This only affects sponsor breaks, not the banner shown above the composer, and it is live today for anyone seeing a Freebuff Pro break.

c4093bf714387f3c5bda94d19d5181c0543054e1.text: When you hit the daily limit on free usage in the CLI tool, the screen now shows how many whole days are left (like "26 days") instead of a confusing number of hours (like "622h 18m"). The wording also changed slightly based on whether you're seeing a daily usage message or a Freebuff limit message. Behind the scenes, the app now remembers your monthly usage balance between checks, so even when the server says you've been refused, the display still shows your correct remaining usage instead of a raw number.

a4b3d0fa55c77663581617e15840fb467c110159.text: Sponsor-break headlines that use a special accent word (like "Your next idea. *Live.*") now have a strict rule: the accent must be a single word wrapped in asterisks, and any headline with zero or more than one accent gets shown as plain text without asterisks so it never accidentally leaks markup. Three places that display these headlines only one of them can show the colored accent, so the plain, unaccented version is what the terminal and inline ads will display. A new shared note explaining that break rows are capped at one per user per day is now shown wherever a break's delivery is reported, so builders and advertisers see a single, consistent explanation instead of two different wordings. These changes are live today.

76a5696e5fdd93b9dc8dded8d2d0c8fac82937ab.text: Starting today (2026-09-05), the default AI model that shows up first and selected by default across the command line, web, and desktop interfaces is now GLM 5.3 Flash instead of DeepSeek V4 Flash. Regular users with full access will see GLM 5.3 Flash selected for them automatically, while limited tier users still get DeepSeek as their primary model because GLM 5.3 Flash is only available to them through an earned access system. The model selection table has been reordered so GLM 5.3 Flash appears at the top, but DeepSeek has not disappeared from the list or lost its availability. A fix was also applied to how availability badges are displayed. Previously the picker incorrectly showed operating hours from one model (like "Open 3:00 AM - 5:00 PM PDT") for unrelated models like Luna and

fb0ab0941b7c17b23b57e0d950f836d852c4d912.text: When you open the command-line tool and your account is on the pay-per-use Freebucks system, you'll now see wording like '100/100 Freebucks daily' and '$25 monthly usage left' instead of the old 'shared premium allowance' message, and the referral banner will read 'Open Earn' rather than promising a dashboard view that only Trust can populate. If your account isn't metered, nothing about the landing screen, model picker, or referral banner changes. The fix that keeps your 'don't show the intro again' choice from being forgotten each time you launch is now live.

e6c61f451394b49df437af776c496a0365474fd6.text: From September 5 through September 7 (Pacific time), Solar Pro 4 costs you 0 Freebucks instead of the usual 5. The assistant and the model picker show you a special notice saying it's on sale for the Labor Day weekend and reverts back to 5 Freebucks on September 8. The price and notice update automatically even while you're looking at the model list, and the app wakes up at the moment the price is set to change so it can refresh right on time.

2cd4966460ec52724504da1424e2aaa7f56b6e95.text: When you're watching a show or video that includes paid breaks, the system now more strictly checks that only known break types are used — so an app can't accidentally invent new ones that would clutter reports. For the breaks that actually interrupt what you're doing (Spotlight and Intermission), the daily limit and timing rules are now kept separate from Showcase, which is the same slot that already holds a regular sponsored banner and is just made taller. The dismiss timer — how long the exit buttons stay locked — is now one shared setting used by both Spotlight and Showcase, with the break type identifying which format it belongs to. These checks are in place and being used today.

b9d72aecc22730807ca4c2d450c9f9b1c0c6739b.text: The SPOTLIGHT ad card now measures how long it keeps you from quickly closing it. When that ad pops up, the X, the backdrop, and Escape key stay locked for up to 5 seconds so you can't slip away immediately — but the sponsor's link stays clickable the whole time so you always have a way out through the advertiser. This lock timing is tracked separately from the countdown timer on the regular Intermission card, because tuning one format used to silently change the other. Operators can now turn the lock off completely (drop it to zero seconds) without pushing out new software, and the data will show whether people waited out the lock and bounced or instead clicked through while it was still held.

4ac0d8ab8584d5ada8c2f0bda35ab6b7c974e02f.text: The model picker in the command-line tool now offers GLM 5.3 Flash to users in regions that receive limited access, not just those who already have full access. Instead of showing confusing leftover quota counts, the panel pulls the model's real-time price and your current credit balance from the same source it uses to start new sessions, so the numbers on screen no longer flicker or disagree. Older saved session data still falls back to the legacy quota counts so nothing breaks for users who have not upgraded yet.

b8a55e9b61345917b0f8b470e4c02ab4f4956d4f.text: A new kind of paid add-on lets you accept a small computing job for a flat $2 fee, with the system automatically stopping any job that costs more than $0.50 in computing time, and the whole thing is only turned on when a server is explicitly configured to allow it. This add-on is tied to one specific conversation thread and shows up as a link in the offer details. In the background, the system stopped writing your secret API key into its error logs when something goes wrong during login checks, so that key can no longer accidentally leak out if a technician reads those error messages.

6c846b9d1e27bda1da35cfbe900f062eefb7e2b2.text: If your account is on Freebucks metered billing, the command-line tool now shows a one-time card at the top of its start screen explaining the meter and your current balance, then adds a new 'metered' section to the model picker so you can see which models cost Freebucks and how much; the picker also sorts models by price and shows a pending indicator while a Freebucks request is in flight, and the end-of-session banner and status bar swap your daily session count for your Freebucks balance instead. Accounts not on the meter are unaffected, and the card only appears when your terminal is at least 30 lines tall so it doesn't push the model list off screen.

88e05db4b26f8e58eca99dbae7cf8ef26f22d0a5.text: When a sponsor break appears during your chat and you dismiss it, the system now records how you got out (a deliberate "continue" button, an "X" you clicked, or hitting Escape) and treats early clicks as likely accidental. That dismissal method and timing are tagged to the specific ad test group you fall into, so the product team can tell which break layout keeps people engaged versus which one they swat away. The underlying code that tracks all this is now in place and actively logging behind the scenes, even when no break is shown, so the metrics can start being read immediately.

7d386183ac1fba92b91d0fd6116ed7f61dbacd6d.text: When you look at your balance now, the date that shows when your next plan bonus arrives is clearer about what it really means: it still appears even if you have cancellation scheduled, but only disappears once you no longer have an active plan. The way leftover monthly bonus gets retired also changed slightly — instead of being taken away exactly when your subscription ends, it now stays around a bit longer and is only retired when the next month’s bonus is actually credited to your account, including if you upgrade. This only affects people on paid plans who get a monthly bonus, and you would notice it mainly by the bonus hanging around for an extra moment in edge cases rather than vanishing the instant your subscription technically ends.

f3857f1b81fa3b21e59eba6564a47a8edb64c5f3.text: Advertisers on the self-serve platform now see only generic, safe messages (like 'temporarily unavailable') instead of internal operator codes (like 'primary_allocation_unassigned' or 'holdout'). The system now enforces a default 10-cent maximum bid for self-serve advertisers unless an operator specifies a tighter ceiling, and logs campaign health evidence with validated, opaque identifiers for internal tracking. This affects self-serve advertisers today: they can no longer see internal reason codes that reveal allocation policies, holdout membership, or other internal states.

3de218cfbec42f26a76cf460205d0a5727735c10.text: If the ad offer card temporarily fails to load or comes back from the server in a broken state, the CLI keeps showing the existing card but grays it out and disables the Accept/Reject buttons, rather than yanking the card away. The card only disappears when the server explicitly reports no offer. You'll notice the sponsored proposal still sits above the input but looks dimmed and unresponsive, with a message explaining it's temporarily unavailable. This affects anyone using the CLI while signed in and receiving sponsored proposal offers.

9f81f91397709452f3b757a035fb9e93d0ab9454.text: If you're a subscriber, you can now use Gemini 3.8 Flash again — it was taken away yesterday because it ran slow and dropped turns mid-conversation, and the routing problem that caused that has now been fixed and re-measured. Free users also get it back as an option alongside the other no-cost models. The subscriber lineup is now built automatically from the catalog, and Gemini 3.8 Flash joins the premium group that enforces a daily spend cap so one heavy conversation can't drain the shared allowance. The fix is live today, with all 24 test turns confirmed landing on the fast endpoint.

d573b4d0977a99b5bea28768a03e3731c51343f5.text: The measurement system now has a dedicated way to track the Supabase acquisition format experiment, which splits eligible users into two groups ('display' and 'agentic') using a stable hash of their user ID and a fixed experiment version string. Each user is permanently assigned to one group for the duration of this experiment version, and their metrics are calculated starting from their first eligible event, without making any database lookups or guessing missing data. Only users who pass strict eligibility checks (being authenticated, relevance matched, same-task procedure applicable, and execution surface supported) are counted, otherwise they are filtered out. This change is live today within the codebase, though it primarily adds the measurement primitive without altering access or

d4ee9ca285c94e9348a7da806a9d2b7ecc69807b.text: A small sponsored ad panel can now expand in the CLI's sponsor dock area, letting you see more details about an ad when you press a keyboard shortcut. If you start a new task, switch to a takeover screen, or click the ad, the panel automatically collapses again so it never blocks the view. The panel only opens if your terminal window is tall enough, keeping it hidden on cramped screens. When it launches today, every click sends a single, clean analytics event with the ad's metadata attached, instead of separate events.

df4b9aa599930aa2b2b9b2bd283089261c4d445d.text: When you see an Imprezia ad in the web chat or Desktop app, the advertiser's measurement pixels and tracking frames now load from your own device instead of being skipped. This is required because those trackers belong to the advertiser's measurement vendor, not Imprezia, and firing them from a server would be flagged as invalid traffic due to a datacenter IP and server user-agent, causing the advertiser to not count the impression even if Imprezia reports it correctly. You won't see a visible change unless you inspect network activity, but the system now logs which tracker channels (impression pixels, impression frame, viewability pixels, viewability frame) were attached by the demand partner so missing trackers can be distinguished from dropped ones, and temporary tracking frames are

09fa12bf061ab808dd43735fc2de7beb5288e441.text: When you send a message that uses up too much of your turn's usage budget, the assistant now stops trying to retry the request and instead shows you a clear message explaining that something went wrong with that turn. This only affects you if you hit that per-turn spending limit (a 429 error with code 'turn_spend_limit') — previously the system would retry four times over about fourteen seconds and then fail with a generic 'too many requests' message that looked like an ordinary rate limit. Now, hitting that specific limit immediately shows the server's explanation and tells you to send a new message to continue, rather than making you wait through retries that don't work. This is live today across the CLI, shared error definitions, and the SDK model-provider.

7b211367021e612630a9c1040fea39abdc157e45.text: When you ask the assistant to think through a plan instead of building right away (Plan mode), it can no longer make edits, run commands, write to your files, or commit anything during that turn—it only delivers the written plan in <PLAN> tags and tells you to switch out of Plan mode to have it built. The restriction now lives in the assistant's available tools rather than just in the prompt, closing the gap that previously let a Plan turn silently build and commit a whole feature. This affects anyone using Plan mode starting today.

f25d4059b88ff4bdca2e120522d0970fb8d2d103.text: When you open the Freebucks section of the CLI, you'll now see 'this month' as an option for spending periods, in addition to 'today' and 'this week'. If your account has a monthly dollar allowance, you'll now see a clear '$N left' indicator showing what's been spent and what remains for the current period, instead of just relying on session limits. This helps you understand exactly how much of your plan's advertised monthly budget you have available, rather than guessing.

8870810f21a3f99ee8e7f349bd10e1dce92488d2.text: If you use the web version from a region where access is normally limited, you can now pick from the full free catalog of assistants, including the cheaper GLM 5.3 Flash option that costs only 5 Freebucks an hour (about a third of other choices). You still can't pick GPT-5.6 Luna, which remains locked behind a paid plan and shows up as a locked row in the picker rather than disappearing entirely. The total amount of Freebucks you can spend per day is unchanged, so this just lets you stretch your same daily allowance across more options. This is a browser-only change, so anyone using the desktop or command-line apps still sees the original smaller set of choices.

3160888e27f2fb25238fef56ff8e67b9d8d1f5ea.text: You might notice that the sample sponsored content shown in development now displays a logo image by default in the header, whereas before it showed an empty space where the logo would go. The developers set up a placeholder logo identifier that looks like the real thing to one of their internal image services, but it doesn't actually point to a stored image anywhere. This means automated screenshots and tests can now exercise the logo-loading code path, while the deliberately 'broken' sample row (the failed state) still checks that the header works correctly when no logo is present at all.

0f33961336a021a0fe9943aa72144fec1183c3ab.text: As you watch a sponsored coding run move from offer to completion, the product now records three more steps that were previously invisible: when you close or reject a proposal card, when a run that was started can't actually save any work, and when that work does finally get written to the run's own branch. That last one matters for billing, because payment under the new model is tied to the commit landing on the branch, not to you later opening a pull request. These events are tracked for telemetry rather than refunds—money already moved when you accepted—except that the new commit stage reflects when the advertiser is actually considered to have received finished work. So if you use these runs, you can now see whether a proposal you skipped or a run that looked active never produced a

219a700815b8cd4d3e19ae9761b2127a53a669e0.text: If you've used the chat and seen a partial or interrupted response from the system, you may have unknowingly received incomplete data. This update adds safety checks to ensure the chat only shows complete responses from the backend analytics system, preventing truncated or cut-off results from being saved or displayed. For users in the server-rendered ad experiment (labeled 'chat_assistant_sr'), a new variant of the 'Freebuff Pro' promotion has been added so they see the same messaging as the control group, keeping experiments fair and accurate.

6470ff421860de64df4196f6891f11470625bce0.text: When an ad appears on your screen, the app now records two things automatically: the exact time the ad finished loading and when your device actually displayed it, so engineers can tell whether slow ads are slow because the network is slow or because your device took time to show them. Each ad view and click also gets a single tracking label generated on your device that stays the same even if the app retries sending the data, letting the server tell a failed-and-retried message apart from two separate actions. If you look at the ad feedback screens, you won't see anything new directly, but behind the scenes the system can now skip counting duplicate reports and ignore timing data from older app versions without breaking them. These improvements are live for everyone using the latest app

7c5cc043fcad67cd82f362c61bc4c82cae553a78.text: If you're shopping for a Plus or Pro subscription, the first-month discount now matches how much each plan costs instead of being a flat $3 off everywhere. Plus goes from $25 to $19 for the first month (a $6 discount) and Pro drops from $60 to $45 (a $15 discount), while the entry-level Starter plan stays at $3 off. This means the higher-priced plans finally look worth trying, since a flat discount felt almost meaningless on expensive tiers. The change went live on September 3, 2026.

7bdce0946bbc83e804efd99fca98fa2d99b90e19.text: If you use Solar Pro 4, it now appears in both the full-access catalog and the limited-access trial list, and at full access it no longer counts against your daily session balance. If you work with GPT-5.6 Luna or Gemini 3.8 Flash in the desktop app, the system now holds a single usage slot per tab instead of letting parallel admits pair up ambiguously, and any slot that sits idle for ten minutes is reclaimed automatically. Limited-access users without a paid plan are capped at one slot-bound desktop session, while free users can run up to three multi-tab sessions. The change is live today and is reflected in the public README and Chinese docs as of the September 2026 snapshot.

7faa16471f65d093f3535980864182ff79dac50a.text: When you're offered to do work that's paid for by an advertiser, you now see one clear sentence naming the advertiser alongside two buttons (one to accept, one to decline) instead of a long list of technical details that most people skim over. The advertiser's name is the only text they get to choose, and it's automatically trimmed to a safe length so it can't push the buttons around or sneak in confusing formatting. If an offer shows up without an advertiser name attached, only the decline button appears and the other option quietly disappears. This is live today in the command-line tool, and it now matches how the same question appears on the desktop app.

38b9fb0ffb5f0f14035dcf78969d153d7b0acfd8.text: When an advertiser offers to sponsor a task in the command-line assistant, you now get a separate consent screen before anything runs. Typing the accept command opens that screen and waits for your approval rather than starting the code immediately, so pressing Enter can't accidentally both approve and submit a prompt. The screen is only offered on machines that can run the task locally in an isolated git workspace (for example, it is shown on macOS and Linux but not on Windows, where the card instead explains why it is unavailable). If you decline, nothing is recorded and the offer stays reversible.

18eee2a9d4ab53dcf63a34e2a5b113f86b86f469.text: When you look at your Freebucks balance, the app no longer shows a second, smaller dollar limit that used to appear right beside it. That extra number was a hidden safety cap meant to catch only the heaviest daily spenders, but showing it next to your actual Freebucks balance made it look like you would run out of dollars before you ran out of Freebucks. The cap itself still exists behind the scenes — it still stops new sessions once the daily dollar total is hit and it still appears in operator-only surfaces — but the running total that used to update on every session is gone, so what you see is just the one balance you plan against. The cleaner display is live today for everyone who signs in.

ebb4deb34adc86dfaa1b4584d98edaf6db889f3d.text: When you start a run, the assistant now stops immediately if you cancel while it is looking up your account or registering the run, instead of waiting the full retry period. Previously, a slow or unresponsive lookup would keep the run alive until its backoff retries ran out, even after you aborted; the abort signal now reaches those early steps and the run resolves with 'Run cancelled by user.' If you trigger a run and hit cancel before the first model request, you get a prompt cancellation rather than a long, unbreakable wait.

a852b83bdfb6dbc2fdc996eb33eecc2e1fbb2489.text: The system now records two new pieces of information on every ad-fetch event in your logs: why a particular impression was chosen to enter the durable decision record (the inclusion reason, such as a contested auction win, a direct-sold serve, or a fully-sampled deployment) along with the probability it had of being selected, and which keying secret version was used to generate the user handle in that record. The probability field has a clear split from the existing event-stream sampling field, which only controls how many rows are counted in the raw stream rather than whether a durable evidence row is written, and the old field is kept as a temporary alias so existing dashboards and exporters continue to resolve during a one-release transition. A new exported allowlist locks down which

892f79590b0dbbf4753d4f66051c8b3d8af7a3ce.text: Ad requests that get refused now produce a new privacy-safe log entry that records only broad, non-identifying details like the route, the reason code, and the system that made the call. This log is built to be aggregated across all users at once without ever storing personal data such as IP addresses, campaign identifiers, or bearer tokens. The refusal data becomes available for analysis starting today after this code was merged in. You wouldn't notice anything as an end user, but the system now tracks how often and why ad requests are rejected in a way that respects privacy by design.

9b16ec41446c36cc56ac43f225aa3b720d29d848.text: The system dropped a behind-the-scenes lockbox it used to prove that a user had finished deleting their Adbuff data before permanently wiping their Convex account. After this change, deleting an account no longer has to pass that specific verification step, and the related security code is gone. You wouldn't see this directly, but account deletion now follows a simpler path with that extra cross-check removed.

6b1963707ad3659f9d2308535dff59f317cd8174.text: If you've ever used a coding assistant that helped make a Git commit, you may have noticed a footer line crediting the assistant, like 'Co-authored-by' or 'Generated with.' The change introduces a setting that lets certain runs omit those credit lines entirely, so the commit instead looks like it was written solely by the human running the tool. That setting only applies to sponsored proposals: advertiser-funded code changes delivered into your repository on your behalf. All other runs behave exactly as before.

8221e333895c0933b2ab58d669ac40272c339eb8.text: You may see a new, clearer refusal message when you reach your Freebucks daily cap, since the system now treats each kind of Freebucks (daily plan grant, one-time plan credit, non-expiring wallet balance) as separate pools instead of one merged allowance. This only affects you if you are on a paid plan whose spend ceiling is enforced today; the refusal copy is in place but the new spend-ceiling reason is deliberately excluded from bypass paths so the plan limit always sticks, and it is only live for the audience the rollout targets.

7b65652ad9decd202054622a7fbe267cc7c11201.text: The system now records whether each ad request comes from a high-value, mid-tier, or unknown location, even when it can't act on that information. This way, analysts can tell the difference between 'you is in a Tier 2 country' and 'we decided not to check you's location', which matters for planning geo-targeted ad ramps. The logs also now show whether the ad-decision process is actively placing impressions, waiting, or paused, instead of just stopping entries entirely when the pipeline slows down. These new tracking fields are live in the system's logging today.

4ff67e17e1d2980de3411ac0f573e20160b845d8.text: The desktop assistant now correctly shows whether a sponsored coding task is still running or has finished, instead of wrongly offering a 'Start' button on tasks that are already in progress or have failed. At the same time, it can finally run git commands inside linked worktree folders (the extra project copies some tools create) without dying with 'fatal: not a git repository', because the sandbox now lets those folders see the real project's.git directory. Both fixes are live today for Desktop runs that use a sponsored proposal with a linked worktree.

26a3a70dac0329050970baa5e1d585b22c8ada9a.text: The privacy notice you see when you open the app or read its README has been updated to match Freebuff's September 2, 2026 Privacy Policy. If you looked at the docs today, you'd see that stored data now explicitly includes agent traces (a record of what the assistant did during your session), and that restricted partners can evaluate your connected Cloud repositories or code only when those files were used with a model labeled "May use data for AI training" - they can't repurpose, widely share, or train on it otherwise. For existing users, this change just replaces the previous July 23 notice text with the new wording - it doesn't alter what data is collected, just how it's described and what limits are placed on partner access going forward under the new policy effective September 2.

c6a7eae9e05dad4f07be5d34298dcecf93ed08bd.text: The system now quietly records two new pieces of information about each ad request that happens behind the scenes: a stable per-user tracking number (called the opportunity_id) and a frozen snapshot of the advertising rules that decided which ads could even be considered (called the eligibility census). These tags are stamped onto ad records in September 2026 but nothing acts on them yet -- they simply sit in logs, waiting for the October 2026 rollout (COD-362) that will let first-party ad networks actually serve you personalized ads using your tracked profile.

f27429b2728f0614353df3194a77b493d0444e18.text: For the desktop version of the sponsored proposal conformance tracking, the system has reinstated specific waivers (exceptions) for rows E-3 through E-7, which were previously removed. The desktop application now correctly treats these E-layer items as requiring real backend execution and actual user actions — not test simulations — before clearing them as passed. If you looked at the conformance table today, you'd see that these desktop E-layer rows explicitly show as 'never run' with reasons noting they were measured against fake test runners rather than live runs, and they only clear when manually verified through the Agentic Ads testing runbook.

60123cbaaa09113e6f314b9c877df53e41165095.text: When an ad gets accepted, it can now only be counted as a fresh action once, even if the system tries to accept it multiple times due to retries or delays. This prevents the same ad acceptance from being recorded twice in reports. The fix uses a unique code tied to the ad proposal so that the system knows it\'s the same ad being accepted again. This is now active and affects how ad acceptances are tracked and deduplicated in the system.

7f41c17658f1631e318a9aa7b0e4d9bd26ad58da.text: When you ask the assistant to run a task inside your project folder, the program now gives a clearer message if it can't do so because there's nobody nearby to approve the request on your desktop — instead of just saying the operating system isn't supported. It also stops trick requests that start with a tilde character (~), like typing a shortcut to your home folder, from slipping past the safety check that keeps sponsored tasks inside your project. Finally, the sandbox that runs these tasks has been tested on a real Mac to confirm it lets a normal set of low-level system files through, and nothing more, so the tasks work without letting advertisers touch anything extra.

6edee52fa9c4ab5511163f99269dd8613f0669f2.text: If you sponsor a coding job to run on your own computer, that job is now locked inside a tighter sandbox that matches the operating system you are using: macOS and Linux get a real restricted container, and Windows gets a deny-by-default policy since it cannot sandbox the same way. The rules for what a sponsored job is allowed to touch are now defined in one shared place and then enforced differently per environment, so a change to the tool list is classified once and each platform answers for itself whether it is safe to permit. You would notice this because the sponsored run can no longer reach outside its stated file paths or terminal commands, and if it tries to step outside its boundaries the run fails instead of silently escaping. The local-execution boundary is live today for the

9b2ca33ed534768e4860d8b6949da3934abf2d81.text: Starting today, people who already pay for the subscription no longer see the house ad that tries to sell them the subscription. If you have a paid subscription, the promotional message asking you to subscribe will stop appearing, even though keeping ads is unrelated to your subscription status. The system now checks one quick rule before showing any house ad, and if you’re an entitled subscriber, it simply shows nothing—saving you from seeing marketing for something you already bought.

2a6cd7375ba0be59db222123a7294c0982ad0453.text: The list of email address providers that are commonly used to sign up for things temporarily (like fake or throwaway emails) now has a new way to be accessed by other parts of the system. Previously, this list could only be used internally for checking if an email was from one of these providers, but now it can also be handed over as a complete, read-only copy. This means that any team or service building a blacklist to block sign-ups from these temporary email providers can now easily get the full list instead of having to rebuild or guess at it. It's now live and ready for use.

6a4ad1d04afdcc25bf6aea1e3503199ae65e39c3.text: The free AI assistant some people use in their web browser has gotten a small upgrade: the version it was offering (called Muse Spark) has been swapped out for a newer one on the date this was written (September 2, 2026). If you open the assistant today, you'll now be using the new version instead of the old one, which has quietly retired but is still running in the background just to let anyone who was already mid-conversation finish up. Your past choices (if you had saved a preference) will automatically switch over to the new version, so you don't have to do anything yourself.

56dbe402f41689aa095fa05026ddd53037ff462d.text: When you run a job on your own computer (not on Cloud servers) and close your laptop mid-run, that job can now still send its final status report — even the next morning — using its temporary login token. That token stays valid for exactly 24 hours, which is intentionally much longer than the 45-minute window Cloud-run jobs get, because your local machine can pause whenever you do. A single shared time limit now governs both the token's creation and the automated cleanup sweep, preventing a confusing error message when a valid late report reaches a row already marked for cleanup.

dd1d934b7418b612d453d52e5fc2091011923dbc.text: The command-line tool's landing screen now opens to a different default AI model — DeepSeek V4 Flash (07/31) instead of GLM 5.3 Flash — for everyone using either the full or limited access tier. If you've ever picked a model before and saved that choice, a one-time migration step quietly shifts your saved preference so you don't get stuck on the old one. You'd notice this because the model listed at the top of the picker and the one shown in your first greeting after launch will now be named DeepSeek V4 Flash, and the limited-tier fallback used during planning is MiMo 2.5 rather than the previous limited default. This is live today in the tool's published release.

6891efd69b17644d4cc43382efd3a757e25507a1.text: Each time you triggered an ad auction, you could land in a different ad group on the next request, even within the same session, making it impossible to measure whether first-party ad placements worked for you specifically. Now, a stable per-user salt ensures you stay bucketed into the same first-party ad treatment across auctions, so routing and campaign allocation read a single consistent sample. Ad fetch logs also gained new fields like opportunity_id, policy_version, first_party_arm_bucket, and eligibility census data to connect each auction to the rest of the ad chain and record why campaigns were or weren't eligible. The change is live today for first-party ad experiments.

d227b0349fd05b02d6d5a0f0c628783996fbf89d.text: When you visit a site that uses the hashed-email identity check, the system now records how that check ended — whether a match was found (and whether it was a direct hit or an observed one), or if it was unmatched, ambiguous, gated, consent-denied, or none — and this outcome is logged alongside every click-ID row instead of being kept inside a per-user digest. That means the logs now carry a plain label describing the lookup result, but only the coarse result, never the email hash itself or any user identity, so analysts can see how the identity rail is performing without exposing individual user data. The new logging is live from today and applies to the external-conversion postback stream only.

3975224904d989f60ad8db9139bf51b7390e67c0.text: When a special offer card appears in your chat, you can no longer open its menu or dismiss it with single keyboard shortcuts like 'm' or 'esc', because those keys now do whatever you were already typing in the message box. Instead, you reach the offer's controls through new '/ads:proposal', '/ads:dismiss-proposal', and related slash commands, which work whether the card is visible on screen or scrolled away. The offer card stays in your conversation after you act on it rather than disappearing, so the surrounding text doesn't jump around while you're reading, and a record of the offer remains in the transcript. The rules that decide whether acting on an offer counts as accepting it, declining it, or nothing at all are now handled in one isolated place so they can be checked without running

a90d9c446543900a2ec75675fe03844a537ac3f1.text: When an AI assistant sits idle for a while, it now clears out old conversation history at a different pace depending on which AI model you're using. For example, if you use the DeepSeek Flash model, the assistant will start trimming history after about 15 minutes of inactivity, while other models wait an hour. Importantly, for the fast-expiring model, it won't delete anything unless your conversation has grown quite large, preventing it from accidentally wiping useful context during short breaks. This affects anyone using these AI assistants in long-running conversations.

c10a9f304bd1337ad48ef2b2294d38af5e460dab.text: If you use the free subscription, the message about how your sessions refresh over time now tells you the correct number of days instead of always saying five. The explanation no longer calls it a five-day rule and now matches the longer window that actually applies, and the exact number shown comes from a single shared setting so the words stay correct if it changes again.

e47bf5c35bbc5397a02ad2dc1074907ad4fdf225.text: The ad system now quietly tracks whether your request is allowed to show a hidden, experimental house ad slot tied to campaign COD-358, based on your user ID, your geographic tier, and a secret toggle. This check is separate from the main paid-ad rotation, so it doesn't affect billing or which regular ads you see. You won't see anything different today because the feature is still dark-deployed and does nothing visible, but engineers are now logging eligibility so they can measure who would qualify if they turn it on.

f2ddf900349a34acf802d7645accc70840d0a4f3.text: When you ask the assistant to search the web, you can now tell it to go deeper: instead of returning a list of links, it can launch a small team of automated researchers that read multiple pages and hand you a single, cited answer to a hard question. That deep search is now wired into the assistant’s tools and is live today, but it costs real money per question and can take minutes, so it only runs when you specifically request it. The different levels of effort (a quick pass, a default thorough pass, or an exhaustive frontier pass) and the list of available search providers are now stored in one central place so all parts of the system stay in sync, and the deep-search endpoint has its own longer timeout so it doesn’t give up while the research is still running.

a71de944590b9d02d5c182133e8c17de5e600db0.text: On the chat surfaces, the GLM v5.3 Flash assistant is now thinking deeply again by default instead of doing only surface-level reasoning. Two weeks ago we turned deep thinking off because it was stuck in repetitive tool-call loops, and temporarily lowered the default to a lighter setting — but measurements showed that lighter setting had collapsed to almost no thinking at all (around 300 characters). We've now restored the deepest reasoning level as the default and set it as the only option you can choose from, accepting the same looping risk on purpose in exchange for the assistant actually reasoning. If you use the chat, the clearest thing you'd notice is that responses now take roughly two times longer and contain substantially more internal reasoning before replying.

0d2d7a08594e7172e82d0f59a6a4c8a6bcc001b4.text: If you tried Solar Pro 4 on September 1, you were capped at one use per day because the system thought it was ten times more expensive than it really was. That price estimate has been corrected, so the one-use limit is lifted and Solar Pro 4 now costs the same as every other premium model. When you next use the assistant, you’ll see Solar Pro 4 treated like any other paid model—available under your normal daily allowance, not blocked after a single try. This is live now for anyone who can use the premium model options.

5d679590800f31569758fe1002a5ef087668f7b7.text: Starting September 1, 2026, the Thinker assistant that helps power reasoning on the freebuff.com/chat page switched from Google's expensive Gemini model to a cheaper DeepSeek model. If you use that chat feature, you won't see a difference in how it behaves, but it now runs faster and cheaper behind the scenes. The cost of running that assistant each week dropped from about $2,700 to under $85, so it can keep running without burning through budget. The switch is already live, and the assistant's name and role stayed the same.

48b5fee79a1016800772e01eafa8ceb3db346f98.text: If you use Freebuff while traveling abroad or connected through a VPN, you now get 6 free one-hour sessions each day again instead of the reduced 3. The team had lowered that number to 3 to stop resellers from creating fake accounts in countries where access is limited, but it also cut normal users' access in half. Since that limited mode is the only way you can use the free MiMo model without buying a paid plan, they quickly restored your sessions back to 6 while still keeping the anti-reseller checks elsewhere. So today, limited-mode users have their full set of free sessions again, along with all the other features that were already in place.

3b8fa14a1010363bb909958213fa8beea9c31a30.text: When you click a house ad and then check out through Stripe, the site now carries your click along behind the scenes under a code called 'bfcid' so the checkout stamp can later credit the right ad campaign. That click ID is not trusted blindly: the conversions endpoint runs an HMAC check on it, so a made-up or stolen ID is rejected with a 400 error and only the campaign that actually earned the click gets credit. Developers also tidied up a few internal model lists (renaming LIMITED_FREEBUFF_MODEL_IDS to LIMITED_FREEBUFF_MODEL_IDS plus some line wrapping) without changing which models are actually offered. This is live today for whoever triggers the Stripe checkout path tied to the freebuff ad flow.

e1792f99509f9abc40904b9f4dad683d57510329.text: Ads now count as viewed only after at least half of the ad stays completely visible on your screen for one uninterrupted second while the app is in the foreground — if you scroll it out of view or switch to another tab before that second finishes, the timer resets to zero instead of pausing. This applies to the web and Desktop chat apps, where both track viewability the same way so advertisers get consistent billing; the command-line tool is excluded because a terminal window has no real viewport to measure. Ads can now also signal whether they are merely placed on the page or fully 'viewable,' with older builds defaulting to 'placed' so existing tracking keeps working.

7bcf9ba0b06d17819d238906d0d0436fa1eb432e.text: When you look at your plan details on a smaller line of text—like a bullet point or a preview strip—you'll now see durations written short, such as "24 hrs" instead of "24 hours," so the text fits without being squeezed. This only affects those secondary lines; bigger headline text still shows the full "hours" version. The change is live and applies everywhere those shorter duration labels appear.

161b864dd4f665957ded8250837935b5f8612cfc.text: Sponsored coding runs now show the same progress and wording in the terminal as they do in the web chat — including a final "committed" status that means the work is saved on its own branch, not that a pull request was opened yet. When a sponsored run finishes and commits your code, the terminal will display "Sponsored thread committed its work" instead of a pending-style message, and the same step-by-step labels (Pending, In progress, Done) that web users already see now appear in your terminal view too. The system also sanitizes two sensitive fields — the pull-request link and the advertiser logo — so that a terminal rendering of a sponsored proposal can't accidentally render an unsafe URL or a stale logo token; if either is missing or rejected, you simply won't see that element rather

6341ef3af85281a213d98d6fab35e502e544dbd5.text: If you use the assistant on Freebuff Desktop and your placement omits the surface field (like the Desktop-Below-Chat slot deliberately does), ad delivery and click settlement will now fill in the correct surface automatically instead of failing on a null value. The code now maps each placement id to its surface and returns undefined for any unrecognized id, with a special fallback for legacy CLI-Chat-Inline-N ids that still render the transcript. Existing slots already worked; this prevents storage failures when a named placement skips the surface. This is live today.

321907165f73f9a66f780f275f38e27092f87aa9.text: Starting today, a small share of ad requests in Tier-1 regions that used to go to Imprezia can now be routed to our house-sponsored book instead, controlled by a new dial that defaults to 0% so nothing changes unless turned on. The requests taken by our book sit directly above Imprezia's normal slot, so the two can never overlap and turning the dial up never shrinks the regular ad window. The system now records when our book preempts Imprezia rather than leaving it blank, so reports that count who won each slot stay accurate. This affects ad routing for Tier-1 regions only and is live today for anyone with the feature flag enabled.

01bf3cd467fb1a2700c866b3097fff745b3c0f5b.text: Free users opening the CLI model picker now see three usage bars instead of one: today, the current week, and the current month. These extra two bars show the free allowance you've been granted and how much of it you've already used up this week and month, displayed in the same layout subscribers already see. The week bar rolls forward seven days at a time while the month bar follows calendar months, and as of now these bars are display-only: using more than your weekly or monthly free allowance does not get blocked yet, so the numbers can legitimately show you past the limit until enforcement lands in a future change. This goes live for every full-access free user today, but stays absent for quota-exempt accounts, limited-access accounts, and anyone on a server that doesn't report the new

b6775f5c3e83b041816b59b2c2bb6dcadadf9f91.text: When you open the creative preview in the advertiser console (where you check how your ad will look), the preview now lets you see your ad at terminal widths of 48, 80, or 100 columns instead of the old 20, 48, and 60. This affects advertisers using the freeBuff campaign builder right now. If you look at the preview, the previous 20-column option is gone because almost nobody uses such a narrow terminal, but at very narrow real terminals, inline ads still get their text cut the same way as before. The new 100-column cap prevents the ad preview dialog from stretching too wide and causing horizontal scrollbars, since the dialog renders width in literal characters.

a49b46d62f39fd4cf45e3ba02499b8aefbca0d24.text: When you hit your usage limit and see the paywall screen in the command-line tool, you'll now see a clear upgrade hint telling you exactly which plan to pick or linking you to the plans page — it will never just stop at a dead-end message. Paid accounts that had been capped at the same low free-tier ceiling now get a higher floor of $7 per day (with a $3 minimum for limited accounts), so they can actually use the sessions their paid plan includes. The daily spending cutoff for restricted regions dropped from $5 to $1, since that lower amount still covers a full day of normal use. Finally, the Pro subscription tier is back on the website after the team retuned the advertised totals (this happened on 2026-08-31), so you can sign up for it again if you'd previously been blocked from doing so.

fcb16dec8af815505ae1dcc2d4f8be9c907fc814.text: I'm seeing the technical details of this change, but I need to focus on explaining it in plain language as you've asked. Let me work through what this means for someone who would encounter it. This change affects people using Solar Pro 4, a specific AI model. Starting today, if you're using this model, you can only run one conversation with it per day. Normally, models might let you have several conversations or be shared across all users, but this one is now limited to just one session daily. Additionally, Solar Pro 4 has been 'pinned' to a specific technical endpoint (a particular server route) called 'upstage/zdr' instead of the more general 'upstage' option. The developers did this because there were two ways to connect to this model, and splitting the traffic between them was causing

091a224cd3b63af11dbded3dea62c726a669d112.text: If you sponsor one of these coding tests, the test runner no longer grabs the full before-and-after source code itself; instead it lets your own filtered tool do that, which keeps sensitive paths out. The runner now also accepts a new terminal tool broker and optional tool overrides when it asks the assistant to edit files. This is live today for any sponsored evaluation that passes the collect-diff flag off.

12f8f2bb5b72969b7114cec9f24ae47e7e5e4500.text: On the usage page, the app now reports how many tokens were moved without counting the same ones twice. Previously, when a request reused a previously cached prompt, the number was inflated because the cached portion was added on top of a provider total that already included it. You'll see the total figure correct itself, and beside it a second number showing how many prompt tokens had to actually be processed fresh, which will be smaller on workloads that reuse cached prompts.

21d3b7668e7f43c2bcfbcd065b1915ae4329f6d3.text: When you earn a session by referring friends, your referral reward now gives you an extra session of GLM 5.3 Flash — the same high-tier model that's already your default — instead of the older GLM 5.2 that used to be the special reward. This bonus shows up only for you if you have the full (premium) tier; if you're on the basic free tier, your referral banner continues to give you access to the reward model through the banner. Sessions reset each day at midnight Pacific time and your earned balance, not a fixed model cap, is what limits how many you can use. The change is live now alongside updated help text in both English and Chinese readmes.

70f1d8d632956affcf4ef483ae0c317dfd8d9403.text: GLM 5.3 Flash was previously running with its deepest reasoning mode enabled by default for free users, and on agent-based coding tasks it got stuck in a loop: re-reading the same files, re-planning the same steps, and re-issuing tool calls it had already made, burning the turn on deliberation instead of edits. Developers pinned the default to the middle setting (called 'high') and removed the deepest option ('max') from the list Freebuff itself can pick or offer, while keeping 'max' available for paying BYOK and direct-API callers who send their own requests. If you are a free user hitting this model today, you will notice the assistant no longer spirals into repeated re-reads and re-plans on coding work; if you run your own API key or pay per use, the deepest reasoning setting remains

94eb1cfce38c1ccd0f91a5a7a1e66013863eabbb.text: When ads are served, the system now looks at a single short country tag (like "US" or "DE", or none at all) to decide which ad inventory to offer, rather than guessing from a full address or user identity. In premium countries the old primary/backup ad mix still runs first; in secondary countries, if the paid ads didn't fill, you'll now get a capped slice of free bonus inventory instead; and when no country is known, only paid-network ads are allowed. A new off switch keeps this behavior disabled by default so existing ad routing stays exactly as it is until someone turns it on. The country tag and the on/off state are recorded in a separate, size-limited log stream that carries no IP addresses or user IDs, and it's clearly split from the older per-country pricing data so the two can't be

f3e97864f5d12d3df41f0bc10e08b5afd66dd101.text: When your account is completely unknown to the system, it now safely defaults to being treated as trusted instead of falling into an error state that could throttle your usage. This means free-mode accounts won't get unfairly slowed down if something about their standing can't be looked up. The user-facing names for access levels are now separated from the internal calculation logic, so the labels you see (like 'new', 'verified', 'established', 'core') aren't tied directly to the trust-scoring code behind the scenes. Live today.

dcc6b662d492759a0776826bd0ee32e36480baa4.text: If you set a daily spending limit for a placement ad campaign, you can now choose a cap as high as $5,000 per day (it used to stop at $500), and the slider that picks the amount moves in realistic steps so small amounts like $5 still feel easy to reach. The same limits the website enforces are now also used by the campaign system in the background, so a number you're allowed to type in won't later be rejected as invalid. The new maximum of $5,000/day took effect on August 31, 2026, and applies to any advertiser setting a placements campaign's daily cap in the console or API.

31e6e831630f42720b61aa08561daa941dbf4ed3.text: The assistant's usage screen was showing a number that was too high, so the math was corrected. The total token count now adds up only the words you typed and the words the assistant wrote, instead of also re-counting the portion that came from the shortcut memory. You might notice the usage numbers on your dashboard tiles read a bit lower than before, especially when a lot of the work is being pulled from the memory cache. The correction prevents the system from counting the cached portion twice, which previously inflated the totals by roughly 80% during heavy cache use. This fix is live now across the shared usage types that power those tiles and reports, so the figures you see today should reflect the corrected calculation.

d88c688727818ebcf7ce9bdcdcc18ba16d7946a2.text: Campaigns that pay per click now have a single rule for their lowest allowed price that every part of the system uses together. If someone tries to set a campaign's price floor to a weird, too-low, or invalid number, the system simply falls back to the standard $1 floor instead of letting the price drop below that, which keeps pricing honest. You wouldn't see this visually, but it stops campaigns from quietly serving at prices that look right but bill nothing, and keeps the price a campaign actually charges from drifting apart from the price automated checks expect. The floor logic that four different system layers all need now lives in one shared spot, so they can no longer disagree and let prices diverge.

c3521fd87fc4c8f683e73c08251772dc976ca8ec.text: When you ask to delete your account, the system now creates a tamper-proof digital signature confirming that your deletion request was completed on the Adbuff side before actually purging your Convex account. This signature is generated using a secure hashing method and is only created after the system verifies that your deletion is properly in progress. The verification process also takes extra care to compare signatures in a way that prevents timing-based attacks. If you looked at this change, you'd see a new file that defines how this proof is created and validated using cryptographic signing.

f9b0815704eb34ebed2b8852b1a27c4902664d58.text: The assistant can now show you how much of your free monthly credit balance is left, broken down into daily, weekly, and monthly usage windows, so when you go to start a session it can tell you right away whether your credit will cover it. This only matters if your account is in the Freebucks rollout group; if you're not, you won't see anything different. The numbers come from a new data field added to every login session, so the moment you sign in you'll get an up-to-date read on your remaining credit without waiting for a separate check. Live today for eligible accounts.

443f19f0eae03bcbc0dfb3ac6a5cd869fb9dcbae.text: When you type `/skill:<name>` without adding any instructions, the app now opens a dedicated text area so you can add your own instructions before the skill runs, instead of running immediately. As you type, a live token-count indicator in the status bar updates so you can see how much context your message is using. The status bar also shows real-time context token usage derived from the main agent state, giving you immediate feedback on how much space your conversation is consuming.

8542dfe658589b2433a7d039b031d1e0eab1be07.text: The system now decides how far in advance to trust an advertiser to pay its bills, based on how the advertiser has paid in the past. Instead of a single limit, there's a range: new advertisers need at least two weeks of payment history before getting any extra leeway, and the most any advertiser can be extended is ten days of spending between checks. The system can grow or shrink an advertiser's trust level after each nightly review, but it changes gradually rather than jumping - with one exception: if an advertiser disputes charges, that cut to their trust can happen instantly without the usual slow-down. Who sees this: advertisers whose accounts are charged through the platform's billing system, especially those whose payment limits can change automatically based on their track record.

94288ad24bcefe362692ded7a3a8c692a503ff16.text: If you open three free premium assistant tabs at once on your desktop right now, the cheapest model (by measured per-message cost) is no longer used across all three. The provider's per-message billing started on August 28, and the three-tab rule that limits which models can be picked for this free multi-tab deal is enforced per model — so this cheapest model now fails the test for staying in the list. The list still excludes any metered (per-use billable) models, which keeps your three-tab free allowance from racking up a surprise combined bill. This change is live today for the desktop multi-tab free premium bucket.

a67e89052816db2de4de5bc42c4b6c318f91797a.text: If you pay for Freebuff Desktop, you can now run more assistant sessions at the same time. A free user is capped at one premium session and three unlimited ones; a paying subscriber now gets three premium slots and eight unlimited ones, so opening an extra tab that needs an expensive model won't be blocked just because you hit the free ceiling. The desktop app will notice these new limits automatically and guide you to an available slot instead of stopping you.

fd3c20c290bf78152ecc86ab7ba9191f420ca1ea.text: When you open Freebuff and don't pick a specific assistant, you now get GLM 5.3 Flash instead of GPT-5.6 Luna. That default assistant is no longer capped at just two conversations per day and won't use your paid session allowance, so it draws from the unlimited tier rather than counting against your daily quota. The assistant also no longer labels itself as using your conversations to help train its own AI, so the usual on-screen warning you used to see next to the default choice is simply gone. This is live today for everyone who opens the app or CLI without changing the selection.

e5d41741aeca4ae11989042f2af1647b94c11e41.text: The assistant's deep-thinking AI now responds faster when you ask quick questions, and you can tell it how deeply to think per question instead of always using the same setting. When you open the model menu, a new option appears with three levels — a quick brief scan, a balanced deep look, and the most thorough analysis. Picking quick makes it skip its internal reasoning entirely, so responses come back fast but less detailed. This change is live today for subscribers on the CLI, and it only affects the free-tier deep-thinking AI model.

477b0e47facf165557cca9b60a070dacc3f6f9d9.text: If you pay for a subscription, the model picker in the CLI now keeps your chosen paid model instead of silently swapping it for the free default. When the CLI gets fresh session info, it also stops forcing limited users onto the default model and instead honors what you picked. This is live today for paid subscribers using the CLI; free-limited users see no change.

f4fca07fcd3d2a041699d3c1216bb216d2dae2ec.text: Advertisers now have a new minimum price that applies only to individual clicks from countries where they pay less per click. This is separate from their regular minimum rate, so when clicks from a low-cost country get scaled down, each one will bill for at least fifty cents rather than potentially rounding down to a lower amount. The change is already live in the system and applies automatically to the geo-adjusted pricing; no action is needed to turn it on.

72fffec8570aebd6a07ae1fce403fcdedee01dbd.text: If you use a free account to run the GLM 5.3 Flash assistant, you no longer hit a daily cap of two conversations with it — that limit has been removed. The team checked real usage data and found this assistant is actually the cheapest one they offer, so keeping it capped while the more expensive assistants (DeepSeek V4 Flash and MiMo) run with no cap made no sense. This change was turned on in production on August 28, 2026, and it only affects paying-with-free-credits users; people in limited regions are still governed by a separate allowlist and are not affected.

4a9013b2a97bd2bade3e61b99f3deb7814094eb0.text: Internal logging now records whether a conversion came through a direct server call (labeled 's2s') or a browser-based request (labeled 'client'). This only affects how the company's own monitoring tools sort and filter incoming conversion reports, so engineers can better tell apart the two pathways. You as an outside observer won't see a visible change — it's a behind-the-scenes tweak to keep internal tracking organized.

6ace1d00c9409518218bbf90225391e9002a5b21.text: When you scroll through free posts in your feed, the app now makes sure there's a short, gentle pause between each sponsored item it shows you, rather than clustering several together in one busy moment and then going quiet for a while. The size of that pause is worked out ahead of time using today's date and a little randomness, so it feels like a steady rhythm instead of a predictable pattern someone could time. Because the change only affects which posts get offered to you next, it won't block anything if you finish a post quickly, and the pauses are kept short enough that you won't notice a long wait.

590e6d257bf4128557f1e5823077c586bb424138.text: Tapering ad campaigns now spend more evenly over the course of each hour instead of saving up their budget and bursting at midnight or after quiet periods. If you run or watch a campaign being wound down, you'll see its delivery smoothed out across the hours it's supposed to cover rather than clustered at the start of the day or the moment the clock resets. The per-hour cap also now shuffles slightly in a way that can't be gamed by retrying at the same minute, and every tapering campaign is guaranteed at least one delivery per hour so a slow wind-down never grinds to a complete stop.

bd4a417e32556ffb2004437274d0cdd893ad3907.text: When you're shown a sponsored proposal for a tool (like a coding assistant add-on) and you tap Accept, you are charged your normal click fee, exactly like clicking a banner ad. Everything else the system tracks later—whether your pull request merged, whether the tool installed its server, or whether the company behind the ad later tells us your team started using it—is recorded only to help price future campaigns and never adds a charge. If you look closely, you'd notice that only the Accept event flows through the regular billing path; all other stages are just telemetry. As of the 2026-08-27 decision baked into the code, only advertisers can tell us about your new account or tool usage; they cannot report our internal stages like whether the code merged.

1f35b8067456bba14e902e3018e6c41545b2a64e.text: The system now records a simple, anonymized report every time it decides whether to show you an ad from a specific ad network, capturing only broad facts like whether the ad loaded, how long it took, and which surface (e.g., the web chat) it appeared on. This report deliberately strips out any identifiers, URLs, or raw error messages, so your specific requests and content stay private. You would notice nothing directly, but your activity in the web chat now contributes to these bounded logs.

57c010db236b4b5ffba7030cb4eff4bb50a4a333.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI on a paid plan, you now see a quiet line beneath the model list that summarizes your plan's limits for the day, the last 5 days, and the month. It shows how much you've used against each limit and, when a limit is currently stopping you, names that limit and the exact time it resets. The same summary also appears in the web dropdown and Desktop, so all three places tell you the same remaining allowance and reset time. This went live with the snapshot dated 2026-08-28.

5c0c933cea38831e8f3c2a1042c1852363445159.text: If you run an ad campaign that's being deliberately wound down, the daily spending limit no longer drops in a straight line each day — instead it drops faster at the start and then slows as it gets close to zero, which is what a "make it taper off" curve actually looks like when you graph it. On top of that, that daily limit is no longer a hard all-you-can-spend-in-the-first-hour cap: the system drip-feeds the day's allowance as the Pacific day progresses, so the first users in the morning get a small opening allotment and the rest accrues steadily, preventing the whole day's budget from being exhausted in the first couple of hours. This only affects campaigns that are actively being tapered down — ordinary campaigns keep their flat daily cap. It's live today in the ad-budget code that

8f390e940d2f9457ea52bca4567f727f0a049277.text: When an AI model hides its private chain of thought inside the visible reply text instead of putting it in the dedicated thinking field, that hidden reasoning now gets separated out and shown only in the thinking box rather than as part of the readable answer. Developers who build on this runtime see the reasoning arrive as its own labeled chunk, while end users notice their chat no longer displays raw thinking markers or half-formed thought fragments in the main message flow. This cleanup is live today whenever an AI response carries leaked reasoning of that shape.

42989afa85b9d0c2cf43c220309ef9f05951d3bb.text: The assistant known as DeepSeek V4 Flash is now available during peak hours again, not just off-hours. If you use subscriptions that show a 'Plan paused 5:00 PM-3:00 AM PDT' label, that note has been removed, because the pause it described no longer applies. This applies to subscribers whose plans explicitly list DeepSeek models, effective 2026-08-28.

cb3ef3135c27c68f08c1c3e92290607a08732afc.text: As of August 27th, free users on the GLM 5.3 Flash model no longer have a limit of 2 sessions per day — they can now use it any number of times, sharing the same usage allowance that other premium models use. This change took effect because the team's initial guess that Flash would be too costly to give away for free turned out to be wrong: real-world data showed 93.6% cache hits, meaning it costs about 6.2x less than routing through the service it replaced. Anyone using the free version of GLM 5.3 Flash will notice that the system no longer blocks access after two sessions, treating it just like the other top-tier models without special usage restrictions.

2f4829e864d268f1cd6987537fd7956f6c67d0dc.text: You'll see a Freebuff Pro subscription ad appear in more places now—specifically in the waiting room before your turn, in the web chat, the assistant chat, and the command-line chat, whenever there's no paid or first-party ad to show. The ad copy pulls its price directly from the subscription catalog so it can't accidentally show an outdated price (the starter plan was resized on 2026-08-27, days before this rollout). The Desktop new-tab slot, which renders a card rather than inline text, also gets an image attached to its version of the ad. This is live today, but a common-code-only change like this doesn't automatically redeploy the web app—teams need to manually check and trigger redeployment for the web and freebuff-web surfaces.

3623ca3ffeb9e8ed71a65207075c1d4d18e639f3.text: When you visit Freebuff and no paid ad is available to show, you still see a house ad promoting the Freebuff subscription, but its pricing text now matches exactly whatever plan is currently offered instead of being copied by hand. The campaign builder let you assemble up to 10 different versions of that same promotion before silently refusing anything past that limit, and now you can assemble up to 25 different versions before it refuses more. The limit lives in one shared spot so the form you build with and the engine that actually serves slots never disagree, which is what was causing some builds to be accepted by one and rejected by the other.

ec3142a4e62ca638acd914b68a3842d4e8c347f3.text: The CLI's messaging system now accepts an optional helper that decides which connection to use when sending a message, so automated tests can plug in a fake connection instead of the real one. In everyday use nothing looks or behaves differently: the assistant still connects the same way by default. The only visible change is that when someone cancels a response mid-stream, the internal notes about the aborted attempt are shorter, which makes the cancellation path cleaner but does not affect what you see in your terminal.

02f42768b0bc73acb01625d4d082a2f6f72d497e.text: If you subscribe to a paid plan and use CodeBuff from a limited region, the model picker now shows the models your plan includes instead of only offering the default assistant. Previously, the app's client-side allowlist hid paid-plan models even though the server allowed them, so selecting a plan model would snap back to the default. The app now reads your plan status from your session and appends plan rows to the limited catalog while keeping free-tier models in their usual picker positions. This applies to subscribers in limited regions and is live now.

f68e7ca5489c3652786a98440b44dc36b95d9176.text: Campaigns that were set to lower their daily ad delivery over time now do it smoothly on a schedule instead of dropping off a cliff. If you run a campaign that is not billed by subscription, the system can be told to start at a higher daily cap and gradually ease it down to a target amount over a set number of days, with a small amount of built-in randomness so the cap landing on any given day can't be predicted from a calendar. Each day gets one fixed number for that campaign, chosen with a hash so it stays the same whether you check in the morning or evening. If your campaign is paid through a subscription, the schedule is ignored entirely and you keep seeing the same daily budget you are charged for.

2cf1163dc72fd40df1b7d56a4ed94d668116dc47.text: When the system tries to talk to the advertising service and gets back a 'forbidden' reply, it now logs a clear message explaining that the ad account simply isn't turned on yet, instead of recording a generic error. If the advertising service takes too long to send back its full reply, the system now waits for the complete response before giving up, so it won't get stuck hanging indefinitely. You would notice this today if you were watching the logs for failed ad requests, which will now spell out the account-enablement problem instead of filing it under vague errors.

38feaebb146a689d5dbf3a38b322e7db2e63f071.text: Ads served today now run through a controlled experiment that splits traffic between the existing ad path and two new ones — about 1% of auctions are quietly shown an alternative provider in the background (the "shadow" path) while a small slice actually routes to it live (the "treatment" path). The system records only coarse outcomes for each auction — whether an ad was found, timed out, or errored — using pre-bucketed labels, and publishers can only turn on live routing after a reviewed policy supplies a stable key, so traffic can't be accidentally shifted by a typo. If you watched the logs you'd see new shadow and live status columns attached to auctions, but the exact scores and internal decision IDs stay out of these logs and are only kept on the durable serving ledger.

5c250334a319ef47c7ae2d5653ec7f062e1eead1.text: When you sign up for Placements as a new advertiser and collect your first $500 (which means your ad account has successfully gathered $500 from customers buying through your promotions), the system now automatically adds a bonus equal to the same amount, up to $500 total, with the bonus expiring after 60 days if unused; additionally, any existing advertiser who actively referred a new advertiser that reaches $500 in collected spend will get a one-time $500 reward, though this referral bonus is capped at 10 rewards per person. If you're the type of advertiser who uses promo credits or balances, you'll now see these extra credits appear in your account ledger as distinct entries, and the system tracks whether they add to or subtract from your balance (or if they're being reversed due to a

9188c032117f7f2326e7bec8afb0a1bc62c33c1a.text: When a new ad request comes in, the system now picks a fresh random sample for that specific request instead of reusing the same user-based sample from before, and it does this through a shared method that keeps first-party (direct-sold) ad inventory and campaign selection working in sync. This means a percentage-based gate, like 'try our book first 5% of the time,' now applies per request rather than being locked to a persistent 0%…100% bucket assignment per user. The change is live in the first-party routing logic (the Imprezia experiment and similar flows) and affects how ad requests are sampled at the moment they arrive.

0591414315966ad5f2442f39de7c0ca6a9478558.text: If you're an advertiser who has saved a payment card, the free money you could spend on placements before paying just got cut from $250 to $100. This is live today: your max unpaid balance is recalculated in dollars, so the most you can spend without paying upfront after adding a card is now $100 instead of $250.

bd5c18ff73257a748a3bd0e402e25af4c012649f.text: If you have a paid subscription and live in one of the limited regions where those plans normally open no extra models, you now actually get access to the models your plan pays for meter — including GLM 5.3 Flash, which has taken the place of DeepSeek V4 Pro in the subscription catalog. The change is live today: paying there no longer means paying and receiving nothing. The daily and five-day session counts were also trimmed so the larger plan isn't just a straight-up upgrade over buying three of the smaller ones.

4ff202b7d262eb975b755a5da73965c661801cc6.text: When you hit your daily limit of free sessions, the assistant will now tell you exactly which plan to buy and give you a direct link to upgrade, instead of just saying you're out. The wording about your allowance also now says "hours" instead of vague "sessions," and the spend limit disclaimer now refers to "tokens" rather than "compute." This only appears for people who can still upgrade; if you're already on the biggest plan or aren't in the rollout group, you won't see any upgrade hint.

adbcb4e4a515334bd3f46580fe8188ba3d27bf84.text: If you refer another advertiser to the platform, you will not receive your $500 credit until you has both collected $100 from ad campaigns and actually spent it on an active, reviewed campaign. Previously, the referral program matched the first $500 of a referred advertiser's spending in two $25,000 chunks, and the referring advertiser was rewarded once the referred account had collected $500. Now qualification requires $100 collected and spent, and each side receives a single $500 credit after that threshold is met. This rule is live today for all advertisers participating in the referral promotion.

6f7cf660e827d750b278497432eebfa763ca58e5.text: Ads now appear on the Desktop new-tab screen, not just inside the chat. The ad system now sends a required address header when asking for display ads, which is the difference that stops the server from rejecting the request. Anyone using the app on a desktop and seeing a new tab should now see ads there; chat ads behave the same as before. This is live today.

47c4bf8cf7f311a30adfb47f4ca09d914cc3ce9a.text: If you advertise on a placement that bills per click, it will no longer sell for less than $1 per click, and any automatic price adjustment is capped so a single change can move only 25% in either direction and only after at least 50 clicks have been recorded. Advertisers who run up a negative balance can now be charged against the card they saved on file, and those charges show up as payments on their statement while refunds and disputes from card networks show up as adjustments, with that payment history kept for 180 days. You only see an effect if your advertiser saved a card, your campaign went negative, and a collection attempt actually ran against it; the credit line and reprice guards do nothing on their own, but the collection ledger entries are live today.

c359f63c20bbc0f7d23fb950af7764257b6ec274.text: When a model is temporarily unavailable, the message you see now always names the time zone (UTC) so you aren't left guessing whether '12:00 PM' is local or UTC time. This matters most when you're using the assistant from a remote server or command-line tool whose clock might be set to a different zone than your own — the message now says '10:00 AM UTC' instead of leaving the zone ambiguous. The fix also lets apps that know your location show the time in your own zone, while older tools keep showing the UTC time as a reliable default. Live today in the apps that already use this message format.

b3e1d17c5a89e05ad7692f0dd70466a97851a3c7.text: If your tool keeps hitting the same error over and over (like a retry loop), it will only send the first few copies of that error to the analytics system instead of spamming one report per failure. This affects anyone using the CLI, Desktop app, or server tools — if you look at the error reports, you’ll see a count field showing how many times each error actually happened, rather than thousands of duplicate entries. It’s already live and working today.

9066513a775a950c3c5f620141e41cd8ebfc76b3.text: If you open the assistant in a desktop browser tab and then stop using it for about ten minutes, the app will now give that session back so other tabs can use the slot. The unused portion is refunded, so when you send your next message you simply get re-admitted on the same instance without losing your work. This only affects browser-based desktop users who leave a tab idle; the clock only resets when an actual turn runs, not from scrolling or typing.

e30c58d37ea03426da0f01a727c5acff3895a462.text: For free-tier users of this CLI tool, when you try to start a chat using certain withdrawn models, you'll now see a clear system message telling you that the model is "no longer available in Freebuff" instead of silently switching to a different model without explanation. The developers fixed this so that when a specific model is permanently withdrawn from the free pool (rather than just temporarily unavailable for the hour), the system informs you immediately and doesn't waste your time starting a session that can't actually run — older clients that don't understand this new feature still get told in their own way via the existing availability text. This is live now for anyone using the latest version of the CLI.
