702b43bf6fbd41be7405bc3e02773f21a7888d37.text: When you use the assistant on the free tier (the default and lite modes), it now uses a simpler, more reliable task setup (base2) instead of a newer one (base3) that was finishing less of your work on its weaker model. If you looked under the hood you'd see a switch that picks which setup runs, and two new example setups ready for comparison testing; the paid max and plan modes never switched back so nothing else changes. For now, the only thing you'd notice is that lite tasks tend to get completed more often than they did in the last couple weeks.

389f40a9a9a113232c22a5e93ee40d01a4ee7b08.text: When you run a command in the terminal on Windows, the app now looks for bash in many more places before giving up, so installs that previously went unnoticed—like a per-user Git install without admin rights, Git on a non-C drive, or a Scoop/Chocolatey layout—are now found and used. The finder also avoids the fake bash that Windows ships in its System folder and in the Microsoft Store area, which used to cause confusing failures when no real Linux-style environment was installed. The same detection runs everywhere the app needs a shell (the terminal panel and the per-workspace startup script), so they all agree on whether bash is available. This is live today: no restart is needed after installing Git, and the app picks up a new install immediately.

837519d09bdafee951022bd77b63e5cfc25ecc7e.text: If you use the command-line version of the app during an active GLM 5.2 promotion, you'll now see a short line at the top of the model picker showing how many extra sessions the promo is adding today, the daily limit, and the date the promo ends, plus a button that opens your Earn page directly in a browser. That promo line only appears while a promotion is actually running — outside of one, the banner looks exactly as it did before, and older versions of the app keep calculating your total session limit correctly because the server still sends that number. The promotion's text and dates are defined once by the server and reused everywhere the app shows GLM 5.2 messaging, so the CLI's notice, the desktop footer, the web picker, and the website all stay in sync, and if your terminal can't

1b28a1b851243771ec6e1433673df5e676496f9c.text: When you open a file in the web or cloud version of the coding assistant, it now shows only the relevant line range you asked for instead of the whole file, so large files load faster and stay within your allowed size limit. The web/cloud version got its own set of agent identities so it can run this single-loop harness separately from the desktop version, and a shared service account now correctly attributes your web activity to the web product instead of the command-line tool. These changes are live today for Freebuff Web and Cloud users.

da1f340a36ff033086086da3fe1411e796af2bc3.text: If you use the assistant picker that lets you choose how much thinking effort to spend (like low, medium, high), every surface now shares one single list of those levels instead of each product keeping its own copy. The developers also added a ceiling check so that when a model offers fewer levels, your request is quietly moved down to the highest level the model actually supports rather than being rejected. This only matters for the models that have a user-facing picker today; the rest of the catalog keeps showing the same single default setting it showed yesterday.

9ddaa67d28223f14873db3c78e8fd0fbf98608c1.text: If you use the assistant or any product powered by it, you may have noticed alerts popping up when database response times changed even during normal traffic fluctuations. The system has been recalibrated so these alerts only trigger when there's a genuine performance regression, rather than routine variations in response times or round-trip counts. You would notice fewer false alarms in your monitoring dashboards, with the new rules requiring both a significant ratio increase and an absolute time threshold to be met before flagging an issue. This affects anyone who relies on these performance alerts for operational decisions, as the signal-to-noise ratio of the monitoring system has improved.

97ea5981ff9943999d24543fa28dd5cc6fe5654a.text: The weekly progress line now includes a new 'progress' section showing exactly how many days of the week-long streak are filled, the total number of slots (always seven), and whether the streak has gone past the week with a '+'. This lets the desktop app draw its own circular progress indicators using these counts instead of relying on text-based dots. The change also adds a 'beyond' flag that is true whenever your streak exceeds seven days, which the dot-display portion already showed with a '+' character. This is live today.

db9b6fc11799d1756d2b434b432c8da1f6422046.text: The command-line helper you run from a terminal now offers several AI models to choose from—including DeepSeek, Fable, GLM, Luna, MiMo, and MiniMax—under one new setup that keeps the paid desktop tools separate from the free command-line experience. When you pick one of these models from the command-line menu, the helper starts up correctly tied to that specific model, and the new Fable model is only available through the command line right now, not in the web version. Behind the scenes, these additions also let the team run automated tests and comparisons against the older setup, so future evaluations match one-to-one. One small side effect: the Luna model no longer tries to set its own thinking depth, leaving that setting to be controlled in one central place instead.

85fe163fd7843afe7dc3d07df57d2ac8eade07c4.text: The free assistant toolbox lost three experimental test models (HY3, Ling 3.0 Flash, and Greg 2 variants) that were never shown to users, and added one new one called Kimi K3 Eco that is now available in the free tier for testing. If you browse or pick a free assistant today, you will no longer see the removed test models (they were only used internally), but Kimi K3 Eco may appear as a selectable option instead. The changes took effect on 2026-08-07 for the test removals, with the Kimi K3 Eco addition landing in this update.

fe7b8fad52fa2ea67a8d2cbb86638e7e0cbb7cf8.text: If Bun crashes the very moment it starts up on Windows—and only on older CPUs missing AVX2 support—it now recognizes that specific crash pattern (exit code 0xC0000409 within 10 seconds) and automatically switches to a slower but compatible build, rather than crashing in a loop and leaving you puzzled. At the same time, it starts capturing the last 8 KB of error text the program spits out when it fails, strips out terminal-control codes so they don’t mess up your screen when it prints them back, and includes those cleaned-up messages plus your system’s actual AVX2 status in the crash report so you (or the developers) can see what really happened. The crash report also now distinguishes between “you’re on the standard build and your CPU is too old” (with a hint to switch to the baseline

660747443d071feffcc7ccb584ac2977e631e0dc.text: When someone tries to sign in on their computer using a code sent to a browser or phone and that sign-in fails for any technical reason (like a lost internet connection or a clock that is off), the company can now see that it happened. Before this change, the failed sign-in was invisible to them: their system would record it as if the login succeeded, and then the person simply never appeared, leaving no trace of what went wrong. Now, every single one of these failures is recorded so support can understand why sign-ins sometimes don't work, instead of only hearing about problems when someone files a confused support ticket.

0bbfdeb6b0c850151bbedd015b31cd6c99f9e2a8.text: Research agents now reliably finish their answers instead of going silent mid-task. You, as someone using these research tools, will notice that they produce a complete written summary at the end of each step rather than stopping right after fetching information, leaving you with nothing. The developers added an internal instruction that tells the agent to keep going—either make another search/fetch or write the final answer—so the step no longer ends on an empty thinking trace. This fix is already live in the two researcher agents that handle documentation and web research.

7a29686a3dc1313a85ce61f22d76bc18a78de3f5.text: The sign-in code you get when logging in on a new device now expires after exactly one hour, the same for both the command-line tool and the desktop app. Previously each app tracked that timer separately, so one could expire sooner than the other without any obvious reason. You would not see a new setting or button; the change just keeps both apps from disagreeing about when a code stops working. Because this constant is now shared and used by the response the server sends back, the moment it takes effect is whenever the server you connect to runs this updated code.

ab5e182182a84b9df51cc00e8cdf96ce75d4bc0f.text: The system that tracks how long database lookups take has been recalibrated to match real-world performance after a network change made those lookups about 10x faster. The old limits were based on how fast the database should theoretically be, so every lookup blew past them constantly and nobody paid attention. Now the limits are set just above what actually happens, split into finer groups so a fast lookup (like checking if you're logged in) isn't hidden behind a slow one. Breaches still don't send alerts yet—the team needs a full week of everything staying under the new limits first, so this just quietly starts collecting data today.

bb7dbadf40439cd9a5159185a4d1a242b68f74ac.text: When you use the AI assistant, especially the free version, the system now watches for cases where someone is using a root AI agent (like a main assistant) without any of the tools that the official apps provide. This is flagged as a new signal called 'root_agent_no_tools' to help identify non-official usage patterns. However, this detection is only reported for now, not actively enforced, because the developers found too many false positives that could affect real users, and they plan to build account-wide rules later based on these observations.

68d9a88c81cfd8b1b1de979ca99eb3468290f961.text: Requests that come in through third‑party AI tools (anything other than Freebuff’s own agents) are now downgraded to a lighter model by default, so they no longer land on the full‑power model that paying Freebuff users expect. Freebuff also fixed a bug that was mistakenly flagging its own researcher‑web agent for 100% of its traffic over a month — about 334,000 requests from nearly 5,000 users — because the old detection list had been hand‑tweaked and missed its two signature tools. You’d notice this only if a request from an external tool suddenly switches to the cheaper model, and the system now automatically treats any new tool Freebuff ships as “ours,” so this misflagging of its own agents shouldn’t happen again.

2d6439de4640f2f4642e07c1f8decad1cdb00812.text: When you go to use the assistant on the free plan, the message that explains why you see a smaller set of models (instead of the full catalog) is now written in the exact same place and wording whether you're on the command-line app or the desktop app, so the two can't accidentally say different things. That explanation text — including how your country is named (for example, showing 'Brazil' and falling back to 'BR' if it can't be translated) and the plain list of privacy signals like VPN or Tor — was copied out of one part of the program into a shared spot that both apps read from. If you're on a full-access account you won't see this message at all; it only appears next to the model list when your account resolved to the reduced catalog. The shared text is in place and active today for

4e79ce476b22c73f06a2ca9fe5210d83d1c325ed.text: A new coding assistant option called Buffy has been added that can now read only parts of files instead of whole files at once, and it can shrink down older conversation history so it stays focused during long coding sessions. When you work with Buffy, you will notice it asks you to search for what you need before reading files, and it will read specific sections of files rather than loading everything at once. The feature is turned on only when someone specifically chooses this new assistant, while the default way of working stays the same.

d800f61ca0291aa9270a75e454fb1a4a8ce09712.text: Database alerts now split into two clear reasons instead of one noisy list. When a database request takes too long, you'll only be paged if it regressed against the prior baseline (for example a sudden 10x slowdown), because the absolute budget was over on every lane daily, making every alert meaningless. The over-budget condition is still reported but no longer triggers paging, since it is treated as an aspirational capacity target rather than an incident. The change is live in the alert evaluation for core database cost monitoring.

accfa422f66916c360186c12c240d9279acaf396.text: If you've ever asked an AI agent to suggest follow-up steps at the end of a conversation, you may have noticed the examples were slightly different depending on which agent gave them—one might say 'Split this file up' while another said 'Add unit tests.' Now, every agent pulls those suggested follow-ups from the same guidance, so the phrasing is consistent no matter which agent you're talking to. Behind the scenes, the duplicated instructions were moved into one shared reference that all the agents read from, and the note telling the agents how to phrase those suggestions was updated to focus on outcomes rather than specific files or steps. If you looked, you'd see each agent still suggests roughly three next steps, but the wording and style match across all of them.

87acd39098734f870266915e02267851c4cd4a4f.text: When someone uses the free tier through a tool that isn't the official freebuff client, their request is now routed to a zero-cost model instead of a paid one. The system checks whether the request includes tool names that only real freebuff clients send, and if not, it downgrades the request to protect the inference budget. This started live on 2026-08-08.

405bf49baa05e2abf854e5c051b36ad54a35002f.text: Windows users of the CodeBuff CLI will now see a startup log entry appear immediately when the app launches, before the terminal watchdog process starts running. This log entry (called a 'launch row') gets saved even if security software on your machine interrupts the app during startup, so when you use the --continue flag later, the system still has a record of your last session for the health dashboard. The change adds a new file (windows-terminal-health.ts) that handles reporting failures when the terminal broker or watchdog encounters issues on Windows. The developers removed the old opt-in flag for the terminal watchdog and kept only the opt-out flag (CODEBUFF_NO_TERMINAL_WATCHDOG) for users whose endpoint security policies conflict with PowerShell processes. Live today for Windows

8553a9efe9d42dc01079c1f7a63907ea55ec77d0.text: When the CLI tool prepares its terminal interface for building, it now handles the bundled native files more safely. If something interrupts the build midway, it will keep the last fully-complete bundle so the CLI does not end up with a half-installed, broken terminal library. The terminal interface components were also updated to a newer version (0.3.4).

92a6961b894204c5620f9dd77cd2606e54b9a397.text: You can now stop your typing from lagging behind what you see on screen when using the command-line assistant — the autocomplete suggestions now stay perfectly in sync with every keystroke, so pressing Enter or Tab selects the option that's actually visible instead of the previous one. Skill authors can add a setting to their instructions that hides them from being automatically discovered by the assistant, while still letting you run them directly if you type their name. When a hidden skill shows up in suggestions, selecting it now inserts its exact command into your input so you can finish what you want to say, rather than sending it right away. The way every skill gets assembled behind the scenes is now handled in one place, so the project-level and global skill files load in the same

851f10f5262ed0de613c360e7724ff58e450f0ad.text: When you opened the model picker in the CLI and tapped the banner that said "Use GLM 5.2", Free users were seeing their choice quietly switch back to the default recommendation. The banner is supposed to offer GLM at both subscription levels, but the screen was only treating GLM as a valid pick if you were on the top tier. Now GLM is accepted at every level as long as you still have sessions left to spend, so free users can actually launch the model they just tapped instead of being bounced to the recommended one. If you were a free user who ever pressed that banner and ended up on a different model, it should stick now.

25d69d5854023aae6361a9dbe09ab23090638563.text: If you pick the Muse Spark 1.2 model and it's busy, your request now gets quietly rerouted to GPT-5.6 Luna after just 10 seconds of waiting, instead of leaving you stuck waiting up to 60 seconds. The model picker now shows a tagline of 'Queue' with a dotted underline you can hover to see why — that fallback behavior — rather than the old '1M context' label. The 'NEW' badge that used to mark Muse Spark 1.2 as freshly released has been removed, and the tooltip text shown in the picker is now controlled by a single shared source so the displayed promise and the actual behavior can't drift apart.

55258aabc4592ed2e90fc5d99fd7ae1e8a7bf10b.text: When the assistant runs certain commands on Windows, it previously started a background helper that some security software mistakes for malware, causing slowdowns or interruptions. That helper now stays off by default on Windows, so everyday use on Windows machines won't trip those false alarms unless you explicitly turn it back on. If you need that helper for testing or troubleshooting on Windows, you can enable it by setting the terminal watchdog option; otherwise you won't notice any difference unless you were relying on it.

0f112dfc17a5d2dfc4419d5c4471a7cb8b49276c.text: When the terminal connection helper fails to start on Windows, the app now silently records that specific failure so the team can spot Windows-only regressions later; it does not change what you see or do when running a command. The recording only happens in the interactive window you type in, and only on the rare spawn failure, so it never slows down normal work or affects the detached background helper. If you noticed nothing different but a Windows-only crash stopped working, that crash is now the kind of error the team can track per software version without being blurred by sampling.

fbf092f424327cab5a5086a0cf209d9199dcac73.text: If you use the Freebuff command-line tool to pick which model drives your session, you will now see the reasoning level the model actually runs at right next to its name, e.g. ' · Reasoning: high', and it stays in sync with what the server ultimately sends rather than drifting from a stale label. The model picker and the shared model list now share a single labeled field so the level shown is the level used today. Models with no reasoning levels, or where the provider's default should be left alone, simply don't show the suffix. On the DeepSeek and MiMo lanes the label is clamped to 'high' so it can't falsely show 'medium' while still running as 'high'.

e455a7f11d4caa461b258678a9a3bb975da44860.text: When you run a command inside the AI coding assistant on a Windows machine, it now passes that command to a separate helper process using a single temporary file in your system's temp folder instead of a set of direct communication pipes. This fixes a problem where, after running several commands in a row (roughly 64+), the communication link between the main program and the helper would fail on Windows, causing the entire assistant to close unexpectedly with an internal error. You may notice that commands run more reliably during long coding sessions on Windows, and the documentation now reflects this change. The new method also handles situations where antivirus or search-indexing software briefly keeps the temporary file open, ensuring your command's results are never lost.

3a8cc3135b1201b6403abb26762a309b269c8119.text: When the CLI tries to connect to your free session and gets cut off, it now reports a clear, structured reason for the failure instead of a generic error string—like whether the server might have already processed your request before the connection dropped. You, the person running the free-tier command-line tool, will now see specific messages on the takeover/retry screen: one for a server that is overloaded (503), one for a request that timed out, and one for a request whose outcome is unknown because the server may have completed it before losing contact. A live countdown shows when the next retry will happen, and the wording tells you whether it is safe to retry or whether you should wait. Under the hood, the system remembers the attempt number and the exact next retry time, and it

372bcb13336cfa7eb8060b1b80208c8a9884fb9f.text: If you use the web version of the service, the assistant can now talk through a new artificial intelligence model called Meta Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor. This model is only available on the website and is not selectable in the desktop or command-line apps, because using it everywhere would quickly exceed a strict usage limit that only the website's waiting-line system knows how to handle. The website keeps the model hidden from the menu of choices, but the underlying infrastructure is now in place so traffic can be sent through it and queued when that usage limit is hit.

95f7ba2869aed9e0bd0ef259d86becf75a4ac23e.text: When you use chat or sign in to your account, this app quietly checks how many database requests each action requires and how long those requests take. The system now has set expectations for how much database work should happen per feature (for example, chat completions should stay under certain response times and round trips), and it will flag if any feature starts asking the database for more time or making more trips than expected. This is live today and primarily affects internal monitoring teams who will see automated alerts and dashboard warnings if a feature regresses beyond the defined thresholds.

6059b884a999ffb281a0c15913c659f9bc6f5308.text: The CLI now lets you manually retry a takeover when it times out or the outcome is unknown, instead of forcing you to restart first to check the status. Transient failures (408, 429, 503) are now classified as safe to retry, since they occur before the session mutation commits, so you won't be blocked unnecessarily. If you looked, you'd see clearer messages guiding you to check and retry rather than restart, along with updated documentation for local development prerequisites like Docker and environment configuration. This change is live today in version 0.0.141.

e93edfe8d2d61a6b285ed4e7614d50a8c9de8e29.text: When you run the assistant in the terminal and leave it working, your computer now asks the server for less information each time it checks in, so it won’t slow down or waste bandwidth showing you quota details you already know. If something unexpected changes about your session (like your account identity), the terminal will automatically fetch one full update before going back to the lighter, smaller updates. Behind the scenes, the assistant also tracks which steps used the AI model versus which used internal tools, and it waits before saving all of its work history until the run finishes, keeping things tidy and preventing any single run from creating too many records at once.

b2a5e5362384591ac9d67ae57216ea088c5cc01d.text: When you open the command line tool today, the referral message you see now also shows a line telling you that you can earn a GLM 5.2 session by doing small paid tasks, with a web address printed right there so you can copy it yourself. This appears in all the banner styles the tool shows, including the ones that lock or unlock based on your current session. If you don't have an audience to refer friends to, this gives you a second, region-independent way to earn more access without waiting for referrals to bring people in.

d62db1eebd81b366812817ac479860ba7ab066e9.text: The list of AI models you can pick inside the program has been made more specific and up to date. Where it used to say something vague like 'the best open-source models,' the description now names the actual model that gets selected for you by default, including the newest version of one of them. If you open the program's help file today, you'll see the model names reflect what the program actually offers right now, including a new option you can unlock after earning enough sessions.

956dcf938814d5da8af5f2c1c1216f14d1bcd769.text: If you're using the free version of the coding assistant from a region with limited access (where you normally can't pick certain premium AI models), you can now use the model called GLM 5.2 after you earn a bounty grant. The assistant used to push your GLM choice back to a basic model even if you'd won a reward, so the reward was wasted in those regions; now it honors the GLM selection when a bounty grant is active. This applies today to users in limited-tier regions who hold a bounty grant for GLM 5.2.

ba0d1c06f45f11e6259d8d3c03aee844a0b60a97.text: When the assistant runs a command in your terminal, it used to be able to tell it to wait up to 50 minutes even for quick actions. If something hung, you could end up sitting through that entire wait with nothing happening. The assistant now has a hard upper limit on how long it can set that wait for regular commands, so a stuck command stops on its own instead of leaving you staring at a frozen screen. Anything that genuinely needs more time still has its own way to run in the background or wait with no timeout.

7005d45cc1116a842069903738371fc3c64f2c92.text: When you use the AI coding tool to look at files in a project, it now handles hidden configuration files (the ones starting with a dot, like `.env`) more reliably across Windows and other systems. It correctly recognizes these sensitive files, even when Windows adds extra characters to their names or reads them from different storage areas, and it can now safely skip template versions (like `.env.example`) that are meant to be shared. Behind the scenes, the tool also became more robust when a project lists files to ignore: one incorrectly formatted rule no longer causes the tool to miss other valid rules, so you see a more accurate list of your project files instead of missing some that should be there.

76020951df33514036c99751ccb03abd92b47274.text: Starting today, when something talks to our servers, we now quietly sort the requests by which app actually made them, instead of trusting a client-chosen label that already caused one big mix-up. Each request's identifying text gets shrunk into a clean product name (like the app's name) and, if present, a short version number, while anything weird or too long gets filed under a single safe bucket. Nothing acts on this yet, so you won't see it change any behavior right now, but it gives us a clearer, privacy-safe way to tell which app versions are making requests. If you peek at a request's recorded details, you'll spot two new optional fields for the cleaned-up app name and version alongside whatever was already logged.

adf5bef2be7cd107b6fdefb43b9e9e6fffadf1d7.text: If you open the assistant picker today, you won't see the new Greg 2 Ultra and Greg 2 Super options anywhere the public can click — both are restricted to god-mode access, meaning only those with elevated permissions can reach them. The reason the developers hardcoded them as god-only isn't experimental status, it's cost: these models bill roughly 20 to 36 times more per input or output token than standard options, and they quietly prepend a hidden preamble of around 17,000 tokens to every request, making even a brief message expensive to process. The team placed them in the premium metering pool on purpose, because leaving them out of any billing list entirely would let them run unmeasured, so the pricing guardrail is now live and enforced today.

a47be121a650358f747794cf743870e75d35e6b3.text: Two helper scripts that run specialized agents (one for browser tasks, one for repo analysis) were incorrectly named with a.test.ts suffix, which caused the automated test runner to treat them as tests. Because these scripts need real API keys and stop on failure, they were silently killing test summaries. The scripts were renamed to start with 'run-' and the test runner was updated across multiple packages to explicitly skip end-to-end and integration tests, so automated tests now report properly while the manual run scripts remain untouched for their intended purpose.

c7445e24582aabfa1c2f45c2108982511769385a.text: Free sessions can no longer start on the HY3 model, effective August 4 — the free-tier model and its Atlas companion were taken off the free catalog, quota pool, and allowlist, so a free chat will not be admitted on either one. You would notice this only if you were picking a free model: those two options are gone from the list, while paid users on their own plans can still route to HY3 through the existing paid path. The bundled roots that let free trials spawn subagents are also gone, leaving only paid or bring-your-own-key access.

dd1e2cfc9f90b5c1b0c2e056e7eecf45ae0c7cd5.text: The CLI's chat, feedback, message block, and publish state stores now enable immer's Map/Set support themselves at module load, instead of relying on a single global call during app initialization. If you imported any of these stores directly (e.g. in a test or tooling context) before the app had fully bootstrapped, immer's plugin hadn't been activated yet, so the store would throw [Immer] minified error nr: 0 and only worked when another file happened to run first and enable the plugin. Enabling it per-store makes each store correct on its own import, and makes a store that forgets fail consistently everywhere instead of only outside the app.

2e0d17a8eb3b3bf8b25564ff44b3338348cbfc63.text: When you build your first project on Freebuff's web version, the team is now tracking how you move through two key moments: the short onboarding questions that appear while your first build runs, and the guided tour of your new workspace afterward. If the system decides your idea is better suited for the desktop or CLI tool, it also records when you click through to that alternative, so it can tell whether you actually landed there. Nothing you see changes visually yet — this simply adds the tracking needed to measure where people drop off, so the team can later find out which step (onboarding question, tour pane, or gate redirect) is most often left unfinished.

f28ecce37f526a75beecd2e0c8d82da50630abba.text: The free MiMo Pro assistant has been removed entirely, so you can no longer pick it from the list of available free AI helpers on the web, CLI, or desktop app. At the same time, there was previously a second way to access the GLM 5.2 model (through an older pathway), but that option has now been closed off; if you want to use GLM 5.2, you must use the single remaining route. GLM 5.2 is still locked behind a referral requirement, meaning you can only use it after earning access by referring friends, and that restriction has not changed. As a result, when you open the app, MiMo Pro won't appear as an option, and GLM 5.2 will only be available if you qualify through referrals rather than being visible or usable by everyone.

60dd01fe109f976b0e1e7eea23b9bd0e3ba67b6e.text: People on the restricted free plan can now actually use GLM 5.2 if they've been given a special access grant, such as one earned through a bounty program. The on-screen card that advertises GLM 5.2 will appear unlocked for them, but only when they still have sessions left to spend from that grant. The system no longer locks them out just because of their plan tier — it checks their available balance instead, and only counts bounty-style grants toward giving them access.

4f9fad7460a17948620ee4c82d02a3ddb4bba868.text: If you're using the desktop app and try to take over a single-slot session that's still technically alive on another machine or window you can't close, there's now a new header-based escape hatch that tells the server to end that specific tab and hand the slot to you. The server only honors this takeover when the instance ID you provide matches the exact holder the system just rejected you from, so clicking a stale card can't accidentally disconnect a tab you never saw. This is in place and live today, providing a targeted override for Desktop's 'Use it here' action without risking unrelated tabs.

9bf66ff09f2303f7bc13ebb134678c45869f2e30.text: When you use the free version of the tool during busy times, you may now see a status message that says 'high demand — in line, starting soon...' instead of a confusingly long 'thinking' pause. The tool now recognizes when the server is temporarily slowing down free users to manage heavy traffic, and shows you that it's waiting your turn rather than silently retrying. This only affects free-tier users; paid subscribers won't see this message. The feature is live today.

383fb0ceededb4056d40b1f6db984a321b7feb21.text: When you open the free coding tool, the streak counter next to 'Start coding for free' no longer shows up as empty boxes in older terminal fonts — it now uses simple dots (•) that work everywhere. The streak line also stays properly spaced out, so the day count and its progress dots don't run together into a unreadable mess like 'Start coding for free18 day streak'. If you're someone who uses the command-line version of the tool, you'll notice the layout stays clean whether the streak appears next to the heading or on its own line underneath. This fix is live today for the CLI landing screen.

12660b067482362d977d9d423b6a2c107ad0c76c.text: When an assistant thinks out loud but then stops without giving you an answer - whether it ran out of space while thinking, or just quietly stopped after reasoning - the system now treats that as a recoverable situation instead of silently failing. It will automatically take another attempt so you don't get stuck with an empty response. This matters only when the assistant's visible reply is completely missing, not when it gives you a partial answer.

32b7907dfe18e9fd79fac194172c07fcc816edda.text: When you run a command in your terminal, the assistant now makes sure it properly says 'I'm done' before cleaning up — instead of vanishing in a way that could freeze your terminal, especially on Windows. The recovery messages now clearly tell you to restart and suggest using Windows Terminal or VS Code if something gets stuck. Behind the scenes, it also waits a reasonable, time-limited amount for stubborn leftover processes to exit instead of hanging forever. The change is live today and affects anyone running commands through the terminal interface.

4d3c46a551d4e0e3f37e902090ea267ec9b9ab5e.text: Accounts created at proxyvpn.cn, impact.qd.je, and fincy.qd.je can no longer be used, because these domains were behaving like temporary throwaway mailboxes even though only a handful of accounts appeared on them. Youd notice this when someone signing up with one of those email addresses is immediately rejected, since the system blocks new accounts from these three domains outright. The system now requires a real, active email provider instead of a proxy or single-day signup service.

d1c94381b39773dbd68e9c7ebbd4909724179110.text: When you run a shell command through the assistant, that command now runs in its own separate terminal window instead of sharing the same screen as the assistant. This stops the screen from getting scrambled, cursor positions from jumping around, or your keyboard input from being grabbed by the wrong program while the command is still running. The change is already live for anyone using the interactive CLI today. If you build apps that embed the assistant's SDK to run commands behind the scenes (headless), nothing changes for you; that path still uses the direct runner.

af3257b3b7d7a81bde74a67d84d9a683478b684d.text: Every time the desktop app tried to recover from a failed turn but kept failing, the system already recorded that moment, but it only counted a random sample of those events rather than all of them. Now the system records every single one of those failed-recovery events instead of just some, so reliability metrics won't have gaps. You wouldn't notice this directly, but it helps the developers measure how often failed turns succeed on a second try versus fail repeatedly.

0251dddf1475cf3bd2449b2fe3f4cb429903459d.text: When a request to the assistant takes no data for five minutes straight, the app used to tell you it was almost certainly your network's fault. Now that message also says a slow start on our side counts as a reason, since the system waits through that quiet period too. You'd notice the difference only if you hit that five-minute silence: the wording now lists 'slow model start' right alongside VPN or proxy problems, and retrying your message is still the first thing suggested. This is live today in the assistant's error text.

5423683dc8558497f5168a3e65a61e9a5e01e0ad.text: If you're a free user of the Claude-powered Fable model, you'll no longer see a separate "let's think extra hard" helper join your chat, because your main model is already strong enough on its own. Previously, Fable sessions would waste time spawning that extra helper (up to three wasted attempts in a single turn during live testing) before switching to a cheaper model to work; now it goes straight to the work tools. At the same time, Fable gets its own dedicated code-checking helper that matches its exact model, so reviews stop silently failing mid-session. Both changes are live today for free Fable users.

f56844fd118df56422c40c55968c247d6253c562.text: When you run a program inside the assistant's terminal window on a Windows machine, the terminal previously kept sending it mouse clicks and keyboard focus signals, which that inner program sometimes painted over the main screen as stray letters. The assistant now briefly turns off those mouse and focus signals only while an inner program is running, so the inner program can no longer splatter random characters across the display, and the signals come back once that program finishes. You would notice a cleaner screen with no mysterious report letters appearing while waiting for a program to complete on Windows; the change is live today for Windows users of the CLI.

32405d54b26ef83e80be7c091a8c9610c6bf3b8a.text: On Windows, when you run a command through this tool, the terminal no longer lets the running program secretly take over your keyboard and screen in a way that could interrupt or hijack your typing. Instead, a new built-in guard quietly locks down the interactive terminal right before the command starts and only gives control back after it fully finishes, so background keystrokes, focus switches (like alt-tabbing away and back), and mode-restoration escapes can't sneak in mid-command. Interactive sessions fail safely if that lock can't be set, meaning a command simply won't launch rather than risk corrupting your terminal. This is live today for packaged Windows CLI usage and is verified by a new smoke test that checks the isolation works on a real Windows binary via winpty.

7335066f45ad29fa39ad3f09fa84c45ab1aca737.text: The chat assistant behind freebuff.com/chat now connects straight to the AI provider instead of going through an older middleman service. If you use the chat, you won't see a visible difference in how responses look or feel, but the system under the hood is now using a more direct route to reach the same model. The old connection method is still kept around behind the scenes just so existing setups don't break during the switch, but new chat sessions automatically use the direct connection.

8c9929fa0f77987bcfd64f0625b68a97cf9dc17b.text: When you install this tool on Windows using a shell program called Git Bash, the installer would fail and show a confusing message about a 'remote tape address' instead of unpacking the files correctly. That happened because Git Bash comes with its own version of a file-unpacking program that misread Windows-style folder paths, so the installer now tells the computer to use Windows' built-in unpacking tool instead. This only affects people who run the automated test that checks the installer works after a new version is published; it does not change the tool itself or what you see in normal use. The fix is live today for anyone running that test on a Windows machine.

59b71a2329ee96e2378ae589e09694cfa02eee4a.text: When an agent is working through a task, the detailed step-by-step instructions it uses are no longer baked directly into its definition. Instead, those instructions are now delivered as a tagged message that is added each step and automatically cleaned up after the step ends. The part of the system that trims conversation history to save space no longer needs to special-case a permanently attached instruction block, because the instructions now come and go with each step rather than sitting in memory. If you were watching an agent run, you would not see anything different in its output, but behind the scenes the way it receives and discards its per-step guidance is now simpler and consistent across all agent types.

cfefab1485351974f3ed0461c9d4797fbb251c9d.text: When the program starts up to check for updates, it now strictly verifies that the version number it reads is genuine and properly formatted, rejecting any malformed or suspicious entries instead of trusting them. If an update notice looks invalid, the program treats it as stale and will refresh itself rather than act on bad data. This affects the startup update-checking step across the three main program launchers. The change is live today.

817391fb58001b3bc24fbc42be479676d265d7d0.text: The assistant can now give newly created helper agents the exact same conversation history no matter how they were started, instead of sometimes giving them a version that was missing the final message or one that included extra outdated announcements. This means spawned helper agents will see a cleaner, more consistent view of what has happened so far. You wouldn't notice this directly unless you were watching how these helper agents behave, but those helpers should now act more predictably because their starting information is aligned.

8f24a429cd6addf8fb858155634ef5241fea86b4.text: You might notice your conversations can now run longer before the system starts trimming old messages to save space. The trimming point for most models has moved from 200,000 words to 400,000, so you get twice as much 'workspace' before summaries kick in. The smaller 262,144-word-capacity models still trim at 250,000, and MiniMax M3 stays at 400,000 even though it can actually handle 524,288 words. This is already live, so longer-running chats will simply wait longer before being compressed.

e183deaed6c794aacff15662a87d41c98e3201d1.text: When you're using the assistant in a tab and your internet stutters for a moment, the system used to think your tab had gone away and drop it. Now, each tab sends a quiet 'I'm still here' signal every 45 seconds, and the server waits through several missed signals before considering the tab gone, so a brief connection glitch no longer kicks you off. This keeps your tab's spot reserved during short network blips.

ef5190fe8024ca729df82dfa11c847354a3ca279.text: When the CLI crashes on certain computers due to incompatible processor instructions, it now remembers that and avoids trying the same incompatible version again. The terminal health monitor, which helps repair your terminal after the program exits, can now be turned off with a special setting because some antivirus tools were falsely flagging it as suspicious activity. Theme detection stopped checking Windows PowerShell for color schemes, since doing so was triggering security alerts, and now just defaults to a dark theme instead.

3e5be71544b2879899a0dea5162bf6f7e8195bcb.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, you may now see a temporary, capacity-limited "Claude Fable 5" trial row offered by the server; if the server still has capacity, that row appears and lets you pick that model for a free hour of agentic work, and if an unknown model id is advertised by the server it is ignored rather than shown as a half-labelled option. The picker keeps the offer state across the short refresh gap so the row doesn't flicker away, and the Claude Fable 5 orchestrator is unconditionally listed so that running subagents mid-session do not get 403 errors after the capacity pool runs out. This affects only people who are served an active limited offer on this specific free-tier endpoint; if the server does not advertise the offer, nothing changes for you.

612e2a39e0355c12169f3dd37ce5e3bf09942e02.text: Every chat tab now gets a short, clean title pulled from the first message you send, instead of leaving it blank or making you set one yourself. When you start a conversation, the system reads your first message, picks a headline-style summary of what it's about, and trims any awkward quotes or extra punctuation so the title fits neatly across the tab. This works the same way whether you're on the desktop app or using the web browser version, since the logic now lives in one shared spot that both versions can read. Nothing changes until you open a new conversation, and then the tab label will show something like "Plan a vacation" or "Debug Python code" instead of a generic name.

13b1cfee56ea86d90e68a05afbb0399cc5c062a5.text: When you're using the newest GPT model (5.6) to run agents that have multi-step conversations, the system now avoids a slowdown that was wasting cache work on each step. Previously, deleting the last message between steps broke the model's caching, dropping hit rates to about 63%; now a single resident prompt is held per turn, bringing rates back to roughly 100%. You'd notice this if you were running long agent tasks on that model: they complete faster and consume fewer repeated tokens. This affects only GPT-5.6-style models; other providers like DeepSeek, Xiaomi, and MiniMax that do longest-prefix matching were already unaffected and stay at ~96% hit rate.

6e1168a960e83d3c2651c6765b504f45f0d091b9.text: The cloud planning assistant now uses DeepSeek V4 Flash instead of MiniMax M3 for everyone, including people on the limited regions plan. You get a stronger, cheaper coding model without the old tradeoff between cost and quality, and nothing about your plan determines which assistant variant you get. If you looked at the setup code, you would see the assistant picker always returns the same main assistant and ignores the model argument entirely, while the secondary assistant for limited regions stays only so already-running planning sessions can finish.

f388f14e2b1dcafb2a95799598ceb7e7ac511c24.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, the selected row no longer shows a redundant 'Press Enter' hint on the right side, and the 'a better model exists' message that appears for retired models is now centered on its own line instead of being shoved to the side. The old 'Press Enter' hint was taking up about 17 blank columns of space on every card for no reason, since a green border already shows which row you're on, and the old indentation made the message look messy on the widest rows. Now each model card is exactly as wide as the text it needs to show, so the menu looks tighter and you won't see awkward empty gaps on the right edge of any card.

31ac8a0f82d45b3a6f82a46a9be1a4c6b8ad3b11.text: The Freebuff assistant now shows a clear message when too many people on your internet network are already using the free service at the same time, and it tells you roughly how long to wait before trying again. The limit is based on your shared internet address (the one your whole household or office appears as), and only applies when new sessions want to start—people already talking to the assistant keep going. If you saw a generic error before, you’ll now see a friendly traffic-light notice explaining the hold and that a slot opens soon. This is live today for anyone trying to start a free session from a busy network.

3a7b54b212bfe45eafb19525bbf52041f9b3a6c9.text: If you use the terminal tool to build something on a free plan, the typing that used to quietly run on a different paid model now runs on the same free model its planner already uses. The change landed on 2026-08-01 for free tier users driving the Tmux CLI agent and the Cloud Build model; you'd notice this only if you checked the model name in the agent config, because everything still looks the same to you. The two pieces still start separate sessions, so nothing about starting or reusing your build session changes.

d5ca1376e2a658169fc355905b29159d5af6a85a.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, you'll now see 'DeepSeek V4 Flash 07/31' with a 'NEW' badge, while MiniMax M3 and V4 Pro show a notice pointing to Flash as the recommended default. If you previously had M3 or V4 Pro saved as your preferred model, the app quietly switches you to Flash on your next session unless you manually change it back. The switcher only shows the replacement notice on the row you're actually selecting, so the list stays clean for everyone else. This is live today.

ae8c38c6a145ee540ec48aea9027714917d9da36.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, the list of models shown (both in the main grid and the referral banner) now automatically gets checked against every approval list it has to pass through before your request is accepted, and this check happens on every surface (desktop, CLI, web) using the picker's real list, not a copy. That catches the same kind of mistake that made the earned GLM 5.2 row show up and then fail with an error last time, except this time the picker's offered set is exported so the test reads the actual models rather than a duplicate. It is live today for the desktop picker and the CLI model selector, and it only ever blocks an offering model from slipping through an unapproved gate, not the other way around, so retired models that are still valid for active

b1f68e07ef57b84fe337023718d350a96ec2305b.text: The free assistant can no longer use Kimi K2.7 Code. Starting today, any free request that tries to pick that model gets blocked, and the free model picker now points you at DeepSeek V4 Flash instead, which the developers say is faster and cheaper than the previous recommendation. If you were on the free plan and were using or could see the Kimi option in the model picker, it is gone now, and requests for it return an error instead of running. The change went live with version 0.0.133 of the command-line tool.

ef75fd7a27e09c75d822efcfdaa28b023a03e31f.text: If you use the command-line assistant and have earned a 7-day usage streak, you'll now see a short note about your streak bonus only after you reach that full week; it was previously hinted at before the milestone, which crowded the model picker on small terminal windows. At the same time, the free model list in that picker was reordered so the GPT-5.6 Luna model appears before Minimax M3 when choosing which AI to use. This is live today.

a5cb80f3d735b96b63f2fc075689ab4ed9955056.text: When you open a new chat or start a fresh session, the app now automatically switches you to DeepSeek V4 Flash if you had previously picked a model that's been superseded (DeepSeek V4 Pro, MiniMax M3, or MiMo 2.5). This happens every single time you start a new conversation, not just once. You can still manually pick a superseded model mid-conversation if you want, and it'll stick for that chat, but a brand new session will always default to V4 Flash. So if you reopen the app, you'll notice the model selector showing DeepSeek V4 Flash even if you used a different model last time.

f3e3cce8abe081a471cdf9fbd525426f7fba600f.text: When you open the model picker in the assistant's command-line tool, the recommended model card no longer jumps around or get cut off while the list of available models is still loading. If your account only has access to two models, the list now stays open and shows both of them instead of hiding one behind a disappearing toggle. While browsing the full list, your keyboard focus stays locked on the recommended model when you expand or collapse the grouped tiers, so pressing Enter always confirms the right choice. Behind the scenes, the code that measures the dropdown's height now uses the larger of its predicted or actual size, preventing clipped rows during the brief moment when the model list refreshes asynchronously.

5d8bc0232add269427599ffd4f928ee6a4786f52.text: When you open the command-line assistant picker on a limited free session, you can now choose the referral model GLM V5.2 directly even if it isn't pre-listed, as long as you still have weekly referral sessions remaining and you're unlocked. The app tracks your referral status separately for full and limited access tiers, so seeing the model and its remaining session count stays correct when you swap tiers, and a clear 'none' reply from the server wipes out any stale cached referral info for that tier. Because of this, if the server temporarily rejects a request and retries, the picker still lets you send to GLM instead of silently switching to a default; and when you close the picker, your last chosen model gets saved only if it's a real freebuff model, so referral-only or retired models

7c831448a6e554c45b87894487ebe7421385045f.text: When you ask the helper to run a terminal command on Windows, it now picks a working copy of bash differently than before. Instead of falling back to the Windows Subsystem for Linux version, which can break silently if its virtual machine isn't ready or has encoding problems, the helper only accepts a Git-for-Windows bash or a manually specified one. If you rely on bash being found automatically, you'll get a clearer error pointing you to install Git for Windows or set the custom path variable, rather than seeing confusing command failures.

d248ecc5ad5aafd3b80a52ed21c4244e0aa849d6.text: Skills with nested metadata (like the hermes: blocks that skills.sh serves) used to fail validation entirely because the system only accepted plain text values. Now those nested structures load fine regardless of how deeply they're nested, so valid skills are no longer rejected over metadata that nothing actually reads. Separately, skill descriptions that run too long are now automatically cut to the maximum allowed length instead of preventing the skill from loading at all. These changes are live today in the current version.

0cda526a6c5bbf6cab64dafb874a9774ac1a4299.text: When the tool builds a list of your project files, it now stops silently at 10,000 files. Instead of returning empty results that look like the files don't exist, it clearly warns you that the scan was cut short and suggests narrowing your search. This only affects projects large enough to hit that limit. On Windows, the tool was skipping past your ignore rules (like excluding node_modules) because of path-format differences, so your source files were getting buried under build output; that path-mismatch bug is now fixed.

6cc0c94c19331c4a4009587d3b698916f00f9f0a.text: If you refer friends to Freebuff and they sign up with a GitHub account that's been open for at least four months, you now get a simple daily reward instead of climbing a multi-step point ladder: paid-tier users get one extra daily session with GLM 5.2 (no limit on how many referrals it happens for), and free-tier users get one extra daily session but no more than three per day total. The old system promised things that weren't actually delivered—daily message limits that were never enforced, and removing the 'Powered by Freebuff' deploy watermark—so both of those perks have been dropped entirely and the watermark is now turned off everywhere. You won't notice the referral limit itself changing, but the promise of unlocking bigger allowances and a cleaner deploy as you refer more friends

c22abe9a8900d52fac3c91bd1d12f407e631be0c.text: The assistant used to refuse to answer questions if a provider tried to charge even slightly more than the exact price they thought it cost, which kept causing errors. Now the assistant will accept answers up to a higher price ceiling before giving up, so it works again when prices shift by a small amount. This only affects people using the Freebuff service with the Luna model; the price cap is still set low enough to block much more expensive providers.

254c227edee9d656de7fc74312468062e17f7a1e.text: When you deliberately switch the assistant to a different model during an active session, the CLI now shows you a message explaining why the switch didn't take effect and what you need to do instead. Previously, the app would secretly revert your selection with no explanation, leaving you confused about why you were still talking to the old model. Starting today, if a session is already running on a model and your intentional pick is rejected due to that lock, a note appears in the chat telling you to run /end-session first and that sessions expire automatically after one hour of inactivity. The feature works only for explicit model picks you choose yourself, not for background reconnections.

bfead8065f4f0e68f6247fa51973c73185d00525.text: If you use the free Codebuff service, you can now choose a new AI model called GPT-5.6 Luna. This model is designed to think more deeply by default (high reasoning effort), which the developers felt is worth the extra cost since Luna is cheap per token. The model is only available on free Codebuff traffic and will not affect users of the paid Codebuff Lite mode. Additionally, the system is set up so that if the model's price increases on OpenAI's endpoint by more than $0.10/$0.60 per million tokens, requests will be refused to avoid unexpected charges.

f5526661a4291076b5784de328a4ddb405831935.text: Starting July 29, 2026, the free GLM 5.2 sessions you unlock through referrals now reset every single day instead of once a week. If you're a full-access user who has already unlocked the GLM 5.2 model, you also now earn bonus sessions for keeping a streak of using the service at least 7 days in a row - one extra session per week of streak, up to 4. The reset countdown in your app also now says 'today' or 'tomorrow' instead of 'this week.'.

5b8b58dbe1bc8498ac86a6e8aaa8e6311e86331f.text: You can now earn an unlimited number of free daily GLM 5.2 sessions by inviting friends, instead of being capped at a fixed number. The old premium-only GLM 5.2 model that was sold as a separate paid option has been removed from the model picker, but anyone already using it in a running session can continue without interruption. If you look at the referral screen today, you'll see 'refer more (X earned)' counting up freely instead of showing a maximum limit.

ab4919394f7cd07cc1f360e48f04b600a1f6d40a.text: When you deliberately pick a model to use and the system tells you a session is still locked on another model, the application now ends that old session and lets you switch to the model you chose. This affects anyone choosing a model in the Freebuff area of the command-line tool; before, your selection would silently snap back to the locked model, making it look like nothing happened. You would notice that after clicking a model like GLM 5.2 or DeepSeek V4 Flash, a short message appears confirming your previous session was ended and the switch was applied, instead of the interface appearing to ignore your click. If ending the old session fails unexpectedly, that message updates to tell you the switch did not apply and you should end the session yourself.

9f80be02582ab23c45aa4fd7adf8370b2613ad92.text: Freebuff removed the Kimi K2.7 Code model from the list of free models you can pick in the app, because it costs too much to provide at no charge. If you had previously selected Kimi, the app will now ignore that saved choice and fall back to a supported free model like DeepSeek or MiniMax instead. The model still works behind the scenes for paid tiers and existing server-side allowlists, but it will no longer appear as an option in the model picker for free users.

dde3b3223f5082e1ce6c3d890dfaee4a1c5e91f4.text: The list of AI models in the CLI now shows your session usage right inside the model picker instead of above it, so the model list no longer shrinks your terminal window. The focused-row cue now has a little more breathing room from the tagline, and the secondary details below each model name are centered instead of indented. The referral banner's copy-link button also gained a borderless variant for locked states, where it now adjusts its width based on whether it's bordered or inline. This is live for CLI users in version 0.0.130.

faee98a2042d0b024219330c1f6ae2f6df89cff0.text: When you browse models in the CLI selector, multimodal models (those that can process images) now show a small ' · Images' tag right on the first line of their description instead of taking up extra space on its own. This only affects the CLI model selector and nothing else is changed. If you look at the selector, the layout for both compact and standard modes will now account for the extra characters so everything lines up neatly, and you won't see any model pushed to a second line just because it supports images.

1ba142d747a1c095f2be79abe6b6adefad0c2a28.text: When you open multiple tabs of the assistant on your desktop, some models are now limited to three tabs at once while premium-tier models stay limited to one tab. The limit is enforced at the desktop session layer using a soft gate and a new constant in the shared models file, while the database also keeps the premium slot to one via a partial unique index. If you run several tabs, the server now sends back live per-user session counts and the earliest time capacity will free up, so the model picker can tell you when another tab or device is holding a slot. These counts cover only running, not-yet-expired desktop sessions.

ff0629f1f1b73fec52d0107117f3c27cc46c389f.text: Hosts that run many sessions over the same project files can now supply a precomputed summary of those files, so the system skips re-analyzing the file tree and code tokens on every run. This reduces CPU and memory overhead, and the new option is ignored unless precomputed project files are also provided. It is live today in the SDK for qualifying hosts.

65f20efb85fbaa7d2ec42f484fbbf9b39c57f751.text: You can now pick the GLM 5.2 model directly from the regular premium list in the web/cloud interface, but you'll only get to use it once per day. Before, the special CrofAI-powered version of GLM 5.2 was hidden and only available through advanced settings, and it shared the same daily usage limit as other premium models. Your normal premium allowance stays separate from this one-a-day GLM sessions quota, so using your daily GLM turn won't reduce your regular premium turns.

f377278c442149319ba818d05791b4012b9cf3b5.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, DeepSeek V4 Pro is now the featured default model instead of MiniMax M3. The recommended hero card also gains an AI-training warning that explains your conversations may be used to train the model, and on very short terminals the card's layout is adjusted so its full bottom border stays visible. The browser-based surfaces keep their own default, which still points to DeepSeek V4 Pro today, but can now be changed independently of the CLI/Desktop default.

c8e487a6246813b34d1f8a6942bef69352c80bc4.text: Starting today, the planning assistant that designs your project moves from DeepSeek V4 Pro to MiniMax M3, while the build step that actually creates your code environment stays on DeepSeek V4 Pro. If you are in a limited region, your planning still uses the same budget-friendly model you always have. After you send one blank project into planning on the free tier, you are capped at 12 planning conversation turns, after which you can still build what you planned but cannot keep chatting about it. This prevents a single free account from running an unbounded chat session on a premium model.

075723dbdc661304e710e2b305277f3acfef3101.text: As a full-access Freebuff Web/Cloud user, you can now use the CrofAI GLM 5.2 model (glm-5.2 via CrofAI's direct API) from the same shared daily premium pool that covers models like MiniMax M3 and Kimi, instead of being limited to just one session per Pacific day. If you open a fresh browser or haven't picked a default model yet, the app will start you on DeepSeek V4 Pro rather than remembering your last selection of this specific GLM 5.2 route, since that route is now treated as non-rememberable. The model's label in the selection menu changed from '1 session/day' to 'Strong all-rounder', and the old separate one-session-per-day quota constants for this model were removed entirely. The weekly referral GLM route (z-ai/glm-5.2) is unaffected and still has its own dedicated pool. This change

6fbfd71dd51c396171b911b5fc3894984e0a3dd9.text: If you pay for Codebuff's LITE mode, the assistant now uses a newer, faster, and cheaper model (GPT-5.6-Luna) instead of the previous DeepSeek model. You would notice responses may come quicker and cost less per interaction, though the overall experience stays the same. Free users are not affected. The way coding tasks are graded by the automated judge has also been made more reliable: instead of three judges where one could silently fail and skew the result, it now uses two specific judges and averages their scores, clearly warning you if one fails.

d281d6eedd789ca6b8590df20edb4388379408f4.text: When the assistant asks for a screenshot or image-related tool, the response now always includes a brief text acknowledgment right before the actual image appears. This fixes a glitch where some image-only results were sent back without any matching reply to the assistant's request, which could make the conversation stop working. You wouldn't see the extra text, but conversations with image-returning tools now flow smoothly instead of occasionally breaking.

ac163119e1412375e526494c81ec179739f4ced4.text: When you open the assistant picker in your browser or the new Cloud thread page, the model now pre-selected is DeepSeek V4 Pro instead of MiniMax M3; this swap only happens on the browser/cloud side, the desktop and command-line versions still start on MiniMax M3. The de-emphasized-models list (MiniMax M3 and Kimi K2.7) is now read by the Web/Cloud picker so those two options appear smaller and lower in the recommended list without becoming unavailable. If you are a new Web or Cloud user you will land on DeepSeek V4 Pro right now, and any time that model is the hero pick the interface must show its training-data warning before you can proceed, so nothing changes live for you until you see that notice. The access-tier logic (limited users still go to the always-available flash model, and

cb202d14e1327ee923368b2dc099364b372dac68.text: Free users in regions that were previously blocked from the Cloud custom-stack planner can now use it, while everyone else is moved to MiniMax M3 as the model the planner writes code with. If you pick the planner, the model it promises and the model your build actually runs are now locked together, so a mismatch that would have silently failed is instead caught before your session starts. New sign-ups also hit a daily cap of five blank Cloud projects (the kind that spin up a full virtual machine), replacing the prior shared limit that effectively let about ten boot in a row; the counter resets at midnight Pacific time.

9b8e85b8d0d50bfc0c1bffe9caa17eee7798d1bf.text: When the assistant sends a command to run quietly in the background (like installing a package), you'll see it sitting there doing nothing for a while — that pause is now logged as a normal part of how long the command takes, not mistaken for the app freezing. The developers fixed this so their crash-detection system no longer thinks these expected waits are errors. If you ever look at usage stats, these background waits will now be counted separately from real problems. This is live in the latest version.

9b8ffc8ef8c48601dc234a57e45ebc83b498a5f5.text: The cloud-based coding helper now uses a different AI model to plan your tasks. Where it used to rely on MiniMax M3, it now uses DeepSeek V4 Pro as the default for the main experience. A new experimental model called Ling 3.0 Flash has also been added to the list of models available in the high-access "god mode" setting, though it is marked as experimental and its data may be used for training. The version number of the downloadable tool has moved from 0.0.128 to 0.0.129.

801a9d02c935e19c2f9529d1330b0de6eac555c4.text: When the assistant runs a simple command (like checking a file name or listing a folder) and the result is short enough to read on one screen, it no longer sends that output to an AI model to summarize. Instead it hands the raw output straight back to you. This only affects the built-in terminal helper, and only for quick commands whose output is about 2,000 characters or less. You would notice it by the helper returning results instantly for small commands, while longer output (like a full test run or log file) is still summarized as before. If the output was already cut short by the system, the helper still summarizes it.

622a2a2228556af643a2addd266099af434504f5.text: The app now tracks which desktop features people actually open and use, like panels, worktrees, diffs, skills, terminal, or preview, through a single new event called 'feature used'. This lets the product team see in one view what's popular and what's not, without creating a separate tracking entry for every new feature. Because the team serves roughly 1,000-2,000 daily users, any rare feature could be used by so few people that random sampling would record zero usage; the system avoids that by always counting these events and instead controls volume by only recording when you intentionally choose a feature and by remembering which features it already counted during your current session.

1402b75d5bd6d305c9bb326da1e9fb0c60a4b35e.text: The default, higher-performance assistant model across the editing, reviewing, and brainstorming tools has been upgraded to the latest Opus generation. If you use the service today, your requests are now handled by the newer model version with no action required on your part. Behind the scenes, the developers replaced repeated hard-coded model names scattered across many tools with a single shared reference, so future upgrades can be done in one place instead of hunting through dozens of files. This is live now and means the model powering your assistant is consistently the intended one across every feature.

3c92d4e7bd963920744771f9af70a7740f5db53b.text: A long chat with the assistant now gets automatically trimmed before it hits the model's size limit, so conversations that would have been cut off mid-sentence will instead get summarized to keep going. The trimming happens before each new message you send, and it sizes itself to whichever specific model version is about to read the chat at that moment. You don't have to turn it on or ask for it: the system just starts watching the length of your conversation and quietly keeps the older parts short enough that the assistant never loses the thread. If you leave a tab idle for a while and come back, the assistant still remembers what you were talking about rather than re-explaining the whole thing.

8e2ef71f5db6f210951e6086acaa0618bf80e055.text: The small helper programs your assistant uses behind the scenes—such as the one that runs terminal commands, the one that browses web pages, and the ones that read technical documents—have each switched to a newer version of Google's lightweight Gemini model family. If you looked at what these helpers are running today, you'd see they now use the Gemini 3.5 flash-lite model instead of the prior Gemini 3.1 version. The older 3.1 model is still listed alongside the new one so that existing desktop and command-line tools that haven't been upgraded yet can keep making requests without failing, but going forward new requests and updated tools will use the newer model by default.

c9bdd9c7b58e05b498d296cf64fcaaa3db54890d.text: When the assistant runs a tool command during a conversation, it now checks whether that command's result was already added to the chat history before recording it again. This stops the system from breaking the entire conversation with a 'duplicate result' error when something is retried. If you're watching a conversation that uses retry-based tool calls, it will now keep going smoothly instead of freezing up on a repeated command.

0ff93e746badad951717b0a70386bf5b24701517.text: When a chat session gets interrupted, your conversation history can end up with a half-finished action that never got completed. Now the system quietly removes those incomplete actions before sending your history to strict AI providers, preventing the errors that would otherwise break every future message. You wouldn't notice anything visually, but your chat will keep working smoothly instead of hitting avoidable failures. The system also handles unexpected data formats from clients without crashing.

c731787cd02fea9b5d37c9e5e6fb06c0e3897045.text: When you're using the Codebuff command-line tool and it can't reach the servers—say they're down for maintenance or there's a network hiccup—the tool will now wait a little longer before each retry, and each wait gets progressively longer instead of always waiting the same amount of time. This means you won't see a thousand people's tools all hammering the server at once the moment it comes back online, which gives the server breathing room. This behavior applies to everyone using the Codebuff CLI today, and you'd notice it as slightly longer gaps between automatic retry attempts during an outage, rather than the tool repeatedly trying at a fixed, synchronized pace.

04bceb38336bd18978e6c75daa2b1451b3f51c8d.text: Every few seconds your assistant trims its own memory before taking the next step, and it now counts words locally instead of asking a server each time — so steps keep moving without waiting on a network call. The trim job also keeps cached content for 30 minutes (instead of 5) before rewriting summaries, which stops it from re-summarizing after short pauses. Because the trim job skips the usual tracking ledger, it uses short-lived IDs that are never reported back to the parent run, so it doesn't pollute your run history. If you're running the assistant today, you'll notice steps keep flowing sooner after each question rather than hitting a small network pause.

086e7bfc29fc3edd9f62a2eddbdc8821ff71b409.text: When starting an agent run fails, you previously might have seen a vague "Failed to start agent run" message with no details, especially if your error logging tool silently dropped certain error types. The system now also prints the raw HTTP status, status text, and response body (truncated to 2000 characters) directly to your console alongside the existing logs, so you can see what the server actually returned or what went wrong during the request. This change is live today and applies whenever an agent run start request fails or returns unexpected data, making previously opaque failures diagnosable without needing to inspect code or logs manually.

3b621851400cd86740de15406b74d8f020832c01.text: If you keep coming back to Chatbase day after day, your weekly GLM credit bonus now grows the longer your streak gets. After a full week of daily visits you earn one extra GLM session each week, two after two weeks, three after three, and it tops out at four extra sessions per week once your streak hits 28 days. The bonus only applies to full-access users and resets every Monday, and if you miss a day your weekly GLM bonus drops back to zero until you rebuild your streak.

99f8bdf7238772049723aee6d133b9e2af05e10c.text: When Freebuff Chat recommends a developer service (like a database, auth, payments, hosting, or AI API), any "Get your {service} API key" button now points to the exact tracked setup link that was returned in that prior search result, rather than letting the assistant paste a generic or vendor-homepage URL. The assistant chooses one service to recommend and then references that choice by its search ID and service slug; the system substitutes the precise stored URL at click time, and if the reference is invalid, nothing happens instead of falling back to a guessed link. Verified Freebuff Chat users in the web interface are the only ones who notice this today: the change is live now, and it covers every model that routes through the base-chat agent and the shared tool execution path.

ef69165e2f7db1192f722d33574d63f4d4bc8f4a.text: New people signing up for Codebuff no longer get free credits added to their account. This only affects new signups; existing accounts and those with monthly credits are untouched. The change was made today and takes effect immediately, though the system is set up so credits can be turned back on later by updating one setting and restoring a verification step for GitHub accounts.

2d3b8b08b30dd13c6590106ec5eb4720ffd18215.text: If you use the paid HY3 Atlas assistant through Freebuff, your requests now go through a different AI provider called OpenRouter instead of talking directly to Atlas Cloud. The assistant still works the same way from your perspective, but behind the scenes it connects to OpenRouter to process your queries. A old connection method to Atlas Cloud is kept as a backup, so if the new route has issues, the system can fall back to it. This change is already active today for paid-tier users.

aa75163a8f27b8cfc8af9d2ce07ba5f3253fdce0.text: The app now decides whether a model's conversations might be saved for AI training using a single, machine-checked list instead of searching for specific warning words in text. You'll notice this only when picking a model: a model that previously showed a data-collection warning will now show an AI-training warning, and the wording of that warning can change in the future without affecting whether your conversations are actually stored. The new data-use rules go into effect today.

ff555dfc23f4037715103ed7983c5e934eae5555.text: Your streak now shows the same way whether you're using the command-line tool or the desktop app — a count like "2 day streak" next to a row of 7 dots that fill up to a fully-filled row plus a trailing plus sign for longer runs. The shared rules live in one common place and each app pulls from it; the command-line tool only adds its own need to fit the width of your terminal window. If you looked, you'd see the same dots and wording on both screens instead of one differing from the other.
