If you were previously seeing a vague "location unknown" message when blocked, you'll now see exactly which privacy service is being flagged, helping you understand why access was denied and what you might need to change.

eb47be392d867a2a8a0235cb993ff4d2af6d6c09.text: Starting today, people using the free tier can no longer access the assistant if their internet connection is routed through a VPN, proxy, Tor network, or similar privacy-cloaked service. When a free user tries to start a session, the platform now checks their IP address for these privacy signals and blocks them if detected; the check uses an IPinfo service that requires a new secret key to work. If you use a VPN and attempt to use the free version, you will be denied access instead of reaching the assistant.

f7bda6243190a9d7853e0dfc16c0c808ac7271de.text: When you press Enter in the model picker, the CLI now correctly picks the model your keyboard is focused on (instead of falling back to a stale or unavailable selection), and arrow keys wrap around to the same selectable model when all peers are unavailable. This affects anyone using the CLI's Freebuff model selection screen. If you looked, you'd notice the picker reliably resolves to a valid model even in edge cases, and error messages in the waiting room now appear even when a session exists with a 'none' status.

a2ded144546c3a4535002cb8ae78cda4dcce08ae.text: When an advertisement shown in the command-line tool doesn't include a link, the ad banner now displays the ad's title text instead of leaving that spot blank. You'd notice the banner staying populated with the ad's name rather than going empty when no destination URL is provided. Behind the scenes, a helper picks the title as a fallback whenever the URL is missing, so the banner keeps looking consistent.

d77b15357e72be57e8dc063f158ad87368fb7a55.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, it now tells you in plain language whether the free 'buff' model is reachable from your own clock right now — for example, something like 'available until 5pm in your local time' instead of a fixed Eastern/Pacific window. The CLI now looks at the computer's current time and timezone to figure out your local availability window, while servers that can't see your timezone still fall back to the generic Eastern-to-Pacific label. You'd notice this the next time you browse models in the CLI picker; it's the kind of change you'd only see if you were actively picking a model, and it only helps when the live availability data is actually flowing through, not when an API error forces the stale fallback text.

dffc7e4372e2972a6b191c42e9365ef32a176a71.text: If you use the free GLM 5.1 assistant in the CLI and have already started 5 sessions in the past 20 hours, the app will now show a waiting screen that tells you roughly when you can try again — for example "in ~45 min" — instead of silently refusing or polling repeatedly. The limit is enforced server-side: your sixth attempt in that window is turned away with a clear message and a count of how many of your 5 allowed sessions have been used. Older CLI versions that don\'t recognize the new message will simply back off and retry later, since the server signals the pause with a standard rate-limit status code. This only applies to GLM 5.1; other models in the free tier are unaffected.

a452cabacaf1a0241a39bf657c576840943fba9d.text: When you start a free session, the tool now checks whether it can tell where you're connecting from. If it can't identify a trusted country—for example, because your traffic looks like it's coming through a VPN, Tor, a proxy, or an unknown network—the system blocks the session and shows you a message instead of letting you join the queue. That blocked response carries a placeholder country code of UNKNOWN so the interface can display a distinct screen rather than a misleading country name. The previous behavior allowed connections through when location couldn't be determined; that fail-open path has been removed for both the chat gateway and the session handler, replacing the older country lookup with a new check that only permits connections from verified allowlisted countries.

ff675681689666dabad9e8a9172bc40aaa557b99.text: Starting today, the text ads shown while you're waiting for a response or while a model is thinking now all appear in the same clean banner layout used in the main chat, and the small "hide these ads" button that used to live inside the chat window is gone. For people using the free, ad-supported version (the Freebuff experience), ads may now show multiple promoted options at once instead of just one, because the system fetches several from the ad provider at the same time and picks the distinct ones. If you're not on the free tier, nothing about your ad experience changes today.

8e39fa2e032c9956dd80ae84cc8f4d1c3420dca5.text: If you open the free assistant in the CLI between 9am Eastern and 5pm Pacific on a weekday, you can now pick the GLM 5.1 model; outside those hours it stays dimmed out. At the same time, MiniMax M2.7 has been added as a model you can choose at any time, and the older kimi-k2.5 variants have been removed from the list of models shown in the free assistant. When you try to join the queue for a model that isn't available right now, the interface now tells you that plainly instead of erroring out, and you'll be guided back to the default model. The change is live today for anyone using the free tier of the CLI.

8b4f89224820c1cd509317e70450de8042486e3d.text: If you manage your own copy of the tool, the command you run to update your database layout has changed from a quick-fix mode to a proper migration mode. The old method adjusted the database directly without keeping a record, while the new method logs each change so it can be replayed or reversed. To bridge the gap, a one-time setup script tells the system that all previous changes have already been applied, so only future changes will run.

faa7d7a6e9ebd7897d4497103455f3161c7fc3fe.text: When you're using a free trial session in the chatbot, the status bar at the bottom now shows a button that lets you end that session early and return to the waiting room. The old stop button was replaced with a more flexible button that can show different actions depending on the situation, and the message you see when you end the session is now stored in one place so it stays consistent across different parts of the app. If you're on a freebuff session and idle, you'll notice a clearly labeled End session button at the bottom that was not there before. This change is live today for freebuff session users.

f872c7ae18bc99433babb66eaa22ec7f2a0cf695.text: When you log into the assistant from the command-line tool, it now identifies your specific computer by its hardware instead of by a random, throwaway label that changed every time you started the program. This means your login session is recognized on the same machine later, so you won't be asked to log in again unnecessarily, even if you close and reopen the command line. If the hardware lookup fails for any reason (like some shared or virtual machines), it safely falls back to the old random method, so you can still log in normally.

79ce156d76a8b978bdd7425f4b66bff19b6827c6.text: If you wait in the free session line in the CLI, you can now choose which model's queue you join. A new model selector appears in the waiting room, showing how many people are ahead for each model; tapping or pressing a number key (1-9) moves you to the back of that model's queue. You can also type /end-session to leave your current queue and return to the waiting room so you can pick another model. Your chosen model is remembered locally and sent to the server when joining; if the server says the model is locked (a conflict), a confirmation prompt asks you to confirm the switch.

3e4179228dddec236914b4fd5e0c7538ecb2da92.text: When you open the CLI app and land in the waiting room before your first message, you'll now see ads from Carbon (BuySellAds) instead of Gravity — in-chat ads during conversations still show Gravity. Behind the scenes, a new provider switch passes 'carbon' to the ad-fetching logic, and a new adapter normalizes Carbon's response into the same format the app already understands. The database now records which network served each ad, stores any extra tracking pixels Carbon provides, and allows the payout field to be empty so it doesn't break when Carbon doesn't supply one. This change is live today for anyone who opens the CLI waiting room. Regular in-chat subscribers are unaffected — their ads come from Gravity just as before.

f2386263397b6d6e6d4473c00622d45d3d027ee2.text: When an assistant is in the middle of working through a multi-step task and suddenly runs into an error, your conversation history used to get lost — meaning any progress made before the error would vanish. Now, that in-progress work is preserved so you don't lose what the assistant was already thinking or doing. If you were watching a session and saw it crash partway through, you'd now see the messages leading up to the error instead of a blank slate.

ff385b6c6953eb8d617d7f53e1ce76e4dad57f85.text: The moderation team gained three new internal tools to manage bot accounts: a script to scan for and ban suspected FreeBuff bots (dry-run by default), one to investigate a user's activity, and another to unban users. These scripts interact directly with the user database to toggle bans, look up accounts by email, and report details like message counts and costs. The bot-detection guide is now excluded from version control. Effective immediately, these tools let staff block or restore access without touching application code.

ec7051080c95a60952a7b243e4c7a89a793c63aa.text: The AI coding assistant inside this project can now automatically work without stopping to ask for your permission before each step. A new settings file was added that tells the assistant to run in a more independent mode by default. If you watched the assistant at work, you'd see it move through tasks without pausing to confirm every action, instead of needing you to approve each one. This only affects how the assistant behaves locally and doesn't change anything else about the project.

f7461e3885e81bf95a5058142b2754174f13eb43.text: If you type /refer-friends, /referral, or /redeem in the command-line tool, nothing happens anymore — the commands and the referral-code entry flow have been taken out entirely. You can still log in and use the assistant normally, but the feature that let someone paste a friend's referral code to claim credit is gone. The screen messages and input buttons that guided you through redeeming a code are also gone. No steps to switch it back on exist; the referral system simply no longer responds.

a92b5cf6c09072e0c1e72ed56d9f41922ff0d610.text: If the system that charges you for using the assistant hiccups, your message will still get saved and you won't lose access to use the assistant. Previously, a billing failure could block your message from being recorded and potentially cut off your usage, but now billing is separated from message insertion and retries won't double-charge you. You'd notice this as continued service availability even when billing issues occur, with zero-impact retries preserving your session.

ff89b57040335b83085dbdb299b6133ff2cfd116.text: Starting today, if you open the assistant in free mode and another instance of yours is already active, you'll see a clear message telling you that your session was rotated, instead of sitting in a loading queue forever. When you close or finish a free session, a banner now appears at the bottom of the chat letting you press Enter to join the queue again, but only if the previous run has fully stopped streaming its results. The whole flow is gated by a new auth check that decides whether to show you the waiting room, the live chat, or the superseded-session screen, and it stops polling the server once your session ID has been taken over. This live now for free-mode users who run more than one terminal session on the same account.

7f5b41b7626ba943763be093bc64e920dd6a6956.text: When the CLI tool downloads a new release version and you're connected through a corporate or network proxy server, the download process no longer makes an extra DNS lookup that could fail or leak the internal target hostname. Instead of resolving the download server's address locally after connecting through the proxy, the tool now reuses the already-established secure connection to the proxy directly for fetching the release package. This change affects anyone whose environment sets HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, or NO_PROXY variables, and if you looked at network traffic during an update you'd see one fewer DNS query hitting your local resolver after the proxy handshake. It's live today in the release tooling used by both the stable and staging update channels.

ab21fbbdc4bac114401e4786199d4a3911af6d45.text: When you use the free sessions, your request used to go through a simple up-or-down check that only asked whether the upstream service was reachable, so admission could start even when the upstream was reachable but already overloaded and making everyone wait. Now, before your session is admitted, the system asks a more nuanced question that returns not just "can I talk to it" but "how busy is it," and it halts new admissions the moment upstream latency crosses the 1-second prefill-queue threshold or KV-block memory pressure hits 90%, with memory pressure evaluated before queue latency because it is a leading indicator of load that responds instantly versus the slower window statistic. If you looked at the system today, you would see free-session admission drip one user per tick as before,

5787c43ba551d59afefddbec4a758a87cfc80cc4.text: The assistant renamed the "Free" option in Codebuff CLI to "Lite", which now means a paid tier that charges credits, while the separate Freebuff product keeps its own free version of Lite that always shows ads and never grants credits. If you open the chat in Codebuff, you'll see a new "Build LITE" button instead of "Build Free", and the ad banner logic no longer assumes a free mode means ads are forced on; it relies on your saved settings for the new paid Lite mode. Codebuff's LITE now runs a different model variant called base2-lite that charges normally, whereas Freebuff still maps LITE down to the old free tier with rate limits and zero credits.

8a7cf082bdd478b85aa746ebe42879733bb3ecdf.text: A new behind-the-scenes watchdog is now running: it wakes up every minute, checks on the health of several AI model services, and quietly records whether each one is working normally, slowing down, or having errors. The engineering team can look up that health report whenever they want, and there's also a quick command they can run to double-check things on the spot. One thing that was moved around is now stored in a safer spot, which stops certain setup steps from crashing when the system starts up.

f231508eb3ebf55810bc726751001b8e306fc6f6.text: Your team added an internal test tool that checks how long the AI provider keeps your saved prompt in fast memory before it gets thrown away. It sends one prompt, waits different amounts of time (like 30 seconds, 5 minutes, up to about 35 minutes), then sends the same prompt again to see if the provider remembers it and gives a discount. This only runs on your internal machines and doesn't change anything you see right now, but it will help figure out how long you can pause between questions before you have to wait for the full prompt to load again.

512ebc980642295869b91eb7e8415afe83cb451c.text: The system that tracks how much you've been charged for using Claude through OpenRouter stopped accidentally charging you twice for the same thing. OpenRouter was telling the system the same cost in two separate fields, and the system added them together, effectively doubling your bill on every Anthropic request. Now it picks the higher of the two reported numbers instead, which correctly reflects what you were actually charged, and it handles the case where one of the fields is missing entirely. This fix is live in production.

13d5f6cb9e9e937400c652728747e50e1f01f2e8.text: When you run the assistant through the developer toolkit, it can now correctly pick which tools to use from a pre-approved list. Previously, a small coding mistake caused some valid tools to be silently ignored, so you might have noticed certain actions not working even though they were supposed to be available. This is live today, so tools in the approved list now work as expected.

fa1d71d7675faadfb04596afc792de92d05fc1ab.text: Free-tier users (those who have never purchased credits or a subscription) can now be blocked from using more credits than they actually have, preventing people from farming free credits and spending far more than intended. When a free-tier user tries to make a charge that would drop their balance below zero, the system will now stop the charge instead of letting it go through. Paid users with subscriptions or purchases are unaffected: they can still build up a negative balance, but only new credit grants will clear that debt, not regular usage. This is live today as a hard gate in the billing system.

8470d9d30ed2c3560e382cce65c03bc155141423.text: The team added a new internal tool that lets them dig through their billing records to check whether OpenRouter is accidentally charging people twice for the same request. When you send a message through OpenRouter, the cost gets recorded twice in the system; once as a general charge and once as an 'upstream' charge, so the tool looks at recent messages to see if that's happening for regular (non-BYOK) requests. If you ran this tool today, you'd see a table of messages with columns showing cost, upstream charge, and how they should compare. The fix to stop double-charging is recorded in a separate change in this snapshot, but this investigation script is now in place to help verify whether it's working.

88dfbcfa7ef46bd9d4aeb95446ac0e3ec417e959.text: If you use Claude's long conversations, the assistant used to start forgetting earlier parts of your chat sooner than it should have—around 140,000 characters instead of the full 200,000 it promises. A new automated check now confirms that trimming only kicks in once you truly hit the limit, so your chat stays complete until then. This is already live and protects everyone who relies on long conversations today.

db4d3b66234703d944bc7a867be44b83b0236d59.text: If you use the free version of this coding assistant today, it can now call in a new helper agent powered by Google's Gemini model to tackle hard problems. That helper is added to the list of assistants the free version is allowed to use, and the main assistant is told to spawn it whenever you hit a complex task or ask it to think through something. The older reasoning helper stays available but no longer carries special chat-subscription settings. In short: free users get access to a new, smart second opinion that the assistant is encouraged to use often.

dd383810b20d07df3a1cd71f9be94d9fb173512a.text: When you chat with the assistant on the free plan, it now calls on a new reasoning helper that thinks by reading the specific files you point it at instead of sifting through the whole chat history. That makes each back-and-forth cheaper for the company to run, so the free tier keeps working for more people, but only if you give the helper the right files up front—if you don't, it won't have the context it needs to help. The change went live with today's release, and you'd notice it right away by the updated guidance the assistant follows when deciding what to think through for your request.

894a5b618d53a24c2af1bb8db82fb17bb3494dbd.text: When an AI agent runs out of space to remember the whole conversation, it creates a shortened summary. Previously, that summary listed tool actions with a 'Tools: ' label, which the AI sometimes mistook as a format to copy in its actual responses. Now the summary drops that label and includes a clear instruction telling the AI those condensed markers are just a log of what happened, not something to repeat. This stops the AI from writing out fake tool calls as plain text instead of using the correct tools.

1579802a544a49757295094a45979ea4e0f16c3a.text: When you press Esc to stop an in-progress assistant message, the program now frees up the queue immediately so you can send your next message right away instead of waiting or getting stuck. Previously, the program held onto a lock until the full background task finished, which could block new messages. The fix moves the cleanup into the moment you cancel, and skips redundant resets afterward so a newer message run isn't disturbed.

868fb291a133d92404b1bc086e483a7823cd053a.text: The project removed a large set of files (about 9,300 lines across 57 files) that supported an experimental workflow for automatically improving documentation by running coding assistants against past commits and analyzing the results. That workflow, along with its guides and specs, is no longer part of the repository. Anyone reading the internal docs will no longer see references to it, but this does not change how the coding assistant itself behaves day to day.

9fcd27ae9517496836efbc7244eb02f0c768bc07.text: When the assistant's tools run into a problem, it shows you the original input that caused the error, but it now formats and truncates that input in a single, consistent way. Previously, each tool that displayed error details (like tool execution, output validation, and agent spawning) had its own slightly different logic for converting the input to text and cutting it off, which could lead to inconsistent or messy error messages. The change pulls that repeated code into one shared helper, so every error message now shows the original values cleanly, adds type information for simple values like numbers or true/false, and caps the length consistently at 500 characters before truncating. You'll notice cleaner, more predictable error messages with the original input when something goes wrong

0df74ef688d9809f4d6e1897f386c3e2e38861dd.text: If you install and run this tool today, your terminal will print a big ASCII art logo for a fake product called Expensivebuff, celebrate April Fools with a toast, and then point you to the real tools Codebuff and Freebuff instead. The developers built it as a joke: it is literally the same code as Codebuff, just rebranded with a pricier name for a day. Nothing functional is added or changed; opening it only shows the prank landing page and the links to the genuine software. The joke package is live now as a one-time April Fools novelty.

0f588b09f03c5086960f61d84df918a3e6303686.text: The program's helper guides that taught you how to understand confusing task instructions have been removed. If you were using the command-line tools and ran into a guide titled 'Interpreting Task Prompts (Especially Eval-Generated Ones)', you won't find it anymore. Two testing files that were no longer being used to check the program's behavior have also been deleted, which means some of the checks that make sure the command-line tools work correctly have been cleaned up.

57f569e59749eb959251d5293e64f60294a2c64b.text: Every hour, the system now automatically runs a quiet background check over free CodeBuff sessions and emails the team a report of accounts that look suspicious, like ones with too many shared devices or rapid-fire messages; no one gets banned automatically, the report is just for a human to review. If you're a free user whose activity pattern trips the heuristic, you won't be blocked right away, but your name could surface in that hourly email. The sweep only counts the main orchestrator agent for each session, so extra helper bots it spawns won't accidentally make you look more active than you really are.

c3a379ac7a9ae375387a052e2cb5a2ed48b5cea6.text: If you try to start a free-mode session (the waiting room before you get access to the service) from a country that isn't on the approved list, the system now immediately tells you 'Free mode isn\'t available in your region' and shows your detected country code, instead of letting you queue up and then rejecting you later. This is enforced at the session gate so the CLI, web, and shared types all see the same 'country_blocked' status and stop retrying; older CLI versions fall back to erroring out and backing off on their retry timer, while newer versions read the 403 response body to display the blocked message directly.

c8bfaa1f66a85810bce9989c8fa8719ca8481b80.text: When the assistant runs its automated test comparisons inside a project, it now makes a shortcut so it can instantly read the shared instructions file without any setup. The assistant also keeps a running tally of which instruction files it has looked at during each test pass, printing that tally at the end, making it easier to confirm it actually reviewed the right guidance while the tests run.

3886a0c449d74a23d08ff1e60013f689c18f53ef.text: The project removed several outdated planning and demonstration documents that were no longer relevant, and moved an authentication guide to a more standard location within the documentation folder. This cleanup only affects the supporting written materials in the repository, not the software itself. If you browsed the project's documentation, you would find the authentication guide in the main docs area and notice the old planning and demo files are gone.

5f271d644e4e896d600fdff14f81b27fe5b84d02.text: evalbuff can now test an AI coding assistant in a new way: instead of comparing whole code snapshots, it picks a specific feature, deletes just that feature, and asks an AI to rebuild it from a plain-language description, then judges the result against the original. This affects anyone running or improving evalbuff's evaluation harness, who will see carve-based eval tasks and a configurable assistant model option. The feature-level delete-and-rebuild loop and model selection are live today, backed by two new scripts and one adjusted runner.

5edd8088d621ddf38c76a323de30c93e37f3fc08.text: You may have noticed that when an AI assistant hands back a list of choices or files to read, it used to break if a single item was returned instead of a proper list. That happened because some of the assistants behind the scenes occasionally sent back a single object where the system expected a whole list. Now, the system has been updated to automatically wrap those lone items into a list on your behalf, so the assistant correctly processes them instead of failing. This affects tools like ask-user, read-files, propose-str-replace, read-subtree, spawn-agents, str-replace, suggest-followups, and write-todos, all of which now handle single-item responses gracefully. This fix is live today and required no action on your part.

72144496dd2dac4bf9da952554b34e69a93783c4.text: You now have a new way to see ads when you're using the free version of the tool. Instead of a single banner ad appearing above your input area, you'll sometimes see a set of four ads displayed as selectable cards that automatically adjust their layout to fit your terminal width. When this new format is shown, you pick which ad you want to learn more about, and each time an ad is displayed to you, that choice is counted for analytics. This choice format runs on a 50% split: half of the free users will see the new card-based layout, while the other half continue seeing the single banner as before. Both the old banner and the new card layout now hide the credit rewards counter that used to show how many credits you earned from viewing ads, so ads will only say they help support the free

dd82cab4cfa6b71e670946fd7a226056e84737ac.text: If you cancel a reply while the assistant is still typing in the CLI, your message history stays intact instead of getting lost. Previously, the system released its lock too early during cancellation, letting new messages in before the previous state was saved. Now the lock stays held until the cancelled response fully completes, so the assistant can't accidentally start a new reply with stale context. This is live today for anyone using the CLI streaming feature.

2007a95dcb103c5d503abbef858a5c69af72e12c.text: Evalbuff, the system that watches a coding assistant struggle with real tasks and then writes documentation to help it do better next time, has been rebuilt to work smarter. It now walks through your project's git history oldest-first, and instead of trying one task at a time, it can run several attempts in parallel against each commit, saving its progress so it can pick up where it left off if interrupted. It also squeezes down the verbose logs those attempts produce before analyzing them, so the doc-writing step uses less computing power. On top of that, when an attempt times out, the system now properly cleans up the whole tree of helper processes it spawned, preventing leftover zombie tasks. Everything described here is active as of March 27, 2026.

3f5910ed11a32b551ef094318694f0d7010f09da.text: When the CLI is actively processing or waiting, a new stop button now appears in the status bar, letting you interrupt the current stream. Previously, there was no visible way to stop an in-progress response from the interface itself.

e1b8a1bf045f51ea8c38f67a3bb2bf5006150444.text: An automated helper that checks how well code fixes work has been sped up and made fairer. It now talks to the AI model directly instead of launching a separate program each time, which removes wasted overhead. When summarizing results from multiple reviewers, it now averages the scores instead of picking the middle one, since different AI models have a habit of rating things consistently higher or lower than others. It also ignores boring commits like version bumps and dependency updates, so it won't waste time running checks on changes that don't need human-like review.

97e7cadd60d76206b8344f53b07d5f30a24e3950.text: When you're using the CLI tool on a computer without a graphical desktop environment (like a remote server or Docker container), clicking links to websites (buy credits, OAuth logins, ads) could crash the whole program. Now those link-opening actions quietly skip the browser attempt instead of crashing the session.

a8119a983e8b19a7e803234bb762b0dc4b01c48b.text: The project's main instruction manual has been reorganized: the single large file was split into a quick-start guide at the top of the folder and several shorter, focused guides inside a new 'docs' folder, each covering one topic (core conventions, dev setup, tools, environment, testing). If you open the repository you will now see several smaller documents instead of one thick one, so people building or extending the assistant can find what they need faster without scrolling through unrelated material.

3f47c49de6a9e18c2c045ef8119115eceb591952.text: When you install Codebuff on a corporate network that uses a proxy server to access the internet, the tool previously couldn't download its own updates or check for new versions, causing timeouts. Now Codebuff automatically detects and uses your system's standard proxy settings, so it can download files and check for updates through the proxy without any extra configuration. If you're behind a corporate firewall and set the HTTPS_PROXY environment variable, Codebuff will just work; otherwise, you'd see timeout errors when it tries to reach GitHub or npm. This is already available in the latest version.

49dbb241650a6c468387d87c21dd4677824a39c5.text: The project has added a new system that will automatically study how well the coding assistant reads and follows the project's written guidance, then quietly rewrite those instructions overnight to fix whatever the assistant gets wrong so it improves on its own. At the same time, the old version of that system has been moved into an archive folder, and a short guide has been added explaining how to correctly structure step-by-step automation without triggering type errors. If you looked, you'd see a fresh folder where the improvement loop lives and a new how-to document, though no improvement runs have actually been executed yet.

fb1bbbe130c7397b115ad5517e1765f12d6f348b.text: When you sign up for Freebuff through a referral link, the site now remembers who referred you. If you visit the get-started page with a referrer, it saves that name and passes it along to the next screen, where it tells PostHog which referrer brought you in. PostHog then records the referral as an event and sets a property called `freebuff_referrer` on your user profile. The tracking runs on the web app and is live today.

94809a3c60388d1c7f5a95708bb118a7967338d8.text: Visitors to the new Get Started page on Freebuff's website are automatically shown the correct installation command for their operating system and can see icons for popular code editors like VS Code, Cursor, IntelliJ, and Terminal. The page is now live and publicly accessible; no login or extra setup is required to view or use it. The editor icons are displayed as image files alongside the installation instructions, making it easier for newcomers to recognize which tools are supported.

54f4585e20a1b0c4ece8a8d9197d9697f9df7c36.text: The internal guide for contributors was cleaned up: extra files were removed and outdated sections were deleted, while the project's stated purpose was rewritten to focus on building one flexible learning agent that includes two tools (the free agent and the eval helper). A leftover reference to an unrelated side project was also removed. This is live in the repository today. If you browse the project on GitHub, you'll see a shorter, simpler guide and one fewer extra entry in the code.

4c95226fb382cfcb26fd7b5d09c57377cbfca2d6.text: On some Linux computers, pressing Enter didn't submit your message because their terminal sent a slightly different signal. Now, if the app hasn't seen the normal Enter signal, it treats this alternate signal as Enter instead. This means you can reliably send messages while typing in the terminal, even on those unusual setups. It's already live today.

cdf440c5e1dc88edc40ee6b4f5de4773b3262b66.text: The team added a new behind-the-scenes script that scans the database for people using only the Freebuff model, ignoring anyone who has also used base2 or base2-max. It produces a sorted list showing email, message count, credits used, cost, and last activity for each free-only user, and separately flags anyone with 50 or more messages for closer review. This is internal tooling used today by whoever runs the script, not something visible to users.

1ba9f20469e72bd2b6940227d8811577721861dd.text: When you open the Freebuff website's get-started or home pages, the site now records which buttons you click and which sections you open, sending that information to an analytics service called PostHog. This only works if a specific API key is set up by the site operators, and the data is sent through a proxy so it looks like it comes from the Freebuff site itself rather than a third party. You won't see any visible changes on the page, but your interactions are now being tracked for the team to review.

6bca8a1e31d8ac42f4355e0a255970e4d3e6902d.text: The system now tracks a new measurement for each message: how quickly the assistant starts replying after you send your message (the very first chunk of text), recorded alongside the existing total response time. If you looked at your message history or billing records, you would see an extra timing field attached to each entry, and the billing calculation now includes that same speed metric when counting credits. The change is in place across the database and the internal tools that record messages, so it takes effect immediately for all users.

e205b670db0541ddfbc8996ae2f525fafa58cb1a.text: If you use the service for free, each of your requests is now tracked against several time windows: no more than 15 per minute, 200 per half hour, 1,000 per 5 hours, and 10,000 per week. When you hit one of those limits, the service replies with a 'try again later' message that includes how long you must wait, and the count resets once that waiting period ends. Only free-tier users are affected; paying users and other plans are unchanged. This goes into effect immediately, since the limit is checked on every chat completion request you make.

ea8a3f85557694e0dfe2c37d53bd4840b2ad67a3.text: When an AI runs a long conversation that would otherwise exceed its memory limits, it now keeps more of your recent messages intact instead of chopping them off. The system first sets aside room for your side of the conversation (up to 50,000 tokens) and a smaller pool for its own replies and tool usage (up to 20,000 tokens), then trims older content by summarizing from the latest message backward so the most recent exchange stays complete. You would notice fewer cases where a response suddenly drops out mid-conversation or loses the immediate context it was responding to.

304ebcc5c6ae9afe71d7da416c79dc7ae355c4c9.text: You can now check how often responses to you from the minimax and minimax-m2.5 models are being pulled from a fast cache instead of being generated fresh, with reports broken out by each individual customer using the service. At the same time, the numbers that measure how efficiently these cached responses are being used were quietly being calculated incorrectly—the math was accidentally counting the cached text twice, which made the system look either more or less efficient than it really was. The fix adjusts those figures so they reflect only the new text actually typed out, giving a truer picture of how much time and computing power the caching is really saving. Together, these updates give the team clearer insight into how the cache is performing for both the service as a whole and for

c0d0ea04cec97c6db2e1df022ed57efaa22ce245.text: The team added a behind-the-scenes tool that quietly scans how much the assistant is being used each day. It quietly watches usage numbers like how many times people ask the assistant to do something, how many of those questions get answered using saved shortcuts instead of starting from scratch, and how busy the service gets at its busiest hour. Only the team running the service can use it today. You wouldn't see it change anything you do, but it helps them decide if they need to add more computers to keep everything fast.

889181a5804829704934025f56da75be65588cf0.text: When you paste a file path into the CLI, it now shows the file as an attachment (with a little icon) and waits for it to finish processing before you can send your message; long file names get shortened so they fit in the preview. This works for both individual files and folders, and while they’re loading, the send button stays locked and tells you it’s working on it.

cb8a36a7e4df9697f164823df2c5f9527e440dc8.text: The system now includes a new assistant that can copy any public GitHub project into a temporary folder on your computer and then answer your questions about how that project is organized or what its documentation says, all without changing the original project. You give it a GitHub link and a question, it brings the project to you for reading, and tells you which specific files hold the answers so you can clean up afterward. The assistant is limited to reading files and searching through them, and it cannot write to or modify the original project files.

e29a8bbf9b72ab3941c2fa40ce5cf537ef629c5f.text: The release system now lets you publish the app from any specific saved version of the code instead of always grabbing the newest one. When someone starts a release, they can optionally point to a particular code version, and if they do, that's the one that gets built and published; otherwise it behaves exactly as before. This affects anyone who triggers releases through the workflow. It's live today and ready to use.

a5dffe7095c4de101fb244995422d56488efc270.text: The assistant now routes API requests through dedicated deployment endpoints instead of a shared global address, which is turned on for internal testing. A new benchmarking tool lets the team run the same 10-turn conversation side by side across three providers to directly compare their costs and speeds. Nothing on the screen changes today, but the system is measuring which provider offers the best value for cached conversations.

3fa2a41c386abbc5a4cbf1b45076ac70cb68450d.text: The assistant's testing toolkit now includes a check specifically for how it handles knowledge files. If someone runs the full set of automated end-to-end tests, a new scenario will launch the assistant to confirm it can load and use a knowledge file correctly. This fills a gap in the existing test coverage alongside the tests already in place for agent startup, ads, code editing, and terminal commands.

6a25ed71f39086bc5a602ccda95836735a758390.text: A new internal test was added that measures how well a specific AI model caches large shared instructions across a 10-question conversation. Engineers can now run this test to see how much of the repeated prompt gets reused (and how much they save) when using the minimax model via the CanopyWave provider. One test script was also updated to read its secret API key from a slightly differently named environment variable, so anyone running that script needs to make sure that variable is set with the new name. Both changes are internal tooling only and are not visible to end users.

f689232cfc268ab21eaac235988c85cf986a40f6.text: When you (or the assistant) ask the system to run a terminal command through an agent, it now goes to a single agent called "basher" instead of picking between "commander" on paid plans and "commander-lite" on free plans. The change renames the agent, deletes the free-tier copy entirely, and updates all the help text and internal references so the two old names are gone everywhere you'd look or be told to use. Behind the scenes, "basher" is built from the same lightweight code as the old "commander-lite" and runs commands the same way, so the behavior you get is unchanged - the only visible difference is the new name in menus, instructions, and error messages. The developers note this is live in the current build and that "basher" is the real agent name you must reference (not a tool) when

02ec8206f65656145e2c6e7a4d201323f0a16246.text: An AI assistant can now drive a web browser for you: it loads pages, clicks buttons, fills in forms, and reads what went wrong, all without you typing. You just describe the task (for example, checking that a login form works on a website) and the assistant reports back what it saw, including any errors the browser logged. This works today if you have Chrome installed on your computer. The browser-automation feature is now available as one of the built-in assistants you can ask to test websites and web apps.

499d7efcab4252154770c95067c5a1cb32368b56.text: The Codebuff team added three new guidebooks to help anyone working on the software understand how the different parts fit together. One guide explains the overall structure of the project and how the pieces (CLI, SDK, agent engine, server) depend on each other. Another details how the server reports errors and how those errors get translated into friendly messages you see in the terminal. The third traces how your prompt travels from your terminal through the SDK and agent runtime to the server and back. These are reference documents only; they do not change what the software does today, but make it easier for developers to navigate the codebase.

734d709579253b9ff76e261804262abe28ded7ac.text: Every time a developer changes the code for the Freebuff application, an automated system now runs a full set of tests that simulate real usage - it actually starts up the program, types in commands, edits code, and checks that everything works as expected. This happens automatically for every proposed change before it gets merged, and it even uses an AI helper to verify more complex behaviors. You wouldn't notice this directly unless you're submitting code changes, but it means bugs are caught before they reach you.

189be16225cfa3196773907e41fad7be46f049e4.text: When you ask for a GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3, GPT-5.4, GPT-4o, or GPT-4o-mini model, your request now goes straight to OpenAI instead of being sent through an intermediary service called OpenRouter. You may notice that responses from these models can take longer to start, especially for the GPT-5.x versions, because the system now waits up to 10 minutes for the first response before timing out. If you use the free version in a country where it's not available, the error message you see is now simply: "Free mode is not available in your country." These changes are live today for anyone using the chat completions API endpoint.

15d4c1857812f92171a6bd18590d29ac326492d8.text: You can now type a new "plan" command that asks the assistant to think through how to tackle whatever you're working on, like designing a new feature or solving a tricky problem. The setup looks cleaner: when the assistant offers to review your code, you can pick predefined options or type your own instructions, and the little status labels that show which mode you're in now appear right in the input box. One catch: the new /plan command only works if you've connected a ChatGPT account while in Freebuff mode, so if you haven't authorized ChatGPT yet, that command won't be available until you do.

c9768351b870eb8065212af10a5b889b72b2538a.text: The team added a new script that tests how much a certain AI service discounts the cost of conversation history when it repeats itself. The script simulates a multi-turn chat with a large initial prompt and tracks how the service bills for cached versus fresh tokens across turns. It only affects developers running internal cost tests, so regular users will notice nothing at all.

3ee603e4c5d23af302e6505d2ead236164edf1de.text: The CLI's build process now works correctly again after a behind-the-scenes file was added to help TypeScript find bundled agent definitions when they haven't been generated yet. This affects anyone running the CLI from source, who would have previously encountered a broken build because the auto-generated agent file is created at build time and not stored in version control. The new file acts as a placeholder so TypeScript doesn't fail when looking for the real, generated file that appears later during installation.

789820e7ef5e012252ad895bb9b25c3ad481ddfc.text: The website's top menu bar, which used to sit permanently at the top of every page, has been removed. Instead, on the home page the navigation now appears as a floating overlay that fades in above the content. The menu items themselves changed slightly too: the order was rearranged so 'Simple' is listed before 'Fast', and the speed claim was softened from '3× the speed' to 'Up to 3× the speed'. You'd notice this if you visited the homepage — the navigation looks different and moves in as the page loads.

4a4200f89eab492b59b535f1bb9ed0c8305da26e.text: When you ask for the minimax/minimax-m2.5 model during business hours (10am to 8pm Eastern Time), the system now tries a custom deployment first, and if that deployment is busy scaling up and returns an error, it automatically falls back to the standard version. Outside those hours, or if the custom deployment fails with that specific scaling error, it uses the standard API directly. You might notice slightly different response behavior during peak hours if the custom deployment is unavailable, but the fallback keeps things working.

b02ac2e5d465624aba2bd5134f9aed1dc0684002.text: If you opt in by enabling a special setting (it is off by default), you can now sign into ChatGPT directly from the command-line tool instead of going through the usual middleman service. When turned on, your subscription requests stream straight to OpenAI using a standard secure login flow, and your credentials are saved locally so you don't have to log in again. If you prefer the existing setup or your account isn't eligible for direct streaming, nothing changes—requests still route the old way unless you explicitly connect.

d86a41e78780d812c253791fc73ed3acf2de0e0f.text: When you connect your ChatGPT account to the tool, it now opens a special local web page on your computer that automatically receives your login confirmation, so you no longer have to manually copy and paste a code. After you approve the connection in your browser, the tool exchanges that approval for an access token behind the scenes and signs you in directly. If the token can't be refreshed later, it stops trying instead of deleting your saved credentials, so you won't be logged out unexpectedly. The connection works by routing your requests through ChatGPT's backend, which translates the messages into the format ChatGPT expects.

47abc4663bdbcf07a7201b136720f8760a1852f7.text: The assistant now sends free-tier user requests to a different backend service called SiliconFlow for the MiniMax M2.5 model. If you use the free tier, your conversations route through SiliconFlow instead of the previous provider, OpenRouter. The developers turned off routing through two other services (CanopyWave and Fireworks) for now, and added a special test to check how well SiliconFlow caches repeated conversation history to save costs. You would notice this as the underlying provider change if you were watching network traffic; there is no visible change in the chat experience itself.

a10cd1daaff1e69d6443e01077f1ba771f8afb1b.text: The minimax model that powers deep-thinking responses for free users now connects to Baseten for inference instead of Fireworks. When you make a request, the system detects the model is routed to Baseten and forwards the call there. A new optional key is accepted in environment configuration, but only the minimax model is mapped to Baseten today; other models continue through their existing providers. This is live today for the minimax route.

e5ff7dce443241fe8c79119d00399bca1d6b49f2.text: If you use the chat completions API with a minimax model, your requests are now sent to CanopyWave instead of Baseten as the backend service. Behind the scenes, the system checks a different API key (CANOPYWAVE_API_KEY instead of BASETEN_API_KEY) and uses new internal code to route and handle streaming responses. The developers also added scripts to test this new connection end-to-end and a safeguard that ensures usage is only counted once even if the provider sends billing data on every streamed chunk. This is live today behind the chat completions endpoint.

01ef8856c8985577e3f3562a3be1a0e138ea999d.text: Today, the assistant's underlying interface toolkit was upgraded to a newer major version of its base building blocks across both the command-line tool and the web dashboard. This update touched how screen readers and keyboard navigation interact with some interactive elements, so the developers added extra safety checks to keep those parts working smoothly. The changes are live now, so you don't need to do anything to receive the improvements.

c68871d3a1a0d94c2af8b33a6e17542f2344a22b.text: If you visit a page that doesn't exist on the site, you'll now see a friendly '404 Page not found' message with a button to go home instead of a blank or broken screen. If something goes wrong behind the scenes, you'll see a '500 Something went wrong' message with a 'Try again' button instead of a confusing error. The site also upgraded its core building blocks to the latest version, which keeps everything running smoothly, and fixed a minor setup issue that could have caused display problems with dark mode.

bcc43e4e215493850e86dbffabf5be10c58766df.text: The base2 toolkit now ships with an automated helper that can drive a tmux terminal session from start to finish, including spinning up the session, typing commands, watching the output, and writing a brief report card on what happened. It only runs for developers who explicitly opt into the default set of base2 sub-agents, so most people won't see it until one of those scripts decides to use it. Behind the scenes, a new definition file tells the helper what to look for and how to record its findings, and a short note in the setup code tells that orchestrator to offer this helper whenever it lists the standard base2 tools.

53fc285969ad9e204bfa96d4f93e33e246aaedce.text: A new marketing and login website for Freebuff has been launched. If you visit freebuff.com today, you'll see a simple landing page where you can sign in, and signing in there also signs you in to Codebuff since both services share the same account system. The site also supports logging in from the Freebuff command-line tool, letting you complete CLI login through your web browser.

5e4f6082c14a4145927c879088df38f432796901.text: When you run the Freebuff release command with a version type (like patch, minor, or major), a helper script checks that you have the right GitHub credentials set up, then remotely starts the official build-and-publish workflow on GitHub, which turns your code into a released package on the npm software registry. The release command lives inside the Freebuff program folder, and the main project now includes that folder in its setup so you can run it from the top-level command. This only becomes live today after someone starts the GitHub workflow, which needs a special access token named CODEBUFF_GITHUB_TOKEN to succeed.

c08733b82d4ff63f1214abe238a5535d62c6da00.text: When you open the Freebuff website or save it to your phone home screen, you'll now see the new logo icon and branded favicon files instead of the old browser tab icon. The site's headline and tagline text have been shortened, and the marketing copy now emphasizes 'No subscription. No API key' and '5x faster than Claude Code'. The navbar and footer now display the logo image with a serif font, replacing the previous text-based 'Free' + 'buff' styling.

7f1e8004d8c8c86843581b245eecd821aaad634f.text: If you installed this version of the tool today, nothing would work yet — running it would just print a placeholder message saying it's coming soon. The team replaced all the real functionality (downloading files, tracking usage, cleaning up old versions) with a bare-bones stub, removing nearly 500 lines of code and downgrading it to a pre-release version. This appears to be an early placeholder so the package can be claimed on the package registry, but it's not ready for actual use.

208a1782033a7b51bfb9aa784ca1fc1eea778c5e.text: New planning and setup documents have been added for a project called Evalbuff, which helps AI coding tools understand and review code changes more intelligently. These documents lay out the first version of commands like 'init' to set up the tool in a project, 'context' to find relevant code and notes before starting work, and 'review' to get feedback on changes after they are made. The planning notes also describe future commands for automatically testing code and learning from past reviews. This is a behind-the-scenes addition that sets up the structure and goals for the tool, but the actual working program is not yet built or available.

98ffa6c38ece5e15ad14bfa2d018fcfdc9a9b014.text: A new free version of the Codebuff terminal coding assistant can now be installed and run without any subscription or payment required. Anyone can install it using a standard app-install command, and once running it works exactly like the paid version but with all subscription, credits, and upgrade prompts removed automatically during the build. Starting today, releases of this free version are published automatically whenever a maintainer triggers the release process, with no manual steps left for users to run. You would see it as a separate program you install, with the same core commands and interface, but no options or messages that ask for money.

2651c0b945cdb2bea86e2ebe937914aafe81fde3.text: When you ask the assistant to use the minimax-m2.5 model, it now talks to Fireworks directly instead of going through OpenRouter as a middleman. You won't see any difference in how the model responds, but the request now takes a different path behind the scenes. This only affects that single model; every other model still uses the existing routing. The change is live today — anyone who already had access to minimax-m2.5 before March 9, 2026 still has it now.

d18df47ac9149474c95f6851ef1eacdb47102536.text: The Freebuff version of the CLI is now a separate build that behaves differently from the regular Codebuff release. When you use the Freebuff edition, the assistant calls itself Freebuff instead of Codebuff, ad banners are forced on and replace the usual credits text with 'Ads help keep Freebuff free,' and the subscription, ads, and mode commands are hidden so you cannot change those settings. The release process for this Freebuff build no longer passes an npm authorization token directly and instead signs published packages with provenance so npm can verify the package came from this project's build pipeline. This affects anyone downloading or using the new Freebuff-branded binary; if you looked, you'd see the changed name, the forced ad banner, and the missing commands.

75cfd15b3e81b44411fba88bf35b4f049acf1834.text: The assistant that tests the chat tool now stays in one continuous session instead of accidentally starting over, and it only captures screenshots of the screen when something important actually changes. As a result, each test takes fewer steps to run, cutting the typical number of actions in half. This is live for internal testers today.

80dc53ab3110fbd9c09ce2fa2e90453e4013893a.text: When you ask the coding assistant to look for the most relevant files in a project and you've asked for the biggest, most thorough search, it now looks through roughly twice as many files as before—about 20 instead of 12. Previously, that deep search sent out two separate file-finders at the same time, which could feel scattered; now it uses one dedicated searcher that is better instructed to focus and find the most relevant files. If you request a full scan of a codebase, you will get a longer, more focused list of files back. This only applies when you explicitly choose the most thorough search option, not during regular file lookups.

b94e7d2b8279e30a3d824ae3bd29fb3550cad6fe.text: If you ever need to see exactly what prompts the system is sending to the AI models, the logging got a lot more detailed. When developers turn on cache debugging, the system now saves a complete snapshot of the request — including the raw data sent to the provider, a cleaner version of that same data, and summaries of any images or files attached. This makes it much easier to understand why certain responses are being cached or not, since you can inspect the full picture of what was sent in each interaction. The new debugging output is available today wherever prompt caching is used, and it applies to anyone building or testing features that rely on cached AI responses.

ccbe035eeed0f877262b54c3ef89eae238bf6c35.text: When the Codebuff command-line tool starts up, it now prints a single line of text to your terminal: "Codebuff CLI starting". This line appears immediately before any other startup messages and before the tool processes whatever command you gave it (like --help or login), so you'll see it every time the tool runs. The change is live now and only adds this one line; nothing else about how the tool works has changed.

5a57b7b0e3a433e54369592a9387bc0786aba473.text: The automated grading harness that scores the assistant during internal evals now runs against a special variant of the assistant that has the 'ask me for help' tool turned off. This stops the assistant from interrupting those automated tests by asking follow-up questions. When you run the benchmark it now uses this question-free version, so it finishes tasks on its own instead of pausing to double-check with you.

af100a17c0367293ff1f89ad4e992fb09c1eb5fc.text: Developers working on the agent code can now flip a hidden switch to save a full copy of every prompt the system sends to the AI — including instructions and available tools — into a folder called debug/cache-debug. A separate tool then line up any two of those saved prompts side by side and highlights the exact spot where they differ, so the team can spot why the AI's prompt cache is being busted and fix the cause. The switch starts off, so nothing changes for anyone running the software today, but the machinery is wired in and ready for debugging.

7ea760f09b36d71fd3d7861962cbeb1c146a871e.text: A new behind-the-scenes tool now lets the team see how much money each subscription tier makes compared to how much it costs to serve. It runs only inside the company — not something you'd see — and it skips one specific internal email address. The numbers are printed to the team's console, not to the app, so nothing changes for subscribers today.

b8dbc9e372c1024fe2544204afa2f653d2a22de5.text: The agent can no longer save just a small edit to a file; it must now produce the entire file content every time it writes. This means lazy shortcuts like leaving placeholder comments (e.g., //... existing code...) to stand in for unchanged parts of code are no longer accepted — the system treats them as the literal text they wrote. This makes every save fully deterministic: what the agent outputs is exactly what lands on disk, with no behind-the-scenes guessing or stitching of snippets. It is live today and applies to all agent types that write files.

b0b535caa6390e9423727516bdb009508dc9998d.text: Logged-in users now see a new 'Account' tab on their profile page that displays their email address and whether it's verified. The tab appears alongside existing profile sections like billing and referrals, so if you navigate to your profile you can click 'Account' in the sidebar to view your email and confirmation status. This change is live today for all users who can access the profile page.

d778cfd31d9a38a9c36c52ffd6afc76e8644e817.text: Developers can now use a new tool that lets the assistant create, update, or delete files using a simple text format similar to a set of instructions. This works across the main assistant software, the developer tools they build with, and the command-line app. You'd notice this if you're building or testing the software and want to manage project files more efficiently, especially with the new model-powered assistants that understand this file-editing style.

51ae862692a8812e3a488c2e99e7ff465cf51f52.text: The token-counting tool now uses OpenAI's own counting service when you ask it to count tokens for an OpenAI model, instead of always using Anthropic's service for every model. If you send a prompt and specify an OpenAI model, the system checks whether that model comes from OpenAI and, if so, sends the request to OpenAI's endpoint to get the token count; otherwise, it falls back to the existing Anthropic-based counting. You would notice this because the logs now record whether the count came from OpenAI or Anthropic, and the error message no longer says "Anthropic" specifically when something goes wrong. This is live today and affects anyone using the internal token-count API endpoint.

4b8bba75d06e4e6391c44a38228dc22ee1ca4609.text: If you use the free version of the service, instead of one assistant making code edits and then handing off to a separate editor assistant (now dropped), the main assistant writes the changes itself and brings in a new lightweight reviewer assistant to check the work. You would notice the extra review step appearing right after edits are made, and the free editor assistant that used to run on one AI provider is now running on a different one (MiniMax), while everything else about how you reach the free tier or its limits has not changed for existing users today.

11c57cc42a98cd1125768aad0b0baed8e947a8a4.text: If you use Codebuff in Free mode, your coding tasks now run on a different, presumably faster and cheaper AI model called MiniMax M2.5 instead of the previous GLM 4.7. The assistant that writes code changes has also been renamed from 'editor-glm' to 'editor-lite', and any documentation or in-app descriptions that mentioned the old name or old model now show the new ones. The switch is already in place for Free mode users today.

e561badadd00e446d412965c34523fc16b410a35.text: When you submit feedback from the CLI now, it actually sends your feedback to the company's servers instead of just staying on your computer. The moment you hit submit, the input box locks up so you can't click it again while it's being sent. The system also makes sure you pick a valid category (like 'good result' or 'app bug') before submitting, rather than accepting any text you type. This is live today, and the developers noted that the server doesn't handle duplicate submissions yet, so don't spam the submit button.

d6911b070e2fca4b06bb4d6446002f80b0901b5a.text: If you cancel a request while the assistant is reading a response aloud, any text that was already spoken but not yet saved will now still be kept. Previously that text could get thrown away when the cancellation happened mid-answer, leaving the conversation history with a gap. The system now makes sure to record everything that came through before stopping, so you don't end up missing the last part of what the assistant was saying.

6fc95937c99cd5afd2794e0a27809cbac58ef8cf.text: A behind-the-scenes menu in the app that changed your subscription plan was removed because nothing was using it anymore. No one should notice anything different — it only affected how the app talked to Stripe (the payment system), and since that conversation already moved to a different path months ago, deleting the old code fixes no live behavior. Your subscription, billing cycle, and ability to upgrade or downgrade remain unchanged today.

096c4f88b360493a40e18fdd94aebc5d05e61ad1.text: Your account can now be credited directly by someone with admin tools, as if you had been given a paid balance without going through a public billing screen. A new staff command walks an internal tool through adding a specific number of credits to a user's account, recording the reason and requiring a final yes/no confirmation before saving. If you are an admin, you will see a summary on the screen that shows exactly who is getting the credits, how many, why, and that the grant never expires; for everyone else, nothing about your experience changes because this tool stays behind the staff-only console.

699d843343ded107bec26c518ca069e881b2ee11.text: The 'Pure Usage' subscription option and the related pricing configuration have been removed from the service, meaning users can no longer select that specific billing plan and it is no longer available for purchase. This change affects how subscriptions and billing are handled internally, particularly around payment processing with Stripe, and removes a specific identifier from the user account records. The system and related settings have been updated accordingly, and anyone attempting to use or reference that plan will find it no longer exists.

bd60ddac9276ae1a04e46797b412364126f8e514.text: You can now kick off the BuffBench evaluation suite remotely from a local terminal instead of only through the automated system that already ran it. A new command lets developers start the same test run manually, pointing it at whatever branch they are currently on, and the results are still delivered privately to CodebuffAI members who already had access. The suite itself now runs only the core test agent, but tests five of them at the same time instead of one at a time, so each manual run finishes faster. The new triggering tool is ready to use today.

0ce28d92c11130c01626a552834fb6f82950b74b.text: When you open the AI assistant in your terminal, a new notice can now appear telling you when you've reached your subscription limit, and you can type a command to jump straight to the pricing page to upgrade. This is live today for anyone using the terminal tool, and it also means your remaining credits now reflect whether your subscription plan fully covers them instead of just showing a flat balance. The on-screen status line at the bottom now shows both Claude and Codebuff Strong availability at once, and the automated test checks that verify the billing flow run faster thanks to a switched testing setup.

22fd5ee0dee41fc394c50853ba1146c5b41ceea9.text: If you open the assistant and type the slash command for buying credits, it now takes you to a new, focused subscribe page instead of the old pricing or profile pages, while still accepting the old command name as a shortcut. Everywhere the assistant points you to subscribe — in help text, in the notice shown when you hit your usage limit, and in the referral screens — the wording and links now say /subscribe and open that same page. The subscribe page itself shows only the subscription options and hides the usual site header and footer, and the profile page buttons likewise point to this new page.

6b1070f762c527e6f79877bd43d54a0f30f727c8.text: When you build the Codebuff SDK into a package, the tool that generates the TypeScript declaration files (index.d.ts) now uses a corrected setup that properly resolves all the internal package paths and targets modern ES2023 standards, and if declaration generation fails, the build now crashes loudly with an error code 1 instead of silently warning and continuing. This matters because the tool that assembles the bundled type definitions previously couldn't correctly trace imports across the @codebuff/* packages, which meant the published.d.ts files in dist were often incomplete or missing type information for cross-package dependencies. Previously, when declaration bundling failed during CI, the build script would print a warning and exit successfully (code 0), allowing the release to ship

5060a002502a7eeeac76ff122490f241cbaf594c.text: A new help article was added to Codebuff's website that explains what makes it different from other coding assistants—things like using multiple AI agents working in parallel, finding the right files faster, and automatically reviewing code for bugs before you see it. If you browse the tips section of their site today, you can read this overview that's written in simple terms instead of technical language. It's a public-facing document, so anyone visiting their site can see it now.

c49789dacbe616b50b764519a6b9e1fba1124c78.text: A one-time database repair script that updated old referral credits was deleted from the company's toolset because it was already run successfully in the live system. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance that only affects internal developers who manage the database. You wouldn't notice anything different — the credits have already been updated and are working normally. This change simply removes a leftover tool that is no longer needed.

0c537d8c58401d1f7556324b6050a649c7557709.text: The part of the system that receives real-time updates from the Stripe payment processor was reorganized so that two helper routines are now stored in their own dedicated file, instead of being mixed in with the main processing route. This was a behind-the-scenes refactoring to fix an error that was preventing the payment update handler from being properly loaded by the application framework. If you happen to look at the code structure, you would now see two files where there used to be one, with the main route file simply importing the helpers it needs from the new location, but functionally, the system continues to check whether a payment update relates to an organization or an individual user exactly as it did before.

77ccc55d578796a0ef5a960c972d37396f3103b2.text: The help article explaining where Codebuff's coding assistant works best has been removed from the internal documentation. Nothing on the live website or app has changed - this is purely cleanup of outdated material, since the tips it contained (like refactoring files and generating code) are now considered common knowledge. You wouldn't notice anything different whether browsing the website today or yesterday.

f3e4216c22135a5d963d01eb1b9bcde68c9994f3.text: The system that tracks referral rewards had to reorganize how it stores old vs. new referral data to keep the database healthy. The assistant can now correctly mark existing referrals as "legacy" without running into a database restriction that previously stopped the process. Nothing visible changes for you yet since this was just moving around behind the scenes how the data gets labeled and updated.

ed9b9413bf5867912f4283e6b2e1eb1ada9d16b5.text: When you make the assistant stop what it is doing, the system now handles that stop signal more consistently instead of mixing it with other kinds of failures. This means the assistant is better at telling the difference between 'you told it to stop' and 'something broke,' which should make interruptions cleaner and less likely to confuse the ongoing conversation. It is already live in the current build.

ad68b32f3a5e58be70437c75eb3719f3678fa6a5.text: You can now get help reviewing your code by typing a new command directly into the chat. When you type the review command with specific text, the assistant immediately examines those changes without any extra steps; if you type it without text, a simple on-screen menu appears letting you choose to examine your recent changes, this branch compared to the main version, or enter a custom review request. The feature is live today and appears in the list of available commands whenever you open the chat.

1147209cdb883e00f1cc2a0779c4fdb941e90eb6.text: The system that automatically updates your account's old referral credit records has been changed so it no longer runs automatically during software updates. Instead, the database team now runs it manually as a separate step right after the update is deployed. This was done because the automated system was failing due to a technical limitation in how the database handles new kinds of referral types. You won't notice anything different in your account unless you're one of the few people with old referral credits that haven't been converted yet, in which case your account will get updated manually in the next maintenance window.

415f5a7c7dc0d39a3021bc9a0ea30d5156d3571d.text: When you refer a friend now, you get a single 500-credit bonus instead of a monthly trickle, and those new one-time bonuses never expire. Anyone who signed up for referral credits under the old program is shifted to the legacy track, which still pays out monthly but is drawn down before other credits. The change is live today as part of this week's release, and you can tell it worked by checking your referral history: old entries now show a one-time 500 credit grant instead of recurring monthly amounts.

f4578bf4f4a245399ea58b440a1a3b30bdcb6d04.text: The software team added a large set of tests to make sure that when you (or the program) tell the assistant to stop mid-response, it actually stops and doesn't try to guess or recover in weird ways. These tests check the 'stop' mechanism across several parts of the system (like when files are processed, when multiple answers are requested, and when the system tries a backup model), so that an explicit stop command now cleanly halts everything without triggering fallback retries or leaving partial responses behind. The change is live and is purely internal quality assurance: nothing in the features you see changed, but the behavior you rely on (cancelling a response) is now verified to work consistently.

4b01c207047d44f9acb47b8d4b7e5cafbc8b3fca.text: When the assistant stops mid-response (like when you cancel it), the system now correctly saves your original message even if it never reached the server. This prevents your message from being lost during interruptions, so your conversation history stays accurate. This is live today and affects anyone using the SDK's run loop to handle cancellations.

baebc5a012ae1bdee67470879e1c3764e7f5d652.text: New users signing up for the service now see one long, scrollable page for setup instead of clicking through multiple steps. They pick their operating system from a list, but the system always uses the npm install command, so there is no choice between package managers anymore. When copying install commands, a green check mark and the words 'Copied!' pop up briefly to confirm the code made it to the clipboard. This updated setup experience is live today.

7eca73b597318beaafc519ee42999dce041609a0.text: Organization admins can no longer set up new billing or purchase credits for their organization through the billing pages—the system now returns an error message and disables those features. However, you can still cancel an existing organization subscription if you want out. Behind the scenes, Stripe payment notifications sent for organization-level events are being filtered out, which prevents repeated failed attempts while keeping personal billing working normally. This is already active today.

2303714342ed6476a96c8e2855a5bdaf79d192d8.text: The command-line tool now identifies your computer by looking at its actual hardware, like the network cards and machine ID, instead of just generating a random number each time. This fingerprint is used during authentication and is designed to make it harder to create multiple accounts on the same device. You would notice a slight delay on first run while the enhanced fingerprint is generated in the background, but the system shows you a quick placeholder ID immediately so it feels fast. This feature is live today for CLI users, and the tool also learned how to properly stop and report when you cancel a request mid-way.

94a7f9ff1c0c25651633bfc43107387ccfd5fc55.text: A help page on the company website that repeated advice already covered elsewhere has been taken down, so you will no longer find it if you search the site. The page simply gathered together tips that already appeared in other spots, so removing it leaves the existing guidance intact without losing any real information. If you try to open that old page directly, you will now see a not-found message instead.

d6e7b7ea7418911b23b69894b06833c420876cca.text: The instructions for connecting external tools to your AI assistant have moved from a technical guide section to a quick-reference tips section, and now they lead with a simpler setup file that works across all projects instead of a complex code file for each individual assistant. You can now configure tools like Notion, GitHub, or other services using a single easy-to-read settings file placed in your project folder, with the system automatically checking your project folder first, then parent folders, and finally your computer-wide settings file last. This means you no longer need separate setup files for each AI assistant you create, and the documentation includes clearer examples for common services.

3be3cc2d6566d12b7c78b7c50d84f8e17ee62964.text: A new help guide called Skills has been added to the documentation. It teaches you how to create reusable instruction sets that the assistant can load on-demand, such as workflows for git releases or code reviews. You would notice this if you looked at the tips section of the documentation and saw a new page explaining how to organize these instructions in a skills folder, name them properly, and trigger them using the /skill:name command. This guide is live today and provides the rules for how skills are discovered, prioritized, and formatted.
