986d6a349dc1d95a48794da2396fe718a9c54004.text: The CLI tool used to get stuck repeatedly retrying the same failed operation forever when it couldn't fetch data. Now, when a fetch fails, the tool only cancels its retry timer without resetting its failure count, which lets it give up after the proper number of attempts instead of looping endlessly. You'll notice this if you saw the CLI spinning or freezing during a network error before. This is live today in the CLI.

5802e2b7bdcc4ff1fde7886bf0d390eee994c48b.text: If you use Codebuff over an SSH connection to a remote server, the login process can now work without the graphical pop-up and clipboard tricks that break in remote terminals. Instead, running the login command prints a web address as plain text that you can highlight and copy with your terminal's normal copy shortcut, then paste into your browser to finish signing in. The login screen inside the tool also shows a tip telling you to do this when it detects you are connected remotely. This only matters when you are working in a terminal session that is forwarded or remote, not when running Codebuff locally on your own computer.

cc4298ee5e138871f9e829f103f77bdc50ff2ce3.text: If you visit Codebuff's help site, you can now read a dedicated Privacy page that spells out how the service handles your conversations and data. The page tells you that Codebuff won't let AI providers train on your chats, keeps session logs only to fix problems, shows ads based just on your current session and basic profile, and routes your requests through its own servers without analyzing your code beyond what's needed to answer you. It also says a stricter Privacy Mode that stores nothing is being built for the future, and you can email hello@codebuff.com with questions. This page is live now whenever you open the advanced-help section.

7eef4c4bcf2fad1756b3695692c844f23397deba.text: The assistant can now connect to external tools like Notion or GitHub by reading a simple settings file you place in a hidden.agents folder in your project, instead of needing to configure each tool through complex setup steps. You write your tool names and secret login tokens (like your Notion password) in a plain JSON file, using short placeholders like $NOTION_TOKEN, and the assistant will automatically look up your actual passwords from your computer's secure storage and connect to those tools when you run it. This works today when you build the assistant from the latest code: project-level tool settings override global ones, and if you forget to add a required secret like your API key, it will stop and tell you rather than silently fail.

bf9eddaba35d2a608d7600e78e602ed432fcff3f.text: When you open the CodeBuff assistant from a project folder, it now automatically reads your.envrc file (if present) and sets those environment variables before starting up. This means any secrets, API keys, or configuration values you've already defined in.envrc for tools like direnv will be available to the assistant right away. The feature skips Windows machines, stops searching for.envrc at your git repository root, and warns you if a.envrc file exists but hasn't been approved via 'direnv allow'.

389ccc13f7c34b2bf8d5fdd0580a7575e4dd6bcd.text: The project removed an internal file called LESSONS.md that contained notes about past mistakes and fixes from running automated agent tools. This affects only the development team, as the file was a private log of lessons learned during builds and tests, not something users would ever see. If you looked at the repository, you wouldn't notice anything missing—the file was behind-the-scenes documentation used to help improve the agent system, and nothing user-facing depended on it.

4215b8a2552107b82d15710d0839adeeaf8f7ff9.text: The assistant can now reliably copy text to your clipboard even when you're connected to a remote server over SSH. It tries local copy tools first when you're on your computer, and uses a special escape sequence method when you're in an SSH session. The developers added detailed automated checks that verify both copying methods work correctly, handle edge cases like empty text, and gracefully fail if neither method succeeds. These checks run behind the scenes during development to catch regressions before they affect you.

e32b581101f3fec2bbd000bd15aa0bbde2a77c51.text: When you open the command-line tool to check on your coding assistant's work, each proposal card now shows a status-specific message instead of a generic one when there are no file changes yet. Instead of just saying 'waiting...', it will now say 'generating...' while the assistant is working, 'no changes' if it finished without edits, 'failed' if something went wrong, or 'cancelled' if it was stopped. This change is already live in the latest version of the tool, so you'll see these clearer labels the next time you check your proposals.

a207ad23c2e11b4963b3c78bb4b961eab5e182ca.text: Paid subscribers now get a new 'Strong' plan that gives them faster, batched access to the assistant during the month, with the subscription's allowance taking priority over free, referral, and ad-based credits. Three monthly tiers set the amount (100, 200, and 500 dollars) and each unlocks a set number of high-priority credits granted in blocks that last a few hours, with lower tiers keeping their current limits until the next billing cycle if they downgrade. Stripe payments trigger these grants automatically, and the system now records subscription events (created, canceled, payment failed, tier changed) for tracking. The feature is backed by new database tables and is live as of 2026-01-29 for existing and new Stripe subscribers.

a536f6a827daaf2d25add1d2389f07aaacf2c3fe.text: Your regular quick test runs now ignore the slow end-to-end browser checks that simulate real user journeys, keeping the fast unit tests lean. You don't need to change anything locally; the test tooling itself simply skips those browser-based specs during standard test runs, which should keep CI pipelines and local runs quicker and more stable. Live today; no action required on your part.

ab76a003422420b5fc75e3c52c8003ebbf9e3d9c.text: The development team moved shared definition files (like blueprints for how data should look) from one location in their code to a new shared folder, so multiple parts of the tool can access them without creating a tangled web of dependencies. This is a behind-the-scenes cleanup that doesn't change anything you see or experience today, but makes the codebase more stable and easier to maintain. The code works exactly the same from your perspective—you wouldn't notice any difference.

e025a206c39f203e83d1a6c495d4796c9341aaed.text: The behind-the-scenes wiring that powers the assistant chat and account-management tools has been tightened up so it no longer guesses at the shape of incoming data. The system now enforces stricter, predefined structures for user account details and incoming chat requests, reducing the chance of crashes when something unexpected is sent. Error reporting in session-revoke and Stripe webhook handling is now safer, using precise checks that confirm the true nature of a failure before logging it. These are internal reliability improvements that make the services more robust without changing what you can do today.

65fb6d39db1b4e441db2014a7557538d1c49c8b3.text: When a multi-step editing task is running and you've collapsed its branch in the CLI, you now see a short progress summary instead of a generic preview line. The system counts how many sub-tasks finished or failed and, depending on the phase, shows text like '2/3 completed' while they run and 'selecting best' when it's choosing the final result; once done, it surfaces the reason the chosen approach was picked. This preview is trimmed to three lines max, and the editor now records that reason in its output so it can be shown to you. Live today.

232f0dddb7dbfb8fb89a438ea7021bdfe535329c.text: The engineering team added a large set of automated checks (over 3,500 lines across four new test files) that repeatedly verify the four main AI helpers — Commander, Editor, File-Picker, and Thinker — still behave correctly after other parts of the code changed. These checks don't add or alter any feature you can see; instead, they catch mistakes early so future updates can ship confidently. You won't notice anything different today, but the software is now far less likely to develop surprising problems later.

3478b8b2654ced86779ac295dbea38fc881ad1e1.text: The project's internal testing scripts have been reformatted to follow a consistent style guide, like tidying up the alignment and spacing of code that only runs during development checks. This only affects the behind-the-scenes test utilities used by engineers and won't change anything you see or do. If you looked at the repository now, you'd notice the test files have neater indentation and line breaks, but their actual logic is untouched.

f74b73e042d7d0464901476ba7db59a419999d61.text: The developers cleaned up the behind-the-scenes helper code that runs the command-line tools, fixing formatting mistakes and making the test code more reliable without changing how anything actually works. If you looked at the raw files, you would mostly see rearranged lines of text that import other files, plus safer test tools that pretend to run external programs during automated checks. This is purely internal maintenance, so you would not notice any difference when using the command-line tools today.

dc00f93621c2f362b6ce42898478d547ad915abe.text: The testing tools the team uses to check their software now have a set of pre-made, type-safe mock objects that replace fake copies of analytics, database, crypto, and stream services, so test writers no longer need to use unsafe type casts. A new guide, TESTING_PATTERNS.md, documents the preferred patterns, including always restoring mocks after each test instead of after all tests to prevent state from leaking between tests. These utilities and fixtures are already in the common/src/testing module and are available for any test suite importing from @codebuff/common/testing today.

45df4dfbce44f07701a79a337579475d9a49d48e.text: The developers cleaned up leftover pieces of code in the assistant's computer program that weren't being used anymore, like removing old recipes from a cookbook that nobody ever reads. This doesn't change how the assistant works for you - it's like organizing a messy desk so things are easier to find later and the program runs more smoothly behind the scenes.

e8d70e5016ac1950e34efe657bfe86360a5a2cef.text: When you cancel an in-progress answer by stopping it mid-stream, the assistant now saves whatever it managed to type before you interrupted and adds a short note explaining that you cancelled. The next time you ask something, the assistant will know the previous reply was cut short and can pick up from there instead of losing that partial work.

8565c2d0deb416b5b1d8ac874a160b0d2c52c67b.text: When the site's pages are built on the hosting platform, the system now records every step in a detailed log file so that if something goes wrong, the full error message is shown instead of being hidden. The build process also filters out repetitive warning messages that used to clutter the screen, and on successful builds it automatically checks that a cache of helper tools is ready. This affects anyone working on or deploying the website, as build failures will now be easier to diagnose.

c1d136969c18ef32ecf0f4344f4f50bd7dae232c.text: The assistant built into the command-line tool can now learn new tricks on the fly. You (or anyone using the tool) can drop instruction files into a special folder, and each one becomes a new command you can run by typing its name. The built-in assistant agent has also been taught to use this system, so it can pull in those instructions during a task, such as asking it to review your uncommitted code changes or clean up messy code. This is live as of the January 26 update.

bb10b2d58731901f13f442a1d7875288169459b0.text: When you use the Lite version of the assistant to help write code, it will now ask a different AI helper to do the typing for it. That helper has switched from one provider to a newer one called GLM 4.7. The only thing you might notice is that the code suggestions could come back slightly faster or phrased a bit differently than before.

a6526e0ba5aa3455b1ca4045b2d268af6cdf3d22.text: When an AI agent in the command line shows its step-by-step thinking before acting, that thinking display now appears correctly and disappears cleanly once the agent moves on to doing work. Previously, the thinking text could get stuck looking like it was still being written, even after the agent had finished. Now, if the agent jumps straight from thinking to taking an action like running a tool, the thinking section properly closes instead of lingering on screen.

5938b0ea4263eb3aba69afa997e50c666e945103.text: When you type a prompt into Codebuff in your terminal, your terminal window's title bar now shows your prompt instead of the default title. The title is prefixed with 'Codebuff: ' and truncated to keep it readable. This works even if you're using tmux or screen terminal multiplexers, and the title resets to its default when you exit.

abaf6a1f5f527cefccbffbe1290a64ae4d56158c.text: You now have access to a second high-powered reasoning engine alongside the existing one when you use the general problem-solving helper, so if the default helper runs, it can spin up both models to work through a tough question instead of just one. The two engines are pulled from a shared setup, so they behave consistently, and the change is live today for anyone using the default general agent path.

88c20d8c1cd5cfd16164b551ea88daea3360cec2.text: If you run the CLI in the free tier today, it now calls the free orchestrator instead of the lite one, serves you ads without asking, and tells the billing API you're on a free plan so it won't grant you credits. The old --lite flag no longer exists; use --free instead. You'll see the thinking/reasoning block collapse automatically once your message finishes streaming, and the terminal title updates as you type. This rolled out with release 1.0.598.

7177b06ec8ea56cf4a6e9649698f36682efbcbf5.text: When your account is adding or using credits at the same time as another operation, the system now waits politely for the other one to finish instead of crashing and forcing a retry. This prevents situations where two processes might try to spend the same credits simultaneously, which could leave your balance wrong. The fix applies to credit grants, usage calculations, and organization-level billing, and adds tracking so the team can see when operations are waiting on each other. Everything happens automatically behind the scenes; you wouldn't notice it in your day-to-day usage, but credit operations are now more reliable under busy conditions.

830dba304fb3ad006f48dc4fbdb92f4a43ee1ff5.text: When you're chatting with the AI in the command-line version, you know how sometimes the assistant gives a long answer that's broken into expandable sections (like "thinking", "agent", or "tool" outputs)? Now there's a new keyboard shortcut — just press Ctrl+T — and it will instantly collapse every single one of those sections across your whole chat, or expand them all back open if they're already collapsed. You'd notice this because the help menu at the top of the chat now lists "Ctrl+T" under shortcuts, and the moment you press it, everything tucks away (or unfolds) without you having to click each section one by one.

02c7a7881109b432b27948add88d805127f1447b.text: If you use the free file-picking helper tools (the quick utility assistants that grab files for you), you'll no longer get charged credits when their total cost is less than 5 credits. A new check instantly recognizes those lightweight helper agents and skips billing them entirely, so anyone running their own subscription through the system won't see surprise charges for these small tasks. The billing code now reports back exactly how many credits were actually charged, and the pricing data you see stays consistent whether or not you got hit with a bill.

c00389f164131f883ab0b8a44003e5b46b59c0f4.text: When you switch between typing modes in the command-line assistant (for example, moving into feedback mode), pressing the Up and Down arrow keys to cycle through your previous messages now works correctly without getting stuck in a stale state. The fix updates keyboard handling so that history navigation stays active even when suggestion menus are open, as long as the cursor sits at the start or end of the input line, and it explicitly allows pasting while in feedback mode while blocking other global shortcuts. If you looked, you would notice that switching modes no longer leaves leftover draft text or prevents you from recalling earlier messages with the arrow keys.

11c14d9693c7f917299bcfe143218701ec49f651.text: A new advanced reasoning option has been added to the assistant lineup, available right now, giving the system a more powerful way to tackle especially tricky problems. It sits alongside the existing problem-solving tools and is meant to be used only when the usual methods aren't enough. If you interacted with the system, you might notice an extra layer of deeper thinking kicking in during the hardest tasks, powered by a newer model.

accf15783fc7529ae9cf3942c82da8a8830bfb05.text: The system that checks whether the website is running and reachable has been split into smaller, independently testable pieces. Previously, this check was tightly coupled to one specific way of counting agents, making it hard to verify in isolation. Now, that counting logic is passed in as a swappable component, and a dedicated test file was added to confirm the check still returns the right structure and handles errors gracefully. The visible behavior for any monitoring tool or user hitting this endpoint remains unchanged today.

306f8687ad62f943c366f87e6e2033c7332bef61.text: When the assistant runs a terminal command for you, you’ll now see a small, dimmed timeout label next to the command (for example, "2m timeout") if a non-default timeout was set. The default 30-second timeout is still hidden, so you only notice the label when the command will wait longer—or be told "no timeout" if you set it to wait indefinitely. If you don’t use the assistant’s terminal command feature in daily work, this change has no visible effect.

d00903a709a387517c1ce06ba36ac6372c8f6c8c.text: The team cleaned up and standardized how the code behind the website looks, making it consistent across different parts of the system. If you looked at the code, you'd see things like fixed spacing, line breaks, and formatting applied uniformly to scripts, API endpoints, and user interface components. This is purely a behind-the-scenes housekeeping change with no effect on what the website does or how it behaves for visitors. Nothing new is live today because of this—it's just tidying up the codebase to make future updates easier to manage.

d752f67c2623da1313c5cf5f2f4bd33c4d8caaea.text: Your terminal-based grid interface used to lose visible content whenever you resized the terminal window and the number of columns had to change. The layout now keeps a single, consistent structure for both one-column and multi-column views, with a hard minimum width enforced on each column, so your content stays put instead of collapsing and vanishing during the resize. This fix is live today in version 1.0.591 of the CLI.

28b7135a68ba48fa7c1f4c9f39c5b46dcf657e4f.text: When you ask the assistant to use a tool from another service (for example, a Supabase database), the assistant used to write the tool name like 'supabase/list_tables' with a slash. The outside tools that receive this request (from companies like OpenRouter and Anthropic) only accept tool names made of letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens, so the slash caused it to be rejected. Starting now, the assistant quietly swaps that slash for two underscores ('supabase__list_tables') when talking to those tools, so requests that used to fail should go through instead of erroring out. You can still type tool names with a slash as before, and the assistant fixes it on its end.

76fac870edb54a406f6e2169fe33410dae62b2d6.text: The company updated an internal helper library used by its testing and automation tools to a newer, safer version. This fixes security problems that the automated monitoring system flagged, but it does not change how the assistant works or what you see. Only the engineers who run those internal tools are affected; everyone else notices nothing different.

31c6ff78607c4aea4456865d2a9dd28c5dd44608.text: The CI workflow now runs the billing package's integration tests in a new dedicated job that spins up a PostgreSQL 16 service container, while the general integration test job no longer includes that package or the agents package in its matrix. If you look at the GitHub Actions pipeline, you can see a separate test-billing-integration job with its own Postgres service, and the main test-integration job has been simplified to skip packages needing a database. Both jobs now use fail-fast: false so one package's failure doesn't cancel others. This change is live today and affects how integration tests run in CI.

614f8ba872fc3e99a949642fc3565cf27ec904a6.text: When the system starts up one of its four built-in helpers (Claude, Codebuff, Codex, or Gemini), it now launches your terminal session on its own without needing the AI to be the one actually typing the command, so you don't have to worry about the session starting up reliably. It still starts a fresh terminal session at a specific size, and your work is still isolated from everything else, but the process is automated so you don't have to babysit the command being run correctly.

95a51d89d74b186344a0b8170ae55666a73cfe8a.text: Internal documentation was added explaining how to connect AI coding assistants to external services like Notion and GitHub through a standard integration method. This affects anyone setting up these assistants inside their projects, since the new guide shows them how to configure the connection and what environment details to supply. If you looked at the project's internal docs, you would find a fresh full-page instruction set with examples for both locally-run and remote service connections. The feature described is available today.

9ff89c4b30b689fa83204343720511eda0b2ae6e.text: When the system figures out which of your prepaid credit grants should cover a charge, it now always includes your last active grant even if its balance is zero, so debt is correctly assigned to the lowest-priority grant instead of being skipped. Separately, the system's automatic retry logic for failed billing operations now looks through the full chain of nested error causes from the database to find valid retry codes, preventing false failures when errors are wrapped in additional layers. Both fixes are live today and affect how your account's credit consumption and billing retries are handled during active sessions.

88d198baf9be9c8c93f3a6627003999f13dc81ed.text: When you send multiple messages to the assistant in quick succession, the program now waits for each one to finish before starting the next, instead of accidentally mixing them up. Behind the scenes, the system starts each message-processing step immediately and synchronously, then adds a 60-second safety timer that resets things automatically if a step gets stuck. If an error happens early on, it cleanly clears out the stuck state so the next message can proceed without hesitation. You would notice that queued messages are processed in the correct order, and the assistant no longer freezes or skips responses when you type quickly.

10f424728d116d125676d97dc1e9df848c01bc50.text: The conversational assistant you interact with in the terminal has had its message-handling and state-tracking logic reorganized into separate, reusable building blocks, making the main interface simpler and easier to maintain. Additionally, a new mechanism has been introduced that uses the database to ensure only one instance of certain background services (like a Discord bot bridge) runs at a time, preventing conflicts or duplicate processing. These changes are structural improvements completed today, improving reliability and code organization without altering visible chat behavior.

2818f1b149f3c4ff78171c90c70f018d7af53ab5.text: When you start the Discord assistant, it now checks every 30 seconds that it is still the leader holding the lock; if the database connection drops, it gives up the lock immediately instead of waiting. The bot will retry up to five times before stopping if it cannot acquire the lock, and it cleans up the Discord connection and releases the lock before exiting. If you look at a running bot, it will shut down cleanly when asked and report a clear error if the lock fails too many times in a row. This is live for the internal Discord bot today.

396d0dff0ce1ae452e308763c42339f199e87fc7.text: You, as the system's orchestrator, now have a new high-powered assistant option for finding files: when the "max" mode is turned on (flag), the file-finding agent swaps its brain from its current model to a faster, more advanced one named after a rival tech company, and this switch is automatic - you don't choose the model, just the mode. Behind the scenes, the code that builds these assistants was reorganized to create two versions of itself (a standard one and a 'max' one) and the main brain that decides who to call now picks the 'max' version whenever you ask for more power, so your file hunts in demanding codebases will now lean on this new, stronger model without any extra steps from you.

ab53db5a63d86b5b55078476d10204f4fd18d3cb.text: The parts of the software that decide how much old conversation to keep, and how to squeeze it down when things get long, have been quietly reorganized so that the numbers and helper routines are named and grouped instead of buried as unlabeled values in a long file. A tracking document was also added that lays out the plan for cleaning up the rest of the codebase and marks the first batch of tidy-ups as finished. Nothing about what gets trimmed or how the assistant behaves today has changed; this is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping that makes the trimming rules easier to read and adjust later.

952cafcea60b275942b7d3b676a7f206432289fd.text: Message blocks in the CLI chat now share styling and state through a centralized store instead of passing the same data through every layer, keeping theme colors, markdown rendering, and agent message trees consistent. Text blocks also drop their top spacing automatically when shown right after a tool result or agent message, so the layout stays tight without awkward gaps.

6a8af63cf292d48cb9a2b25b0f6f4e271de4a6ed.text: When an AI agent runs out of conversation space, it needs a built-in pruning tool to automatically trim old messages and keep things moving. That tool was broken: the list of settings it relied on lived in a separate file that got detached whenever the agent was saved and restarted later, so new agents couldn't start up at all. Now those settings and helper routines live directly inside the tool's core routine, so the agent always carries everything it needs to prune conversations on its own. If you watched the process closely, you wouldn't see a visible change in behavior, but the pruning logic now consistently triggers without crashing. This is already in place and running today.

be7a47c3aba6efd68c6a94469ef976b2bf075c1b.text: The chat screen code was split into smaller, organized pieces behind the scenes, so the main chat file is now shorter and easier to maintain. You won't notice anything different when using the chat, since nothing about how it looks or behaves changed. The development team marked step 1.1b of their cleanup plan as done in their notes.

58d6c0e7ad61d7c3ba8d057744585e0890655cb3.text: When you chat with multiple AI assistants at once in the CLI, the app now handles the color scheme for code snippets more gracefully even if one wasn't fully set up. Instead of forcing a color palette to exist and potentially crashing, it quietly lets the palette be missing where it's not needed. You won't see a difference in how things look unless a palette was previously missing and causing issues, in which case the app will now avoid that error and continue displaying everything smoothly.

392655319d5814d42edd8cc06aef380791cadfe6.text: If you turn on Max mode, the review step now runs several specialized code checkers at once instead of reusing the same assistant used for writing. Each checker examines the code for a particular concern like security or speed, and you see their combined findings in a single report. The change is live for Max mode sessions today.

0f4b98503ecce31555b4a32e0f293d39ab4bed3f.text: The system dropped two of its more complex multi-step review helpers: one that ran several reviewers and picked the best result, and a separate planning helper that coordinated multiple agent types. If you're a user, you would not notice these directly, but you might see a different review helper name appear in places that previously referenced them, and any workflows relying on the now-removed helpers will need to be swapped to the replacement review helper.

01c06622102352f6714739724f42933b4e0a4983.text: The CLI team cleaned up how the assistant renders text blocks on your screen, making the code simpler and more reliable without changing how anything looks. If you were watching the terminal output, you wouldn't see any difference — the blocks still appear in the same place, with the same spacing — but behind the scenes the logic that calculates margins (the empty space around each block) is now shared in one place instead of being repeated in many spots. The refactoring also added a safeguard so that when your terminal window gets too narrow, the layout automatically switches to a single column instead of squeezing into multiple columns and becoming hard to read.

4a88477aab83e69caeceb7e109b377707d815e1d.text: When you use the command-line assistant to ask you a question, the screen that shows the question and the answer choices has been reorganized behind the scenes: the question title, the list of options, and the place to type a custom answer are now separate, easier-to-maintain pieces. The option that lets you type your own answer instead of picking from the list used to be called 'Other' and has been renamed to 'Custom'. Everything works the same way for you right now - the wording change is just a label - but if you look closely at a question prompt, the custom-answer button will now read 'Custom' instead of 'Other'.

3a2107e4d0372944191f09aa2bd398224ef0d7b0.text: When the CLI program hits a problem while running, you'll now see a clear error message in a red-bordered box at the top of your screen, instead of a plain text error. The program automatically hides any error messages that are blank or just spaces, and the error text uses your chosen color theme so it matches the rest of the interface. This only affects what you see on your screen while using the command-line tool; it doesn't change how the program behaves or what it sends to the AI.

c6ed3479cbb3d26b18acd3af1544904e8faba7e0.text: The chat window you see now lines up multiple conversation threads in a tidy grid instead of a single stacked column, and it shows a quick summary at the bottom telling you how many threads are still running, how many finished, and how many hit an error. When several tool calls happen back-to-back, they now group together with just the right amount of space between them so the timeline stays easy to follow. If you look, each thread still scrolls and updates live, but the overall page feels more organized, like browser tabs in a row rather than a long list.

9495948aaae1dfa6fe453d655f21443e1515ecf2.text: If you run the CLI and a conversation message contains agentic work, its on-screen layout is now assembled from smaller, single-purpose pieces instead of one big chunk of code. The visible result for you is the same today: the same blocks (message grid, tool calls, thinking, user content) still render in the same order and style. This is purely behind-the-scenes reorganization so the code that draws those blocks is easier for the team to maintain; no access, plans, or features changed, and nothing is live that wasn't already live.

b9c092fdbe928382fd8f37fe37866ddbe2a6f7ed.text: When multiple AI agents work on the same task in the CLI, you can now see their outputs side-by-side in a clean grid layout instead of stacked vertically. The internal code that builds message displays was also reorganized into smaller, dedicated files, and the system now tracks UI-only error messages that show up as banners without affecting the actual AI response. This reorganization is already live and makes managing parallel agent work smoother in your terminal.

3f158d6374927f48c756d865153280f5ac0f8f4c.text: The CLI’s helper code that organizes assistant messages now uses one flexible grouping routine instead of separate ones for each case. It can collect runs of implementor agents, runs of non-implementor agents, and runs of tool calls through a single shared mechanism, and add-tool names are derived from base edit names rather than listed separately. You wouldn’t see this directly, but the underlying message handling is tidier and easier to maintain as a result. The JSDoc comments on most exports were also removed during the cleanup.

20e9efa656734873d9199d96b1ba3b17a19582d0.text: The command-line version of the tool gained two building blocks for organizing what you see on screen. A new grid layout helper arranges items into columns that shrink or expand based on available space, so lists and buttons can flow side-by-side on wide screens or stack into a single column on narrow ones. A paired error-boundary helper acts as a placeholder container that can swap in a backup message or view if the content it holds fails to render. These pieces are now present on disk and in the test suite but sit inside the interface layer, so you would only notice them if a future screen is built using them; the layout itself already reacts to window width, while the error boundary today mainly reserves space for parent components to plug in real fallback behavior later.

954d9565fd3c0c0a4c907dcd4210d4995637e0e8.text: When you type an @ sign in the command-line assistant to tag someone or something, it now works even if the word before it ends in an apostrophe (like typing "Bob's" then @name), instead of ignoring the mention. If the assistant pops up a follow-up question while you're typing and you answer or skip it, your original text stays in the box instead of being wiped out. Text the assistant shows you, like command output and the top status bar, now keeps any important spacing at the start of the lines, so things like indented lists or tree diagrams line up correctly. This is live today for everyone using the command-line version.

abbc9730a4783f84c1fa9c128fd4e1864f1381b9.text: When the command-line tool displays information that is normally spread across columns, it now checks how wide your terminal window is and automatically rearranges that information into fewer or more columns so it fits without getting cut off. The arrangement is worked out from a few width marks (around 100, 150, and 200 characters), and each piece of information is shifted into the next column in turn, so widening or narrowing the window immediately lines everything up again without you having to do anything. This new behavior is already live for the command-line tool.

253c4754e42312935287f7d0996ea9335394fa10.text: The four command-line testing helpers for Claude Code, Codebuff, Codex, and Gemini now pull their shared setup from one central place instead of each carrying around a long copy of the same instructions and rules. If you looked, each helper file would be much shorter and the common prompts and validation rules would live together in dedicated spots, so adding or changing something across all four only happens once. This is already live: anyone triggering automated CLI tests or code reviews now relies on that single shared setup.

eabf40e54495c612d5a6308fc4f4f4be9ebf08fd.text: The automated helper tools that check and run the Claude Code, Codebuff, Codex, and Gemini command-line programs can now do code reviews, not just tests. When you ask one of these helpers to look at someone's code, it will spot problems and suggest fixes, listing the file name, how serious the issue is, and concrete ideas for making it better. The same session logs you already save will now also include the helper's list of found issues and recommendations, so you can read them later. A few helper tools additionally let you scope the review to just changed files, recent commits, or your own custom set of files.

0a378efeb66ac84c6014c50df46a5e923c81f781.text: When you run a CLI command that displays a conversation, the program now processes each type of message block (like reasoning, tool calls, or agent responses) through one centralized utility that groups consecutive blocks of the same kind before passing them to the display layer. This means you will see reasoning blocks streamed together, tool calls batched as a group, and agent responses rendered according to each handler—instead of each individual message fragment triggering a separate render call. The change is internal to the CLI and does not alter what you see on screen; it just cleans up how the rendering code repeats itself between the BlocksRenderer and AgentBody components.

ed73d8422680785fdd74ad2bbf8c7bd0db804414.text: When you send the CLI multiple messages in quick succession, it now waits for each one to finish before starting the next, instead of potentially mixing them up. This prevents confusing or overlapping responses when the agent takes a turn and you queue up more input during that turn. You won't notice anything when typing normally, but if you paste several prompts back-to-back, they'll arrive in clean, separate turns rather than jumbled together.

85062102870de68eb7871eb8917d67e6e0ad6979.text: When you're typing a long message across multiple lines in the command-line version of the assistant, pressing Ctrl+J now reliably starts a new line instead of being ignored or acting like Enter. Previously, the software only recognized Ctrl+J when it arrived as the raw two-key combination, but most terminals quietly translate Ctrl+J into a linefeed character before the assistant ever sees it, so the shortcut silently failed. The fix tells the input field to also watch for that linefeed character and treat it the same as Ctrl+J, making the shortcut work consistently in regular terminal windows today.

4a9f5399ab66052e1793f774e3c50fae738fd4cb.text: When you attach files to a message in the CLI chat, it now treats both images and text files as the same kind of thing instead of handling them separately. The shared attachment preview card that shows next to your message now supports both media types through one consistent interface, and removing an attachment works the same way whether it's a picture or a document. This is live today and affects anyone using the CLI to chat with attachments.

27a1225a727911ef4aff187402652ae400435967.text: The internal testing team now has a new automated assistant that can test Google's Gemini command-line tool by simulating a real terminal session. This new assistant creates a virtual terminal window (like opening a new browser tab, but for typing commands), types in Gemini commands, watches what appears on the simulated screen, and then records the results to check if everything worked correctly. If you looked for it, you would find the recorded test results saved in a debugging folder, and the team's testing documentation now lists this new Gemini test assistant alongside the existing testers for other tools like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. This is live today as part of the internal testing infrastructure.

83be8c8402aadb3865406aa15d9a7571a11dc597.text: The testing system that checks terminal-based AI assistants now works with multiple assistants instead of just one. Previously, the system could only automate tests for a single AI coding tool called Codebuff. Now it can also automatically test two other popular AI coding assistants - Claude Code and Codex - using the same terminal automation approach. The developer who runs the tests writes a description of what to check (like 'verify the help screen looks right'), and the system spawns a simulated terminal session, sends the commands, captures what appears on screen, and reports back whether it worked. All session activity is logged to a debug folder so anyone can review exactly what happened during testing.

b9eb4a78d7ce4a1295a83fb65a3d201e7b6a8521.text: When you run the assistant on a project, it now also reads a set of notes you keep for yourself in your home folder (files named knowledge.md, AGENTS.md, or CLAUDE.md), combining those with the project-specific notes so you get both your personal defaults and the project’s context. The tool looks in your home folder for those files and treats them as read-only, meaning it won’t edit your personal notes. If you don’t want that behavior, you can pass a new option when starting the assistant to point it at different files instead. You will notice the change the next time you use the assistant on a project, because your personal notes will start influencing how it responds without you having to copy them into each project.

5a6348b74a6f86c73f6698bf81502dc5bbdfebf3.text: The nightly check that makes sure the app works end-to-end now tests the full website instead of just the documentation pages. It does this by spinning up a throwaway database, loading the right test data into it, running the complete set of simulated user journeys against the live web app, and then tearing the database down when it's done, so each run starts from a clean slate. A safety switch makes sure this only ever happens against a local database unless explicitly told otherwise, so test migrations never accidentally run against a production system. If you watched the nightly report, you'd see far more detailed browser-based test results covering real website flows rather than just doc-page checks.

9032b27453a861dee6a007ef1d04cbde3a8aa9dc.text: Pages like the affiliates, pricing, privacy, and terms pages now load faster because they are built ahead of time instead of being assembled on every visit, which means you see them almost instantly. Pages that list individual agents and their versions are set to refresh their content every 10 minutes so information stays current without slowing things down. If you looked at these pages right now, you would notice they load immediately instead of showing a loading spinner while the content is gathered.

2379ebdd7dc0b899dfde10e53aad5d0ee1475536.text: When you paste text into the command-line version of Claude, it now shows up as a little preview card the same way images do, instead of dropping straight into the chat box. If the pasted text is long, you'll see a small banner near your input area showing a brief snippet and character count, and you can review or dismiss it before sending. This makes big blocks of pasted text easier to control and less likely to flood your message by accident. The feature is live today for anyone using the CLI.

88a0c20e49d2b40a3d2eed9eae481241d55ab176.text: Old draft documents describing possible future features were deleted, and several links in the online documentation were fixed so they now point to the right pages. You'd notice this if you opened the help or agents guides: links in the customization and quick-start sections now go directly to the correct sub-page instead of landing on a general page where you'd have to scroll to find the topic.

44e0ce088a75fb8768a03c6447855d81243e7e7f.text: The docs writing guide now checks your documentation for problems automatically, like awkward headings, repeated words, or leftover TODO notes, and flags them before publication. Every night, the system runs a full test that reads through the docs like a visitor would, clicking links and checking content to catch anything broken or hard to read. You won’t see this directly, but if you write a doc with a sloppy heading or a stray TODO comment, it will be caught instead of slipping into what people read.

b15da6fa4c00648fae15b7f32d8ad34708cbbccd.text: If you click Docs or the Help section in the site navigation, you will now land directly on the Quick Start guide instead of a blank page that forwarded you onward. Clicking Docs opens /docs/help/quick-start right away and the links in the footer and top bar go straight there without an extra stop. The change is live today for anyone visiting the docs pages.

0e8618beae7340f8c5738483e0c57729269e6573.text: The agents store page now loads with just basic agent info upfront, then pulls in usage metrics like run counts and spending separately after the page is already showing. If you visit the store, you'll see agent listings appear faster with less data transferred on the first load, while popularity and usage stats still fill in as before but through a dedicated metrics endpoint that serves cached data. The change is live today for the store page and affects anyone browsing the agent directory, with metrics now cached for ten minutes server-side to keep response times quick.

eed20257d2a0c7bd1e6c832bba3408e3259d147e.text: When you sign out of the command-line version of the app, the system now knows exactly when each login session (token) was created, because every session gets a timestamp the moment it starts. That timestamp lets the logout process quietly retire only the sessions that are still within a safe deletion window around the moment you signed out, instead of guessing which ones to touch. For you, this means signing out on the command line cleans up your active sessions more precisely, and you won't be accidentally signed out of a session that is clearly outside that window.

8a8f1bf4b2dc63db9287af5c37347c3ab5de358a.text: The public agent store pages now include hidden labels that tell search engines exactly what each page is about, like whether a page shows a single AI tool, a company profile, or the full catalog. If you look at the page content in your browser, you won’t see anything new appear, but a search engine reading the underlying page will find a structured description it didn’t have access to before. Behind the scenes, the tool that tracks every public page to submit to search engines also got leaner and faster. The same descriptions were also added to the publisher profile pages and the detailed AI tool pages. Who it affects today: visitors arriving via Bing, Google, or other public search engines (not Codebuff app users or CLI users). They’ll see search results with richer previews of Codebuff

428186cb3b0d7e93b1e3fa1dc6be1ae6c15eebbd.text: When you sign out of the CLI tool, the system now also clears your web-based login sessions and releases any device identifiers tied to that account, so your online and command-line presences are fully disconnected in one action. This affects anyone who logs in through the terminal and then uses the same account in a browser. If you were to look, you'd see the logout endpoint returning a cleaner state where no lingering web sessions remain attached to your identity. Behind the scenes, the authentication logic was reorganized into dedicated modules for session and onboarding handling, but you won't notice that unless you're managing the codebase.

f043ef6f04e61d61a7fa203fb69d671a68154339.text: When the software runs its automated checks on the server, it now sets up the necessary login credentials automatically so the checks don't fail halfway through. This only affects the testing system, which means you won't notice anything different when using the tool, but it makes the checks more reliable.

0ccf198a02188bd380c1a2e571fa25dde374a379.text: When you see an advertisement banner in the app, the button text now comes from a dedicated 'call to action' field if the ad has one, otherwise it falls back to the ad's title, and finally to 'Learn more' if neither is available. This means advertisers can now control the exact text on the button (like 'Shop now' or 'Sign up') instead of relying on the title, which might have been too long or not button-friendly. The change is live today for anyone seeing ads in the app, and if you looked at an ad banner you'd just notice the button text may be different or more specifically chosen than before.

7f153b3f0c5abe6ea4067329c8b7c289695ba2c9.text: When you click buttons and other interactive elements in the command-line interface, the text inside them no longer gets accidentally highlighted. The system now consistently prevents text selection across all clickable areas, so tapping a button won't leave stray highlighted text behind. This affects everyone using the CLI today.

6de489d104eb2a8c5df33254babcbdd8082b6853.text: The company's main web pages (homepage, pricing, and affiliate program) now include extra information that helps search engines like Google better understand what each page is about, similar to how a library book has a detailed label. Visitors would notice these pages have clearer titles and descriptions when they appear in search results or social media shares, and the pages load with better organized behind-the-scenes metadata. The team had to rearrange some code from single files into separate pieces to make this metadata work properly, like moving ingredients into separate bowls before mixing them together.

19fc2d7d12eb4a9df4f71aa489b76a7e9db64550.text: If you downloaded the software toolkit for adding AI features to your own apps, you may have noticed it was larger than necessary because it accidentally bundled some internal helper files alongside the real tools. The toolkit maintainer removed five duplicate copies of those internal helpers from the published package, so future downloads are smaller and won't include confusing extra files that shouldn't have been there. This is already live, and the only thing you'd notice is a slightly smaller download and no more stray files showing up if you peek inside the toolkit's contents.

1bb18115cb107d956fa0026d5b9ae840db62b72e.text: If you ask the assistant to read files containing secrets (like passwords or keys), it will now refuse and show them crossed out with a '(blocked)' label, while files that are just examples (like.env.example) still show up with a '(allowed - example only)' note. This protection applies when you run the tool through the command-line interface, and it kicks in before the tool even checks your project's ignore settings. The change is live today, so the next time you use the tool on a project with secret files, you'll see the blocked files displayed but never actually read.

86c38afdba3b611d829db4e2619dbf70f304b910.text: When the web server starts up, it now quietly catches any unexpected errors that happen in the background instead of letting them crash the whole server. This means visitors are less likely to see a '502 Bad Gateway' error message when something goes wrong during a request. The server logs these serious mistakes for the team to review later, but keeps running so other visitors can still use the site. This fix is live today and applies to anyone using the web application.

0a2247ae002a0eb868ab0a38bedb597749cce5d6.text: The app now shows error messages the honest way instead of guessing at them. When something fails behind the scenes, it checks first whether the failure is actually an error message before deciding what to display, rather than treating every unknown thing as if it carried a message it might not have. For you as someone using the publish command or the profile sections like API keys, referrals, or security settings, this means the messages you see when something goes wrong are more reliable and less likely to disappear into confusing empty text. This improvement is already live.

46b792bd9bd8339b916315562ec5968dbb00d212.text: If you have ever needed to inspect or replay an automated test that ran inside a special terminal session, you can now open those saved sessions in a new browser-based viewer that lets you watch them back, scroll through the full log, or export a small animated movie of the screen. you also has a hidden mode that hands the same session data to an AI as plain text. The script that starts those sessions was also simplified so it can be reused by other tools. Anyone running the command-line test suite today can launch you with a single command and immediately see interactive or exported playback.

28e56655182b955afbc04b30e07a97e31ac28efb.text: The internal system that estimates how much a task will cost has been corrected so that images sent to Anthropic's models are counted correctly. Previously, images had to be sent as base64-encoded data, but now the system also recognizes regular web links (URLs) to images. If an image doesn't have valid data or a proper web address, it is ignored entirely instead of causing errors. This fix is part of an internal token-counting tool and improves the accuracy of cost estimates before you actually run the task.

1ad9d6062d128b5250882fff882cec350009cef9.text: After someone changes how the CLI looks on screen, there's a new automated helper that can open a real terminal window, type commands into it, and take screenshots of what actually appears. This catches visual problems that normal tests miss, like text getting cut off or layout looking wrong. The helper automatically saves full logs of every test session so developers can review exactly what the terminal showed. It's live today and ready to use right now.

aa14cd499b507412ae2183857efaf076e008124b.text: You can now type Chinese, Japanese, and Korean characters one piece at a time into the CLI's text input, instead of each character being ignored or split apart. Previously, the input only accepted keys with exactly one character, so multi-character symbols from input method editors slipped through the cracks; the new check quietly recognizes these multi-byte symbols as legitimate text. The change is already live for anyone using the CLI's multi-line input box.

bc83390be8a7c2995938a7162af2209a82b77017.text: When the assistant shows you several implementation proposals side by side in the message log, they now appear as a responsive grid of cards instead of a single vertical list, so you can compare file stats, inline diffs, and status of each agent at a glance. As you resize the terminal, the grid automatically adjusts from one card per row on narrow windows up to three cards per row on wider ones, distributing the agents across columns for balanced reading.

1146a2d326051ac01289ba442e7403ff3c7a019e.text: The development team cleaned up a folder in their project that contained duplicate, automatically-generated files. These files were copies of other files and served no purpose, so they were deleted. This cleanup helps keep the project organized and prevents confusion from stale files that might otherwise be accidentally used or edited. The project itself works exactly the same as before.

7541b151819f14294dcb1f61a07acf13772ab145.text: If you use the CLI tool to check your activity, background refreshes no longer get interrupted. Previously a small part of how the tool remembers what to fetch changed on every screen update, which silently restarted the timed fetch loop and could stall live data. That part now stays put so polling keeps its schedule. The change is live today.

f9864d271e8f84678643282a52af796dc759f60c.text: When you're not typing or actively using the terminal, the assistant now pauses background checks for things like your remaining credits instead of repeatedly polling the server while idle. When you start interacting again, it picks up where it left off. Previously, these background checks kept running even when you stepped away, which could become unreliable in terminal sessions.

24d04f4074629d1766bd27fde3f4e62e4fc104ec.text: When you are using the CLI chat, you can now type /chats (or /history) to open a screen that shows your past conversations. From that screen, you can browse or search your chat history and pick a previous conversation to jump back into. The feature loads the most recent 25 chats immediately so the list appears fast, then continues scanning up to 1,000 total chats in the background for thorough searching and resuming. This is live today in CLI version 1.0.577 as a built-in command—no flags or extra setup needed.

21d528e58eb8198508c6d0df275cccfcef7bd886.text: When Claude reviews your code changes in Max mode, it now switches from Claude's native reviewer to a specialized agent powered by OpenAI's GPT-5 model with high reasoning effort. This means Max mode users will get code reviews generated by GPT-5 instead of the default Claude reviewer, while Basic and standard users continue receiving reviews from the original code-reviewer agent. The change is live today for Max plan users, and the reviewer now makes file edits directly rather than outputting text comments.

57a4cce906474762dd99bec2de2d4763f45cc23b.text: If you pay for Claude as a subscriber, you can now connect your account inside the assistant by typing a special command, which opens your web browser so you can log in and approve the connection. Once connected, a status line appears below the input box showing your remaining usage quota and when it resets. The connection uses an OAuth browser flow, exchanging a code for tokens and polling for quota data behind the scenes.

2c0db067743914f34017ba345f6613ac4d70948a.text: If you use the command-line tools built from this code repository, you may now see agents moved into a dedicated folder called 'agents' that the tools bundle directly, while the original spot is now used only for agents specific to this repository. You won't see a difference in commands you run, but the developers can now better organize which agents ship with the tool versus which stay local. This change is already in place and affects how agent code is structured behind the scenes.

20aaa76bb2a5342c178b3789fe752caa38a69235.text: When you type a message to the assistant in the command-line tool, the system used to run a custom check in the background to decide whether to stop or let your message through. That custom check, along with its supporting bookkeeping about your session, has been removed entirely; instead, the program now relies on a built-in web-standard cancel mechanism (AbortSignal) to handle stopping mid-response. If you look, you won't see a visible difference while chatting today, but behind the scenes the code that handled your typing is much simpler and is being phased in across the CLI and agent components, with supporting files already deleted and type definitions updated to expect the new cancel signal rather than the old manual check functions.

43603d527a501ae9d4a2c02e8adfd19f2d8582b0.text: The assistant now gets an exact count of how full your conversation is from Anthropic's servers each step, instead of guessing. This more accurate count powers the context pruner, so it knows precisely when your conversation is about to hit the limit and when it is safe to skip trimming. Right now this runs automatically as each agent step executes, with no extra action needed from you.

a2ce12824d8a873e296bd31e89399fd48d753401.text: When your conversation with the assistant gets very long (near the 200,000-word limit), the system now replaces all that old back-and-forth with a single, concise summary message instead of simply cutting out pieces it thinks matter less. This means you keep more of the story without losing important details, because the summary captures the whole conversation in roughly one-sixth the space (15% of the limit). Long individual messages—whether from you or the assistant—are trimmed to keep the most important beginning and end before that summary is created, and this new behavior is live today in the agent’s context-pruning step.

0791333cfed30bcc55af1240090ed5e06d47fbd3.text: If you run the CLI with a new hidden switch turned on, it will start printing debug notes about which parts of the screen are drawing themselves repeatedly and unnecessarily; this only happens when that switch is active, so most people will see nothing different today. The change adds a new environment variable called CODEBUFF_PERF_TEST; when set to 'true', the CLI logs detailed re-render diagnostics for the message display and conversation branch components. Developers working on the CLI can use this flag to identify and fix sluggishness caused by redundant interface updates without modifying any code.

0c321bca7d1954fc485583b706ac234bb750cc42.text: The team cleaned out some old, unused testing tools that were left over from earlier experiments - roughly 470 lines of code were removed while only 2 were added. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance that makes the system a bit leaner and easier to maintain going forward, but you wouldn't notice any difference in how the product works today.

5ed90fba63526c235aca49db1a3eee6e5da4591b.text: When the CLI has trouble reaching the server, it now decides whether to keep trying based on standard web response codes (like 408 for timeouts, 429 for rate limits, and 5xx for server errors) instead of a custom error tracking system. This means the login check and message sending will show you a clearer status: 'retrying' when it can try again, or 'unreachable' when there's no point continuing, and you'll get one consistent message if you run out of credits. The change is live today for anyone using the CLI tool. What you'd notice is that errors during login or sending messages behave more predictably and the prompts guiding you to fix issues (like adding credits) appear consistently.

37126c04f583af9a61215363c0d25648e999776c.text: When you run out of AI credits in the command-line tool, you now get a dedicated screen that replaces the normal text input area, showing a friendly message that your credits are gone and automatically checking every 5 seconds whether your balance has been restored. While on that screen, pressing Enter opens your web browser directly to the credits page where you can buy more, unless the tool has already detected that credits are back—then it quietly switches you back to normal chat without needing to buy anything. The Escape key or Ctrl+C still exits the screen so you can walk away at any time. This only affects people using the command-line version of the assistant.

d117982018b999e2bc02269627b1a86a340f4bd8.text: The development team deleted 24 temporary error log files that were accidentally saved in the project's main storage area. These files contained records of automated test failures ('Failed to start agent run') and were never meant to be permanently kept. If you browsed the project folder, you would no longer see these outdated error reports cluttering the test results directory. This is routine cleanup that keeps the project organized so only intentional, current files are tracked.

98340cb75d0702cc2595c7854cf89ae6a688c748.text: The app removed several behind-the-scenes steps it used to perform to decide whether to send your usage data to the analytics system, and now instead just turns on directly when needed using settings read from the environment. You won't notice anything different while using the app today; this is internal cleanup that makes the analytics setup simpler and removes some code that only existed for testing. The change is live as of the snapshot date and doesn't add new features or change how your data is collected.

6a7669dddb1114ca0408761d28ca816510effac8.text: When you type the new commands to turn ads on or off, a small strip showing a relevant ad now appears above where you type your next question, and the system adds credits to your balance each time one of those ads is actually shown to you. Ads are pulled from a service the app recently started using, rotate automatically, and open your web browser when you click one. This is live now for anyone running the app from the terminal today.

72f3a8e02425af57ec6dbd8d21d7e683e26688c9.text: Two logo images (one regular, one with a black background) were added to the folder that the website uses to display public files. If you visited the site today, you wouldn't see them appear anywhere yet; they're now stored and ready for the website to use them in places like browser tabs or app icons. This is a behind-the-scenes addition that makes the logos available for developers to reference, but it doesn't change what visitors see right now.

022a5647165db9116361662682f5cf37bb262932.text: A new financial reporting tool has been added to the company's internal systems that automatically pulls revenue data from Stripe for the last four months of 2025 (September through December). This tool calculates total sales, processing fees, refunds, and net revenue for each month, then prints a clear summary table showing how much money came in, how much went to transaction fees, and how much was lost to customer refunds. Only internal staff with access to the company's systems will see this report when running the tool, and it works by reading transaction records directly from Stripe's dashboard-style data, automatically detecting whether it's looking at test data or real customer payments based on the secret key used.

c269c1cfc765ce0e176612df2263b72579883001.text: Events your app sends to analytics will no longer be lost just because tracking happened before the analytics client finished setting up. Instead of requiring the analytics client to be turned on ahead of time during website startup, it now quietly starts itself up the first time an event is actually recorded. If you were watching the website's startup logs, you would no longer see the usual messages about connecting analytics at the moment the site launches, because that step has been removed entirely. This is live today for the web app.

8042f539c522106d8d639e58a570428e440c407f.text: When the assistant works on a long task, it sometimes needs to tidy up its memory to make room for new thoughts. The cleanup process now protects the most important actions—like reading files, updating task lists, and writing changes—so those aren't accidentally discarded. Large outputs from tools are trimmed automatically, and older, less important tool interactions are removed first. If you were watching, the assistant would keep working on your task without losing track of the files it's editing or the steps it's following.

1b45d60b9cf8d19c8b38a282e5ebf8df09d38281.text: When an AI tries to use one of its tools and that tool fails, the assistant now reports the failure directly as an error message instead of stuffing a fake tool reply into the conversation history. This stops confusing, orphaned messages from appearing in the chat log when something goes wrong. You'd notice fewer broken or duplicated entries in the conversation when a tool call errors out, and the system is live today.

98e09dcabaff3ff8b117fa4969eb003807818ee7.text: When you close the program, your terminal screen no longer gets left in a messy, unreadable state. Previously, the program shut down without first telling the fancy text interface to clean up after itself, which could garble your terminal output. Now, the program properly resets your terminal's special modes (like mouse tracking and full-screen display) before it exits, so your command line stays clean and usable.

4974a0ac14084386cac2c89eaa485117378bb084.text: The website has switched to using Next.js's native startup hook to initialize analytics, replacing the old manual initialization code. This means analytics will now start automatically when the server boots, without needing to import and run it from a separate file during layout setup. The change also added a webpack fallback for the 'path' module to fix bundling issues with logging libraries. This is a behind-the-scenes refactor that should make analytics initialization more reliable, particularly in ensuring PostHog events are not missing.

33f4f1ee757625a0beb228f8c27292ecb28a5bad.text: When the database temporarily stumbles under load, the system now waits a short, slightly random amount of time before trying again instead of all parts retrying at once. This makes the database less likely to get overwhelmed during busy periods. The retry now covers specific types of connection and timeout errors that used to stop operations mid-flight. If you run the software today, you would notice fewer failures when the database is under stress.

7d12c4b1de13b91b3d3233fbad77912dd0adf21e.text: Behind the scenes, the team updated the software libraries the tool depends on to keep them current and patched, which quietly improves reliability for anyone running it. They also moved test-only setup code out of the production modules into separate testing files, so the live tool no longer carries test logic that could clutter normal operation. Additionally, the BigQuery mock setup is now included when running tests, making automated checks more consistent. These changes are maintenance work today; you won't see a new feature, but the tool's underlying setup is cleaner and its test suite is more reliable.

32ed3cd539855c9528c7f60d1257416f86260b78.text: The project's instruction manual had a small animation showing how the coding assistant works, and that animation has been removed; if you open the main guide, you'll no longer see the moving picture at the top. The project also deleted the animation file itself to make the codebase smaller, which means the guide now starts directly with the explanation of how the assistant improves on other tools.

eaab1c00c97488d39d1212c7b8b7036f4ca9088b.text: When you open the terminal in your home directory or a folder nearby, the project picker now correctly appears to help you choose a project. Previously, it would sometimes pop up in folders where it wasn't needed. The fix replaces scattered checks with a single, clearer rule: show the picker only when your current folder is your home directory or an ancestor of it. You'd notice this if you regularly navigate from your home folder — the picker will appear when expected and stay hidden otherwise.

025f9ea3de3e383d108eb9fee90cfcc744d54b60.text: Test runs that used to run during every code change now happen once a day in the background, so routine checks finish faster. The tests that need real online services no longer start up during work hours at all. If you run them yourself, you'll need to turn on a special setting before they will talk to the live system.

1ac0923d47a048c8e0030e8f5cb25a901b2e9fb7.text: When you visit the billing setup page to enter your payment method, the page now loads Stripe (the payment processor) once when the page first opens, instead of reloading it every time you click to pay. This means the payment screen should open a bit faster since the Stripe setup work is already done and waiting for you. The change affects anyone setting up billing on the web app and is live today.

8edcd033320d505662b983af3d38e3114fe9ff4a.text: When the assistant hit an error talking to an AI provider, the logs would dump a huge wall of technical detail including the full request URL, headers, and response body. Now the logs just show the actual error message, so troubleshooting is easier and quieter. Behind the scenes, the code that shapes those error messages was merged into one shared spot and gained the ability to optionally include the raw error detail when developers specifically ask for it, which some streaming connections do.

46b77ba9352d95676ad63add9be1a82e9098ebbd.text: When you run the assistant setup command, it now creates a ready-made folder at.agents/types with starter template files for defining agents, tools, and shared types, so you don't have to write those from scratch. At the same time, if the assistant runs into a tool whose input format can't be safely converted into a shareable schema, it no longer crashes; instead it skips that tool's schema and continues working with the rest. You'd notice this if you just set up a new assistant project and opened the.agents/types directory, or if your project includes custom tools that previously caused setup or runtime errors due to schema conversion problems.

057da0ff3ce9dd133cdf56c49d9ed0db162833ab.text: When you use purchased credits towards a service, the system now tells Stripe (the payments processor) that those credits were used, so your billing stays accurate. This applies right away: any credit consumption that happens through the chat APIs now reports back to Stripe after the transaction succeeds, and your account now stores a link to your Stripe customer record. Behind the scenes, the system avoids sending these reports during automated testing or when Stripe isn't fully set up, and it uses a unique key per message so the same usage isn't counted twice.

017ae9888f1491d0d8f2eae5c59d16f2688cf46b.text: The software now asks the server for only the specific pieces of user information it still needs, instead of downloading the entire profile each time, which means faster loads and less data used when checking who you are. If you watched the network traffic, you'd see smaller requests flying back and forth and a local copy of your info that gets filled in piece by piece rather than replaced all at once.

d785ad2d1cc547704386b254e06d567c35ad9757.text: When you open the tool without a project open, or from your home folder, you'll now see a project picker screen letting you choose which project to work in instead of landing in a confused state. Once inside a project, typing /help shows a help banner with keyboard shortcuts and tips right in the interface, and the program's top and bottom notifications have been restructured so future messages can be added more easily. These changes are live today.

9a06ffce0d6666c7b244ebee6f272b9f45a70bf8.text: When you file a credit-card dispute over a charge, the system now starts sending you a friendly email that tries to resolve the issue directly rather than letting it escalate. If you keep disputing charges (five within two weeks), the system automatically suspends your account: instead of chat requests hanging or timing out, you'll see a clear message saying your account is suspended and to email support. Behind the scenes, Stripe's dispute notices trigger an automatic check that counts your recent disputes and, once you cross the limit, flips your account to banned. Everything is wired up and live today, so new disputes from now on will be tracked and acted on immediately.

7f1db058a8bc17e8cad49d2b7ea6e1c0a8dc9e13.text: Blocked accounts can now be officially flagged in the system instead of just being hardcoded, so the chat API will check this flag and refuse service with a deliberately vague error to avoid tipping off the blocked person. Two specific users who were previously blocked via a hardcoded list are now being handled through this general-purpose flag, and while the system is set up to do this, it's unclear if any new accounts have been added to the blocked status yet.

a769cf4ed37e181a5d9d727c67c7ff433b584c37.text: When you ask the assistant something, your question now shows a tiny copy icon right next to the text instead of on a separate line below it. Hovering over that icon (on a computer with a mouse or trackpad) highlights it and shows a checkmark once you've copied it. The icon stays dimmed until you move your pointer over the message, so the conversation still reads like plain text at a glance. This only affects your own messages, not the assistant's replies.

96a4cd5c691a14a39fbfe73bf3a1c2c1ebf38c0e.text: The AI coding assistant now drafts code changes using structured tools instead of pasting raw text, so when you ask it to edit files it produces cleaner, more reliable edits that apply correctly. You'd notice the assistant no longer fumbles edits between multiple draft versions—it writes out each proposed change as a discrete step before committing to one. This affects everyone using the AI-powered editor features in the CLI and makes multi-prompt comparisons and best-of-n selections more robust. It's live today for all users of the CLI editor agents.

2322b7a1c5f6744d284f7cd524d33e4eec3ffc66.text: You may have noticed pages on the site occasionally took a moment longer to appear or threw a temporary error while the team upgraded the web app's foundation; some dynamic address segments (like specific referral links or admin trace pages) need their path parameters to be resolved in a new way, so each affected page or API endpoint was updated to await those values before rendering. If a route parameter (for example, a feature flag key, an agent version, or a client request ID in an admin tool) is requested, the page now waits for it to be ready rather than assuming it is immediately available, which prevents crashes on routes like the agent page, admin orgs features, trace messages, trace timelines, client sessions, and invite handling. This is a behind-the-scenes maintenance step to

05491fbab4eac3f56281ee813f35728748bb9eee.text: When you look at a published agent's page on the store, you can now see a visual map of which subagents that agent uses, shown as a clickable, expandable tree. Behind the scenes, the system fetches all of those related agents in as few as six database lookups instead of potentially hundreds, so the page loads quickly. The map only appears on agents that actually have subagents configured, and it lets you expand each branch or jump to any subagent's own page.

a4f80a52b115799c9bdc515677f0388daba736ae.text: A help article that explained how to undo, redo, and compare your changes while using the assistant has been removed. If you used to browse the built-in documentation to learn about undoing mistakes or syncing your work with git, that page is gone now. This only affects the in-app help content—it doesn't change how the assistant actually works, so your ability to undo changes or use git is exactly the same.

0ced308f91700a9f6d7f376a08f190cc7bca3e4d.text: When the team's automated test helpers run, they can no longer interrupt themselves to ask you questions mid-task, because a new self-driving mode has been turned on for them. That mode quietly lives behind the scenes and only affects how those internal helpers behave during evaluation runs. You won't see or touch it unless you're setting up those test runs, but if you were, you'd notice the helper just keeps working without pausing to ask for your input.

b4dd83faf2eb1c5d5e60489c8387f81d8b3a539a.text: The assistant and its tools were updated to use a newer version of the data-checking library (Zod) across all its main pieces, and the website's content-management system was swapped to a community-supported fork (Contentlayer2) to keep working with that library. You wouldn't notice anything change in how the tools behave, but these upgrades keep the software stable and able to receive future fixes. These changes are live today.

6b4ec78c720a54ba6603924840420f20036fa492.text: Codebuff refreshed its written guides and help documents so they match how the tool actually works now, removing outdated pages and fixing inaccurate descriptions (like correcting that it uses a newer, more capable AI model than previously stated).
