The documentation system itself was upgraded behind the scenes to a newer version of its publishing framework, which should make the docs render and load correctly going forward. These changes are live today for anyone reading the online guides.

c905bee12e1bb67dc7d8d5779e871b2e315ec8d8.text: When you start using the assistant before logging in, it tracks your activity anonymously using a temporary ID. Once you log in, it now properly links that anonymous history to your real account, so your pre-login actions aren't lost. This is a behind-the-scenes improvement to how usage is tracked, live today, ensuring more accurate analytics for the team. You won't notice any visible change, but it helps provide better service by understanding how people use the assistant from the very first interaction.

e8889743c35d14d3e1dce50c5f4e6a4fb5723ee4.text: When you run the /init command to set up a project, it now creates a starter knowledge.md file instead of a codebuff.json configuration file. The system no longer reads JSON configuration files for file change hooks, and instead relies on knowledge files to determine what commands should run to verify edits. If you looked, you would see the /init command description changed from 'Configure project for better results' to 'Create a starter knowledge.md file', and the assistant no longer checks for a codebuff.json file during responses - it only looks at knowledge files for verification protocols.

eafae3baf8a8c76c7baf5da8c1f1deda373e37a6.text: When the tool asks you to pick between branches or review skipped questions, the labels it shows you now read more naturally — "Your answers:" instead of "Your 3 answers:" — because the numeric count is no longer tacked onto words like 'question' and 'answer' in those headers. This makes the prompts feel less robotic and more conversational while you're interacting with them. The change is live today in the command-line interface.

da195774d6bbcaef8fd202be64a8c675eb00fbda.text: When you open an agent's page, you'll now be sent straight to the most recent version of that agent instead of landing on a generic page. Previously, opening an agent page would show you a version-less view, but now the system checks which version was created most recently and automatically takes you there. You won't notice any extra steps—the redirect happens behind the scenes, and the page still loads the same agent you were looking for, just the latest build of it.

c119924adde2adf1c18a026d98240bebd563d2c7.text: A new automated helper called the 'Buffy the Max Evals Orchestrator' has been added to run evaluation tasks without interrupting anyone for input. It skips the usual prompts that ask you questions or suggest next steps, so it can operate entirely on its own. If you were watching an evaluation run, you'd notice it no longer pauses for confirmation or recommendations. This change is part of the internal agent definitions and is already in place.

c7e5ac5c9632319d3cba4aebe761309f32c656b0.text: You will now be prompted to re-authenticate automatically when your login token changes, instead of the system silently reusing an old session. Behind the scenes, the app stopped depending on a legacy name for the secret API key and now reads the key from a single, consistent source whether you are running locally or in a continuous-integration pipeline. If you use the CLI in a CI environment, set the key under the new name; the old name it looked for before is no longer read.

cdbf0ac186158369f2a0a744f25ce56b78f4bd70.text: When the assistant needs to understand tool instructions written in simple tags like <type>click</type>, there is now just one place in the codebase that does that translation, used by both the command-line tool and the web dashboard. The old duplicate copy in the internal package now just points to that single shared spot, so anything running in a browser gets a version that stays browser-safe. Automated stability checks and test runs no longer waste time spinning up unused pieces of the system that haven't been touched. What you'd notice if you looked today is a cleaner flow with one less place for the XML-parsing logic to drift out of sync.

ae954b5a7e2e340c5b47c21c7af5f0eaffd3d44b.text: If you run the Codebuff command-line tool, your terminal settings (including new scroll speed and Zed editor detection) now load through a single, locked-down source instead of being read loosely from anywhere in the system. The tool also sets up default settings automatically whenever you run automated checks, so tests behave the same way every time without needing manual setup. What you'd notice: your scroll speed and terminal theme detection stay consistent across different shells and test runs, and the tool no longer accidentally mixes your personal environment variables with its own.

d8e58ef8a1ca185fabff999e600f1e3cd4d310cd.text: When you copy something in the chat, the little tooltip that explained the copy button now disappears right away instead of lingering. The copy button, which used to sit next to the timestamp on your messages, now appears inline with your message text, so it stays close to what you actually copied. If you watched this happen, you'd see the button pop up near your message content and the hover hint vanish instantly after clicking.

af236d6388eb1416df385631d1e23f7f0ca94306.text: Starting today, the coding assistant that works behind the scenes in Claude's integrated development environment has been upgraded to use a newer, more capable model (GPT-5.2) for generating code, and it now has a new workflow where it can draft suggested changes and send them to a second AI to review before applying them. If you ask Claude to make a significant code change, you will now get suggestions produced by the upgraded model and evaluated by both the existing assistant and the new one before anything is written, giving you a better chance of a correct and clean edit.

4a1ada9b8f349517688429aa120711147b1b7fe4.text: The code that powers web search and document search now shares one common set of tools for parsing requests, checking API keys, and charging credits, instead of each route keeping its own copies. As a result, search requests are handled through a single internal pathway that can extract fields from incoming data more consistently, and header information from search responses is read in a uniform way. If you use these search features today, nothing about how you interact with them changes — the work is behind the scenes, tightening up how the system checks your access and bills you without altering the search behavior itself.

008d91d863e7bf116e83aaf241e191f2d94628d6.text: When you run certain helper commands that work with your internal database (like setting up the database tables or opening the database browser), they now run a little bit differently under the hood. Previously, these commands were routed through a compatibility tool that made sure your secret configuration files were loaded correctly. Now, they call the underlying tool more directly. You likely won't notice anything different when running these commands, but if you do, it could mean those commands no longer automatically read your local settings file.

a61071b5cda4641493bb22d6fa4f4382765163d0.text: When you're asked a question in the terminal and you use the arrow keys or hit Enter, the way options look as you move through them just got cleaner. The selected choice now stands out with a highlighted background and bold text, and the keyboard hints at the bottom tell you exactly which keys do what (arrows to move, Enter to pick, Esc to skip). These are visible right now the next time the assistant asks you to select from a list of answers.

b61898eefd0b58773daa08d6fda070349cc2cb5d.text: The program now reads its settings through a single, organized system instead of grabbing each value piecemeal from the background. This lets the team test features in a controlled way and stop crashes caused by typos or missing values. Right now, this rewrite touches how the CLI spots whether you run it in a terminal or through an app, picks your default editor, and decides if it should use a special fast file-search tool. Most people won't notice anything new today because the visible behavior stays the same, but the program becomes more reliable and easier to maintain.

bc4b22cd288f7e377c95386b69528cb760453a5b.text: Internal database tools now run through Bun's runtime so they can read your local environment settings automatically, preventing connection errors that happened when they used the default tool runtime. This only affects engineers running database migration or administration commands, and there is nothing you need to do differently. The change is live today.

55668e77242f539867994ee0e9589c7517c02533.text: The assistant can no longer run untrusted JavaScript in a locked-down QuickJS sandbox; the underlying engine and its configuration options (memory limits, stack size, interrupt handling) have been deleted entirely. The web-facing sessions API had a broken database import path that pointed at the wrong module, which stopped it from loading session records correctly. The import has been corrected so user session endpoints work again. These fixes are live as of 2025-12-12.

bc6c3285b51a0a3b9102806c5e632bda264fc4e9.text: When the assistant is typing out a response one word at a time, it now groups small updates together and applies them roughly ten times per second instead of updating the screen with every single letter. This keeps the display from flickering or stuttering during fast streams, and if anything goes wrong while the response finishes, the system still automatically cleans up the background timer so it doesn't keep running. You won't see a new button, but the chat display should feel smoother and steadier when messages appear quickly.

ba9dc9b36ea82fdfdd28d57e5a11e0247658aa2b.text: When you use the CLI tool and it asks you multiple questions, instead of seeing one question at a time with a progress bar moving you step-by-step, you'll now see all the questions laid out at once. Each question can be expanded like a collapsible section to show its options, so you can open the ones you want and fill them in any order. Once every question has been answered, the tool automatically submits your answers without needing a final confirmation screen. This affects anyone who uses this CLI tool's ask-user feature to interactively input data.

1a2cf0fbe4bde70934185dd2a9319a10ab848d63.text: When you have a long chat with the assistant in the terminal, the conversation now loads in batches of 15 messages at a time instead of all at once. A new 'Load previous messages' button appears above the visible messages, which you can click to bring in older parts of the conversation one batch at a time. This makes the chat faster and more responsive when you've been talking for a while, and prevents the terminal from slowing down or freezing with very long histories.

a49d960c315177906c541d3a90a7b20997248dce.text: The system now records two new kinds of failure that can happen when an agent tries to run, so the automated checks that grade agent behavior can catch and verify those failure modes going forward. The affected work is the evaluation harnesses that test agent runs and tool restrictions internally. If you looked at the project today, you'd see new error-record files under the evals folders that capture traces where an agent run failed to start or where a restricted tool was attempted; these files are in place now and are consumed by the evaluation tooling.

ae711f9e5b384f72d415333d5c13a5dd558ea0ac.text: When the assistant asks you a multiple-choice question in the terminal, the updated screen now handles your selections more smoothly and remembers where you left off so it can jump to the next unanswered question. Past follow-up questions that the assistant suggested earlier are now shown only as text, so you can review them but no longer click them. The message area also knows whether a response is the very last one in a thread, which lets the new display logic highlight and disable the older follow-ups appropriately.

bcc048163c83d0fd4387a65d618b83d057caa839.text: You can now ask your computer to tell you whether your project's helper programs — the database, the admin screen, the toolkits, and the website preview — are actually running, just by typing a single check command. Instead of guessing from error messages or opening a bunch of windows to see what's alive, the command quietly pings each piece and reports which ones are connected and which ones are missing. The same list you already use to start or close down those helpers now includes a quick status option.

9f05d5e37cd1d2cb1f08fcb363cd8757202763a5.text: The documentation that explains how to use Codebuff has been reorganized. Instead of having separate pages for special commands and other use cases, all of those examples and tips are now combined into a single page called 'Where Codebuff Shines.' If you were reading the documentation and looking for tips on shortcuts or example commands, you would now find them merged together in one place rather than on separate pages. This change is live today as part of the documentation refresh.

804b82f7f33e98081bab24a56f5900b97b9306d0.text: Some experimental or outdated assistant setups that were sitting in the main project folder have been shut down and put into a separate 'archive' folder, keeping the active workspace tidy. The team deleted one assistant variant entirely and moved the rest to a 'graveyard' area so they are out of the way but still preserved for reference. If you browse the project structure, you won't find these old assistants in their previous location; instead, they now live in a clearly labeled archive section, and their internal references have been patched to still connect correctly to the active parts of the system.

7599418572c1441af7650256cd7f765a9c1fd5ad.text: The scripts developers run on their own computers to start and stop the local development tools were rewritten from old shell scripts into the same language used to build the project itself, and you start and stop everything by running a single command from the terminal. When you hit Ctrl+C to stop, all the background pieces shut down automatically, and if you're working on a separate branch at the same time, stopping on one won't accidentally kill processes from the other. This is an internal developer tool and is live today with no effect on the app itself.

86940e3ca7662f0c32805c5120ee221e1f891fa6.text: When you're typing a slash command (like /exit or /new) and a menu of suggestions pops up, picking one now runs it right away instead of just pasting the command name into your message for you to hit Enter on. If there's only one match and you tap Tab, it runs that command immediately, unless the command is marked as risky (like /exit and /quit) which still needs an explicit Enter. Commands can now also list extra shortcut names (aliases) right in the menu, so you can see that /exit is also called 'quit' or 'q'. The system also enforces upfront whether a command needs extra typed-in arguments, so you get clearer errors if you forget them.

2307e67c59b431d1eea7c06cded952f4eac3c4d9.text: The documentation you read on the website got a refresh. The section called 'Getting Started' is now titled 'Quick Start' in the sidebar, making it easier to find the basics. The help articles themselves were also rewritten to be shorter and clearer, with less repetition and simpler language, so you can get answers faster without wading through extra text.

67f392b73e9fdf36e30a5dd617111234600aed47.text: When you ask the assistant to help, it can now offer clickable suggestions that show common next steps based on what you just asked it to do. Instead of typing out your next request, you can just tap one of the suggested prompts and it gets sent automatically, so you don't have to think about how to phrase it. This only shows up for certain plans or modes, not in the simplified lite version.

b57c75e9cf2999ad20b2fcf006ae127d321935fb.text: When you're typing a slash command like /help in the CLI and there's only one match, pressing Tab now just fills in the command name without running it, and you need to press Enter to actually execute it; this prevents accidentally triggering commands like /exit when you meant to keep typing. Commands that don't accept arguments (like /help) now quietly ignore any extra text you typed instead of showing an error, and the /new command gained a 'reset' alias while /feedback lost its 'bug' and 'report' aliases. Behind the scenes, the command system was reorganized using a factory pattern that makes it easier to register new commands consistently and handle keyboard shortcuts more reliably.

13fc2cfee4abcf05831876306a576f0712a2c6f9.text: When a developer asks the system to review code changes, the assistant now uses a more advanced model to do that review. The separate definition for the old opus-based reviewer was removed, and all the places that triggered code reviews now point to the single code-reviewer, which runs on the opus model. The reviewer is now explicitly told it is a subagent and must not use any tools, so it only offers suggestions rather than taking actions. This is live today for developers using the default, max, or fast modes.

f194a6ef6209225032bae93d1e2ed9dc22de5318.text: The assistant now solves coding tasks by trying multiple approaches in parallel instead of one. For bigger, more complex requests, it generates a few different solutions at once and then picks the best result, which should give higher-quality code. You wouldn't directly control this, but the assistant's code changes are likely to be more thorough and reliable than before.

c70c387429ae44627e8946895102985eeba9625b.text: When you install the testing version of the tool on your computer, it now cleans up old leftover files automatically and shows a welcome message telling you that you are using a beta version. The tool also stores its files in a dedicated folder in your home directory instead of scattered around in its installation folder, matching how the official release version works. If you ever uninstall the testing version, it removes the tool files from that folder so nothing is left behind. This only affects people using the pre-release or testing version of the CLI tool.

815680200858cf794d4d933963073d133036449f.text: The team added tougher training tests that teach assistant programs how to edit real software projects more carefully. These new tests are designed to challenge the assistants with trickier, multi-step editing tasks across several popular codebases, so the assistants have to gather information, make changes, and verify their work in a more realistic way. The harder sets are now in place and ready to be used by the tools that evaluate how well the editors work.

bc4fcd1010aebb128c6059d556a1035f7c2e0b75.text: The company added tougher training problems for Codebuff, Manifold, Plane, and Saleor to the internal testing set used to measure how well automated coding tools perform. The tooling picked harder past code changes by asking a separate program to evaluate and select them, then wrote the results into new benchmark files. This only affects the internal evaluation system that the engineering team uses to score coding agents, and it does not change anything you can see or use in any product today.

ad5815a052e41a708572f75b0f8e23fb3f334e5c.text: The team tore out an old, separate backend system and the old command-line app that sat on top of it, folding all of that work directly into the main command-line tool. You would notice this by looking at the project folder and seeing those two old pieces gone, with the setup guide and roadmap rewritten to describe a single, simpler way to run things locally. If you were setting up the tool yourself, you now point it at the web app for login instead of running a separate backend server alongside it, and several outdated settings (like a Google project and a Relace key) have been dropped from the example configuration.

6808457153458c235fb9ad603598efad7169a0a3.text: Contributors who want to work on the Codebuff codebase no longer need to install two extra tools (infisical and direnv) or run a multi-step setup just to get their local development environment running with secret keys. Now, after cloning the repo, a contributor only needs to copy a single template file (called.env.example) into place and fill in their own values, which is a one-step process. If someone does want the more advanced team-wide secret syncing, that option still works, but it requires an extra step (allowing direnv), and it is only for team members, not for every personal project. This simplified setup is live today: anyone who pulls the latest code will see the easier instructions in the contributing guide and the removed tools from the required setup list.

67927deabf1e7c17f14dc4a40e14675ddaa51550.text: The system now has a new test that checks whether it properly trims down saved conversation history when the total size (including the system instructions) gets too large. The test uses a sample saved state where messages and the system prompt together exceed the limit, confirming the trimming logic handles the combined size correctly. This only affects internal developers maintaining the system, not anyone using it — it just adds more assurance that the trimming feature works as intended.

ea9359be498583c1243a988d5e0f24d75c3c4744.text: The team cleaned up the website's code-quality warnings, which is the kind of behind-the-scenes housekeeping that keeps things running smoothly but doesn't change what you can do on the site today. The visible result is that the code now follows consistent style rules, like finishing sentences with proper punctuation and using the right variable types, so future edits are less likely to introduce bugs. If you were to look at the website, nothing would appear different, but the underlying code is tidier and easier to maintain.

9b5726e3d5abbd49741ca2d372762ea3d6f573fa.text: When a developer needs to remove a temporary copy of the project (called a "worktree") that was set up for testing, the cleanup tool now first makes sure no background processes tied to that copy are still running before removing it. It also checks that the copy's name is valid, gives clearer warnings if something is missing or won't delete, and runs a bit faster. This affects anyone on the team who creates and deletes these temporary project copies during development. The change is live today; you would notice it only if you use the cleanup command yourself, since it's an internal developer tool.

cd38d63bce75c5439f033ec51998cad44bcbffe0.text: When the assistant logs what it's doing, it now builds that logging information in one shared spot and sends clearer, more consistent details to PostHog (the analytics service). If you're watching logs in real time, you won't notice a difference; behind the scenes, errors that happen while tracking usage are now caught and reported with more context, so issues are easier to diagnose without breaking your session. This affects anyone running the CLI or using the web version today.

c56032f0efb738f1db1176c56d141ea141329c41.text: When an assistant spawns a helper to work on a sub-task, that helper no longer automatically receives any images the main assistant was looking at. If the helper genuinely needs to see those images, it has to request them explicitly through the includeMessageHistory option, instead of getting them by default. This went live as part of an agent runtime update that landed in a snapshot on December 8, 2025, alongside other changes like the read-subtree command accepting an empty path string and the thinker agent switching to Claude Opus 4.5. If you were watching a sub-task unfold and it previously seemed to 'just know' about an image from the parent conversation, it will now ignore that image unless the parent deliberately includes the full message history when handing off.

c84b6395e68969d2ebfb3208b9545e5863d4b364.text: When you use the CodeBuff CLI or web tool, your errors and events are now collected by a single shared helper that decides when to actually send them out. This helper waits to group related errors together until it knows which user you are (or your account id), and it makes sure nothing leaks out during local development. As a result, your error reports should be more consistent between the command-line and web versions, and developers won't see random test errors appear as real analytics data.

7969fc0fd749ae2267eb95e123836faf47d9a149.text: When you go to publish your agents, you'll now see a new toggle that lets you include reverse dependencies - agents that call/spawn the ones you've selected - so the confirmation screen shows the full picture of what would be affected. Bundled agents (pre-packaged ones) no longer appear in your publish list, and the system now sends the complete set of your local agent IDs to the server so it can catch any missing dependencies before publishing. You'll also see little chip labels showing your selected agents with the ability to remove them individually.

f72d0dd5b11234985d46b0b123d92e3a19403fcc.text: The system that tests the assistant against real-world coding jobs now runs across many projects at once instead of just one, so it can see how well the assistant handles tasks from programs like Codebuff, Manifold, Plane, and Saleor in a single pass. It also gains a new check that flags which tasks the assistant consistently struggles with (scoring 7.5 or lower), so developers can focus on the hardest problems. You would notice this if you looked at the test results: instead of separate runs for each project, there's now one combined report listing multiple repositories and a new section calling out the most difficult tasks.

99bb1e61a149a143d39b030770c2d8af2bda629d.text: When you run the CLI tool, it now carries the agent definitions it needs inside the application itself, rather than going looking for them in hidden project folders every time. This means you no longer need certain extra files sitting around on disk for the built tool to work. The developers added a step that scans the agents folder and bakes their contents directly into the program files before it is packaged. You would notice this if you tried to run the tool without its usual agent files present, because it would still work the same as before.

8dbf674f3b0ae4511f43298d862b6d39f35a28c0.text: When you type /publish in the command-line chat, you now get a selectable checklist of your local agents to pick from instead of the old text prompt. The checklist shows each agent plus how many other agents it depends on, and you can pre-select some by listing them right after the command. Once you confirm, the tool tries to upload the chosen agents and reports plain success-or-failure feedback. This is live today for anyone running the updated command-line tool.

73e2e27486bcd494c28452c302fe43729555ccaf.text: When an AI helper runs out of thinking space, it used to forget your messages too soon because it didn't account for the space taken up by its own instructions and tool descriptions. Now it factors those in, so it keeps your conversation history longer before trimming. This matters to anyone using an AI agent that relies on multiple tools. You'd notice the helper stays on task longer without abruptly losing context. The fix is already live.

a52a4c209234fb70a8bdbc8a3eebffd7ab9dbd88.text: The SDK now ships with a complete set of automated tests and ready-to-run example scripts that developers can use to verify their integrations and see common workflows in action. When you open the SDK package youll find a dedicated testing area organized by category-streaming, multi-step workflows, custom agents, and specific features like file handling and step limits-along with step-by-step instructions for running each group. The examples show how to perform tasks such as reviewing code, generating commit messages, and explaining code in plain language, all runnable with a single command after adding an API key. This makes it easier to catch problems and learn patterns without writing tests or scripts from scratch.

eb64e4dca0d7fb6e502fed42022b45e424628c86.text: You, as a developer working on this software kit, no longer need to remember several different commands to check that everything works—there's now a single command that builds the software, checks for code errors, and runs all the compatibility tests at once. The team replaced the old collection of separate instructions in the project file with one new verification script, and added a shortcut to skip the build step if you just want to run the tests quickly. You'd see this as one command replacing several, and if you looked, you'd find the old separate scripts are gone and a single new one in their place.

03169275bafd4f0e1a8d59e760bd6754af1a012e.text: If you build tools or apps that rely on this toolkit, you may have hit confusing type errors — especially around message-building helpers — even though everything looked correct on the surface. The toolkit now imports those helpers from its own internal location instead of an external package path that was causing mismatches, so type checking resolves properly. A new command was also added to the toolkit’s build steps that automatically tests type compatibility across different project setups, removing leftover cached copies first to ensure a clean check. The fix applies today to anyone installing or updating the toolkit, and you’d notice fewer mysterious type failures when integrating it into projects that use strict module or bundling settings.

e4f52de6c61a65b94a47553497bc4757ed4129ab.text: When the assistant works through a problem step by step and shows you its reasoning as it goes, you may have seen some words appear twice in a row. That happened because the tool was saving up pieces of text and then replaying them, instead of just passing each piece along once. The extra saving and replaying has been removed, so the text you watch stream in now appears only once, matching what the assistant actually says.

62f371ab9f8fea40c134bacc74ed3c184f655dc9.text: When you type a multi-line message in the terminal assistant, you can now click anywhere in your text to move the cursor there, instead of nudging it character by character with arrow keys. If you highlight some text with your mouse and then press Delete, only that highlighted part disappears rather than everything from the cursor to the end of the line. The assistant also figures out the real width of your terminal window on its own, so text wrapping behaves correctly even when tabs or wide characters are involved.

aea1cc2b5b0e724c255ce1d78154608df8b26933.text: When you have a long conversation with an AI assistant, the system sometimes trims older parts to stay within limits, but it had two problems: it guessed how much room messages took by their text length, and it sometimes left behind mismatched tool calls and results. Now it counts messages more accurately—giving each image a fixed 1000-token cost—and it quietly removes any tool call or result that lacks a matching partner before and after trimming. You would notice that the assistant no longer trips over context overflow errors or broken back-and-forth tool sequences during long sessions, since both fixes are internal and already active in the current CLI version.

edd9eca23e7811ca00573e211e858edc4aa7f537.text: When the assistant's conversation memory gets trimmed down to save space, it now keeps tool-call and tool-result pairs together instead of deleting them individually, preventing errors that occurred when only one part of a paired interaction was removed. This affects how the system manages long conversations internally, and if you were watching the trimming process happen, you'd notice that related back-and-forth actions are no longer at risk of being split apart.

7c8087db46d5abfaf5dfb9640efc89ae25f661fa.text: When the assistant tries to type answers inside a terminal window that's being driven by an automation tool, the letters get cut off and only the last character shows up. To fix this, the assistant now wraps every message in special invisible markers that tell the terminal the text is arriving all at once, so every letter gets through correctly. If you watched someone script the assistant inside that terminal background, they would have seen words arrive incomplete before, and they would see them arrive whole now.

9f1a79a6d7d0f1cecaba8752a6e24eb445937f47.text: When you launch the CLI, it now checks your terminal's color theme a split-second before the main app loads, instead of doing it in a separate step later. This prevents your terminal's theme information and the app from competing for the same input channel, which previously caused them to clash and could produce a blank screen or wrong theme. You won't see a new option or setting—the fix just makes the existing automatic dark/light mode detection work reliably every time you start the CLI, with no extra steps on your part.

cc9334c64de77cce03e96f47dd083d245f3f2ba9.text: When the CLI starts up, it now figures out your terminal's color theme directly as part of its normal launch sequence, rather than launching a separate helper process to do it. That extra process—and all the code that paused and resumed your keyboard input around it—has been removed. You shouldn't notice anything different while the program runs, but startup involves one fewer moving part, so there's less chance of the input briefly freezing or the theme check interfering with the terminal interface as it appears.

8f4f6608f9fdb8c08ae534463c5d1d935eff66ea.text: The default base2 assistant now automatically includes an editor helper when it runs, instead of requiring you to turn that editor on manually as a separate setting. When you launch the default base2 assistant, it will spawn an editor agent alongside its other helpers so you no longer need to start a second "base2-editor" assistant to get editing support. The editor's instructions were also softened for non-GPT-5 models, telling them to think before acting instead of demanding they think very hard. This is effective today for anyone using the default base2 assistant, and the old separate editor definition no longer exists.

ceae0abf396aea5f2e5e76df7dfd68ad992f1308.text: When you run the CLI and the assistant is thinking out loud, any reasoning markers embedded in the streamed text are now captured as a dedicated thinking block instead of leaking into the visible response. This only affects the CLI experience today: the streamed output is parsed so that the start and end of a reasoning section become a structured block with a flag marking it as reasoning, and partial markers split across pieces of text are buffered so they don't get chopped up. If you watch the CLI output, you would see the assistant's thinking wrapped in a collapsible reasoning section rather than mixed into the main answer; the developers confirmed this is live and intended for CLI users, and noted that previous helper code for tracking open/closed thinking state was removed because it

0a44c0a2733540c97459a99ac77c0e684b0d6660.text: When you start the CLI, it asks your terminal what color scheme to use by sending a special color query. That query used to wait forever if your terminal never answered, which hung the whole startup. Now every query gives up after a short, fixed limit, and the whole detection step is cut off if it drags on, so startup always moves forward. You will notice that the dark-or-light theme still gets picked when your terminal replies quickly, but you no longer sit staring at a frozen screen when it does not. The bundled interface library was also bumped to a newer patch release, which is the kind of behind-the-scenes update that fixes minor glitches without changing how anything looks.

55d40fae1f7ec759ffa4c4b7a171c7534b2953e4.text: When you send a message in the CLI, the program now uses smaller, organized pieces of instructions behind the scenes instead of one long tangled sequence. This makes it easier to maintain and test, and you won't notice any difference in how messages are sent. The change was rolled out as part of an update that also added new checks for terminal compatibility and updated the model options for developers.

afde2ad4554beaf169454cafe821a670be200bc4.text: The CLI's message-sending code was reorganized behind the scenes: the logic that builds and updates chat responses was moved out of one large file into a new dedicated file made up of small, focused functions. This does not change anything you see or do in the CLI today, but it makes the codebase easier for developers to test and maintain. If you looked at the project structure, you'd see two new or modified files in the utils and hooks folders holding the moved logic and new unit tests covering it.

a77640d86b6a0a36d02fd56722d9c56ebee86fa0.text: Today, when you use the CLI to chat with the assistant, the behind-the-scenes logic that sends your messages has been cleaned up. Instead of one complicated internal function, the work is now split into smaller, dedicated helpers, each doing a clear job. If you looked at it, you wouldn't see faster responses or new features - the change only makes the code easier to maintain and fix down the road. A few redundant steps and duplicated settings were removed so the system has less clutter to sort through every time it processes your message.

92a7fd201b02dc80c3408f37fbecd7a9d2d25462.text: The release scripts that package the CLI now ignore harmless error messages that appear when checking the installed version, so version-detection during installs is more stable and no longer trips the project's code-quality checks. If you reinstall or upgrade the CLI, you might notice fewer stray warning lines and slightly cleaner terminal output; the version-checking step itself behaves the same way. The change also tidies up a few unused bits in the build and release tools, which is behind-the-scenes cleanup that keeps releases consistent and helps catch future mistakes early. This is live today for anyone installing or upgrading the CLI through its normal installation flow.

b71bb469a43dea417bca0074e86030b73297a566.text: When you type a command right after /bash (like /bash ls), the tool now runs it immediately instead of asking you to confirm first. The system automatically handles how the command output appears - it shows as a live updating message during ongoing conversations, or gets added directly to the chat history otherwise. This means you can quickly run bash commands without the extra step of entering a separate mode.

a759cb9d36b85b618122e8a256b15d405f192a81.text: The team deleted the old evaluation system and moved everything into the newer buffbench folder, so all the testing tools now live in one place instead of two. You would see the old git-evals folder is gone and the same files (setup-test-repo and pick-commits) now sit inside evals/buffbench. The standalone command-line tool for cloning repos and the script that emailed results were both removed, so cloning must now happen through the main workflow and results are no longer emailed automatically.

387cbcfa0baaef8026e24eb202aeb6e82b14828e.text: You can now include images when chatting with the assistant in the command-line tool. Instead of only typing messages, you can attach a picture by running a command like /image path/to/photo.png, or by copying an image and pasting it directly into the terminal. The assistant sees the image alongside your text, and the interface shows a small preview of any picture you've added but not yet sent. This works today in the CLI, affects anyone using the command-line chat, and is live now.

091c6d50b52bdf05cee2bb5910bc5d426d9c30e4.text: An internal orchestrator now has a faster, lighter mode that uses a different AI model and skips some of the slower analysis steps, so certain automated coding tasks can run more quickly when full rigor isn't needed. The lite mode also swaps in a streamlined planning step and routes implementation work to a GPT-5-based editor instead of the heavier review process. This is a behind-the-scenes change for internal tooling that controls how the system breaks down and executes coding requests; if you rely on the older default flow, nothing about your experience changes. The new mode is in place today, but only takes effect when an internal process explicitly opts into it.

db30e8c193515679b6ced7ca24cf99f050a99089.text: BuffBench now lets you run Claude and Codex CLI tools alongside Codebuff agents to see which one performs better, requiring those CLI tools and their API keys to be installed globally. The system parses the external agents' JSON output into the same step-by-step format used by internal agents. If you use 'external:claude' or 'external:codex' as agent names, the tool spawns those external CLI processes with permission-skipping flags and tracks their actions for comparison. Errors get saved to files, but malformed tool calls don't.

56ecce97fc37d6e98ea499132138fc28cf9d4170.text: The system's internal assistant workflow now includes a required 'think first' step before making code edits. When you ask the assistant to edit code, it will pause and lay out its plan before writing anything, and a new orchestrator role has been added to route certain tasks through this more careful editor path. This applies to how the assistant processes your requests behind the scenes; if you use it today, you may notice a brief delay while it decides how to proceed before changes appear. The mechanism enforcing this is already live.

8a3d8338e4d6d3cbb867738a67237e66820dbbf4.text: When you run a terminal command in the CLI, the command and its result are now shown in your chat history without being sent to the AI model for reasoning. Previously, bash commands were injected into the AI's context so it could react to them; now the system only updates your UI history. This affects the terminal command flow across the CLI, and you would notice that bash output no longer influences AI-generated text.

515b7693ac6b2f8378ca9df3d5d8bc4de82744e4.text: When you run a command in the CLI chat, the result now appears immediately as a placeholder and updates asynchronously once the command finishes, instead of waiting and replacing the whole message. The CLI treats your bash command output as regular chat context, so the AI can see what you ran (including the working directory and timing) right away. If you’re watching the terminal, you’ll notice commands show a live status and their output flows into the conversation without freezing the chat. This is live today for CLI users.

de8732e50334a2b2c36715e242966b1cfd39981e.text: When you interact with multi-step AI agents (like the best-of-n editor), those agents used to read each other's responses as plain text and try to guess what tools were being called. Now they talk directly using native tool calls, so there's no guessing game — the system knows exactly which helper is being invoked and with what input. You'll notice subagent tool calls are now correctly attributed to the agent that spawned them, and results from spawned helpers come back as clean structured data instead of messy text that needs to be parsed. This makes agent chains like editor-best-of-n more reliable and easier to debug.

780933c2773c184d84d5bba9e3d500642f7c9bfc.text: When you run a command in the CLI, it now shows a dashed, ghost-like preview that stays on screen while the command runs instead of flickering in and out. Finished commands are added to the chat history all at once in a single smooth update rather than one at a time. This makes the terminal feel steadier and less jumpy when you trigger several commands quickly. The change is live today in the CLI.

10614922a610bd81b6f9491aa50eec0f47a193fa.text: If you run the automated coding evaluation called BuffBench today, it will test only two assistant configurations instead of four. The two removed variants were extra flavors of the main assistant that used a different model and a setting that made it relax while reading files; the remaining two cover the standard tier and the top tier. The model used to pick between competing code drafts now spends more thinking steps on the top tier, and the top-tier draft-picking sequence now uses a different mix of draft-writing models. Nothing changes for the main coding assistant used in day-to-day work; only the internal evaluation harness is affected.

2ff04a605d1bc4152b2e674d27b7a1ae8b2cf4a7.text: If you have auto top-up turned on, you will no longer see the pop-up warning telling you that your account balance is getting low, as long as you still have some credit left. The app now checks whether your card will automatically add more money when you run low, and if so, it stays quiet unless your balance drops all the way to zero. That means the warning banner only comes back when you're truly out of credits, not just when you cross the usual 'getting low' thresholds.

9bfbea1d4e17832f2fed4e58702550e75b34fdcb.text: When your account balance gets low, a warning banner now pops up automatically in the chat window instead of staying hidden until you ask for it. The program quietly checks your usage in the background and shows the banner when your credits cross certain warning levels, then hides it again after a few minutes. You'd see this if you open the chat and notice a colored status notice at the top without having to request it.

40b0eaac602f290e5127508fe56c6bdcae1b990e.text: The testing system that checks how well the coding assistant works has added a new, more powerful model option to run against. If you looked at the evaluation setup, you would see it now runs three configurations instead of two: the existing strong mode plus the new model variant that reads files more calmly. The change is live for internal testing and benchmark runs, not something end users toggle directly.

d05275532c93db7601d0c45d5740b32db33fd084.text: When you're typing in the chat input box and a menu of suggestions (slash commands, mentions, or files) is open, the program now handles your arrow, tab, and escape keys in one consistent place instead of checking for them in several different spots. You will notice this if you open a suggestion menu and use those keys: the up/down arrows, tab, and shift-tab move through the list predictably, and escape or ctrl+c exit cleanly, because the same logic decides what each key does instead of different parts of the screen disagreeing. Behind the scenes, the old scattered keyboard checks were gathered into a single helper, so adding or fixing a key behavior now only needs to happen in one spot; until that central helper is wired in everywhere, those keys still fall through to whatever each screen

9bcd14928a9295924c79855964f0e6bf45828ee4.text: When an AI agent takes a step, it needs to decide which extra tools it can use. That decision logic was moved out of the main step-running code and into its own helper so it can be reused and tested separately. You won't see a new tool appear, but the code that picks which tools are allowed is now cleaner and easier to maintain behind the scenes. This is already live today.

ea119d20250121da03859f9303b2533c2ae3fbd0.text: When you ask the assistant to tackle a particularly tough, multi-step problem, it now hires a different, more capable helper to do that heavy thinking instead of the one it used before. You won't see this directly—you'll just notice that the assistant's deep, deliberate reasoning runs through this new helper under the hood. The old helper is no longer part of that high-complexity workflow, so anything depending on that specific chain now uses the replacement. This is in place and working today, not a future change.

05880abe323b6862e31bc5691a6b42f68cf89cda.text: When you use the CLI to log in, publish your agents, or claim a referral bonus, the program now talks to the website through a single, well-behaved helper that bundles up your login token and translates error messages, instead of each command crafting its own request. If a network hiccup happens, the helper can tell a temporary problem from a real failure and retry only when it makes sense, and every part of the CLI shares that one helper so error handling stays consistent. The changes are live today for anyone running the CLI commands that log you in, fetch your account details, publish agents, or redeem referrals, so you may notice friendlier error messages or smoother retries where things used to fail silently, while the behind-the-scenes behavior you see day to day otherwise remains

170f4ac03f25ef3c2252ed382a85a261e2ec9b00.text: The usage banner now shows different text and colors based on your credit balance, and it updates automatically when credits change. You'll notice the banner displays whether your balance is loading, shows colored alerts when credits run low, and appears or disappears depending on your remaining credits. This logic was moved behind the scenes to make the banner's code cleaner and more reliable, though what you see on screen stays the same.

90505cc2fddb0cba143ef0524cd598d693a6e012.text: When a banner pops up in the command-line tool, it now uses one shared template instead of slightly different copies in each place it appeared, so the look and behavior stay consistent. The banner adjusts its width and spacing to fit the size of your terminal window, shows the message text, and has a small close button that changes color when you hover over it. This is live today as part of the latest command-line tool release.

8ebd20c4b4f1601b4f4b8e63f40b4dcd7aabcb60.text: When you run the assistant in a terminal window, the layout of banners and buttons now adjusts based on how wide or tall your terminal is, using clear cutoff points (very narrow under 80 columns, narrow 80-120, medium 120-160, wide over 160) instead of a single rough check. If you shrink your window to be very narrow, side margins on banners and some buttons disappear so things still fit on screen; as you widen it back, that spacing returns. This only affects the CLI interface you see right now while typing, and the behavior is live today.

7028a55d670b1caeee9913d27ac38648c1def091.text: If you use the assistant inside tmux, it now tries several different ways to ask your terminal what background color theme it should use, instead of relying on just one method that often failed. It checks whether tmux is configured to let color requests through, sends the request wrapped correctly for tmux (or other multiplexers), and if that still doesn't work it falls back to reading theme hints from your terminal's environment variables. You would notice this as the assistant's colors matching your terminal theme more reliably when running inside tmux, which previously often caused mismatched or default colors.

3e144e64550be90029e056b819564add6e1f6c9b.text: When you chat with an agent that runs your code, it can now pause mid-conversation and show you a fill-in form with multiple-choice questions, navigable by keyboard, then wait for your answers before continuing. The form supports single- or multiple-select (radio vs checkbox style), an "Other" text input with length limits and validation, a live progress indicator, and a final confirm screen summarizing your answers. This is live today for the Base2 planning agent, whose instructions now tell it to ask clarifying questions via this form before writing specs, while the general chat interface simply subscribes to display such forms whenever an agent triggers them.

9fdebef076cb48328a0f9c9a11f584f8055fcfda.text: When you're typing a question to the assistant, there's now a new way to switch how the input bar behaves. Instead of a simple on/off toggle for running commands directly, the input bar can be in 'default' mode (normal chat), 'bash' mode (run terminal commands), or 'referral' mode (a new mode with a special icon). The settings for each mode are now defined in one central place, so the look and behavior of the input bar adjust based on which mode is selected. If you press backspace at the start of the input while in bash or referral mode, it exits that mode instead of trying to delete text.

4b7158cceb1db887ffbcdf0de8daff9da37ee0bd.text: When you type a referral code into the CLI, it now automatically adds the 'ref-' prefix if missing and corrects the casing, so you can type 'ABC123' or 'REF-ABC123' and it will be standardized to 'ref-ABC123' before use. If the system fails to fetch your account details (like your name or subscription info), it will now throw a clear error instead of silently returning nothing. You'll notice fewer confusing mismatches when entering referral codes and clearer error messages if something goes wrong with account-related commands.

282c13d7bfc774cac3a990c988aa21586a6e3762.text: When you're chatting with the assistant and press the exclamation point to switch into bash mode (for running terminal commands), it now switches modes only when you type exactly one exclamation point by itself. Previously, typing just an exclamation point at the start of your message would remove that character and keep the rest of your text intact, which sometimes led to unexpected behavior. Now, pressing the exclamation point by itself cleanly enters bash mode and clears your input, so there's no confusion about what text remains when you start typing your command.

c397e4bb6633591bbc0be0ca45900bf89bd1453c.text: The chat tool you use in the terminal now has a new /referral command that lets you redeem a friend's referral code for bonus credits, or type the command with no code to see and copy your own shareable referral link. Behind the scenes, the way the tool handles special input modes switched from a simple yes/no toggle to tracking a named mode (default, bash, or referral), so adding new modes in the future is easier. If you looked, you'd see a small banner appear in referral mode that either shows your link or says it's loading.

e2ac3956fd4bbb82821a0b344e7968826d14ead8.text: When you type a command like /help, /login, or a referral code that starts with ref-, the program now handles it through a clear, organized lookup table instead of a long list of special cases. This makes it easier to see which commands exist, what short forms they accept, and where each one sends you. You won't notice anything different right away unless something previously broke; the change is a behind-the-scenes tidy-up that makes future command-related tweaks safer and easier.

b3f58f1583db98cf167f1d2bbdfbc14633a78799.text: When you ask the command-line tool to work in its highest-powered mode, it now delegates the toughest coding steps to a newer, more capable assistant model instead of the one it used before. If you watch it solve a complex edit, you'll see it quietly hand off planning, editing, and review work to this stronger model running behind the scenes. The older, faster assistant is still used for everyday tasks, so lighter jobs stay quick. Live today for anyone using the max mode.

85840c1a181ec17e838f801af87b2b9b01367759.text: When you switch between the normal, max, and plan assistant modes in the CLI, your chosen mode now sticks around after you close and reopen the terminal instead of resetting to the default each time. Behind the scenes, your last-selected mode is saved to a small settings file on your computer, and when the CLI starts up, it reads that file to restore your preference; only the three valid modes are allowed to be saved, and if the file is missing or corrupted, it falls back to the default. The CLI version was bumped at the same time, so this behavior is live today for anyone using the current release.

7d389c79603ffef1b287f51493b37f177be2c7ec.text: The row of buttons that appears beneath each assistant reply (copy, timer, and feedback thumbs) has been pulled out of the main message component into its own self-contained building block. This means the main message display no longer has to manage the logic for showing whether a reply is still generating, how long it took, or the thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback state, so future tweaks to the copy button, elapsed-clock, or feedback controls can be made in one place without touching the larger message-rendering code. Nothing you see or click changes right now the buttons work exactly as before, but the codebase is now cleaner and easier to maintain behind the scenes.

7e2ec29d0364ae0695fbedbda96acd28f950c322.text: If you watched the agent work, nothing now looks or feels different; the behind-the-scenes wiring for how individual agent actions (like adding a note, recording a sub-goal, or searching code) get processed got reorganized. The code that runs each action now returns its result directly instead of wrapping it in a second helper object, which cleans up how the system keeps track of things internally. You would only notice this if you poked at the agent's internal structure: the extra bookkeeping object and its associated type are gone, replaced by a simpler, direct response. This is the kind of change engineers make to keep the system stable and easier to maintain long-term, not something that changes what you see.

983639b668d1cc516831efb9419a9d975d92b17a.text: The agent no longer keeps a duplicate copy of the conversation while it works. Previously, it stored messages in two places: a temporary working list and the main conversation history, then copied them back together. Now it writes directly to the main conversation history, dropping the extra copy. If you watched the process closely you'd see fewer memory hiccups and less redundant bookkeeping behind the scenes.

db2ca99cf368616723532902ed6e235764f3b653.text: The assistant's instruction manual is no longer being stuffed inside a shared pocket that every tool reaches into; instead, each tool now receives the instruction manual directly as its own parameter when it is called. This is a behind-the-scenes cleanup that changes how the assistant pieces are connected internally, without altering what you see or how the assistant behaves when you interact with it. Engineers working on the assistant will need to pass the instruction manual explicitly in fewer places now, but everyday users will not notice any difference in performance or features.

a7162eb89147da6766c7f3a6c4a462233712bd0a.text: A small clipboard icon now appears at the bottom of each message in the CLI, letting you copy the full message text to your clipboard with a single click. Hovering over the icon expands it from a small symbol to [⎘ copy], and clicking saves the message exactly as it appears. The assistant also copies messages to the clipboard almost instantly when they arrive—dropping the delay from two seconds to a quarter of a second—so pasted text shows up faster. Both changes are live today.

08a7817c1c838ec7cdebaf79ca7c965080490573.text: The system has renamed a couple of internal labels it uses to describe tools (like the assistant's search or coding helpers) so they follow a more standard naming convention, which makes the tool descriptions show up more consistently and clearly. It also removed a validation step on the server that was checking incoming messages before processing them, meaning messages are now accepted and handled without that extra filtering layer. If you use the agent, you'd notice tool call descriptions reading more predictably, and the backend processes WebSocket messages with one less validation hurdle. These changes are live and take effect immediately for anyone interacting with the agent runtime over a WebSocket connection today.

bd4783f5a274f641b8397c5dc54f7ec6cf1514d7.text: When you ask the assistant to do a thorough code review (the "max" mode), it now uses Google's Gemini model instead of GPT-5 to compare multiple review suggestions and pick the best one. You won't see any menus change, but behind the scenes the assistant spawns several reviewer agents at once, collects their feedback, and lets Gemini choose which comments to surface to you. This only affects the detailed review step you opted into; everyday, faster reviews are unchanged.

b3c4c6eb3f506c1a924a0017b5c0c51182b1a08c.text: When you type something the program doesn't like, instead of seeing one big error message at the very top or bottom of your screen, you'll now see a small pop-up box attached directly to the message where the problem happened. This makes it clearer which part of what you typed caused the issue, so you can fix it without hunting through a general error list. The program still catches the same mistakes; it just shows them closer to where they occur.

9a112b81ee00de1ca0b1a37baca1fd690857420d.text: When you interact with the assistant through the command line, you can now type commands directly into your system shell by typing the word 'bash' or an exclamation mark at the start of your message, which keeps every following command running in that shell mode until you turn it off. The input area also hides the mode toggle while you are in bash mode, giving you a little extra room, and pressing Escape clears your current input instead of doing nothing. This is live today for anyone using the command line version of the assistant.

4c9ea8c6a70b5c8f93c498d2bbdab2cd5be618cc.text: When you click away from the terminal window, the blinking text cursor in the input box now stops blinking instead of continuing to flash while the window is unfocused. The app detects whether your terminal supports focus tracking by waiting for a moment when you first click back into the window, and only then enables the blinking behavior; until that first focus confirmation arrives, the cursor stays steady. This affects anyone typing at the command-line chat prompt and using a terminal that reports focus events to the app.

83a4bfe07f54a7f57b4113d5a721808b10825acf.text: The default code review step in the project pipeline now uses Google's Gemini model instead of the previous generic reviewer. If you look at the project's automated workflow, you would see the review stage is sourced from a newly added Gemini-based reviewer definition, while the higher-tier review path still uses GPT-5. This change applies to the default review path for contributors today.

c0f35bea0a53ef0a7958fb98c7668ad80c21dafa.text: You can now share your custom agents from the command line by running the new publish command, which sends your local agent templates to the backend server. Before uploading, the tool checks that you are signed in and handles network errors; if something goes wrong, it tells you a message instead of crashing. This works today: when you run the command, it intercepts the request before the main app starts, uploads your agents over a secure connection, and then exits. If you tried it before this update, that command did not exist.

05d94aa57087efb9bd2d9a9c9eb7f1213f66ee15.text: When the CLI shows you multiple AI assistants of the same type working side by side, they now get labeled with numbers to tell them apart—like seeing "Sonnet #1" and "Sonnet #2" instead of two identical "Sonnet" names. This only happens when more than one assistant of the same kind appears together; a single assistant still shows its plain name. Behind the scenes, the numbering logic was moved into a dedicated helper and calculates each assistant's position among its siblings before the label is drawn. It is live today as part of the CLI.

a699bc369f2f25900e4f3af0411d4bf507745b25.text: The assistant system has been simplified so that one of its two backup editors is no longer an option. One of the assistant's older helper tools, specifically the one that used a different AI model (Gemini), has been removed, and any jobs that used to automatically switch to that editor now always use the new main editor instead. This means the set of editors the assistant can pick from is smaller, and some older backup worker files have been moved into an archive folder. This change affects how the assistant coordinates its editing process internally.

5c377ee1a4e4a7d7d2e4e12ee8f5b862fcd1db8e.text: The coding assistant that helps you review and pick the best version of your code now has just two modes instead of several: a standard mode and a max mode. If you choose the max mode, the system will use a more powerful model to generate and compare multiple drafts before settling on the final version. The older options that let you swap in different AI providers have been removed, so the choice is simpler but less flexible.

98f07dd7fb0a63a48e64aa38200065139812ee04.text: When you run the development version of the CLI tool, it now reads the SDK code in its original source form instead of first compiling a separate copy. If you ran the development command before, you may have seen it silently rebuild the SDK behind the scenes as a fallback; that fallback step is gone, so the dev command starts up directly from the source. The type-checking step also no longer builds the SDK types beforehand, and a few helper scripts and special module declarations were removed since they are no longer needed. This is live today and affects anyone running the CLI in development mode.

666b406a3a8eb7e05f5a1e266501426ff5e1d65c.text: When you ask the assistant to do something and it temporarily can't (like the server being busy), it now automatically tries again on its own instead of giving up right away, waiting a bit longer between each attempt. If something looks wrong with your login details, the system now treats that the same as a login failure so it cleans up properly and can try again with corrected credentials. These improvements are active in the software development kit that powers the assistant today, so you should see fewer dropped conversations caused by temporary errors.

97e8da47b7b1afc60b74c77a65dad1b03cb6f850.text: When you chat with the assistant in the command line, parts of the screen that show your messages now refresh less often and feel more responsive. The program now keeps certain background instructions steady so they don't restart every time something changes, which means your feedback buttons and message areas behave more predictably. You will notice smoother interactions without extra loading flicker while the assistant is thinking or waiting for your reply. This improvement is live today and works automatically with no setting to turn on.

405e44db858954df8326fe7a6fea528a24e364b1.text: You will no longer see the 'Showing latest X of Y messages' notice at the top of chat history. Instead, all messages load directly without the threshold or scroll-up behavior. The underlying mechanism that hid older messages and kept a count has been removed, so chat history renders as plain text without any virtualization logic.

ed6e1d350c8d06b15507c0b82ce54a65bf0a01d2.text: After installing the Codebuff command-line tool, you now see a friendly message in your terminal that walks you through how to start using it—telling you to open a project folder and run "codebuff" to begin. The tool still secretly removes an older version of itself during setup, but now also prints these simple getting-started steps right in the terminal. If you install the desktop app version separately, that version's setup no longer waits to check for typing errors or run tests first, so it installs faster.

07c317efa31f9cbb124d001bd1d75765f81015d9.text: You will now see clearer, more specific messages when the assistant fails to log in or loses its internet connection, telling you what went wrong in plain language instead of a generic error. The fix also makes pressing Ctrl+U (the shortcut that deletes a line of text you are typing) behave correctly on long messages that wrap across multiple lines, clearing back to the start of the visible line rather than the original line. These improvements to on-screen error text and text editing are live today in the command-line tool.

956847a245a4e27dc28944d5383f52f75f040a16.text: When you ask the CLI to send a message and the server doesn't respond (due to a temporary network hiccup or a busy server), the tool now automatically retries the request a few times using an exponentially increasing wait between attempts instead of failing right away. While it's retrying, a small banner appears at the bottom of the status bar letting you know that your message is waiting in line to be delivered. This only affects people running the CLI tool directly on their computer; if you're using a web interface or a pre-built app, you won't see any difference. The retry and banner are part of the live behavior today, not just a setting that's been turned on but unused.

14efb668c81fd4179c4c7c316074e0490899497e.text: Your assistant's helper-agents now get their answers back in a simpler wrapper. Instead of one agent's result being hidden behind a nested 'output' field, the content you actually read sits directly under the message, and each tool's name shows up once at the top level so it's easy to spot which tool produced which line. This is already live for anyone using the helper-agent kits, and the cleanup touched over sixty agent definitions, but you won't see extra steps appear; the only difference is the structure is flatter and easier to follow when you glance at the conversation log.

13a08d80e24c9b421d2f26752ba2d6fd68653d11.text: When you paste text into the CLI's multi-line input box, it now inserts the pasted content at the cursor position, just like before. The difference is that the software now uses the text field's built-in paste feature instead of a separate helper program that was doing the same job. This simplifies the code but doesn't change how pasting works for anyone using the command-line tool.

aa78173fbc0077512011a1b80bec9b6ddb9f1778.text: The CLI tool now has better control over timed actions that used to cause glitches. A new system lets it schedule and replace timers by name, so if the same timed task is started again, the old one is canceled instead of piling up and potentially leaking memory. It also cleans up all remaining timers automatically when it closes, preventing leftover actions from running after you're done. This makes background tasks in the command-line interface more reliable and responsive, especially during rapid updates or shutdown.

6c564150707150f8c838ff312c839dffdbc13b6b.text: If you use the Codebuff assistant and it suddenly can't reach its servers or your login expires, it now fails in clearer, more predictable ways instead of a generic crash. The assistant will recognize whether the problem is a bad login (like a wrong password) or a flaky network (like a spotty Wi-Fi drop), and it will automatically retry sending your message up to three times, waiting longer between each attempt (roughly doubling from one second to a maximum of eight seconds each time). This behavior is already live today and built right into the Codebuff tool you interact with when it tries to send or recover messages.

6ad51cc53cbb42ea703dec7a8fb785fd94d9f4d3.text: When you open Codebuff in your terminal, you'll now see a notice at the top telling you about a recent visual update and inviting you to share feedback with the /feedback command. A revert command (npm install -g codebuff@legacy) is shown so anyone who prefers the old look can opt out. This notice appears by default for all users the first time they launch the updated app, and it stays dismissed once you click the close button, tracked by a new visibility setting the program remembers between sessions.

174a50a54c312498a093de80f3ec16c356aef3fa.text: When you run the usage command in the CLI, the assistant now shows your quota information through a refreshed system that avoids making the same request over and over, even if the banner is hidden and shown again. The usage banner you see will update automatically when you view it, and the assistant no longer needs a separate step to handle errors when fetching your data, since the new system manages that quietly in the background.

979ee8921cd8ab662050d2321fb6408b9e591d3a.text: The text box where you type your message to the assistant, along with its helper buttons and menu, was pulled out into its own reusable section of the program. If you use the command-line version of the assistant today, your typing area behaves exactly the same — you will not notice anything different on screen or in how you interact with it. Behind the scenes, the team took the old, bulky input code and split it into a neater package, while keeping the rest of the chat window untouched.

8e91efe579ef943192965ebf293613d30cea3125.text: A new guide explaining how to test AI coding assistants was added. The guide lays out step by step how the testing system gives each AI the same task, lets them work at the same time, and then checks their answers with three independent AI judges that each compare the work against the real example. It also shows how the system can run test commands or install tools after each AI finishes and how to read the final score reports. If you ever wanted to see how different AI coding helpers rank against one another on real programming problems this guide tells you exactly how that process runs today.

1df0789330bbb5b37778fc7427c7a9d00d04bcc1.text: When you run the usage command in the CLI, your credit and billing information now appears in a persistent banner at the top of the screen instead of a temporary message that disappears after printing. The banner stays visible for 60 seconds before auto-hiding, and you can close it manually with a close button. It also adjusts how it wraps its text based on your terminal window width, using warning-themed borders for visibility. This change is live today for anyone running the CLI who checks their usage.

adfbddada89a400496438ee1acbad5535695d75a.text: You know the little usage banner that shows your credits at the top of the CLI? It now refreshes itself automatically while it's visible, so the numbers you see stay current without you having to do anything. When a run finishes and the banner is showing, the CLI quietly reloads your usage data in the background and updates the display; if something goes wrong, it just keeps going instead of breaking your chat. This is live today — you'll notice the banner updating on its own as you work.

3d3296b4ea103f3c01c2f2683fb9131c1bd7fe2b.text: A new version of the code-writing helper is now available that uses Google's Gemini model instead of the usual OpenAI model to draft code edits. When this Gemini-backed helper is turned on, it swaps out the normal editor and skips the step that asks the AI to 'think out loud' before writing, while all other helpers keep that thinking step. The change is already live in the codebase today, behind a flag that switches the editor role, so anyone running that configuration now gets Gemini-powered editing by default.

e9d1ea54241dc3e7fbc4bc6f095b629e39adb630.text: You may have noticed that messages in the command-line assistant were sometimes appearing as blank screens instead of showing your conversation history. Behind the scenes, the team upgraded the interface library so that chat responses now display correctly without disappearing. The fix is live today, so the next time you run the assistant from a terminal, messages should appear normally instead of as empty space.

0ec450befdd1e05d7accdeb197863e3ce5b0ff8d.text: You now check your account's billing and usage directly through the web dashboard's billing section instead of the older CLI tool command. The assistant can now look up usage data for entire organizations, not just individual accounts. If you're an organization admin, you'll see team-wide usage and billing details that were previously unavailable.

ce8746f8d07699fe23e93474228befa70626b689.text: The Codebuff assistant (used inside Cursor and other editors) now brings its own private copy of ripgrep — a tool it needs to search through your code — and unpacks it automatically when you start a session, so you no longer have to install or configure ripgrep yourself. This matters only if you previously ran into errors because ripgrep was missing or the wrong version; the assistant simply works now without that step. You won't see ripgrep anywhere, but if you open your editor's logs you might notice a brief message about it extracting the tool the first time it runs after the update.

bf3c551cdc5273e913222fa3304231bd2edc66d3.text: You can now publish new versions of the assistant's command-line tool by choosing whether you want a small bug-fix update, a medium feature update, or a big breaking update, and a helper script will handle bumping the version, packaging the downloaded files, uploading them to GitHub, and creating a release announcement for you. This automates what used to be a manual, error-prone process of editing version numbers and uploading binaries by hand, so releases are less likely to break or get half-finished. The system also quietly removes the downloaded program files from your computer if you later uninstall it, cleaning up after itself. This is already live: the automation is wired up and ready for the next time developers need to ship a new version of the command-line assistant, and it

1816b44e4fbfc3c1759cb4fb3289d89be63229c2.text: The assistant software you install on your computer now comes with its core engine already packed inside the installation folder, instead of downloading it separately the first time you run it. You'll notice the installation completes in one step with no follow-up download, and the engine files are removed automatically when you uninstall the program. This only affects people installing a fresh copy today; existing installations keep working as before.

9eebdf564d275d8fd08af15dbccf386a11fb4938.text: The team deleted an old, unused configuration for a specialized code-reviewing assistant variant that was never actively used. You would not notice anything different in the product today, since this was simply removing leftover settings that no features or users relied on. This is behind-the-scenes cleanup of dead code, with no impact on your experience or any live functionality.

349207f275379f7a4070094f7183c47a4cbe8cc0.text: When you start the coding assistant from a terminal, the setup work it needs to do is now split into two clearer steps behind the scenes. The main startup logic in the entry point was moved into two new focused modules: one that handles the core app initialization (finding your project folder, enabling data structures, and loading your color theme) and another that deals only with detecting your terminal's color support through a background probe. This is purely internal housekeeping that reorganizes how the assistant prepares itself before showing its interface, so it should feel no different to you, but the separation makes the OSC color-detection path easier to isolate and maintain.

2bf17736b6335ff9b84f30e0cf4c849cee0561a3.text: Starting today with version 3.2.5, the CLI tool downloads its core program directly into its own folder as part of installation, instead of first unpacking it during the release process. This means that when you uninstall the tool, the downloaded program is automatically removed along with everything else, leaving no leftover files behind. If you look at your system, you’ll no longer find an extra hidden folder storing the program separately. Note: This change applies to the CLI release-staging installer and may not affect your current installed version.

c07be589486b045d51cf600a1718cbaa589b98cf.text: The Buffy orchestrator (an internal coding agent) now has a new path to run on Google's Gemini 3 Pro model instead of Anthropic's Claude Sonnet or OpenAI's GPT-5.
