If you opt into the Gemini-flavored definition, the orchestrator and its best-of-N editing/selection sub-agents swap in the Gemini model, and the set of available sub-agents is dynamically trimmed to match. In other words, the internal agent family now includes Gemini-based variants that use the same workflow but a different model under the hood.

d1991436ee87e7a50aa5cd1c8955c64e174dbe1d.text: When you submit feedback on a response in the CLI, it's now tracked more reliably across the interface, so the feedback controls won't accidentally react after you've already sent your input. The way feedback is collected has been reorganized behind the scenes, making it easier to manage your feedback choices and ensuring the system remembers what you've already submitted. You may also notice new, clearer options for what kind of feedback you're giving.

60e64003fc6cb8f91ece050371c5f18470cdcb96.text: Starting November 18, 2025, the multi-model reasoning pipeline that compares several draft answers before picking the best one now uses a single evaluator regardless of which underlying model is asked to think. Instead of running one of two separate evaluators when the newer model is selected, the system always routes every comparison through the same single evaluator component, and it no longer prepares, loads, or falls back to the separate newer-model-specific evaluator. The older-model-specific evaluator is also gone entirely. You would only notice this if you were watching which helper gets called during reasoning: it is now always the same one. This change applies only to the internal best-of-n reasoning step and does not affect how the drafts themselves are generated.

5dc3cb8f5d3c297141fdf29dc54d7b791705484c.text: You can now get a smarter writing assistant. When your agent is set to its top-tier "max" mode, it now uses the same high-quality model (Claude's Sonnet) that the default editor uses, instead of a different model (GPT-5). This means the way it picks the best of several drafted edits is unified onto one proven system. You would notice it by watching the editor draft multiple solutions and then have one consistent reviewer choose the best one, rather than two different reviewers being used. The old, separate selector that used GPT-5 has been removed.

63695fd1cb54c891cbf6a049de88203803551ea0.text: The team turned off several experimental helper modes inside the assistant that tried different ways of reviewing code or making decisions, then deleted the four switch files that turned those modes on. From your side nothing looks different: the assistant still runs the same default helpers instead of those extra ones. You would only notice if you were looking at the backstage configuration, where those options and the files that defined them are gone, leaving only the standard set of helpers to run.

94368ccf248874fa609a0c64672134d6f3eff6b2.text: You now have a new way to pick up a conversation where you left off in the command-line tool. Instead of starting a fresh chat every time you open the assistant, you can run it with a flag that reloads the most recent conversation, including the context and progress from before. If there's no prior chat to resume, it tells you that instead of crashing. This works today whenever you start the command-line tool with the new option.

9aba6179f07afd42472ea2c8568b264599736692.text: When you talk to the assistant in the CLI, things like thinking blocks and agent lists now start collapsed by default and remember whether you opened them, instead of the screen tracking all of that state separately behind the scenes. The app still stores that open/closed choice, but it does so right inside each message, which simplifies how the chat components work. You would notice that expanded sections stay open if you opened them, while everything else stays tucked away until you pull it up again.

02673a5a36c56079121349f82cf8ef8292adafdc.text: The CLI now offers a /feedback command that opens a dedicated input area, and every message shows a feedback icon you can click to open that same area. You pick a category (good, bad, bug, or other), type your thoughts, and submit, with Escape cancelling and Ctrl+C clearing the entry; the feedback text is kept separate from the main chat input so typing does not shift or resize the chat box.

415d0e7edf82282fe445e5e53a4eb9b400c129f7.text: When you ask the writing assistant to come up with multiple versions of a solution, it can now do that directly in one go instead of spinning up a separate helper agent for each version. Behind the scenes, the assistant hands off the request to a built-in 'generate several' option, and all the different answers come back together in a single list for you to pick from. The old helper agents that used to handle this step have been removed, so the whole process is simpler and faster. You won't see two different agents running side by side anymore; you'll just get the batch of responses in one place.

0113870be5722e9f1d35500ebd97af8f509a77a6.text: The CLI tool removed a block of internal code that handled keyboard shortcuts like '/login', '/logout', and '/exit'. This code was no longer being used by the main program, so deleting it cleans things up without breaking any features you use. If you typed those commands now, nothing would happen differently than before—the removal only stripped out unused logic that had already been replaced. This is live today as behind-the-scenes cleanup with no visible effect on how the tool works.

9f957b42e3f0b7bf8a9c2bee7c06ece6c64b34ec.text: If you or your integration cancels a run (for example, by stopping mid-response or timing out), the agent now stops immediately instead of continuing to call tools or send output. A cancellation signal travels through the same internal pathways used during normal runs—including the SDK's run() function, the core agent loop, and the real-time WebSocket connections—so the stop is respected consistently across the entire flow. When you cancel, you see a brief 'Run cancelled by user' error instead of partial tool calls or streamed output finishing.

67fc4211757842802ad66af074415327313236a9.text: The assistant can now talk directly to the newest GPT-5 model when you ask for multiple responses at once, skipping the usual middleman server that routes requests to different AI providers. If you look for it, you’ll notice a new settings field has been renamed to make GPT-5 think harder, and a placeholder for a new API key now sits alongside the existing ones. This is live today for any request that asks for GPT-5 and multiple answers, so you’d get a faster, more direct reply.

e8e8a05fcb281138c308840f70c28154e8cb3b42.text: The agent system now includes a new specialized assistant that uses an advanced model to help make tough implementation decisions, and the team can choose to activate it when orchestrating tasks. When enabled, this assistant is added to the team lineup alongside other specialists and receives extra instructions to consult it at key decision points. You would notice a new orchestrator option available today that includes this decision-making assistant, identifiable by its nickname 'Buffy the Max Decision Maker Orchestrator,' when selecting task configurations.

90e3928e01d3d9600e466ed7c4d8c06492a4f80d.text: If you use Codebuff's assistant tooling to analyze a project that lives in a Git repository, the SDK can now run Git commands through a custom shell handler you provide instead of always using the built-in one. This matters when your environment restricts or redirects how shell commands execute, because the initial project snapshot (files, recent changes, and commit history) is now fetched via whatever command runner you specify. If you don't supply a custom handler, it falls back to the standard Node.js shell, so everyday behavior stays the same. The feature is in place and ready to use.

0aed1a8c261a72a8b5f60878d41693f4c6b846f2.text: The status area at the bottom of the CLI chat has been completely redesigned into a single, cleaner bar. Previously, the status indicator showed text like the assistant's current state and elapsed time, but it was a separate component; now it is consolidated into a new StatusBar that also includes a scroll-to-bottom button that appears only when you have scrolled up away from the latest message. The developers also added a pause queue feature, allowing you to temporarily stop and resume the incoming message stream, which is especially useful if you need to catch up on text that is scrolling by too quickly. Additionally, the text input area's cursor now correctly handles tabs and control characters, preventing it from jumping to incorrect positions when editing your prompt.

e6fbb859c88a1211185293e12729a369875e7ead.text: When you ask the software to write code for you, it now uses a faster method that tries to get the whole job right in a single pass instead of generating multiple drafts and picking the best one. This only affects users selected for the new 'base2-with-editor-implementor-gpt-5' configuration in the internal testing environment, and it reduces the number of tasks running at once to keep things stable during evaluation.

99166d1235b91ccda0f08ade523e00c5be5c439d.text: The command-line assistant used to draw every kind of message—lists of helper agents, formatted text, thinking notes, tool actions, and step-by-step plans—all from one giant, tangled block of code. Now those different pieces are each handled by their own dedicated drawing routine, so the code is easier to read and fix. You wouldn't notice a change in what appears on your screen today, but the display logic behind the scenes is cleaner and less likely to break going forward.

3158a6f1ae2d7f078f8cf682a48a83f6c8cab8c2.text: When the assistant uses the built-in tool to look something up in a library's documentation, the command-line interface now draws a compact one-line entry for it instead of leaving it blank. You would see a single bullet line showing the library name and the topic it's reading about. This only covers displaying that summary line; there's no button to expand or collapse the details. The change is live today as part of version 1.0.512.

5aff4e9abb7e273137e9897ed92e08089e85afca.text: You can now tell CodeBuff to use your own OpenRouter API key instead of using theirs. When you run a command, CodeBuff will check for an environment variable named CODEBUFF_BYOK_OPENROUTER and, if it's set, send that key along in a special header so the request is billed to your OpenRouter account. The system was also updated to track these messages and skip charging Codebuff credits when this happens. This is live today for anyone who runs Codebuff with their own OpenRouter key.

7e505fbceb0d2c91b30efceb72f8fa23075e3d00.text: When you ask the assistant to look something up on the web or read documentation, it now sends those searches through Codebuff's own web service instead of the third-party services it used before. Any credits you spend for these searches are reported back by that service and added to your running total, rather than the assistant trying to calculate the cost itself before charging you. If you use web search or docs search, this is already working now, and you'd see the cost show up accurately in your usage. The change also removes older checks that required extra identifiers to be present before a search could run.

fa9ae200a8deda63f5cf9923794dbd56a1c79403.text: A second automated assistant has been added to the team that checks code changes. It affects the internal agents that review edits, not anything you interact with directly. If you looked, you would see a new agent variant named like a code-reviewing orchestrator and a new option that turns on automatic code review after edits. This is live today in the internal agent configuration only.

bde7e88d8f549ae4e56913c25ca9e5b07384692c.text: When you write a multi-line message in the CLI and press the up or down arrow keys to navigate between lines, the cursor now moves to the correct line based on how the text actually appears on screen. Previously, the program ignored how lines wrap when they get too long, so pressing up or down could jump the cursor to a completely different part of your message. This affects anyone typing or editing long, wrapped messages in the terminal interface.

166714289a14e603703e5a97e3eb9e7b5fc299e5.text: The code review assistant now has specialized versions built for the latest model, so when that model is in use it picks the right setup instead of the previous one. The review results no longer include a separate explanation field showing how the choice was made. If you use the review feature with the new model, you'll get reviews tailored to that model without the extra reasoning text. This only affects internal reviewers and works automatically once the new model is selected.

2dd14a8796d9eb5e03b00d4d8f713f044fc3f6e9.text: The assistant can now run several code-review agents at the same time, compare their different suggestions for fixing your code, and then pick the best one to show you instead of just giving the first review it comes up with. This ensemble approach to reviewing code is turned on for the default and GPT-5 versions of the tool, so it's available today whenever those review agents are used. If you look under the hood, you'd see one 'orchestrator' agent spawning a few 'worker' agents to each write a review, followed by a final 'selector' agent that chooses the winner.

56d7380c078b5768aad603721901a06a31c2fbff.text: The agent runtime can now answer questions by searching the web or product docs, in addition to using its built-in knowledge. When you ask something that needs up-to-date or specific information, it will fetch relevant results from those sources and include them in its reply. This means explanations can be more accurate and current rather than relying solely on what the assistant already knows.

3e90de9474241a1f14dfd9cb1639ab10178b0823.text: When you click and drag on buttons in the terminal app (like the scroll-to-bottom arrow or the branch toggle), the app used to crash because the text got accidentally selected during the drag. The app now uses a single, consistent button element across all its clickable areas that actively prevents text from being selected during mouse interactions, so dragging no longer triggers a crash. If you look, every clickable control behaves the same way and won't highlight text mid-click. The fix is live today for anyone using the terminal-based chat interface.

f98abc6747424c58719df37a51f6b84c20983172.text: When you start the app, it now figures out and applies your color theme (dark or light mode, plus your terminal and editor settings) all from one central place instead of looking it up from a separate theme list. The theme it picks now also gets a built-in name label so other parts of the app can identify which look is active. If you watched the startup sequence you would see theme detection and setup happen in a single coordinated step rather than being scattered across separate files. This is live today for anyone running the command-line version.

519af8336763e7adef1740f28d0e5442e21bbe9b.text: You can now type `/usage` or `/credits` at the command prompt to see how many credits you have left and when your quota resets. The assistant looks up your account balance from the server and shows it to you right in the chat, with color highlighting to make low balances easy to spot. This works immediately for anyone who is signed in; if you are not logged in, it will ask you to log in first. The list of available commands in the slash-command menu has also been updated so `usage (credits)` now appears as a built-in option instead of staying hidden as an unused placeholder.

fe344e336954a2f3fb7ec20e5b5f8669b7569448.text: The assistant that translates your requests into the right format for the AI model now always picks a return value, even in edge cases where it previously left one out. This stops the system from throwing a type-check error during its own build checks, so the conversion step finishes cleanly and reliably. You wouldn't notice anything different when using it, but the underlying process that prepares your prompt no longer fails unexpectedly. The fix is live today.

267fadde6c1040b10f172801f22c71887f9357ea.text: The AI assistant can now work with a wider range of model providers right out of the box, without needing each one to be programmed in individually. Behind the scenes, the team copied and adapted the code that connects to OpenAI-style services into a shared internal toolkit, adding support for conversations, image inputs, structured responses, and usage tracking. If you looked closely, you'd see the system now understands extra details from each response (like which model was used or why it stopped) and can handle both full replies all at once and streamed responses chunk by chunk. This change appears to be live today and affects internal systems that rely on pluggable model providers.

3e8ea0f28e6db2832558a3ccd7aa75929ca6539b.text: The CLI interface has been refactored to reduce unnecessary screen redraws, especially during streaming responses. MessageBlock now splits its content rendering into a separate memoized component, and AgentBranchItem uses standard React composition with children instead of content props. Additionally, the debugging hook now checks for the 'dev' environment instead of development mode. These changes make the interface feel smoother and reduce flickering when content updates, particularly noticeable when watching agent responses stream in real-time.

fd4c93b3bfb2e431317665fc6cb87aab12607158.text: When you open the assistant in a terminal, it now asks your terminal a quick yes/no question to check whether the terminal supports special color commands before trying to use them, which prevents the program from freezing on terminals that don't understand those commands. It also gets better at figuring out which kind of command prompt (like PowerShell, bash, or zsh) you're using by checking your system settings, so it can correctly detect whether you're on a dark or light theme, especially if you use PowerShell on Windows. These updates apply to anyone running the assistant from a command-line terminal today.

c6b9afa2061bd4a1e20b1640ed273858e0765870.text: The command-line tool now shows a scroll-to-bottom button when there's more chat content above, and the status bar at the bottom has been redesigned to display elapsed time and connection status side by side. The timing and connection info update live during your session, and the toggle that switches between modes now lays out its pieces using a more stable arrangement so that animated text no longer causes display glitches. If you use the CLI chat, you\u2019ll see a new button to jump to the latest messages and a cleaner status line, with fewer visual hiccups when things are updating in real time.

a1aefce57da230dee0f784dbc22ad0c7bf3c735f.text: When you run the assistant through the command line, it no longer checks for a live connection every 30 seconds no matter what. Instead, it starts by checking within 10 seconds, and after several successful checks in a row it gradually waits longer between checks — 30 seconds, then a minute, then up to ten minutes — so it stops poking the server when everything is calm. The moment a check fails, it snaps back to checking every 10 seconds until things look healthy again. If you watch the logs, you would actually see messages noting when the wait gets longer or shorter, so the CLI now adapts how often it listens to the server based on whether the connection keeps looking good.

480358465d3d5ec1266aded222aff5c88af41c89.text: When you ask the assistant to tackle a really tough, open-ended problem, it no longer commits to its first train of thought. Instead, it now quietly generates several independent lines of reasoning in parallel, then privately compares them and keeps the strongest one before replying to you. The end result is that your answer reflects the best of multiple attempts rather than the first pass. This is now turned on for the models it ships with today.

946bf225ab7b2e053524aa25771b29338303fb5f.text: When you press Ctrl+C in the CLI, the first press now clears your current input line instead of immediately trying to quit, and the second press cleanly sends your usage statistics before exiting. If your conversation grows beyond 60 messages, only the most recent ones (plus a small buffer) are kept actively loaded and rendered on screen, while older ones are tucked out of view to keep the interface responsive. The slash command and @mention menus now intercept keyboard input more precisely, so navigating them with arrow keys or selecting an item won't accidentally trigger broader app shortcuts that happen to use the same keys. These refinements rolled out today for CLI users on the default setup, with the virtualization behavior kicking in automatically once your message count crosses the

2ff2d8eec8ff45929540bff08232b4e4464f8563.text: Developers added a behind-the-scenes debugging tool to the assistant's on-screen chat interface that silently tracks why individual message boxes pop up on your screen again. The tool is turned off by default, so you won't see anything change now, but it gives the team a way to catch and fix glitches that make parts of your chat window re-render unexpectedly. If you looked at the code, you'd see this tracking helper living alongside the existing code that already stops message boxes from updating unless something actually changed. Today it sits in place doing nothing yet, waiting for someone to flip its switch when they need to hunt down a rendering bug.

a9d2c6d98e6eedaad2e8a51a891427487fd486fc.text: When you ask the agent to find relevant files in a codebase, it now uses a single, faster built-in file-finder instead of the old specialized one that was deleted. That finder has also switched to a quicker AI model (Grok 4 Fast), so it should locate files more rapidly while reading up to 500,000 tokens of content. This affects the main task-planning agents and research helpers in the.agents directory, so you'll notice the file-search step in your plan or implementation runs a bit differently and completes faster. The change is live today; the deleted agent is gone, and all references point to the new one.

10a77c9cf193eaa4205656f7aff9ba657d7bc8e2.text: When the assistant reasons through a problem, you now see its thinking in a collapsible section that starts folded up, showing just a short preview instead of the full internal monologue. You can click the header to expand or collapse it at will. This applies to the reasoning text the assistant generates while answering, and it only appears in the command-line tool.

aa16ab568526a0366456d84cfe7d74dfc841e6b0.text: Behind the scenes, the internal labels used to identify certain specialized assistant tools have been flipped from 'best-of-n-editor' to 'editor-best-of-n' (with the GPT-5 variant adjusted the same way). Anyone who builds or maintains these internal tools will now see the reversed naming show up consistently in the configuration files and the instructions those tools follow when they spin up helpers. Functionally nothing behaves differently: the tools still do exactly what they did before, only the internal name has changed.

dcc0065a1c0ba72393551fd5c6456a307d8fee71.text: When you chat with multiple assistants in the terminal, the chat window now draws each assistant's messages using a single reusable block instead of rebuilding the layout logic every time. This makes the conversation area more responsive and easier to maintain behind the scenes, especially as messages stream in and you expand or collapse different assistants.

4b5f5e457dba3f9e2a25d53c69f5b72dcb13e8b1.text: The on-screen countdown that shows how long the assistant has been working now lives in its own independent display box, so when the seconds tick by only that small box redraws instead of the entire screen flickering. Any place that showed the timer now receives only the moment the assistant started, not the whole ticking object, which is what stops the rest of the interface from refreshing on every pulse. For the first second of activity you'll just see the word "thinking...", and after that the elapsed seconds appear as usual. This smoother behavior is in effect starting today.

8e9cece8db39ed643d192cde78ced48c799c5b56.text: The command-line version of the assistant now draws its title banner separately from the chat window. When you open the tool in your terminal, the logo and header appear in one dedicated strip while the conversation area below behaves independently, so resizing the window or switching themes updates only the relevant section. This split is already in place for everyone running the CLI starting with the 2025-11-08 release; no setting needs to be turned on.

674e32910ecd258cdbe5a385d3840d4e213ebf8a.text: When you're chatting with the assistant in the terminal and it's still thinking or generating a reply, each part of its response used to redraw itself over and over as new text trickled in, which could make the display look jumpy. Now, the terminal interface is set up so those in-progress message sections only refresh when their actual content changes, keeping your screen steadier while you wait. You'll still see the same streaming output, just without the extra, unnecessary flickering as things render.

61bec3cb33c0182c25640c2d39b15877a9d7f62b.text: When you ask Claude to find files matching a pattern, it now shows you a concise one-line summary in the chat instead of a verbose tool block. This makes the conversation flow more naturally while still telling you what was searched and where. The change applies to anyone using the CLI to interact with Claude's file-searching capabilities, and it is live today.

f949ce7dcdca3fbf5acfd0c4b50009fbd789d7bd.text: When you switch your assistant between its fast and deep reasoning modes in the command-line chat, a subtle horizontal divider line with the mode name (like "FAST" or "DEEP RESEARCH") now appears centered in the conversation to visually separate the sections. This divider shows up on the first message of a new mode and whenever you change modes, so you can easily tell when the assistant's behavior shifts. The feature is limited to the command-line interface chat rendering.

de236d698f9b83773b4fe50cfb93f0ed1600ff5e.text: When you type a message in the command-line assistant, your input now appears inside a single-line box with simple border characters, giving it a cleaner, more defined look. The shared border style was moved to a central location so all parts of the interface use the same borders, and the previous box styling code in the agent branch item was removed. If you use the CLI chat today, you'll notice the input area is now neatly wrapped in a box instead of being plain text.

3c4d47aa33f92d6dbde97c28f2db636c0242cf4f.text: When the assistant finishes a task, it now clearly tells you whether it succeeded before you try to use its work. Previously, you might have tried to use the results even when the task failed, causing confusing errors; now you must acknowledge a failure first before accessing results or error details. This affects anyone using the SDK to run agents programmatically, requiring a small adjustment in how you write code that calls the assistant.

e986021ad3703043db335b6e60ab5d8c54d0d3fb.text: When you type a message in the chat input box, the text now wraps accurately at the correct column instead of breaking a few characters early — so lines fit the full visible width without awkward premature line breaks. The width of the "FAST", "MAX", and "PLAN" mode toggle button is now calculated from its actual rendered size, preventing the input area from being narrower than expected. These fixes are live today and apply whenever the CLI chat input is displayed.

bddfb8a52d16bf2c1b157382e392a17f8e9af54d.text: When the CLI tool displays the result of a new action called "read subtree" — which reads a tree of files and folders — it now shows the list of paths it found instead of leaving you with a blank or generic result. The list appears as a simple comma-separated line inside the existing result display, with no expand/collapse option. You would notice this when inspecting a tool result that involves browsing nested directories; the concrete paths of the files visited are now visible. The change is live today, wired into the tool registry alongside the other display rules.

622efe1d9de19eeababd42d2999e49fe8402869d.text: When you start a coding assistant session without telling it which project files to load, it will now correctly go find those files on its own instead of silently skipping them. This fixes a bug where the assistant was always pretending it had an empty list of project files, which prevented it from discovering and using your actual project files during the initial setup. You'd notice that your assistant now properly recognizes and works with your project files right from the very first interaction, rather than missing them entirely. This update is live today.

569aa21fe301a74f85f40a3ccb2076ccdbf45035.text: When you interact with the assistant through the command line and it finishes what you asked, the response now shows a clear, bold "Task Complete" bullet point so you can easily see that your request was finished. Previously the completion of a task didn't have a distinct visual marker in the terminal output. This new on-screen element appears automatically whenever a task is marked as completed, making it easier for you to spot when the assistant has finished its work.

d34e86a543f72eb11f0f9838621009f07726377e.text: The assistant's file-searching tool now returns the correct files when you ask it to look in a specific folder. You would notice by getting only the matching files from that folder instead of getting files from the wrong location. The tool now properly filters files based on the folder you asked it to search in before using the search pattern.

3a4bb9426497e14f22ec68a982cf95cee262406b.text: When you tell the assistant to edit or create a file in the terminal, the list of changes now appears as color‑coded lines instead of plain text—added lines show up in greenish‑yellow and removed lines in orange‑red. Those colors and the side‑by‑side view come from a new built‑in display component that the editing tools now share. If you watch the terminal while a file gets written today, you’ll literally see the additions and deletions light up so you can spot what changed at a glance.

38c345fddae2e93c0411fd400c8b9f1158694321.text: The CLI chat interface was reorganized so that the single large screen file no longer handles everything itself; instead, it calls on smaller helper modules that each focus on one job—like managing login state, handling what you type, watching terminal size, or showing validation warnings. You won't see anything different on screen right away, but the program will now be easier for developers to maintain and extend. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping that went live today.

a2aaf401d7a8857b5e12643832b10b438c5e867f.text: The toggle that switches between the assistant's speed modes was rebuilt so it now looks and behaves like a set of connected buttons instead of separate labels. You'll notice it expands automatically when you point at it with no delay, and it now avoids the quick pop-in and pop-out flicker that happened when you moved your mouse near it. This affects anyone using the command-line version of the tool who switches between the speed settings. It's live today as part of the latest command-line update.

0a30509a990ed2c22278282e35da2d4736ec06f9.text: When the assistant wants to show you the contents of several files it just read, it now draws them in the chat with a nicer layout: the tool name sits on the first line next to the first file path, the next two file paths each get their own line, and any remaining paths are listed together in a compact row. This only affects how that particular tool result looks in the terminal-based CLI, so if you run the assistant in that interface you’ll notice the cleaner grouping whenever it reads multiple files at once. It went live today with no switches to flip.

181a942c1336c3e198f43edca9e10af0a0d2c9ac.text: When the assistant runs a tool like searching your code, the CLI used to have one central place that decided how every tool's results were displayed, and each tool's display rules were mixed in with that place. The display logic for each tool has now been moved into its own separate folder so that each tool (like code search or listing directory contents) describes how it should look on its own, and the main message panel now simply asks a central list which tool should handle the display. A reader would notice nothing visually different today, but the system is now set up so plugins or extensions can register their own custom ways of showing tool results.

982826a24ba6ed6d3f5ad0b1bc764d9df640dc9e.text: When the chat tool runs into a problem talking to the AI assistant, it now logs the error details in a clear, organized way instead of dumping a messy technical error message. If you ever had to ask for help debugging a failed chat, you'll now get a cleaner report with the error type, message, and where it happened, rather than a jumble of system text. The change is live today and only affects what gets recorded behind the scenes when something goes wrong.

2bb32123f60ddb7e4005bec14aae94e29a6404b3.text: The website that shows agents and their metrics now checks its data connection during the build process, so if the connection to the database is broken, the build fails immediately instead of silently producing an empty site. After the build, the site also warms up its cache automatically when the hosting platform (Render) pings its health check endpoint, meaning the agents data is ready to serve the moment real traffic arrives. The automated tests that previously ran one file at a time now run together in sequence, and the old interactive debugging tool that used to open on test failures has been removed, so if something breaks, engineers will need to reproduce the issue locally rather than debugging it live.

d965302b24714790de558e0250541d964f2ccd44.text: The assistant's file-reading helper (the part that explores your project folder and lists your files) now does its work in the background instead of pausing everything while it looks. This applies to the core engine, the command-line tool, and the evaluation test system, so operations like scanning directories, checking file stats, and reading gitignore rules no longer freeze the interface when they touch a slow disk or network drive. You would notice the experience stays responsive during project indexing, but only on versions dated November 4, 2025 or later; older builds still run those same file operations the old synchronous way.

8123b654697ca99500ce7f3f86f90ddde3c5eaaf.text: When you type messages in the command-line assistant and send them, those messages are now saved to a file called message-history.json in your settings folder. The next time you open the assistant, your previous messages will still be there so you can scroll back through them using the up and down arrow keys. The list is capped at 1,000 messages, and if the file ever breaks or contains corrupt data, it will simply start over with an empty list.

90a461c2e715db1aa14e174c1ce7893bd9bb47c1.text: The text-based interface you see while chatting now has a refreshed look: toggle switches and status labels appear as raised, button-like badges instead of flat boxed-in text, and the color scheme is applied through a new unified theming system. The behind-the-scenes code that manages these toggles was split apart and rebuilt so that agent-related displays and tool-related displays each have their own dedicated handling, and the markdown content shown in those toggles is now wrapped in a text container before being displayed, preventing the interface from crashing when it tries to render certain styled elements. This rollout also pins a specific version of the underlying terminal rendering library, adjusts how the login state is tracked during loading, and adds theme hooks that let the

3baf4009a3728d1df7aaa75537148ebee2048f61.text: When you start the assistant, it can now figure out your terminal's color theme by checking your terminal directly (right inside itself) instead of launching a separate mini-program to do it. While it checks your colors, your terminal won't process your keystrokes so nothing gets mixed up or lost during the check. If the developers want to see what happened during this check, they can turn on a special setting to log the details. This is live today the next time you open the assistant in your terminal.

31feeceadd86485c98003c47fe88d70126e4d4c9.text: When you open a project, the assistant now looks for instruction files using a specific order: it checks for a file named knowledge.md first, then falls back to AGENTS.md, and finally to CLAUDE.md if the others aren't present. Previously, it would grab whichever of those files it found without preferring one over the other. This means projects that include an AGENTS.md file will automatically be picked up and used without you having to manually tell the assistant where it is. The new behavior is live today, so you can drop any of those three files into your project and the assistant will find and read it according to this priority.

0a6469f29d60e48a1aa18c4a6fc74281273689a4.text: When you start typing a slash command, the suggestion menu will now match your keystrokes even if the letters aren't side by side, and it will highlight exactly which characters from your typing appear in each command name or alias. For example, typing 'lo' will still surface the logout command, and the matching letters within 'logout (signout)' will be shown in a different color so you can see why it appeared. This works for the agent and slash dropdown menus in the CLI today, so anyone triggering commands by partial names will see more forgiving and clearer matches.

291adef5277d360edd064523a5171b088904db0a.text: When the assistant is working through a list of tasks, it can now show you that list directly in the terminal interface. You'll see checkboxes next to each task—empty boxes for things not done yet and checked boxes for things that are finished—which makes it easier to track what's been completed and what's still pending at a glance. This only applies to the command-line interface that developers use to interact with the assistant.

22452ae741879dd71b30193efb8585f9f1419bdc.text: When you're chatting in the terminal and messages scroll past, the speed now changes smoothly based on how fast you're scrolling, instead of jumping at a steady rate. You'll notice that flicking through a long conversation feels more natural and less jerky, while casual scrolling stays controlled. The change only affects the terminal chat window, so your browser or desktop app behave exactly as before.

fdd062321c48cef702d2cbe04a635f597f994f4c.text: When you open CodeBuff in a terminal that reports its own colors (like certain terminal apps), it now picks the right light or dark theme automatically instead of guessing from the operating system. Your terminal is asked, 'Hey, what color is your background?' and CodeBuff matches that so text is easy to read. The login window also switches to a 'surface' color for its background instead of the main theme background, which keeps it looking consistent on more terminals. This works today in the CLI, for anyone whose terminal supports color-querying via OSC sequences.

328e5f2b849e1242af413cc72549754d1caba9ba.text: The store pages now go back to asking the API for the assistant list instead of pulling it directly from the database. That means the data-fetching logic lives in one consistent place again, and a leftover data file was deleted to match. If you browse the store you will not notice a difference: agents still load and show the same as before. Behind the scenes, your request now travels through the API route the way it did prior to the last inline update, so the same caching rules apply. This is effective today as part of the current deploy.

ed8123417d0efdc798db9c0b825982936b241ea0.text: After you ask the assistant to make a plan in the command-line version, two new buttons appear: one green 'Build Fast' and one red 'Build Max.' Clicking either button switches the assistant to the matching mode and immediately starts building with the command 'Build it!' instead of making you type it yourself. The change is live for anyone using the command-line tool today; no separate update is required on your end to see it.

3e5f667a18687dab45fb0713e3f550d2d907a1cd.text: You can now type /init in the chat to kick off a new session setup, similar to how you might type a command to create a file or run a search. This new command is wired into the existing set of slash commands you already use, so it behaves just like them — you enter it, hit enter, and the assistant starts whatever /init is programmed to do. The change also quietly reorganized some shared definitions into a common library that several parts of the app now reference, which is why files like message-block.tsx, branch-item.tsx, and login-modal.tsx show up in the change. It's live today, so if you open a fresh session, /init is available right away.

78f004a6bcef7bc20cec2153b55127a5629fde98.text: When you visit the store's agent listing page, the site now pulls the agent data directly from its local database instead of making a separate request to its own agents API. This removes an extra network hop that could fail during the site's initial generation, so the store page loads more reliably. The shared data-fetching logic now lives in one place that both the page and the API can use, and the change is live today.

22e79b1075811c2c7819a1d4a55763cc5bee77c5.text: A small behind-the-scenes cleanup in the command-line program made its internal code easier to follow and less error-prone, but it doesn't add any new features or change how the program behaves today. The team pulled the slash-commands (the /help, /login and similar shortcuts you type in) out of the main file and gave them their own home, and they also gave the two operating styles ('Fast' and 'Max') a single shared label so every part of the program agrees on what those names mean. You won't notice anything different while chatting, but the program is a bit tidier under the hood.

5ddb0fc5ffa9423bb1ffbc77f93ca30b0c0e92fb.text: The assistant can now produce a written implementation plan without actually writing any code or files, letting a human review the approach before any changes happen. It does this by adding a new planning mode that skips the step of automatically searching and reading project files. The instructions for the multi-attempt orchestrator were also tightened so it only uses the conversation history as context and never accepts a custom prompt. These changes are live today.

f1a628329680e646e1a2935eb032d53ebbea8ead.text: If you use the coding assistant in its internal testing mode, the program that coordinates multiple helper agents to write code has been simplified. Instead of maintaining two nearly identical coordinator programs that differed only by which AI model they used, they now share one coordinator that picks the right model automatically. The only visible effect is that the internal name used to reference the non-GPT-5 coordinator changed from 'best-of-n-orchestrator-fast' to 'best-of-n-orchestrator'; everything else you'd experience stays the same. The old coordinator program file was removed, but the GPT-5 version still exists and simply calls the shared coordinator internally.

9ada540db1aacc997d1ddadd035e472ff92c638f.text: If you use the "max" version of the system, it now automatically uses the newer GPT-5 model instead of requiring a separate setup for it. The old separate GPT-5 worker has been moved to an archive folder and the code has been simplified so that only the "max" option turns on GPT-5. This means you get GPT-5 capabilities right away when you choose the max mode, without any extra configuration.

35af4be2c9b2244cf105c95a6f98d6fa70e95db0.text: A background assistant that drafts code changes has been renamed from "orchestrator" to "editor", which better reflects its role of editing code by testing multiple options and applying the best one. The underlying process remains the same, but the updated name and slightly adjusted instructions make it clearer how it should be used when making code improvements.

c4525b44712ca41a7f4033b0e62143368d3e62a4.text: The AI assistant you interact with can now pull back a quick snapshot of the project's folder structure along with the key variables defined inside your files, all in one response. When you (or the assistant) ask it to review where things live in your project, it will hand back a condensed view that covers directories, file names, and parsed variables, and if that view gets too large it will trim the deepest files and drop file variables first until it fits a default size limit of roughly 4000 tokens. You would notice this as a faster, more focused answer about your project layout instead of a long, unfiltered dump of every directory and file.

e1f201cd8af7a5715d954f825612b6eaa46eb3a2.text: When you ask the assistant to search through code, it now looks through your files in a more reliable way that doesn't break on file names containing colons, hyphens, or unusual characters. Instead of stopping mid-search when it finds enough results, it can now cut off early, so you get your answer faster without waiting for a full scan. This works today when you use code search in the SDK, and you'd notice it handles tricky file names and search patterns it used to skip or misread.

f89e20d18a57f969a42bea09e939d8ed96a976d3.text: When the assistant finishes its work in a session, it now must explicitly signal that it is done using a new 'task completed' action instead of just stopping on its own. The developer notes that this action should be used when the request is fully fulfilled, when you need to ask the user a clarifying question, or when you are stuck. If you configure an assistant to have this action, it cannot end its turn any other way; only older assistants that lack the action will fall back to the previous behavior of ending turns implicitly or with an end-turn command. You would notice the difference as a new final step that requires a deliberate choice before a session closes.

080f9aa96b9ef948fc728b2ff672e2f06ef960ef.text: The assistant system can now choose to use a newer AI model called GPT-5 when working on coding tasks. This change is specifically enabled for internal agents that handle planning and writing code, and it is live today for those internal workflows. If you were looking at how the system picks which AI model to use, you'd see GPT-5 as an option and notice that the assistant now skips certain steps and tools it doesn't need when using this new model.

8952cbcc915f0cc3d0f70839b57f1aaa25344e60.text: A separate, older release channel for the Codebuff assistant binary is now published to npm, so people who depend on the previous generation of the tool can install a stable, known-good version even as the main version moves forward. The release runner now picks a platform-specific binary from GitHub, and if a downloaded binary is broken or was killed mid-download it deletes the bad file and tries again instead of leaving a corrupted install in place. This only affects the legacy distribution stream that users explicitly opt into; the main release flow is unchanged.

155ad8212eb92a904c328576c5868bcf81d8bbbb.text: The assistant templates that define how data types work in agent projects no longer rely on a third-party validation library called Zod to define their type shapes. Instead, they use straightforward TypeScript type declarations directly. This means the template files are simpler and load slightly faster, but the end-user experience of using or building an agent stays identical. There is no behavioral change for someone running or writing an agent; only the underlying template structure was refreshed.

118c2379ba39f52f9819c3bdb88abf2c64ed5301.text: If you run an agent in fast mode, it now automatically runs its best-of-n quality-checking layer instead of needing you to turn that on separately. The two standalone best-of-n entry points that existed before have been removed, so fast mode no longer has a separate toggle for this behavior—it always includes it. If you looked today, the fast configuration would no longer list the old separate agent flags and their dedicated files would be gone, leaving one consolidated path that always runs the best-of-n orchestrator in fast mode.

80ddeb3b78ea643c7dd930a00fd5a84c50c18e57.text: The CLI chat can now run agents directly on your own machine instead of needing a remote server, and it shows how long each response takes as it streams in. If you watch a conversation, you'll see elapsed time ticking next to the status indicator and inside each message block while the assistant is thinking, and the terminal now renders markdown tables and line breaks more cleanly. When a local agent fails validation, the error messages come back clearer and formatted for the chat window, and the login screen draws its logo through a shared hook with an optional sheen animation. These pieces are live in the local-agents integration and the streaming/timestamp tests as of the snapshot, so you can try them today by running an agent in local mode and watching a streamed reply.

d71a65c907b832d925e31556da4166a017e5d09e.text: When the system generates code, it now asks two different AIs (Claude and GPT-5) to independently draft solutions instead of relying on just one. A separate AI evaluator then compares both drafts and picks the better one. This means code changes are still being reviewed by humans, but the initial suggestions now come from a more diverse set of AI models.

314ec8b2f756cd6ca4003b1500289ab4c60e6c27.text: The steps that publish the software kit to the public have been merged into a single process, replacing two separate workflows that used to run one after the other. If you watched the automation that ships each kit release, you’ll see one combined run instead of a setup stage followed by a separate build-and-publish stage. The kit itself behaves exactly the same today; only the behind-the-scenes publish pipeline has been simplified, so releases should be easier to follow and keep in sync going forward.

11a280be3f2a39b4fc22ce2e965a5e692fbb2238.text: When you send the assistant a single block of text as a prompt — like a long instruction or request written as plain text instead of formatted chunks — the system now correctly marks that text so the assistant can reuse its response for follow-up questions without re-reading the whole thing. You get faster, cheaper answers on repeat questions because the service can pull from its short-term memory instead of starting over. This fix went live today and affects any plain-text message you send through the system.

888d9b98c8467caaf5a53bbf9da90537b710ab91.text: The company cleaned up the internal naming of its coding assistants, dropping an old prefix so the assistant names are now simpler and easier to read. Three duplicate helper files were removed and their useful parts were merged into two main files. Since this only affects how things are labeled behind the scenes, you won't notice any difference in features or performance.

2529ad939468c6fc9138040858a51345d47a14de.text: You now have a faster way to generate multiple solutions to the same coding task and pick the best one. When the base2 assistant is set to the 'fast' mode with the best-of-n option, it spawns five parallel implementor agents and then uses Claude Sonnet 4.5 to evaluate and select the single best implementation, outputting only that implementation's ID. This new fast variant is live today for anyone using the fast best-of-n workflow, alongside the existing slower best-of-n option.

e6045ca354143caf0820bbbd035f2a6e1ec4eff3.text: The program now reads its settings through one central, well-labeled catalog instead of hunting for each value in a big pile of raw system settings, so the backend and the command-line tool stay consistent and are less likely to misread a value. If you ran it today, the behavior is unchanged; the swap only makes future settings easier to add and verify without rewriting every file that uses them.

1c3a5ebec14f47ed14f2b4f689efe2d6cbeab4ac.text: The assistant can now take on a more collaborative approach: instead of one agent drafting all the code, it can spawn several independent agents in parallel, each proposing a different way to solve the problem, and then automatically pick the strongest proposal before applying the changes. You would notice this happening through a new option in the Base2 agent framework that, when enabled, routes a coding task through an orchestrator that manages this multi-agent review process rather than editing code directly. This is live today for anyone configuring the Base2 agent with the best-of-N mode, which adds several new specialized roles (the implementors, a selector, and an editor) that coordinate automatically.

fc982fd79f84dd0ac4833998c807ed0fff0ead8e.text: The CLI and backend stopped using a shared configuration helper for reading secret settings and went back to reading those settings directly from the system, restoring the old login constants and analytics checks. This means environment variables like your API key and PostHog keys are now read the same way they were before the centralized refactor, so nothing should change for you day-to-day, but it rolls back the recent move to a single shared config file. The change is live now and affects anyone using the command-line tool or hitting the backend auth/analytics flows, reverting to the previous direct access pattern.

673ae6eb753ef1ce2137c5cca9a434c2febe1a9e.text: If you run Codebuff from a terminal, it now reads your secret key and settings from one consistent place instead of hunting through many scattered spots. This prevents the wrong value from sneaking in when it runs locally, behind a proxy, or in CI, and it keeps debug logs and login links working the same way everywhere. You probably won't notice anything different day-to-day, but things like starting the app, signing in, and sending usage stats should behave more reliably across different setups.

75052a57cb38efdbfaa4ef1a7008bc571c1693a3.text: A new helper robot has been added to the internal research team that quietly asks for more files when it feels it doesn't have enough context to answer a question. The robot watches what the team has already read, checks if a specialized file-researcher has suggested new files, and when there are unread files that might matter, it prompts the team to read them by saying 'Let me read more files' and then signals to take another step. This only affects the internal research workflow and doesn't change anything you would see directly.

75ecd3cceb3e27353e7638fc45a129076604b8f5.text: The database lookup path that powers your agent runs and message cost tracking has been switched back to a shared location, so all parts of the backend now pull from the same source again. If you were poking around the code, you'd see backend files importing from '@codebuff/common/db' instead of the 'internal' folder. This also tidies up a handful of agent definitions and the editor settings file, but it won't change what you see on screen.

f78605fb0b4af7357f0caa33ed2e61997598d4bf.text: The codebase that powers the CLI and agent tools has been tidied up so that all of its files follow a single, consistent layout. If you opened one of these files, you'd see things like long lines broken into shorter ones, lists of allowed tools put on a single line instead of stacked, and files ending with a blank line. It's the software equivalent of giving every document in a filing cabinet the same font and spacing, making it easier to read and quicker to load, though it doesn't add any new features.

2fce2191f4800b36c2dd3c3d392801d9b30bcbd7.text: The CLI's automated assistants got their code reorganized and reformatted. Agent definitions like code-sketcher, file-explorer, planner-pro, and deep-thinker received prettier formatting changes—some lines were reformatted or collapsed into single lines. The CI testing configuration now explicitly includes new packages called 'internal' and 'billing' in its test runs. The backend's agent-run.ts swapped its database imports from '@codebuff/common/db' to '@codebuff/internal/db'. If you opened the assistant definitions, you'd see cleaner line wrapping and spacing; if you used the CLI, you wouldn't notice any functional difference today since these are formatting and import path changes.

3b8d54596cb77ac70305951fb8c03549cd220b00.text: Behind the scenes, the team moved the part of the code that talks to the database out of a shared tools folder and into a more restricted one used only by server-side code. This means the customer-facing pieces (like the web app and billing pages) now get their data through a more carefully controlled path, while the shared tools folder no longer carries the heavy database dependencies that only the server needs. If you looked at the code, every place that used to say 'database, please' to the shared folder now says it to the restricted one instead, and the shared folder itself is slightly less cluttered as a result. This kind of cleanup doesn\u2019t change what you see in the app today, but it makes the system more organized and keeps internal server details safer from accidentally

06170a5c256b6641cb7305534ade2d1d2a62288d.text: If you try to publish or check an agent through the website, the system now runs the spawnable agent validation logic from a different internal location. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping: the same checks still happen the same way, just moved to a more organized spot in the codebase. You won't notice anything change in how validation works or what errors appear when you submit an agent.

b73182067dbc1e12e451cfe68a116d5fde00e879.text: When the system sets up its automated testing and release pipelines, it needs to know which secret values (like API keys) to pull in from the stored vault. Previously, the script that decided which secrets to grab worked by eyeballing the source code with text-matching shortcuts, which could break if the code's formatting changed. Now that script instead reads from a clearly-defined catalog of every environment value the system actually uses, so it only pulls in secrets that truly belong there and ignores anything extra or irrelevant. This affects only the behind-the-scenes release and test automation, so you wouldn't see it change anything directly in the product, but it makes those automated steps more reliable and less likely to fail because a code comment or line break shifted.

9e9b23e7ac1a281ad1912d1c07960d4a4884a258.text: When you sign in to the CLI tool using the terminal login screen, the part that fetches your login link and opens your web browser now lives in a separate helper instead of being baked into the login screen itself. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping for the developers who maintain the code; your sign-in experience stays exactly the same. The change is live today in the CLI's login flow.

3a2c574687a93973dc409e2bc24e73548821dced.text: The behind-the-scenes organization of the login screen in the command-line tool was tidied up, with no change to how the login screen looks or works. Engineers split the login screen's behavior into smaller, separate pieces—one piece handles keyboard shortcuts like pressing Enter or the letter C, another watches the server to see when your login finishes, and a third draws the shimmer animation on the logo. This is housekeeping that makes the code easier to maintain and less likely to break, but you as a user would see nothing different when you log in.

e69082cb5a257484951b8a4f9001d3933472d8da.text: A new planning assistant has been added to the internal agent system that helps decide what to do next in a conversation. Before each action, it trims down the accumulated conversation history to keep things focused, then asks two different thinking helpers (one powered by a model from Anthropic, one from OpenAI) to each suggest a possible next move. The suggestions are used purely as inspiration; the new assistant writes its own real next step based on them, then those draft ideas are cleaned out of the message history so only the final step remains visible.

07594b7fc745e85de00e5a770d386b1a33c4d789.text: The helper now always writes out a step-by-step plan before doing your project work, instead of only doing so when specifically asked. Previously, you could turn this planning feature on or off, but now it runs every time by default, so you’ll consistently see the plan appear as you work through a task.

4005dbdd6d12b10eec8c128e43eb3e7e66ad7d4f.text: When you install the assistant software development kit (SDK), it no longer silently clears out secret settings the moment it starts. Instead, the production publishing process now supplies those placeholder values directly when it prepares a release, so the kit ships without any built-in code that wipes or overrides configuration. If you were inspecting a freshly installed SDK, you would no longer see the hidden routine that used to blank passwords and API keys on startup; the kit simply exports its types and waits for your own configuration. This is already live in the current SDK releases.

7981212c645f49747a55c7c94e942b2df9b7295d.text: The team undid a recent reorganization of how the company's apps read their secret settings. Previously, developers had moved the rules that validate those settings into a separate file, but this change moves all of those rules back into one main file. This only affects internal developers working on the codebase; outside users and apps will not notice anything different. It is live today.

335496eda9f44762cff28f27e66aee18f07eaafd.text: An internal AI assistant used for testing code fixes got a new sibling that plans its work as a running checklist instead of a short bullet-point list. The checklist version is live now and is being tested head-to-head against the original, with twice as many tasks running at the same time to see if it works better under pressure. You wouldn't see anything change in your own tools today; this only affects the behind-the-scenes bots that help developers test themselves.

dcd79cd82cba676be30221112be9339bb7d2411d.text: When you start the program for testing during development, it will now first try to run normally, and if that fails for any reason it will automatically build a missing piece it needs and try again. This means developers no longer have to manually build that piece before testing, since the system now handles it behind the scenes. The change is live today whenever someone runs the development start command.

2bc8607144b44f0342871f5137124d47ebd4d133.text: When you give the AI assistant a task with multiple steps, it can now keep a running checklist that shows up in your conversation. Instead of just talking through what it's doing, the assistant writes down each step and marks them off as it finishes, so you see a clear list of completed and pending items. The CLI interface renders these updates as a checkbox list, suppressing intermediate chunks for cleaner output. This is live today for anyone using the agent runtime to run multi-step tasks.

3959bf7b5f948219edcc6b32903f7ba5ff9bbcc3.text: The command line tool now remembers you're logged in instead of asking every time, so signing in works smoothly without repeated login prompts. Behind the scenes, the program swapped out its homemade login tracking for a standard system that manages your session more reliably. If you use the tool today, logging in and staying logged in should feel steadier, and the developers added new tests to catch login problems before they reach you.

4b4381d637361188165ada3105540ee032520149.text: When you open the CLI login screen, the layout now adapts smoothly to different terminal sizes using a single shared rule set. Instead of each part of the login screen calculating on its own how wide or tall the terminal is, they all ask the same centralized helper for breakpoint flags like isNarrow or isVerySmall. You might notice the login modal renders correctly no matter how small or large you resize your terminal window. The helper uses fixed thresholds: width below 60 columns is narrow, 60–99 is medium width, 100+ is wide; height below 15 rows is very small, 15–19 is small, 20–29 is medium, 30+ is large. This is live today for anyone running the CLI login flow. The new helper replaces direct inline calls, and the login screen now reads from it directly rather than duplicating the

b01a1c0afbc112e10ba2514f475cb882bd19c679.text: The SDK release process is now automated, so releasing a new version happens through a defined workflow that builds, tags, and publishes to npm with less manual effort. Sensitive API keys and environment settings that were baked into the build are now applied at runtime, meaning they are cleared when used in production but still work in development. This affects developers using the SDK—they'll get more reliably published versions and safer handling of credentials without needing to manage secrets during the build step.

8f6d890f97c0a175dd83c06284794c714b302c9f.text: The decomposing thinker agent can now start fresh with just the files you give it, instead of carrying along all the previous conversation history. It also accepts new fast-mode configurations that let it skip validation steps and use the decomposing thinker tool directly. Researchers no longer spawn this agent, but a new fast-track copy does.

e0d6df3ed1ceb4316fe837bb9bd6693f25c5a544.text: When you ask the coding assistant to find something across your project's files, the results now come back grouped by file with each file's matching lines listed together under its name, instead of one long list of file-and-line snippets. This makes the output easier to scan and uses less of the AI's working budget, so searches stay faster and cheaper. The change is live now for anyone using code search through the assistant.

9984487d7cff85d054cb969e1e2b75349057bd9f.text: You asked the assistant's code-search tool to look for text inside files, and it used to mix up the file name when that name contained a hyphen or a colon. Now the results are sorted correctly again. The fix also tells the tool where to find lines that are just context around each match, so nothing appears out of place. The corrected behavior is live today.

8450f267d05089ebc24e215e2003a8986d3e03e1.text: Starting today, when you open the CLI chat, a new assistant message appears at the top showing the list of agents that were loaded into memory. The message is collapsed by default, like a folded paper in a notebook: you see a short summary line and can expand it to read the full list if you want. The software also cleans up a few extra blank spaces and awkward line breaks in that message and in the formatting around login, giving the list a cleaner look on screen. The list only shows on startup, only when at least one agent was actually loaded, and only in the CLI chat window, so if you just open the command line or use a different part of the app you won not see it. The feature is controlled by a new type of message content and a matching display component added directly into the chat

9e226827a42b370975fde54a1ecf394e5e93c85c.text: A nightly automated test of the coding assistant now exercises a faster configuration that skips final answer-checking steps. You wouldn't notice anything directly since this only changes which version gets tested each night; the test will simply run the quicker, less-validated variant instead of the usual fast one. Behind the scenes, a new agent profile was registered and the nightly test list was pointed at it, so the test harness now measures the no-validation flavor. This is live only inside the nightly evaluation runs today.

ef910125a487c7bb1f4af9bf66edd54e011c1d06.text: When you chat with multiple AI assistants at once, their responses now stream more smoothly and reliably to your screen. The system was reorganized so that the way text pieces (chunks) are stitched together and filtered behind the scenes moved from the chat interface into the core engine that powers all AI conversations. This means the same reliable streaming logic is now shared everywhere the software is used, instead of being duplicated in just the chat window. You won't see a new button or setting, but you should notice fewer glitches and interruptions when assistants are typing their replies in real time.

776aabb75bf7a85f3f1c12b8889fa00c8a438a8e.text: The internal tool that grades code submissions stopped crashing when it received unexpected data chunks — it now ignores them instead of trying to display them. The assistant's user profile lookup was also split into a smaller, self-checking piece so the system can catch errors sooner and keep the default profile fields (like ID) intact, leaving your experience unchanged.

9872a589671e7f8e7ac108bb1947ff5ad280e7f0.text: The assistant used to have two ways to run: a quick mode that skipped checking your work, and a quick mode that also checked it. Now there's just one quick mode, and it always checks your work the same way (running type checks, tests, lints) before finishing. If you used the separate checking variant, it's gone; the quick mode now includes checking by default. Developers who relied on that separate option will need to switch to the standard quick mode, which behaves the same as the old checking variant did. This is live today: both quick and full-power modes now run validation steps as part of their process, with no separate variant to choose.

c2167451749849219ea711fd55c2327e67980f75.text: When you ask the assistant to tackle a coding task, it now follows a two-step research plan. First, a smarter research agent explores your codebase, gathers the key facts, and produces a written report plus a list of the files that matter for your request. Then a deep-thinking planning agent takes that report and file list to draft a detailed implementation plan, which a separate coding agent will later carry out. The practical effect is that before any code gets written for your request, the assistant pauses to read the relevant parts of the project it hadn't seen yet, rather than guessing from memory. You won't notice the extra step, but the resulting suggestions should fit your existing project structure more closely.

b5676a455ce66a06314c0fcdb60608a69b6c8f3d.text: When an assistant streams a response that includes tool calls (the special XML blocks the AI uses to invoke functions), the SDK now processes those blocks chunk-by-chunk in real time instead of feeding them through a callback that runs after the whole response arrives. This means you see the assistant's regular text flow more smoothly, with tool-call tags filtered out as the stream comes in, rather than having them cleaned up in a separate pass. The change live as of October 25, 2025, affects anyone building on the SDK to handle streamed agent responses, and the behavior is noticeable if you're consuming those chunks directly in your application.

37316d850d1997c2d84a80ef8a56b2e0b1be07cb.text: A version of the coding assistant that normally moves fast has gained a new, slightly slower mode: after writing code, it now automatically runs your project's checks (typechecking, tests, linting) before telling you it's done, rather than leaving that to you. The internal evaluation harness now runs this new mode on five tasks at once instead of several older speed-focused variants. If you were watching the test suite, you'd see fewer broken runs getting reported, because the assistant's output is getting a basic sanity check inline.

ce5838beffc746f29d2f2bf0de4c4f3a94e0d140.text: The system that handles your account information was reorganized internally, moving its logic to follow the app's standard structure. You don't see any difference in how things work, but behind the scenes the code now lives where the app expects it, making it easier to maintain. This is an internal housekeeping change with no impact on your experience.

72ac5ceeece0f9f634230cac977a7c635aef9f3e.text: When the shared code that the command-line tool depends on gets edited, the tool now automatically runs two safety checks — one to confirm it still type-checks, and another to rebuild it — before anything ships. The new validation script launches the command-line tool inside a terminal multiplexer, waits a few seconds, and then scans the startup output for words like 'error', 'failed', or 'exception', flagging any problem it finds before a real user would see one. This is live for developers working in the project today.

3dcb91e7fcf9a52146e59b4f81ff2207cbf1c5d8.text: When you start the program, it now shows the login screen as a floating window that sits on top of the main chat interface instead of replacing the chat with a full screen. You can see and interact with the chat behind the login prompt, and closing the login window reveals the conversation that was loaded underneath.

a9da3c1510b478d14fd8521ec25bf8837589d04c.text: The CLI used to quietly hide error and warning messages that mentioned PostHog, an analytics service, by intercepting what got printed to your terminal during startup. That filtering step has been removed, so those diagnostics will now surface normally in your console output when running CLI commands. This only affects the analytics setup in the command-line tool. This cleanup is live today.

c3b8d4b4dfd7542eda0fa4be8083d839a55ce90a.text: A new behind-the-scenes debugging tool was added to the evaluation system used to test the AI assistant's performance. The system now quietly records detailed logs of what happens during these tests to a file, but only when running locally or on a developer's machine, not in automated test or production environments. If you look at the test-running area of the code, you'll find this logging is now connected to the AI assistant client, so developers can trace exactly what the AI does during evaluations. This change is already live in the codebase, but it only produces visible output for developers running tests outside of CI or automated test environments.

02faa42bd585e2ed567dd8cdb7a1f761febfc97c.text: Each time you ask the assistant to do something, that request is now tagged with a unique run ID that follows the request through the entire process. This lets the system trace which large language model calls and tool actions belong to your specific request, making it easier to debug or analyze what happened during a run. The run ID is passed through the core contracts used by CLI hooks, evaluation scaffolding, and the agent runtime, including the live-user-inputs and send-message paths. If you looked at the internals, you'd see new runId fields added to the types used by SDK calls and agent steps, plus new dependency wiring like the agent-runtime being added to the SDK package. The feature is live today on 2025-10-23 and affects CLI users, the evaluation harness, and the agent runtime

e323769925c2d3bf9766a629afcec59219b54378.text: The developer tools now include two new helper assistants that work behind the scenes on coding tasks. One helper (Buffy) coordinates the work by sending out specialized sub-helpers, including another helper (File Researcher) that quickly scans code and produces a short written summary of the relevant parts plus a list of files. These run automatically when developers use the orchestrator path, which was added today as a new internal workflow. Nothing about the product itself changes; this only affects how the internal development assistants search and report on code.

df596975d3847f148250d348fada73ef08f30465.text: When you open CodeBuff in your terminal, you'll now see a login screen that shows a web address and a button to open it. Your terminal will wait there until you sign in through your web browser, and once you do, your credentials are saved locally so you don't have to log in again every time you start a new session. You can use the commands to sign in or sign out at any point. This is live now for everyone who runs the terminal version of CodeBuff.

b28837b59c4e660e1f3643c81e0d0336ccbddaf4.text: The team reorganized how the base2 assistant variants are stored on the internal server, moving them into clearly labeled folders (alloy, task-researcher, orchestrator) and deleting an old unused variant. Nothing you see changes today because the runtime behavior stayed the same, but the housekeeping means future edits to specific assistant types are easier to find and keep separate.

a25fb6d74829e92aca5c6f1c6715d0495dd6ae8d.text: The coding assistant no longer checks its own work or runs validation steps before finishing — it skips those review and testing phases entirely. If you watched it work, you'd see it make edits and then immediately wrap up, without spinning up extra helper agents to double-check the results. This makes each coding task finish faster, but removes the built-in quality checks that used to happen between writing and completing the changes.

221cb2ec11a00626b71169de7fda5ebe803df7dd.text: The command-line assistant no longer fakes replies when it can't reach the AI service, so you won't get those pre-written 'All changes have been applied successfully' style messages anymore. It also stopped logging routine notes about your system's color theme, which means less clutter in your terminal. Behind the scenes, it gained a new way to organize and track chat sessions under a debug/chats folder, making it easier to manage conversation history. If you use the CLI, you'll notice responses now only come from the actual AI instead of placeholder text.

cc27f91eeec33217f8e98e84c0868ba74c7bb117.text: If you run the BuffBench evaluation, it now only tests two specific assistant configurations (the strongest one and its simplified version) instead of four, and it runs them twice as fast by handling more tasks at the same time. At the same time, the team added two new pre-built assistant types and gave the existing GPT-5 worker a more powerful engine, so it can tackle harder tasks. These changes are live today for anyone running these internal evaluations.

604846184451b01b03c7fcaeab0acf8e869c5ace.text: The SDK no longer includes a helper that used to run an external binary and turn its text output into structured events you could react to in real time. If you relied on that streaming bridge between the SDK and the binary, it is gone, and the diff shows no replacement being added in the same snapshot. Other SDK capabilities around agent runs and logging are still being wired up, but this specific streaming path is deleted.

92fa5b6572b619e73ecb6997537100f031e0825b.text: The assistant has been taught a new rule: once it announces it has finished a task, it must fall silent and not say anything else. Engineers also added several experimental assistant modes for an upcoming internal evaluation, so test runs can compare how different thinking approaches behave. These new modes only affect the test environment today and are not turned on for regular use.
