033073467c13ccad942aecb26c18cffd9d6cef5d.text: The assistant can now stream answers through the software development kit, which means programs embedded inside other apps can tap into the same live, word-by-word answer flow that the main web version uses. Behind it, the system now talks to three AI service names at once and reads the correct license key up front, so third-party integrations no longer have to guess which provider settings apply. If you build or run such an embedded app, your streamed answers will behave the same as the browser version instead of falling back to a simpler mode.

f86de95b1d62b244097e2d98d780082948a198df.text: Staging deploys for the CLI tool now happen automatically whenever someone pushes code or opens a pull request that includes the tag '[codecane]'. The build process switched from using Node to using Bun, which is a faster JavaScript runtime, and a new shared setup step was added to handle Bun installation and caching. Windows was dropped from the release build targets, so releases are now built only for Linux and macOS. These changes are live today for the CLI staging environment.

d4b22ca4cb6a8e01715bda743269445dd9a291b1.text: The system that breaks big coding jobs into smaller steps has quietly switched the helper it uses to do the actual work, so each step now has the helper explicitly open the relevant files first and ask a separate tool to clean up unused information before proceeding. The new helper also stops itself after 15 tries to avoid running forever, and the people planning each step now write smaller, clearer goals instead of listing separate success conditions. If you used this system, you would notice that each step reads the files it needs up front and the whole job is less likely to stall on its own; behind the scenes, the instructions for planning steps were also reworded to nudge the helper toward smaller, safer changes.

a1f6959919ec9099adb2ffeba70711cb3e8ce760.text: When you're chatting with the assistant in the CLI, you can now choose between two modes: a quicker, simpler mode (shown in green as FAST) or a more powerful, thorough mode (shown in red as 💪 MAX). You switch between them by clicking the colored label or pressing the Shift and Tab keys at the same time. Whatever mode is shown when you send a message is the one the assistant will use to answer you, and your last choice stays set for future chats.

d110a2c2f3d458cfef54d4fd5c9a5a6eb697c2e2.text: A coding assistant can now split a big project into smaller, independent chunks and tackle them in parallel, rather than working through one piece at a time. When you give it a large task, it plans the work in rounds, hands each round's pieces to specialist helpers, and keeps going until the whole job is done, so large jobs finish faster. This new planning and parallel-execution capability is live today for the internal orchestrator agents, and one existing helper was renamed so it matches its actual configuration file. If you look, you would see the orchestrator calling multiple helpers at once instead of waiting for each step to complete before starting the next.

013dbab32556cccf8a74b982f53ef25827eda6e5.text: When you run the assistant from a project folder, it will now look for a hidden folder named.agents in that folder or any folder above it. If it finds custom agent instructions written there as plain text files, the assistant loads those and uses them instead of its default behavior, letting you keep specialized assistant setups per project without changing global settings. You would notice this the first time you launch the assistant in a folder that contains a.agents directory; nothing changes for folders that do not have one.

4e92bc395cc55fd95fb15c8a50a444daf5706bc8.text: When you run the assistant, it quietly calls on a background helper called the context-pruner to tidy up long conversations. Starting today, that helper's status messages and progress logs no longer flash across your terminal screen. If you watched the CLI output, you'd notice those background lines are missing, even though the pruning work is still happening behind the scenes.

be0477d25a58aa37c00a90666c4324daed2215ab.text: A new internal test helper for the company's coding assistant has been added and switched on in the evaluation suite as of October 21, 2025. This helper is a faster version of an existing learning assistant, but it deliberately keeps only half of the past mistakes it has collected, so its suggestions are built from a shortened history. The change is live for internal testing only and does not change anything visible to users of the product.

3e97921e5764810a9aea89b47879d7db60aa5f66.text: When you send your API key to the service, the system now creates a written record of what happens during that check, so problems can be traced later instead of silently failing. This logging is now passed along automatically to every place that verifies an API key, including the real-time connections and web requests. If you looked at the code today, you'd see the assistant tools for the SDK gaining the ability to run locally with database access, though the main visible difference is the improved error reporting path.

a7d0c59f9544e21786009224776572e99b86bead.text: When you run the assistant in your terminal, the status messages and error notes it prints out now follow a single, consistent layout instead of mixing different formats from different parts of the app. Behind the scenes, the terminal interface switched its logging system to match a shared format already used by the rest of the application, so messages like 'Failed to copy to clipboard' or 'Starting mock response streaming' display their extra details (such as the prompt or theme name) in the same structured way everywhere. The assistant now logs errors and info with the context details first, then the human-readable message, making troubleshooting output easier to read whether the error came from copying text, sending a message, or detecting your system's light/dark theme. This is live

fc82d19e497c6cb5d7a9fb7f9362d60fcaa5e28d.text: The engineers removed four experimental helper versions of their main coding assistant, named after the character 'Buffy,' that were used to test different ways the assistant could organize its work. These four variants—designed for different review, simple, and validation workflows—are no longer part of the project. If you browsed the repository today, you would not find the folders or files that defined these test configurations, since they have been permanently deleted from the codebase. This is an internal cleanup and does not change the behavior of the assistant you interact with.

f5518d5397c26749a6b2cd39a6709a5526f4cac8.text: The system now offers three strength levels for its main helper: a quick-and-light version for fast answers, the standard version you were already using, and a new power version that brings in an extra specialist agent to tackle harder jobs. If you look behind the scenes, the quick version still skips a couple of check-in steps, the standard version works as before, and the power version activates an additional worker alongside the usual reviewers. The internal tester that judges how these helpers perform has also been switched to run these three versions side by side, with each version handling up to ten jobs at once instead of the old setup.

59e96da1f633f267818239be9917755f2badf9da.text: Starting today, when you ask the assistant to pull up an agent from the database, it will securely send along your API key as a bearer token, so the backend can verify you're allowed to see that agent and return it. If you're running tests or using the web-socket tools, the same key now travels with the request automatically instead of being left out. Behind the scenes, the code that fetches agent templates passes this key through wherever it needs to, and the test setup was combined so both old and new checks use the same key handling. The feature is live now for anyone authenticating through the supported entry points.

89e2d03b6a4c4a7814164710cb2ba630889c5b02.text: When you use the CLI tool to grab a binary release (like a packaged program), it now goes through an intermediary address instead of hitting GitHub directly. That middleman takes your request for a specific version and sends you along to the real download on GitHub, so if the team ever moves the files to a different storage place later, old CLI versions won't break. This only affects CLI downloads through this proxy—existing download links or direct GitHub access are unchanged.

9e0f3be93e18a8e8f31cc12e5d3a8f0335c8ed52.text: The team added a new internal guide named LESSONS.md under a hidden folder called.agents. It is not visible in the app today and does nothing for users; it lives only in the codebase to help the developers who write automated assistant tools learn from past mistakes. The guide collects real failures from previous runs (such as a scrollbar that looked wrong in Firefox, tests that broke when text changed, and tools receiving unclean data) and pairs each failure with a concrete fix the assistants should follow next time. If you opened the project files, you would see a 1627-line notes file written in plain headings and bullet points, added on October 21, with no changes to anything you use.

d07d04a7a916e8569ee9f892c2c14325d8de2ccf.text: The engine that powers the assistant's step-by-step reasoning was relocated into a shared runtime package, so the main application and evaluation tools now pull it from that central location instead of a local module. This is behind-the-scenes reorganization that cleans up how the system starts up and runs, removing tangled dependencies between parts of the code. If you were watching how the assistant boots up, you'd see it loading the same reasoning step from a shared toolkit rather than from inside the main application itself. It's live today as part of the normal startup flow.

6228a229e658078389efd88abab51065b7d00d39.text: The system has removed a behind-the-scenes analytics tool called Benchify that developers were using to collect usage data. This cleans up how the system counts changed lines in files and removes the extra tracking setup, making the code simpler and faster. If you are a user, you will not notice any difference in features, but the system is now slightly more streamlined without the unused tracking code.

1c72ab87bf40bd2711815869577aa2238562f7f1.text: When an AI agent attempts a coding task and runs into trouble, this change lets the system generate a short written analysis explaining what went wrong and what the agent should have done instead. You can turn this analysis generation on or off with a new toggle, and when enabled, the system saves these write-ups into a designated folder instead of cluttering the debug logs. The system now also stops saving certain noisy error messages (those involving malformed JSON from tool calls) to reduce clutter. This is already live in the internal eval tooling used by the engineering team, so if you run a buffbench evaluation you may notice the new output folder and cleaner debug logs.

ca96b87b2988625b3712f7378dbe1ee031345095.text: The team moved the Relace AI assistant code from the main backend into the shared agent-runtime package, so the assistant's rewriting logic now lives alongside the other AI providers instead of being tied to the backend. The backend's fast-rewrite feature now imports the assistant from the new location, which means this refactor is already live today for anyone using that rewrite feature. You wouldn't see a difference in the assistant's output, but the code is now organized so other tools can reuse it without pulling in backend-specific dependencies.

d5aabc7f690bcc1fa48f578c345bd408077031b7.text: The behind-the-scenes helper that gathers and formats the agent's final answer was moved into the shared agent-runtime package, so the main runner now imports it from there and the old helper file was deleted. Internal files within agent-runtime switched to relative references for two of its own utilities. Nothing you do changes today, but the codebase is now tidier and that helper is one step closer to being reused by other agent setups.

d1533e56edba105fab205460f2dc35e3cab79ecc.text: The agent now has a new way to decide what to send back when it finishes a task: it can return only its final reply, return every message it produced, or hand back a special structured result when one is expected. If you were watching the agent's output, you might notice it now consistently picks the most recent reply from the assistant instead of including the opening setup prompt, and it gives a clear error message if no reply was ever produced. Alongside this, a written checklist was added explaining how files should be moved into the agent-runtime package and what import paths to fix, so future moves follow the same rules.

0fa400c780a526b82f5635c0b10b4bd994e5569f.text: A new helper script is now available so the team can take two sets of AI-coding-assistant test results and automatically line up the tasks both runs attempted, then print side-by-side numbers for overall score, cost, and time. When you run it, you hand it two folders of result files, and it quietly skips any task where one run crashed or scored at or below 1.0 before showing mean, min, max, and spread for each assistant and the head-to-head deltas. The script is in the repository today, so anyone running BuffBench comparisons can start using it immediately; no existing workflows change, and nothing currently depends on it except people doing these paired evaluations.

d45606cc2a9f1501a2563557ab9ac4af6140c871.text: The assistant's instructions and prompts were moved from one part of the codebase to another, and all the places that used them were updated to point to the new location. If you looked at the code, you'd see imports referencing a new package path instead of a local folder. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping; nothing changes how the assistant behaves today.

877c6debf1fb947279badda7fe9a5dbd7b2cfe0c.text: The coding assistant now has an optional helper it can send out first to read the relevant files and gather facts before it starts planning or editing. That helper is required to hand back a written report of just the facts and a list of the files it examined, so the main assistant works from a focused, pre-filtered set of information instead of rummaging through the whole codebase itself. This new "research-first" option is in place today for teams using the GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 orchestrator variants.

66f86aa8018078b5e9dbccdbf92dfbadb8b4c4f9.text: A new internal assistant named "Buffy the Orchestrator" is now available to help handle complex coding tasks by coordinating several specialized helpers. When assigned a tricky coding job, Buffy can call in a task researcher to investigate the problem, a planner-pro to map out the approach, and other tools to search files and write code. Buffy uses a powerful model (Claude Sonnet 4.5) to manage this teamwork. This is a behind-the-scenes addition to the company's agent tooling, so you won't see it directly unless you're working on one of these coding tasks.

ac5e30fa879ae975f6c86c1c2981ac1be6d1307e.text: When two people open the same assistant conversation at the same time, the assistant now reliably stops the older session instead of letting both run. Previously the list of active conversations was kept in one place and shared by whoever asked first, so it could get mixed up; that list now lives inside the engine that runs the assistant and is passed in fresh to each session. If you open a conversation that someone else is already using, your new request quietly takes over and the earlier one stops responding. The change is live now.

fb08bf54f6dd19d6ea8727fe6da1fca4faf3aa98.text: A new AI coding assistant called Buffy the Orchestrator is now live to manage complex programming tasks, which means the system can now break down big coding jobs into smaller research and implementation steps automatically. Buffy uses a structured research agent that returns required analysis, key facts, and relevant files, so the quality of task breakdown is now enforced rather than optional. This affects internal coding workflows starting today, and you would notice if you asked the system to tackle a large multi-step development task, it now routes through Buffy's layered planning approach instead of a single direct agent.

28cef1c635daa836d6369ba622fb266f28014157.text: A new faster mode was added to the internal agent orchestration system, letting a lightweight version of the assistant skip extra planning steps and move straight to getting things done. The system also updated the underlying AI model used for searching code references, and renamed a couple of internal helper steps to clearer names. Additionally, outdated instructions for running services locally were removed from the project knowledge base. These changes are live for internal use, affecting how the assistant behaves when operating in the new fast configuration.

9c60bc01fa615522d05499dc45aa413a107712e1.text: The assistant now has a new helper that uses a more advanced model to think through the best ways to solve a coding task before starting. When the main orchestrator gathers information about a request, it can now summon this planner to compare five different approaches and pick the simplest one that still meets all requirements. This only affects internal agent definitions used by the development tooling; there are no visible changes to the user interface or command-line commands, so you wouldn't notice it directly unless you're looking at the backend wiring.

0d1a74e3de45c233e1f518a9bdc94a416a09880b.text: The coding assistant can now tackle harder problems by splitting them into two steps: a research pass that gathers facts and relevant files, and an implementation pass that writes and reviews the code, with the overall coordinator handed off to a newer Claude model and the hands-on work done by a newer GPT model. If you watched it work, you would see it first ask a specialist to read and report on the task, then spin up further sub-agents to plan, edit, and review the actual changes before finishing. The updated evaluation test used to judge these agents against a custom-tool coding task, so the improvement is live for the internal benchmark rather than for most outside projects.

4d3e9e5c93a2bd32cd0bcd7fc8ff5a734ffbb2e6.text: When you stream a response from an AI assistant, the text now shows up in clean, complete chunks instead of broken pieces, because the system stopped cutting off and restarting sections of text mid-stream. If an assistant is building up its answer while also handling tool-use tags, the system now flushes those pending sections only when it actually has meaningful text to send. You would notice fewer jarring interruptions and less empty or garbled text appearing in the middle of a streamed answer. This is live today for anyone using streaming responses.

3212f215c6793cc65f8922d41ff7c5e10062898c.text: The agent registry has been reorganized so it lives in one shared location that the backend now reads from, which lets the backend, real-time connections, helper tools, and eval scripts all tap the same source instead of each keeping their own copy. You won't see a new button or different output yet, but this kind of cleanup is what makes it safer to add new capabilities later without breaking the things that already work. It also fixes a long-standing tangle in how new agents get started, which in practice means the system is slightly more reliable when spinning up fresh agent runs. This is in place today as part of the normal build.

7584c09b880d1c005a7c1350be3091c8867b7ef9.text: When you run an AI assistant that uses helper agents, you'll now see the helper's written replies show up on your screen as they happen, instead of all at once at the very end. Previously, the system held onto any text written by subagents or before a tool call until the entire run finished, so the display waited. The system now tracks where each agent's current text section starts and flushes that pending text to your view the moment it encounters a tool call or switches to another agent. You'd notice helper-written text appearing live in real-time during a run today, backed by new tests covering this behavior.

742227da10913c4864e05563894dc6636d1b29ed.text: Pull requests on the main code branch that contain the tag [codebuff-cli] in their title now automatically kick off a staging release pipeline. This pipeline builds complete standalone program files (binaries) for Windows, Mac, and Linux whenever such a pull request is opened, so the team can test the packaged application across different operating systems before a final public release. You would see new automated checks appear on those pull requests, and the system now ignores the temporary bin folder during builds.

98ec8fd6847c39221b548818d3fac2e4e667fbe0.text: You now get three flavors of the same helper instead of one: one that runs a code review step, one that skips the review, and one that adds an extra validation step on top. Each helper is a prepackaged instruction set for handling coding tasks, and the only difference between them is which assistants they're allowed to call in for help. The helpers are defined but not yet wired into any menu or command you can pick today, so having them in place changes nothing you can click yet.

d75bbf2e220f6459116eda5a1da3dbbf1c1455cd.text: The chat endpoint now accepts complete replies all at once instead of only streaming them piece by piece, so you can get a full answer back in one response when you call the API. While it talks to the model provider behind the scenes, the system now also saves each back-and-forth question and answer into a long-term storage bucket, which lets the team analyze usage and costs later. This means anyone integrating with the chat API today can choose to receive full responses rather than streamed chunks, and those conversations are being recorded for analytics.

05ccf5598533c54b5979d13a0f2b4f00029c83b0.text: If you run a BuffBench evaluation, you can now choose exactly which individual tasks to run instead of having to run them all at once. You simply list the task IDs you want, and the system will work through only those specific items. If you type an ID that does not exist, it stops and shows you a list of the IDs that are actually available, rather than silently skipping it. This change is live as of today for anyone using the BuffBench evaluation tooling.

a7f0d37e617bdd35f08684e595b68dd9ab2fa8b2.text: When you ask the assistant a question and a tool runs behind the scenes, the program used to sometimes show you the hidden instruction text (the part that tells the tool what to do) mixed in with the readable answer. Starting with version 0.4.3 on October 17, 2025, that instruction text is now stripped out before the reply reaches your screen, whether the response comes all at once or in pieces. You will see cleaner message replies without any leftover command codes leaking into the conversation, and this fix now applies consistently across the whole CLI and SDK instead of relying on separate filtering in the chat display.

94b2449a8e687af2090225001ed7a82e5bd2ee57.text: The assistant can now log each individual step it takes while working through a task—like recording each action with details such as step order, credit usage, and success or failure status—for internal agents tracking agent runs. This new logging capability is live today for developers building on top of the agent-run system, allowing them to monitor and debug agent behavior step-by-step. If you looked at the system, you would notice that agents send detailed step records to a dedicated endpoint during execution, rather than just reporting a start and end.

6d5d85a97e7ba2b986693b1be3634ec15c18fc17.text: The assistant now accepts a new input that lets you tell it exactly which file system to use when it looks at your project files, instead of always using the default one. This affects the parts of the tool that read your folders, check which directories exist, and save changes, so you can now point it at a custom setup like a browser environment or a sandboxed drive. If you were building custom integrations, your calls need to pass this file system explicitly now, otherwise you'd see it fail to find or save anything in your project.

dfcc0c1cd89e33166928cf814c16441c9a486715.text: When you ask the assistant a question and it answers bit by bit, the words sometimes showed up twice on your screen, or a chunk of the reply went missing mid-sentence. The fix introduces a smarter way to stitch each incoming fragment to what was already shown, so now what you see builds up one smooth, correct sentence at a time, with no repeats or gaps. It's live today in both the command-line tool and the SDK that powers it. If you watch a streamed response now, you'll notice the text grows steadily without the earlier jumps or duplications.

51003b6481c11dec1f8774b062fd13a541cb0923.text: The system that automatically tests your AI coding assistant now gives the evaluation tools a snapshot of how your agent is configured (its tools, prompts, and settings) right from the start of each test run. Previously, each check-up point had to pull that information separately, which meant the analysis could miss the full picture of why an agent acted a certain way. Now a single check evaluates how well one agent performs across many different tasks and highlights its strengths and weaknesses, giving a clearer report on how your assistant behaves overall.

3196d7975658d2aa215bde9d557f885ff429629e.text: When the assistant finishes editing files in this internal coding workflow, it now hands the work off to two specialized helpers instead of one general reviewer. One helper critiques the code like a meticulous editor, and the other tries to build and test the changes, automatically fixing any errors it finds, similar to running spell-check and then proofreading in sequence. Anyone using this base2 workflow today sees that handoff happen automatically after edits, because the new two-step check is already wired in.

28d09e3c03b10bd8e7c228d543f199df7d6eefd2.text: When you paste text into the assistant's text input box, it now inserts exactly what you copied instead of mangling it or losing focus on the typing area. Previously, pasting long blocks of text could cause the input field to lose focus or the cursor to jump, forcing you to click back into the box before typing could continue. The fix restores reliable bracketed paste handling, so multi-line pastes work cleanly and the input stays ready for your next keystroke.

58b1334d6359b8685011bf063a677132bd80010c.text: When you send a chat request through the API, the system now records specific events for each step - whether it was a successful request, an authentication failure, not enough credits, the start of a streaming response, or an error. Previously, these were tracked with a single generic endpoint, making it hard to see which part of the chat process was failing or succeeding. This gives better visibility into how the chat completions feature is working in real time.

1f3b425d12af04a4f15409814f92d25504d156d3.text: When you paste text into the command-line assistant with the usual paste shortcut, it now appears exactly like typed text, because the tool switched from a company-specific interface framework to the standard version everyone else uses. If the assistant's code relied on a special paste-only signal to behave differently when you pasted versus typed, that signal no longer arrives. The change is live now for anyone running the command-line version of the assistant.

cc2883fecaaa85f7851fa637d0588641ee402a1e.text: You now have a new way to tackle big coding projects: an assistant can split the work into two stages, first using one model to think through and plan the steps, then using a second model to actually write the code. This new setup lets the planning step focus on mapping out the task while the coding step handles the implementation, which should make complex requests get completed more thoroughly. If you looked at the system today, you would see this two-step planning option available alongside the existing one-step setup.

01bfdc23bd9397068024c9bf4e2f4d9814b6f718.text: Starting today, programs that talk to the run-tracking system can now officially tell it when a run has ended, reporting whether it finished normally, hit an error, or was stopped early, along with how long it ran and how much compute it used. Behind the scenes, the system now records a completed-run event for analytics and validates the reported status and usage figures before accepting the message. If you watched the run list, you would see the run flip to a finished state immediately after one of these new completion notices arrives, instead of staying open until the system noticed on its own. The feature is live for any caller sending the new finish request; it does nothing for callers that don't use it yet.

b1a181070db578e9feec494db57db5c8a4b10f4f.text: The team moved the user-information lookup logic into its own dedicated module outside the main application folder, and the web endpoint now simply calls into it. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping — the way the system retrieves your profile information hasn't changed, and you won't notice anything different. It's live today as part of the ongoing internal cleanup.

10088392e2eb8b537251237bfe6aec441e246e20.text: When you call the agent-runs or me API endpoints, the system now records a tracking event for each request, validation error, and creation success or failure, sending that data to the analytics service. This means anyone inspecting network activity or logs will see additional event entries alongside the existing responses, but the core request and response behavior stays the same. The tracking is active today for both endpoints.

0260e2a5776f290b8693d0b81ec1aa0f78a639c1.text: When you visited the website and hit an error, the page would break completely and show a blank screen. Now, a friendly error page appears instead that tells you whether the problem happened on the server or your browser. The website will keep building successfully even if there are minor coding mistakes, so visitors still see a clean message instead of a crash. This fix is live today.

1bd41f380e7a779b9e3c3ef1fd975816f87337fb.text: The system can now record when a tracking run starts. When an approved app or service kicks off a run, the platform generates a unique ID, checks the credentials behind the scenes, and begins the run in the background. If you were looking at the logs or tracking tools right now, you would see these new run entries appearing for authorized callers instead of nothing happening. Test accounts will show the start event but skip saving it to the live records.

0dda1c76174ec6037b663966e6af6886394d0473.text: You can now fetch information about a specific assistant directly from a new web address, so tools that connect to that address will find the same assistant details they always expected. The new address simply forwards requests to the existing system without changing how anything works.

897473eb30202ae3a838084cfd3ce2d284ae7c1b.text: The system now uses a newer, smarter helper model for complex tasks. When you give a big request, the main assistant can automatically bring in a specialized worker that uses the latest model to plan steps and edit files, then coordinates it inline. A few existing instructions were also tweaked for consistency. The feature is in place now and will activate on supported task flows.

1b6e682c0a89942a889cbddd445fe81d890dd139.text: A new web address is now available that lets a tool or app ask for basic details about the signed-in account, like its unique id, email address, or linked Discord id. You send a secret key for identification, and you can choose which of those three pieces of information you want back, with the account id returned by default if no preference is given. This is live today and ready for internal tools or authorized programs to use.

245b514c5b58cf559f26b3bcd2498d628f7527a6.text: The assistant that picks out which files are relevant to your code question now gets help from a faster, cheaper model called haiku to do the legwork of searching. Instead of the main helper doing the file search itself, it now asks a specialized sub-helper to list the files, then reports the results to you. You would notice nothing different except this now flows through that extra step using the newer model. This is live and affects the internal tooling that powers file-related answers.

64a1b8036aef020f928c091d19a11d0af0f5adf3.text: A new helper for the codebase search tool now looks through your project files in two passes: first it lists up to a dozen file paths it thinks matter, then after peeking at those files, it gives you a refined, shorter list of the most relevant ones. If you use the file explorer, you should notice it picks more accurate files and stops listing ones that turned out to be irrelevant. It's live today.

de8997f72f16d19ca4777f92a437418d4e13c860.text: You can now launch a new terminal-based chat interface for the assistant that renders rich formatting and supports multi-line input and nested sub-agents. Behind the scenes, the streaming pipeline now tags every response chunk with which agent produced it (via parentAgentId and forwardToPrompt flags) so that conversations involving several layers of helper-agents display correctly in the new terminal UI. Live today as an initial release: open the terminal, start the new interface, and you'll see styled markdown messages and branched agent conversations instead of plain text. The developers warn that the terminal UI is strict about how spaces and text elements are written, so misusing them can blank the whole screen.

e99abbdeb5d459542a4979625d0d14ff56808962.text: The behind-the-scenes communication between different parts of the system has been reorganized so that shared tools like logging and sending responses are passed around more consistently. This touch-up spans several core backend areas and cleans up duplicated wiring, but you wouldn't see any change in how the product behaves today; it is purely internal housekeeping to make future updates easier and less error-prone for the team building the system.

d73d54376969f1c711478bbd0f076f9a04560729.text: You can now ask the codebase assistant to find files for you using a lighter, faster model, and it will locate the most relevant files without doing text searches. The system now routes file-discovery tasks to this new setup, so results should focus on file locations and brief relevance notes rather than deep code analysis. This is live today as part of the agent tooling.

bdcd0fc3a36048a7ff5e8c5fda9b3e10bfc3bef3.text: A new set of specialized assistants is now wired up to use the latest underlying model, so internal tooling that previously relied on the older model can hand off tasks like editing and review work to versions configured for the newer one. The main control assistant now explicitly delegates to the new editing and review assistants during normal operation. If you looked, you'd see fresh definitions for planning, editing, and reviewing roles that all point to the same newer model instead of the previous default.

b1e58232082fb2f114b1c486a0c981745684c05e.text: A new helper called base2-max has been added to the internal toolbelt for the team that builds and tunes AI agents. This new helper runs a context-pruner before each step, then repeatedly calls a gpt-5-powered single-step agent until the task is marked complete, letting the existing max-style agent delegate work to a gpt-5 model instead of handling every step itself. Nothing about customer access, plans, or regions changed, so everyday users of the product will notice nothing, but engineers running or configuring these agents now have an additional gpt-5-driven path available when they use the base2-max agent.

5e38e4869cf7477ce6189a7abd4f9d7a0da75f67.text: Each night, the system now runs a specialized evaluation routine that tests how two specific versions of the assistant (called "base" and "base2") perform on a set of benchmark tasks, then automatically emails a summary of the results to the team. Previously, the nightly automation ran a more general evaluation tool. This new process specifically executes performance and cost measurements for those two assistant versions and sends the formatted scores via email, so the team gets a direct comparison of their nightly performance without needing to dig into logs.

5f818783ccab888062b1eb7844c09409d94d235d.text: The way the system asks for and receives files from the app has been reorganized so that the file-reading tools no longer depend on a single, hardcoded connection method. Instead, the tools that search and display file contents now receive the file-fetching helper from whoever is running them, letting those tools work through different connection styles without changing their own code. The reorganized file-fetching now also guarantees each returned file ends with a blank line, keeping file contents consistent. Existing tests for the tool behaviors remain in place and continue to pass under the new structure.

99bbe8a0f1e12a65d4886899760bfff6a70c84d0.text: The software's helper tools used to be hardcoded to talk to one specific communication system, so swapping out how the assistant talks to the outside world required rewriting core files. Now those tools receive that communication method as a parameter instead, like handing someone a phone rather than bolting a specific phone line into their desk. You won't see a new button or setting, but the system is now structured so developers can plug in different ways for the assistant to receive data and send results — including ones that fail faster if something stalls. This is a behind-the-scenes change that affects only people editing the program's internals today.

86a36594559cec23d4854b9b692970c1798efbc2.text: The team retired an older planning agent, moving it into an archive section of the project where unused pieces are stored. This means that specific tool, which was designed to generate and evaluate multiple plans before choosing the best one, is no longer active or in use. If you went looking for it, you would find it set aside among other retired components rather than running like the current tools do. This is an internal change, so it does not affect anything visible to you today.

216cd365f94b3b646f227df539f642d06f3903b2.text: When you ask the planning assistant to come up with the best possible step-by-step plan, it no longer just tries once or twice. It now quietly generates five different draft plans at the same time, then picks the single best one before presenting it to you. So you get a plan that’s been pre-filtered from several options, rather than the first good-enough version the assistant landed on. This only affects internal planning behavior behind the scenes; nothing you see or do differently is required to get it.

7627eca0d19fc59601017560f61194990dbc4589.text: The team tidied up how the assistant's responses and conversation messages are built by moving two key pieces of logic into their own dedicated spots. If you watched the codebase, you'd see that the behind-the-scenes functions for shaping what the assistant outputs and how user messages are assembled are no longer tangled up in the main workflow file. This doesn't change what the software does for anyone, but it makes the code easier to follow and adjust later on. It's purely structural housekeeping affecting the backend system.

2309aac671735329bfa6b89c0341ea02472b0a6f.text: The company moved 14 unused helper programs (like the brainstormer and reviewer tools) out of the active workspace into a separate 'graveyard' folder where they are kept but no longer run or affect daily operations. Anyone working on the system will see these tools have changed addresses, requiring updated connection paths, but regular users won't notice any difference since these programs were already inactive.

4bc5155e0063793c6285961c97b6583514497964.text: When the assistant decides how to plan a coding task, it now occasionally brings in a fresh second opinion before settling on a plan. This new reviewer isn't told about the earlier back-and-forth with you, so it examines your request purely on its own merits rather than being influenced by previous discussion. The net effect is that some key decisions get a clean-slate review, which should reduce cases where the plan quietly drifts from what you actually asked for. This behavior is already in effect for tasks that run through the main planning flow.

5256ed43f35086dd245541f379056b01f9478c9c.text: The assistant system now picks a single smarter helper to plan tasks instead of juggling four separate helpers. When you ask it to build something complex, one dedicated planner evaluates five different ways to tackle it and chooses the simplest strong option before the rest of the team gets to work. This streamlines how your requests are broken down internally, reducing handoffs between helpers. It is live today as part of the base orchestration layer.

3d4f0d2ab93aede0e51defcef464ee8187d4c6ef.text: A new automated testing system for AI coding agents has been added to the codebase. This system can now run AI agents against specific programming tasks, automatically track their work including time and costs, and score their performance. If you look at the repository, you'd see a brand new folder dedicated to these evaluation tools that weren't there before, making it possible to compare how different AI assistants handle real coding challenges.

a99f06f816ff8cc9b9d1ebbf4b58bcaee3acb8c2.text: A new behind-the-scenes helper was added that coordinates other assistants during complex tasks, directing them to gather information, review work, and edit code in organized steps. It only affects internal development tools and doesn't change anything you see or use today.

8b710f3cd6cbf7024b4e0781198404c3a95f93a7.text: The team added a tool that can read and print score tables from buffbench log files, making it easier to review how different setups performed. They also tweaked the logging system to prepend a task number to file names, so files sort in the correct order and are easier to trace. Additionally, they adjusted the main runner to use a simplified agent, bumped the concurrency limit, and force an exit at the end. These changes streamline internal evaluation and make log analysis more practical.

2a6146f7c62ae4e182807a21b0a9dd6f313391e5.text: A large test-result file that had been accidentally saved into the project has been deleted, trimming the codebase by over 65,000 lines. This file was a leftover record of test specifications and mock data used for checking how child agents receive conversation history, so removing it only cleans up the repository without altering any live functionality. If you browsed the project's internal folder, you would no longer find this bulky JSON artifact sitting alongside the actual test files.

0eef90fdb385962768014fbfeb736944533b5462.text: The app's backend now checks agent names through a single, shared validation step instead of repeating that logic in multiple places, and the agent runtime can read an agent's stored profile directly from its database connection. Developers calling agent setup will notice their templates resolve using this new shared lookup, while end users can expect agent name validation to behave consistently across the service. This goes live today across the backend service, touching the agents and prompt-building layers.

36e8766564f6d51a15cc9158805e0a3833b763ba.text: When you ask the assistant to run a terminal command, it now uses a faster model called grok-4-fast to execute and analyze the output before relaying a concise summary back to you. Previously the assistant would run commands but the analysis step was less streamlined. This means you get quicker, more focused responses when the assistant needs to inspect system information, run diagnostics, or check logs, without waiting for slower processing. The feature is live today in the internal agent definitions.

26f55166262409e7b9a8944e374bb3eb5cfc59da.text: Today, if you looked at the code, you'd see the parts that talk to external AI providers are now being told which provider to use instead of guessing that on their own. The backend still does the same thing — rewrite code, find files, run reviews — but each task now receives its AI helper as an explicit input, making it easier to swap providers or test changes without breaking the rest of the system. Nothing about what the tools actually do has changed yet; this is purely behind-the-scenes wiring for future flexibility.

52c8877220a91be43ee357fbfa420cfb20765347.text: If you use the lighter-weight version of this coding assistant, you'll now get access to a faster, simpler thinking helper that runs on a newer model, alongside a more streamlined review helper. The assistant will spawn these lighter helpers instead of the full versions, and it no longer sets up formal step-by-step plans before diving in. Behind the scenes, the instructions it follows were trimmed so the lighter mode doesn't include the background planning steps. These changes are live for internal use today.

78bed8cfae272b337de52963663a166f825d2a99.text: If you run the test suite with a command like `--agents base,base-lite,base2`, the system now runs each of those helper versions on the same problems at the same time and then shows you a side-by-side scorecard so you can tell which version is best. Previously you could only ask about one helper at a time. The comparison report is generated automatically and saved alongside the regular test results. This only matters if you are the kind of person who launches these automated helper comparisons today.

de251aa9733c0427d81579d1aa9ee04acce9304a.text: When you look at a past software project to check how a new feature performs, your tools now download only the essential history of that project instead of the entire record, which speeds things up and uses less storage. Each test run also now records the exact version of the code its results build on, so it's easier to trace back to the precise state later. This change is live today and affects only internal benchmarking, so you wouldn't notice it directly in your normal work.

95b4d8e4868428e74c708595676fb1544ea43d4c.text: Today, when Buffy the Orchestrator runs a complex coding task, it can now choose a more powerful teamwork mode that lets it spawn an extra helper agent to read and explore code files more thoroughly, and that helper will stream its findings back live instead of hiding them. You would notice this only if you ran Buffy on the 'max' teamwork setting, where the helper it calls in for exploring files will now report its progress in real time so you can watch it work.

7749099ba5a987c262d8317c33e33939f501e333.text: Behind the scenes, the code that builds the code-reviewing assistant (the part that scans changes and flags issues) was reorganized: one definition file was removed and its building blocks were merged into another. Anyone who runs or maintains the reviewer tools will see a different file layout and one fewer configuration to update, but the review experience itself behaves the same. It is live as of this snapshot and has no effect beyond the internal reviewer setup.

fc27ede766ebfca965131039f32ae18434d4ee70.text: Imagine you and your team have a shared digital toolbox where you keep all your project files. Every time you run a test to check how well your AI helper is doing its job, the system was saving detailed log files of each test right inside that shared toolbox. These log files were cluttering up the space and making it harder to find the files you actually cared about when you looked at the project history. The system now automatically hides those test log files so they no longer show up in the shared project history. Any leftover log files from previous tests have also been quietly removed. This means the project history stays clean and focused on the actual code changes. If you were to look at the shared toolbox now, you would only see the project files and code changes instead of a bunch

4c9651734f95d5b3926d7844c6ec39778fe81550.text: If you ask the assistant a question, it can now call in a helper that finds everywhere a function, variable, or setting is used across your project before answering. The question-answering helper was rebuilt so its setup and word choices live in one file instead of three, and it dropped a couple of tools it no longer needs. This is live today for everyone using the ask mode.

14a5ce45cb782f613a2510abd25835090bdf2574.text: Starting today, when the system runs its automatic quality checks, it now defaults to only the essential core set of tests rather than running the full suite. This means fewer tests run by default, which should make those checks faster and more focused. If you maintain or rely on these checks, you'd notice that some additional test scenarios that previously ran automatically now need to be triggered separately. The new default keeps things streamlined for everyday use while still keeping the door open to run the broader set when needed.

53fa11877ff1d106dd40de5c02a90f6c28d829a1.text: The system that runs the assistant's responses now receives its language-model connection from a shared, passed-in source instead of importing it directly. This affects every part of the app that generates a response — the live backend, the automated tests, and the evaluation harnesses — and means all of those pieces now use one consistent way to reach the AI model. If you looked behind the scenes, you'd see the model-calling helper moved from a hardcoded import into a named slot on a shared toolkit object that is passed around and frozen in place.

a28a7ed3c7d8a2c540f9e6ff28b28e98b721b1de.text: The team took a piece of wiring that connected the agent's brain (the reasoning engine) to the rest of the system and moved it from a plug-in slot to a direct connection. Instead of telling every part of the system to bring its own copy of the brain module, each part now simply asks for what it needs at the moment it needs it. This means the agent's ability to stream replies is now handled through one consistent path rather than being passed around as a dependency, making the wiring simpler and the flow of requests more predictable. You wouldn't see a visual difference, but the system is less likely to get tangled or confused about which brain module is in use.

92cfaa2fba620a3dd322f335dbe7404d20edcfae.text: The system moved all its helper-assistant setups from a single messy folder into organized subfolders named base, editor, and researcher, and gave each helper a file whose name matches where it now lives. If you manage or rely on these helpers, you would no longer find the old top-level files like ask.ts or base.ts; they now live inside.agents/base/ instead, and any references pointing at the old names were switched to the new paths, including some IDs that changed from researcher-docs to researcher-web/researcher-docs. Three of the deleted helpers were removed because they were duplicates or unused, so spawnable lists that used to mention them now point at the surviving IDs. Live today across the 33 changed files: the move is complete, imports follow the new layout, and the

054041acb6e82c577f3982b1034a97b83a4c459b.text: The codebuff assistant had a bunch of shared definitions (like logging formats and data types) living in a separate package called @codebuff/types. That package has been deleted, and everyone who needed those definitions now imports them directly from the @codebuff/common package instead. If you peek at the project structure, the scattered helper files under the old package location are gone, and the corresponding files inside the common package now hold all of these shared definitions in one place. The end user sees no difference in how the assistant behaves today, but the codebase is now tidier and easier for the team to maintain.

6d7f3c94aceba9530dabc3995117e1c05f8bf4a4.text: The main helper that runs your coding tasks has been broken into a team of more specialized helpers, each focused on a narrower job like searching code, listing folders, or sketching out new code before it is written. What you experience is that planning, reviewing, and thinking steps now route through these dedicated roles instead of one general one, and one old helper named Buffy the Orchestrator coordinates them. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping with no direct change to any app or command you run today.

acb4b791af9df7d35ef2a3c504e513d0b0c208af.text: The backend team updated several behind-the-scenes functions so they now receive a logging tool through their parameters instead of fetching a global logger. This lets each request or session carry its own tracing context, making logs easier to follow. Nothing changes for you as a user right now; this is internal housekeeping to improve debugging and traceability.

d54e005911ba295594a81002a5df5118606ecc13.text: The backend now wires up its helper tools (like logging and run tracking) by handing each step an explicit bundle of dependencies, rather than having each step reach out and grab them directly. What you experience: the agent flow keeps working the same way today, but the internal plumbing is decoupled so steps receive what they need through shared context instead of hardcoding imports. This is live now and is purely a refactor - no new visible behavior, just cleaner connections behind the scenes.

cd81abc72c44a39f5550d54709d18321ddde4d6a.text: The engineering team wrote down a step-by-step plan for how they will change the way internal logging works in their backend code. This is just the planning document—no actual code or behavior changes are live yet, and it only affects internal tooling that developers use. If you looked at the repository today, you would see a new planning file that lays out how they intend to pass logging utilities through function arguments instead of having it available globally, along with reminders to run a full type check afterwards to catch any mistakes.

8034a4a5b3321cc0de16275a6666bf236f9d5a39.text: The system lost its old shared error-reporting tool and now each part builds its own simpler version instead. If you looked at the code today, you'd see fewer files pulling from a single central logger; instead, the billing helper dropped its reference to logging, the monthly usage script writes errors directly to the standard error stream, and the text-replacement step now uses a nearby local logger. Nothing about what users see changes, but the behind-the-scenes reporting is now spread out rather than gathered in one place.

b944aae38e42c85cf9f5f7e23fc28d02f577f59f.text: The assistant can now find and inspect files in a project by name pattern, like asking to see every config or test file at once. A new file-finder lets it search using patterns such as "*.json" or "src/**/*.ts" and a directory-listing tool shows what files sit in a given folder. Both tools are live today, and the finder returns results sorted by most recently modified, capped at 15 matches per search with a hard limit of 250 across all searches.

13355c40a4d053d8e7aa3b8743ae336090f1c146.text: If you have the Max plan, your coding assistant now switches to a stronger model for deep thinking and for reviewing your code changes — and it does so more quietly, since the review step only runs on meaningful edits rather than every little keystroke. Behind the scenes, the assistant merges its two thinking modes into one, stops asking for your permission to think hard, and removes old debug logging so the process feels smoother. Your work history and file retention settings also got cleaner, and the assistant now keeps track of a few more details when summarizing long conversations.

3d73b9cbc895bfda6a7d9324ba27c8feca06db19.text: When you publish or validate an agent (like adding a custom helper to your workspace), the system now needs to be explicitly handed its logging tool instead of grabbing one it keeps around behind the scenes. Think of it like a restaurant kitchen: previously, every station would sneak over to a shared spice rack to log notes whenever it needed; now, the manager must hand each station its own labeled spice kit at the start of the shift. You won't notice this directly, but if you ever look at the validation process logs, things should be slightly cleaner and more predictable, since each step is using its own designated tool rather than reaching into a shared, invisible supply closet.

0d7b7f07109f706992af0ec4989624acd875abbb.text: You might notice that logging messages and database-related definitions now live in one shared location instead of being tied specifically to the agent runtime component. The agent run startup and completion functions have been simplified to reference these central types directly rather than defining their own. Nothing about how agents actually run has changed—it's just cleaner organization behind the scenes.

153fcfae637fec18f12587de88627705769fe527.text: The app removed two pieces of old, unused code that were quietly failing to do anything: a helper that tried to log errors through an analytics service it could never reach, and a set of utilities meant to encrypt and store API keys that no part of the product was actually calling. If you looked at the settings or logs, you would notice nothing changed because nothing was reading or using that code to begin with. This cleanup only deletes dead code and updates the internal documentation, so it is safe and live today with no effect on how the app behaves.

243fded6c481960d76415bde7cf0cf85a7aa19b1.text: When the assistant starts, finishes, or records a step in an agent run, it now always receives a logger so it can write debug, info, warning, and error messages through that single consistent object instead of a hard-coded one. This lets callers such as the step loop and programmatic step runner pass in their own logger, so log messages stay tied to the right run and the code can be tested with controlled output.

34aaac5a5350b143cdc652ec1ef92b41735eb3d4.text: A new, still-empty building block called the agent-runtime was added to the project's shared toolkit, and the main backend now lists it as a dependency it expects to use. If you looked at the project's configuration files today, you'd see references to this new package, but because its source code is empty, it doesn't actually do anything yet — it's just scaffolding waiting to be filled in.

7ec84dff520dcaf25b9420a1ef1b38101a944510.text: The internal team moved all the deep-thinking helper definitions into a single dedicated folder, so anything that looks for those helpers now uses the new path. Two old helper files were removed, and the remaining ones had their instructions cleaned up to no longer depend on shared persona settings. If you looked at this change today, you’d see one folder of related helpers instead of scattered ones, but the actual thinking behavior you rely on stays the same.

7b7a1af5be96f149c61ee71628ff4a0c01d5d0fb.text: A feature that let one assistant silently spawn and coordinate multiple helper assistants in the background has been turned off and its supporting pieces deleted. You would not see a new button or option for this anywhere—any workflows or automations that depended on that background spawning will now run without it, and the assistants will only do work the direct way instead of quietly farming parts out to other assistants behind the scenes. The change is live now for anyone using the assistant, because the code that powered it is no longer part of the system.

fb9fee641c9ea126a149f3a94e369c1f3e03ee12.text: When you ask the coding assistant to tackle a tricky problem, it now pauses to think through several different angles of the problem before it starts planning, like having a careful brainstorming step before making a to-do list. This slower upfront thinking is available right now when the assistant runs its standard multi-step coding workflow. The assistant can also search through code examples more thoroughly during its research phase, and the read-only helper that explores your files can no longer launch other assistants, keeping it strictly in observation mode.

7a7299fde3edbc83b67c25d47b495b78ee484c2e.text: The team published their internal game plan for the next few weeks, so anyone watching the project can see what they're focusing on right now. It tells you that the engineering staff are rebuilding the command-line tool from scratch with a new visual interface, moving more of the work onto your own computer instead of a remote server, and building a smarter version of their automated programming helper that you can try out today by typing a special command. Nothing changed in how anything works yet because of this—it's just a posted schedule of where effort is being spent.

99daf6cd36cecea2d6ae560cce6af1933756a196.text: The main helper that runs your coding tasks was rebuilt to coordinate work in a new way, and it now uses an upgraded model to do so. As part of the same update, several older variants that relied on a different provider were removed, so only the new setup remains active. If you were watching the internals, you would see the old coordinating files gone and the new one in place; from a user standpoint, nothing you directly start has changed today, but the system behind it now runs on the newer configuration.

a57d231d62f6756512255fb072978e000f8a5f30.text: The assistant now groups together many small text-editing requests to a file and applies them all at once, instead of editing each one individually, which makes large multi-edit changes faster and less likely to fail partway through. When several edits are bundled, an AI helper can review and apply them as a set, and if an edit can't find what it's looking for in the file, the system returns a clear error instead of silently doing nothing. You'd notice this as smoother, more reliable edits when the assistant rewrites chunks of code, especially when files end up with no net changes (an error is now explicitly returned instead of a vague 'no change' message). It's already live today.

2fd2162227a4d7519fa36e6b74cd6aa08e2a6942.text: The system now lets the assistant use a new external model provider, so it can access models that weren't available before (and this is live as of the snapshot dated 2025-10-06). When the assistant answers you, it can also save extra details about how it thought through the answer, including the actual reasoning text and how many reasoning tokens it used. If you look at conversation records, you'd see new information stored alongside each message showing which assistant agent produced it and what kind of internal reasoning happened, even for messages where some previously-required reference fields are now allowed to be missing.

ea10e06cb24feaed39a4c389d96a2360748a7b91.text: Starting today, when one assistant hands off work to another assistant (for example, a planning assistant asking a code-editing assistant to make changes), the receiving assistant can now see the full back-and-forth conversation from before the handoff. Previously, the receiving assistant only got a brief summary, so it often missed important context like earlier decisions or files already discussed. To make this possible, the system was also simplified: the assistant that coordinates the handoffs now only does two jobs (sending work and reading files), and the editor assistant gave up its own copy-paste tools in favor of reusing the parent's prompt. You would notice this as smoother, more coherent multi-step tasks that don't lose track of what was agreed upon earlier in the conversation.

ab9a465cd44a06f4e7484961f052349e6057b54a.text: Behind the scenes, the engineers moved some helper code that sets up temporary test repositories into its own dedicated file, making it easier to reuse across different parts of their internal tooling. Users would notice nothing different since this is purely an internal cleanup with no impact on functionality or performance.

c5e091f351e22120b69ed60b8044a2468ed47272.text: An internal planning tool now uses a specialized helper that breaks big tasks into smaller pieces and assigns them to other helpers at the same time, then combines their work into one plan. If you looked, you would see a new configuration file that tells the system how to run this process, but it only affects how the company's internal tools are built, not anything you directly interact with.

5739bfadbdf38fe5daaf3236439480bcc64280b5.text: A new automated assistant was added that can independently test the system's planning capabilities by cloning repositories, running evaluations, and comparing file states before and after. At the same time, the order of instructions given to the system was changed so that a critical rule about which tools are available now appears before the descriptions of each tool. If you looked at the system's behavior, you would notice that the new assistant can dynamically load and test different planning agents, and that the main system now receives its tool-access rules earlier in its setup. The change is internal and affects how the evaluation and planning workflows operate behind the scenes.

c06f476a31525cc3320c0b1a24108623d72dee22.text: Every time an assistant message is processed and costs need to be recorded, the system now tries to save that cost to the billing database up to three times before giving up. If the save ultimately fails, it throws an error so that no cost data is silently lost. This only affects internal billing and credit-consumption tracking behind the scenes; end users will not notice any change to how the assistant works or how their account is billed.

bd9fe14e9a9f7e7eccac7c665a2b4c3ab339ab48.text: When you run a search or use the AI tools inside the CodeBuff app, the software needs to know where its own helper files live on your computer. In older versions, that lookup broke when the app was packaged in a way called ESM, which meant searches and code analysis could fail silently. Now the app finds its files reliably whether it's running in the older or newer packaging style, so both full-codebase searches and automatic code navigation work again. You won't see anything different in the menus, but things that used to error or hang now just work.

0fc18275eb2baded595dd1e540728d2500a1bf1b.text: The coding assistant can now tackle bigger, multi-step jobs by breaking them into pieces and assigning each piece to a smaller specialist helper, rather than trying to do everything itself. Those specialists handle narrow chores like researching, planning a step, editing code, or reviewing the result, so a complex task gets handed off and coordinated automatically. If you watched it work, you'd see the main assistant pause, spawn one or more of these helpers in turn, collect their output, and then either continue or hand back a finished result. The change is already in place for anyone running this setup.

973aecfde121f57ce98402c67bfbee039783f032.text: A new research assistant can now search through your Notion notes and documents and find answers to specific questions, while a second assistant coordinates it by breaking big research topics into smaller questions and running those searches in parallel. These assistants are defined in two new configuration files that were added, and both connect to Notion using a shared integration token. If you looked at the files, you'd see the first is a specialized search tool that knows how to read Notion databases and pages, and the second is a coordinator that can spawn multiple instances of the search tool at once to gather information faster. This is live today for anyone using the internal agent system.

5dbf30d40c060361a702724debed8c886992a656.text: When you type `codebuff` at the command line, the placeholder file that used to greet new custom agents now shows up-to-date, simpler instructions written in plain commands you can copy and paste. Behind the scenes, the list of allowed AI helper tools was pared down—some older planning and output-control tools that nothing calls anymore were dropped, a couple of remaining tool groups were folded into broader, easier-to-read categories, and the configuration for connecting external services like Notion now lets you add private headers when running on your own computer. The bundled agent template also switched its default AI model from the previous recommended model to x-ai/grok-4-fast. These changes are live today wherever you download the latest version of codebuff.

6dc7848401b4167696523c366bc851a214df64e7.text: Clicking a documentation section now takes you to its own page instead of scrolling down within a single long page. The old behavior, where clicking a subsection link jumped the view to an anchor and relied on a smooth-scroll effect, has been removed; the sidebar now links directly to dedicated subsection pages. You would notice this if you use the internal docs site: navigation lands on clean, separate pages for each section, with prev/next buttons between them, rather than a single page with hash-based scrolling. This is live today for the docs navigation described above.

3620c288dfece6087a7f7d091063a55c3c2e4b4d.text: The agent reference page now pulls the actual TypeScript definition file live from the source code via a new internal endpoint, instead of showing a hand-maintained static copy that could drift out of sync. Anyone reading the docs on the website will see the current agent definition content automatically refreshed rather than a potentially outdated snapshot. Behind the scenes, the display component fetches and renders the freshly read source file on demand, so the documentation stays in step with the real code. This is live today and applies to the public-facing agent reference docs.

3827ca8068cbbf8e9617771fb87c2aad118cf0d9.text: An agent (the automated helper that builds and modifies code inside a project) can now be told to talk to external services called MCP servers. These servers act like extra toolboxes the agent can reach into on demand, so instead of only using the built-in tools, the agent can pull in custom tools defined by whoever set up that server. To use one, a project’s configuration lists the server by name (names cannot contain a slash) and optionally which specific tools to allow, written as serverName/toolName. When the agent runs, it asks the server for that tool’s instructions and then uses them just like any other tool during a turn. This is live today for projects that configure one of these servers; if no server is configured, nothing changes for the agent.

c2d4eb320cca5c35bca24e82ff9c634af2faea5d.text: When an AI assistant built with Codebuff works through a multi-step coding task, it can now stream live status messages—like 'reading file...', 'planning edits...', or 'found an error'—directly to anyone watching the process in a web browser or app. Previously, these behind-the-scenes logs stayed hidden in the backend until the whole task finished; now they appear in real time over the connection as the work unfolds. This affects developers building custom coding assistants with Codebuff's agent tools, especially those using simple text-based scripts (QuickJS) or full TypeScript setups. The feature works today: log messages written by the agent's code are now sent instantly to the frontend instead of being held back.

0ec2e79975f296601020169fd6c259534ccaa6bf.text: When you use the assistant without manually telling it which files to look at, it can now automatically find and read your project files on its own. It does this by scanning your project folder and skipping anything listed in your.gitignore file, so only relevant files get pulled in. You don't need to configure anything—if you don't specify files, this auto-discovery kicks in by default. The change is live today as part of the SDK.

4f5be7d3fa2bcdae47b3f4fe5d36ad6d39aca23c.text: A new assistant profile has been added to the company's internal toolkit, joining the existing lightweight assistants used for automated tasks. This new profile uses a different AI model that can think a little harder before responding, giving it medium-depth reasoning. If you are a developer building or modifying these internal agents, you can now select this reasoning-capable profile instead of the basic lightweight one. The capability is available right now in the internal agent directory, though only developers who explicitly choose it will see any difference.

6d42091e2faa4f5c79eee73cc40ee4d28d9a6bb2.text: The behind-the-scenes process that prepares and publishes new versions of the software has been simplified. Instead of using a complex system that generated special GitHub credentials on the fly, it now relies on a single pre-existing token stored in an environment variable. This removes the need for multiple helper scripts that handled cryptographic keys and token generation, and the documentation has been updated to reflect the simpler approach. The release process is already using the new method, so maintainers will see fewer steps and less custom logic when triggering releases.

88cc7bfb2f724ceaa5fe526249535c48b9c81920.text: A new lookup_agent_info tool has been added that allows the base agent to resolve and retrieve metadata for published agent IDs (like @publisher/agent-id@version). When you reference a full published agent ID, the system now validates it exists and returns its schema details before spawning. This affects the base agent factory and tool registration, enabling proper agent ID resolution today.

b4d321ea165cad7843a03d33175ae27b9a852895.text: When you visit the agent store page, it now loads faster and shows your login status correctly right away instead of flickering between states. The site moved the heavy data loading step to happen ahead of time so the page is ready before you see it, and it checks who you are on the server side so the navbar doesn't get confused about whether you're signed in. These fixes are live today.

c8c024256c6cb507648ff71a950cc7cfad6686c2.text: The main assistant that handles complex tasks like coding and research has been upgraded. Previously it used one specific AI model, but now it uses a more capable one, and it can bring in other specialized assistants to help it (like ones that research code, think through problems, or review work). If you give it a medium-to-hard task, it will now automatically create three different plans in parallel, compare them, and pick the best one before presenting its final answer to you. This should make the overall result higher quality since it's actively comparing multiple approaches, though the process might take a little longer as it runs through that comparison step.

3e3516db79eb7d4d1c78068c6055a0422f907602.text: If you log into the site and then open any page, the navigation bar at the top will briefly appear empty before your profile and links load in a split second later. The page still works the same once everything finishes loading, but there's a tiny flash where your account stuff isn't visible yet. This only happens on pages the site builds ahead of time for speed.

f02a7c97178c2c26cf1945adbcc1c610e2d5ecbf.text: When you visit the agent store page, you'll no longer see a gray loading placeholder animation while the content appears. The page now loads straight into the full list of agents without any intermediate loading state, because the separate loading screen file was deleted and the page generation settings were changed. The list also now starts with 24 agents already visible immediately rather than beginning empty and filling in as data arrived.

4101de8d3133d6f28bd1e3cf4036e89fbf98ad9a.text: Visitors to the store page will now see a simple loading animation with placeholder shapes while the page prepares, instead of a blank screen or delayed content. The store page has been switched to build as a static page ahead of time, which means it loads faster and can be served from a global cache, with the content refreshing automatically every ten minutes. Additionally, the agents list that the store page pulls from is now cached for a shorter duration of five minutes, while allowing cached copies to stay fresh for up to an hour, and responses are explicitly labeled with their type so browsers and caches handle them consistently.

79d51fed4589d252018daf3777dad93fefe52ac9.text: The separate guide file that walked people through building custom helper assistants has been folded directly into the main project instructions file, so there's now only one place to look for that information. You would notice this if you opened the project folder and looked for the guide — it's gone, and its contents now appear inside the main instructions document instead. This affects anyone reading the project's starter files to learn how to assemble or customize the assistant's teamwork setup, and it took effect with the version that ships this combined file.

2ba83d6f2b6309166d7ce9651e2f9cc7c5017f73.text: The system now has a set of checks that watch how it reacts when the assistant tries to use a tool but sends something broken, like instructions written in the wrong format or a request for a tool that doesn't exist. These checks make sure that when that happens, the system records the mistake properly instead of passing bad information along or losing track of where things went wrong. You wouldn't see this directly unless you were looking at logs or testing edge cases, but it means the system handles messy or incomplete inputs more reliably instead of crashing or silently dropping parts of a conversation.

5260144d060b2c381010cf1ca060693304002c37.text: When you ask Codebuff to do a coding task, you now get back a result object you can save and hand back for a follow-up, instead of starting each conversation from scratch. Behind the scenes, the connection logic was moved into a single, simpler entry point, so the same agent can keep context between runs. You'll notice this if you chain two prompts together: the second one will remember what the first one created or changed without you having to paste or describe it again. This behavior is active today for anyone using the SDK.

0eed7b6589e7b36cd6e6cd9ae178c2fa5a515632.text: The agent store page now loads faster for visitors because the list of agents is assembled on the server ahead of time instead of building it in your browser. If you opened the store page, you would still see the same search and sort options, but the initial list appears sooner since the heavy data work is done before the page reaches you. This is already live for anyone viewing the store page today.

24d738b56c7b9032b26da7d3c6f96ce6aa5d9477.text: The Agent Store page now loads faster because it builds the page ahead of time and only refreshes the agent list every 10 minutes instead of every minute. If you're browsing the store, you'll see the same agents for up to 10 minutes before new ones appear, but the page will start showing your login status a moment after it loads instead of waiting on the server. The timestamp next to each agent ("2 hours ago") now updates in your browser rather than being locked in when the page was built, so it stays roughly accurate as time passes. This is live now, so you can look at the store and notice these differences today.
