02e75684b4c2ef0f4086c3c69f34e137baf5fef3.text: The SDK now ships with its own copy of ripgrep, a fast file-searching tool, bundled directly into the package for Windows, macOS, and Linux on both Intel and Apple Silicon processors. Previously, it relied on an external copy from a separate project, which meant it could break if that external project changed or became unavailable. If you inspect the package, you will now see ready-to-run search tool binaries sitting inside it, and the package will automatically pick the right one for your computer instead of going looking elsewhere for it.

d8f79b328cee11300b8803578baf05e40b15223a.text: The research tools can now use a faster model to explore codebases and documentation. When you ask the assistant to research a topic, it will spawn specialized sub-agents that use this new fast model to search code, read docs, and explore files, completing research tasks more quickly than before. This affects anyone using the research features internally.

16e270c1ee516c18480d506077f8731686374a02.text: You can now save a helper as its own app command. After running a setup command, you can type that helper's name directly instead of opening a separate program and asking for it. The setup works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, installs the helper into your settings folder, and gives you commands to add, remove, update, check, upgrade, or list your installed direct commands.

c126a30593d7f3279168703bbadd1c5ebe150d6f.text: The team removed four old assistant setup files that were no longer being used anywhere in the system. These files described 'Buffy Lite' helper variants and their sub-agents, but no active configuration actually referenced them. If you looked, you would find the folders ".agents/lite/base2-factory.ts", ".agents/lite/base2-lite.ts", ".agents/lite/editor-lite.ts", and ".agents/lite/reviewer-lite.ts" are gone, and nothing that remains depends on them. The change is live today and simply clears out unused parts of the internal tooling. — no behavior you rely on is affected.

d56bf0c09c00ed6c386b397de5a6ec801fc303ef.text: The helper kit that other software uses to talk to Codebuff can now be loaded in two different ways: one for modern projects and one for older projects. If you're building something that uses Codebuff's tools, your project can now choose whichever style of importing it you normally use, and it will work without conversion steps. The two separate packages are built side by side, with the modern one being the default for new projects. If you looked, you'd see two different bundle files in the output folder, one labeled for modern style and one for older style.

c97840e55968fed1a1bd564b80b38c9cb390ef26.text: The onboarding wizard now shows a different number of steps depending on whether you arrived with a referral code, and referral landing pages reuse the same step flow instead of a separate page. If you click a referral link, you'll see the welcome card and then proceed through the standard setup steps with the referral code already filled in, rather than being sent to a dedicated referral-only screen. This is live today for anyone signing up through a referral link or visiting the referrals area.

47b7615d03ac29d103611335675885e9881daaa7.text: The team cleaned up leftover API keys from the configuration files, removing two keys that were no longer being used by the system. If you were setting up your local development environment using the example file, you would now use a single key called CLAUDE_CODE_KEY instead of separate keys for Anthropic and OpenAI. The internal tool that runs automated tests now correctly maps this new key to the system it needs. Since these were inactive keys, most people will not notice any difference in their day-to-day work.

936ef5a2c914a6cca745be0ce2a2f2de0d3eaa91.text: When someone clicks a referral link to join Codebuff, the page now stores their referral code more reliably in the browser before showing the signup screen, so the credit is less likely to get lost. The back button on an agent's detail page now has a safety net: if there's no history to go back to, it sends you to the store page instead of doing nothing. You would notice a smoother experience landing on a referral page and a back button that actually takes you somewhere useful even on a fresh visit.

927d66df680ac2e25db6584e11a45e7ad74b0580.text: You can now run a new terminal command that adds one or more assistant IDs to the list of assistants a project is allowed to call. Running the command prints which IDs were newly added and which were already on the list, and it updates the project's settings file directly. Nothing else in the project setup is touched, so existing settings stay in place. The feature is available today through the command line.

27921c25ca825f1c4a385e257f3cd63e0525de64.text: When you open the app on a phone or smaller screen, pages like your profile, the store, and agent usage charts now spread out or stack neatly instead of getting cramped or cut off. The sign-in screen was also updated so that after you log in you can return straight to the page you were heading to, and links from email or the command-line tool work as intended. You'd notice cleaner layouts with less sideways scrolling and a smoother transition from signing in to getting back to your work.

6cb0d214c2573ba320cd6c7560ed76b5d193e9bf.text: The agent store page on the web now loads faster when there are many agents listed. Instead of rendering every agent's full card in the browser at once, it only shows the ones visible on your screen and swaps in new rows as you scroll through the 'All Agents' grid. The page also adjusts how many agent cards appear side by side depending on your screen width, fitting one card across on a phone, two on a tablet, and three on a desktop, with virtualization kicking in only when the list gets long enough to need it. This change is already live today.

afa50cef2b2e3ad224709a400c644332f20f04fe.text: You know how when you want to run an agent from the command line, you'd type something directly? Now the tool quietly puts the agent's name into your input box first, so you can just press enter and edit it before running. In your web browser, when you look at an agent's details, the little usage numbers that used to sit in a separate box now appear right next to each version in the list, and the buttons for running and saving an agent have swapped their icons for a 'play' symbol and a bookmark, with clearer messages that pop up after you click. None of this changes what the agents can actually do—it's all about making the screens and commands look and feel cleaner.

7bc9570e4ad49fbf79acbfba3ba99e0cb16505ef.text: On your agent detail page, when you view a specific agent, there is now a new "Save this agent" button sitting next to the existing "Copy ID" and "Run agent" buttons. Clicking it copies the text “codebuff save-agent [agent-id]” to your clipboard and shows a small notification confirming the copy. The button appears for anyone viewing the agent detail page and is active today.

eb99717911a7e0fc2ef460c70a6d43a57c6a0b37.text: When you view a specific version of an agent in the web interface, you will now see two buttons: one that copies the agent's ID to your clipboard, and another that copies the full command needed to run that agent (like 'codebuff --agent <id>'). If you visit the public agent store, each agent card will also show a button that copies the same run command. These buttons save you from having to manually find and retype the correct command each time you want to launch an agent.

978c4a991cb11b15be437b2d5cf4306f5bfbba4a.text: A new four-part digital assistant has been added to the internal system, working together to fetch information from the web, clean and organize it, and then present the most useful results. Each part has its own specific role: one searches the web, another sorts and formats the data, and a third ranks everything based on what matters most to you. This assistant was assembled in September 2025 and is now available within the tool's agent registry, meaning you can use it today to run a complete search-and-filter workflow that previously required manual steps.

5d4b23f4c8f3bc3ce0316fbd71079e19376bc001.text: When you open the detail page for a specific version of an agent, its technical definition now displays as neatly formatted, color-coded text instead of plain, unstyled JSON. Each important setting like the agent's name, instructions, and step-handling code appears with its own readable formatting, making the configuration easier to scan and understand. This affects anyone viewing agent definitions on the internal web publisher detail pages, and the improvement is already live.

b276ed02a2b173d435dbf891dbdacba22661dbd5.text: When you ask the assistant a question, you can now drop an image file path right into your message, the way you would attach a photo to an email. The tool you talk to will shrink and compress that image (up to about two megabytes) before sending the picture along with your text to the assistant, so you can ask questions about screenshots, diagrams, or photos instead of only typing. If you look closely at the new message you send, you will see a little paperclip note summarizing how many images were attached and their total size in kilobytes. This works today in the command line tool and the backend that powers it, with no special switch to flip.

a843dae88c94285ab67804c71d9532639cbf1f1e.text: The agent store page now loads list views much faster when you browse completed agents. The system added targeted indexes that act like sorted filing tabs for already-finished agents, so the database skips the slow full table search and pulls results by agent name, publisher, version, or your own completed runs instead. You can scroll and filter the completed agent list without waiting on long loading pauses, and the lookup for your past runs shows up quicker when you open the store.

f870afd6fc98c6d4c282d57a9999e52146eb929c.text: Starting today, the system that sends back AI replies now watches each chunk of text itself and cuts the reply off the moment a predetermined stop marker appears, instead of waiting for the upstream AI service to do it. This affects you if you are streaming a response through the core prompt path, because the new manual stop-sequence handler now controls exactly where the streamed text ends. If you watched closely you would notice the reply stops mid-stream right at your configured stop sequence, with no extra trailing text, and any buffered text up to that point is still flushed out before the stream closes.

d7a030548ce8b3024c8b5795729b434eb1588f54.text: Codebuff has published a new document at the top of its project that spells out how community members are expected to treat each other, what kinds of behavior are not allowed, and how to report concerns by emailing support@codebuff.com. The rules apply to all official community spaces and events, and they were adapted from a widely used public template. If you participate in Codebuff's community or contributor activities today, these are the standards you are now held to.

b64c31d77633c6c4dfdca27101978ce88f907f05.text: When you are looking at a specific publisher's page or that publisher's individual agent details, the 'Back' arrow now takes you to wherever you were before instead of always jumping to a fixed page. The site added one shared back button and swapped out the old, page-specific ones, so navigation follows your actual browsing history. This is live today for anyone viewing publisher and agent detail pages.

62a47a4cb7e9dedbc891f8bdf0790a6fe2730408.text: The system now has a new helper that can automatically review code changes before they are finalized. When someone on the development team asks for a review, this helper looks at what changed using the project's version history tool, reads the affected files, and brings in another helper to find any related files that might be affected. It then gives written feedback on what could be improved. This only affects the internal team's workflow and does not change anything you see as a user today.

549a261f62cac8282808c079f3e2fd5e9c269a86.text: If you're reading the Web docs and looking for a hand‑held guide, you'll now see a new 'Walkthroughs' entry in the sidebar. Opening it shows the first walkthrough, a step‑by‑step tour for creating your first custom agent, presented in the same guide format as the rest of the Web docs. Clicking either entry loads straight to that page on the site, so it's live today for anyone browsing the Web docs surface.

148d1c73f460f72e3b864797d647b486d87a3358.text: CodeBuff published a short page telling people how to privately report security problems: if you find a security flaw, you should email support@codebuff.com rather than posting it publicly on GitHub issues. Nothing else in the product changed, and the new reporting instructions are live and visible today.

916ee1fedd8e7caee71faabe679cf983a460b5e4.text: When you browse the agent store or view an agent's detail page, you'll now see a small circular picture of the person who published it beside their name. If that publisher hasn't uploaded a picture, the space will show the first letter of their name or ID instead of appearing empty. The system now pulls that picture from the publisher's profile information, which it didn't show before.

3c8986b38c45b4cb0a7a607c87feda29a41c3a70.text: The tool now has two new assistants available. One reads your project code to find the right build and test commands, while the other runs quick, read-only terminal queries using a faster model. These assistants were moved and renamed, with the main one shifting to a top-level folder and gaining slightly more codebase awareness. The changes are live today as part of the September 12, 2025 update.

1a1d4cdf5378c1fe6c4acc06753065b07d358393.text: The contributor setup instructions now guide you to load all the necessary secret keys (like API keys for various services) into a tool called Infisical by importing a template file named.env.example, with a specific note to manually fix the database password line. You'll also find a new step-by-step setup guide document linked from the main instructions, and the service startup order is now explicitly listed as backend first, then web server, then CLI. If you followed these steps before, you now need to use the new import command and adjust the database URL to match the local Docker credentials.

2383f28ac6ccdf104d0779c41385815a9b771162.text: The project stopped keeping a private setup file that links your computer to your secrets workspace in the shared code folder, so that file no longer gets accidentally shared or exposed. Instead, each person now creates their own matching file locally by running a new setup command described in the contribution guide, and the project now treats that personal file as something to keep private. If you clone or look at the code, you won't see anyone's workspace id anymore, and if you join development you'll follow the updated guide to make your own private link.

453e865754de799ccde739180429a59055b326b3.text: Today the lightweight assistant you can ask to brainstorm ideas switched to a smarter model that thinks a bit harder before answering, instead of the previous quick-thinking version. That assistant also lost a helper that used to let it stop itself mid-conversation, so from now on it will keep using tools until your request is fully done rather than pausing early. A new, even simpler assistant called quick was added for tasks that need a fast, no-frills response. You will notice this if you ask either assistant to do something multi-step, because they will work through it continuously instead of stopping after a single partial reply.

36a870f0b74b53e35d8e041aba31f694241b393d.text: When the assistant looks back at a list of files it already read while working on your project, the tool now correctly pulls the file details out of the right spot in the response, so it no longer crashes or misreads the information. Previously, the code tried to read file results as if they were all stored in the same format, but the file-updates tool wraps its results in a different shape, causing errors; now the parsing logic understands that difference and handles each tool's output correctly. This affects any task where the assistant reviews previously read files, making that step reliable instead of failing silently or producing wrong results. The fix is live today for all agents using the updated tooling.

3d6dbdecbf5f64d99a76f7b4048292718de656ac.text: The assistant used to automatically check which of your files had changed since you last looked at them — comparing new changes against everything you'd read before, filtering by token limits, and deciding what to re-read on its own. Now it has stopped doing that automatic checking. When you ask it to look at a file, it reads exactly the file you named and nothing more, without trying to sneak a look at other things it thinks changed. If you used to rely on it noticing file changes between turns without being told, that behavior is gone — you now have to explicitly ask it to read the files you want it to see.

3388b22dcf16bb140ef45efb664609f8cd806e68.text: The project cleaned up its written guides: a separate page about setting up a development environment was removed, and its instructions were folded into the main contributor guide alongside some light editing of the project's front-readme. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping that tidy contributors will notice as a single, slightly neater place to read setup steps, but it changes no behavior you'd run into day to day.

10dc52b48ef20a6d1b1bb2336e1d72e07ca6e8fa.text: The project team added a new guide that explains how outsiders can pitch in by fixing bugs or adding features. If you open the main project page, you'll now see a link that takes you to step-by-step instructions covering everything from installing the right tools to submitting your proposed changes. The guide lives alongside all the other documentation but is meant only for collaborators, not casual visitors.

bb06e768c5ec19d836ce6d5a783a773fcdb2edaa.text: On the page for a specific version of an agent, you can now see a new summary card showing how much the agent has been used this week and overall. The numbers include total runs, money spent, average cost per use, how many different people used it, and the date it was last run. While those numbers load, you will briefly see gray placeholder boxes instead of blank space or a spinning icon. In the shared agent directory, you can also choose to sort the list by how many unique users have tried each agent.

1ab6c9fe589d8ff53eb1081fc765ef8369fc8a6d.text: The agent store cards now lead with the agent's ID and a version badge rather than displaying the name first, making it easier to identify and reference specific agents at a glance. Money amounts now show as '$1.5k' instead of '$1500.00' when they hit a thousand or more, and time stamps update in plain language like 'just now' or '3 hours ago' instead of showing a raw date. Anyone browsing the agent store will notice these cleaner, more conversational labels right away.

705d777231f507599c088d705abf026809c24d12.text: Publishers in the database can now only be owned by either one user or one organization, but not both at the same time and not by neither. This prevents confusing situations where a publisher record might accidentally be linked to both kinds of owners or to no owner at all. If you looked at the publisher records, you would see each one clearly tied to exactly one owner type. A separate cleanup also ensures that step numbers within an agent run stay unique. The change is live today.

37d4c0c6379ab72349d088dcacde4751484385da.text: When the assistant runs a helper agent for you, it now prints a clear, labeled header at the start and end of that helper's work, like 'My Agent (id123)' and 'Completed: My Agent (id123)' with a divider line, instead of a plain dashed line that could interrupt the loading spinner. The header is only shown when that helper is the main task you're waiting on, and the spinner pauses and resumes smoothly around it so the output stays tidy. If you watch a subagent run, you'll see these cleaner headers appear without the spinner glitching. This behavior is live today.

c6fb1afec11328d13b53737412783f6da3c8867e.text: The CLI tool now displays your messages with proper formatting instead of raw text. When you're using the command-line version, text now appears with styled headings, indented bullet points, highlighted code snippets with colors, and proper spacing between sections. Previously, the assistant's replies would show up as plain text without any structure, so reading long responses with lists or code examples was harder. This makes reading conversations in the terminal much easier on the eyes.

9ac5443e315c21de8ba4985c35904715089c1111.text: The system now quietly records how much each AI task costs and how many steps it takes, storing this information as you work. When you run an agent, it starts a new entry, logs each step's credit usage, and closes the run with final totals. This data lives in two new database tables that the team can later use to show you detailed cost breakdowns per session. The change is live today, though you won't see new UI yet since it's the behind-the-scenes logging.

6ecd771c6dee76e84c4e74609480d586da55cb6a.text: If you open the project's main guide, you'll now see a side-by-side chart showing how it stacks up against a rival tool, plus the opening paragraph no longer leads with the score. The opening paragraph no longer leads with the score. The setup steps that used to sit in one block are now split into two labeled sections—one for installing and one for running—so it's harder to mix up which command comes first. The picture that shows how the different parts work together has also been shrunk to roughly half its previous width so it doesn't push the rest of the page too far down.

c75a1f2e2a6788f8446606eb76b184240799e7e0.text: When you visit someone else's referral page while signed in, you now see a GitHub sign-in button instead of a generic link if you're logged out. The page no longer shows a 'that's your own referral code' message inline; instead, the 'Complete Referral' button only appears for logged-in users who aren't the referrer. A new 'Refer Friends' link has been added to your profile dropdown in the navbar, and referral codes are saved in your browser when you sign in through the referral flow. These changes are live today across the web app.

ba774d8acf8e4a056c909ec349e40dd903eca391.text: The program's internal address book for how the assistant reads and understands messages was cleaned up so all the related definitions now live in one place instead of being spread across several files. If you looked behind the scenes you'd see the old separate pages for messages, images, and tool data were folded into a single reference sheet, and any code that used to fetch from the old pages was quietly redirected to the new one with no change to what you actually see. The change is live today and only touches how the system organizes itself internally.

70fb491f3bb5270529d59de8f19e1625fe4d958c.text: A new section showing how different AI coding tools compare has been added near the top of the homepage, right after the main welcome banner. If you visit the site today, you will see a highlighted block titled about coding agent evaluation, with animated badges and a chart comparing results, plus a new image illustrating Codebuff versus another tool. The homepage now loads a bit more content immediately, and the new section uses subtle animations that fade and slide into view as you scroll.

505330cc75765c46a02fbd4f458988652ccc8a3f.text: The coding assistant can now hand off quick, read-only terminal checks to a new specialized helper, so it can peek at your project's structure or search code without touching anything. You wouldn't run or install anything different yourself; when the assistant needs a fast fact about your codebase, it may now spawn this helper instead of doing the work directly. The main assistant and its scouting helper also received minor prompt updates and an additional search capability. This behavior is available as of the September 6, 2025 snapshot.

c2c9848af041c2011b6589328393a5d8f5c8869e.text: When someone updates the standard starter templates for AI agents in the main project, those template files now automatically get copied over to a separate shared repository that other teams and projects can pull from — no manual copying or syncing needed anymore. This keeps everyone using the same base set of agent instructions without someone having to remember to copy changes by hand. You wouldn't see this happening directly, but if you rely on those shared agent templates, your copies will now stay up to date automatically whenever the main project's starter files change. The system uses a secure token to authenticate the transfer, so only authorized updates are pushed through.

7cacb9278a28ef9cf803ee44ca5fa20eb8c7befc.text: The team deleted an internal planning note that described an idea for later splitting the security settings page into two separate pages: one for API keys and one for profile-related items like usage and sessions. Nothing on the website changed as a result. If you opened the website today, your security settings page would look exactly the same, because the plan described in the deleted note was never built.

4d4c11a1815e6f6aae3b2d54412259d47f310bbd.text: The code-map package now loads its language-parsing engine dynamically at runtime instead of bundling all the pieces together at build time, which means the WebAssembly files for each programming language are resolved on demand when you actually need them rather than being included unconditionally. This change is live today and primarily affects anyone using code-map's parsing features, who will see fewer upfront loading costs for language support they don't use. If you looked at the internals, you'd notice the bundle size for the core package is significantly smaller since the language-specific parsers are no longer statically imported.

9262fa52938d34fe8f183cebb2185ab96660e167.text: If you click or type a referral link on the website today, you'll see a page that tells you the code isn't applied online — instead it shows terminal-style install instructions for applying the code yourself in the Codebuff command-line app. Behind the scenes, the site now keeps your referral code safe while you sign in with Google or GitHub, and if it ever gets lost, a small recovery step on the home page catches it and finishes applying the credit for you. This only affects people signing up through a referral link; it doesn't change anything for users logging in normally without a code.

d95fe720bdf34f2f88719ba73aa0de98350d46ae.text: If you open Codebuff's main project page, you'll see a rewritten introduction and a short looping demo showing the tool in action, plus a new diagram explaining how it coordinates several AI agents at once instead of relying on a single helper. Anyone building custom workflows now has a step-by-step guide and clearer sample files describing how to define their own agents, choose which AI model they use, and mix automated steps with AI decisions. A separate setup guide was added explaining how to run Codebuff locally for development, covering the required tools and environment. The supporting command-line and agent-template files were adjusted to match the new documentation structure, so the published materials stay accurate as the system evolves.

ca45080a3851f24c32b1dd46f90f0bfe88953620.text: If you looked in the project's folders today, you'd find that the internal team removed several files they used to run automated tests, which were scripts and lists for checking the software against outside programming problems. These tests helped them measure how well their code fixing tool worked, but they are no longer using that system and have cleared it away completely.

4131f72b6d59d7515ddb9b7e4bd0dafafd86f182.text: The assistant's message definitions, which previously lived as local files in both the main project and the starter template, are now pulled from a shared library called the SDK. This removes about 430 lines of duplicate type definitions across 15 files, leaving a single, authoritative copy maintained by the SDK. If you were to look at the project today, you would see those local message-related files gone and imports pointing to the SDK instead, meaning any future changes to how messages are structured will come from that shared library rather than being edited locally. This is live now and affects anyone using the starter template to build new agents, since they will inherit the SDK-managed types instead of local copies.

6110c51f2dffffc23fb6da01a37c49b92ff1b1ec.text: If you set up new agent templates from scratch, those agents now carry their own copy of the message handling code instead of pulling it from the shared toolkit package. The system added local blueprints defining how messages, images, files, and tool calls are structured, and rewired the template generator to use these local copies. Nothing changes for agents already running, and the toolkit package remains available for other parts of the platform; the shift only affects freshly created agent templates going forward.

f2cffd61c66eb9ac5e9522464891bf06bba9dd96.text: When a new project is created, it will now include a small configuration file in the custom assistants folder. This file tells the system that the folder holds your personalized AI assistants and describes what they do, along with the license terms. You would only notice this if you looked inside the assistants folder of a freshly created project; it does not change how the assistants themselves behave.

19e85ab18e8d389872435c9d4876a8b648ce0353.text: The team added a new guide explaining how they test the coding assistant's skills. Instead of just running simple quizzes, they now measure how well the assistant can rebuild actual software changes from real open-source projects, with an AI judge checking the work across correctness, efficiency, and code style. This guide lives only inside the company's internal testing system and won't change what you see in the product today.

6ebb174737994de585f600048ff23914815abe74.text: When you ask an agent to look through your code for matching text, it now actually scans your project files using a fast search engine instead of doing nothing. The search stays inside your project folder, so it can't wander into parent directories you didn't intend, and if the results get extremely long, they're cut off at a fixed size so nothing overloads the conversation. If an agent tries to run file-change hooks (like commands that trigger when a file is edited), those now quietly report that the feature isn't available in this environment rather than silently failing. Only tools that are officially published can be swapped out, so custom or experimental tools can no longer override the core published ones.

eb115012aa8c6a80a4369c0e1ea8b8ed69360262.text: You can now run a single command to set up a starter kit of example projects in your local folder. That kit includes sample projects, a how-to guide, and the rules the system uses to recognize your project files, all pulled from the same shared library that the existing agents feature uses. The new setup command is live today and ready to use.

10584871295dd90cfc84bf2a76fb1051c99eab71.text: The team reorganized how the assistant definitions store their settings and model references, moving the old configuration values into a separate labeled folder behind the scenes. If you looked at the code, you'd see references that used to point to the main settings file now point to a folder marked for legacy configs, but nothing about how the assistant behaves has changed. This is purely organizational cleanup with no visible effect for anyone using the system today.

091316b99d0fb730930f36691bf6f3c2bbf33f8f.text: When new agent projects are first created, they now include a copy of the standard Apache 2.0 license file, so anyone who gets or copies that starter project will see the licensing terms right away instead of wondering how they're allowed to use it. This only affects the initial project templates bundled with the software—it doesn't change how running agents behave or add any new functionality.

0877d4fc8a5d95fa8771ee023cc57ce37ffb52b5.text: A new lightweight coding helper called Buffy Lite is now available internally, which coordinates planning, editing, and reviewing for coding tasks. It still uses the same main orchestrator model but swaps in two different specialized models for the editing and reviewing steps, using a faster editor model and a chat-tuned reviewer model. The shared definition logic is now reusable, and the new files define how this lighter helper behaves. This is live today for internal use.

2c1a76aa597223d1c5191df56e4f5babbe66f89a.text: A duplicate assistant-checking helper was removed from the shared toolkit that both agents and the main program use, so only the primary copy of that validation logic remains. This is behind-the-scenes cleanup that doesn't change any visible behavior today, but it reduces maintenance confusion. If you looked at the project's internal files, you'd see one fewer file where the same check was duplicated.

c843bdf400fd6e53f65a28448561938e60c13222.text: When you or the system asks whether a listed helper-agent actually exists and can be used, the system now checks in two places instead of one: your locally defined agents and the published agents stored in the database. Any helper-agent reference that cannot be found in either source is now flagged as a validation error, so publishing or validating a set of agents will fail if a referenced subagent is missing from both sources. You would notice this if you try to publish or validate agents through the web interface and a referenced subagent no longer turns a blind eye — it now produces a concrete error instead of being silently allowed.

ad994723e7d3e52dd280a5a26510dc186736b5d9.text: If you look at a message record or a trace of an API call, you'll no longer see a fingerprint ID attached to it. The database column that stored this anonymous identifier has been permanently removed, and the code that used to write it there no longer does. The backend systems that relied on linking messages through this ID (including a script that counts daily active users) have been updated to work without it. This affects anyone viewing message traces or running analytics that depended on that identifier. The change is live today.

9a0d9dde91e6e1e9f77b647b1044da90ecf9de04.text: The system cleaned up its internal test dataset by removing entries that were created by failed generation attempts. If you looked at the test cases used to train the assistant, you would see that broken or incomplete test scenarios were stripped out, leaving behind only valid and runnable examples. This affects the quality of the data the assistant learns from, but you wouldn't notice it directly in your conversations.

bc640140ba10e9abbeb99e6ec3a0c221813071e2.text: The team removed some behind-the-scenes debugging tools from the system that were used during development but aren't needed now. These tools wrote log files to the server's filesystem and resolved file paths for prompts, but since the system doesn't rely on them anymore, they were deleted entirely. The logging system also had some leftover code removed that wasn't being used. Nothing you see or do in the application changes - this is purely internal cleanup. If you happened to look at the server's file structure, you'd notice these debugging files are simply gone.

b586383b9e0c3122140d7f2f73f2b6e9c1a96c45.text: When an AI helper uses a tool (like reading files or running a search) and gets a result back, that result is now saved in a clear, structured format with labeled fields for tool name, unique call ID, and output, instead of as a loose piece of text. A new setting lets the system quietly skip recording these tool usage notes in the message history when it’s not useful to keep them—like when a background check or summary step happens, keeping the conversation thread cleaner. If you looked, you’d see that messages from tools now show up as a distinct “tool” role rather than mixed in with regular text, and some internal helper agents that organize or clean up the work no longer leave behind noisy tool call records. This affects the AI agents that work behind the scenes on your code changes,

cd8111d1d5f25cde8bacdd7a96153a2e0acc3fc6.text: You won't see a new feature, but the assistant's behind-the-scenes machinery for editing your files just got simpler and more reliable. The team deleted their hand-written patch code, the thing that figures out how to merge suggested changes into your existing files, and replaced it with a widely-used off-the-shelf library called diff. That swap is live today for the desktop app and the programmable toolkit, and the two spots that actually apply your file edits now also explicitly catch and report the rare case where a change can't be merged instead of failing silently.

89d2af15b727726b51ca33f8b2c29abb0eb63a16.text: The project now has two new documents attached to it. One is the full legal text of the Apache License, Version 2.0, which spells out the rules for how the software can be used, shared, and modified. The other, called a NOTICE file, simply identifies the project by name as 'Codebuff' and states that it is copyrighted in 2025. If you were to look at the project's main folder, you would see these two new files sitting there at the top level.

ddcb7593efc6020e53cff6e078c3a80ba3eb8175.text: If you visit your profile page without being signed in, you now see a helpful "Sign in to Codebuff" card with a button to log in, instead of a blank or confusing page. The sign-in button has been improved to optionally track when people click it for analytics purposes, and it now preserves referral codes when you're signing in through other flows. The setup instructions for developers using the software development kit have also been simplified to a single clear line that links directly to where you get your API key. These changes are live today and affect anyone visiting the profile page while not logged in, as well as developers following the SDK setup guide.

6fb0494b34834fad98b268ce430968f4c42f5985.text: The software now uses a single, updated way of packaging conversations with the AI assistant, replacing an older, now-deleted method that translated between formats. If you looked at the code, you'd notice every part of the system that sends or receives messages now imports from the same shared message type. This is live today for anyone running version zero point one point seventeen of the tool, which includes the new message format along with instructions for setting up API keys and custom tools.

7c2cb2b0bdf6644394975a621161b7434a7ad7d3.text: When a developer saves a test file, the system now runs all unit tests across the backend, npm-app, and common packages using a single consolidated step instead of searching and running each test file individually inline. If every test passes, you see one clear success line; if any test fails, you still get the full detailed output so problems can be debugged. The new runner also handles the case where a package has no test files, reporting zero tests rather than erroring out. This is live today for internal developers working in those three package areas.

2cc0ca11dba0871a5942ca10a900f91d78806dfb.text: The planner now uses the GPT-5 High model exclusively for complex tasks, switching from a model that handled everything. If you triggered a plan, you'd notice it's labeled for heavyweight work and is slower because it's reserved for genuinely complex problems. This only affects the internal planning agent — not any direct user-facing feature yet.

7466d3853b0137fcc88e3d7c0d73074a79e73ae0.text: The internal tool that the assistant uses to read documentation now provides a clearer instruction for looking up MongoDB setup help, including the specific topic it covers. This behind-the-scenes fix corrects how that lookup request is formatted so it matches what the system expects, and it keeps the related automated checks in sync. You won't see any visible change in the assistant's responses; the correction prevents type-validation failures that could otherwise cause that documentation lookup to break during development.

e8eef4d62176ab5156b486e6d83d2f72c334f468.text: If you run the automated tests that check how the assistant behaves, those tests now talk to the assistant through the same connection method a real program uses, rather than a separate shortcut built just for testing. In practice, you would not see a different conversation or a different answer, but if something fails to output anything, a new debug print will help figure out why. The change only touches the test and evaluation setup, so nothing a regular user does with the assistant is affected. It is live today for whoever runs those evaluations.

8d9b622db70eb7529fbf3ef5c456d40717ae4d48.text: The assistant now has a new, more precise way of understanding the different types of messages it sends and receives, kind of like upgrading a filing system so each note is sorted by a clearer, stricter label. This affects the core messaging layer, so anyone working with the assistant's message-handling internals (such as developers extending the agent or tooling) benefits from fewer mismatches and more predictable data shapes. Because the new message types replace the older ones across multiple files, the project becomes easier to refactor and less likely to break when adding new message parts such as images, files, or structured reasoning. The change also tweaks a decision flag so that certain tool calls no longer automatically signal the end of a step, giving the agent more control over

027e8428279173140bdc3e9fea47749a558c554a.text: If you open the app, the separate menu items for security tokens, usage, and referrals are now gone and replaced by a single Profile section with tabs. Your personal access tokens now live under the label 'API Keys' instead of 'Personal Access Token,' and the old direct links to those pages will automatically send you to the right tab in your profile. Anyone who clicks or bookmarks the old addresses lands on the new tabs without breaking older links.

d6c91af4a750ea1fe31cd5be1b235db36ac9d682.text: The system now keeps a running tally of how much money each assistant session costs as it works, instead of only calculating costs at the very end. This only affects backend agent execution and cost tracking, so you wouldn't see a direct UI change, but the system can now report accumulated costs accurately for parent assistants that spawn subagents.

124fcefd042d4100e46408a1420e80fabb78874c.text: The software's research assistant can now send out two new specialized helpers on your behalf: one that browses the web for current information and another that reads technical documentation. These helpers were already available to be called but the main research coordinator now actively knows to use them and can launch as many of the web or documentation helpers as you need in a single request. If you asked the assistant to research something, you would notice it is now quicker to pull in up-to-date web results and official documentation alongside its normal file searching, and you may see it spawn multiple searchers at once instead of just one. The change was released today.

eae7f3081d5c6ab32780795d8f4ef127ab28d74d.text: The account security page now uses a single, simpler action to log you out of sessions or revoke access tokens, instead of handling each one separately through different hidden paths. When you sign in and visit the security settings, you'll see two tabs — one for web sessions (your open browser windows) and one for app tokens (programs accessing your account on your behalf) — and you can now revoke multiple sessions or tokens at once. Behind the scenes, the system checks that requests come from the official site (origin checks) and clearly separates web logins from long-lived API tokens so each kind is managed correctly.

9757c03ed1ba4909a173c2faf0d12868e49a6ea3.text: When you go to revoke an API key in your profile, you'll now see a styled pop-up dialog instead of the browser's plain default alert. The new dialog lets the team match the look of the rest of the app and shows a clear message, a cancel button, and a confirm button that can show a loading state while the revocation happens. This replaces the old browser-native confirm window that looked out of place in the settings page.

f0605b5664fecfd89a9ec8d12a364fd983f7079b.text: The assistant no longer asks an AI assistant to guess whether new files are worth reading before actually looking for them. Instead, it always goes straight to finding the relevant files. You would not notice this directly unless you use a prompt that previously would have been skipped, in which case you might now see the assistant look at more files. This change is live today.

68bf922740c07889ebec41c5baf8b20276eb4a45.text: A new helper called Buffy can now spin up a quick-answer agent named Lewis & Clark, which is good for fast questions about your codebase or the web. The main editor helper can now call in a researcher for background reading, and that researcher no longer pokes around in your files or code—it only searches the web and reads docs. If you work with these helpers, you'll see Lewis & Clark as an option and notice that the editor can fetch research on its own, while the researcher sticks to web findings instead of browsing your project files.

c2bc8bb0d5595c79cbd8aba647ba40ede710ac4f.text: The evaluation system that tests how well the coding assistant works now has a choice: you can run those tests using either the default assistant or a new option that connects to a different AI model (Claude). Previously, every test run used the same assistant. The system was also updated to use a new setting name for linking to your referral page. If you run these test commands today, you can add a flag to switch which assistant gets tested, and referral links will point through the new address.

b705b7fe7d3472c6a391bb2f2b385fa2d1268fce.text: When you manage your login sessions or API keys in your web browser, the system now double-checks that any action you take (like revoking a key or logging out) actually came from our own app, making it harder for malicious sites to trick you. Your active sessions are now tracked as simpler, clearly labeled types (web browser, API token, or command-line tool), and the system automatically sorted your existing sessions into these new buckets so you don't lose access. You would notice that actions requiring confirmation now prompt you more explicitly before deleting something important, and your session list will appear cleaner with consistent, predictable labels. These security and cleanup changes were part of the update released today.

5c24bec1121904e88098db764a25ff597fb953e7.text: A new, more advanced version of the coding helper (GPT-5 with high reasoning effort) is now available for tasks like planning, editing, reviewing, and deep thinking. The underlying planner tool was reorganized so the same structure can support different AI models, while the existing planner still works as before. If you look at the agent settings, you'll see new entries for these GPT-5 variants, and the editor will now show output from the new GPT-5 helper alongside the standard one.

c695f86e44302c6a1e0f2d23567241b6c845b879.text: A new layer of automated helpers has been added behind the scenes to make coding tasks easier to manage. Instead of one tool trying to do everything, your request now gets handed off to a team: first one agent makes a plan, then another writes the code, then another checks it over, and a cleanup tool trims away extra conversation details after each step so things don't get cluttered. These helpers are already active for internal systems that run and coordinate these coding chores, so you might notice smoother, more organized handling of complex tasks without seeing the change directly.

dd30e468c06834f763d571ea1e541e74bf2c4c16.text: When an AI assistant that can take multiple steps (like reading several files or making several edits) reaches its limit, it now stops cleanly instead of getting stuck in a loop. The system now tracks a 'steps complete' flag that lets these multi-step agents know when they've hit their step cap, so they can break out of their work loop gracefully. This affects the built-in agent types that handle complex tasks, and while you wouldn't see a visual change, the assistant will stop more reliably when it runs out of allowed steps instead of potentially continuing or behaving unpredictably.

552f74d95ca2a9be9a5be74d209437d5961b6fb7.text: Three different ways the assistant starts up a helper agent (inline, async, and regular spawn) used to each carry their own copy of the same checks and setup steps, so fixing a bug in one place often left the other two still broken. The shared checklist and setup work have been pulled into one common helper, and a new test file now checks that permission rules are enforced consistently across all three startup paths. Nothing visible changed for how you start a helper agent, but future fixes or new safety checks now apply to every startup method at once instead of needing to be copied three times.

0d765207f7655da140fd151321189db7228110ab.text: The AI assistant now automatically cleans out old information from its memory before moving on to each new step, so it can work faster and avoid hitting its memory limit. It does this by quietly removing the oldest tool results and messages it no longer needs, without showing you extra output or popping up new windows. This runs automatically whenever you use an agent, including the standard coding assistant, and you wouldn't see any visible change in the interface except that long sessions are less likely to get cut off. The change also adds test coverage so this cleanup behavior won't accidentally break in the future.

32031c5c322d983799c40181e0f7450c1f34da31.text: When the assistant spawns helper agents to work on a task, it now strips out system-level instructions before sharing the conversation history. You won't see this directly, but child agents will no longer inherit the parent's system prompts, keeping their context cleaner and avoiding mixed instructions. This is a behind-the-scenes improvement to how multi-agent conversations are managed internally.

1369f2367c82b7d9d228b2bcf3651ce999e05db0.text: The interactive coding tool now hides playful surprises inside its text-based interface. Typing certain words triggers animated celebrations: confetti bursts of code symbols and emojis, a cascading green-code rain effect, and a slow typewriter-style message reveal. A new digital assistant named Chloe has also been added to help create such fun features. These additions are documented in a guide for the team.

b02e0dc13c89be729db385f032d7aa2c9716b15e.text: When the assistant starts a new helper agent during a conversation, that helper used to receive the parent's full instruction set, including internal system-level guidance that isn't meant for child contexts. Now the system filters out those internal instructions before passing along the conversation history, so child agents only see the actual back-and-forth dialogue. The change is live today for both the immediate and background-style spawning paths.

ef9914ece072339229d796de949244cf5b381d2f.text: Starting today, the assistant can build a map of your code project—showing the file structure, how often each part of your code is referenced, and which pieces call which others—right at the beginning of a run, instead of starting with that information missing. This happens when you provide project files through the SDK, so tools and agents that rely on this map now have it available from the start rather than finding it empty.

584bcc4789235699a30cc12d7dc9fb116854e467.text: The system added a new way for multiple AI helpers to team up and think through tough problems together. Instead of one assistant tackling a complex question alone, it can now break the problem into parts and send different specialized helpers (each tuned for deep, balanced, or creative thinking) to work on pieces in parallel, then stitch their answers back together. If you look closely, you'd see fewer wordy step-by-step instructions baked into how these helpers are built, replaced by a leaner setup that lets each helper focus on its one job before passing results along. This is live now for internal use, so the assistant can quietly summon these coordinated helper teams whenever a question is too big for a single pass.

1ada6a5e7e9e376dbc88aefefdd09eb4c1f13404.text: The AI assistant you talk to can now use your own custom tools that you define, not just the built-in ones. When you give it a project, any custom tools you've set up are now included in the instructions the assistant reads, so it knows what extra commands are available and can run them during the conversation. The assistant also understands your tools even if they're described using standard JSON schema format, not just its native format. If you looked at how the assistant talks about its available commands, you'd see your custom tools listed alongside the built-in ones, properly formatted in the examples it shows.

647453e06d65bb13a105495c642cfbe337e6ed40.text: The system that checks the code for mistakes was finding errors in how one of the internal helper libraries was set up, so the team corrected a reference path that was pointing to the wrong folder and cleaned up some minor formatting. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance that keeps the development tools running smoothly; it doesn't change what the assistant does or how fast it responds. If you looked, you'd see a small edit in one of the type definition files and a few test files, but nothing you interact with has changed.

47b52b66e011bdec337bd279e9beb35d33ff0e83.text: Behind the scenes, engineers adjusted one of the system's internal parts so that a specific set of rules about which helper agents are allowed to team up can now be checked separately and more thoroughly. They also added a fresh collection of automated checks that put those teamwork rules through their paces. You wouldn't see anything new on your screen; this is housekeeping that helps the team catch mistakes faster and keep the helper-agent matching reliable.

4cb06d0fd7555769708e20cfe6d06e19b5b3c846.text: The system now has a single, shared set of rules for understanding agent IDs—identifiers that tell it which publisher and agent (and optional version) to use—instead of each component making up its own rules. This affects how the platform recognizes and matches agents when one agent tries to use another, and if you watched the process, you'd see the matching logic now consistently handles cases where a publisher prefix or version is missing rather than silently failing. The new parsing approach is live today as part of the updated agent spawning flow.

4a6592fd618e1061f9a2c285c0de8d725af04ab0.text: The assistant's tool-calling system was reorganized so all tools now use one shared set of definitions instead of separate copies. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping—if everything is working, you won't notice any difference. The change makes the code easier to maintain and keeps tool behavior consistent, but doesn't add any new features.

cd9cd6a6b5319406034db4db7032e58ccb439a1a.text: You now have clearer instructions for building and customizing specialized helpers called agents. Instead of writing helper rules in a basic text format, you can now write them using a more powerful programming language, and the guidance shows you how to add fields that tell other helpers when it's useful to call on this helper, how its results should be structured, and how to control the helper's behavior step-by-step with code.

a3dd658db8918e671462b308acebea0fa7ad771d.text: The system has switched from using a borrowed third-party component to an in-house copy of that same component, so it can now be adjusted to match how the platform talks to a particular set of AI models instead of being limited to whatever the outside provider decided to support. Any cost calculations that were previously being ignored for these AI models will now be counted again, so billing and usage tracking should go back to reporting the real numbers. You wouldn't see this directly, but if you were watching how much different model calls were costing your account, the numbers should now line up correctly again.

7d1f2e244237cc544b5e843e338dc7dfe1104e66.text: The team added a small configuration file inside a folder that holds the assistant's agent code, which tells the system how to build and check that specific folder on its own instead of relying on the main project setup. This means the agent code can now be tested and type-checked independently using its own settings. If you were to open that folder, you'd see a new file listing basic project details and a command that runs the type-checking tool locally.

dc4ed3ac98a63e8da6104544e6ce162a7060f41c.text: The team replaced the actual step-by-step checks that test the help-document tool with a fake version, so the tests no longer wait around for slow real steps to finish and they clean up properly afterward. You wouldn't see this change yourself, but it means the automated checks behind the scenes are more reliable and faster now, with fewer random failures.

97ee03b06fb332b51bbda94fa43c7d8066ef8f42.text: Your CodeBuff assistant can now check whether an agent ID it doesn't recognize locally is a valid, supported agent before it starts a coding task, by looking it up against a remote list of approved agents instead of just asking you to fix it yourself. This check happens automatically in the background during startup when you have credentials configured, and common valid agents are remembered for five minutes so repeated checks don't overload the system.

c42281bf67b57f5c7c743bf40c51389d2fd4fa58.text: If you ask the assistant to run a terminal command (like listing files or checking status), it can now actually do it instead of saying it cannot. The command runs on your machine in your project folder, captures both normal output and errors together, and stops automatically if it takes too long. You get back a single block of text showing what the command printed.

138c15f63fda36edbfed7fb7a1cec204ba7468e3.text: Developers building desktop apps with the Codebuff SDK can now attach images and other files to prompts, and reshape the conversation history before a run happens. Under the hood, helpers like `generateInitialRunState`, `withAdditionalMessage`, and `withMessageHistory` replace the previously hidden session-state setup inside the client. You'd notice this if you're wiring up multimodal prompts (e.g., feeding an image URL into an agent question); the sample walkthrough now shows an agent analyzing an attached image. Live today with SDK 0.1.8.

8da355b2536ec849a8f7882e6e8f1685d5f5110f.text: The internal research agent now runs on Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro model instead of the previous Claude version, meaning the system's automated research helper switched to a different AI provider. The default custom agent template that came bundled with the tooling has been removed, so new custom agents must be built from scratch rather than starting from the old example. These are internal-only changes that don't affect end users directly.

60c5963bcfeb53629c083a3d27b096801d61dc4e.text: If you use Codebuff's command line tool or its backend API, you now authenticate the same way in both places: with a single standardized key header instead of juggling two different header styles. This replaces the old "Bearer token" and "X-API-Key" headers that were handled differently across the CLI and backend, which previously required separate logic in multiple files and left debug logging scattered in the code. The authentication flow now consistently reads one header for agent validation and organization coverage checks, removing manual parsing steps and cleaning up duplicated credential management. This is live today for internal use.

dcdbad70987dbbed158437edf5945378daa46784.text: A new helper named "Mitt the Git Committer" is now available inside the development toolkit. When a developer asks it to save changes, it runs Git commands to review what changed and the recent commit history, reads any relevant files, then stages the right files and writes a commit message in the standard format with the Codebuff footer. The helper is defined and ready to use today, so developers can simply request a commit and let it handle the review and saving steps automatically.

0b98c636bc02df17e4290325671290101fc8b210.text: The team moved a set of placeholder labels — short text tags used inside the assistant's instructions — from one definition file into the secret-agent definition file, and updated the few files that read those labels to point at the new location. If you opened the relevant instructions file today, you'd still see the same tags being referenced; they just come from a single place now. The old prompt template files in the backend templates folder were also deleted, since that prompt logic now lives entirely in the agent prompts folder.

f8aedbbad52d1cf631dec4235a048727dd1d22a9.text: The project removed some old example files that showed how to build simple assistants (like a code reviewer or commit message writer), along with a chunk of placeholder definitions that were no longer needed. What you see in their place is a fresh starter file that walks you through building your own assistant from scratch, with comments explaining each part. If you were browsing the examples folder before, those sample files are gone, and instead you now get a single templated file pre-filled with guidance notes rather than a working example. This is live today for anyone opening the repository, replacing clutter with a cleaner getting-started path.

1a557775785ad1c09f91bd4298339db34327e55c.text: When you build or use an AI assistant built on this platform, the way you tell that assistant to run tools (like searching the web or reading files) has changed: instead of labeling the information you pass to a tool as 'args', it is now labeled 'input'. This affects everyone who writes or uses agent definitions, because every tool call they configure will use the new label, and older references to the old label would break. Behind the scenes, the underlying AI and validation libraries were also upgraded to newer versions, which is why the argument label had to change.

edd38c58d55ce1fdb236bf4f31a5969f705391fb.text: Developers who build custom AI workflows now have three ready-to-use templates showing exactly how to define an agent that reviews code changes, writes git commits, or explores a codebase by coordinating multiple helper agents in parallel. The system that validates these agent definitions was also tightened so inputs and outputs must follow a stricter format, and one property name in the step-by-step workflow was corrected from a technical term to 'args' to match what the code actually uses. If you look at these examples today, you’ll see concrete prompts and step sequences you can copy and adapt, and the corrected naming means your own agent definitions will align with the updated expectations.

d7a8b17ef8b1cc0a5f2dd7248083ee62b5aabe76.text: The assistant's instructions have moved from being copied into many places to living in one shared spot, so every variant of the assistant pulls from the same central instruction set. You won't see this in the app today, but it makes future updates easier to roll out. This only affects the engineering of the system itself.

bf9c8d683ccfa2c3c637566de185e420353f9089.text: The team rolled back two pieces of the system that power the AI assistant behind the scenes: the engine that interprets structured data and the toolkit they use to talk to AI models. A newer version of both had just landed moments earlier, so this undoes that move and returns to the prior stable versions. If you use the assistant today, you will not see any visible difference in what it can do, but the underlying plumbing that keeps it running is back to the version the team had already tested and shipped.

e8a75d0c6b54a8e77eae376869f38c2aa8b7fc17.text: Behind the scenes, the assistant's internal plumbing was upgraded to newer core libraries, which required renaming how the assistant's built-in tools talk to each other. If you peek at the configuration files that define what the assistant can do, you'd see every command that used to be written with a field called 'args' is now written with a field called 'input', plus a few other minor adjustments to match the new tooling. This is live today and doesn't change what you experience, just keeps the foundation up to date and consistent.

b9be8087852566eebb4f957a163e292428599b14.text: The command-line assistant can now correctly recognize an agent name even when it's typed without a prefix or a slash. When you type in a name that doesn't match anything local, it automatically adds a default prefix so the system knows which organization the agent belongs to. At the same time, the team moved some behind-the-scenes logic for displaying run traces into a dedicated spot and cleaned up error messages when publishing, so failures show clearer details and helpful hints instead of one jumbled message. Lastly, the list of recent sub-agents now closes when you press either the Escape key or the letter q, matching a friendlier standard for exiting those views.

f973ae976bba995a74979542f236e73f602a2e57.text: When you publish an agent that includes other agents as sub-parts, the system now handles finding and checking those sub-agents in one dedicated place instead of doing it inline during publishing. If a sub-agent reference doesn't include a specific version, the system can now look up the most recent published version from the database rather than requiring an exact match. This applies to anyone publishing agents through the internal publishing flow, and publishers will see fewer validation errors when referencing sub-agents without explicit versions.

6fc0452c5f167554ccecad4fb532262c8cc4d898.text: You can now tell when another assistant should call on this one by reading a label that says 'spawnerPrompt' instead of the old, more confusing 'spawnPurposePrompt.' Every built-in assistant template and the starter file you edit to make your own assistant have been updated to use the new label, so anything you write or copy from the examples will match. If you open the project's agent folder, each assistant file simply swaps the old name for the new one with the exact same description of when it should be summoned.

cc66bae453842ec9a247c477ad02f5701ee998f3.text: The behind-the-scenes software that checks and organizes your project's settings was upgraded to a newer version, which means the team can now add new configuration options without breaking how data flows through the system. For users, this doesn't change anything you see directly today, but it sets the stage so that when new settings get added later, they'll work smoothly instead of causing errors. Internally, the code that formats configuration details for the AI assistant was also tweaked to handle these updated checks more cleanly. All of this went live in the backend code on August 12, 2025.

80b22c7a54f1b774f28e3ea4f109ed5120ce4a22.text: The assistant platform rolled back its underlying data-validation library to version 3 while keeping the newer version 4 import style for its built-in helper tools and prompts. If you looked at the running system today, you'd see the validation engine behave like the older release (for example, reporting errors through its 'errors' listing rather than 'issues'), even though the helper definitions still read as if they were written for version 4. The switch affects anyone running Codebuff agents that rely on those built-in tools and prompts, since those now import their schema definitions using the v4 path while executing on the v3 core.

3d8ece358a740c6718282091c53b1d051ecf78dd.text: The example agent templates that you see when building your own AI coding assistant (the.agents folder files) have been moved into a shared location called the common package so the whole system can find them consistently. This means if you create a custom agent today, the starter templates, type definitions, and example files still exist and work, but they now live under common/src/templates/initial-agents-dir instead of the project root. The developer comments in the moved files confirm this is for anyone writing custom Codebuff agents who imports the type definitions to get code suggestions and safety checks while building, and you would notice the import paths in the source files now point to this new shared location rather than the old root-level folder.

ac9fff6cb1c8f512e0cb3565c2abb8f63f85f4b0.text: The example helper agents have been reorganized into a clear three-level structure (basic, intermediate, advanced) with simplified names and removed redundancy. If you looked at the collection now, you'd see the old 'diff-reviewer' helpers split by skill level, the advanced section consolidated into a single 'file explorer' helper, and the main 'changes-reviewer' and 'git-committer' agents given clearer instructions about when to run and which tools to use. The older 'outputMode' and publisher metadata have been stripped out so the agents rely only on their spawn instructions and explicitly listed tools. This is live today for anyone using the provided example agents (for example, developers building on this template project), but it does not change how the core system works for end users.

940b78477765f959e0aee72c7a109ba1b82126ab.text: The agent builder template was moved from the backend service code into a separate folder (the `.agents/ directory), decoupling it from the backend code. If you looked, you would no longer find the assistant's full definition inside the server folder where agent templates are listed, and the list that previously loaded it from the old location no longer pulls from there. This is internal housekeeping that reorganizes where the agent's instructions and tools live, making it easier to manage independently, and it is effective today.

73da134833ad2e089ad6654266aa3a2f399a1552.text: The core assistant definitions were updated so that internal helper tools like adding subtasks and launching background agents are now properly recognized by the base assistants. If you look at the built-in assistants, they can now be configured to use these internal tools without type errors, and the shared tool list was moved to a common location so both the public assistants and the SDK share the same source. Some tools such as spawn_agents_async remain commented out, so it does not gain full public access yet but lays the groundwork for it. This is live today as part of the base type definitions.

7695a102f6c1720f224a9d7a8e1b11448b12d4de.text: Custom AI assistants you build now live in a dedicated folder called.agents at the root of your project, instead of being scattered inside the app. You can run them with 'codebuff --agent your-agent-name', publish them with 'codebuff publish your-agent-name' so people worldwide can run them, and edit the starter template (my-custom-agent.ts) which now points to the correct type definitions. Each agent is a single file that spells out which AI model to use, what tools the assistant can access (like reading files or running commands), and when other assistants should call it.

fe3e591cef9c316211695f4cf7a7f637d6485807.text: Behind the scenes, the developers renamed an internal building block called AgentConfig to AgentDefinition across all of the agent files. This is purely a housekeeping change: the developers cleaned up the code, swapped old words for clearer ones, and aligned the system prompt language, but nothing you do with the agents has actually changed. If you opened one of these agent files today, you'd notice the variables now read 'Definition' and 'spawnableAgents' instead of 'Config' and 'subagents', but the behavior stays exactly the same.

d5344c2e9ca9f5578066a53e68ae9ee17a036b92.text: The assistant can no longer spawn specialized helper agents that share its conversation history. This only affects internal development tools, so you won't see any difference in everyday use.

f64d2087ca0c709d15abdfcebdebb20e57e13fb0.text: A starter template for building your own custom agent was added to the project's main agent directory, so anyone creating a new agent now begins from a ready-made example instead of starting from scratch. The example reviewer agents, which help check code changes, were also switched to use a newer advanced model. If you looked at the project, you'd see this new template sitting alongside the existing example agents, with the examples now pointing to the updated model version, and the agent builder no longer auto-loads the older sample agents by default; everything is live and usable today.

641cba2e0c6951478f1d34a9de5066bfa07baf3b.text: The system now keeps track of helper assistants inside another assistant using a clearer name, so when one assistant calls on smaller specialist assistants to help with your request, they're stored under 'subagents' instead of the old 'spawnableAgents'. If you looked at how the system organizes things internally, you would see this consistent naming and a more explicit rule telling developers that any assistant they want the main assistant to be able to call on must be referenced by its full name including publisher and version, or by a local file name. This change is live today and affects how nested assistants are tracked and spawned.

d774a1190033ba81f120a60be3c9821e52c7588b.text: If you use Codebuff's assistant that spawns helper assistants to tackle parts of a coding task, those helpers can no longer exchange notes with each other or with their parent assistant using a dedicated messaging tool. The feature that let one assistant send a structured message (prompt plus extra data) to another has been removed entirely, along with the special instructions that told the parent assistant to use it. Async-spawned helpers still run independently, but they now report results through the normal task-completion flow instead of interrupting each other mid-task. The change is live in the 2025-08-10 release for anyone using the async multi-agent workflow.

ab87eb2287659131d7dcc6e88f70971ab7161251.text: The setting that tells an agent how to format its final answer used to be called 'json', but it now expects the name 'structured_output'. This only affects you if you have written or edited your own custom agent configuration that uses the old name in that setting; built-in agents and examples have already been switched over, so they keep working without any action from you.

1a03c37bb1e3db631749b6fcec1dd888e5a7df49.text: Starting today (August 11, 2025), the assistant now checks your custom AI helper configurations through a regular web request instead of during its initial startup handshake. This means if you use tools like Codestream or Cursor to build custom agents, the validation of those configurations happens separately from establishing the main connection. You won't notice a difference in how quickly the assistant starts up, but behind the scenes it's now validating your agent templates through a dedicated check that authenticates using your session. The old method of embedding validation in the startup response has been removed, along with outdated documentation files that listed supported agent types.

2a564ae89f287d49c1639bf3038f84292f1028d3.text: If you write a configuration file that tells your assistant which helper agents it is allowed to create, you used to list them under a setting called 'subagents'. That setting has been renamed to 'spawnableAgents' in all the built-in agent recipes and the configuration-reading code, so you must rename the field in your own files too; any file still using the old name will be ignored. Today, when you run the assistant and do not pick a specific agent, it now looks first for the 'spawnableAgents' list in your config file and, if absent, falls back to the new default list defined in each agent recipe. In short, your helper-agent list setting works again only after you rename it from 'subagents' to 'spawnableAgents'.

eb2d3ba2ded99f971b20ba32e93cf80fcc985c37.text: The system now includes three ready-made example assistants that show different ways to review code changes, from simple to more advanced. It also tidied up how assistant-building parts connect to each other and adjusted how assistants talk to one another behind the scenes. If you looked at the new examples, you'd see them guide an assistant through running a diff check and reading changed files; if you looked at the configuration files, you'd notice labels for output styles changed from one term to another and one messaging feature was taken away. These example assistants are available now as templates you can use or copy.

121d2628a543f2565607534a6ef1313a72f1dbce.text: If you build custom Codebuff agents, the type information (like what settings each agent needs and what tools are available) now travels inside the SDK package itself instead of being pulled from a shared internal folder. This means your editor will continue to offer autocomplete and error-checking for your agent files when you use the SDK, even if you install it without the full monorepo setup. The change is live in the SDK build pipeline as of today.

1b182fcbea278b555d09041f57880dba147187f4.text: The assistant can now launch a mini-assistant that works inside the current conversation without losing track of what has been discussed. When you ask it to do something, that mini-assistant sees all the messages so far and any new notes it leaves behind stay in the conversation when it finishes. Unlike other delegation tools, this one does not come back with a summary result; it simply stops, and you have to take back control manually. The change landed on 2025-08-10 and is part of the backend system, so you would notice it if you use the assistant through a developer tool or integration that exposes the new capability.

842c13227ee038cd86127c984d9b1e06d59da640.text: A new testimonial PDF from The Flex has been added to the public-facing testimonials folder on the website. If you visit the testimonials section of the site, you will now see this document available alongside others as part of the marketing content. You don't need to do anything to access it, as it is automatically displayed to anyone viewing that page.

7b74c69b7e9bae928f3a4856871b35ce53c9be3f.text: When you ask the assistant to read files from your project, it now uses a built-in version of that file-reading capability instead of relying on a separate app's code, and you can now set which folder counts as your project's home. The assistant also refuses to read any file over one megabyte in size and will not look outside of your designated project folder, so stray or overly large files will come back with an error placeholder instead of being read.
