6c61620ce9e92107cc1368c32299260afec1c851.text: If you write a small program that talks to the assistant, your code now connects through a live two-way channel instead of the older polling method, and it can let the assistant edit your files for you (creating or patching them on disk). Your program can hand the assistant its own custom versions of file-reading, file-writing, search-and-replace, and terminal commands, and each connection now gets a random session name instead of everyone sharing the same one, which reduces clashes when many programs talk at once. The assistant still uses the same underlying engine, but the way your program listens to it and gives it tools to work with got simpler and more secure. These updates are in the just-released SDK version, so you can start using them today.

7b17f6ed1a64395d1a122323932488f7bd0c21cc.text: The Codebuff assistant software has been updated to version 0.1.0, and it now connects to the system using a newer networking method called WebSocketHandler instead of the older CodebuffClient that has been removed. The software also dropped several automatic features you won't see anymore, like checking for outdated versions, generating commit messages from your code changes, and certain types of server messages. If you are a developer building apps on top of Codebuff, you will need to update your code to use the new connection method, but the core task of writing code for you continues to work the same way.

2d55670bb0b79b4ddc3d8fd834329dfcf06a6dfe.text: If you visit the web app, you'll now see an Agent Store link in the main navigation menu. Clicking that link opens a new page where you can browse published agents in a searchable, sortable grid. Behind the scenes, a new API endpoint pulls agent data from the database and returns it with basic usage metrics, and the CLI tool sheds some unused code that no longer serves a purpose. The store is live and visible right now to anyone who opens the site.

9ffa0d8df053b386eb3457bbae9c37d455ef1905.text: If you've had a CodeBuff account for more than a week, the referral banner that used to pop up at the top of the page will no longer appear for you—it only shows to accounts less than seven days old. To make that happen, the system now checks the date your account was created and hides the banner automatically once that week is up. You wouldn't notice this unless you're a very new user: new accounts still see the banner as before, while older accounts simply load without it, no action needed on your part.

117ab40956c9ab02b23ad4d8b937ec63d95b7e6b.text: When you or your team refers to a built-in agent (like CodebuffAI/claude-code), the system used to quietly strip off the "CodebuffAI/" prefix before looking it up, and also applied hidden rules about which tools or sub-agents were allowed. The system now uses the exact name you type, with no automatic cleanup or override enforcement, so the name you request is the name it tries to load. Users writing agent configuration files in the Codebuff platform won't get silent rewrites of their agent IDs or unexpected rejections based on the old override rules.

bd373f80a8158ef1b961df7d31f0721a7ca65b8e.text: The coding assistant's instructions were stored as one long line of text with \n characters instead of real line breaks, causing the prompts to render as a single run-on paragraph. A new conversion step now properly formats these instructions so they display correctly with line breaks, headers, and spacing as intended. You would have seen the assistant's behavior guide as one unbroken block of text instead of the readable, structured document it was meant to be.

3191ed4ac57c59d4757a76ad30a2528bb2c7ee49.text: A new toolkit for developers called the Codebuff SDK is now available, letting them write programs that can automatically run AI coding agents to edit code, start new conversations, and read responses as they happen. The publishing process has been set up so the toolkit can be downloaded from the standard package directory, with scripts that convert internal dependencies into ones it expects to find already installed on the developer's machine, and the package is public under a permissive license. Today, anyone can install it, provided they have the matching command-line tool and an access key already in place.

ca3a556f4227a0de6fda1901881bb725210d9c76.text: The system renamed an internal label that describes the kind of progress update your assistant sends back while it's working, so that developers see a clearer, more consistent name in the code. If you watched the assistant respond in real time (like a streamed word-by-word reply), nothing about what you see changes—the message format and timing stay the same. The update also tightened up how agent templates are recognized, which mainly affects reliability behind the scenes. It's live today as a housekeeping cleanup, not a new visible feature.

39fe906737675184504341cc8944ff08505797d9.text: A coding assistant you can run entirely for free on your own computer now exists. The change adds a new team of specialized helpers, each with a clear job: one writes code, another finds the right files to edit, a third researches questions online, and one reviews work for mistakes. The main helper coordinates them, just like before, but everything talks only to free, publicly available models instead of paid ones, so nothing in the tool uses a paid service anymore.

1e55a7a09e3b4a2387941c0bafd712a2a9350e68.text: The SDK stopped repeating itself by storing its internal binary name in one shared spot instead of pasting the same value into two separate files. You won't notice anything different unless you're maintaining the SDK itself; the change only tidies up how the code is organized behind the scenes.

c35393f6a7ed440d91bdc773b0808a28c4219fa0.text: The product can now capture a more complete and consistent snapshot of any error that occurs internally, so when something goes wrong the system records the error's message, the detailed step-by-step trace of where it happened, and the type of error it was. This behind-the-scenes addition affects how errors are collected and stored for troubleshooting, not anything you see directly. It's in place today as a building block for more reliable error reporting.

1c316bcad2efcdbee05d33df22ed000f37001826.text: If you use one of the project's coding assistants, you'll notice nothing changed on the surface, because the assistant still shows up with the same publisher and version label it always has. Behind the scenes, that label used to be copied and pasted into nearly every assistant's settings file by hand, so the team gathered those duplicate copies into one shared file that all the assistants pull from instead. This means future updates to the publisher or version will only need to be made once, and the old separate file for the version has been retired. The consolidation touches all the built-in assistants, but because the values themselves didn't change, your experience stays exactly the same.

9d120f68d2646f2a13a56e363472b375ef11d7cc.text: The agent-builder now skips checking that every listed parent instruction refers to an existing agent, so templates with unknown parent entries are accepted instead of producing a type-check error. If you author an agent template with parent instructions, you'll no longer get blocked at validation time for referencing agents by identifiers that the builder can’t confirm exist. This is live with the latest release.

894cacff0897a61b5df730cbcefcaae4677c9038.text: The team reorganized where a specific description field sits inside the configuration files that define how the AI assistants operate. Instead of sitting near the top of each assistant's settings, the "parentPrompt" field has been moved to the bottom, near the end, for all 19 assistant configuration files. This is purely a behind-the-scenes structural change to align with internal expectations about field ordering. You would not notice any difference in how the assistants behave, as no actual content or logic was altered.

02d9b66bb03af49cd3065afe48de04a50a7657f9.text: The team has laid the first bricks for letting external tools talk to Codebuff: they added a new, empty connector kit that other software can import to start chats and continue existing conversations with Codebuff. Right now this connector is private and unfinished, so nothing is using it yet; it only knows how to hand out placeholder results and read an API key passed directly or via an environment variable. If you are building an integration and imported this kit today, you would get back empty conversation responses until the real logic is filled in. This is in place but does nothing yet.

96d4ec940f3afb32bfae952aa445e2ef1da0b6b1.text: You can now publish several agents at the same time instead of one by one. When you run the publish command in the terminal or send a request to the website's API, you can give it a list of agent IDs and it will upload all of them together, reporting success or failure for each one. If some fail, you get a clear list showing which ones had problems and what went wrong with each, plus any available publishers you could choose from.

9a98a9628e12ff6a1307e44d61b40004daba75a2.text: When you publish an agent now, you must declare who is publishing it directly inside the agent's own config file, using a new "publisher" entry. The separate command-line flag and the web publishing form no longer ask for or accept a publisher ID; instead, the publishing endpoint checks that every agent you try to publish in one go lists the same publisher, and rejects the request if they do not match. If you have been publishing agents, you will need to add your publisher ID to each agent's config before you can publish, and you can only publish agents that share the same publisher in a single batch.

6e38dc70e63b946baf6670a2ddb020327e66d3e5.text: When you use an AI coding assistant, it can call on smaller helper AIs (subagents) to do specific tasks like picking files or exploring a project. The system now makes sure every main assistant explicitly requests a specific, agreed-upon version of those helpers by name and number, rather than just saying 'give me the file picker' with no version pinned. This means the helpers the assistants use are predictable and consistent, so today's assistants will reliably spawn the same version of their subagents that the team tested them with. If you looked at how the assistants are configured, you'd see each one now lists its helpers with a shared version tag and identifies itself as published by Codebuff, instead of each listing helpers by plain names.

fd9f50be684550f2b3fbcfa836b96452fa2eb901.text: Today, the example agents have been made more generic and the configuration system has been simplified. The example agents (formerly named things like level-1-code-reviewer) are now simply called example-1 through example-3, and the system that loads them will only pick up files with this naming convention, making them clear templates rather than specific use cases. The agent configuration options have been streamlined by removing several prompt fields (parentPrompt, systemPrompt, instructionsPrompt, and stepPrompt) and adding a new, more structured agent builder file that provides clearer guidance for creating new agents. If you looked at the system now, you'd see simpler, more generic examples and a cleaner way to start building your own agents, with the new structure available today but

2637bb80b7ac6d1705dcaf06445567cad5a15abf.text: The project added three ready-to-use helper assistants that you can pick from depending on how involved the task is. The simplest one just reviews your code for obvious mistakes, the middle one writes and runs tests for your code, and the most advanced one reads documentation, searches the web, and builds a plan before writing docs or guides. These helpers come pre-configured with specific skills and tools, so people building on top of this project now have starting points instead of writing everything from scratch.

881fb5fbfe4559d46b200b3d4e61a7338ced2ea6.text: When you ask the system to create a new custom assistant for a specific job, it now uses a single smarter base assistant that can spawn the right specialist builder on demand, instead of relying on one standalone assistant-builder tool. Existing configurations that previously pointed at the old builder need to be updated to reference this new base assistant, so any saved setup files will stop working until changed. You would notice this the moment you try to create or edit an agent: the process now flows through one central assistant that dynamically picks the best builder for the task.

434a95f4e3ce4356ef0633e6edac259e23aa45fe.text: If you ask the system to load an AI assistant that lives in the database, it now handles version labels like 'latest' correctly, checks that the assistant is valid, and quietly skips any that are broken instead of stopping everything. When building a collection of assistants, it first gathers all their names so it can spot duplicates, then validates each one and reports failures by logging them and returning nothing, rather than crashing. This behavior is live today, so any assistant loaded from the database now passes through these safer checks automatically.

859ad7e54b51989ecc9de21310bc696b4f363f20.text: The engineering team added a set of automated checks that repeatedly verify the part of the system that decides which assistant template to load and where it comes from, including which one wins when both a local and a database version exist. The new checks also confirm the database cache can be cleared and that locally assembled templates are properly validated before use. This behind-the-scenes work does not change anything you can do today, but it makes the registry more reliable and catches future mistakes before they reach production.

6afaedf2780868da8f1e615d1c61b6447edd597a.text: If you open a publisher's page on the web app, you used to see a row of buttons, each labeled with a different version of the agent (like v1, v2, up to six of them), with the newest one highlighted. Now that row is gone and in its place there's a single line of text that just says "Latest: vX", where vX is whatever the most recent version number is. You no longer have quick buttons to jump between older versions directly from this page—you'd need to go through the main agent listing to find them now. This is live today in the internal-facing area of the site.

3102f4b997c556abb4927abb8f962063ed2b521e.text: The system now saves the settings for each helper assistant in a dedicated folder, so the main assistant can tell them apart and hand off the right job to the right helper. You as a user won't see a new button or menu, but if you peek at the code you would spot 12 new files living in a.agents/ folder, each spelling out how one helper should chat, which model to trust, and what tools it can reach for. The main assistant also got an updated address book that lists these helpers, so starting today the project is wired to keep them organized even if nothing behaves differently on the surface.

4f44503c013b7a94ff1a6e6467767916a8e70b0b.text: Organization managers opening an organization's Settings page will now see a "Create Publisher Profile" button that takes them to a fresh, guided setup page instead of landing on a flat list of publishers. The old Publishers link in the navbar menu has been removed, and the main Publishers page now only shows existing profiles without offering a way to start creating one. The new setup page walks you through picking ownership, then entering basic and profile details. It is live today.

64b95a78547e1abc8015aa371bc89af4e516d578.text: The team added a new automated reviewer that runs only inside the company's internal code workspace, not in the public tools people download. Whenever someone asks for a review, the reviewer checks which files changed and reads them over. You, as an outside user, won't see this appear or behave any differently today.

8bb59e8230290449320080bd9ac6b9474da8830d.text: If you go to the Publishers page, you'll now see the step-by-step guide for creating a new publisher profile right there, instead of being sent to a separate new page. The links in your organization settings and the user menu at the top now take you directly to that same page, and one section about billing has been removed from the settings screen so publisher management is the main focus. This is all live today, so anyone creating a publisher profile for their organization will use this single, consolidated flow.

410255d3bae0bcbd08a406fcbb9782f9d246456a.text: When the assistant needs to decide who should handle a task, it now uses a pre-packaged set of instructions that travel with each session instead of looking them up in a shared global list. This means agent templates (the predefined roles and prompts) are bundled locally per session via 'localAgentTemplates', passed directly through the options of mainPrompt and runAgentStep, rather than fetched dynamically through getAllAgentTemplates calls. The result is faster startup and no risk of circular dependencies or stale global state affecting agent behavior mid-run. You, as the reader, would notice nothing directly unless you were looking at logs or timing: sessions launch a bit quicker and template resolution is more predictable.

3205731013904f23094a12865f5ef90d9627bfd9.text: Organization settings pages now show a list of publishers (the profiles that own assistants) along with how many assistants each one has published, and you can click into any publisher to see their assistants grouped by name with a full version history. Each version can be opened to view the assistant's code and configuration as formatted JSON, with a version picker and download options. Publishers also get a validation step when creating a new profile, and the org-level publisher API requires you to have at least a member role on the organization before it returns the list. This is live in the web application as of the 2025-07-31 snapshot, behind the normal organization access controls.

dd600ffc724ef2fde296d49ca596f6bd7b0ebe14.text: When someone signs up as a new publisher, they'll now go through a step-by-step form instead of one long page, and as they type their publisher ID, the system checks live whether that ID is already taken. The old way waited until the end to catch problems, so now you get instant feedback if an ID is unavailable or doesn't match the required format. This is live today for anyone creating a new publisher.

75420684d805f178a5c0f7e11c47fe5fcf46d9eb.text: Publishers—creators who distribute content through the system—can now be owned by an organization as well as by an individual. If you create a publisher, the record no longer requires a personal owner; instead it tracks which individual created it and optionally links it to the organization, so a team can jointly maintain the publisher while a specific person is credited as the creator. The old rule tying every publisher to one person has been removed, and new publisher accounts accept an optional organization, with the creator always specified.

d207ff68dfbf510eba4f15c6cc46e761542d8fe8.text: The place where you start creating a publisher has moved. Instead of going to a separate page at /publishers/new, you now go to the main publishers page at /publishers, which opens a multi-step form. If you were in your organization's settings and clicked to create a publisher, that link now takes you to the same form with your organization pre-selected. Everything you need to set up either a personal or organization publisher is now handled in one guided workflow on the publishers page.

9616ee028343f0afa46ce10206604a4dbb2bf11d.text: When you ask the system to read and check your custom assistant templates, it now does the checking directly in one quick step instead of setting up a separate tracking object that remembers previous results. You won't see any difference in what gets built, but the behind-the-scenes checking used to rely on a stateful service that loaded templates asynchronously; that service is gone, replaced by a single synchronous function that both the main backend and the web publish-endpoint now call. This means validation errors and converted templates come back together in one pass, with no lingering service state carried between calls.

7e79c46ba0f7f6e3c4d607e71e98154f679615b8.text: The app tidy up its behind-the-scenes wiring across hundreds of files so all the helper pieces are imported in a consistent order, with type-only helpers clearly separated from the ones the app actually runs. You won't see this directly, but it makes the code easier to maintain and speeds up type-check times. It landed on July 31, 2025 in the core backend services.

e25b24b2a4d4c19eed5b79143ac0402cf1a8cf33.text: Behind the scenes, the system that tracks assistant versions switched from storing them as plain text strings to using neatly separated version numbers (major, minor, patch). This makes comparing versions and automatically incrementing them more reliable, so when one gets published the correct next version number is picked without mistakes. If you look at the publish workflow now it accepts these structured version numbers and converts them back to the familiar format like '1.2.3' before saving. The tooling flagged it notable because the old string-based logic was causing incorrect version bumps.

5b00580593d2c47f24f40c05b5f72666e3b6dc7a.text: The app used to rely on an outside company's rules to describe how messages between you and the assistant are structured, and now it uses its own built-in rulebook for those same messages instead. Nothing you see or do has changed—conversations, replies, and file suggestions work exactly the same. What you might notice if you peek behind the curtain is that several helper tools that shuffle and organize message history were renamed internally, and one old, unused check that looked for repetitive replies was quietly removed. This is finished and live, but it only cleans up how the code is organized rather than altering any feature you interact with.

f49314023bf975ad86703ecb51e01505d994ea66.text: The team ran an automatic code formatter across the entire project, which silently cleaned up how the code is laid out in files—standardizing things like whether text uses single or double quotes, how lines are spaced, and where line breaks go. If you opened any of the project's files today, you would see neater, more consistent formatting, especially in configuration and documentation files like the agent definition and workflow settings. This is purely cosmetic housekeeping—no features or functionality changed, it just makes the underlying code easier for future developers to read and maintain.

dbdbac636d7ae581f4c058f33979eb1fcbdceafd.text: When you go to publish an agent through the command line, the program now tells you exactly what went wrong if something failsâlike pointing to the specific spot in your settings that needs fixing instead of giving a vague error message. At the same time, you can now create and manage a publisher profile through a new section of the website, where you can set a name, add a short bio, and upload a profile picture that gets saved to the site's image folder. This profile system is live for anyone using the web interface to create or edit profiles, and the improved error reporting is active for anyone running publish commands from the command line.

2662f7293d022e8ac34e3f8d864764ab5a5eec4c.text: Assistant configurations are now tracked separately for each publisher, meaning two different publishers can no longer accidentally share or overwrite each other's identically named assistant setups. Previously, an assistant named "HelpfulBot" at version 1 was locked in a single shared slot regardless of who created it; now, each publisher gets their own unique slot tied to their identity, so Publisher ABC and Publisher XYZ each keep their own independent copy. If you work with multiple publishers or manage assistants across different teams, you'll now see distinct, non-conflicting entries where there used to be potential collisions. This is live today for all publishers.

7c98630f058946cec393077942e0d9217d856554.text: The system behind the scenes now ties each AI assistant to the specific person who created it, so published assistants are linked to real accounts instead of being stored as anonymous templates. The old way of bundling an assistant definition under a generic 'template' label has been replaced with a versioned record that carries the creator's identity, and the dynamic loader now pulls definitions from this new structure. You won't see a new button yet, but assistants that get published going forward are recorded against the publisher's account, and deleting a publisher now removes all of their published assistants automatically. The database migration that makes this possible is part of today's build, meaning the publisher-assistant link and the cascade-on-delete cleanup are live behavior

242dd5da37af12c3be0e1a5b921b5bdd8704ee73.text: The pieces that define how custom agents are built and run have been moved from the backend into the shared 'common' area, so both the backend and any other code that relies on these shared definitions now pull them from one central place. As a result, the backend no longer ships its own copy of these types and instead imports them from common, while its old local reference point now quietly forwards requests to the new home so existing code keeps working. You wouldn't see a visible difference in behavior, but the system is now organized so future features built on these shared agent-building blocks will be easier to maintain and less likely to break.

4a70a14b99fb697cf0cd5d3d87abb837c7ae6141.text: A new specialized research assistant named Charles has been added to the company's internal tool kit. Charles is specifically designed to answer detailed questions about deep sea sardines and marine biology. If you're an internal researcher or team member looking up information on sardine behavior, migration patterns, ocean conditions, or conservation efforts, Charles can now be summoned to gather and summarize scientific sources, using web searches and document review tools. This capability is now available within the internal tooling environment.

e6c1628bdbfc15462fed7b29f44bb28c4e873fe5.text: The system moved all of its tool definitions and related settings into one shared location so the main engine can read them from a single place. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping, not a new feature you can use yet. The only visible difference, if you looked closely, is one fewer setting passed when checking whether the assistant should stop; the assistant still stops at the same moments it did before. It is live today as a refactor: existing behavior is unchanged, just reorganized.

2ec998359ef71cd986d5804c00e5fee78967a336.text: When you set up a new agent project, the system now automatically creates a clear, typed list of every action the agent is allowed to take—like searching files, editing code, or controlling a browser—instead of leaving those details as a vague, unstructured checklist. The agent builder writes this list during initialization, generated from the same source that defines each tool's rules and parameters, so every tool name and its expected inputs are spelled out in a shared reference file. If you peek at a new project's configuration, you'll see the agent now knows exactly which actions are available and what each one requires before it can run, rather than guessing at shapes that might not match. The change is live now: any freshly generated agent project will include this typed tool set and

61db08a8e6fabb1ca7e0b43c2df3e6c5d362e0bd.text: You (or your organization) can now publish and install agent templates through a new built-in store. The system now remembers who published each template and keeps a unique name (slug) for each publisher, so you can install the same agent name from different publishers without collisions. Behind the scenes, versions like 1.2.3 are stored as major (1), minor (2), and patch (3) so filtering and updates work cleanly. Note this change is live in the database schema today, but no templates or publishers are visible in the store until someone actually adds them. Existing behavior is unaffected until content is submitted.

a29a854c99017a698e7c8c673e870465919ec957.text: If you write or customize your own AI helper inside Codebuff, the system now gives you a printed instruction manual and spell-check while you build, so you catch mistakes before you run it. The built-in helpers for committing code and keeping project notes were rewritten to use this same safer setup. A new creative brainstorming helper is also available out of the box, ready to toss around ideas whenever you need a thinking partner. Everything is live starting today for anyone putting together their own custom AI helpers.

1797faae3610cb0eeb52e971c4c56c8c3a5b9397.text: If you watched the assistant work, you would now see it occasionally stream extra, structured bits of information alongside its regular text replies. These structured bits are non-language data the system uses to coordinate actions, and a few specific places in the flow intentionally skip over them so the main conversation stays as plain text. The change is live today and only affects how the assistant communicates with itself and the display layer, not the visible chat you see.

1f0bac25584d68b774ebefd686e230f6994935ec.text: When you ask a file-picking helper to find something in your code, it no longer relies on a pre-written opening message that used to trigger its tool calls. Instead, it now generates each action step-by-step from scratch, and the system feeds the results back in as if you had typed them. If you looked, you'd see fewer canned phrases at the start of its replies and more direct, on-demand tool usage. This is live today for anyone using agent-powered features.

eb753bc25cc19785667584465261ff304d1be965.text: The system renamed the labels it uses for custom agent templates—the field called 'name' is now 'display name', 'purpose' is now 'parent prompt', and 'spawnable agents' is now 'sub-agents', along with a few other similar changes. This matters only to people who have written their own agent templates; if you have, your templates will stop working until you update them by replacing the old label names with the new ones. If you just use the built-in agents and haven't touched the templates yourself, you won't see any difference. The change is live today.

0d509da06d767843f74d01b88828b6c01df5cdb5.text: Starting today, the team added a new automated check that runs the assistant's quality tests every night at 9 AM UTC, so problems are caught even when no one is actively watching. They also sped up the existing daily check to test ten things at once instead of one, which means results come back faster during the day. You wouldn't see anything new on your screen, but behind the scenes the system is keeping a closer eye on how the assistant behaves and catching issues sooner.

b268e180b5be256164c1f42f74b623a2be7e8701.text: The way the code-writing helper gives you its final answer has changed: it used to send you a formatted report, and now it sends you a structured JSON output instead. If you watched an agent work, you would see it end its turn slightly differently and produce a machine-friendly summary rather than a narrative one. The git-committer agent also switched to a different AI provider (Claude Sonnet 4), and templates that define optional output fields now default to JSON mode automatically. This is live today and affects any template or consumer reading the agent's output state.

060cf727c4c9dcae216f8f887bf820cb28086186.text: Each helper your main assistant can summon (planner, researcher, reviewer, etc.) now receives a clear, automatically updated roster of the other helpers that exist, so when one of them decides to call for backup it sees the same current list instead of a stale, hard-typed one. Behind the scenes, the list is generated once and plugged into every helper's instructions, and the wiring that previously tangled tools to specific helpers was loosened, letting the system keep everyone in sync without circular references. The result you'd notice is fewer 'agent not found' surprises and helpers that more consistently know which teammates are available to be spawned.

7defa45899aaab83853bd9a61504b3badc2f8359.text: You can now write custom AI assistants using a special scripting style that lets you define exactly how each step of the assistant should run, giving you precise control over things like which tools it uses and in what order. When you place one of these script files in your agents folder, the system checks that the script follows the correct format before activating the agent, and if the script is missing or formatted wrong, the agent will be skipped with a clear explanation. A sample script showing how to use this feature is included so you can copy and adapt it for your own assistants.

9758acce4176bfc120ebe727e1aa3b3cf929eeb7.text: If you build your own helper inside the Codebuff toolkit, the system now hands you a ready-made checklist of allowed settings, so filling in your helper's personality, model, and capabilities feels more like picking from labeled boxes and less like guessing. The toolkit will warn you the moment you type an unsupported tool name, model, or agent to spawn, preventing silent mistakes before they run. You don't need to change anything in your existing helpers to keep working; the new definitions are purely additive safety rails for authors writing brand-new helpers today.

63d17bdb944e23096a21bf27ad1de36e2e2e758c.text: The software's testing tools now have a new helper that makes it easier to temporarily swap out parts of the system during automated tests. Instead of directly replacing code modules (which could accidentally break other tests or leave things in a wrong state), tests now go through this single, safer method that keeps track of the original code and automatically restores it when the test finishes. This change affects the test suite used by the development team and is already in place across many test files.

fd29880e6f8f8d07f16002d301aa6354878cec5c.text: When you run the CLI tool with the --trace flag or type /subagent, you can now watch the assistant's subagents working in real time. Instead of waiting until they finish, their responses stream to your screen as they generate them, and a log file is saved to your.agents/traces folder so you can review what happened later. The developer tests now run in a consistent order, so results are less likely to change between runs. This is available today.

ad6627939eca72397fd71d101ead016fb6d72d94.text: The backend now builds each assistant's set of available helpers fresh on every request instead of keeping one shared list stored globally. If you use the chat, you won't see any visible difference, but internally the code is cleaner and won't carry leftover state between your conversations. One unused instruction file was also deleted, and the system now checks for valid assistants at the moment it needs them rather than trusting an always-on registry.

8d04c33a5fe3b083a08af02baf11408a378043a3.text: The system can now run step-by-step agent instructions written as text (in addition to traditional code functions), executing them inside a safe, isolated environment that prevents crashes or runaway resource use. When an agent template provides its logic as a text string rather than a built-in function, the backend routes that string into a sandboxed JavaScript engine instead of calling it directly. This sandboxing limits memory and stack usage so one badly behaved agent can't take down the rest of the service. It's live today, and when this cache is cleared (triggered by the existing cleanup routine), any active sandboxes get torn down along with the cached generators.

fb4a3fa673956b8c5e83855c4107a4bd1b38d04e.text: The system now has a unified way to run its automated agents and a new built-in helper that explores your codebase by searching multiple locations at once. Previously, tool-running and turn-ending logic were split across separate files, which made the flow harder to follow and maintain; that split logic has been merged into a single programmatic step handler. A new "file explorer" agent template was added to the registered list of agents, and the old file-pick agent now also spawns the file explorer as one of its available sub-agents. If you use or rely on these agents, you will notice smoother, more consistent behavior when automated steps end, and the file explorer will automatically fan out parallel searches instead of one at a time. This is live today for anyone using the agent

12f543cffc41f69df54a321881500e52ab4253a1.text: The assistant can now use two new tools to manage the conversation history directly: one adds a single message to the end of the discussion, and the other replaces the entire history with a fresh set of messages. Previously, the system built and adjusted the message list in one central place behind the scenes; now that responsibility is handed over to these tools, so the conversation flow is controlled through them instead of a single hidden routine. This is live today for anyone running the agent step logic.

16d12e771a8c781b3fc6ad05bb19ead604b2ad9e.text: The AI assistants in this system now define themselves using a more powerful, typed scripting language instead of simple configuration files. If you looked at the folder where assistant profiles live, you would see text files with.ts extensions replacing the old.json files, and their internal definitions now include type-checking tools and schema validation. This affects the core system's assistant profiles, such as the creative brainstorming helper and the automated git commit tool. The change is live today and is already wired into the loaders and templates that the system reads.

08db44aed164aaed864bc8b391b83b7b07f23915.text: The written guidance for building helper assistants has been rewritten: the section showing how to tweak an existing assistant is gone, replaced with step-by-step instructions for making one from scratch, and a new field lets an assistant give specific directions to the helper assistants it creates. If you read the docs today, you would no longer see the old override instructions and would instead find advice on defining each assistant entirely on its own, plus a new section showing exactly how to hand off guidance to sub-assistants. The change is live in the documentation now, affecting anyone reading the internal agent-building guides, but it only reorganizes and clarifies existing capabilities rather than adding new ones.

0c7e401f9f5a66c8471545377d7077c7a2078105.text: The project's safety checks now look at a wider range of files. Previously, the automated checker that scans for code mistakes ignored test files during its regular sweep. Now, those same test files are included in the automatic review. This means more of the project's code gets reviewed at once, catching potential problems earlier in the development process. You wouldn't see this directly, but it helps prevent certain types of errors from slipping through.

67de04e383d347076dc197675c3549846bb12642.text: A parent agent can now see specific, written instructions for each of its helper agents, so it knows exactly when to spawn each one. These instructions are embedded directly into the agent template files, like adding new rules to a playbook. You would notice this when a parent agent spawns a helper, because it now comes with clear guidance baked into its prompt about the helper's role. The change is live and applies to all templates that include the parent instructions field.

5dd32714276f230b86c332ffa34a5a09c244e232.text: Internal test scripts for the assistant's grader now get fully checked for mistakes, so developers catch broken helper files before they cause failures. Previously, the system skipped type-checking those test files during setup, leaving issues undetected. You wouldn't see this change in everyday use, but it tightens behind-the-scenes quality control for anyone contributing internal evaluation code.

0995194bd0e08148b005dfd48dfcfaff02af2422.text: Two outdated setup files that told the assistant how to behave were removed from the project. These files were for internal tools only and didn't change how the assistant works for you. You won't notice any difference in conversations. This is just behind-the-scenes cleanup to remove confusing and unused instructions.

85179603f1b471b7a414fa3df09b6ddac8f9598c.text: When you ask an AI agent to do a task, it now formats its internal thinking and tool requests using a mix of JSON and XML tags instead of pure XML. This affects how agent templates like "brainstormer" and "git-committer" handle stopping conditions, switching from template-specific stop sequences to global constants. You'd notice the assistant's internal tool calls look cleaner and more consistent, though the end-user experience of interacting with the agent remains the same.

0a9d706727c7518decfaf051516b4b4c3123e044.text: The system that runs automated assistant tasks has been reorganized so that all agents go through the same single pathway, instead of having a separate, older route just for programmatic agents. If you watched the logs or configuration today, you would no longer see the term 'programmatic agent' as a distinct category; instead every agent is handled as a step in a unified flow. Behind the scenes, the short-term working memory for each agent is kept in the server's memory rather than passed around, which is an internal housekeeping change aimed at stability. Note: the evidence shows a placeholder that throws an error still exists, so this consolidation is in place but does not yet enable programmatic agent execution.

ff8a3a3182fec78b4c070d595efa07a8e9d21174.text: A debugging interface was added to the internal admin web application that lets support staff replay and inspect individual client sessions as an interactive timeline of messages, tool calls, and responses. When you expand a session on the timeline you'll see a chat-style view of what the client and assistant said, with any tools the assistant decided to call shown as clickable references so you can trace the steps that led to a particular outcome. The change is live now in the admin tool and only affects internal staff who have access to these trace records; regular end users of the service are not impacted.

e3e403b364549a6ef6a9301f44b8b531f0480fb5.text: The assistant can now dispatch helper assistants to work on tasks in the background while it keeps talking to you, and you (as the person watching) can cancel a question you started typing if a background helper is the one actually responding. Under the hood, a new manager keeps track of every helper that is spawned, routes messages between them, and makes sure each helper only acts when its chat session is still active; meanwhile the code that checks whether your connection is live now requires a session ID and can tell the difference between "stop letting me type" and "I changed my mind, drop what I started." If you looked, you would see multiple assistants moving around in your chat at once, and a single text input box could get cancelled by either you or an assistant without confusing

87fcf2384eafe3573e1e9364834648f15e4ebd68.text: The assistant's specialized tools—like spawning helper agents, deep reasoning, updating reports, and web searches—have been rewired into the main tool system instead of running through a separate test setup. You won't see a new feature, but if you watched how tools are loaded, you'd notice they're now registered uniformly alongside the older tools rather than being flagged as experimental. The internal tracking of conversations and tool IDs has also been tidied up so tool results link back to the correct request instead of generating new IDs mid-processing.

9d5cb14ac691fc930b3a0f38680493a348f98607.text: Starting today, the system loads your custom assistant templates from the project's active configuration instead of searching for files on disk, so missing or misplaced template files no longer cause validation errors. If a template omits the "override" field, it now defaults to false instead of failing validation. This affects anyone using custom dynamic agent templates in their project.

236b55735026f8576be5e9243729b501cd47ca67.text: A new reference page for agent configuration has been added to the documentation, giving users a complete guide to all the fields they can adjust when customizing AI agents. This includes detailed examples of the JSON structure for both overriding existing agents and creating new custom ones, with a directory layout example showing where these template files are stored locally. The page is live now and appears under the "advanced" section for anyone looking up agent customization options.

b4a95d509ff96b964c2809e742867f056076edf7.text: The documentation for customizing agents now lets writers embed live flowcharts and sequence diagrams directly inside the pages you read, instead of showing the raw diagram text as plain code. When someone marks a code block as a "mermaid" diagram, the page now draws it as a picture right there; behind the scenes the site pulled in a new diagram-drawing library and taught the existing code-block component to hand those blocks off to a dedicated diagram component. If you browse the agent-customization guides today, you'll see diagrams render as graphics rather than as indented text, and the sidebar that lists all the docs lost its Project Showcase section while a couple of mobile layout tweaks were made so things don't get cut off on narrow screens.

44d9fc7837de87a7a7b7fb7700a29da7ab52f2f3.text: The assistant can now search for and retrieve relevant files from your project when working on code tasks, instead of only reading specific files you point it to. When you ask the assistant to work on a codebase, it will automatically find files it needs to understand your project, which should make responses more accurate and complete. The developers added a switch to control how much file detail gets collected, and noted they might want to enable that on a per-project basis in the future. This feature is live and actively available when using the assistant on code-related tasks.

23741261a65e50b975cf7a876cf542bf57ec0c69.text: You can now find a new "Agents" section in the documentation sidebar, giving you direct access to three guide pages that explain how to customize the AI assistants, create your own, and adjust their built-in prompts and settings using simple text files. Each guide walks you through editing JSON-style configuration files stored in your project, so you can change things like which AI model an agent uses, what instructions it follows, and what tools it can access. These documents are live today and appear alongside the existing Advanced topics in the docs.

65c432bc959509a143dd2f09a601266ef1731f8a.text: Starting July 10, 2025, the assistant gained the ability to read files you point it to as an active tool, previously it was restricted to a work-in-progress list. When the assistant selects this feature, it directly accesses your project files and returns their contents to you in the conversation. You would notice this when the assistant reads a file and shows you its contents without needing manual copy and paste. This change affects all users interacting with the assistant where file reading is supported.

978abcd00776ef588b41d9e2be44c5f376659813.text: The development team added a pair of helper commands that let a developer spin up a separate, isolated copy of the project for testing a feature without disturbing anyone else's work, and tear it down again when they are done. Each isolated copy can run on its own custom port numbers, so multiple test versions can run side by side. If you browse to the repository today, you will see two new one-line commands in the project's main instruction list that launch these setup and cleanup helpers. The underlying machinery is in place and wired up, so running the new commands will create and destroy these isolated workspaces as described.

1fc362b6a7a23cc3872263dc1a88a0757a7f9fc1.text: A new automated helper has been added to the development toolkit that can write git commit messages for you, summarizing code changes with structured analysis and standard footers. It's registered in the system's list of available assistants, but it is marked as experimental and known to need debugging before it's fully reliable. If you looked at the development environment today, you'd see this new automated committer option listed among the available tools, though it may not work correctly yet.

d2fe4f46e112bf9f79fd35ba031fe70166efb744.text: The assistant can now create a structured plan for tackling a task instead of just jumping in, which means it will think through steps before acting. It also starts tracking when it writes to a knowledge file, so activity on those files gets recorded. If you looked, you'd see the assistant lay out a plan and save progress notes in one place.

83c0bac173fc5dac8df83a1a7809e8860dfd426a.text: If you build an agent that's described in a template file, the system can now read and check that template's custom input rules in a more reliable way, using a shared library instead of hand-written conversion code. When a template's rules can't be turned into something the system understands, you'll get a clear note about it and that agent will simply be skipped instead of causing a hard failure. There's also a helper added for writing tests that need a ready-made project context.

d529db2f4104336c563aab75c217cf016b55da40.text: The assistant can now make targeted edits to specific parts of a file instead of rewriting the whole thing or inserting changes at the end. This works the same way the existing write tool does, so the assistant can both create files and surgically replace text within them. The feature is live today for any workflow that already used the write tool, and no new opt-in is required.

13a1a2ddd2f03b45a2fcbab38bebb96475902f41.text: Custom agent setups that pull in instructions from other files can no longer point to locations outside the approved templates folder, and absolute paths are now blocked outright; any such setup that fails this check stops right there instead of being loaded. This protects the system from configuration files that try to read from places they shouldn't, and anyone building or editing these custom agents would see these problematic paths get rejected during validation rather than silently accepted.

cea53e5a106c68ce3a20245020fbfb58be1328d3.text: If you asked the assistant to look up documentation for a specific library or topic, it can now actually do that by pulling in real reference material from an external documentation source. Behind the scenes, the assistant checks that all the required internal identifiers (user, step, and project) are present and correctly matched before fetching anything, logs how long it takes and roughly how much it used, and only then returns the relevant docs to you. This is live today: the documentation lookup feature is turned on and wired into the backend, so anyone who triggers it gets real results instead of a placeholder or error.

aa1b41fd45dd6eb6706bda6ccd9a5a3f04f28a7a.text: The assistant can now create or overwrite files directly as part of its workflow, instead of that action being held back as unfinished. For you, this means file-writing steps that the assistant kicks off will actually complete and flow through to your project, rather than stalling out partway. Behind the scenes, a new handler wires file-writing into the active process and removes it from the list of tools that are still being built, with a streaming callback so results come back to you as they're produced. This is live today for internal backend usage.

d35987b91ed8bd157c650ffff4512394c650fca7.text: When you start your local development server for the project, it now waits until the server is fully up and running before starting the client application. Previously, both would launch simultaneously, which could cause errors if the client tried to connect before the server was ready. The startup script waits for a specific 'server is running' signal before proceeding, preventing these timing issues during development. This is a behind-the-scenes improvement to the development workflow.

53dc30d932a3f65ce7a28198d6e2bc21ccf0909b.text: You can now add a JSON file in your project's.agents/templates/ folder to customize which AI model an agent uses, what extra instructions it follows, and what other agents it can call. When the system starts that agent, it reads your file and layers your choices on top of the built-in defaults before the agent ever responds. The customization is live today and works for agents like the code reviewer. If you looked, you'd see your project now recognized and using your personalized agent settings instead of the standard ones.

5b9b71c236ae63df0ea980f8afb1f58905adfd89.text: Developers can now define AI assistants using actual code instead of relying solely on text prompts that another AI interprets. When a code-defined assistant is used, the system runs its built-in generator function directly and processes tool calls step-by-step, bypassing the usual prompt-based override process. An example code-defined assistant was added to demonstrate this new approach, so you would see it listed among the available assistant types. This is live today for internal and developer use.

2ff11c230959e2b2bcc003a223a25934a80827ca.text: I changed how the internal system passes information between its steps so each step now returns a consistent format: a text result plus an optional state for the next step. Handlers that previously received an extra settings object now get their request and state as direct inputs, and one tool, find_files, was moved into a not-ready category and its working file removed. For anyone observing the backend today, tool steps will consistently produce a result string and structured state rather than mixed return shapes; the find_files capability is temporarily unavailable internally. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping that does not change what end users see, but standardizes how the system talks to itself between steps.

b275c1a52b7e523d172dfe4fe96066f35bad3782.text: The assistant's behind-the-scenes tool-handling system was rebuilt to be more consistent and less error-prone, but you wouldn't notice any difference in how it behaves. Internally, the way the assistant reads and acts on the tools it's allowed to use (like searching files or running commands) has been reorganized so each tool gets stricter, clearer instructions, which should make future updates safer and less likely to break things. Some configuration was also moved and cleaned up, but again, nothing you can see or do differently has changed yet.

7140c172231339f503372d9bbce45094a3ae0423.text: A new built-in assistant called "Brian the Brainstormer" is now available alongside the existing team of assistants. When the system is asked to run a brainstorming task, it now knows how to load and use this new creative partner, which is described in a separate instruction file. If a task tries to use an assistant that doesn't exist, the error message now lists all the assistant types that are actually available. The list of assistants that any given assistant is allowed to hand work off to is also kept up to date automatically as new assistants are added.

9b31b16ab18e95ee465852912a8f8e612e0e0a64.text: The team removed an old testing setup that was used behind the scenes to check that parts of the backend work correctly. This setup included configuration files that handled how tests run and how environment variables are loaded during development. You won't notice anything different - it doesn't affect how the app works for you. It's just internal cleanup of tools developers used during development, and since nothing depends on it anymore, it was deleted.

097d5b66abe48120ca14ff7580d5945f7d095775.text: The assistant no longer bundles three jobs together when it takes a step: deciding which files to look at, running a tool, and updating what you can see. Instead, each job now lives in its own module, so if one part breaks, the others keep working. You would not notice anything different right away, but the system is now easier to maintain and less likely to choke when a file lookup or tool call takes time. The split is live today for anyone running a session behind the scenes.

c05fd779259e5639b1c7ab03beb7da0b7c5df23e.text: When you ask the assistant questions using the latest Claude model, the system now tries answering through Google first, then Amazon Bedrock if Google is unavailable, and only then falls back to the original Anthropic source. This reshuffles the order of providers behind the scenes so responses come from whichever service is fastest or available, without you noticing any difference except potentially quicker answers. The change also cleans up how those cloud services connect, keeping the system organized for future features, and it went live today.

400f9755ae3ab7aa9d5d11fc17dca2aa413b42b1.text: The system now includes a new helper assistant that is purpose-built to design other assistant personalities, so adding fresh roles no longer requires hand-writing every detail from scratch; you would notice a new "Agent Builder" option appearing whenever someone goes to define or extend the roster of available assistants.

ef15e7858ec99e23e936839f8bcb220101667bed.text: If you use Claude models through this service, you'll now get them via OpenRouter instead of Anthropic's own API. The system dropped its old Anthropic connection and rerouted all Claude traffic through OpenRouter, which means the behind-the-scenes plumbing changed but the end result for you stays the same: you still get Claude responses. The change also tidied up how internal references to Claude models are written, and it's already in effect today.

2c1155c49a69577aa2964aee4e854904ff3285fb.text: The system that powers AI assistants has been reorganized so that each assistant is now defined by its role (like 'ask' or 'thinker') instead of being tied to a specific AI model like 'Gemini 2.5 Pro'. This makes it easier to swap out which AI powers each assistant without needing to hunt down and change configuration references everywhere. If an assistant setup goes missing, you'll now see a clear error message explaining exactly which one is missing instead of a confusing breakdown.

a7addaf7d9ce6fe2416b953ebcd02e9bfd03fed5.text: When Claude fails, Codebuff retries the request via OpenRouter instead of giving you an error. The retry chain uses the same Claude model names mapped to OpenRouter equivalents, with fewer retry attempts for fallbacks than the primary API. You would only notice if the primary Anthropic API call failed; otherwise, your chat works exactly as before.

1b1d47513ef9ed9fa7e565580077d8f9d29633f9.text: The assistant's available tools (like searching code, running commands, spawning sub-agents) used to all live in one big file, and now each tool has been split out into its own file so the system is easier to maintain and extend. If you watched the assistant work today, you wouldn't see any difference in what it can do or how fast it responds - this is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping that reorganizes the code without changing behavior. The team also tidied up how the assistant looks up which tools each type of helper agent is allowed to use, pulling that information from a shared, central location instead of a local list that each part of the system used to carry around.

da73133a25d61bd1bebac97cc84e4d9f56d139eb.text: When a developer opens a pull request to test the new CodeCane feature, you'll now get a pre-release version automatically published for testing on the beta channel, without needing a manual approval step. This was made possible by splitting the old monolithic release process into modular workflows, where the staging workflow checks for '[codecane]' in PR titles and triggers the appropriate build and release pipeline. If you're working with CodeCane during development, you can rely on fresh binaries being available in the beta channel right after submitting a PR with the right tag.

77ed9c98ca9647885e2623ef13430e6ade412bf4.text: When a developer on your computer runs a local test of an agent's tool results (the pieces of information the agent sends back to its brain), the system now forwards the exact error message returned by the tool straight back into the conversation, so the agent sees what actually broke instead of a generic failure. This only affects developers actively editing and running the tool-call test files in their own terminal today; there is no visible change for end users or in any deployed feature. The test suite is the only place this new forwarding behavior is wired up right now, so until more tests or code start reading that forwarded message, it exists in the codebase but does nothing beyond the single test path. You would only notice this change if you are one of the developers opening the

eeab42f0181892f83d261d1db9dbd374c07f1028.text: The app now quietly hides certain confusing error messages that would normally pop up in the background when it tries to load a terminal feature, so you won't see scary crash-like text during startup. It also cleans up how unrelated noisy messages from an analytics tool are blocked, making the code easier to maintain. If you happened to be watching the background logs closely, you might notice fewer red error lines; otherwise, your day-to-day use looks exactly the same.

16923279ae32387da295cc3c5b23b8813379b09a.text: When you run common project commands like tests or your local server, the system now automatically loads your secure login credentials for databases and other services behind the scenes, instead of requiring you to manually trigger a separate setup step each time. The old approach asked you to run a special helper script before every command; the new approach quietly checks whether the command you typed needs those credentials and, if so, fetches them automatically. If you look at how things are wired together, you'll see that the list of commands needing credentials is now defined inside a single launcher that replaces the old helper, and the project's setup instructions have been rewritten to tell you to install one additional tool and grant it permission. This is already in place in the

90aae81dbea5378d1a84ce40d5b0dda7798d5576.text: The team deleted an old planning document that laid out a step-by-step approach for automatically supplying secure access credentials to development tools only when a specific task actually needed them, so routine tasks like installing packages would run faster and with fewer exposed secrets. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping and has no effect on any product behavior you would see. If you opened the code repository today, you would notice that the old planning note is gone, and nothing else changes.

fa45f1d2216ed59290203a42196afe3f32f0c4a1.text: The software project has been reorganized so that its different parts can be built and packaged more reliably for distributing pre-compiled programs. Previously bundled together components have been separated into distinct, clearly named packages, and a new automated process now compiles standalone executable programs from the code. If you were to look at the project today, the build process runs separately for the web interface, type checking, and the main application package, and certain internal configuration and dependency setups have been adjusted for this new structure.

9729e46d239e367d119ee1a76c7702c767548232.text: When you use the assistant built as a standalone program (not running inside a code editor), the text-search feature now works again: the program unpacks its own search tool on first use and remembers where it put it, so searches stop failing. If you just updated to the latest version, the next time you trigger a code search you should see results come back instead of an error.

6bd1bce94a1cbcc102aa1d630b4f29404fb89271.text: The system that tracks when billing data fails to reach Stripe from your assistants just got more flexible. Previously, every recorded failure had to be tied to a specific assistant message, and Stripe was the only provider it could handle. Now, failures can be filed by provider name without needing a message link, so it can track billing sync problems across different providers, not just Stripe. This is an internal cleanup, so you won't see a visible change unless a billing sync fails, in which case the error log will now show the provider that caused it.

202feaac7b6dd5ffe35f8729a3d9b1eaa7facccf.text: The app now watches for signs that you're frustrated and quietly records when it happens, without showing you anything new on screen. For example, if you bang out five or more keystrokes within one second, enter the same command three times within thirty seconds, quit right after an error appears within ten seconds, or wait over a minute while the loading spinner is stuck, the app logs a private 'rage' event to help the makers understand what's going wrong. You won't see a pop-up or message from this, but the team building the app can use these logs to fix the spots that make you want to smash your keyboard. This is live today for everyone using the app.

970af3ad42e94e09d6e70f1783316a4ab33a5793.text: A new option for the assistant's brain, called 'experimental,' is now available to choose from, and it runs on Google's latest Gemini 2.5 Pro model designed for tougher reasoning tasks. If you opened the list of available brains, you'd see this new one alongside the existing default; picking it switches the assistant to that newer model. This is live today, so anyone who can select an assistant brain can now try the experimental one.

f115e675e6f741606cdced358761c2d60b9e0f94.text: When you start a new conversation with the coding assistant, you can now choose between two pre-configured versions of Buffy instead of only one. One version, called 'Lite', uses a faster model so you get answers more quickly, and the other, called 'Max', uses a higher-quality model so you get more accurate answers. Both versions share the same updated instructions that let Buffy track which task she's working on and keep correct records when she edits your files, and this choice is available today when you create a new session.

cf9187cabf960dc9d7457161194f2d56e84d58fa.text: The assistant's internal way of talking about tools it can use has been redesigned. Instead of calling a tool by one name and its settings by another, every tool now uses a consistent format with a clear tool name, a unique id, and a single 'args' block for inputs. This change touches how the assistant plans its next action and how it reads back the results, so behind the scenes the flow is more uniform, though you wouldn't see any difference in how it behaves today.

6039f909d5badf56d3f464c831966286a764b894.text: Only people on Codebuff's official admin email list (like the core team members) can now open the admin section of the app—if you're not on that list, you get bounced out. Admins can also check their Stripe subscription and billing portal status, and they alone can see private git evals while everyone else only sees public ones. The old list of admin emails was moved into a shared internal spot so every part of the app checks the same roster instead of keeping its own copy.

c001a7c6320bd9578c5c98c1cc80fbee819185ff.text: The list of pre-built assistant setups was moved into its own dedicated file, so the file that defines how each setup looks no longer also holds the list itself. Only the assistant's internal code reads this, so you won't notice anything different when you use it, but it makes future changes easier to sort through for the team maintaining it. No behavior changed for you — it's straight behind-the-scenes housekeeping.

b4063deba5c1f9345768ae7d4775644bd3762d39.text: The automated system that used to package and publish ready-to-use program files for different operating systems after each major release has been turned off and removed. If you looked at the project's release pages today, you would no longer see the separate download links for those packaged program files that were previously created automatically. This only affects the behind-the-scenes process of creating and sharing those release packages; it does not change how the program itself works or gets installed from its standard source. The project will now rely on its regular installation method for all users.

75e6c77beb02137e71b96ea0df60d8ba7ed005e6.text: Today the coding assistant works a bit more simply behind the scenes: the separate "manager" layer that once oversaw multi-step projects has been removed, along with two extra terminal tools (kill the terminal and wait/sleep) that were only usable by that manager. If you looked at your terminal right now you wouldn't see any of those pieces anywhere - the project's remaining terminal tool just runs a command and waits for it to finish on its own. This means the assistant now runs as one direct agent instead of as a manager telling another agent what to do, and anything that used to rely on the manager's special tools will no longer work.

e64b7691fdaa078c65efdf09e0d54c56f4eae8b8.text: The assistant now runs on a newer, more capable model and has a friendlier, more proactive personality built in, so conversations should feel more helpful and engaging. A helper system was added so the assistant can spin up its own specialized sub-agents when needed, letting it delegate parts of complicated tasks instead of doing everything itself. This is live today for users of the main assistant.

edcfdeff27d8b493d92cf258fb91f25cb98a6ac5.text: Starting today, the project's release process now automatically builds ready-to-run programs for Windows, Mac, and Linux whenever a new version is published, dropping them into a shared download folder so testers and developers can grab the latest builds without running the code themselves.

1a4ed158f86d613e27df141446b335949495d638.text: Admins on the Evals page can now click a control next to each benchmark result to make it publicly viewable or hide it from public view without deleting it. The new visibility toggle checks that you are logged in as an admin (the same people who already manage the system) before letting you flip the public/not-public switch for any result. Behind the scenes, the list of who counts as an admin was consolidated into one shared place so future admin-only features use the same definition, and the extra metrics shown on each result (average completion and code-quality numbers) now update correctly. If you are not an admin, nothing on the page changes for you today.

75183ae0d850204e81d037acb0d05a7a544a3fdf.text: If you run the assistant and a project has no configuration file, or your settings file is broken, it now quietly uses a sensible built-in default instead of stopping and leaving a key setting unset, so the assistant no longer needs to guess what to do when configuration is missing. The built-in default sets the maximum number of steps the assistant can take to a fixed safe number, and this rule lives in one shared place that both the assistant and the background research tool read from, so the two can no longer drift apart and cause confusion.

8e43ddbb832c3f82ba86c2fd5ea3233861b0e657.text: Organizations that pay for seats (per-person billing) now keep their Stripe invoice in sync with their actual headcount. Accepting an invite, removing someone, or doing a bulk invite will each update the paid seat count in Stripe right away, and any over- or under-charge is credited or billed in the same cycle using prorated amounts. If Stripe rejects the update for any reason, the membership change still goes through and the problem is logged but won't block the user signup or removal flow, so this behavior is live for seat-based organizations today.

3287b282081f25efe4bb87a438c8108859d0c07e.text: The system that checks how well the assistant performs on coding tasks now runs those checks in parallel instead of one after another. Instead of waiting for each repository test to finish before starting the next, the system splits the work across multiple processes that run at the same time. This change only affects the internal team that evaluates the assistant's performance; you wouldn't notice it in your daily use.

df512fead49f7da75f8cf81837b34b7e39ea9cc4.text: The project deleted a large folder (230,000+ lines across 1,500+ files) of old test data and removed it from the build's workspace settings, so the test fixtures used internally during development no longer exist. This is purely behind-the-scenes cleanup: you, as a reader, would notice it only if you browsed the repository and looked for a folder named "test" to inspect sample data (it is gone). No features, behavior, or customer access changed; it is housekeeping that does not affect anything running today. The deletion was flagged as notable internally, but it has no visible effect on the product.

70fe182b1cb2be918bd0e2afa142c2294b1fdd27.text: The team moved the collection of build tools into a shared folder alongside other project packages, so all projects are now organized in one consistent location. If you looked at the project's configuration, you would see the build tools living under that shared packages area instead of being listed separately. Anyone working on this project would now find the tools grouped together with everything else, rather than tucked away in their own standalone spot.

c4c187769c73e73062c9573a1486dbd5787d7679.text: When the system runs many evaluation jobs at once, it now caps those jobs at 20 simultaneous processes instead of letting them all start at the same time. This prevents the system from getting overwhelmed and using too many resources when lots of evaluations are triggered. You wouldn't notice anything directly, but the system stays more stable and responsive during busy periods.

0275ec9804c5514f3ff2beb4f2eb9faed02d7ff8.text: Starting the backend, shared libraries, and evaluation tools now uses a single, consistent way to load sensitive project secrets (through a tool called Infisical), instead of each script repeating that logic inline. The new helper automatically detects whether the secrets tool is installed and, if not, simply runs the code directly so nothing breaks. If you work with these parts of the system, you'll see cleaner, shorter startup commands with one place controlling how secrets and settings are loaded.

668035297dccf48b348d35b23ec1fb68661d6851.text: You can now ask the assistant to investigate multiple questions or topics at the same time instead of waiting for answers one by one. When you request this, the assistant spins off several small helper agents that gather information in parallel. Each helper stays in read-only mode, meaning it only looks things up and gathers facts without changing anything, and it runs with lighter, analytics-free settings. Once all the helpers finish their research, the assistant collects and presents what each one found, then uses that combined information to form its final response or plan.

e71a0c76c384f58a533c7df9415092a95a800006.text: The system now keeps a permanent record of how well it performs when editing real-world codebases, like a report card that shows up in a new leaderboard view. Every time the team runs a batch of automated coding tests, the results — such as accuracy, cost, and which AI models were used — get saved into a new database table and displayed on a public page, so you can compare performance across different models and repositories. This makes the evaluation data visible and trackable starting today.

a5423aef9cac05dd20553c49818748e32620efa2.text: Developers removed the old, manual system for managing passwords and configuration settings, and replaced it with a secure password manager called Infisical. This change affects everyone working on the code, including automated testing systems, and it means that sensitive information like API keys is no longer stored in plain text files. When you look at the project setup, you will need to log in to Infisical using its command-line tool instead of copying a sample settings file. Automated checks and test environments now get their settings through secure scripts that pull from the password manager, removing the risk of leaking secrets.

08d9ecfdfbc411d9281fe3a7476b732bc412485b.text: The development team has set up an automatic system that will run quality-checking tests on their software whenever someone commits code with a special tag in the message. These tests, which verify the assistant's responses against certain criteria, will only trigger for internal commits marked with a specific keyword, so they won't run during normal development work. If you were watching the build system, you'd see a new automated job start up whenever someone pushes code with that tag, running tests to ensure the AI behaves correctly.

7f28828ae0cf979cb67ac6bf24258b68423d2891.text: If you notice the assistant getting stuck repeating the same action over and over in agent mode, you might now see it abruptly stop and ask 'How would you like to proceed from here?' instead of spinning forever. Behind the scenes, a new automated check reviews your recent conversation whenever the assistant has just taken several turns without handing control back to you, and if it looks like a non-productive loop, it forces a natural break. This only kicks in when the assistant has gone well past a few consecutive turns with no end-turn gesture, so normal chat flow is unaffected. The behavior is active today for agent conversations meeting that condition.

6b6e431e66f67bfc112370bfb18a950dfc7f4ca4.text: Administrators can now adjust which AI models are available to a specific organization directly through a new section of the admin dashboard, rather than only through code changes. Behind the scenes, this required adding a new protected admin page, a way to fetch and save each organization's model settings in the database, and a confirmation step so only authorized staff can make these changes. If you looked at the admin interface today, you would see a new menu option for managing organization models that did not exist before.

40154da3140adb1a3d3901a729d4fd31825fe613.text: When you run programs in this tool, the assistant keeps track of where lines of text begin and end to avoid printing too many blank lines. The old method guessed using a simple count of recent characters, which mistook colored text codes (invisible instructions that change colors or move the cursor) for actual blank lines, causing it to wrongly merge or split your output. The new method carefully reads each line, strips out all invisible formatting codes and zero-width characters, and only then decides whether a line is truly empty, using a more reliable marker to know when one line ends and the next begins. This is a behind-the-scenes housekeeping fix that makes the text output you see cleaner and less jumpy, especially when programs print styled text.
