0422ab89d021af35cd82ac61b3382e427563442a.text: Organizations on the paid plan can now choose which file-selection model their team uses and set custom limits on how many files the assistant can look at at once. You’ll spot it when you open the file picker for your org: instead of the default behavior, you’ll see the model and file limits you chose. The company added a new settings page (stored in a database table) that lets org admins pick from the available models and adjust how many files to pull in for different tasks. If an org hasn’ set any preferences yet, or if the settings get removed, the file picker quietly reverts to the standard default behavior, so nothing breaks.

210b7c44b78d37b414f98d5d8a36ed65a8052783.text: The evals tooling now compiles to a shared output folder and the root build command runs across all projects automatically instead of listing each one. If you watched the repo, you'd see build errors vanish for eval scripts because they now run from compiled files, and a new configuration file in the evals folder declares how builds, eval runs, and cleanup steps work. It's live today and affects anyone running evals or full-repo builds.

76edaada622722b10c9a81e1277ae796a06a3744.text: The code that checks who is allowed to use the backend and who can log in to the admin panel used to live in two separate copies - one in the backend code and one in the web code. Both copies contained the same list of admin email addresses and the same logic for validating login tokens, so when the team needed to update either one, they had to remember to change it in two places. The team moved that duplicated authentication logic into a single shared location inside the codebase, and then pointed the backend, the website, and the evaluation tools at the new shared location so every part of the system now reads from the same source of truth. The list of admin email addresses was also carried over unchanged, so the same people who could previously access admin features can still do so.

da734278793e858621e4ec242f7cc47c6d2af6d0.text: You can now type a single command, "npm test," and your project will automatically check its backend, shared code, and web application for broken pieces, all at once, instead of running each check separately. This combines the scattered testing steps into one organized routine, making it harder to skip tests before sharing your work. The project now understands how its pieces depend on each other so it can decide what needs checking when something changes.

6aabac5a3b27729e7bb58fcd22f42d6fbe75afb0.text: The team deleted an old internal planning document that described how they were thinking about building a new way for the assistant to handle multi-step coding tasks. It was a 140-line file sitting in the project's main folder, and nobody was using it anymore to guide development. If you opened the project today, you just wouldn't see that document there. It was housekeeping, not something that changed how the software works.

6b06d7c2d22dda3b3b6b3ea9522dc25892387fe8.text: When the tool runs commands, it now splits the work into two cleaner jobs: one for commands that run in the open (like typing into a shell) and one for commands that run quietly in the background while you wait. This means background processes are no longer kept alive by accident after the assistant finishes with them, so they clean up properly instead of lingering. You won't notice a visual change, but behind the scenes the terminal handling is organized into two focused sections (foreground and background) instead of one crowded file, and a small helper was added that prevents duplicated text when stitching output together.

be9cd704489e65d16e3104d8e3959dcf43776d8f.text: The system that sends and manages team invitations has been cleaned up so that adding, resending, and removing people from a group now goes through a single, more organized set of pathways instead of several separate ones. As a result, invitation links sent by email now always point to the correct company web address, even when the request comes from a background job or a different internal service, so people who click the link land on the right page without errors. If you invite someone to a group today, the invite page and the team settings screen you interact with have been updated to match, so the experience is more consistent and less likely to break. The change is live now for all organizations using the team management features.

88cc4d16628ef964c963ec43cc6b6b3503ac213e.text: A new behind-the-scenes helper script has been added that can automatically write weekly summaries of what changed in the codebase. When it runs, it gathers recent development notes, asks an AI helper to organize them into a readable weekly recap, and files that recap in the right place for people to find. If you browse the project's history folders, you'd now see this new automation tool tucked in with the other developer utilities.

3af6aacb66eb3ab5ef49661a6bad7562394f88f5.text: The assistant published its release notes for the past three weekly updates, gathering them together under a single Q2 2025 section so they're easy to browse in one place. If you looked, you'd see three new changelog pages covering new AI model options (including a newer Claude model and an export command to save conversations), clearer slash-menu commands, and behind-the-scenes work to make the assistant's responses more consistent and reliable. These notes are now available to anyone viewing the changelog tab today.

d2eddcb6a9a9369239a4a5cf928f1716e4b5a4f3.text: The system now routes all its emails through a single, well-maintained email service connection, instead of each part of the app building its own. This means email-sending from both the evaluation results and the web signup flow now share one reliable method that handles errors and logs failures properly behind the scenes. You won’t notice a visual difference, but emails like invite links and eval summaries are now less likely to silently break if the service misbehaves. The change is live today for anyone receiving an invite or an eval email.

16dc62f59d5bb5a4150395fe5f0cf7cd4403b3db.text: Every organization now has two settings that used to have default values but are now required when an organization is created: the balance that triggers an automatic top-up, and the amount to top up by. If you create an organization through the web interface, the form you fill out must include both numbers explicitly; the system will no longer assume a starting threshold of 500 or a top-up amount of 2000 if you leave them blank. Behind the scenes, the database no longer keeps those default values and refuses to store an organization record unless both fields have real values in them, so the web form and the database now enforce the same rule together.

6dde6b9b6c63d71a7a11cbd578ac948a35de43bd.text: A new automated test script was added to the project's evaluation suite to verify the end-to-end functionality of a sample "cat app" backend and command-line interface. This test can be run using the npm script test:e2e-cat-app and will start the backend, interact with the CLI, and validate expected behaviors within configurable timeouts. It affects developers or CI systems that run the evals suite by adding a new validation path for the cat app integration, ensuring it works as expected from a clean state. If you looked at the project, you'd see a new test file e2e-cat-app-script.ts and a corresponding entry in package.json, with no impact on production user-facing features today.

5014af4859bbde92fd438d261f1a1fd362e106f4.text: You can now start an /agent mode from the command line, which lets the tool act as a supervisor that plans out multi-step coding tasks and drives the normal coding assistant through terminal commands, including a new ability to forcibly restart a stuck terminal session or pause execution for a set amount of time, with the terminal-command feature now accepting an empty command for timing purposes; these new controls only work in that /agent mode, not in regular use.

663ba6dc6110c21286c3f0c2de6893729e5323d9.text: If you're an organization that uses the service, you can now check whether a specific repository is covered by your organization's billing through a new API endpoint. The usage reporting system can now fetch billing data specific to your organization instead of just personal usage, and it will gracefully fall back to personal usage if there's an issue fetching org data. Behind the scenes, a new tracking system follows who you are, which org you're working for, and which repo you're using across requests, so billing and usage data stays connected to the right organization. The pricing plan names in the configuration were also updated to reflect team-oriented billing instead of individual plans.

1b50daa17311dc7c04d314fa4e1180db472f1065.text: The team reorganized how the assistant handles tool instructions, moving the detailed tool definitions into their own clearly separated section so they can be managed independently. While doing this, they also tightened the type safety around how tool calls are validated, reducing the chance of mismatches between what the assistant sends and what the tools expect. If you were looking at the code, you'd see tool schemas are now more cleanly isolated and the callback logic uses stricter typing; from a functional standpoint, this is behind-the-scenes housekeeping that makes the backend easier to maintain and less prone to type-related bugs.

71a5dd348de49a75dc8e6d8851dfd82cc295591d.text: Developers can now check how well recent AI model upgrades perform by automatically running old prompts through both the old and new versions and comparing the results side by side. This behind-the-scenes tool sorts through thousands of saved conversations, picks out a representative sample, and labels which ones should be used for testing rather than training, so the team can see concrete accuracy improvements before rolling updates out. You won't see this interface directly, but it helps ensure future model updates pick the right files more reliably and accurately over time.

2d55accd2d926586bb9c73324740db2a1231bae9.text: Every time you run a set of evals, the system now writes up a quick human-readable summary and fires an email to whoever is configured to receive results, so you no longer have to dig through files to see how things went. The summary includes total runs attempted, how many succeeded, and the average scores for helpfulness, completion, and efficiency. To send the message it talks to an external email service, and it silently skips sending (with a warning) if the required API key hasn’t been set yet.

9426dab66658a087315d9ad066c87850a87b75c6.text: When you (or the assistant) edit a file, the editor can now automatically run extra instructions right after each save. For example, it can run a spell-check or code-style check on just the file you changed, without you typing that command yourself. Project owners turn this on by listing those instructions in the project's settings file, where each instruction runs only when certain kinds of files are edited. All of this is live today: if a hook fails, its error gets reported back so you see it right away.

3f77b33e6a7c75596e1cc3d0512e80c541ff2678.text: Every part of Codebuff that talks to its AI helper (the one that writes and edits your code) now speaks the same language when it passes along the conversation history. Previously, different backend pieces each translated the chat into slightly different message formats before sending it off; that translation layer has been removed in favor of one standard message shape used everywhere. As a result, when you ask Codebuff to do something complex—like figure out which files you need to have read or rewrite a section of code–the AI receives your conversation in a single, consistent format, which makes the responses more reliable. You won't see a new button or setting, but behind the scenes the message handling is cleaner and more uniform across the whole workflow today.

770ce41fcad5f7ed8dde633ec3ae95b6eb7d908e.text: The admin tools that help manage and evaluate how well the assistant performs its tasks have been rewired to use a single, shared method for talking to the AI instead of one approach specifically for Claude. You won't see a difference in how anything works right now, but behind the scenes, grading runs, relabeling files, and generating diffs all now go through the same internal channel, which simplifies maintenance and ensures consistent billing and logging for these internal operations. Several older, duplicated ways of calling the AI have been removed.

c07b0311eeb0e5956971f4e517f4dfddc9cadb64.text: The team removed the code that let the system talk to the Deepseek model, which had been used to send requests, wait for answers with timeouts and retries, and quietly strip out image data (since Deepseek didn't support images yet). No one should notice anything different when they use the product right now, because this is behind-the-scenes cleanup; the feature still works the same way until they switch to a different way of calling Deepseek or another provider. If you opened the code folder, you'd find that one file gone and all its helper logic with it.

7c67da92e90a02e3ba79b831a02000b24e604e1b.text: After each automated test run of the assistant's responses, the system now automatically generates a written summary of what went well and what problems came up, including which issues are most important to fix first. This only affects the internal team who runs these test evaluations; you wouldn't see it in normal use. Behind the scenes, a new step reads the test results and writes up the findings, but if that step has a problem, it just logs a warning and lets the rest of the testing continue without stopping.

b2abad5b36ea9b7fbf26f3272d0afb631866f9a1.text: You wouldn't notice anything as a user, since this change only affects the internal scheduling tool the development team uses to run automated quality checks. That tool previously had a daily check-in that tested the assistant's coding help every morning, and that scheduled daily check has been removed. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance, so it doesn't change any features you use today.

6913a7ebac0d7da3c464aa06bc09de0d9baa87a5.text: The app now sends all its requests to language models through one single connection method instead of keeping a separate shortcut just for OpenAI. As a result, the code that talked directly to OpenAI and routed traffic through an analytics service called Helicone has been deleted entirely. Internal developers will notice the unified module is now the only way any backend request reaches a language model, and the extra OpenAI-only setup is gone.

f6094b46efc0702c2e9effdb80f3195d0c1908a8.text: The system now has a new set of practice tests built from real past work done on Manifold Markets, letting the team automatically check that its AI-writing helper still behaves correctly as they tweak it. These tests are only used by the developers internally to catch problems before changes go live, so you won't notice anything different when using the assistant.

427525b708f93cfa71fc8788d46092e8ee7747e4.text: The software stopped maintaining two separate Gemini connection methods and now uses a single, shared path for all Gemini conversations. If you relied on internal admin tools to re-label conversations, you may need to restart the process because the message-handling step changed how messages are prepared. The old Gemini-specific connection files were deleted, and the system was simplified to remove outdated message types that nothing actively used anymore.

1ebf8d9b68b11b6e094c42a279daf6cc6d916a0f.text: Until now, the evaluation system could only pull code from one specific repository. It now accepts any repository URL you give it, so teams can run evaluations on their own projects instead of being limited to the Codebuff repo. When you provide a URL, the system automatically figures out the right folder name to download it into. This works for both public and private repositories, with the system using a security token to access private code if needed.

122102bb87087439ec17c52fdcb6f3653592f174.text: Starting May 28, 2025, when the automated test suite runs each day, it now downloads the codebuff project into a staging folder before executing evaluations. Previously, the test environment expected this repository to be present but did not explicitly fetch it, which could cause failures if it was missing. You would notice this as a new step appearing in the daily test logs labeled as setting up the codebuff repository before tests begin. This step uses the organization's GitHub access token to authenticate the download, making the repository available consistently for every evaluation run.

a7c06a2712110372bea2d081c80dda845602e9ec.text: If you're an admin running the internal trace-relabel tool, traces that were previously scored without full file context can now be re-run using Claude 4 Opus with that full context. The new script filters down to only the traces still missing an Opus-with-full-file-context label and processes up to 20 of them at once in batches of 5, so you'll see a fresh set of Opus-scored traces in the data store whenever you fire it. Nothing changes for everyday users; this only affects the internal dataset used to judge and improve model selection.

f227db9b854ccb84a908c2d46dae7b0c5eb0e012.text: The development team removed some leftover code that was no longer being used to connect to two external AI services (Gemini streaming and OpenRouter). These functions were sitting in the codebase—dead weight that nothing actually called anymore—so cleaning them up makes the system simpler and slightly easier to maintain. If you looked at the code, you'd see one fewer file and shorter files with that unused logic taken out, while day-to-day behavior stays exactly the same.

0adc47918fccab0706e1a2b9ddf4b7f6126a2e32.text: Every day at 8 AM UTC, a hidden helper inside the company's code repository now wakes up and runs a set of automated checks that test how well the AI assistant performs on sample coding tasks. These checks save detailed reports for the team to review, and the results live in a private internal system that only staff can see. Nothing you use changes, but behind the scenes the team gets a fresh daily snapshot of AI quality.

a566ec2b780dc09c4cded7008af0081931421420.text: The assistant can now automatically collect and review examples of how it handles git-related tasks, building a library of past interactions to improve future git work. When applying edits to files, it also stops crashing if a file path is malformed or unreadable, instead skipping that file and continuing with the rest. Together, these changes make the system both smarter (learning from git examples) and sturdier (gracefully handling bad paths) when updating your project files.

358d0db78fa82fc0c46511254ba6315755ace647.text: The system can now check three pieces of code at the same time instead of waiting for each one to finish before starting the next, which makes checking multiple code versions faster. This only affects the internal team that tests how the coding assistant behaves on different code histories, not on anyone using the assistant day to day. If you watched this testing process, you'd see it log that it's running three checks at once instead of one, and save progress files appear sooner as each batch finishes.

693635b17ac0bc709ac805ab46be6dbc2543146f.text: Tests that calculate credit usage and auto-recharge behavior were occasionally failing at random because leftover fake data from one test was 'leaking' into the next. The code now clears all fake data in one shared setup step before every test runs, so each test starts with a clean slate. You would see fewer surprise failures on the testing dashboard, especially in the billing and usage tests that had been flaky.

a5eb09dc80f7f241cc343e69e090224dbd8f5c54.text: The team deleted a 302-line document that was sitting inside the npm-app package because it was just a copy of information kept in other places. You as a reader wouldn't see or read this file in your day-to-day work, but editors and contributors will notice that the duplicate notes are gone when they browse that package. Keeping the information in only one spot means the team won't have to update the same text in two places every time something changes.

ac9a7f7354e3dd3e6e28eb67521b4d340722c6aa.text: The tool that helps decide which code files matter most for a request can now be automatically graded by another AI model, so teams can see how well different versions perform side by side in a new admin page. When an admin opens that page, they will find a new section for relabeling past decisions, and the backend now pulls in extra context from related training traces to help make those judgments. Support staff and internal users will notice the new grading and relabeling pages are available today, while the underlying query system now also lets developers ask for traces with or without associated relabels or training-context data using optional filters.

8af577c6c9d73bcdc8f71a16cb91a4dcbe24c86d.text: Messages you've already finished now load faster, because the app looks them up using a combination of the account that owns them and the time they completed rather than just the completion time alone. Behind the scenes, the app's filing system was switched from a single column to a two-column lookup (completion time plus account), so searches that filter by 'my finished messages from today' no longer have to scan every message in the system. The improvement is live for anyone whose account stores finished messages, and you would notice it mainly as pages that list completed messages loading smoothly under normal traffic. The app now uses a composite index named message_finished_at_user_id_idx that covers both finished_at and user_id, replacing the old single-column index.

e2fd961bd1c659ed789bcf6030462ce804e2e40a.text: When you ask the assistant for help with how to use it from the command line, the simple, everyday options you might need are shown first, while the more advanced settings are tucked away so they don't clutter the main view. You can still access those advanced options by typing them in directly, they're just not advertised in the default help text. The list of available options and their explanations now live in one shared place so the help screen and the on-screen menu stay consistent with each other.

b68ef311d4d1f636c5975523293b15ff7a545c47.text: When the assistant looks at your files to decide how much to keep and how much to cut, it used to pick the sample files using randomness that could change every time, so the same set of files could lead to slightly different estimates. Now it uses a fixed, deterministic method seeded by the file list itself, so the same files always produce the same sample and the same token estimate. You as a user would notice that the system prompt generation behaves consistently instead of showing occasional drift or flakiness in how your file context gets truncated. This fix applies to the backend service that builds system prompts for the assistant and has been live as of today's date.

c60fa21bba1531e05cc683abfb8272cae2bc712f.text: Today, the assistant stopped using its brand-new way of reading incoming message streams and went back to the older, stream-based method for understanding replies and tool calls. If you were watching the system handle long, multi-step responses, you might notice it once again breaks its output into smaller chunks rather than tagging and parsing whole sections at once. Behind the scenes, the team also removed an experimental parsing tool (along with its tests) and restored a previously used library. The old streaming logic is now live in production right now.

1b79a6d5380dfdf14a4e6a99cc1a63b5f9ad8b91.text: When the assistant writes tool-use blocks (like when it tells the system to write a file or run a command), the software that splits up the incoming text stream now uses a proper XML parser instead of rough text matching. This means nested tags and attributes inside those blocks are read correctly instead of being misread or dropped. You’d notice it mainly if the assistant previously failed to act on a well-formed tool call that contained attributes or nested tags—those now parse and execute instead of producing errors. The change is live today across the tools you can call, such as write_file and the various agent actions.

9a4ad025abb84b7082bf8324947873c15ea25c51.text: The AI assistant now reads its own thinking process using a more reliable method, like upgrading from a shaky pair of reading glasses to a proper magnifying glass. When the assistant works through problems out loud, this new system handles complex reasoning steps and nested thoughts without breaking down, so you're less likely to see errors where the assistant suddenly stops or gets confused mid-explanation. Behind the scenes, this makes the assistant more robust when it needs to think carefully or follow multi-step instructions.

11f760c6a76e7b6e3d6dd8b13ecb1f8ef7cf4d8c.text: The app now keeps a quick-reference list of when each message finished, so screens that show messages sorted or filtered by completion time load faster instead of sifting through every message each time. You won't see a new button or setting, but if you open a list heavy with completed messages, it simply appears without the usual pause. This is already live today for anyone viewing message lists, and developers will find the matching reference recorded alongside the rest of the database layout so the optimization stays in sync as the app evolves.

0963ba72ae47c80f897f4c8c270729c0d9dc18e7.text: The npm-app build process now runs an automated code check that catches certain import mistakes before compiling, and the lint configuration was moved to a newer format to support that. Files that imported code out of order or used the wrong import style for the pino logger were corrected so the new rules pass cleanly. If you build or review npm-app, you will see the lint step appear in the build sequence and the previously failing files no longer trigger import-order or named-import warnings. This change is live today for anyone building or linting npm-app.

a5ebaaba019755369adf2ce7acd08962010cade2.text: When you paste text that contains special symbols written in a shorthand form (like < for a less-than sign), the program now turns all of those symbols into their proper characters correctly, even when the symbols arrive in pieces across multiple chunks. You wouldn't notice a difference in the final text, but while the text is still being processed you might briefly see leftover ampersands if the previous logic left them in. Who is affected today didn't change.

91d4333a25cace02ad7b83b188ff28b4c05f9d77.text: The team removed the old way developers ran tests on their own computers and instead improved how the company's automated testing service stores and reuses downloaded dependencies. Now the automated tests run faster and more reliably because they skip re-downloading things they already have. If you looked, you'd see the automated testing setup now covers more of the project's parts and prepares its settings earlier before running.

2c1460fdd43768d35ec6d4898ba2243fe7a8428b.text: When the assistant reads a file as part of understanding your project, that file's summary now includes a new section listing which other files reference or call the key names defined in it, capped at 25 entries per name to avoid bloating the conversation. This appears in the project analysis views that shape what the assistant knows about your codebase, so you'll notice richer context when the assistant discusses how files relate to each other. The feature is live today as part of the project context that's assembled when the assistant loads your project.

687e4dbb50a8b1bf82f5dbe8fb29d44140c0b176.text: When you visit the landing page and click the big button in the hero section, it now says 'Get Started' instead of 'Try Free'. Clicking that button opens a new step-by-step installation guide that walks you through each editor (VS Code, Cursor, IntelliJ, PyCharm) and lets you copy the terminal command with one click. The competitor logos like Cursor and Claude Code were moved into a shared 'logos' folder and new IDE icons were added, so the guide shows recognizable pictures next to each option. If you're building the project from source, the README's setup instructions were simplified to a single command.

1e5e715fbfb1d537c35ac58d4cdab501b5fd5220.text: Starting May 1, 2025, the system that runs automated code checks before merging changes now sets up its testing tools directly inside each check instead of using a shared setup file that was shared between all checks. This means each check is now self-contained and less prone to issues caused by that shared file, which fixes a problem that was causing test run 16 to fail. The shared setup file is no longer used or included. The internal team that works on the codebase is the one affected by this change, and they would now see each testing job configured separately in their workflow files instead of calling one common setup step.

b2d17e9d5315f24fc2136003a3213616d6fb86b4.text: The build system used by the project's automated checks was reorganized so the setup steps live in one reusable place instead of being copied into every check. If you watched the checks run, you'd see them start faster and behave more consistently, because they now pull from a single shared setup instead of each defining its own checkout, dependency installation, and caching. The special flag that tells the software it's running inside the automated system is now set at the top level for all checks, rather than being written into a settings file during setup. This is internal plumbing; nothing about the product you use changes as a result.

5a61a5397e376f1a3e8a62cd0f9ab1012066eaf3.text: The company has added an internal tool that lets staff pull a monthly report showing how many credits, messages, and users were active during a given billing period, along with a ranked list of the top ten heaviest users. It's a behind-the-scenes script for employees, not something you would see or interact with; if you were to look in the system today, you'd find this new option already available for anyone with the right access.

497d434f8bf4f962710d0b0404f4460fe6404d93.text: You can now ask the assistant to make a small, targeted edit inside an existing file, swapping out one exact snippet of text for another, instead of rewriting the whole file. The assistant looks for the precise old text you point to—including spaces and punctuation—and replaces just that piece, then shows you where the edit happened. This is most useful when a file is very large or when the normal full-file save doesn't apply cleanly. It's live today.

1f43c1b870135fc0ecb44ac13dcb0dcdf9c5dbaf.text: Developers can now run the project's automated checks (building, testing, etc.) directly on their own computer, instead of only running them on the cloud. A new tool was added that sets up a local simulation of the cloud system, and the team also simplified how the checking steps are organized so they run a bit more efficiently. Everything is ready to use today if you're a developer working on this project.

e42ccfe65840d616173d0151a2b9917a7e5cb817.text: The system stopped running two separate checks on every code change and now runs them as one step instead. If you looked, you would see one fewer status check reporting in for each change. This only affects people working on the codebase itself, not what you see when using the app.

fb2d1dfca2916877ffe136e6f82f171d831b5726.text: If you open the configuration documentation today, the technical reference for the project settings file now reads like a structured, annotated outline instead of plain prose, with each option shown in a JSON-style layout and helpful notes about what it does and its default value. The underlying engine that builds this reference switched to a format that prints the settings in tidy, indented blocks and includes descriptions and default values inline. This affects anyone reading the built-in documentation for the configuration file, which is now rendered as formatted JSON rather than generic text.

ad147ec5f9339ffaf17daf1f1acca40b87dd987d.text: Your computer now remembers the results of repetitive tasks like building or checking your code, so the next time it needs to do the same work, it can skip straight to the finish instead of starting over. This means tasks that used to take minutes might now finish in seconds, especially when nothing has actually changed since the last run. The system also now treats a section of code called BigQuery like a first-class part of the project, so any code that depends on it can be checked and built independently. You wouldn't see a new feature or button, but behind the scenes your development tools are faster and more organized.

17c71f6cd1a840b7e8b7eb26f2282ef90885a5bc.text: You probably won't notice anything directly, but behind the scenes the team reorganized how the app talks to Google's BigQuery storage. Instead of parts of the code digging through a messy shared folder to find BigQuery tools, they created one clean, clearly labeled package that everything now pulls from. This is housekeeping that makes the system easier to maintain and less likely to break when they need to update those tools later.

ff5f5f89dccaaaea3cd2e126a02983444710922a.text: The build system that prepares the web app and the npm tool for release has been switched from a set of manual scripts to a single coordinating tool. Instead of separately running several build commands in different folders and copying files by hand, those steps are now defined in one place that understands the order and dependencies between tasks. What you'd notice: running build, clean, or typecheck now uses fewer commands and produces the same result faster because it only rebuilds what actually changed. This is live today across the main project files.

75e00b83dadca24eafbd038d5231929ab455518a.text: The product now records two new tracking events—when someone signs up and when credits are granted to an account—alongside the already-tracked prompt activity. These tracking events are sent to PostHog with near-immediate delivery thanks to configuration tuned for minimal delay. If you're an admin or analyst watching usage dashboards, you'll see signup and credit-grant actions appear in reports that previously only showed prompt-based usage.

2d7d7a990ff33bd90041223f1a955d5b4c987e17.text: If you need to work on projects for this company from a Windows computer, there's now a step-by-step guide explaining how to set up your environment. The guide includes login details and access information for a shared Windows machine, as well as instructions for installing necessary tools using an automated package manager. This document is only for internal team members and doesn't change anything in the main software — it's just a new reference file to help developers get started more easily.

12424332f7ce042f336c1443112487c5463cd0c2.text: The assistant now silently checks whether git (a tool for tracking code changes) is installed on your computer and reports that fact back to the developers. You won't see anything different, but the developers gain a small piece of information about how often git is available across user setups. The check itself was already working; this change simply makes that information visible in analytics.

e981392bdbddda96419fd5168ddf806ca16b28d5.text: When you run commands in the tool, any time the output has three or more blank lines in a row, the software now automatically squashes that down to just two blank lines. This happens everywhere the tool prints text - command results, error messages, status updates - so nothing has extra gaps anymore. The change took effect today for the assistant's responses to your commands.

02c69f33e90bac403ed0165a7a303ca88d3ff3f5.text: The app now keeps two kinds of logs in tidy, separate files instead of mixing them, so you can inspect detailed debug information for the backend (/debug/backend.log) and the app (/debug/npm-app.log) independently. Behind the scenes, a new analytics event called Background process started is now tracked, and the client uses a shared logger that automatically attaches your user id and session details to each log line. This means your logs are easier to read and the background work the app does can now be analyzed for reliability.

03cbe0d68e2b22eb3a810c1fb8abb04ed6ba6901.text: The software now quietly tracks how people use it by sending anonymous usage data to a analytics service called PostHog. When you open the app, it logs that you started it, and when you send a message through the backend, it logs that interaction too. The data is only sent in production, and the system waits to make sure all the tracking information gets sent before it closes. If you are using the app, you probably won't notice anything different since this runs in the background.

ea533f8d06f0c48e553825c246cc202f920dced6.text: A behind-the-scenes setting that checks for mistakes in the code is now switched on and stays running while developers work, instead of being turned off. Any developer on the team who opens their coding tools will now see automatic error reports appear in a shared log file, whereas before the checker was disabled and not actively watching for problems. This is housekeeping that helps catch coding errors earlier during development.

b72ea4bebd2954faa734ef250ea33eaaa5fee143.text: Starting with version 1.0.244, the app stops saving detailed debug logs to a local file when running in its live environment. If you are using the production version, logs that used to be written to a file called npm-app.log will no longer be saved there. Instead, the app only keeps logs in its active memory while it is running. This change affects anyone running the app in the production environment, which is now live today.

6202b3322489c22213ee330a765a775ce8e78633.text: Anonymous users who interact with the assistant without signing in will no longer trigger pricing calculation errors, because the system now defaults to a flat 1 cent cost per credit when no user account is linked. The pricing logic has been moved out of the shared core code and into a dedicated billing module, which the backend now imports directly, and the continuous integration system has been updated to build this new module before running checks. The old standalone auto-top-up handling and direct credit-granting functions in the backend have been removed and replaced by the same shared module, keeping billing calculations consistent across the entire platform. This fix is live today.

b907db6d8af65b13a0871fa4cf04eb63ce3da8e3.text: You can now visit /config on the Codebuff website, which takes you straight to the configuration documentation section. The page that displays the structure of the configuration file has been redesigned so both the assistant and people reading the docs can follow its layout more easily, with clearer descriptions and nesting. When you run the setup command that creates a starter configuration file on your computer, it now points to this same /config address. If you open your browser and go to /config today, you will land on the documentation page that explains every option you can set in your configuration file.

c2c62ac86efaf3f89c920c7159e13dd4ae856f94.text: When you run the assistant inside a project, you can now type a setup command that walks you through creating your configuration file instead of having to write it by hand or know its exact format. The configuration file can now be written with helpful comments included, the same way you'd annotate a document, and the assistant will read and follow those extra notes. Behind the scenes, the instructions the assistant receives are wrapped in a clearly marked section so it treats them as firm guidance rather than casual notes, and a short optional description field can be added to that configuration file to label what it's for without affecting how things work.

2f0ded02ccab4cb1346a9f602d6391424b860994.title: Sponsored proposal card gains post-code setup guidance
2f0ded02ccab4cb1346a9f602d6391424b860994.summary: SponsoredProposalViewModel gains a nullable setupGuide field plus setupExpectation, and the CLI SponsoredProposalBlock now renders inline setup prompts for the offered state and a dedicated Setup → verify section when setupGuide is present. The advertiser CTA label changed from “Create your ${advertiser_name} project” to “Set up ${advertiser_name}” and is now grouped under the setup prompt, keeping the CTA out of destination territory per the VM-33..VM-36 conformance checks added in sponsored-proposal-conformance.ts. Scope covers CLI (sponsored-proposal-block.tsx), shared core (sponsored-proposal-view.ts, sponsored-proposal-conformance.ts); the guide is only populated in ctaStates and stays null otherwise. setupGuide steps describe review, account setup, and verify-in-app without claiming live integration verification, since a finished run only proves local work.

a843b8817e843fe1808f0aeeff438fd28e185b5d.text: The hidden admin tool that lets staff reassign AI conversations now requires a verified admin login before it can be used, and it has moved to a simpler, cleaner web address. You'd notice the old, randomly named address no longer loads, while the tool itself — used only by four specific staff members — still works exactly the same once you sign in.

9c2c4c5c3d6899dc23a34a8fb9ead53e1c827e80.text: The web server now saves its activity logs to a file called web.log instead of only showing them on the screen, which makes it easier for developers to troubleshoot problems when working locally. The login screen for the web interface has also been split into two separate pieces: one that shows a code entered during command-line authentication and another for the general sign-in view. If you opened the web login page in a browser, it looks the same to you; these are behind-the-scenes changes for local development and logging.

99c163f037a9735d9c356e9c2e363dca52e23cd2.text: Nothing you can see or touch has changed in the app today; this work is purely for developers maintaining the code. The team added plain-language explanations to the configuration files so that when someone looks at or generates documentation for the config structure, they see helpful descriptions of each setting instead of bare field names and types. These descriptions are now stored alongside the field definitions and a new utility can turn the whole schema into readable text, but that text never appears in the running application or affects how configuration is validated.

f49acb7d1549800c1a73424b8600eccb51894aa7.text: Starting today, the system handles credit checks and monthly resets in a way that prevents two people (or two parts of the system) from using the same credit at the same time, which previously could cause credits to be spent twice or monthly grants to be added twice. When you log in or check your usage, the system now makes sure your monthly credit renewal happens safely before showing your balance. If you looked at your account, you would see the same credits and resets as always, but behind the scenes the system is now coordinating these updates so they do not interfere with each other, and it will automatically retry if there is a temporary conflict. This is a live fix for the billing system.

74c651a6db4b3716ce750abc7a823dd307a2e085.text: When you ask the assistant to help find or use files in your project, the system now records a detailed log of every step it takes — which files it looked at, what it searched for, and in what order † to a secure database. This gives the team invisible breadcrumbs to trace exactly why the assistant picked certain files or skipped others, even mid-task. The change is live today for everyone running the assistant through the web interface; if you use it, each of your sessions is now quietly being logged behind the scenes so problems (like a missing file or a slow search) can be investigated later. There are no visible differences in how the assistant behaves right now — it just gains the ability to be understood better if something goes wrong.

7f6e2d2aa73926aa1bf8671f77e819316faf0a09.text: You now have a new admin page where staff can manually ask the system to re-label or analyze file-picker activity for a specific user. When triggered, the system pulls relevant traces for that user and runs them through two AI models (Claude and Gemini) in small parallel batches, then stores the new labels in BigQuery. The database column names used in queries were also corrected to match the actual schema (created_at, agent_step_id, user_id), fixing potential query errors. This is live today in the admin interface.

ed236a0bceda603c16863ddda5d7a664ee35b143.text: When you open the tool for a project, it now checks for a codebuff.json file and can automatically start background tasks like a web server, so you don't have to run them yourself before getting started. This works through a new settings file that lists which processes to kick off, and the tool will validate the format before launching them. Anything in that file is kept out of the project's searchable content, and the background tasks are labeled differently so user-started processes stay quieter. This is live today and works whenever you launch the tool with that config file present.

132778b796b180f9021119dbd0f749076993f323.text: The assistant can now think through responses in a step-by-step way when using Gemini, a newer model provider—similar to how a person might pause to organize their thoughts before answering. It also now accepts the same set of stop commands (like specific phrases that end a response) across different AI systems, making behavior more consistent. You wouldn't see a dramatic difference unless you're using advanced settings that rely on these features, but the system is now more unified behind the scenes. This is now live and part of the core system as of April 2025.

60a75f471aa4a05410ab3d44b15e09560ad01c1e.text: The team split up one large internal command file into smaller, focused files that each handle a specific job - one for checking API keys, one for showing code changes, and one for the hidden easter egg feature. This is purely behind-the-scenes organization work; everything still works exactly the same for anyone using the tool. The only noticeable fix is that the checkpoint system now correctly saves snapshots even when there are no changes to save, which prevents it from unnecessarily creating checkpoints when it shouldn't. Nothing the reader would see or do has changed.

5246b83c5432b876374e1cf0450c5f6e869f243b.text: When the assistant's streaming XML parser encounters a tag that isn't allowed by the expected structure (like a <video> tag inside a list that only expects <item> tags), it now includes that tag's full text in the output instead of silently dropping it. This means you'll see the actual <video> text appear in your response stream rather than having it vanish completely. This affects any content that previously contained unexpected tags, which will now be visibly preserved instead of being stripped out.

e9194839f09c07d29defdb1e2d66f2f35bb5e3f5.text: The internal code that manages the assistant's undo, redo, and checkpoint listing commands has been moved into its own dedicated file, so the main startup file is now shorter and easier to follow. Anyone maintaining the tool sees the change immediately: the command logic they used to find in one large file now lives in a clearly labeled section, and importing it behaves the same as before. No new features or options are introduced; the assistant's ability to rewind or list conversations works exactly as it did today.

ffd640ed3f0aaaf6f7ff5b5a308e62e4c7d330f4.text: The assistant software can now connect to and use a new kind of custom-trained AI model, allowing it to generate responses through either real-time streaming or complete delivery. Behind the scenes, it adds a new internal module that routes requests to a specific fine-tuned model endpoint, and it includes basic cost-tracking for usage of that model. A small example was left in the code showing how to try this new model, alongside notes indicating the team plans to clean up some temporary message conversion code. This is now in place and ready to use.

894cfcb85b60b8b9fd0edb37d03319389a5bd171.text: When you ask the assistant a coding question, it now automatically pulls in relevant documentation from Context7 and tucks it into the prompt it sends to the model. That means the assistant starts answering with the official docs already in hand, instead of trying to recall everything from its own training. You'd notice when you ask something like 'How do I use React hooks?' the assistant can reference specific, recent documentation snippets directly in its reply, because the background integration fetches and injects those pieces before the conversation even reaches the model.

7fe3167b36cb8dc119d4736b84a649eadc1a022b.text: The system that records what happens inside the app now uses a separate, more careful helper for breaking up large pieces of information before writing them down. You won't see this when you use the app—it only changes how the program stores its own logs behind the scenes, but it should now handle big messages more reliably without choking on things like empty text or unusually long single words.

c01863b6a8c0af42bab2e1e3e61cb367e548302b.text: The assistant can now see what's happening in programs that keep running in the background (like a long download or server). When you run a background task and then ask another question, the conversation now includes any output that task produced since the last message, so you don't have to check a separate terminal window. The new information is capped at 5,000 characters per stream to avoid overwhelming the chat.

68f85fd4c9cc9441b1cfb768df3f7aa65ab024af.text: When the system logs large pieces of data, it now correctly breaks them into smaller chunks that fit within the size limits, instead of failing or producing unreadable errors when the data is too complex. Previously, deeply nested objects or very large text values would cause logging to break; the logging process would choke on structures that contained other structures or arrays. Now the system carefully splits these complex data shapes into multiple readable log entries while respecting the size limit, so you will see complete, well-formed log lines instead of truncated or broken ones when inspecting logs that contain large or nested data.

ae194dc9bbd65478c8aed2c99ffbb238a6cbee6a.text: The website's buttons and overall look changed to a bold, high-contrast style: pricing and login buttons now have a stark black-and-white appearance with a slight shadow effect instead of the old blue and purple gradients. The referral and pricing pages switched to green-themed gradients for their cards. The browser tab icon (favicon) now displays correctly, and the main headline on the homepage ('Direct your codebase like a movie') was capitalized. You would notice these changes immediately if you visited the pricing, login, or referral pages.

59567a4df76501aeb4f2605211f209875554ce97.text: The affiliate program now lets each participant claim a custom username and raise their referral cap from the old default to 500 friends they can recruit. Your referral page address changes from a fixed system name to whatever username you pick, and the credit reward per new referral is halved from 500 to 250 points. If you're already signed up through an existing program link, your old address still works, but new links must use the new usernames. The higher 500-referee limit is live right away for anyone who fills out the new affiliate settings page.

e149d3a326e893650d788669092b77b0fdca2a5b.text: When you ask me to run a command in the terminal, I can now choose to let it keep running in the background while I do other things, instead of waiting for it to finish first. A new setting tells the system whether a command should run right away (like before) or be set aside to continue on its own, with its results saved so you can check them later. I'll also clean up and stop any of these background tasks automatically when our session ends, so they don't keep running unnecessarily.

ceb58b10a8882ac97daad91a16c76253b2104648.text: The app can now remember your secret login tokens for other AI services securely, instead of keeping them lying around unlocked. A new locked storage box was added to the database, where your tokens are scrambled with military-grade encryption that only your account can unscramble. If you signed in and connected an AI service like Google's Gemini, your token would now be tucked away safely in this encrypted box rather than stored in plain sight. This protection is active today for anyone using the newer features.

6baeeab1a6450bcd49bfb45b5356164a89a1442c.text: When the assistant reads back a long chat to fit it into its memory, it now trims the conversation more aggressively—keeping only the 5 most recent terminal command outputs in full and simplifying the rest—while also filling only half of the available memory space instead of all of it, leaving room for new messages. If you look at a trimmed conversation today, you’ll notice older terminal outputs are shortened and the overall message history is more compact. This affects the internal tool that prepares the assistant’s chat history before it responds, and it’s already live in the codebase.

aeca6290626a96dea7060dcddef7e3461aa5262f.text: A new event page has been added to the website that displays details for the upcoming Codebuff Hackathon at Mox in San Francisco on April 13th, 2025. The page shows the event schedule, location, and prize tiers including monthly Codebuff credits for the top three winners. Anyone visiting the site can now navigate to this dedicated page to view all the information about the hackathon, though registration details are noted as upcoming.

2af716acdbb25762ae53b86c5352ec5e04848fe2.text: If you send messages that contain special invisible characters called null characters, the system now cleans them out properly before storing them. The system used to remove these characters by converting messages to a simplified format and back, which sometimes broke or slowed things down. Now it uses a smarter method that goes through the whole message and removes those characters safely and quickly, so your messages get stored correctly no matter what's inside them.

f22b4d03a0a972455c39ad9e224a836ac651dc3e.text: Starting today, people using the premium "max" option to spend more for better results will now get conversations powered by Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro model instead of the old default. When you type a message in max mode, your request goes to a new streaming path that tries Google's service first, and if that doesn't work, it can still fall back to the older providers. You won't see a setting to turn on or off: the model choice happens automatically based on which plan tier you're on.

1b0767f9b5193fe1c26fc42e2e1ed981a863ab50.text: When you sign in with the command-line tool on more than one computer, each tool now gets a slightly different identity tag. Previously, two identical machines could end up with the same tag, causing their login sessions to mix up or overwrite each other; now the tool adds a small random value to the tag so every machine is uniquely recognized. If you looked at the login process, you would also notice that the tool no longer automatically creates this identity tag for you when requesting a code, that login responses now include when they expire, and that logging out clears the stored signature so it cannot be reused. The system also stopped writing your access token into debug logs when sending prompts or connecting, so less sensitive information is recorded while you work.

d7303e3a320dfe599bb499741c829f30c2eb2801.text: If you write a label with extra spaces around the equals sign, like mylabel = "hello" instead of mylabel="hello", the system now reads it correctly instead of ignoring it. Tests that check this labeling behavior were reorganized into a single folder so they're easier to run and maintain. You wouldn't see any difference unless you're someone writing or checking those labels, which is mainly the internal team.

083ba34e1b8127271cab8501c442e98772ee098e.text: The Discord bot that helps link your Discord account to your Codebuff account has been rebuilt from the ground up to use Discord's newer, more reliable connection method. Previously, the bot relied on a separate service that handled interactions differently; now, it connects directly to Discord using an updated library, and the old connection method along with its supporting setup files have been removed. If you notice anything, it might be a slightly smoother experience when using the bot, though the basic functions, like running the '/link' command to connect your accounts, should work just as before. This change is internal and mostly affects how the bot operates behind the scenes.

f33f7ec279296b67b59b9f69f02db55a99716de9.text: The assistant can now record what it writes to your files while it works, helping developers trace errors if something goes wrong. At the same time, an old method for the assistant to act on your behalf directly in your browser was removed, since it was no longer needed. You wouldn\'t notice either change just by watching, but if a problem happens, the logs will contain more detail about what the assistant tried to save.

f6f380735fd0aeab7a8a51079c3187d36fbcec08.text: When a developer who uses this project saves a file, Visual Studio Code will now automatically tidy up the order of its internal code references, keeping them grouped and alphabetized. This happens behind the scenes because the project added invisible configuration files that tell VS Code to run this cleanup every time a file is saved. Any developer on the team who edits code will see their files automatically stay organized without having to manually fix line ordering.

454988686e03f8ea672270fc20dc55814ba53a36.text: You can now link your Discord account to your existing profile by typing a slash command like /link <email> inside any Discord server where the bot is present. The bot verifies your request using Discord's signature, limits each person to five commands per minute, and replies only to you so others can't see your email or response. Behind the scenes, a new column in the user database stores your Discord ID, and the bot responds with messages that disappear after a short time to keep your information private. The developers note this integration only handles slash commands today — listening for new messages or member joins would require additional setup in the future.

254095ba25df1931af14d0fc48f39aef06460ad6.text: The main page's big banner section used to stretch to fill almost the entire phone screen, which pushed important content off-screen. Now, on mobile devices, that banner shrinks to a normal size so you can actually see and interact with the demo content below it. If you viewed the site on your phone before, the hero area would take up nearly your whole screen; now it only takes up the space it actually needs, and the IDE demo below it is formatted to be readable on smaller screens.

3ea21c0bf5c767ff7bf49eacc27f03ae18ed0e61.text: This is behind-the-scenes software cleanup that changes how the tool talks to itself when saving and loading your work. Internally, the system now tags every conversation with a unique ID so responses can be matched to requests, and instead of checking error messages as plain text, it uses structured error types that the main tool can catch and handle smoothly. You won't see this directly, but it makes checkpoint-related errors (like when saving or restoring your session) handled more reliably and consistently.

7013cc6a0c68f7d94e42951b34cc6db0284c07db.text: When you visit the site, the browser now loads the company logo immediately instead of waiting, so the logo appears faster at the top of the page and in the footer. The site also uses refreshed favicon images — the small icon shown in your browser tab — including new versions for standard browsers, Apple devices, and a separate light-themed icon. If you looked closely, the call-to-action text block at the bottom has slightly more breathing room beneath it. This is a live visual refresh; no new features, just snappier branding.

3f1365de20974594e130701a2f8ad0e9a14cc010.text: The landing page now fills the entire screen with a redesigned hero section that transitions to a demo more smoothly, and documentation pages have prettier arrow buttons for moving between articles. These visual updates are live today and affect anyone visiting the main website or browsing documentation, making navigation feel more polished and the initial page load feel more immersive.

2f0ded02ccab4cb1346a9f602d6391424b860994.text: When you run a sponsored proposal in the CLI, you'll now see inline guidance telling you the expected setup path: 'Code → account setup → verify' when the proposal is in the 'offered' state. After completing the code step, a dedicated Setup section appears with a 'Set up [advertiser name]' button that walks you through review, account setup, and in-app verification without claiming the integration is live. The guidance is only shown for proposals that include a setup guide; other proposals render as before.

b9940e9407b6dd65b151a988c0fd5b6e2a9ebef9.text: When you run the tool, it now checks whether another copy is already working in the same project before it starts any background tasks. If it finds an active instance running, it skips launching those duplicate background processes, preventing conflicts and wasted resources. You would notice that the usual startup messages about launching development servers or background tasks might not appear if the tool detects a similar instance already running, since it will gracefully avoid duplicating the work.

b9c4a393b92b8814c33c7952356a3d0145ed9a72.text: Users with auto-top-up enabled will now have credits automatically purchased and added to their account when their balance drops below a threshold they set, so they don’t run out mid-use. The system charges their saved payment method immediately, grants the credits right away, and temporarily disables the feature if a payment fails; balances update in real time based on actual usage. This is live today for paying users who opt into automatic top-ups.

c7f818857794f59f69a714a1c2c0afaa3b28d4f7.text: You can now ask the assistant to use OpenAI's newer gpt-4.1 model when you run it, and you can pick that model from the command line instead of relying on the default automatic choice. The assistant will figure out which model to talk to (OpenAI's gpt-4.1, the usual GPT-4o/O-mini set, or Anthropic's Claude) based on what you specify or the cost mode, and it tracks the price of using gpt-4.1 just like the other models. If you look, you'd see a new option named --model you can pass in, and when gpt-4.1 is selected it quietly skips a reasoning hint that doesn't help that particular model.

8807e7c761039f32d9662636b84e3cd83336fa36.text: The public-facing landing page at the website's main entry point has been visually and structurally rebuilt. Visitors will see new sections for showcasing products, demos, and comparisons, along with refreshed page layout, spacing, and visual styling. The page is now built from reusable building blocks that make future updates easier to manage, and several placeholder or competitor images have been added or swapped out, such as badges for Claude Code, Cline, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

e9e6bfa2552ed87cced63694ac7f044c0ff7ee82.text: A developer added a hidden debugging switch that, when turned on, writes out a snapshot of the assistant's current prompt and instructions to a file on disk so the team can inspect what the assistant was told in a given moment. The snapshot is gated behind a flag set to off by default, so nothing changes for you today, but when enabled it saves the system prompt and recent messages into a local folder named system-prompts for later review. The same change also makes the assistant's context and user instructions only appear when an actual prompt is present, which is a behind-the-scenes safety tweak that does not affect how you see responses right now.

ec645def0e60d84b36ae620b6159b65ab5840651.text: When the assistant tries a fast rewrite using one service and the result looks incomplete, it now retries with a different service that can produce longer answers (up to 16,000 characters instead of 8,000). This means you will see fewer half-finished rewrites when asking for long file changes. A small helper was also added behind the scenes to reliably extract the rewritten code from the response. This is live today.

fde2dbec23446274503a18292ca9b8e43f4d0afa.text: The assistant can now connect to Google's Gemini AI models, not just Anthropic and OpenAI. Your personal API keys for these services are now stored encrypted and protected, so the system keeps them safer than before. If you provide a Gemini key, the assistant uses your key first, then falls back to others if needed. This is live today for anyone supplying their own API key.

e8b6afa4c44e491938b76bfcdd87c865aeabfd12.text: The assistant no longer carries a running list of previously read files into every new question it considers; instead, it relies solely on the conversation history to decide whether more files are needed, and it will not request more than 30 files at once. A reusable snippet of instructions has been replaced by a single, explicitly marked copy that the system can reuse, making the assistant faster and cheaper to query. This is live today for anyone using the backend service.

2d86909ff04f6c3d79bf105e6115e6ee399e7b9a.text: When you start a new conversation with the assistant, it now automatically reads a broader set of files right away, even if you've only sent one message. Previously, the assistant would hold back from reading many files unless the situation clearly called for it. The change also fixes a formatting issue in how file paths are listed, making the file-reading process smoother. This is already live, so you'll notice the assistant pulling in more context from the start of your chats.

be93e9c7a9ad166a3f966d7670e62899912a0d7c.text: Behind the scenes, the assistant's internal tool-processing system was cleaned up and made more flexible. Previously, the code that simplified file-reading results was tangled up inside the main tool parser, making it hard to reuse for other tools. Now, a single, more general-purpose helper was extracted into its own module, and a new specialized version was added to also clean up and simplify the verbose output from terminal/shell command executions. While you won't directly see a new feature, the assistant's backend is now more organized, easier to maintain, and prepared to consistently tidy up a wider variety of tool outputs it generates, including those from terminal commands. This is a live internal refactor available today.

404c7a37e1937c7e68170eb5ae9823377e24a22e.text: When the assistant shows you the contents of a file, it used to stop right at the end of the text with no space before whatever came next. Now a blank line automatically appears after the file content, so the next message or block of text starts neatly separated instead of running together. If you looked, you'd see a small extra gap where file contents are displayed, making things a little easier to read.

a1241ac65cad91f81e70464f7c18445e72511a07.text: The assistant can now skip a slow step when rewriting code and jump straight to the rewrite, saving time on edits. If you watch the assistant work, you'll notice it stops checking whether a file was already updated before re-editing. This only matters if you're the assistant itself doing the work, so you won't see a new button or setting.

4456de5e52c0de58db25dd6050493865b3c6d245.text: The system that writes code edits now has clearer instructions for keeping the right comments and dropping the unnecessary ones, so edits keep helpful notes from the original file without clutter. The automated helper is also told it must run any new practice checks it writes and make sure they pass before finishing. These are behind-the-scenes tuning steps; regular visitors to the app won't see any changes yet.

ae551e15b0befaf867661627e85e5bb8e2c6650d.text: The app now records detailed internal notes about what it is doing as it runs, saving them to a file on the server rather than just keeping them in memory. These notes are stamped with the context of each operation so you can trace what happened during a specific task, and they are written at a very low level so almost nothing that occurs goes unrecorded. If you looked at the notes file, you would see a running log of the app working through requests with timestamps and labels indicating how important each note is. This is a behind-the-scenes tool for people who maintain the app; it does not change anything you experience directly while using it.

09dcc50f0c0925f20cb6c989762653af1215cae7.text: The system now runs a new background report that tallies how many paid credits active subscribers used over the past week. If you're an administrator running this report, you'll see three numbers printed: the grand total of credits used, a list of each subscriber's individual usage ranked from highest to lowest, and a day-by-day breakdown of consumption. Only people whose subscriptions are currently active are counted, and the report pulls its numbers from the database of completed messages. The report is ready to run today.

0d502c7e7288be983f9f95e1a7200f7d3e7a1c8f.text: After the assistant sends you a message, you'll now see how many of your usage credits that message cost, shown to you right away. This works through your active connection to the service, which pushes the cost information to you immediately after each response. The change also adds a new endpoint for checking your usage and moves authentication handling so that credit tracking works consistently across both real-time connections and regular API requests.

3b70e6d56a4ea8c7675e02b1a9ff78f0f0583529.text: The software now handles a situation where the usual place it looks for code to test against doesn't exist, by falling back to a common alternative location. This affects automated testing systems that verify the software works correctly against real-world bug reports and fixes from open-source projects. If you looked at the test setup configuration, you'd see it tries one git branch first, then automatically retries with a different branch name instead of failing.

0579cdcab13ae9aa373130a9429d3fcf6e6cf9a4.text: When you type what looks like a terminal command, the system now checks whether it's really a command on the remote server side using an AI classifier, instead of guessing locally with simple text matching. This means the assistant no longer needs to ask you twice to confirm that you want to run your own command—it just runs it. You would notice that commands prefixed with ! or /run, as well as plain commands the AI recognizes as terminal instructions, are executed immediately without extra back-and-forth. The client-side lists of command keywords and prefixes have been removed in favor of this centralized, smarter detection.

a3a13cce00f8d4cbe5fcd7b096f420f3a4d0d716.text: The assistant now saves your progress in a separate background worker instead of blocking the main interface during git operations. Previously, when saving checkpoints of your conversation and file state, the entire application would pause until the git commit or restore finished; now those git tasks run on a worker thread, so the interface stays responsive. This only affects the internal checkpointing system used by the agent infrastructure, not something you interact with directly.

4d89fd90e801069dd11296321a667c3c061b1280.text: The system now runs a larger set of practice coding problems from well-known projects like Django, Flask, and scikit-learn to check how well it can solve real bug fixes. These problems come from a standard collection called the Princeton Lite SWE-bench dataset, and each one links a specific project to a known issue that developers had to fix. If you looked at the project's testing setup, you'd see a longer list of these problem IDs and new entries pointing to each project's code repositories. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping to improve the assistant's coding accuracy, and it's already active today.

8585e19830ddf9f824141cb980e20d73a1f52a12.text: The project's automated testing system now actually runs the code's tests instead of just checking if it compiles. Previously, when developers submitted changes, the system only verified the code was valid but never executed the actual tests; now it runs the test suites for the main components to catch bugs before they reach production. The behind-the-scenes file organization was also tidied up, with AI model integrations moved into a dedicated folder, though this has no visible impact on how the software behaves for users.

f0e8228f1223b9bd2fe7743bd6403bb76ab3389a.text: When you ask the assistant to edit a large file, it now uses a more powerful model that produces search-and-replace edits more reliably. Previously, edits on big files could fail to parse and produce broken results; now those edits apply correctly. The change also records an extra detail (the assistant's full reply) in internal logs when this large-file path is used, so engineers can debug failures more easily. This is live today for large-file edits, and you would notice fewer failed or partial edits on big files.

a9f9898592d18ccc113e4156257eff05c4e01d28.text: Long conversations can now be trimmed automatically before reaching the assistant. When you have a back-and-forth that exceeds the maximum conversation size, the system now removes the oldest parts of the chat while always keeping your most recent message, so you lose the distant history but preserve the current thread. This keeps single chats from being cut off mid-sentence when they run too long, and it applies specifically after the conversation hits that size cap.

bda7d09c830d4d1ea86649fdafff1fc84d4ff379.text: If you were using Claude Sonnet to write or work on a large task, the system now limits how long its replies can get, freeing up space so it can remember more of your conversation at once. The assistant can still read the full context of your request, but it will keep its responses shorter to make room. You would notice this if you asked it to do something that previously produced a very long answer, and you would get a more concise reply instead. Non-Sonnet models were not affected.

11d9e80aab463dc74f7ece14f1c7e90f330c30df.text: The documentation site now shows a side-by-side comparison of Codebuff and Claude Code using a new table format that lets visitors copy feature details to their clipboard with a click. Visitors reading the advanced docs will see this comparison page, while subscribers who hit a payment issue during an upgrade now get a clear message about unpaid invoices with a direct link to pay them, instead of a generic error. These changes are live on the docs and subscription confirmation pages today.

10630e0f5e067bf2525c12ceac195107ca6bdce2.text: When you ask the assistant to think through something, it now prints a short status message that ends with a blank line before it starts working. That's purely a formatting tweak so the output looks a bit cleaner while you wait. The same change also pulls in a separate collection of example projects used behind the scenes to test the system, but that's only relevant to people running the tests.

7560af255e825a03c221890bd46c9d9c271e5142.text: When the system asks an AI to look at files and decide what's relevant, it now uses a single smarter fallback path: it tries one AI service first, and if that fails or misbehaves, it quietly switches to a backup, then another, without interrupting the task. The instructions for how to talk to the Google Vertex AI service were rewritten so they match that service's exact format, preventing the errors that happened when the system sent instructions in the wrong shape. The result is that file-finding and planning steps behind the scenes are more likely to succeed on the first try and recover automatically instead of failing outright, and the Google Flash model now waits a bit longer (doubled tolerance) before giving up on slow replies.

34743caca48b5ea49a0adc6d8d66baa034df4dc1.text: The main landing page of the app was updated with new headline text: 'Upgrade your coding agent' and a subtitle that says it can run in your terminal or IDE. The old gradient-colored title was replaced with a solid blue color. A new benchmark dataset was also added as a submodule to help evaluate AI coding performance. These changes affect anyone visiting the homepage or testing AI coding capabilities.

9124f763c550afc4dcb723c93b33cc6cd4cb1140.text: When you log in, check your login status, or log out using the command-line tool, your computer now talks to the server using standard web requests instead of a constant live connection. This makes those actions more reliable, especially on unstable networks. If you looked at the tool, the login flow wouldn't appear to change, but the behind-the-scenes communication is more robust.

d100b687b82eff62836f87e7f3b2b3bf049539ee.text: The assistant now treats bigger files as normal instead of flagging them, so longer documents you send in will be handled the full way without getting cut off as "too large." When checking size, the system now adds together both the original content and the new edit you made, and the cutoff moved from 10,000 to 11,000 tokens. A new piece of extra code from the manifold project was also pulled into the repository. If you looked at your work on GitHub today, you'd see the file-size rule relaxed and a new submodule folder added.

00b34952856356dd00deaf3449c680432a85ff03.text: The version number for the AI assistant tool was updated from one release to the next. This is a behind-the-scenes change that helps the team keep track of which version is currently available, similar to how a product might increment its version number when packaging a new release. You won't notice any difference in how the tool works or looks. This change is live today as part of the latest release.

bcf9cb8a8fdb47d3878144182788e4c59c5c5a19.text: The assistant's cost tracking was restored so that billing calculations run correctly again when tracking how much each conversation costs. You would notice usage being recorded properly in the backend system, with quota and subscription status now clearly separated so subscribers skip quota limits while still being tracked for billing, and the old verbose billing documentation was trimmed down to core information.

892afc07c227187bb69953d291875bd56e3b3bb4.text: When you ask the AI to use a computer (like clicking buttons or typing), it can now optionally take up to two pictures of your screen to show what happened before and after each step.
