These pictures, which look like regular screen photos, only appear when the AI is actively controlling a browser session and only the highest-tier models like Sonnet can receive them; other models automatically strip out the images so they don't break. If a picture fails to take for any reason, the AI just quietly logs a note and keeps going without stopping, so your task won't crash even if screenshots miss.

b79a553e5af77db115cbd740b9712c11e5519174.text: When the assistant is busy thinking or working behind the scenes, you’ll now see a smooth spinning indicator instead of inconsistent or missing loading messages. The program now uses one shared spinner component across the command-line tool and web demo, so loading states appear reliably whether you’re in the terminal or trying the interactive demo online. You won’t see random pauses or flickering messages anymore—just a clean spinning icon that disappears once the work is done.

1f91f2ea178b06aa306692ce6a76f859b8e945c7.text: When you ask for help finding files to work on, the system now uses a different, more cost-effective AI model (Gemini Flash) for the initial file selection step. This is a behind-the-scenes change to make file discovery faster and cheaper, and it affects all requests that involve finding relevant project files. You won't notice a direct difference in behavior, but the system now skips the older model for this specific step and uses simpler logic for deciding how many files to look at based on your pricing tier.

864595917326240c53d73457c3fbcf724748c311.text: The tool that lets you browse and inspect web pages no longer downloads its own hidden copy of Chrome — instead, it uses the Chrome you already have installed on your computer. What you'll notice is that the tool can now only look at pages: it can load a page, scroll around, take screenshots, or type text into fields, but it cannot click buttons, submit forms, or otherwise interact with page elements as if you'd clicked them. If the tool tries an interactive action, it will refuse and report the limitation rather than proceeding. The tool also quietly retries a few more types of connection hiccups (like a frame getting detached mid-action) before giving up, which makes it more resilient when pages update themselves while you're watching.

2d126431420f2215e48033847ab6b90fbb58e8a8.text: The assistant can now tap into Google's Gemini models running on Google Cloud as a backup option, so when it needs to pick or read your files it has another route available if the primary one fails. Behind the scenes, your project must supply a Google Cloud project ID for this to work, and the system translates its usual message format into the structure Google's servers expect, including how images are packaged. If you looked, you'd see newer log entries referencing Vertex AI alongside the existing model calls, and the internal notes now list how each provider wants its images and messages shaped.

a1b4ad89172ca55f1348017a4d8d39dd3b5cda4a.text: When the assistant counts how many tokens are in your long messages, it now remembers recent answers instead of recomputing them every time. Each time you send a message longer than 100 characters, the system checks if it has already calculated the token count for that exact text, and if so returns the stored result immediately. It keeps this memory limited to about 10,000 recent messages, automatically forgetting the oldest ones to make room. The whole thing is live today and you would notice it as slightly faster and more consistent response times when working with repeated or similar chunks of text.

7951ebc176382f24ef2511c6ace5aa7d79107e79.text: A new internal tool now quietly tallies how often people make 24-hour edits to files in the system, giving the team a way to measure that activity without touching the product itself. If you opened the company's internal scripts folder, you'd see a small TypeScript program that searches the last day's records for edit-file actions and reports total edits, how many messages included edits, and the average edits per message. The script is live and functional for internal teams who need the metric, but regular users won't see or interact with it.

36b930f637bf4d39a76afa4168b6599bd3d3572f.text: A new troubleshooting guide has been added to the help section, showing users where their chat history is stored on their computer and offering solutions for common connection errors. The FAQ page was also updated to make the data storage explanation easier to understand.

7deebad01fa66f3133bcfb51bb0b8858de07d74a.text: The assistant's code-editing system has switched to a faster, newer method for applying your edits, so file changes should go through more quickly instead of the slower, older process it used before. This only takes effect once your account is set up with the new service, and you wouldn't notice anything different on your screen unless an edit fails, in which case it would let you know rather than quietly making a mistake. If you look under the hood, you'd see this commit already requires the new setup to be configured before it can run at all.

bb02aa5925d19c1d2dd7ddf2b8956ffa5a54e687.text: The assistant can now control a web browser to click around websites and take pictures of what it sees, which helps debug tricky problems. When it does, the system automatically shrinks the picture files so they work with every AI model you can talk to, and each model gets the picture in the exact format it understands. You'd notice this today as the assistant handling tasks that used to require you to describe what's on your screen.

c5e75252efbb9d315d2d643f8129097d798bdcfe.text: The project deleted three old note files that contained outdated plans and scratch work from previous features no longer in use. These files lived at the top level of the project and held written-down reminders about how certain settings should work and what still needed building, but they had not been updated and no longer matched the current system. If you happened to browse the project root, you would notice these three text files are gone, but nothing else around them changed and nothing stopped working as a result.

516276fff8cc25ae3416775e22882d6188d62508.text: Imagine the team kept a long list of all your files to help the assistant understand your project, but that list was getting too heavy to fit. They moved just the part that trims the list down when it gets too long into its own tidy file, while everything still works exactly the same way behind the scenes. This is purely housekeeping: nothing about what you see or experience changed, and the developers also fixed a small numbering typo in their internal guide as part of the same cleanup.

3be38cadbf028f05ba3e84a6299acc75f85a1636.text: If you opened Codebuff's web instructions document today, you'd find it's been heavily condensed — what used to be a long guide packed with detailed steps about colors, screen effects, and technical layout rules has been rewritten into a short, bare-bones reference. This was purely a behind-the-scenes cleanup of internal documentation, so nothing on the actual website or app works differently now, but anyone who previously relied on those detailed setup notes will find the file much shorter and less instructive.

6a47827d9d8c4751aefe4c42e306352b10b62412.text: The assistant now picks the most useful parts of your project files faster by keeping only the top-ranked sections and dropping the rest, instead of sorting through an entire list every time. This happens behind the scenes during prompt assembly and you would not see a visual change, but the assistant should be able to prepare its response a bit quicker when working with large codebases. The improvement is live today.

84b162580ec88b3547c69a8d9a12db719b78c5a0.text: A new internal tool was added that lets the team run a script to see how often each AI model is being used, how many tokens it's consuming, and how much it's costing. There's no visible or user-facing impact from this addition; it's purely backend tooling for analysts to review model usage statistics. This change is live as of February 1, 2025, but only affects internal operations, not customer experience.

34f77ef4ed2a509623586b69f494640e8ddef825.text: The team added a new reporting tool that counts how many unique people use the assistant each day, looking at daily activity logs. It works by checking who sent messages over the past week and tallying them up by date. This is an internal tool only, so you won't see it anywhere. The script is ready to use now, giving the team a quick way to track daily usage without leaving their development environment.

480d5741a0687e926e8a97b5ccee533b6dad3d0d.text: If you press Ctrl+C while a command is running in the terminal, it will now actually stop that command instead of just stopping the assistant. The time window to press Ctrl+C twice to fully exit has been extended from 3 to 5 seconds. This makes interrupting long-running terminal operations more reliable.

50c6ad5fbee31d741b783327a0547e32812f951a.text: The team cleaned up how the command-line tool starts up and listens for your typing, moving chunks of setup code into organized sections so it's easier to maintain. This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping with no visible change to how the tool feels or behaves. It is live today for anyone using the command-line version of the app.

1e76e4dac70f2d76f74309a5050cdfeee74db946.text: The team added a tool that pulls a spreadsheet of every customer's email, name, sign-up date, and whether they have an active subscription, saving it to a file with today's date in the name. You'd notice this only if you're an admin who runs system reporting: instead of manually querying the database, you'd now run this tool and get a ready-made spreadsheet. The data itself doesn't become visible anywhere new to ordinary users — it's just a new way for the team to export what's already stored.

61893b46b9498b063a99cd33325ef541e74eec83.text: A new internal tool was added that scans Stripe billing data to find customers who went over their plan's included usage and calculate how much extra revenue that overage generated. It only looks at active subscribers with at least two paid invoices, identifies tiered pricing items on the most recent invoice, and compares usage against the first pricing tier to compute overage amounts. The script then groups these overages by plan and prints per-plan summaries including total overage revenue, average overage per customer, and usage distribution buckets ($0-$50, $50-$100, $100+). This is behind-the-scenes housekeeping for internal analysis, not a change to what subscribers experience when billing.

05e0047e93e5b1604d9473f8fe69e71bb3babb2f.text: A new help page was added that shows example questions you can ask the assistant, like writing a commit message, explaining how authentication works, or generating a script to calculate monthly churn. It also includes tips for getting better results, such as being specific about which files you're working with and using knowledge files to teach the assistant about your project's patterns. You would see this as a new section of guidance documents alongside existing tips.

c3285d6f774d056d14008c9b204f0f9fe321e922.text: When you run the program without pointing it at an existing project folder, it used to crash while setting up where to store your chat history. Now it notices there's no project folder and falls back to storing that history in the current directory instead. The net effect: you can run the --create command to scaffold a new project from a template even when you're standing outside any existing project, and the program won't blow up just because it can't find a root folder.

842a3c9fe971c84b9a74440c96a10f741ff14816.text: Code examples in the documentation now automatically get styled consistently instead of requiring special formatting each time. When someone writes a code block in the docs, the site will now wrap it in a nice preview box that shows the code with proper styling and includes a one-click copy button. This makes all code examples across the documentation look uniform and easier to use, so you can copy commands or code snippets directly without worrying about formatting differences between pages.

f68b71753130d7822e19cfc2c1b30632ffcc8a34.text: When you change your subscription plan, the page you see after the change now shows your updated plan details and limits instead of a simple generic confirmation message. This affects anyone who modifies their payment plan through the web app. If you looked at the new page, you'd notice it displays your current plan type and what your new limits are, while still confirming the change was successful.

7736bf8c71d2c5a5423312f7ca7527e8c58a083f.text: The documentation sidebar on the website has been reorganized into three labeled sections — Intro, Advanced, and Project Showcase — making it easier to find articles for your skill level. Articles about how the assistant processes requests, works with large codebases, and uses AI models have moved from general help and tips into a dedicated Advanced section. The FAQ now includes questions about what tasks the assistant can perform and its data handling practices for users evaluating trust.

039bf9ca922ea15e5f3b37416477787374bf7c31.text: From now on, every time someone sends new code to the main project, a check automatically runs to make sure everything still works together before the code is accepted. If you are a developer working on this project, you will get faster feedback about whether your changes break anything, and you won't have to wait as long to know if everything is okay. If you looked at the project's settings, you would see a new automated process that tests the code every time it changes.

541a515f763b1e86d86d008093c8f3c36a7401e2.text: The team moved a small utility called 'sleep'—which makes the app pause for a moment between steps—into a different folder that already handles similar tasks. This doesn't change any visible behavior you'd notice, but it helps keep the code organized so future work is easier to maintain. Nothing you see or do in the app will feel different because of this change.

ab8eb3dee6f2248a3e095e2fcd0e240267d2e358.text: The website now sends analytics events to PostHog through a proxy, so visitors' browsers route tracking data through the site's own domain instead of hitting PostHog's servers directly. Event names were also standardized to a consistent format (like 'subscription.payment_completed' instead of 'clicked "Try For Free" button'), and the team stopped sending irrelevant data like UI theme preferences while adding consent tracking so they can measure how many visitors decline analytics. This is internal housekeeping for the product team's analytics dashboard—no changes that visitors would notice in the site's appearance or behavior.

275ed4dc5f8440c970f6ea2e64b099b22a9164cb.text: The assistant now gathers information about your computer—such as the operating system, processor count, and the command-line program it uses—in a single organized step before doing its work, instead of scattering those lookups throughout the file-handling code. If you were watching the setup process, you would see this behind-the-scenes detail collected cleanly rather than mixed into the larger file-scanning routine. Affected area: the internal file-scanning tool the assistant uses to understand your project before responding.

d02430ff07e656278bf8926cafb01b6e4c831e18.text: The assistant now runs terminal commands through a single dedicated module instead of scattering that logic inside the general tool-handling code, so long command output that could overwhelm the view gets cleanly cut off with a clear marker telling you it was shortened. If you watched the system work today, you'd see terminal-related behavior behaving the same from the outside, but internally the command-running and shell-setup code lives together in one tidy place, making it easier to keep working correctly. This is behind-the-scenes cleanup that doesn't change what you can do, just how reliably and clearly the assistant handles terminal tasks.

473544be8885257c683c7ec3ff33551956ac9a17.text: A new internal tool now calculates how much the company makes on average from each paying customer each month. The tool pulls every payment received through Stripe during the past 30 days, converts that amount from cents to dollars, totals it up, divides by the number of customers, and then prints out not just the average but how many customers fall into different spending ranges. Since this is an internal-only script that runs manually, you won’t notice any change when using the product. If you’re an employee with access to the system, you’d see this new script in the scripts folder that can be run to instantly report the latest customer spending numbers.

6573107d01347935aadf697c09bca758bdb5e9ce.text: Visitors to the landing page can now play with a simulated coding terminal right in their browser—typing example commands and seeing responses—backed by an AI assistant model running live through a new web endpoint. While there, the site asks for permission before tracking how people move around with PostHog analytics, and only starts collecting that data after you agree, respecting privacy settings like Do Not Track. If someone looked closely, they'd see a new consent banner and notice the terminal demo has built-in limits to prevent abuse, like a cap on how often one IP address can send requests.

aeb348fdcaeca28f3de97d59c3083b2144f69a25.text: If you look at the tips section of the website, you'll now see a new page called 'Knowledge Files' that explains how to create and organize plain-text files (named knowledge.md) to store important project context like coding standards, architecture decisions, and best practices. The existing guidance about where the assistant works best has also been updated to clearly mention these knowledge files, removing some redundant tips. This helps you understand and use this feature effectively.

9432f8961c0bcaa8d7a21768f833e02d4c7fadac.text: When you open a terminal inside the app on a Windows computer, it now picks the right command program based on what you're already using. If you're in PowerShell, it opens PowerShell; if you're in the regular Windows command prompt, it opens that instead. This fixes cases where the terminal would previously force PowerShell even when you weren't using it. This change is live as of January 7, 2025.

9330c43a06996ca4d64ff92f38d1b661facd6df4.text: When the software opens a terminal window on a Windows computer, it now always uses PowerShell instead of trying to figure out which shell program you were already using. It no longer runs extra checks to detect whether you were in PowerShell or the older Command Prompt, and it has stopped defaulting to Command Prompt when it couldn't tell. The effect for you is that any automated tool that opens a terminal on Windows will start PowerShell, regardless of what shell you had open before; on Mac and Linux the behavior stays the same.

3abfb85ab2fa33ecb2e02d339132beb0b4f78461.text: The assistant's terminal command system now uses a real, always-on shell instead of launching a fresh process for each command. This means command output appears exactly as it would in a normal terminal, with errors mixed naturally into the same stream as regular output. The system also gained a test framework and helper functions to verify the terminal behaves correctly, plus handling for stopping commands that take too long.

ae3804a62d8269be646f6b94cd9436b94a56492b.text: The tool that runs shell commands in the assistant's coding workflow has switched how it captures command output. Instead of merging the normal output and the error output into one combined stream, it now returns them as two separate streams, so you can tell which messages were errors versus regular output. This also means the special terminal emulation software has been removed entirely, and the older, simpler method for launching commands is back in use. A couple of leftover pieces that only existed to support that older setup were cleaned up or stopped being tracked, but the way commands are run and their results shown is otherwise unchanged.

0d8894ca77aef154b2d414afb75c21846988c335.text: You can now upgrade your own plan directly through the service between the existing Pro and Moar Pro tiers without contacting support. The pricing page now lists each tier separately, and during the upgrade flow you will see a confirmation screen showing your new price, the prorated charge for the rest of the billing cycle, and the upcoming recurring amount before you finalize the change. The single old subscription price setting has been replaced with separate price entries in the environment for each tier’s base and overage usage, so both the fixed part of your plan and any pay-per-use charge update together when you switch. This upgrade capability is live today for Pro and Moar Pro subscribers using the Stripe-powered subscription change endpoint.

017f18a6991ec32e11a7e393b70e282c9bd49f21.text: When you run a command-line tool on Windows, it now automatically uses the same shell program you're already working in instead of always forcing PowerShell. If you're in Command Prompt, it opens Command Prompt; if you're in PowerShell, it uses PowerShell. The tool now checks what shell is currently running before starting a new terminal session.

502c8a171f713aaf91af8ed3ead28e0668af5971.text: The website's homepage and pricing page got a visual refresh, so the main landing message and plan-selection layout will look tidier when you visit. Case-study stories were lightly revised, and the moving text ticker at the bottom of the home page now scrolls a bit faster. If you browse the site, you'll simply see a cleaner layout and snappier marquee motion, but the tools you use stay the same.

4a1c1090ec8373b0f2e1242fab2d79bf473ee973.text: The assistant no longer creates knowledge files during planning, and now uses your cost preference to decide which model to use. You would notice that the assistant skips a file-creation step and instead asks the model based on your budget choice. This is live today.

6290ea41cfa2cd1c46381d5fe38cd3182e9405f2.text: You can now watch the intro video on the home page even if your browser prefers the webm format over mp4, since the site will automatically pick whichever version works best for your device. Behind the scenes, the video element now includes a remote-playback lock and preloads the clip ahead of time, so it starts up faster and won't accidentally cast to a nearby TV or streaming stick without your permission. The new video file and updated page are live today, so the next time you load the home page you'll get a smoother, more compatible playback experience without changing any settings.

0676fd902eaef8c6d6bcc3f00447aa92c784b079.text: When the assistant runs commands in your terminal (like running a script or checking files), it used to run them in a way that mixed up the output and error messages separately. Now it uses a real terminal emulator inside, which keeps all the output together, preserves colors and formatting, and behaves more like when you type commands yourself. If you watch the assistant work in a command line, you'll see colors and formatting that were missing before, and commands won't get stuck as often because it can restart the terminal cleanly if something hangs. This is already in effect today for anyone using the assistant through the command-line version.

6a7f6623edd8adaa109fc0a08f77ad85b5d3f01d.text: When you open the site today, you'll see a short headline that says 'Code faster with AI' instead of the old multi-section layout, along with an autoplaying, silent video demonstration right on the page. Previously, you had to click a button to open a demo in a pop-up window and read a terminal install snippet; now that demo plays directly inline as a video. The site's description text that search engines and link previews pick up has been updated to match the new headline. The change is live and visible to anyone visiting the home page.

a698cd8441363e0d429b1e191b7295ce9880620c.text: You can now check how much steady monthly income your paying subscribers are bringing in by running a simple command. The new tool asks Stripe for every active subscription, skips anyone whose subscription is set to end at the next billing cycle, and adds up just the base subscription price. It then shows both the monthly total and a year-long estimate. This is available today and documented in the billing guide. What you'd notice if you looked: the system already excluded usage-based charges and canceled subscriptions, and now also skips any subscription scheduled to cancel at period end, making the revenue figure reflect only ongoing, committed subscriptions.

65cfd5a0fcd047942bd548117e6700b37a1f0581.text: If you use the Lite mode (a cheaper, faster option), your requests are now handled by DeepSeek Chat instead of the previous model. When you type in Lite mode, responses will come from this new model, which costs less per message. The system now tracks the cost of these responses at the new rates, so billing reflects the cheaper pricing.

beb0a7f320489f054fabc167238bb0bce726e643.text: A new story about a developer named Oliver using the coding assistant has been added to the internal documentation. If you browse the case studies section, you will see this new page describing how Oliver used the tool to build a grant application platform, alongside existing stories. This content is only visible inside the company and is not published for the public.

79d15dd36fb8d58a489777bc568e4330ec072627.text: The assistant can now reach the o1 model through a single external routing service instead of talking to OpenAI directly, which means responses still come from o1 but travel over a different connection. OpenRouter now handles o1 requests, so the team added a new key it checks for at startup and updated the planning step that prepares answers. You would only notice this if you were already using the o1 preview feature, because the switch happened quietly behind the scenes and the assistant still produces the same kind of answer.

c95d630de7b6227d3f518d884f37df8b8ff987dd.text: The help article that answered 'How does Codebuff actually work?' and 'What models do you use?' has been moved out of the FAQ section and into the dedicated documentation pages, so visitors now land on cleaner, standalone articles instead of a single crowded FAQ list. Behind the scenes, a new link-handling piece was added so links inside these docs behave correctly whether they point to another page on the site or to an external address. The content you read is the same, just reorganized and given its own space.

d591118f115c70fea467813f8f7b134c374153b8.text: The documentation sidebar on the company website now includes a News section that automatically displays the latest articles from https://news.codebuff.com/feed. Sponsee profile pages (accessed via URLs like /some-sponsee) now render consistently regardless of whether the sponsee name in the URL is typed in upper or lower case. The backend assistant flow now logs errors and defaults to non-unbounded iteration when checks fail, improving reliability. Additionally, the troubleshooting guide has been removed, and the codebuff dependency has been updated to version 1.0.119.

ca0c95cf0318ef95b381c1d8b11ae04d7628e905.text: You can now choose how much you pay for each task you ask the assistant to handle, and the assistant will pick a different level of effort based on your choice. When you pick a lower-cost option, the assistant does a simpler, faster analysis; when you pick a higher-cost option, it does a deeper, more thorough analysis and looks at more files. This only affects tasks that involve the assistant actively working on your project files, not the basic replies, and it's controlled by a new setting you can send alongside your request.

8151ce2028b89f39a1159fe0f49102ceb2c92046.text: When you ask the assistant to figure out a big, tricky code task, it can now use a smarter, more careful planning model to lay out a detailed step-by-step solution and stream the whole plan back to you piece by piece. The assistant also now correctly charges you for how expensive that new model is per word of input and output. Behind the scenes, when you ask for progress on a long-running task, the assistant now requires you to explicitly say how you want to be billed before it builds its next message.

b2172514822c8405c13432c4393f6620ff737fe8.text: When you ran the tool, it used to automatically save your code changes to Git with a single on/off flag. Now you choose to stage changes yourself using a new --git stage option, so the tool prepares your files for you to review and commit instead of committing them right away. If you looked, you'd see the old auto-commit step is gone and replaced by a step that runs 'git add' on the specific files that changed, plus clearer wording when the system is busy. This is live today for anyone running the tool from the command line.

78eb505f1c5078acce40199d97be44e615b6d675.text: You can now choose how much money you want to spend versus how good the answer is by picking cheap, normal, or expensive. A cheaper mode uses a faster, cheaper AI model and only looks at fewer files, while the expensive option uses a more powerful model and considers more files, giving better quality results at a higher cost. This setting works whether you're asking the assistant to do a task or to figure out which files are relevant, and it's available now when you interact with the tool.

369b8b051db0507ebe41a6534a560ceccfaa8c66.text: The troubleshooting guide page has been removed from the website, so visitors looking for step-by-step help with common problems like connection issues or permission errors will no longer find that dedicated page. The software now includes a new tool called Codebuff as part of its core setup, which was added alongside some behind-the-scenes reordering of development packages. If you browsed the site today, you'd notice the missing help page and the updated package, but the overall experience remains unchanged for most users.

3f43ab01953a8cbdde6b426d491904ef631e4fb1.text: You can now see the latest CodeBuff news articles directly in the documentation sidebar and site footer. When you open the docs, a new 'News' section appears under the sidebar with links that take you to the full articles on Substack. The site also pulls in the RSS feed through a background connection so the list stays updated automatically, without anyone having to paste in new links by hand.

c16ab111a0ff3d9731c3811d694badb5d4a9ee0c.text: Each message sent to a request now records how long it took to get an answer back. When you look at a past message in the system, the time it spent waiting for a response is shown alongside other details like cost. This only affects messages processed after the latest update.

39e050a949b84a3ea36138b1395939eadd927ad7.text: The tool the assistant uses to count words in your messages was quietly updated, and the project's package list was rebuilt using a different tool. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance that doesn't change anything you see or feel when chatting. If you're a developer on the backend team, you'll need to reinstall dependencies with the new package manager before the changes take effect.

f670fdb7932f87bef16edeb24cf73db2b5d6077d.text: If you pay for the higher-tier plans, your monthly bill is getting cut in half: Pro drops from $99 to $49, and Pro Plus drops from $500 to $249. Your access to features stays the same, but the number of credits you get is also being roughly halved at the same time, so the cost per unit of service stays consistent. The company is also rolling out a behind-the-scenes switch for existing subscribers to move them to the new prices without losing track of how much they’ve already used this month, so invoices stay accurate. Nothing about this was live before now—the new prices show up on the public pricing page.

fbdf1f044cfb39225553aa6fb9ef6979dd190732.text: You can now find a full documentation center on the website, where articles are written in an extended Markdown format and organized by category in the sidebar. Behind the scenes, the database layer was rolled back to an earlier version of its ORM tool and the project switched to using Bun for all package management tasks. The sidebar on the docs pages can be opened, closed, and pinned with a keyboard shortcut, and your open or collapsed preference is remembered via a cookie. Because the site now rebuilds documentation from source files at build time, a new generated cache folder appears and is ignored by version control.

440d6914d76a8fac849413795f68ccbba9626f70.text: The assistant can now connect to Google's Gemini model in addition to the ones already supported. If you looked at the settings, you'd see a new option for a Google-based AI alongside the existing choices. A secret key for Google's service was also added to the system's configuration, and usage of the new model is being logged for tracking and billing purposes.

7d1b3f6252a10308fd6aae37a6e9a158297260fd.text: A new customer quote has been added to the company's website, featuring feedback from JJ Fliegelman, the founder of a business that used the product. If you visit the website and check the testimonials section, you'll see this new review highlighted, along with an image that confirms the quote is genuine.

c485b69b4b1315b0b638e015cb7eb291a7e2624d.text: When you finish a Codebuff Pro payment, LinkedIn can now properly record that a sale came from its ad. Previously the tracking was set up on the checkout button itself and relied on passing along an ID through several links; now that ID is carried through the payment flow and the actual LinkedIn notification happens once you land on the payment-success page (the "Payment successful!" screen with the credits image). This only affects visitors who arrived at Codebuff via a LinkedIn ad and then upgraded to Pro — they get counted as a conversion. It is live today for anyone using the web app.

f65adba28db3fa54b0d303b79ce91026b28f437c.text: When someone clicks a referral link from a YouTube creator, the site now recognizes who sent them and shows a personalized welcome message with you's name and any bonus they might get. A new landing page checks the link's address to verify it's from a real partner, saves the tracking info, and then sends the visitor to the main page with special tracking tags. The navigation bar no longer shows the Referrals link unless you're logged in. This works today for visitors coming from YouTube creator referrals.

9137ca0c8cffe43534f1fce215958517349f4c46.text: The system now files messages in two new organizational drawers—one labeled by who sent them and one by where they came from. This is the kind of thing you'd notice as faster loading when looking up usage history tied to a specific person or connection, because the computer no longer has to flip through every message to find the right ones.

ee0663dbef0086abfcdbabc749210904cf8dc92c.text: When someone upgrades and comes from LinkedIn, the system now passes along their LinkedIn tracking ID automatically through Stripe's checkout, so the payment success page can record the conversion without the old manual URL building. The tracking code for LinkedIn is currently switched off (commented out), so while the new handoff is in place it won't actually fire yet. You wouldn't notice anything right now, but the plumbing is ready for when LinkedIn tracking is turned back on.

519f59e3da75e0220722ce9094577d3b11f6afd5.text: When you sign up for a paid plan on the website, the system now consistently records whether you came from LinkedIn's ad tracking, whether you clicked an upgrade button in the pricing page or the account menu in the top-right corner. Before, those two places handled the tracking separately, which meant some LinkedIn referrals could be missed. Now both paths use the same shared logic to log the attribution before sending you to Stripe's secure checkout page.

40a018d94ff478a6678ecebaed3245b9b3d97178.text: Each fingerprint record in the database now stores the moment it was created, automatically set when the record is added. You won't see this date anywhere in the app, because it's behind-the-scenes data that only the system uses for tracking. The column is already live, but nothing in the current app actually reads it yet, so it does nothing until a future feature starts using it.

6f27f4d86abf2ba45057e82294ed8f3b753a7746.text: The assistant used to keep going and automatically decide when to stop based on checking your conversation with it, but that system has been turned off. Now the assistant relies on a simpler approach: it counts messages and stops after a set amount rather than analyzing whether the task is done. If you were using the assistant and noticed it no longer seemed to adapt its behavior based on conversation progress or model checks, that feature is no longer active, and any tools or prompts that depended on it have been removed.

6b20e41107c04b8870bc35225d6371acaeb2289b.text: The coding assistant can now better decide whether it has finished what you asked or is stuck repeating itself, instead of blindly running a fixed number of steps. When you give a broad 'do everything' instruction, it checks your intent first and lets the task run longer when that's genuinely what you wanted. If you look at an ongoing session, you'll see it pause for your input only when it makes sense, rather than stopping on a rigid schedule. The assistant must also install any new tools into your own project folder, not somewhere shared on your computer.

07a24a2fcadc2a4f836f299fb5bdb8b8efd755a9.text: The assistant now watches conversations more intelligently to avoid getting stuck in circles or running forever. Instead of just counting messages, it checks whether the task seems complete or the conversation has gone quiet, then decides to pause or keep working. You, as the person watching the assistant work, would notice it stopping sooner when progress stalls instead of looping endlessly. This makes sessions more efficient and prevents wasted effort, though the core interaction of asking and editing remains unchanged.

35aa8ccddea9fc4b5f340b447a07c4ffd3b2eed3.text: A developer added a new script that lets Twitch chat messages be sent directly into the Codebuff coding tool running inside a terminal window. Every minute, the script checks a special website for the latest chat message and types it into the Codebuff session as if someone were typing it manually. This affects anyone running Codebuff during testing, because their terminal will start receiving chat input from Twitch viewers. The feature is documented internally for testing purposes and is limited to the development environment.

87b543491dd17629e88ab979f6ced010e6b0e050.text: When you land on the homepage through a LinkedIn ad, the site now quietly saves a LinkedIn tracking ID to your browser's local storage so your visit can be connected to future actions. The homepage reads the tracking ID from the URL and stores it, and a new guide documents how this ID follows your upgrade or checkout steps later using LinkedIn's tracking tag. This means LinkedIn can correctly attribute your eventual subscription to the original ad, even if you don't sign up right away.

b5d976e118da6f39dce3ab47189176b981991272.text: When you delete your account or request your data be removed, the application now automatically deletes the stored conversation records tied to you instead of leaving them behind. The payment system also stopped forcing a fixed quantity on checkout so it can switch to usage-based billing, and the pricing page was tweaked so a line break keeps the cancellation link readable. These changes are part of moving to usage-based pricing and are live as of the November 2024 migration.

7e274e30d3106b8379bfe073e95d045d0adf1a88.text: A new customer quote from Stefan Gasser, the founder of a company that used the product, has been added to the website. If you visit the site, you'll now see his testimonial alongside others, featuring his photo and a story about how quickly his team was able to convert their app's design from dark to light mode. This gives visitors another real example of the product in action.

040218df9cf8ad4facc6f386fc53d9a01781eb67.text: From today, when the assistant suggests changes to a file, it now wraps the before-and-after snippets in the familiar git-style merge markers (the same conflict dividers you see in code reviews), replacing the older angle-bracket <search>/<replace> tags. If you ever read one of these change suggestions, you'll now spot the classic <<<<<<< SEARCH... =======... >>>>>>> REPLACE blocks instead of the old XML-looking tags, making the proposed edits easier to scan for anyone used to git. The assistant still does the same job of proposing file edits; only the container format of those edit snippets changed.

07bc5c57d8a158315a50f61e8112658f4751cf58.text: The documentation folder for the Python version of the coding assistant was cleaned up and made clearer. Internal developers looking at this folder will now see straightforward, step-by-step guides for setting up a local Python development environment and for publishing an updated package, plus an explicit note that only the npm version is currently available for installation. The published package information file was updated to match these documentation changes. These changes are live in the internal docs today.

7fecc6d01a9c82b8b07cb0b1994513c9af0b8f17.text: When you close a chat session, you'll now see a number showing how much of your usage came from that specific session, alongside your overall monthly total. The system tracks credits consumed during your current WebSocket connection using a session identifier, and this per-session count is included in the usage data returned when a quota check or exit happens. This lets you see exactly how much you used in the session you just closed, rather than only seeing your running monthly balance.

8be7449b6eb2832f7ff0ac7ff3d70d09cbd76ebc.text: The home page now shows a frequently asked questions section, so visitors can click on a question and see the answer expand right below it without leaving the page. The answers live in a single list that the home page pulls in and displays, which is why the page needed new code to arrange and render each one as a collapsible item. If you scrolled to the bottom of the home page today, you'd see a new 'FAQ' heading followed by questions like 'Do you store my data?' and 'What models do you use?' that open on a click.

9f3905939a7734c5d57e5693ceac0a1e6bbd136a.text: The assistant can no longer look up prediction market questions from the site Manifold Markets. If you asked it to search those markets, that option has been removed. The change is internal and live now.

f087bd5656693d637cf464a906611af5b1e75fc0.text: You can now see a new testimonial on the website from Shardool Patel, a founder, who praised the service by saying it feels like hiring an engineer for $100 a month. A photo of Shardool Patel and a proof image of the testimonial were added alongside the quoted text. This testimonial is live on the website today for anyone browsing the web testimonials page.

7906dec3b6cc6fe8901f20be64d91f53dd7dc7e7.text: The coding assistant formerly called Manicode now has a new name, Codebuff, everywhere it appears in this project's setup files. You won't notice this if you already installed it: the old npm command `manicode` still works today because this commit only updated text inside the Python placeholder project that isn't released yet. If you're helping build or document the Python version, you'll now see the name Codebuff in the installation instructions, the project's internal knowledge notes, and the spot where the program prints its 'coming soon' message.

8b9d6a0c26752b5619ee9f05bfae867010999bdb.text: Your monthly usage limit now resets automatically at the start of each calendar month, even if you haven't used up all your credits yet. Previously, the system only reset your quota after you had exhausted it, causing delays for users who hit their limit at the wrong time. The assistant now checks the date before each use and resets your quota on schedule, without waiting for you to run out of credits first.

f3375a1a8bd642bea10b8a5b44708e10d9fb89fc.text: A new person's story, Omar, now shows up in the list of testimonials on the website. You would see his short quote and photo in the same section that already showed other stories from people like Stevo. The website visitors reading the testimonial page will now notice this extra entry alongside the existing quotes and pictures.

8d4806b72aeef12acede91d4f443273c851313ac.text: A new testimonial from Stephen Grugett, a founder and CEO, is now displayed on the website's testimonial section. The website also updated existing testimonials to use a consistent format for titles, changing 'Founder, CEO' to 'Founder & CEO' for clarity. If you browse the testimonials page, you'll see Stephen's quote about a positive experience alongside updated titles for other founders. This change is live today.

c1afad717e45147f90d5bc436067481baaee7a71.text: Visitors to the web landing page will now see a horizontally scrolling section titled "What Developers Are Saying" featuring rotating testimonial cards with quotes and developer names. The testimonials pause automatically when a visitor hovers their mouse over them, allowing time to read each quote before the scrolling resumes.

f3fcbc871040f310e55a4afa21ce90c78594c3dc.text: When you visit the company's main website page, you'll now see a section called "What Developers Are Saying" featuring a scrolling reel of customer quotes. Each quote appears on a clickable card that takes you to proof of what the customer said, and the cards scroll sideways in looping rows, some moving right and others left. The company added photos of the people quoted and screenshots as evidence, and updated the website's structure to make this scrolling display work.

15e35c14bf1a5b1d7cbc4ee3a7bbbc5d638dd3e0.text: You can now click the demo video thumbnail on the homepage to open the video in a clean pop-up window, instead of having it play embedded in the page. This keeps the rest of the page visible and lets you watch the video in a focused view, with a close button to return to the homepage.

6604b7989b06a7bd740d399288d947e70cd1a9fc.text: Previously, there was a single global cap on how many people any one user could refer. That cap has been replaced with a personal limit stored on each user's account, so each person's allowance can be set individually instead of everyone sharing one number. If you looked, your profile now carries its own referral allowance and the system checks that number rather than a shared constant; the referral page now reports how much room you have left instead of just saying you're blocked.

acdc10a9b34eb900af1f7790a360e03f8b4166ae.text: When you ask follow-up questions that depend on files the assistant already looked at, responses will now come back faster and with less wasted work by the AI, because the system now caches the background instructions more reliably instead of rebuilding them from scratch each time. The assistant now organizes project files by their actual versions, so small edits to a file no longer invalidate the reusable portions of the prompt; this affects every session that loads multiple files before answering. If you watched the system internally, you'd see it reuse cached prompt blocks around stable project context while only swapping in the specific file content that changed; the timeout for gathering files also increased to 200 seconds, so slower file sets have more room to complete.

535fbc2e860e08b374e529e1f128cb9c3480fc0e.text: When you run out of quota, the app now shows different messages depending on whether you're a paying subscriber or not. Subscribers see a warning about potential overage fees, while non-subscribers are blocked from using the service. The system now tracks and displays your subscription status alongside your usage data, so the app can tell the difference between someone who should be blocked and someone who should just be warned. Paying subscribers also now have a lower quota limit of 10 million credits instead of 50 million, and overage charges have been raised to 95 cents per 100 credits.

82b15d5ad5695e1a3a697c4b27d66978ef1d9319.text: Users now get a clear signup date and a quota reset date that lines up with their Stripe billing cycle. Previously, your quota reset date could land on today's date instead of the end of your billing period, which meant your usage limits might not refresh when expected. Now, when someone signs up or upgrades, their reset date is set to match when their Stripe subscription actually renews. The system also records exactly when each account was created. These changes only affect the account and billing records—they don't change your plan prices, usage limits, or the features you see.

a30788b1d677be33608e2c8be3336a4511d02c14.text: The team moved the customer quotes that appear on the homepage into a single, dedicated container used only for storing that kind of text, while the page that displays them now simply reads from it. You would not see the quotes change or move on the site, but if someone opened the storage container they would find a tidy list of the three quotes ready to be shown. A new optional slot for a picture was also added to each quote entry, though the homepage has not been updated to use it yet, so the slot sits empty and invisible for now.

6ab694669541596938b3e537b1e11c0c1baef90f.text: When the system edits a file and a piece of an edit doesn't quite line up with the existing text after a few retries, it now switches to a different AI model to make sure that piece gets applied instead of being skipped. This only affects the internal editing workflow and doesn't change what features are available today.

8e47d113a1f9db946d06668bcf24a5d862996195.text: When the assistant compares two versions of a code file to figure out what changed, it now falls back to ignoring extra spaces and indentation if an exact match fails. This means differences in how lines are spaced or indented no longer cause the comparison to break or miss the actual edits. Internal tools that depend on this comparison process are now more resilient to formatting-only changes.

f257801349ff1a8f88a5e39c15887849d0d04de9.text: The referral system now reports clearer failure reasons and lets visitors check referral links without signing in. When you look up someone's referral code, the site no longer blocks you with a login prompt and instead returns whether you has hit their referral limit. A small on-screen notice now appears above the top menu so important messages stay clickable. The homepage also swapped its spinning globe graphic for a different background and tidied up how some text is laid out.

de1b1be8b4adbf10c2464601af2a658d1558639b.text: The website now shows a playable YouTube video of a demonstration right on the home page, so visitors can watch how the tool works without leaving the site. The small icon that appears in a browser tab has also been swapped to a different picture format, and the logo at the top of every page now uses that same updated icon image. Anyone opening the site in a browser will see the new video and the refreshed logo.

8d675ea7bdec92d5bc572b07f6fc7cc157393dd3.text: When the assistant rewrites a file you're working on, it used to regenerate the entire file from scratch, which meant it had to reproduce every line correctly. Now, it can make targeted edits by finding a specific block of text and replacing just that part with a new version, leaving the surrounding code intact. The assistant also got more reliable at locating your project's configuration files on different computers, so it stops misreading settings in some setups. These improvements apply to all conversations today.

ea33b2602d1ba8b3b3423a203455f67393d23ee6.text: You can now open a dedicated page in the app (called '/usage') to see how many of your monthly credits you've used and how many are left, and the same numbers are shown through the navigation bar as you move around. Behind the scenes, the part of the system that keeps track of credit limits was moved out of the server-only code into shared code that the web app can read directly, so it no longer has to fetch the numbers indirectly through a separate server request. Starting today, when you visit that usage page, the server asks the updated credit tracker for your current month-to-date usage and the date your credit counter resets, and it sends back exactly those four figures: credits used, total credits, remaining credits, and the next reset date. Anonymous visitors do not get this page.

6e292a9504ec4e5d29ec15854e8d1b2f3cb3549f.text: You can now read the full Privacy Policy and Terms of Service directly from the website — they show up as new pages linked in the footer and top menu. The homepage also gained a one-click button to copy the install command, so you no longer have to manually select and copy it yourself. These pages use a styling add-on that makes long legal text readable right in your browser. If you visit the site today, you’ll see the new footer links and the copy button on the main page.

18d586d784dc4c6623376cc3f76ed08df8848b2e.text: If you're signed out of your account, you'll now see a 'Continue with GitHub' button directly on the login page and on the referrals page, instead of those pages just telling you to log in elsewhere. The referrals link in the top menu is now always visible to everyone, even when you're not signed in, so you can navigate to it without being logged in first. Behind the scenes, the team moved the sign-in button code to a dedicated folder and replaced an image-loading library with a simpler standard image tag.

7d5989ef8550811be44d7bed834b6f5347e679b6.text: The assistant now loads your project information in the background instead of making you wait before you can start typing. When you open a project, the assistant can take your questions right away rather than pausing to check its version or scan your files first. This means less waiting time between opening the tool and being able to ask for help. The change is live today for anyone running the latest version.

9b36eea10a2b242a13c6fc88ddef508a0624fcbc.text: Starting today, if you run a local development version of the assistant tool, it will read your login credentials from a file named 'manicode-development/credentials.json' inside your computer's hidden config folder, instead of the shared 'manicode/credentials.json' used by the real live service. This keeps your work-in-progress login info from overwriting or mixing with the credentials that the actual deployed assistant uses when you're not actively developing. The change only affects people running a development copy with the ENVIRONMENT variable set; if you just download and use the regular app, nothing looks different to you.

41b405b65610a0b6602197b616c9e653ffdd6e6b.text: When a user hits their usage limit, the system now sends a clearer 'you've run out of credits' message instead of a generic error, and it includes a personalized referral link to earn more credits. The pricing page has also been improved to explain usage limits and referral rewards, and the support contact email is now configured for billing-related questions. These changes take effect today for all users, improving the experience when limits are reached or help is needed.

5d7f6c6f547418d57c5d5c81f1a61442518d3ee2.text: You now have new tools that clean up code comments and turn raw code patches into training examples for AI. If you looked, you'd see a new folder of scripts that combine datasets, standardize placeholder comments across languages, verify patches stay consistent, and split results into shuffled practice files. The changes are live today in the developer tooling that prepares future AI training data.

23d30e803574b62295d5a2fc559c005f163595ad.text: You can now invite friends using a personal referral link and earn 500 bonus credits for each friend who signs up, up to a maximum of 5 successful referrals. A new section in the app shows your referral links and tracks how many bonuses you've earned. Behind the scenes, the team also switched how the app's web address is stored in configuration (renamed an internal setting) and raised the testing credit limits so developers can experiment without hitting usage caps, which only affects local development environments.

97a524e86e58a1203a38a17e13cf91bf8e10c892.text: The referral program's credit-awarding logic was moved into its own file so it can be reused by both the sign-up page and the referral redemption endpoint, keeping the behavior consistent everywhere the feature appears. While doing that, several pages were fixed so that apostrophes in messages display correctly instead of breaking the site's build, a sign-in button now uses the site's standard image component for faster loading, and an error message about using your own referral code was cleaned up. These changes affect anyone signing up with a referral code and anyone visiting the referral pages, who will now see properly displayed text and consistent credit rewards.

996ccc5a44c36603479e0c9e51952148f7e46493.text: When you interact with the assistant over a WebSocket (the live connection used for real-time chat), every log message it produces now automatically includes three hidden identifiers: your fingerprint ID, auth token, and client request ID. This means that instead of seeing a single disconnected log line per event, you can trace an entire request from start to finish across all internal systems without any code changes. The logging system now uses a context-tracking mechanism behind the scenes that automatically attaches your session information to every log entry made during your interaction, so support engineers can quickly find and understand your specific session's logs without manually searching through unrelated entries.

09b8f1d5bef7c0a6f14c8762231d44747146125e.text: When you run the auto-commit command, the software now asks an AI assistant to write a clear, human-readable summary of your changes instead of using a boring, generic message. The AI looks at what files were modified and generates a short description following standard commit conventions. You would notice this if you use the command, as your git history would suddenly have meaningful descriptions of what actually changed rather than generic placeholder text.

603b1250745ae26f6cdf68e8fb64d1d93e4cb220.text: When the code assistant makes a small edit to just one part of a file, it sometimes leaves out the rest of the file, which used to make the system accidentally delete the missing parts. The system now notices when the assistant did that and automatically marks the missing parts with a '... existing code...' label so they are preserved instead of being removed. This only affects single-edit requests and nothing changes for regular edits, but if you ever see that label in a suggested change, it means the surrounding code was intentionally kept intact.

f0ea9490c29d6691ba8bf669a849f2f7322788c8.text: Starting today, the system that runs in the background now keeps track of how much you're using it, and it applies different limits depending on whether you're signed in, have a free account, or pay for a subscription. If you're just visiting without an account, you can use it up to a point before being asked to sign up or log in; if you have a free account, you get a bit more; and if you're a paying subscriber, you get a much higher allowance. When the system checks your usage, it now also factors in the cost of the specific features you're using, with a small built-in margin added on top, so heavier tasks count for more against your limit. Anonymous visitors who exceed their cap will be prompted to authenticate to keep going.

d213792a89fde8df257d192a0c03dcd4afd7ce83.text: When the assistant looks at your project's recent changes or its file structure, it now keeps those descriptions shorter so they fit within a size limit, and it counts how much text there is more accurately. You will notice that details about your files and recent edits are summarized instead of shown in full when there is a lot of them, and the assistant gets a bigger allowance (80,000 units) to describe your project's file layout. The change is live today.

c409707321172e20165a3a6116c0b53ad8c1beec.text: Starting October 2024, the system now tracks how much you've used the AI assistant and assigns a cost to it based on the model type (Claude or GPT) and the length of your prompt and responses. Your usage is tied to your session, so each conversation you have is recorded for potential future billing. You won't see direct charges today, but the infrastructure to calculate costs—like $3 per million input tokens for Claude Sonnet—is now in place and running behind the scenes. This affects anyone signing in through the CLI tool (npm-app), as the new flow requires your credentials to be polled rather than pushed directly.

1376cfaf7769ce0f595c8ff7d0ea4db561e39a28.text: The software behind the assistant used to print all its operational messages in a messy, informal format using basic console commands. Now, it uses a structured logging system that formats every message consistently, making it easier for the team to search, filter, and understand what the system is doing. If you looked at the system's technical documentation or logs today, you'd notice the messages follow a standard format and can be sorted by importance levels like error, warning, or info. This change affects how the team maintains and monitors the system, improving reliability and debugging.

2f64ead5948cd33b095aaf39edff7eb9de28698e.text: When the system tries to apply a text update to the end of a file, it used to miss changes sitting right at the very bottom or get confused by lines starting with a backslash. Now it properly handles both cases, so the update reaches every line reliably. If you maintain or upgrade a project by pasting an update file (a patch), it now succeeds on files that previously failed at the last line.

16e9952360cc28c2219d8a130db5581b6c2d076d.text: When you log into the command-line tool on a new computer, it now shows a one-time code on a screen that you visit in your web browser to prove it's really you, then the browser opens and you can finish signing in through your normal Google or GitHub flow. That code is generated by the backend, checked against a secret value known only to the system, and tied to your specific device using a fingerprint-like identifier so your session on that machine is linked to your account. If you use the command-line tool to sign in, you'll see a link appear that opens automatically in your web browser before redirecting you through OAuth. This feature is live today for anyone signing in through the CLI, replacing the previous method that was having environment configuration problems.

92334a746484a4e10f1626df1a0b36e664295bb6.text: Signing into the assistant from the command-line tool no longer works: the feature that opened a browser for you to authenticate has been removed entirely. If you relied on logging in through the CLI, that path is now gone; you will need to authenticate another way instead. Behind the scenes, the code that managed one-time login codes and session tracking was deleted, along with the settings and documentation that supported that login flow.

cb6b625beb5195bce2988325c81047a4223bbf27.text: The assistant's instructions for how to find and read files, and how to run shell commands, were rewritten to be clearer and more detailed. A new section on using these tools was also added. These changes help the assistant behave more consistently and effectively when working with files and commands. The update is now live.

af4c1ae2a9c6c51b83636a9a8cdb2c647f2061a6.text: When you ask the assistant a question, a behind-the-scenes helper reads your chat to find the most recent message actually written by you. Previously, that helper could mistake the assistant's own tool feedback for your real question, which made it think you'd gotten fewer replies than you did and might cut off the conversation too soon. Now the helper skips over those internal tool notes, so it reliably stops at your genuine prompt. This only affects how the assistant tracks its own reply count, not anything you can directly see.

950bb55122c3a51a3df5b29e2d21a3e20c051552.text: The code-scanning and code-understanding helpers that the app uses to read your project files have been moved into their own dedicated folder, so they no longer travel bundled inside the main shared toolkit. If you looked at the project layout today, you'd see a new top-level folder holding those helpers, and the shared toolkit's build steps and project wiring now skip over the scanning tools entirely. This is live now, so users running the app get the same scanning behavior, but the engineering team can now maintain the scanning tools independently from the rest of the shared toolkit.

1957662225e21cadeedeb264f448951360602776.text: Manicode now checks for new versions directly through your web browser connection instead of asking a separate server each time you start it. When a newer version is available, it automatically updates itself using whatever package manager you already use (npm, yarn, pnpm, or bun), and it shows a green message telling you the update succeeded. If the version check fails or you're offline, the tool still starts normally without waiting for it.

169a24a087447e04cc889302f8535c7e730a9598.text: The coding assistant no longer uses its old built-in way of calling helper tools during conversations. Instead of automatically running code or searching files through a special tool interface, it now reads and responds to simple text tags you include in your requests (like marking sections with tags the system looks for). If you were using a workflow that depended on automatic tool actions from the assistant, those will stop working; you'd need to include tag-based markers in your prompts instead. This change is live today across the core assistant and file-generation features.

8a1b30b651eb64c1d661a51db93cd339e895f109.text: Starting today, you can sign in to your account using the command-line tool instead of needing a web browser. When you run a login command, the tool generates a one-time link and automatically opens your web browser where you complete the usual sign-in steps; once finished, your command-line tool is authenticated. The backend now issues time-limited, single-use login codes tied to your device, and the session tracking system has been updated to remember your specific device. This applies immediately to anyone using the command-line interface.

0fbcd881c6a38f09658a71033ea07c5f1c2748a6.text: When you ask the assistant to work on something, it now talks to you in smaller, steadier pieces instead of sending whole paragraphs all at once. You’ll see messages like 'Editing file: [filename]' appear as each step happens, so you know what’s being changed right when it happens. The way it gathers and displays replies behind the scenes was also cleaned up, removing an old draft file that was only used for testing. These tweaks are live today and affect anyone using the assistant.

a05cfb6fe95189eae4071effa32404356c159d61.text: The app now supports a light-colored mode in addition to its usual dark look. When you open the site, you'll see a light background with dark text instead of the previous always-dark theme, and a toggle to switch themes has been moved from the bottom corner into the top navigation bar. This is live today for anyone visiting the web app.

9eef70a6a490319f0a7d38ad9d4a9aefdc1c1d86.text: The team moved all the database setup code from the backend and web folders into one shared folder called common/src/db, so both parts of the app now use the same database configuration. If you were looking at the backend's code, you'd notice the database files are gone, and instead there's a new setup that uses Docker and special scripts to automatically start a local database and run migrations. This means developers can now spin up the database with a single command instead of manually setting it up, and the web app's authentication code has been updated to use this shared database setup.

135d30ff7623de37a897108855894a232e7e4dad.text: When the system tries to apply a suggested edit to a file, it reads the edit's surrounding context lines to figure out exactly what should change. A small flaw in how those context lines were gathered could cause it to misread edits that started with deletions, potentially applying the wrong change. The logic was simplified so context is now collected consistently, and new tests were added to confirm edits that reorder imports and delete comments are applied correctly. This is a behind-the-scenes bug fix with no change to features or behavior.

2d267eda1e830442ec31c63f2c1ecafd89bc7669.text: The team removed an old configuration file used only to set up a database migration tool behind the scenes. This file lived in the backend code repository and told the Drizzle Kit tool how to connect to PostgreSQL databases when generating schema changes. Since the tool is no longer used locally and database migration setup has been centralized elsewhere, the unused config file was deleted. This change only affects developers working directly in the backend codebase; regular users will not notice any difference in functionality.

a2e91c18f510cd091d55929f54451a7f9871800f.text: The company's main website homepage got a visual redesign, swapping the old simple welcome screen for a modern animated layout. You would now see a spinning 3D globe with glowing lights marking key locations, alongside floating particle beams that animate in the background, replacing the previous static text description and sign-up form. This change only affects the public website viewed by visitors; the underlying tools and services users interact with remain unchanged. The new design is visible to anyone visiting the website today.

9f62f7976a0b44e340a50ec5458112cb4d199167.text: You, as a developer using the internal patching system, submitted a patch that rearranged the `setupSubscriptions` function inside the `Client` class without any issues, and the system correctly applied that structural change. The new test verifies that `applyPatch` reliably handles patches that move code blocks around, rather than just inserting or deleting content in place. No visible behavior changed for end users today; this is behind-the-scenes work to keep the tool reliable when refactoring internal code.

3cbefde8c7b78bb988f91f34a80100034bf2d3dc.text: When the system applies a set of edits (a patch) to a file, it previously miscalculated where one group of edits ended and the next began, which could cause it to skip over lines that should have been kept or changed. This fix corrects that calculation so patches are applied accurately, and the developers added realistic test data (a sample D3 graph patch and its expected result) to verify it works on complex updates. The fix is live today in the core editing utility, improving reliability for anyone generating or applying structured code changes.

d98196190301f2ed83ec0c225b91cae0f4b83acd.text: The team added a large, fake project folder structure to their testing materials so they can check that their knowledge file generation works correctly with complex, realistic data. This is an internal testing tool that helps developers verify their code handles real-world folder layouts, and it is live today for anyone running the project's tests. If you looked at the code repository, you would see a big new test file with a detailed mock of folders and files, but regular users would not notice any change in the app.

c587aae615c068ba13fe9290e69628519c378849.text: The backend system now checks its own settings more carefully when starting up, throwing a clear error if any required secret (like an API key or database address) is missing or malformed, instead of failing silently later. When the backend is running, an automated monitoring tool can now ping a simple "/healthz" endpoint to confirm the service is ready and alive. The team also removed the old, manual scripts and files used for building and deploying the backend server, suggesting those steps are now handled in a more standardized or automated way.

7615438e2c03a608ae43b0f591a801fcce0c6c06.text: When you apply an edit to a file, the editor now uses several smarter strategies to find the right spot in the file, instead of relying only on the exact line number. This means edits are more likely to apply successfully even if the file has shifted a little or has different spacing. You would notice fewer edits failing when files have minor changes or formatting differences. This is live today.

1a7ece065b2da90198d92d34b291f8249a4ac162.text: When someone proposes a change to the code, the system will now automatically ask Brandon and Jahooma to review it, instead of leaving it up to chance or manual assignment. At the same time, the backend added a tool that helps it make decisions based on different patterns, which fixes a problem where a needed piece was missing and could have caused things to break. If you looked at the project right now, you would see these two behind-the-scenes updates already in place.

c6622fefa7dabd0a797510e1c1fb6654b21cd60b.text: The assistant can now automatically create or update a special notes file whenever you and it make meaningful changes to your project while chatting. After a back-and-forth chat where you didn't ask it to run any specific tool, it uses a separate AI step to review what happened and write down helpful, non-obvious context into a.knowledge.md file in the right folder. This happens in the background as part of the same session, so you'd notice a new notes file appear (or an existing one get an extra tip) right after a chat that involved real code changes.

76dfa7f9bf87f34de548b671ec1be25be897ce64.text: The backend software had some incorrect file references that were pointing to the wrong location. The team corrected these references so the software can properly find and use its utility functions. You wouldn't notice anything different unless you were looking at how the system organizes its files internally.

a9461c25625621ba785fe8d226cef84808e7c1a8.text: The application can now save and look up information about people who sign up, using a proper database system hosted on Google Cloud. When you start the application, it automatically connects to a secure tunnel to that database and begins tracking each person with a unique ID, their email address, and the date they joined. If you look at the project's setup notes, you'll see new instructions for developers on how to connect to this database locally using a Google-provided credential file and a tunneling tool.

c11faad368a762482fa6cd50bb9d1658ab05786f.text: When you run the new starter command on a Mac, the app now opens two separate windows for you: one for the app's engine and one for the visual app. The visual part only launches after the engine confirms it is fully ready, so you won't see connection errors. The setup steps were also rewritten in the guide to match this easier one-command flow, with a note that it only works on macOS for now.

94d47b15dbe328f9fbc8d5a9cc615f38a5387fcc.text: A new guide was added that explains how to start the coding assistant's two-part system on your own computer. It creates a helper file with placeholder slots for three AI provider keys, and the main start command now launches the background engine and the interactive chat window separately instead of only the chat. A single script opens both pieces in their own terminal windows so you can see both the tool's log output and your conversation side by side.

d9881d19056719643cd0b0466eeb4f153f175028.text: When the assistant needs to talk to many services at once, it now limits how many it contacts at the same time to 20, so it doesn't accidentally overload anything. The tasks still get done and you get all the answers back in the right order, just without hammering the server with too many requests at once.

34de88ced7e058b1b2b9c7869a6a649994be1525.text: If you open the project folder now, you'll find a friendly guide at the top level that explains what the assistant does and how to run it, plus a ready-made file you copy and fill in with your artificial intelligence account keys. When you type the new run commands from a terminal, the app launches its front-end and the behind-the-scenes helper at the same time without needing to remember long addresses or file locations. The project is pinned to a single version of its tool manager today, so the setup described in the guide will behave the same on every person's computer, and the added helper package simply lets those run commands stay written in plain English.

ee96fe281beb7224909fb3ab0b3a87cd0cb7c7fd.text: If you use the code visualization tool, it can now map out Ruby, Go, and PHP code in addition to other languages it already supported. At the same time, it stopped supporting Elisp, Elixir, Elm, and OCaml, so if you rely on any of those, they will no longer appear in the diagrams. For C code, the tool now uses a more accurate set of rules to understand the structure, making the maps slightly more precise.

d9857812d3dab70010a4ae80c0f94bf3a971ee32.text: If you write a computer program that prints a greeting, this change swaps the old way of doing that simple print command for a more structured approach using containers and templates across 15 different programming languages. Instead of a single function that just outputs "Hello, World", the example code now defines a named object to hold the greeting settings, which makes the example more representative of real-world coding. This is housekeeping inside the software's internal test examples, so you won't notice anything different if you aren't writing code, but programmers building tools or learning these languages will see a more consistent and realistic pattern.

d802a8ae32441e522f6c35f2d9c292c92a28d5b1.text: The version of the software was bumped from 1.0.57 to 1.0.58, and a new command was added that lets developers start the assistant pointed at a test project built with the Litestar framework. This live today: after updating, anyone running the new start command will see the assistant initialize against Litestar sample files instead of the default project, and both the main package and the backend package now report the same newer version number.

bbf6819d104cc6b0a9d35f4b7b934df6402ef550.text: The assistant's two main software components were each nudged up to their next minor release number, moving from one version to the next. The release also added two new test fixtures, which are sample codebases the assistant uses to practice handling Java and Python projects during automated checks. For you as a user, nothing in the assistant's behavior or features changes; these are quiet housekeeping updates that happen in the background to keep the system organized and ready for testing.

915f42f128f863efc7d80675193e0ed20ffdc966.text: When the code-reading tool looks at files, it used to rebuild its reading engine every single time it opened a file, which slowed things down.
