Now it builds the engine once, saves it, and reuses it for all the files it reads. At the same time, it got better at spotting names in files that are set aside to be shared with other parts of a project—specifically, names written as exported constants and exported variables—so they show up correctly in the generated map of your code. These engine improvements happen automatically behind the scenes when you ask the tool to analyze your codebase.

de7f68d523d5b79acadd2e592f2e95d3b4f6c12d.text: The assistant can now read and understand the structure of source code files written in many programming languages, including TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Go, Java, C#, C++, PHP, and Rust. Previously it could only look at text; now it uses a parsing system to identify specific code elements like function names, class definitions, and type declarations. If you opened a supported code file, you would see the assistant correctly recognize and label its core building blocks instead of treating them as plain text. This applies right now to anyone who asks the assistant to analyze or navigate code in these languages.

2b08698b2f0fce32c9a3570cfb3d8a760ea48ded.text: The assistant's project file browser now respects a project-specific ignore list (a.manicodeignore file) in addition to the standard.gitignore. When looking at a project's files, it skips anything listed in either file, so project authors can hide their own private folders (like __mock-projects__) without changing Git settings. If you check a project that has this file, those extra items simply won't appear in the tree view.

c89d785b3f6f9163b1b55b24d2d198bb8a96a325.text: The team added a new set of helper tools that can study how the project's code changed over its past thousand updates. When a developer runs the tool, it looks at the before-and-after versions of files, asks an AI assistant to explain each change in plain language, and saves the results into a temporary folder to build a training dataset. This only affects developers working on the project's internal scripts, and they would notice it by seeing new folders and instructions appearing in their local development environment after pulling the latest changes.

21d52d137265dd24d44ac81648e97905031c04c8.text: The team moved the assistant's file-editing and project-scanning tools into a shared module so the chat app and the command-line tool can both use the same code without duplicating it. When the assistant applies your code changes, it now writes them based on a project folder you specify explicitly instead of guessing, which makes editing more reliable. Behind the scenes, the test suite that guards this behavior switched from Jest to Bun, which means the checks run a bit faster, but you wouldn't see that directly unless you were running the tests yourself.

fff6d38300ea5fd18de41bda42feca55b47a16c7.text: The assistant now generates code changes through a new AI model instead of the old local logic. If you asked it to edit a file, you'll notice the generated edits now come tagged with line numbers and structured file-change objects rather than raw text patches, and edits take longer to finish because the model is allowed up to 200 seconds to respond. This switch is live today for all interactions that trigger patch generation.

a0572b1406dc1d4d9e8b2fe6b1d90181befe47a0.text: The dataset builder now reads from a list of projects instead of one fixed folder, so it can pull code samples from both Manifold and Litestar in the same run. Each project gets its own labeled output file, and the helper that shuffles the samples now comes from a standard utility library added to the project. If you looked now, you'd see separate dataset files named after each project appearing in the output instead of one generic file.

2190b8d08c3d40aabf14682199e64cdbe8dbe628.text: When the team deploys new backend code, the script now labels each uploaded image with the machine's name and a timestamp instead of always calling it the same default name. This means you only build and reuse images that actually belong to this specific environment, so a test setup can't accidentally grab production code. Behind the scenes, the build process also skips copying debug logs and dependency files, keeping uploads smaller and avoiding stale debug data leaking between versions. The engineers also noted two new bugs they're tracking: the terminal sometimes won't release control after running commands, and reconnection attempts may report success without actually resuming work.

c7ae728112c6ae83fc2f5f49c91203c25092d701.text: The company's own programmers added a complete, realistic copy of the Manifold Markets website's internal code into their testing area. This fake copy includes all the configuration files for their hosting, databases, and code-checking tools, so when they run their automated tests, those tests can practice working with code that looks just like their real, messy production system instead of simple fake examples. Your experience as a user does not change at all because this copy only lives inside their testing system. You can tell this is test-only because everything is tucked away under a 'test mock projects' folder, and the programmers explicitly said it only affects their backend testing infrastructure, not the live website you use.

432ee9ff077425f6d079b8c56f8e22710c413c72.text: The team added a written plan that describes upcoming features for logging in and paying for Manicode: a username/password login for the console, a PostgreSQL database to store accounts, Google and GitHub login buttons, referral links, Stripe payments, and per-user usage limits. The change is a planning document, so nothing new works today and users will not notice anything different. Anyone tracking the project's roadmap can now read the full set of intended authentication and billing steps in one place, rather than scattered across notes. The project's running checklist was also updated to mark a few finished items and add a couple of new behind-the-scenes notes.

2e6270d27fa41c8624131a57ae90f25a9c51c50f.text: When you open the app, it now quietly asks the server what the latest version is, and if your copy is outdated, you'll see a yellow warning telling you to update (with the command to do so). The server compares your installed version against the version baked into its build, so the moment a new release is deployed, older copies of your app start nudging you to upgrade.

a38a3180d7a9e25f1a83f4c3365fddcd90bdd4e6.text: When the assistant works on files behind the scenes, it now holds back the actual file contents so they no longer get streamed out to whoever is watching. Instead of sending the raw text of each file as it works, the assistant only shares the surrounding explanation and uses internal callbacks to handle files separately. If you were observing a live session, you'd see the assistant's commentary continue without the file contents being dumped in the middle of the stream. This behavior is live as of 2024-08-22.

7f031f9931b38b8a8ed67b0739ce455014a82dc9.text: The software's testing system now includes a new practice scenario that mimics how it handles messy, incomplete, or incorrect responses from the AI assistant. This helps the team catch problems before they reach you, but it doesn't change what you experience directly. If you've noticed the assistant occasionally stumbles when processing complex file changes, this update strengthens the behind-the-scenes checks to improve reliability over time.

0fa2bf1bc2ec6a37c2fcd6db54d64bfdeaa4799b.text: You (the developer) now use Bun to run the project instead of Yarn. When you start the backend, build the app, or install dependencies, your commands use the faster Bun tool directly. The documentation and every start script inside the project have been rewritten to call Bun, so commands like `bun add`, `bun install`, and `bun run` replace all the old Yarn ones.

66ed712e83dd5455a0196c11ef8b78ee1c8e04f9.text: If you typed the assistant's command in a terminal right now, it would print a short note saying the Python version isn't ready yet and point you back to the npm install. A new, empty Python package folder named 'manicode' was added to the project, containing only placeholder text, a license, and packaging notes so developers can later build the real Python version that mirrors the npm tool. The change is already in the code repository, but no actual coding help happens yet when you run it.

92b54a227398657bed70dec701400db26f76f0f5.text: The project's notes were mixed together in one place, so the team split them into two: one for big-picture wishes and one for specific tasks that need getting done. This mainly affects the developers working on the project, who now have a cleaner, action-focused list to track and check off problems. If you looked at the notes now, you would see the to-do items like fixing bugs with pasting text and handling file changes organized separately from the brainstorming ideas about new features.

fe97f7321e301d188dc28144a30295ea016a2de6.text: When you start the assistant, it now quietly reads details about your computer's hardware—things like the make and model, processor, and operating system—and turns that into a unique, scrambled code. That code is sent along with your connection so the service can tell your machine apart from others. It only affects people using the internal command-line version of the assistant; regular users won't see anything different, but the startup might take a fraction of a second longer as it quietly gathers those hardware details in the background.

efc5cb41ea406771cacb3a3acdb5cae91fe7f81e.text: When the system talks to the Claude and OpenAI assistants behind the scenes, it now quietly tells them to pace themselves: roughly 2,000 paid calls per user per day, with usage tallied in cents, and any overages throttled back. This rate limit lives in a small shared settings file that only the backend server-side code reads, so everyday users won't notice anything different unless they hit those usage caps. It's live today for any backend requests routed through the updated API connections.

961453dae185cb06f8ea4b20d52122f7d30cbe8b.text: When you ask the assistant to work on your project, it reads through your files to understand the context. This change puts a cap on how much of those files it reads at once, keeping the most important files first until it hits a limit of 100,000 tokens of text. Any file that would push it over that limit gets shortened and marked as truncated, so the system doesn't get overwhelmed by very large files or projects with tons of content. This affects anyone using the assistant to review big codebases, and you'd notice it if you're working on a project where some of your files suddenly show up with a truncation notice instead of full content.

7f1629543df85669e89ad87d7d0d978f06bbe5fb.text: The assistant now starts by looking at the code changes in your message first, instead of summarizing your request at the beginning. This means the order of its reasoning steps has shifted: it still explores options, explains its plan, and records any lessons learned, but the code review step now leads the process. The change is live today and only affects this internal backend system prompt.

be899b33d927028a64cef09a21a1ba9e30cb5252.text: When you run the tool from the command line, its text messages now appear in different colors: blue for file version navigation, green for loaded files, yellow for stopped responses, magenta for the exit message, gray for file change logs, red for errors, and cyan for file lists. You would notice the status messages stand out more instead of all being plain text. This affects only people using the command-line version of the tool, and it is already live today.

c4091bc7c28991d8a7f85c28f5a5998885e26ad1.text: When you ask the assistant to rewrite a file, it now follows a smarter two-step editing process instead of one fixed method. If the original file is very large and the new version is much shorter, the assistant applies the changes directly to the original text (preserving its structure) and then converts Windows-style line breaks back to match the original file's format, reducing formatting errors. This improves reliability for large file rewrites but only affects that specific size condition. The change is already live today as part of the assistant's update.

d4581ed59329811065c9d3431dc6ef61fa4ea739.text: The test that checks whether the assistant's code-suggestions match the expected output was failing only because of a single stray space character in its reference data. The stray space was stripped out so the comparison passes cleanly. This is internal housekeeping for the test suite and does not change any feature you use.

d2809905e36a4015a9511174f278231dd93fccc4.text: The behind-the-scenes instructions that tell an AI assistant how to write code changes were reorganized to be clearer and more step-by-step, making it less likely to guess incorrectly when filling in missing parts of a file. This affects the internal system that generates code edits, and if you looked at the instructions given to the AI, you would see separate sections for discussion, planning which parts need expansion, and then the actual code output, rather than mixing those steps together. No visible feature for end users changes; this is stability maintenance to improve the reliability of automated code generation.

e68c4539c90295fa30bbd970b4c3b662be9bd7e1.text: You don't see anything different when using the tool, but behind the scenes the system that generates file comparison messages had a minor cleanup: a stray blank line was removed from the end of one of its instruction templates. This keeps the generated prompts consistent with how the assistant is expected to format its replies. The change only affects internal backend logic used during diff generation and is live today.

8e31d5f27feb75694e2cb28ae6031dac8c82da56.text: When the system compares your old and new file content to show you what changed, it now converts Windows-style line breaks to the standard format before doing the comparison, so diffs come out consistent regardless of which operating system created the file. This keeps the displayed changes from showing spurious differences caused only by line-ending style. You'd notice cleaner, more accurate change listings when working with files that originated on Windows. The fix is live as of today in the backend prompt processing.

cd5349e25eadd27f76346cd021b6d2160cae5f04.text: Our system that figures out how to edit code files now gets a clearer, more detailed set of instructions when it tries to piece together what the edited file should look like. Instead of just seeing the file changes, it's now shown a couple of examples of how it should format its response and explain what changed, which helps it produce cleaner, more consistent results. This affects how the system processes code edits in the background. You wouldn't see this directly, but if you were reviewing the system's work, the explanations and final file output would be more uniform and complete.

554f7982b3450290329a9a3826bcf8ab5ca1c872.text: The team added clear licensing information so that anyone who downloads the assistant's public toolkit knows exactly what they can and cannot use it for. The downloadable toolkit is now explicitly marked as free-to-use MIT licensed, while the rest of the project (the servers and private parts) is marked as proprietary and confidential. If you looked at the project's main description file, you'd now see a new line stating the proprietary status, and a new guidebook entry explaining that only the toolkit portion is open for public use — everything else requires explicit permission. This change is live today: the licensing facts are now clearly published and in effect, though the proprietary protections themselves existed before this update.

8d613fb0a458e56d1fb49cb6068b27c77b9e11c4.text: The coding assistant no longer needs to manually browse your project's folders to find relevant files before answering your request. Instead, a quick, lightweight scan now happens first to identify and pre-load the most relevant files based on your project structure and conversation history, then passes them directly to the main assistant. You'll notice the assistant starts working with the right files already open, saving the time it previously spent figuring out which directories and files to read.

11ccbdb184aab6cb277ee80ccf773aea3f0cc099.text: When a developer publishes a new version of the software to the package repository, the system now automatically strips out development-only libraries before the package is uploaded, making the downloaded package smaller and faster for end users. Before this change, anyone who installed the software got the full development dependency list bundled in; now they only get what is needed to run it. The build process also injects a production setting directly into the main script, so the software knows to connect to the live service rather than a local test environment when used by regular users.

d37dfa943b0da5dda6fe0f9b33eb8e6f0993ec64.text: The backend service can now be packaged and deployed automatically using containerization tools, making it easier to update and manage. When you deploy, it will bundle the backend code and its shared components together, build them, and push the packaged version to a hosting platform. Additionally, the assistant now checks if a file already has the correct content before rewriting it, avoiding unnecessary changes. These improvements streamline the deployment process and reduce redundant work.

33d729465cbb73556b089f0c5501ec4357605772.text: The AI assistant can now fetch and read content from any web page you point it to, similar to how it already opens files in your project. Instead of only reading local files, you can give it a link to online documentation, APIs, or articles, and it will pull in the text so you can ask questions about it. Behind the scenes, the system was reworked to handle different tools through a shared registry, so adding capabilities like web scraping fits into the same flow as reading files. This is already live today, so if you ask the assistant to look at a URL, it can do it on the spot.

f1744c6fb4c1c5e1c281acd92756d59a40c9453e.text: The assistant can now answer questions about uncertain future events by looking up live prediction markets. When you ask about something like an upcoming election, it searches a site called Manifold for yes-or-no betting markets on that topic and shows you each market's current probability as a forecast. Each result includes the market question, its probability, and a link to the full market. This works today as part of the assistant's internal tool set.

c0839d542c602e23c2260a2e68fb6b4732c9630e.text: When you save a helpful webpage link (like API docs) into your project notes, the assistant now automatically reads that webpage's content and pastes it right into your notes too. So instead of just storing the link, you'll see the actual text from the page appear in your project files, making it easier to reference later without visiting the URL yourself. This works behind the scenes whenever the assistant checks your project files.

0c7c30edebde240f56733da60cdae23a4f9a6ff1.text: The helper tool that runs from your command line now ships with a short guidebook inside its install package, so anyone who grabs it gets instructions on how to use it and how to keep a running notes file alongside their code. At the same time, two small spots inside the tool were taught to point to that guidebook and the ready-to-run version of the tool itself, so future copies of the tool include both the user directions and the working program files. Today, if you installed or downloaded this command-line assistant, you would see its README guide and the finished program files bundled together instead of one or both being left out.

80b9a1ddfa78dd182116dabcfbf1c851628d97c1.text: The project has been reorganized so the part you interact with can now be installed and run as a standalone tool, rather than only working as a piece of a larger code collection. If you looked, you would see a new self-contained folder for the interactive tool with its own setup files, and the supporting pieces it depends on were adjusted to build correctly independently. A stop signal was also added to one of the backend instructions so automated code edits are told explicitly where to end their response. This is live today as part of the current source.

12e25be8a163cb29d77631abc7a6a4ab76ee970f.text: The team added a new test case that checks whether the assistant can correctly identify and handle a file that has been changed in many different ways all at once. This helps make sure the diff-generation feature stays reliable as the code evolves. You wouldn't notice anything directly, but it makes the system more robust behind the scenes.

3383120ca5be7ec0dcab06028a1a41a518b54b68.text: The AI coding helper now has a new internal guidebook that explains how its own project is organized, so it can better understand where things live and how they fit together when it's working. This guidebook lives in a file called knowledge.md and describes the project's layout, the main building blocks that make up the tool, and how it's all put together. If you looked inside the project, you'd see this documentation file has been added; it also mentions that the AI is designed to keep updating these guidebooks as it learns more. This is behind-the-scenes documentation that helps the AI operate more effectively within its own system.

1a0cb9c328cdeba83a093af35e3751910662ac21.text: The assistant can now expand shortened code diffs—where unchanged sections were collapsed into placeholder comments—into complete file versions by consulting a new model, using a sliding-window matching technique to compare old and new content. The documentation now explains that larger window sizes catch more scattered changes but cost more processing time and may blur big structural edits, and teams are advised to test different sizes for their codebase. This improves the accuracy of showing exactly which lines changed during collaborative coding sessions, so reviewers see fewer ambiguous gaps in the diff.

b00d1c37492084dec807ea468716e4c9c55c361f.text: The assistant's response engine has been split into two clearer parts: one that manages the live conversation flow and tool usage, and another that handles turning changes into actual file edits. If you watched it work, you wouldn't notice a difference in behavior, but the system now keeps the main chat logic and the file-editing logic in tidy, separate boxes, which should make it easier to maintain behind the scenes.

fc982c8568ae25d4a81d20d465653d8b72cc2069.text: The backend now uses a new approach to generate code changes: instead of comparing files directly, it asks an AI assistant (GPT-4o) to rewrite a shortened version of your file into full code, then creates a clean, patch-style update that's easy to review and apply. If you're an internal developer or someone reviewing automated code changes, you'll notice the updates now come as precise patches showing exactly what changed, rather than messy full-file comparisons. This makes it easier to see what the system intends to modify and reduces noise in code reviews.

f8e7677a226835196471a95b36e1b5501fa393de.text: The build system now ignores test-only sample files when putting together the backend code, so it no longer trips over placeholder data meant only for testing. This affects the internal build process and won't be visible to you as a user, but it keeps the code-assembly step from stumbling if you were to rebuild the backend locally. The mock-data files themselves still exist and run during tests exactly as before.

4ae0090ae9f7110e93090689876343fb1f83ee1b.text: When the assistant finishes responding to you, it now signals the end with a shorter marker '[END]' instead of the longer '[END_OF_RESPONSE]' you may have noticed before. The instructions telling the assistant how and when to stop were also tightened up, so it is nudged to include that marker and you are more reliably prompted to continue if it forgets. Behind the scenes, the developers deleted the old helper file that connected to the assistant and removed a leftover line that asked for your input twice. This is a small consistency and cleanup change, so you will mainly notice the slightly shorter ending token if you were watching for the old one.

f50c11cd424aa5fa7d072d06cbcb7380dfac2d84.text: When the coding assistant writes instructions for making a code change, its prompts now have to ask for labeled, lettered groups (A, B, etc.) for each separate edit, along with the right indentation details for each part. If the system can't find an exact match for a requested change because of spacing issues, it will retry by adding extra spaces and tabs (up to a point) so the edit can still apply. If a perfect match still can't be found after that, the change falls back to being reported as unmatched rather than silently failing.

a528a49ef6a21a7bd4e5990ebb4fb03a5fcda199.text: You won't see a visible change in how the app works, but behind the scenes the team removed an old collection of shared tools and now each part of the app grabs just the specific helper it needs directly. This makes the code easier to follow and keeps unused bits from sneaking in. While doing this, they also stopped printing a small message in the logs whenever a file was updated or created. The app behaves the same way today; these are internal cleanups to keep the project tidy.

29d41099d146c6cf01e4c86de2f6f7a08e259dc8.text: Your coding assistant now does a better job when you ask it to edit code that already contains comments. It can now reliably preserve those existing comments while making changes, instead of accidentally dropping or breaking them. The team added new example files that specifically test this comment-handling behavior, and they reorganized where example files live so related pieces are easier to find.

e7f52632973782fea2bf03ea76964af888d84850.text: The assistant's code was cleaned up so it's easier to maintain behind the scenes. The parts that handled typing, settings, menus, and connections were moved out of one big file into separate files, and the way chats are tracked was updated to keep better track of the current chat. If you looked at the files, you'd see a cleaner and more organized structure, but your experience using the assistant stays the same. This cleanup is already live.

e7b486a15b295697e22197dd56f26405c827fd92.text: The system now includes a new test that checks whether the assistant correctly updates code when lines shift due to changing indentation (like when code blocks move in or out of functions). The test uses two example files showing a before-and-after version of a script, and it verifies that every change is applied accurately so the final result matches the updated file. Since it is a test, you will not notice any change in how the assistant behaves today, but it helps ensure future code updates handle tricky formatting changes without breaking.

e350c7f460b34059eb4cdd72a9683eb4e6695258.text: The team added a testing system behind the scenes so the assistant can now automatically check that its responses stay consistent over time, mainly benefitting developers building on the platform today. They also moved the assistant's continuation logic into its own folder and simplified how it handles follow-up answers, though most readers won't notice this directly. Additionally, the assistant now strips out meta-comments from code changes it generates, but this only affects developers reviewing the diff output.

be19b40c22d27853ff48643096530f0cfeea490f.text: The team gave the backend a built-in way to automatically check itself for mistakes, similar to how spell-check works for a document. When they make future changes to the assistant's behind-the-scenes logic, it can now catch problems before they reach you. This only affects the staff building and updating the assistant, not your experience right now, since it's purely a tool to help them work more carefully.

2edfac49059f0f236e622e58f9ba59f67f9e5d16.text: The assistant now saves your conversations so they stick around between sessions instead of disappearing when you close the program. Each chat you have gets stored as its own file in a local folder, and you’ll see a new chat ID printed when you start a conversation. Your chat history is now saved in the background automatically.

122ee89d87e5519937008129f0e0add084d67079.text: Today, if you ask the assistant to edit a file, it will no longer accidentally process the same file twice in one request, which could have caused conflicting or duplicated changes. While working, you (or anyone watching the backend logs) might also notice a new plain-text file named debug.log being written in the backend folder, capturing a step-by-step trace of each assistant task for troubleshooting; this file is not tracked by the project's file history tool and is wiped clean each time the server restarts. The debug log is always on for now, so no setting must be toggled to see it.

918a7aa4253a876c3a47f6c56395745454283c0c.text: When the software runs its automated backend tests, it now automatically reads the same configuration settings (like API keys and database paths) that it uses in normal operation, instead of starting up empty. Previously those tests ran without any environment settings loaded, so anything depending on them would fail or behave differently than expected; now they load that configuration at the very start of the test run. If you looked, you'd notice the test runner quietly logs a message about loading environment variables before any tests begin, and backend tests that rely on those settings now work consistently instead of being skipped or erroring out.

6d8a809148fcc144292078d1af3ab89a7d607005.text: The team added a plain-language guide that explains how the assistant's brain works, so anyone joining the project can quickly understand how it thinks, talks, and edits files. If you peek at the project, you'd find a new 113-line guide in the backend folder that spells out each piece and leaves sticky notes (TODOs) for future improvements like login checks and speed limits.

6cd4d481c83bb4d6faae74a0c776ca1556ff0977.text: The assistant now reads a special notes file called knowledge.md that lives in your project folders and can use those notes as extra guidance when helping you. You'd notice this the next time you ask for help in a project that has a knowledge.md file: the assistant is expected to look at it, and if one is missing you may be asked (or the code nags) to add one. The change also makes the assistant stop pretending it will read a file that doesn't actually exist, so it will quit promising to show you file contents that aren't there.

4e57e9c38ddbb65ddb0564ce4b99c1b2c5331296.text: A new reference document was added internally that captures ideas about how the Manicode assistant could gather and use knowledge, written in plain language so the assistant's builders have more context when planning features. It only affects internal planning and product direction, not anything you can touch or see today. If you could open the repository, you'd see a new 151-line notes file alongside code changes that support how assistants read and act on documentation like this one.

e6578a9d7b4b1c9b7b82f7d175ec1782913ce13e.text: When the assistant finishes writing a response, it now uses one single, shared stop signal instead of several copies of the same hardcoded text, so the system stays consistent and easier to maintain. The assistant is also being told to skip trying to open files that aren't part of the project, which prevents it from hitting errors when it looks for something that wasn't provided. For anyone watching, you won't see a dramatic change in behavior right away, but the assistant should get along a bit more smoothly without stumbling over missing files.

4b3edc7eee72aa55a274b36f9281093957978009.text: The helper built into the code editor now calls itself 'Manny' instead of 'assistant' in its conversations and written instructions, so when you talk to it, the program identifies itself by name. When the Manny helper tells you what files it changed, it says 'based on Manny's instruction,' and if it gets confused about which files it has already looked at, it will skip re-reading those same files again to save time. Manny is powered by the AI engine behind Claude, according to the project notes.

2d2e8dd1108a5a2feda2bc02ed593179b79aaf3c.text: When you connect to the assistant through a web browser or app, the server now handles your connection through a cleaner, more organized system that can keep track of who is subscribed to what updates. Previously, all connection handling happened in one dense block inside the main server; it has been split into separate modules so that managing your session, sending you streaming responses, and recovering from dropped connections are each handled in their own well-defined place. You will not see a different interface, but the connection is now more resilient: if your network drops for up to one minute, the client will automatically reconnect and resubscribe without requiring you to restart your request. The system also now records the "system" role in conversation history and encourages

e35b16b9b2fd62ce6f2305a2e603b07be9a26f4e.text: When you run the tool, it no longer talks to the AI helper directly — instead it opens a live text channel to a separate program on your computer that manages the back-and-forth. That helper program connects to the Claude AI and streams replies back piece by piece, so you see words appear gradually rather than waiting for the whole answer at once. The new system also stops looking for specific files to work with, so it can no longer pick or edit a file on its own from this interface. This is live today and only works if that background program is running.

06e4e19ee1b5c95ea7566e30c5ae0a69345bddc8.text: The team pulled the assistant's shared helper functions (like cleaning up data and filtering lists) into a single shared code library that both the main program and the backend server can use. Instead of each part keeping its own copy of these helpers, they now both pull from this one common library, which keeps things consistent and easier to maintain. You would notice the backend server now builds its code into a dedicated output folder and starts up from a cleaner project layout, but the assistant's behavior itself stays the same.

66ba78e74d208e853547e8331136229c4c1ba045.text: The team split a large, all-in-one control file into smaller, dedicated files that each handle a specific job: one manages the connection to the assistant, one builds the instructions it works from, and one reads and writes code files. From a reader's point of view, nothing looks different right away because the program still does the same things, but the project now keeps each kind of work in its own organized space, so adding or adjusting one part (like how file exchanges look) won't accidentally break the others.

4eb9084f29628018a8f1d25677eb365fc6ff82bd.text: Starting today, the assistant inside the coding tool can now look at and read multiple files in your project on its own while it works, instead of relying only on a single pre-loaded description. As the assistant talks through what it is doing, you will see it pull in the real contents of the files it mentions and reason about them live, which should reduce mistakes when it edits your code. Behind the scenes, the system was also reorganized to keep those file-reading steps stable and recoverable if something interrupts the work.

0d9e257b88312ce91939b721a634a9c1ff1851ef.text: The manicode tool, which helps automate parts of software development, has been split into its own separate package instead of living inside a larger shared codebase. If you looked at the project, you would see a new setup file for compiling the code, an updated project list of required libraries, and the main code renamed and reorganized into smaller, self-contained helper files. Several old project-specific files and debug logs were also cleaned up from the shared ignore list, and a few new utility helpers for working with lists and objects were added locally.

bd7d722103b0942a6a51ab1fa30bc4236e2dc4c3.text: The developer-facing instructions that guide how file edits are written changed: instead of marking old and new sections separately, you now paste the whole file and use comments like '... existing code...' to show what stays. Behind the scenes, the system reads those shorthand comments and converts them into precise before-and-after snippets to apply. Files are also processed at the same time instead of one after another, which should make multi-file edits feel quicker. This is live today for people writing edits inside this tooling, but it doesn't change the final result you see.

aa91f013a9f0cb8d35f70d8ce5fa0f7f48f785b1.text: The team added a new assistant tool for developers that can automatically write code based on plain-language requests. When a developer types a description of what they want to build (like a new page showing live market activity), the tool figures out which existing files are relevant and generates the necessary code changes. This is intended for internal use by the development team and is ready to run today.

2a92180a36c023f405081b2ff39b4be06887ea0c.text: The release number for the freebuff command-line tool was bumped from its previous value to a new one, but nothing else changed about how it works. If you are a developer who installs or relies on this tool, you will now see it reported with the new release number when you check for updates or download it, but the actual behavior of the tool itself remains exactly the same as before. This kind of change is purely a behind-the-scenes housekeeping step that helps keep software versions organized and trackable.

cad79f08e6293749c664db735a10c1cce98c40e1.text: You work at a shared computer that doesn't have the company's secret login keys, and you want to confirm your coding tools still work. You can now run a tiny, pre-approved practice test directly with the specific version of Bun the company picked, skipping the automated login step that usually blocks setups without those keys. The test runs a small set of three checks on a country-code list, and it passes as long as that one file is present—no full setup needed.

da165be855e3ab42d7ee67881a23710c0617542c.text: Your subscription dashboard now keeps the most recent cost summary on hand even if the background refresh gets interrupted, so the last calculated numbers and their timestamps stay visible instead of disappearing. You'd notice a new set of status indicators—showing whether the data is fresh or stale and whether a refresh is idle, running, cooling down, failed, or unavailable—alongside the cost figures, saved time, and next scheduled refresh. This small, behind-the-scenes addition sits in the shared core types and is ready for the rest of the system to read, but doesn't change anything you see yet since no surrounding logic has been wired up to use it.

ea08076516aa21e440150902f9290c71b0336b98.text: If you looked at the page that tracks how much paid subscribers are spending each month, you would now see a few extra checkmarks next to that total, most of them just recording that the system is still waiting on a more precise number rather than giving you that number yet. The team that reads those reports gets a clearer view of whether the newest daily total is fresh, missing, or stale, and can tell at a glance when the system has stopped short because it lacks the cost basis needed to turn a Freebucks allowance into a real dollar forecast. Those new labels are in place, but the underlying allowance-constrained estimate they describe still shows unavailable, so today nothing about your bill or the public dashboard changes.

fb17d9888659f8054532d4a90a7b8bb5027043e9.text: Verified Y Combinator companies now have a new promotion ready: after collecting $1,000, they will receive a one-time $1,000 credit. The rules are recorded as fixed limits and thresholds, but nothing in the product uses them yet. Who is eligible today did not change, but the groundwork is in place. Today the constants sit unused, awaiting the logic that will grant the credit.

2f90af6aca5f096834b3755d3076f56cc36c5d9b.text: The freebuff coding assistant's downloadable package quietly moved to a new internal version number. If you reinstalled or updated the tool today, you'd get version 0.0.175 instead of the previous 0.0.174, but nothing about how it behaves will feel different. This is just routine bookkeeping that labels the current build so package managers and installers can tell it apart.

8134f2f8f7a358cb93c871c34e16d99ef6b98e5f.text: No user-facing change happened here. The words you briefly see when hovering over the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash option in the model picker were corrected in the program's test suite, so any future build checks match the new tooltip text rather than the old one. Nothing you use today is different because of this.

4ff23980eed8bb8c8060150d73829847ba390d48.text: When the system runs an automated check that makes the assistant answer a quick question to confirm it is working, the check no longer asks the assistant to add two numbers together. The old question asked the assistant to add 4187 and 2359, which sometimes produced a wrong answer and failed the check, so the check now asks the assistant to reply with only the English word for the number 7 in lowercase. This affects only the behind-the-scenes automated test; it does not change the assistant you use day to day.

2e67ad0b60df355424e672d6a635b6d5ab2cdad8.text: The team wrote down how they check that the main builder app (the tool that creates websites) is still working before it gets rolled out to real users. This matters because that app now deploys automatically, so a broken build would reach users instead of getting caught first. The checklist they documented pins the tool's Node version (so a mismatch doesn't silently break it) and runs a mini end-to-end test that actually loads the assistant SDK and runs one chat turn through a seeded session, with all the outside services faked so only an internal failure stops the deploy. It's live alongside the rest of the testing docs today.

c293aca107f890c0d45d6739e4905bbb80e97aac.text: When you check your usage credits, the system no longer shows a special "peak" price surcharge badge for Flash models, because Flash now uses a flat rate instead. If you were using an older server or app that still expects that peak badge, it will simply leave the field blank rather than breaking. This only affects how the credit details are displayed behind the scenes; your actual usage and billing are unchanged.

217906d84aa2113d8c363debba204695a6e074db.text: When the CLI's freebuff landing screen shows a rate limit warning, users will now see a direct link (https://freebuff.com/freebucks) suggesting they can turn on auto top-up to keep working instead of just being told to wait or pick a cheaper model. This change affects only users who hit rate limits while using the CLI's freebuff landing screen. If you looked at the screen during a rate limit, you'd notice the addition of the auto top-up link alongside the existing message about waiting or choosing a cheaper model.

286d268c11543e5525d49ce12cd2d707cdd5ecbc.text: When the automated test that checks the live coding session runs and an assertion fails mid-way, the test previously left a real coding session open on the account, which could stay active for up to an hour. Now the test tracks whether it has already ended its own session, and if not, it automatically sends the command to end the session during cleanup, but only if the chat screen is still showing (not the initial landing screen). You would notice this only if you were watching the test run or checking for leftover sessions on an account afterward.

3cb1fb6862cca34e8ccbba778c11ca697e2a9e05.text: If you run the web app under Node (the way production does) instead of the test runtime, a recent assistant feature that crashed on every request will now fail the build instead of reaching production. The docs now tell contributors how to reproduce that production-like check locally, and to do it they start a local copy of the company database and run a simulated session, admission, and chat flow. It's live today via the build process, and it affects anyone who builds or deploys the web app: a broken assistant route now blocks the build on main rather than silently shipping.

c53b6a752b9954bbd96a70f0d3eafd60c350491f.text: The test that double-checks mission prompts are correctly set up has been updated to match how those prompts are now written in the code. The prompts themselves haven’t changed—what changed is the test’s ability to confirm they’re still present and formatted correctly. Since this only affects the testing process and no live software was modified, there’s nothing new for you to experience in the app today. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance to ensure ongoing reliability, not a new feature.

871e0ef0f989d23273c778f4b30eb541c6d0deed.text: The app's build number ticked up from a version ending in 172 to one ending in 173, a routine step in rolling out updates. You wouldn't notice this yourself, but it signals a fresh package was assembled for distribution. It's live today as the current release.

abd23ca628058b352e08b9fc4028f775b2c72042.text: The coding assistant's packaging and distribution version was bumped from one release to the next. This is a behind-the-scenes housekeeping update that helps keep the tool installed cleanly for anyone downloading it. You won't see any new features or behavior from this particular change. It is live today as part of the release.

02082cce25560ae06491ef8c0ef30c6518b5afc7.text: You don't see anything new yet: the developers added a set of checks that confirm how the system decides which waiting agent should get paired up with a real one when several are spawned at once. The tests verify that the first matching agent in line wins, that names are matched loosely enough to ignore extra version or scoping details, and that an agent placeholder gets moved out from the main list and tucked under its parent agent once it's resolved. This is behind-the-scenes work that locks in the matching-and-nesting behavior today so future code can rely on it being correct; there is no new user-facing capability from this change alone.

2c8541e90dcc9e7641fe7d4ba7c03e1eea64bfa4.text: The label for your monthly spending limit on the plans page now reads 'model spend' instead of 'tokens,' so the dollar amount (like '$4.10 of $25 model spend') and the raw count of tokens are no longer called the same word on the same page. If you can see dollar figures, your recent-usage card also shows an estimated cost in USD, rounded to cents, labeled clearly alongside the token counts. If your account isn't allowed to see dollar amounts, that estimated cost field is simply absent, so the card disappears rather than showing a number you shouldn't see.

81f78e0c885af9edb97960bf8e8497cf1a45e6a1.text: The system now keeps a certain type of temporary login token out of the shared project storage, so those short-lived credentials can't accidentally get saved or sent somewhere they shouldn't. If you looked at the project's ignore list, you would see a new line that tells the system to leave those tokens alone. This only affects people working behind the scenes on the project, and it is live today.

54ba9b4874e7b588f9f771155853fa42e2218765.text: Nothing changes for you today. The software that ships the assistant got a routine internal version number bump from 0.0.171 to 0.0.172 in the packaging file, which is behind-the-scenes housekeeping for the release process and produces no visible difference in what you experience.

a8def7f03d62efcc46ff246bb83a69443036aa27.text: The CLI removed three helper functions that used to work out agent family trees and figure out which agents were visible, leaving the core message-tree builder intact. If you opened the CLI source today, you would find those helpers gone and the remaining tree-builder code unchanged. This only touches internal tooling, so there's no visible change in behavior for anyone running the CLI.

7539eacf2a73bfcbfdb5e37cf88fdcc494361cf5.text: When the system tries to load an ad and the ad service responds with an error like a generic '400' or '500' code, the system now also captures and records the first part of the actual error message that comes back. You would notice this in the logs: instead of just seeing a status code with no explanation, you would see a snippet of the specific reason the ad was rejected. This only affects the internal logging behavior and is live today, so it won't change anything you see in the app, but it helps diagnose why ad loads are failing.

95e3f5f94d99ac80eeac8306d46296208263d5bd.text: Premium session users on free tiers can once again start up to 5 paid chat sessions per day instead of the reduced 4 limit. This restores the original session count that was lowered when experimental Level tiers were retired, and removes the old level-based override system entirely. You would notice this if you checked your daily session allowance setting, though most regular subscribers using the main service won't see any change in practice.

8d21e42dbfa0c7509ffc294601a55f9a95a2cd25.text: When a single response hits its usage limit, the message you see no longer speculates that an assistant got stuck in a loop — it simply states the turn reached its limit and your session is fine. This wording is shared across the web, command-line, and desktop versions, so everyone gets the same clearer explanation and can start a new message to continue.

ec6003e6dc37caba65b92c4eca3adb7595eca4e3.text: The tool that packages the coding assistant for installation bumped its version number by one small step. If you downloaded or updated the assistant today, the version you get is now one patch newer than before. Nothing about how the assistant works changed in this step; this is just the behind-the-scenes numbering that gets updated with each small release.

5454338099733607d45ae7442117bf2879569637.text: When you're in a region with limited access and open the assistant picker, the first model shown is now the cheaper GLM model instead of the previous default. The cheaper model can be locked if your account has no earned reward balance, so the picker now keeps a separate always-available fallback model that you can actually join onto when the cheaper one is unavailable. In practice, you'll see the cheaper model lead the list while a guaranteed-usable fallback waits one step deeper, and the public description of limited-access regions now lists the cheaper model first. The tooling flagged the split as a minor change and it is live today.

f1ebb9710b9ba26d96f19a1cf8e6fb2e2ae71c8b.text: If you are an advertiser, your assistant's use of a new MCP tool it calls on your behalf is now recorded in a way that tracks which advertiser account made the call, the tool used, whether it worked or failed, and how long it took. The system only logs those specific details and deliberately never records the content you sent or received, so your data stays private while helping your advertiser account's activity get counted properly.

f396f4ef37618acc07c9b6c7e461695e3d357e72.text: If you use Freebucks, your account can now do about 25% more work in a day before hitting the daily limit — the cap went from three times the value of your Freebucks up to four times. So if you used to run out of compute partway through the day, you'll be able to keep going a bit longer before your sessions get refused. The on-screen message you see when you hit the cap now says 'four times' instead of 'three times.'.

d3d99f4c5a6e4bc6fbb83c81ea8b7a63cb53e0b4.text: The assistant's release packaging was bumped from the previous version to 0.0.169, a routine internal update that does not change your experience. You would only notice if you were inspecting the published package metadata, where the version number now reads 0.0.169. This is live today as part of standard release housekeeping.

52fa3fb94d1b2957fdefa82afae8158a0ae19cff.text: The team updated their list of files that the system should track by default. They told it to start watching a sample setup file used for local development, so that file won't be skipped anymore when working on their project. They also added two more items to the list of things the system should ignore, to keep the project cleaner and free of unnecessary clutter from certain tools used during editing.

54ce330ea151686b4a999b1318617b6c6a069644.text: If you use the command-line version of the assistant and check your free daily usage, the header now shows how long until your free allowance refreshes, like 'resets in 4h 12m', matching what web and desktop users already see. This only appears when the current time is available, and it doesn't change who can access what; it just adds the countdown to the existing usage display.

20289ffb12000c10fd26cd3735849066e963d1cc.text: When someone sends a conversion back to the ad server after a click, the system now quietly notes why the click ID was rejected if it failed a shape check (missing, wrong type, empty, too long, or containing control characters). If you review the logs you’d see this extra label on those specific failed events, but none of the actual click value or request details are recorded. This is live today for server-to-server postbacks on the Conversion API path.

8fafc97b35aa47a8dcea952690e2a8bf115f2da8.text: The assistant now waits a little longer—15 seconds instead of 10—before giving up when it can't reach the model and decides to switch to a backup plan. This mainly affects you when lots of people are hitting the model at once and every key to get in is temporarily blocked. With the new key-pool system, the assistant now automatically tries another available key behind the scenes before waiting, so the longer window is only the final fallback when nothing works. If you looked, you'd notice a slightly longer pause before the model switches rather than an immediate switch on a busy moment.

f1654d2c20dcf2cc75a464b7c6707d1cfeef6711.text: You may have seen a small note marking Solar Pro 4 as experimental before, like a 'preview' label on a menu item; that label is gone now. The model definition had a single flag removed, so Solar Pro 4 now appears as a regular, standard option rather than an experimental one. You would notice that label or warning indicator no longer shows up alongside the model, since shared interface code stopped displaying it once the flag was dropped. Who is eligible today did not change; this only removes the experimental label from how the model is presented.

e2b7fe5a4ebe36206150cc194cc297fc0c8bd251.text: Starting today, when the system sends information to its advertising partner called Gravity, it now passes along the real browser or app details from your device instead of pretending you are using a regular web browser. If your device did not send those details, it falls back to the generic browser information so nothing breaks. This fixes a problem where roughly three-quarters of traffic was being incorrectly reported as regular Chrome desktop users. You would notice the difference only if you were checking the advertising reports, where the traffic now shows up with its true source.

bb9e8822ea946d45870d09ff2ad8db35f872bbda.text: If you use a Freebuff subscription plan, your Freebucks wallet now shows one combined balance made up of two different parts: permanent Freebucks you earned through bounties, referrals, or grants, and a monthly bonus tied to your plan that expires when the new month begins. When you spend Freebucks, the system always uses your expiring monthly bonus first, so you won't accidentally lose that time-limited allowance while keeping the Freebucks you earned permanently. This clarification only updates how the wallet's behavior is documented internally — your balance and spending order stay the same as of today.

2476a76f4dd8eb14dba89d848e676146c839a7e5.text: The system that records settlement data now has a place to store a specific metric identifier alongside each record. This means when settlement information is logged, it can also carry a label that pinpoints which exact metric is being tracked. This affects internal logging utilities used across shared core components. Today this field exists in the logging definition but nothing is writing to it yet, so you wouldn't notice any change in behavior right now.

2a92b62f5263e702f76e3a7c3b9f89b29a046710.text: The release number for the assistant's installer was bumped to 0.0.168, so anyone downloading or updating the tool through official package channels will pull the new package instead of the one labeled 0.0.167. No features, models, or behaviors changed; this is purely a behind-the-scenes version-label update to keep the distribution tracking consistent for automated builds and install scripts.

6e53c6db1674d4f343f2392092a6f316fa9644fb.text: When you open the app, a menu label and the balance shown next to it were sometimes based on different calculations, so they disagreed. The app now reads the access tier that the server itself attached to your session response and uses that single, authoritative value for both the label and the balance, so they always match. If a server response carries no tier, the app falls back to its previous behavior. This is live today and affects the menus and balances shown to accounts whose server response includes the tier.

23c15cfd4656c6eb305dfe9e4bbab938ebadbed8.text: Your ad system can now log a safe, stripped-down record when an advertiser pulls their reporting data, capturing only the bare details needed (like advertiser ID, request size, and how long it took) while explicitly blocking any sensitive query contents from being saved. This is live today for anyone hitting the advertiser reporting read path, and if you checked the logs, you'd see a new structured entry appear only after qualifying requests, with no raw parameters or private data attached.

13c3ba7d0b36a754116bac24f76957a3eebb9f64.text: When an ad request is made on either rail (provider waterfall or first-party), this change adds a single field called 'request_id' to the log that records the completed ad fetch. If you looked at the system's records for ad requests today, you would see this new identifier appearing alongside the existing auction-level 'opportunity_id.' The 'request_id' serves as a unique handle to correlate all activity tied to a single HTTP ad request, distinct from the placement-level identifier, and acts as the key for batching related decisions in the outbox.

6222be5e6b2164b7dae9ff261d06be5fc88c2b47.text: If you are offered a sponsored task to run, you no longer see a line telling you that it will use your session and credits like any other task. The offer now simply says the task runs in its own worktree, and the detailed explanation of why that cost still applies (the advertiser-paid system for these tasks has no server-side reader yet) is left in a code comment instead of being shown to you. The change is live today for anyone who accepts a sponsored proposal in the assistant. Until the billing system can report usage on the server side, the text stays silent on cost rather than risk implying the task is free.

477a8a0d84c0b6cd3c5181ef0a6498eec2079321.text: If you use the service on more than one device, and another session of yours has taken over, the system now tells your client device exactly how many other sessions are active on other computers or browsers, instead of just quietly forcing you to close it. The session-checking machinery and the list of possible responses from the server were reorganized into two separate checks: one that decides whether you can be admitted to the free service (still covering things like being on an unknown location or running low on free balance), and a separate, dedicated flag that says your session has been superseded by another login elsewhere. This is a behind-the-scenes rearrangement of how the server's replies are categorized; no new user-facing features were turned on today, since nothing is yet

d4bc77782d48297b04fb290ea5fb43ca4dae0d37.text: Your coding assistant's packaging version number ticked up from one build to the next, which is the behind-the-scenes housekeeping that happens each time the team prepares a new release bundle. If you download or update the assistant right now, you'll be getting version zero-point-zero-one-sixty-seven instead of the previous number; otherwise, nothing about how it works has changed. This is just a label swap in a manifest file, so you won't see any new features or behavior differences when you use it.

9ede9a4a53b7798cd504493c12aa75323f7a0225.text: The testing documentation now states clearly that the main test group never connects to the live production-switch system. This keeps tests from breaking when an operator flips a production flag that has nothing to do with the test, and it applies to every package's test run in both local and CI environments. Tests that need a non-default setting must set it themselves within the test instead of inheriting it from the environment.

390944fda9461b1401383ef148dfcd844f8d4427.text: The app now has new automated checks that make sure pressing the up and down arrow keys places your cursor in the right spot when viewing wrapped lines of text, correctly clamping the column position when lines end early and handling edge cases like the first and last lines. These checks are live today and run behind the scenes during development to catch any regressions in cursor positioning logic, though you won't notice any change in the app itself since it's testing existing behavior.

59cca53dfb5bc9c9c03141f91494646de4a40ce3.text: The system stopped trying to give some readers a sticky first-party ad experience that stayed the same across visits, rolling back a recent experiment. Instead, ad requests now skip tracking extra correlation fields like an opportunity id and policy details, which removes behind-the-scenes logic that previously kept certain users in the same ad auction bucket. The change is live and affects how ad delivery data gets logged internally, though you wouldn't see it directly as a reader.

26f3b123cc05ef5f25fd8b0fe2adf7fbbdeeb691.text: When you see a promotional message in your feed or sidebar, the system is now clearer about two distinct modes: a default safety net that only appears on rare occasions and is intentionally not repeated for a given user, versus a regular paid promotion that still respects the standard limit on how often the same person sees it. The change is to the written rules inside the advertising configuration, so it is live today in any environment pulling the latest published code. If you looked now, you'd notice the documentation explicitly states that the safety-net fallback is off by default in production and that repetition is avoided by showing varied messages within the capped promotion, not by relying on the uncapped fallback alone.

2a958f98f5f8c683057d7419feae9093bea14cfb.text: When someone adds money to a Freebuff placement using a card, the name that shows up on their bank or card statement will now include 'FREEBUFF.COM' as a suffix. This is a small adjustment to keep those one-time charges displaying correctly within Stripe's 22-character limit on the Codebuff Stripe account. If you looked, you'd notice the statement descriptor for one-off card charges now ends with 'FREEBUFF.COM' while subscription products still carry it directly on the product name. This change is live today.

605ba1edc6365594cf457c25adab324cb801d41c.text: The test setup now forces the 'god quota exempt' feature flag to be turned on before any test runs, so that production settings from the CI environment can't accidentally override it. If you looked at the test runner output around 2026-09-01, six exemption-related tests went red because the production environment had flipped this flag off. From now on, only tests that explicitly set this flag themselves will run with it off.

c179bfcc451be624a8bffc032075ba836a5a967b.text: When fractional data allowances are used, some on-screen usage rings can show ugly long decimals like 0.7000000000000002 instead of a clean 0.7; this change adds checks that make the display logic round those computer-math leftovers back to tidy numbers before showing them, so the rings stay readable and correct. Nothing in the actual product changed today—this only adds test coverage for an existing rounding fix, meaning the safer display behavior was already live and these tests just lock that behavior in place to prevent it from breaking later.

8592ea01be0a05c20e0741bc3b1dfe82c4694e7b.text: You won't see this if you're browsing the web app or using any feature day-to-day. Behind the scenes, the system now keeps a local-only working folder used to pick up where a batch of ad requests left off, and that folder is now explicitly blocked from being saved into the shared project history. It only affects people who build or maintain the software itself, not people running ads or using the product.

ae136bca432c7f3c74cb18d6c7fda924de2d8a12.text: The version number for the CLI release package was bumped to 0.0.165, which is a routine internal update that helps track which version of the software you're running. This change only affects the people who build, package, and deploy the CLI tool, not the commands you type or the features you use. If you checked the version number reported by the installed tool, you'd see 0.0.165 instead of the previous 0.0.164, confirming you have the latest build.

3dd1da66d178a91f9d099d3370564ecb00dde3dc.text: Nothing new for you to use yet. Engineers quietly bumped the build number of the assistant's installation package to the next release in the normal publishing schedule. That number is what people see when they check the version they installed or when the tool lists updates, but the bump itself adds no extra capabilities and most people would not notice it.

210f7ac71cdb6b0f59662b85b4b86cdf0ef5e723.text: You may have noticed that clicks on ads in some countries used to be skipped entirely if the revenue would have been too small, usually below 5 cents. Those clicks now generate a minimum charge of 10 cents, so that ad inventory gets monetized instead of being left with no value. This only affects the smallest payouts from low-converting countries, leaving larger ad rates untouched.

d49020039fb91ec4c15dbfeaf70940853e84f5e8.text: When you click the button to connect your GitHub account on the referral banner, it now opens your account page at the website's /account address instead of the old /web/settings address. This affects anyone using the command-line application who clicks that GitHub linking button. If you looked at the link before it opened a page ending in /web/settings, and now it opens one ending in /account. The change only applies to the version of the command-line tool released today.

d36ecd09839c43b9c0949a8ad83ea5a171cba6bc.text: When the system decides which ads to show, it now logs more detail about why it can or can't reserve ad slots based on how often someone has seen them. Specifically, it tracks the maximum time it's allowed to wait for a slot and all the reasons a slot might be unavailable, not just the first one. These new data points are recorded in the system's internal logs but don't change how the ads you see work today; they're being collected so engineers can better understand and improve the ad selection process in the future. This change is live now.

646e9fe14848ff98d26448d1c90f42422e3dbe8a.text: Your copy of the coding agent got quietly re-tagged to version 0.0.161, a routine numbering bump with no new features or behavior changes. If you install or update the agent today, you'd see this new version number reported, but everything it does would work exactly as before. This only affects people pulling a fresh install or updating the software; existing users notice nothing unless they check the version number.

9c2974837d8b90725ae61ebe6ac5c8c7f29ea493.text: A set of new checks was added to the command-line tools' quality tests to confirm the countdown timer displays correctly under various scenarios like partial days, past dates, and invalid inputs. These checks verify that users will see accurate time remaining messages such as '4d 7h' or 'now' without any changes to the visible features. Since this is test-only additions to the internal suite, you wouldn't notice any difference in your experience today, but it helps ensure the time formatting behaves reliably.

9c1de51074bf984f2827742fffce78a1e7580203.text: A developer set up the project so that spreadsheet files containing your email address and other user data are now automatically hidden from the shared codebase, preventing accidental exposure of personal information. This affects only the internal development environment where engineers build features, not your account or any service you use. If you were to look at the project files, you simply wouldn't see these sensitive export files listed anymore.

df7e3aa400c51c34ba5185d01ce1527c892a671f.text: You probably didn't notice this one because it doesn't change what you see on screen. Behind the scenes, the assistant removed a redundant nickname for an internal helper that formats the countdown text on those usage banners, and pointed every place that needed that text directly at the real helper instead. If you happened to be reading the code itself, you'd see one helper being called in two screens where a duplicate wrapper used to sit.

23c05c4a5fce1db9301b66529c2dd543d51c1e77.text: When the system calculates how much each ad click or thousand impressions actually cost you, it now separates two different numbers: what the billing ledger says you were charged versus what the delivery rows themselves recorded as charged. Previously, a manual back-bill or adjustment line in the ledger would sneak into the cost-per-click and cost-per-impression ratios, pulling them away from the real per-action price. Rate metrics now divide by the delivery-charged spend field, so manual ledger-only corrections no longer distort the average costs shown in reports. The new field is added alongside the existing spend total, so any report or dashboard that reads placement totals can opt into the cleaner rate numbers.

7266e1b5944dd0a7094a9cbaa49361d470b67c9e.text: Nothing visually changed for you today, but the system now has a guardrail that stops a silent mistake from hiding future problems. When the paid plans page lists which assistant models each plan includes, it used to quietly swap in a default model (MiMo 2.5) if it couldn't find a plan's listed model in its own catalog; that mismatch would have made a plan look like it offers fewer models than it really does, with no error message. The new check is a test-only addition that forces every model tied to a paid plan to be confirmed present in that same catalog before anything ships, so any future drift between the two lists will trigger a failure and get caught immediately rather than slipping through unnoticed.

1312fa1702921f9df8394bf191da9ef062fba043.text: Your house ads — the small promotional messages we show in your feed — can now correctly display our app's icon next to them. The system that places these ads was previously unable to fetch a static image for the icon and would show it missing or broken. This fix lets the ad display code fall back to the proper icon image, so the promotion looks consistent and complete to you whether you see it in the feed or elsewhere.

179f317de8d228cc02d32ac4730781a8c0aadbc9.text: The version number for the CLI release package was incremented from 0.0.159 to 0.0.160. This is a minor change limited to packaging metadata, with no functional code modifications. The update helps identify this specific build but does not alter any features or behaviors you would experience.

d40c36e4aae67b74e3067d4c23a2c1c3db9bf665.text: If you manage a software project, you know that sometimes extra folders get created when different parts of the system want to work independently — in this case, the tool the assistant uses to explore code can make its own full copy of the project to avoid messing up the main one. To keep those temporary copies from accidentally being saved into the project history (which would create confusing duplicates of important migration records), a small instruction was added to tell the project to ignore a specific folder where those copies live. If you look at the project settings file that controls what gets ignored, you will see a new entry pointing to that folder, ensuring only the main project stays clean and tracked.

7bb5501109a4dd88daf5e262cb1356b7b815b200.text: The progress bar that shows you how close you are to the next level now always stays within the correct range instead of dipping below zero or jumping past the maximum. This keeps the visuals steady and readable for anyone looking at their level progress on the web app, desktop app, or command-line tool. If you watched the bar before, you might have seen it flicker past its bounds when your raw progress landed outside the expected window; now it stays put at the edge instead.

f7d35db5a5e064e98c9f12739e68f1583ced9c5d.text: Freebuff now counts your GLM 5.3 Flash usage by how many times you start a conversation, not by how much you talk. If you use GLM 5.3 Flash, you can start at most two conversations per day instead of the previous fractional session limit. The in-app display now shows 'starts' instead of 'used' for this model, and the shared premium allowance still charges you for any extra time you use, rounded up to the nearest tenth of a minute.

ed224f5a8768b78f3333974446054d71497e4419.text: The software that runs the coding assistant quietly moved from one minor build number to the next - think of it like the program printing a slightly newer release label on its package whenever someone installs it. If you reinstalled or updated the tool today, you'd see the new label appear, but nothing about how it behaves would feel different. This is purely behind-the-scenes housekeeping so the published package stays consistent, and the change is live as soon as you pull the latest release.

1d9a61e734810b53404ced16489971b33109725e.text: On the Freebuff website, the premium assistant model is now locked behind your paid subscription — you can no longer reach it from a free web session. Starting today, web visitors without the proper paid-tier account key are turned away at the door before the assistant even loads, while people using the desktop app or the command-line tool keep getting the same free access to that model they always have. The restriction also kicks in during the model's busiest hours (roughly early morning to late afternoon in your local time), when the web paywall automatically closes entirely — even subscribers are blocked then — to avoid paying twice for the same expensive service. If you hit the web version outside those hours as a paying subscriber, you'll simply see the standard assistant; free web

b42492330322ad9c82caf4620c05e4ab36d661d4.text: On Linux computers, the software stopped saving and reusing downloaded helper packages between test runs; instead it grabs a fresh copy each time, which the team found actually finished tests faster. If you run checks on Linux machines, your jobs start a little sooner because they skip the step of unpacking a large saved package, but Windows and Apple machines still reuse theirs. The system still keeps smaller, faster-to-move caches for a few build steps and the helper tool itself, so those parts stay quick.

15ebdcb20344b1faa17ff5345846ba1241d3e664.text: When the assistant writes a response, it sometimes tucks thoughts into hidden tags that look like parentheses with a 'think' label — the opening and closing of those tags can arrive split across separate pieces of text. The software that reassembled those pieces was misreading the splits, which could drop stray closing tags or glue text together wrongly, so the reconstructed message came out garbled. The fix teaches the parser to treat a lone closing tag as its own boundary, and tells the text-joining step to blend consecutive pieces first before hunting for tags, so each tag pair stays intact and the assembled output keeps its intended structure. This works today for everything you see in the CLI; there are no new commands or settings to use.

fbda78872046ff7f2223c83c8093d1d1f9237dca.text: You won't see anything change on your screen. Behind the scenes, the system now ignores a temporary settings file that employees use when starting up the ad pilot feature, so that file can no longer be accidentally saved to the shared project and expose real advertiser information.

c5e4bf5459e0119e774dbda81d74d89d580f6c6f.text: If you use Freebuff on the web, in the app, or on your desktop, the message shown when model limits change has been updated. It now tells you that you get a normal daily session allotment with no separate caps per model, and that MiMo and DeepSeek V4 Flash stay unmetered. The old message about V4 Pro switching to V4 Flash while a provider recovered has been removed. This text is live today wherever the notice appears.

4e45c27aa823ee8d4a0abe9d493d85479e030149.text: If you use the assistant and V4 Pro is temporarily offline because its provider is recovering, V4 Pro will now quietly answer using V4 Flash while it gets fixed, instead of returning an error or a notice about unmetered MiMo/DeepSeek V4 Flash. Freebuff has also added a new capped Flash front lane, FusionCode, which is live today and lets providers join a specific routing path. You wouldn't see FusionCode directly, but if you notice V4 Pro responding slightly differently during a provider outage, that's this change working behind the scenes.

a4d50e7363432ab28c574b022a0b2fc76de0ab2a.text: When an ad is shown to you or you tap one, the app now quietly logs that click or impression along with a few details like where it appeared and which provider served it, so the team can measure how well first-party ads are performing. These new tracking events are live today and feed into the app's existing analytics pipeline.

29e42653f8ec332f88173a5a05520ff6f8119655.text: When the system says your allowance is used up because of a VPN connection, the message now tells you clearly that connecting directly instead of through a VPN will restore it. The developers added checks to make sure those messages mention VPN and connecting directly, so you know exactly what to do. This fixes a gap from August 24 where people hitting the rate limit only saw a generic message without that guidance.

ff5d55049a4f9d7a0175b82bbc68a7c75c89e811.text: When you open the model picker, the Premium section now lists a different model called DeepSeek V4 Pro instead of DeepSeek V4 Flash, which moved to the Unlimited section. The test files were updated to verify this new ordering and to confirm that V4 Pro correctly shows both its training warning and its usage quota chip, which Flash used to carry when it was the Premium model.
