Before this, the cursor keys and Tab did nothing, and you had to know the keyboard shortcut (Enter for take over, Escape for exit) without any on-screen cue about which action was active. The screen is live now, so anyone starting a second instance will see the border appear around a button as they navigate with the keyboard.

8fa7488daf630728e2d15dc62d3e14b3f3544e07.text: When you open the list of AI models you can pick in the CLI tool, pressing Tab and Shift+Tab now reliably moves your selection forward and backward through the models. Previously, depending on your terminal, those keys could be missed or handled inconsistently, so sometimes nothing would move. The keyboard handling was reworked to translate key presses into a clear forward/backward direction and stop the keys from triggering anything else at the same time. This is live today for anyone using the model selector in the CLI.

53bd37e42721c3c82f38c6e13eeca9ad1f6ef2fa.text: A reference to a missing documentation page was removed from the AGENTS.md file, which lists helpful guides for developers. The linked file had already been deleted from the repository, so the entry was simply pointing to nothing. This only affects the AGENTS.md listing and nothing else, leaving all other references intact. The change is in place today.

30a74b13655cdf54bdb92695b32a79061bab3395.text: When the assistant tries to use a tool that doesn't exist or is used incorrectly, the error was previously shown to you in the response. Now those errors are hidden from your view—they still happen and get handled internally, but you won't see them mixed into the assistant's replies. This only applies to tool call failures, and it's live today.

e5a769f1aecce74e5f931b8b7686d435fd3bce7e.text: When the assistant uses a reasoning step (like the 'thinker') during a task, its final written conclusion was getting hidden in the terminal output before it could be seen. The terminal now displays that final conclusion correctly, so you will see the full chain of reasoning instead of just the intermediate steps. The fix affects anyone running the assistant in a terminal who relies on reading these reasoning blocks.

19fd493012e249d012cb6ac432019b0b6305b69c.text: The small status line at the bottom of the command-line assistant no longer labels your remaining time as a "Free session," because that word was already implied and only added clutter. If you use the assistant in a terminal, you'll see the same quota and time details, just without the redundant "Free session" text taking up space. The change affects only the on-screen status display.

497dd729d369e5f79ccc4448f522620ebed335b1.text: The assistant's test code was being too strict about what kind of data it could handle, so the developers relaxed that rule. This mainly affects the people building and testing the assistant software itself — if you're just using the assistant, you wouldn't notice anything different. Behind the scenes, the testing files are now a bit more flexible, which should keep the software stable without changing how it works for you.

c237e011f8bf96dcaedb048c20f4bec2649ad6a1.text: You now see a single number in the status footer showing how many premium sessions you used out of the 5 available each rolling 20-hour window, regardless of which premium model you pick, replacing previous per-model usage lines. The list of premium models shows only a tier badge per row, and MiniMax models simply label themselves "Fastest" with no usage tracker, since they are unlimited. If you looked, you would no longer find per-model "X/Y used" hints on each row or separate quota lines in the waiting room screen. This is live today.

c7a858cca6e4e756fd504ebd1e57ab981ff4eecc.text: When the assistant runs out of space to remember a long conversation and needs to summarize what happened earlier, it now writes shorter, cleaner notes. Lines that used to start with 'Previously' now just describe the action directly (for example, 'inspected files' instead of 'Previously inspected files'), and each note about something you asked is labeled simply '[USER]'. The result is a more compact summary that takes up less room in the conversation, leaving more space for the actual discussion. You won't see this summary yourself unless you dig into technical logs; it only changes how the assistant internally tracks what was done earlier in the chat.

225ff3c73330ef6e3e8feddd60540221ddf3b765.text: The system now has a new end-to-end test that verifies a specific agent correctly resumes work from a previously summarized conversation. This test uses a complex, realistic scenario where part of a coding task (like adding a helper function and running tests) was summarized mid-conversation, and the agent must continue without restarting or copying the summary's format. It checks that the agent makes real tool calls (like editing files) and avoids mimicking the text style of the summary itself. This is a testing improvement behind the scenes; it doesn't change what the agent does for users today, but helps catch regressions in how the agent handles resumed conversations.

ed6b40772029fa12c2b2aa696281378a75f40235.text: The status bar at the bottom of your screen shows your remaining session time and, if applicable, which model you're using. The tool just trimmed the redundant "Free session" label from that display, so it now shows only the model name (when present) and the remaining time. You would notice a slightly cleaner, less cluttered status bar, with the same information minus the extra words.

9b64c59cc76e48d59c00491ff539a53a1f2e6b92.text: The diagnostic log now shows the path to the tree-sitter WebAssembly file under the label "globalThis wasmPath" instead of "env.CODEBUFF_TREE_SITTER_WASM_PATH". This lets the diagnostic read the file path from a global variable that is always accessible, instead of from an environment variable that is blocked by an architecture check in certain pre-initialization files. The change affects the CLI smoke diagnostic output that CI logs and bug reports display when smoke testing fails.

2bb6ffca346d7996349f7df48f315d184562788d.text: When the software starts up and can't find a required helper file, it now automatically downloads that file from the internet and saves it locally so future starts don't have the problem. This only affects users running an older version of the setup tool that updates the main program but forgets to include the helper file, leaving them with a broken installation. You'd notice a brief message on your screen during the first launch explaining the download is happening, after which the software works normally on its own.

c44bdd892aa4070a170df2a76b3dd1f17b9c08b9.text: When the assistant starts up and runs its quick self-check, it now has a backup plan for finding the tree-sitter grammar file it needs. If the normal setup step fails to hand the file over (which happened on Windows where the program path gets confused during startup), it falls back to looking for that same file in the same folder where the program itself lives on disk. By the time the assistant actually begins running, that disk path is reliable on all systems. You would notice this as the self-check passing instead of failing with a missing-file error during startup, especially on Windows machines.

1c308ad5aa42aea42643a76b6d4e64e48279bbb6.text: When the program looks for its helper file that understands code structure, it used to accept a shortcut path that the system couldn't actually open, causing confusing 'file not found' errors even though the path looked valid. Now it only uses paths it can truly read, skipping those broken shortcuts entirely. You wouldn't notice this directly, but the program will be more reliable when setting up code analysis features instead of suddenly failing during initialization.

a3399902180bb42581d2a6eff6229153d3b3d389.text: When you start the assistant on a Windows computer, it needs to find a helper file called tree-sitter.wasm that was placed next to the program. On Windows, the system was looking in the wrong folder for that file, so the assistant could fail to start properly. The fix tells the assistant to check the path of the file you actually opened instead of a temporary internal address, with the old method kept as a backup. If this works, you won't notice anything different except that the assistant starts up reliably instead of getting stuck.

ba4858b418fe880ea4af7d324806a355ed56c701.text: When you run the assistant on Windows, it needs to load a grammar file called tree-sitter alongside the program. That file used to be found too early in the startup process, before Windows had settled on the correct disk location, so it was silently skipped. The lookup now happens later, when the program can see where it actually sits on disk, so the grammar loads reliably. A diagnostic option (--smoke-tree-sitter) was also added so developers can trace what Windows reports at that startup moment.

249bd7f3b2b65513814d63081e8f4fc4adbdccb6.text: When the assistant's built-in syntax check crashes during automated testing, the system now prints a short report to the test logs showing exactly where it looked for the required parsing helper file and what files were actually present in that spot, plus key environment settings. Previously, these crashes left no clue about whether a file was missing, misnamed, or simply not placed where expected. If you review CI logs from today, you will see this extra diagnostic block appear only when the syntax check fails, helping developers understand why the check broke in any given environment.

5e57c1f796855869d728591ba4b167d523bcd33c.text: Every time someone pushes new code, the system now runs a quick Windows test that builds Freebuff and checks it actually starts up without crashing. This test would have caught a recent bug where Freebuff appeared to work but then broke silently on Windows machines after OpenTUI was upgraded. The test specifically looks for late failures that happen after the initial boot, which the old Linux-only checks missed. This is live today for anyone developing or testing Freebuff on Windows.

a5d75a28b2b4267967854295d903874554669bd0.text: When you run the assistant on Windows, it loads a small engine that parses code files. That engine used to fail to start because Windows' file system couldn't locate its packaged file correctly. The build scripts now place the engine file in a dedicated local folder before packaging, so the assistant's built-in loader finds it reliably on Windows. The file is treated as temporary — it's added during builds, deleted after, and automatically cleaned up even if the build process crashes midway.

2c4b87305949af8fff3128a2d055e243801a2d64.text: The assistant can now check that its embedded tree-sitter language parser loads correctly before doing anything else, by running a hidden command during automated testing. Previously this check lived in an early-loading setup step that relied on a special await keyword, but on Windows machines that keyword didn't actually pause execution, so the parser got checked too late and the test command was mistakenly rejected as an unknown option. The check now runs directly in the main entry point before the command-line processor starts, so the early-loading setup only publishes the parser data and the main program synchronously runs the parser boot test when that hidden command is given.

5e43e630ff377c5e94bd665b5f692c6aa5446abf.text: When the desktop app is built, the program now writes its tree-sitter parser files using a method that Windows tools can't accidentally shrink away or ignore during the build, then double-checks that the files were actually saved correctly so a broken version won't be released. This only matters to people running the self-contained desktop build of the assistant; regular installs that pull the parser files from the internet when needed are not affected.

b463207c112fdd3a17ba8a3b2693f83088a63a76.text: When you run the assistant's built-in code analysis, the helper that understands programming languages is now checked automatically before each release: if the language-reading component didn't get packaged correctly, the build stops instead of shipping a broken tool to you. Developers building the assistant will now see a clear failure if the language module is missing, and the program can verify its own language feature with a new diagnostic command. If you use the assistant today, you don't see anything new yet, but you're protected from future releases that might accidentally break code analysis.

cb069ac68216580c5dd2fb7e7e24606106126599.text: The developer tools that check whether the environment is set up correctly now also recognize a helper module that prepares the WebAssembly component used for code mapping. This affects only the internal tooling area and was added to the allowlist that governs which modules can interact with environment variables during startup. If you inspect the tooling configuration, you'll see the new entry listed alongside an existing entry for loading terminal variables, both of which are now permitted to access environment settings during initialization.

74abc489274e376070953134b985d7a893394cea.text: Live today in the web app's test suite, the behind-the-scenes checks that confirm buttons and pages work now run without crashing when certain modern web features load. The fix patches in missing pieces like text handling and network requests that JSDOM (a fake browser used only during testing) doesn't include by default, so tests involving Next.js server code and OpenAI integration no longer fail at startup. If you opened the test files, you'd see they quietly add these missing tools at the very start now — React and React DOM now resolve from the main project folder, and a small TypeScript rule was added to stop the assistant's command-line installer from choking on a WebAssembly import during setup.

5743114d091cefdc1bda82f2525713d077e6ba42.text: The release process for the command-line tool can now build from a specific version identifier instead of always pulling from the latest main codebase. This only affects the internal team who triggers production releases, since they are the ones running the workflow. If you were watching the release setup, you'd see a new option to specify exactly which code to package, rather than it automatically grabbing whatever is newest.

70f7a46adf8f52052d3296d9de39e15f79535ad3.text: You interact with the CLI tool the same way as before, but pasting text with formatting or special characters now gets cleaned up automatically so it won't mess up the input field. The assistant's terminal interface now uses a newer version of its text-based UI library, which improves stability and reliability. If you use the CLI today, you won't notice a visual difference, but copy-pasting from other applications should work more smoothly without garbled text.

adef8ed677d3b8bbf057bae008263a01a245d22b.text: If you use this tool from a Windows command line, the code-reading helper now starts up reliably even when bundled into a single executable. Previously, the startup process tried to find a helper file using a Windows-style path like B:\~BUN\root\..., and the system would incorrectly report that path didn't exist even though it actually worked when read directly. Instead of searching for the file at startup, the program now loads the helper's contents into memory once when it begins, then hands those contents directly to the startup process, completely sidestepping the broken path-checking step. The fallback approach of finding the file by path is still available for development tools and tests that don't bundle everything into one file, and the Windows executable path takes the new

d4d2c0a14efc1143775dca97336dd6ea21ccb3ae.text: The command-line version of the assistant temporarily went back to using the previous screen layout engine, which fixes a few glitches some people noticed with the newer one. Pasting text into the assistant now works more reliably, and the screen properly returns to where you were when you close the program. A supporting piece of code that powers the editor behind the scenes was also rolled back to an earlier version. If you use the command-line assistant today, you should see fewer weird display issues and cleaner paste behavior.

2ae871eaca3d57a0d7002b3a0fc77b334a91f44f.text: The AI assistant built on Kimi K2.6 can now be used at any hour of the day, even outside its previously restricted availability window. This affects anyone using the service through the Fireworks serverless API, where the model was formerly only reachable during specific freebuff deployment hours. If you looked at the system configuration, you'd see Kimi K2.6 removed from the hours-gated model list, while other models like z-ai/glm-5.1 still remain restricted. The dedicated deployment for Kimi K2.6 stays disabled, meaning it routes entirely through the always-available serverless path now.

2974f323e3997b744e9210484e13afe6a2b69787.text: The program now checks that its text-based welcome screen actually appears on startup, instead of only checking that no known crash messages showed up. This catches silent crashes, frozen screens, and new error types that the old check wouldn't recognize. If you run the program and the welcome screen never appears, the startup test will now fail and show you exactly what the program printed before it went quiet. This is live today for anyone running the automated startup test on the assistant.

83b6eacae7bb294f340070cb93b108c286f5b9e1.text: If you live in Liechtenstein, Austria, Singapore, Malta, or Israel, you can now use Freebuff’s free mode. The service checks which country you’re connecting from and only lets people in approved countries sign up for the no-cost tier; those five countries were just added to that approved list, so the gate that was previously closed to them is now open. The one place you’d actually notice this is the FAQ on the homepage, which now lists those five new countries alongside the ones that were already supported.

13805acab332ef9046b6b7681285c5b221755c0b.text: The terminal interface that the tool renders its output through was upgraded to a newer version of its display engine. This means how text and interactive elements appear in the command-line window is now handled by updated technology, which should make the screen drawing more reliable. Users running the tool from a terminal will see the same overall behavior, but the application now uses a more current system for managing the full-screen text display, and pasted text is cleaned of hidden formatting characters before it is processed.

2d282ce3f002e05f6fa23ee3e753dcf71e878f2b.text: Starting May 3, 2026, the tool no longer silently inserts a required phrase into your requests when connecting to newer Claude models through Anthropic's OAuth system. Developers building applications using the provider now send your prompts exactly as written, without the extra system-level prefix that was previously added behind the scenes to meet authorization checks. If you relied on that automatic prefix being attached, your requests will now reach the API unmodified, which may change how some integrations behave with Claude 4+ models accessed via OAuth.

12a85348fc6f4c647e2df06bf06fea631467ed6f.text: When the AI assistant tries to use a tool (like running a command or opening a file), it usually sends the instructions as a neatly formatted message. But sometimes, due to quirks in how different AI systems talk to each other, that message gets jumbled up—like a letter sent in the wrong envelope—so the recipient can't understand it. This update teaches the system to recognize those jumbled messages, try to fix them automatically, and, if it still can't make sense of them, clearly tell the assistant what went wrong instead of silently failing. So if you noticed the assistant occasionally struggling with tool usage before, it should now recover gracefully from more of those hiccups.

8698c9a9a2ae2c01a1619cfeacbc4f38e2e5b815.text: When you sit in the waiting room before your assistant responds, the area where an ad banner will appear now holds its space from the moment the screen opens, rather than staying empty and then suddenly expanding once the ad loads. This stops the rest of the text and buttons on the screen from shifting downward when the banner pops in. Anyone watching the waiting room during an ad-supported session notices a smoother, steadier layout. It is live today in the assistant's command-line interface.

a81339bb43003d5c6f7e97fa18865c42e93b7543.text: The list of models you can pick from while you wait in the CLI tool no longer turns the model name green when it's selected. Instead, a green border and arrow point to the chosen model, while the name itself stays in its normal color, so the highlight is quieter and the text doesn't jump out at you. This only affects the waiting-room screen you see when using the command-line tool before you get connected.

721d1d5c2d85cc0acd878e826b4fd832cd95810a.text: When you open the model picker in the CLI, you've probably seen lines like 'Kimi K2.6 — 3 ahead' telling you how many people are supposedly in line. That counter is gone now: rows just show the model name plus a short status like 'Closed' (when it's outside its scheduled hours) or 'Limit used' (when your personal quota is burned through). The data still comes back from the server, but nothing in the interface reads it anymore, so you won't see a number change anywhere — the picker is just cleaner and a bit narrower, with secondary details tucking onto a second line when your terminal is too small for one row. One unrelated tweak landed in the same snapshot: the Kimi K2.6 tagline flipped from 'Smart' to 'Balanced' in the picker's constant list, so that label (if the interface shows it) now

61ebc7842f5ed64de0431a0a74a94c99ef4903e9.text: The agent runtime now saves the reasoning thoughts the model generates while answering, and replays them as part of the conversation history on the next turn. If you look at a multi-turn conversation, you will see the model's internal reasoning from earlier turns carried forward to inform its next response. This only affects the agent runtime's behavior today, as the flag controlling it has been flipped on in the constants file.

32aa640716e4d7af9ee0b5feac31802250ef2782.text: When you use the freebuff deployment during its scheduled hours, a newly added model called Kimi k2.6 is now restricted to those same hours, joining the older GLM 5.1 model that was already limited this way. This means that outside of freebuff deployment hours, you cannot access Kimi k2.6 through the serverless option, and you will get a clear model_unavailable error if you try. The change is live today, and it only affects users attempting to use Kimi k2.6 or GLM 5.1 outside of the designated freebuff deployment hours.

18cde84c6d5b59255165d0fca707419bd82be4ca.text: A specific assistant in the base2 agents area was renamed today. If you looked at the list of available assistants, this Gemini-powered one would now show up with a shorter name ("Buffy the Gemini Orchestrator") instead of the longer previous name. The change only affects the base2 agents directory, and it's live now.

fdadc4602f1fdbda8a076cd0af48714c5c9c4ab3.text: The base2 assistant can no longer generate or display on-screen visual layouts or forms. If you interacted with base2 and expected it to produce a visual interface element, that capability is gone today. The change is already live in the base2 agent as of May 1, 2026.

fdf34b7667ba21a400fdba34045282e9a10e3725.text: When you're connecting a new service that needs an API key, the assistant will now show you a clear, clickable button labeled 'Get your [service] API key' instead of just text. This button links directly to where you create your account and get your credentials, making the next step obvious and easy to follow. You only see this button when you're actively integrating a service and credentials are required.

40185a3e1bcea3e4c2bc3b4b4c2cd1d9db18f8b7.text: When you click a button in the command-line interface that opens a link, it no longer tries to tell you whether the link opened successfully or not. Instead, the button briefly flashes and then returns to normal, giving you a quick visual acknowledgment that your click was registered. This means you won't see any text indicating success or failure after clicking, just the momentary flash effect.

14559962af1f8a3de237b44dbaa9c22904093da8.text: When you tell the system to start an agent, you can now type the agent's name with underscores in place of hyphens and it will still find the right one. For example, if the agent's real name uses hyphens like "my-agent", you can now write "my_agent" and the system will treat them the same when looking it up. This only works for the agent name itself; the publisher and version parts stay exactly as typed.

8cc765a6f0e563278323a30c4ab4f69bf8d90b0b.text: When you open the model picker in the command-line tool, each model now shows a small badge telling you how much of your daily or per-session quota you've already used for that specific model, so you can see upfront whether it's already exhausted before you pick it. Navigation was cleaned up so your arrow keys move through every model in the list rather than skipping over ones that look unavailable, and the picker decides in real time which ones you can actually join based on live quota data fetched from the server. The live quota data now includes a new rate-limits-by-model snapshot that the picker reads to display those per-model exhaustion hints, and this is already in place and active today.

d727cd453111a7a6c890e0addf6884f095b552a0.text: The waiting room for the free assistant used to let operators adjust how long it stays open after a session expires, but that knob is gone. It now stays open for a fixed 30 minutes, matching what the instructions already said. If you run the assistant and check its settings file, the old switch to change that time is no longer there. The change is live today.

ce0dc1e52d1066d1087b9fbc7bd57403bfff2e9c.text: When the internal tools run their automated tests, they now automatically use a test-only access key for the CanopyWave service instead of needing someone to provide one. This only affects the behind-the-scenes testing environment, so regular users won't notice any difference. The change makes the automated tests work consistently, similar to how other services like OpenAI already have their test keys set up.

537da7262e41c2b3153deaff46ba434318c2f83f.text: When the assistant asks helper agents to do things like search code, it now calls them by name using underscores (for example, code_searcher) instead of hyphens. This matters for you only if you watch the assistant's internal tool calls, because the names it sends to those helper agents now match what the underlying AI providers expect, so calls that used to risk being misread will now line up correctly. The old internal nicknames for these agents are still used behind the scenes for bookkeeping, but the names that actually leave the assistant and reach the helper agents now use underscores everywhere they are listed and when results come back.

8ebb2284766ba0abd76aa21b0077a4b2bc319ac6.text: The free coding mode switched back to using the GLM 5.1 assistant instead of the Kimi K2.6 assistant. If you use the free or lite mode of the coding tool, you are now talking to GLM 5.1 again instead of Kimi K2.6. The program tried Kimi briefly, then reverted to GLM 5.1 as the default for these free modes. Anyone who had picked a different model and saved that preference still sees their saved choice the next time they open the tool.

894c58555c70298811bb100eb79190a867c79a13.text: The GLM 5.1 assistant now serves requests through the standard public access hours instead of a private reserved connection that was active all the time. If you use GLM 5.1, your requests will only be processed during Freebuff's published availability hours, even though they are now handled by the shared public system rather than the dedicated one. The private connection itself is turned off and no longer accepts traffic.

fbd3b1e27f7f8ecab654c9e7ca58e5e2557aa928.text: Developers running the app on their own computers can now test the free-tier access gate locally: requests coming from their machine (like 127.0.0.1) are treated as US-allowed when the environment is marked as dev, so they don't need a real country lookup. In production, this path is never used because Cloudflare always supplies a country code. The feature only applies when the local dev flag is set; if your machine isn't marked that way, nothing changes for you. This is already live in the codebase, so developers with the right flag can bypass the country check right now.

362f5d536d5e38b3a744f5c96daba82a0d815412.text: If you're using the GLM 5.1 model, you'll now hit your usage limit sooner. You can still start 5 sessions (meetings with the AI), but they roll off a 12-hour window instead of the previous 20-hour window. So if you've been maxing out your 5 sessions, you'll need to wait a shorter time before slots free up and you can start a new one. The CLI now shows clearer messages about when your oldest session will expire and let you start again.

19bb1512b49bc195eb4ee2a72e73ecf14ca26ba4.text: The assistant can now route requests for the Kimi K2.6 model through CanopyWave, a service that handles pricing and model access. Previously, this model was not available through CanopyWave, but the update adds it alongside pricing details ($0.95 per million input tokens, $0.16 for cached input, and $4.00 per million output tokens). You would notice this change if you tried to use the Kimi K2.6 model and expected it to work through CanopyWave, because now it does instead of falling back to other routing.

b8fada28b29c3dca484789f94f35ad43ebc85bbf.text: When you use the free or lite version of the assistant, it now uses a different AI model called Kimi K2.6 instead of the previous one. This affects everything from the main coding helper to the file finder and code reviewer, so all the free tasks you ask it to do now run through this new model. The new model has the same usage limits as the old one — you can use it for 5 sessions at a time, and each session lasts up to 12 hours. If you open the app today and use the free version, you're already using Kimi K2.6 instead of the older model.

20dc66e496fe49e4981becbf1c5a5839f1584836.text: The assistant you chat with can now switch between two different AI models during internal testing, instead of being locked to one. When testers run the long-running CanopyWave test, they can choose either the default MiniMax model or the kimi model by typing a simple word, and the system will use the right pricing rates for whichever they pick. If someone tries to use a model the system doesn’t know, it will stop and tell them rather than guessing. One of the test scripts is now also set to use the kimi model by default, which can use more of your tokens when it thinks through answers.

e6dbaa57c4631c420cc9490b6751d5d568719e12.text: Small print next to ads now appears in bold instead of a faded style when the ad doesn't include a website link. This only affects the brief labels you might see in the command-line tool. Nothing else changed - the layout and content of the ad banner look the same.

dc84d374a148fa96a6056bf8bccca23e68eca5b9.text: The assistant is now available to help during deployment hours every day instead of only on weekdays. You'll see the schedule now says '9am ET-5pm PT every day' and the time shown is in your local time. This is live today, so if you previously couldn't access the assistant on weekend mornings or afternoons, you can now do so during those hours.

8cfc4b0c1c15bb82cadba7a997f4383b4bd3ac16.text: When you open the app and are placed in the waiting room—the screen shown while you wait for your turn—the app now requests a different kind of ad to display there. The system tells the ad service that this is the waiting-room screen, and the service responds with ads specifically chosen for that spot. The ad shown will look the same interactive style already used in choice-based ads, just pulled from waiting-room-specific placements. This is live today for anyone who sees the waiting room screen.

08c9f24906e3ca2a5798360242009f7f70f5714c.text: The Terms of Service page now shows a newer update date and lists Manicode, Inc. instead of Codebuff, Inc. as the company that owns the trademarks and copyright. If you read the agreement today, you'll see the updated name and the fresh date at the top, plus the correct company name in the section about intellectual property. This change lives on the public website now.

f13eed31aadf22362eae2419ff326f18199b31b6.text: When you use the assistant with lite cost mode, your requests now go through the standard Fireworks API pathway instead of erroring out or relying on custom model deployments. Previously, lite users who encountered deployment hour limits, cooldown periods, or 5xx server errors would get blocked; now the system automatically falls back to the standard API when you're on the lite plan. You wouldn't see this switching happen, but if you're using lite mode and the custom deployment is unavailable, your request will still complete instead of failing with an error. This applies only to web users who have lite cost mode enabled.

fa3c0324cf252ceff341f9dbc08e52dba3e051d5.text: When you open the app and there's no conversation yet, the waiting room now tries one ad network first and, if that can't find an ad to show, automatically tries a second one so you're not left looking at a blank spot. This affects anyone who uses the free tier or lands in the waiting room before their chat starts — you'll just see an ad load instead of a gap, with no action needed on your part. The new double-check behavior is already live.

25f8b89c42ac2c35f0d8d4681987dfe169e3280c.text: When you start using the MiniMax model through the free session system, the server can now let in far more people at the same time before making anyone wait. The limit that decides how many get in immediately was raised from 200 to 1000, so heavy bursts of usage won't trigger the waiting line as quickly. This only affects how the free session system handles MiniMax and does not change how long your session lasts once you're in. The change is live in the server configuration.

2ce07f2db82e2bbb24f2499cc3bdc767670f3d6c.text: If you are using the CodeBuff CLI's free Chat mode and the service determines your location is not eligible, the session now ends cleanly with a clear country-blocked message instead of leaving you stuck waiting. The waiting room releases your spot immediately, and your chat window switches to show the blocked status with your country code, so you stop sending messages into a session that will no longer respond. This is already active for free mode users hitting the country restriction today.

a372554f76118600c0116e7f7d4422c4e8f7e84b.text: When the AI assistant asks another tool to run, it sometimes sends the instructions as one long, messy text string instead of a neatly filled-out form. That confused the system and produced a vague error message instead of a helpful one. Now, the system first tries to tidy that string into the proper form before checking it; if it still can't, it tells you exactly what went wrong so you can fix it. This applies only to the background assistant runtime, not to anything you see in the app's menus or command line.

49b8b2cfa951743de1affca7625fc4165d9a670c.text: The system now quietly checks whether someone signing up for the free tier is likely outside the service's intended English-speaking and western-European audience, by looking at their display name (Chinese/Japanese/Korean characters) or email address (common Chinese providers like qq.com or.edu.cn schools). But it only treats that as a yellow flag when paired with very heavy usage — at least 300 messages in 24 hours, or 500 depending on context — and even then it only nudges the overall abuse score, which is meant as background evidence, not enough to ban someone by itself. Reviewers were also told that being from one of these regions alone shouldn't trigger a ban, since real users from diaspora communities (for example, a Chinese student studying abroad) can trip the same signal, and the

4c3be9e5f60b0c89fb7fa8cb42e5d335d949e375.text: When you open the app and it asks you to pick a project folder, that screen now appears before anything else. Previously, a login screen or a 'please wait' queue could flash in and replace the folder picker, making it look like the app kicked you out. Now, even if your login fails or your session hits a queue, you'll always get to choose your working directory first, and only after that will the app prompt you to sign in or tell you to wait.

2d3a32bd4522b027f88c1460088a2331a540ab22.text: The abuse-detection system now gives a score reduction to GitHub accounts that are at least 1 year old (-20 points) or 3 years old (-40 points), recognizing these as strong counter-signals that indicate a real, established person rather than a temporary bot account. This means a newly created account showing very heavy usage will no longer automatically be flagged as a high-tier threat if it's linked to an old, legitimate GitHub account. The review team was also given updated guidance on not over-flagging established users unless additional suspicious activity is independently detected.

b234a41d2a82101d48b6df162b29f0896fe3a70a.text: The system that watches for suspicious activity on free coding sessions now gives users the benefit of the doubt when their behavior looks human. Instead of only flagging red flags, it also looks for quiet gaps (like a 4+ hour break suggesting sleep) and diverse tool use (real users hop between bash, file picker, code reviewer, etc.; bot farms stick to one). When a suspected bot shows these signs, reviewers see the counter-evidence right alongside the flags and are told to lower their confidence. Live today for the internal team reviewing abuse cases.

a33580f1172d15cc5251c499c83675894751aa40.text: When the abuse-detection system looks at whether a user behaves like a bot, one signal it uses is how long the biggest quiet gap is in their activity over the past day (if you go hours without doing anything, that's a sign you're human, not a bot). Previously, the system only counted gaps between messages, so it might miss a long stretch of inactivity right after a user's account was created or right up to the current moment, especially for brand-new or recently-active users. Now, the system clips the time window to start from the later of the user's account creation time or 24 hours ago, and it also factors in the gap from the last message up to right now, so fresh accounts or users who just stopped being active get credited properly for that quiet time. This is live today in the internal

76c3d44991d7a4d6424bb1d484b73cb453902454.text: When you're using the Freebuff session in the CLI and that session ends, the follow-up suggestion buttons will now turn gray and stop responding to clicks. This prevents you from accidentally triggering actions on a session that's already closed. If you look at the follow-up buttons after your Freebuff session ends, you'll see they're disabled instead of being clickable as they were before.

0706c98b582684fbc935fa4a36f3575f310b5e6c.text: When your chat session ends in the CLI, the software now takes you back to the model selection screen instead of automatically putting you back in the queue. This affects anyone using the command-line interface to interact with an AI model. If you looked, you would see that after a session ends, you are now asked to pick your model again and confirm by pressing Enter, rather than silently rejoining the waiting line.

2e3f02b8ddbf01d0944290ed1180467912f8d048.text: When you end a freebuff session using the /end-session command, instead of being put back in the queue to continue waiting for a model, you are now returned to the model picker screen where you can choose a different model to start a new session. The system now resets your session status to 'none' and shows the model selection screen, so you can pick a new model and manually rejoin the queue by pressing Enter. This change affects users who are using the freebuff mode of the CLI, and it is live today as of the current release.

fb2656966ba564e13d588d8ca0a06658d1e5e422.text: If your account is banned, you'll now see a clear 'Account unavailable' message right away instead of spinning in the waiting room. The system now checks your account status when you try to join, so banned accounts are turned away at the door rather than quietly inflating the queue numbers. You won't be able to enter the queue at all, and the counter you see will no longer jump around when banned accounts are cleaned out.

212bab08e71dc3d7dec495ba7d7e2600c0ec77e2.text: When someone asks to join a free session for a specific AI model, the system now checks how many people are already using that model. If the number is below the model's set limit (for example, 50 for one model or 200 for another), the new person skips the waiting line and starts right away. Only when that limit is reached does the queue kick in. If two people ask at the exact same moment and both see room, the system allows both in even if it slightly exceeds the limit, since the numbers are chosen with extra space to handle that.

de32834c77187d82c06aef4462df5c10149f4546.text: The Terms of Service still describe the exact same service at codebuff.com, but the legal name on the page changed from "Codebuff, Inc" to "Manicode, Inc. (DBA Codebuff)". This is purely a corporate renaming behind the scenes to match the company's actual legal entity. Users will notice nothing about their experience, payments, or access since it only updates how the business is formally identified in the legal text. The change is live now since visitors can read the updated Terms of Service page.

f7c7870d8533395e47d9a3ea1216b0036f9c204c.text: When you're picking which assistant model to use in the CLI, the app now makes sure you can always actually get one -- even if your preferred choice (GLM) is temporarily unavailable due to its scheduled hours. Instead of silently flipping you over and then 'remembering' that fallback forever, it keeps the switch in memory for this session only so your real preference stays saved for next time. The fallback model it lands on is MiniMax M2.7, which is marked as 'always available.' This is now live behavior in the model picker and session joining flow.

8ce2c7174ebedbe8117bf44377c553ceee8be468.text: The system that watches for fake and abusive accounts is now better at telling the difference between a real busy developer and a bot. Instead of flagging heavy users just because they type fast, it pays closer attention to natural human habits: whether someone pauses for at least a few hours between sessions (bots usually don\'t sleep), whether they use a mix of different tools, and how long their linked accounts have existed. This means genuine power users are less likely to get mistakenly blocked, while accounts that act like bots around the clock (roughly 18+ hours of near-constant activity) or pair heavy usage with a brand-new linked account are more likely to be caught. The change is already live and in use today, so the impact is happening now rather than waiting for a future

58e7f306da16d24c097bda7826d08d1444777da7.text: When the system checks who gets to use the free service, it now also kicks out anyone who has been banned, freeing up that spot right away for someone waiting in line. Previously, a banned person kept holding their slot until it naturally expired, blocking others even though they were no longer allowed to use the service. If you watch the queue move, banned users disappear and new users get admitted faster within the same check cycle. This is live today as part of the regular admission process.

08b69435f21d290eebafab30f3bc456f29616697.text: When you open the app and don't have a paid subscription, a small ad banner may appear at the bottom of your screen. Previously, the system sometimes served two different layouts (a single-banner or a multi-choice design), and the code had to decide which one to show. That split has been removed: every non-subscriber now gets the same single ad array pulled from one shared pool, and the banner simply reads whatever list of ads comes back. If you look closely, the ad spot now always behaves the same way instead of occasionally switching between two slightly different presentations.

b0d0e55a348de37244c1edb5c8c97017e573c350.text: The system no longer sends requests for a specific AI model to a particular provider account that was previously handling them. If you tried to use that model, your request would now be routed differently or not at all, since the connection to that account has been turned off behind the scenes.

72afab04704468996fb3c2eef1150ff28633b78e.text: When you open the model selector in a narrow terminal window, the two model buttons now stack on top of each other instead of squeezing side by side. The program checks how wide your screen is and how long each button's text is, and if they wouldn't both fit comfortably, it switches from a horizontal to a vertical layout. Up and down arrow keys now move the highlight between the buttons, so you can navigate without accidentally leaving the selection screen.

938191c3f2cdcda8e5f2613ed2f250a2c8b8ee6e.text: When a Freebuff session ends, the model picker briefly showed "No wait" on every row before refreshing the real queue lengths. Now, right after a session ends, the picker immediately fetches just the up-to-date queue lengths in the background, so you see the correct "N ahead" hints instead of the misleading "No wait" flash. The hint stays blank until the real numbers land, and live queue data is fetched as soon as you pick a model to join. This is live today for Freebuff session users.

46bf7033c9cdd02a76ffed40eab17c2ee9a3c1d9.text: The waiting-room system now logs how many people are actually using each AI assistant model at the same time, rather than a single total number. Previously, all models’ active users were lumped together into one count, making it hard to tell which assistants were busy. You wouldn’t notice this directly unless you watch the server logs or dashboards, but from now on those monitoring tools will show a per-model traffic chart that updates every few seconds, so developers can spot which models are overcrowded. This is live today and affects how the system watches and balances load behind the scenes.

6f2d8fa236055ec7e5f93209d3d93f8808c2eb1f.text: When you now open the assistant in the command-line app before you've joined a queue, instead of seeing a blank shimmering "Joining..." message, you'll see a landing screen that lets you pick which model you want to use right away. Before you pick, the app quietly checks (without reserving anything) how many other people are waiting in front of each model's line, and shows those live counts next to each option so you can pick the shortest wait. Once you choose a model, that's your commitment — you're placed into that model's queue and either start chatting immediately (if no one is ahead of you) or move to the waiting room with a real numbered position. This only affects the pre-join flow: if you're already queued and switch models, the old behavior (losing your spot to rejoin the back of

50f2ade2171191f6369ab907ee04f50cf76f3dfb.text: The assistant picks a model in the command-line menu. Previously each model showed a short description as a trailing hint on the right edge, which forced that hint column to be wide enough for the longest description (so the buttons jumped around less, but left extra blank space for short descriptions). Now that same description appears right next to the model name, and the trailing hint only carries the queue status, so it is fixed to the width needed for 'No wait' or '999 ahead' and no longer stretches to fit any description. You would notice the right-side hint is more predictable and tighter, and the model descriptions now look like 'DeepSeek V3 · Powerful reasoning model' inline instead of sitting in the trailing column.

b3c8862230764bfcb68cdd4001824885c81ee8cb.text: The team added one more AI model called minimax-m2.7 to their internal testing list, so they can now run long-running checks against that model to make sure things keep working smoothly. This only affects the behind-the-scenes testing tools used by the people building the product, not anything you'd see or use today, so nothing changes in your experience right now.

1d89739afa72e15aba869e50191b1be62a0cb290.text: When you're picking which assistant model to wait in line for, keyboard users now use two steps: arrow keys move a highlight to preview a model, and Enter then confirms the switch. This matters because switching lines costs you your spot in the old line — the system re-queues you at the back of the new model's line — so this preview step keeps you from accidentally losing your place just by tabbing too far. Mouse clicks still switch immediately as before. You'll notice a separate highlight that follows your arrow keys without triggering a change until you press Enter.

f953ae68f3b5abf9b56cc7d69b56ecd0e9266e25.text: The web system now knows how to route requests for a newer model version when it needs to call it. You wouldn't see anything new yet, since nothing in the product actually asks for this model today, but the configuration change is live and ready for anyone building or testing internally.

a3087a33f8fffc6f3dbdc169bb6f0c191af8d792.text: When you're waiting in the Freebuff queue (the spot that shows you're in line for a busy AI model), you'll now switch between model buttons with Tab, Shift+Tab, and the Left/Right arrow keys instead of pressing number keys — Up/Down won't accidentally change your selection. The "N ahead", "No wait", and tagline text next to each model stays the same width as the numbers tick down, so buttons no longer shuffle around and jump. The "Wait" label and your wait time on the waiting room screen are now shown in the same muted color as the rest of the labels, so they don't draw extra attention against the other info.

1242b4e38947578ec285e80ed8d498ad170ecd86.text: The token counter — which estimates how long your prompts and replies are — now defaults to counting with the latest assistant model unless you explicitly pick a different one for counting. If you're a developer or power user calling the token-count API from a non-Claude provider, you may notice slightly different totals coming back because the default model used for the math has changed. This is live today, so the next time you call the endpoint without specifying a model, the counts will be calculated using the new default.

b76f9be64e0489961fd31dbb625d9181a9355b1d.text: When you open the command-line app and land in the waiting area, the model picker now sits at the top, directly under the message telling you that you're in the waiting room. Below it, the estimated wait time and other status details are grouped together in their own box with consistent spacing. The picker itself uses the same row-based layout style as the rest of the screen, so the visual separation between choosing a model and reading your status is clearer and easier on the eyes while you wait.

47084a9dee1e018602723f65e34025c41255896d.text: The documentation that explains which AI models power the product has been updated to reflect the actual models currently in use. If you read the guide to what models are used, you will now see Opus 4.7 listed as the main orchestrator model instead of the previous version, and the descriptions of sub-agents (the specialized assistants) now correctly name models like GPT-5.4 for reasoning and Gemini Flash Lite for research. The free usage tier is also now consistently referred to as 'Lite mode' in the docs, and references to the Claude Pro/Max subscription connection feature have been marked as deprecated. No code or features changed — only the published documentation was corrected to match reality.

a51a9349ec1bcbe51bad6bdacccd11215310bff7.text: When you see the waiting room screen in the CLI, the text that shows how long you'll wait no longer has a shimmering animation. Instead of the words 'any moment now' or a formatted wait time animating with a shimmer effect, the text now appears as static, plain text. This affects only the CLI waiting room screen experience.

8c694456f59d1ebdf7c410ea979a0a59596156c3.text: Behind the scenes, the development team updated their internal test setup to stop pretending a field called 'referral code' still exists on user profiles, because that field was already removed from the actual user database. This means nothing changes for you right now, but if you're a developer looking at the test code, you'll notice the fake user profiles no longer include a referral_code line. It's purely housekeeping to keep the tests matching the real data structure.

2118e41fd1ff01f99c589aaa4be5eb359cbcdf06.text: Free sessions handled by Fireworks will now be marked as struggling when their slowest typical response takes longer than half a second, instead of a full second. The system uses this early warning to stop sending new sessions to that backend before most people notice things slowing down. If you watch response times right around the threshold, you'd see the 'degraded' flag appear sooner than before.

dd373b9102d0ec75fe327a1e3b7dcd2b0f654270.text: If you were running the tests that check what happens when someone hits their weekly usage limit or the five-hour session cap, those tests are now given up to fifteen seconds to finish before failing, matching the slower pace these particular checks can take. You wouldn't notice this while using the app itself, but if you are keeping an eye on the development process, any of those limit-related tests that occasionally timed out too quickly will stop reporting failures caused by speed instead of mistakes.

9996bc60d46e06a5738df6d568f147ca937513ab.text: When an account gets suspended, the message it shows no longer mentions billing issues and instead uses a more general wording. This keeps the written guidance in the documentation matching what the service actually tells people who hit that error, so anyone reading the docs sees the same example message they would encounter in the product today.

87c6e90052b803282e0edd7017a42409e9b36784.text: When you hit the subscription limit during a chat, the interface no longer freezes with a stuck "streaming" cursor. The session-ended message now appears correctly and stops the continuous loading indicator, so you can press Enter to rejoin. This restores control during the grace period and prevents the appearance of an unresponsive session.

20e84ced412bc793ededb64af3c50bca6765fe5b.text: The internal test account team@codebuff.com can now skip the waiting room that normally queues free sessions, so automated tests run by that account won't get delayed or fail when the waiting room is active. The system now checks whether the logged-in user's email is on a special bypass list and, if so, treats the session as if the waiting room were turned off entirely. This is live today for only that one account and prevents test flakiness during CI runs; no other accounts or real users are affected.

bf7bf87c62b0dba407d2ee2b03899d2c7ec13677.text: When you and other free-trial users start a chat, the system now checks how slow the "waiting line" feels for the slowest 10% of people instead of the typical (median) case — and it stops letting new people in earlier, when the tail is still only mildly slow, so your queue time is less likely to climb into the seconds. The threshold also changed: the system now flags a problem once that slowest-decile wait nears about one second instead of when the average wait tops just a tenth of a second. This behavior is live now in the free-session area of the app; you'd notice it as the assistant occasionally becoming unavailable sooner under heavy load, rather than staying open until waits are already long.

2dee392b72ade5fa5f5da75c8c821c8bc8c2b96c.text: When your account gets suspended while using the chat service, you'll now see a clearer message that simply says your account has been suspended, rather than explicitly mentioning billing issues. The behind-the-scenes code that routes chat requests was also cleaned up to fix messy formatting, but this doesn't change how the service works. You wouldn't notice any difference in functionality, but if your account is suspended, the error message you see will be slightly different.

234adfdc33d52adb8e03da558d111ef5755d7630.text: If you join the free session waiting room, the time shown next to your spot now counts down using roughly 24 seconds for each person ahead of you instead of a full minute per spot. This only adjusts the little estimate you see while you wait; it does not change how fast spots actually open up. The waiting room is still limited to free sessions and is gated by the CLI, so only people starting a free (Lite) session through that entry point reach this queue. This estimate is live today.

6736dfa66d6bf15eb812a131068343af0029f59d.text: Starting today, when you open your chat history in the CLI, your session no longer gets deleted or dropped back to the waiting room afterward. Previously, viewing your history would unmount the underlying surface that keeps your session alive, which erased your session record and forced you back into the waiting room upon return. Now the history screen renders inside the same surface that holds your session, so the session stays mounted and intact while you browse. This affects anyone using the CLI to access chat history, and you'll notice the app no longer kicks you out or resets your session after viewing past conversations.

e0ba3a65c9a4f579af2ffd0f2ed6342ef0513646.text: When you're waiting in the free-tier session queue, the app now shows a wait estimate of about one minute for each person ahead of you in line, instead of trying to match the actual backend processing speed. If you're in position 2, you'd see roughly one minute; position 5 shows about four minutes, and so on. The estimate no longer reflects real-time system delays, like when the service pauses admissions during an incident, so it's a simplified rule-of-thumb meant to feel more human-friendly than a technical countdown. This change is live today for free-tier (Lite mode) users in the web app's waiting room.

9278d13d86080c3293753ec84c110db59e73deab.text: You no longer get disconnected when asking a really deep-thinking AI question that takes a while before it starts streaming an answer. The system used to give up after 10 minutes of waiting for the first response, but now it waits up to 30 minutes for OpenAI, Fireworks, OpenRouter, Canopywave, and SiliconFlow models. If you looked, you'd see the same setting changed from 10 minutes to 30 minutes across the five provider setups. This change is live today.

c0061ed43bee434c65385d84134b8f5dd2b1dd6c.text: The system that watches server responsiveness just got more cautious: it now flags slowdowns as 'degraded' when the wait time before answering a question hits 125 milliseconds, down from 200. This doesn't change how fast the assistant answers, but it makes the internal monitoring react sooner when demand rises, so overloaded conditions show up earlier in operational dashboards. You wouldn't notice this directly, but if you peek at the backend health panels, the 'degraded' status will light up a bit sooner during busy periods.

1b47ff6b79bfe5516520bd9bc28dee1c2a2c21c2.text: The system that checks whether our AI service is working properly now uses stricter rules to decide what counts as a problem. When the system tests itself to make sure it's healthy, it pretends there are fewer pending requests in its queue before calling it 'good' - specifically half as many as before. This means the test data has been adjusted to match the tighter standards, so the system won't incorrectly report itself as healthy when the queue starts backing up sooner. You wouldn't notice this directly, but it helps keep the service reliable by catching problems earlier.

504f80c1ed8afbd7081ff99a1932d9757ff74cdf.text: The promotional banner that used to appear at the top of the website has been taken down, so you'll no longer see that strip of marketing text when you visit the homepage or any page on the site. This is a behind-the-scenes removal of a visual element that was being shown to everyone who viewed the web pages, and it is already live today.

3888bda6dbbd4b0dd55364e5781ae9d17b2661b5.text: If you run a waiting-room flow, the system now records how many people are actively in a session on a steady loop, not just when the number jumps. Those recordings show up as their own chartable stream tagged for waiting-room metrics, so you can watch queue depth and active usage move together in the log aggregator. The change is live today for anyone going through the free-session admission flow.

59640d5c70dd5863abcdf66110b1b7247c66af05.text: If you use the service, you may notice the system now flags slowdowns and memory pressure sooner than before, so requests can be held back or redirected before they start feeling slow. Internally, the thresholds that trigger those early warnings were lowered, meaning the system reacts to smaller delays and tighter memory use. Nothing about your access or features has changed.

eeffc4f2b7cd78031922b0fd8b22c77f57557e4f.text: Two background tests that occasionally caused the automated checks to fail unpredictably have been temporarily turned off. If you run or watch the chat completion test suite, those two specific scenarios will now skip instead of running. This only affects internal testing; no live feature or subscriber behavior changed.

528904b505179630fec4697946d63df856a51e4c.text: Two background checks that simulate a person editing code and running shell commands have been turned off so they no longer run automatically. Those checks were also given a longer wait time before giving up, increasing the grace period from two minutes to fifteen. If you opened the test dashboard today, those two checks would appear grayed out and skipped rather than passing or failing. The change only affects the automated monitoring system; nothing a person sees in the product itself has changed.

79becb7d0014169ea4b07db5f350afbcb8d29669.text: The status bar now shows a countdown of your free session when the assistant isn't actively working, so you can see how much time you have left (for example, '1h 30m left') and it turns orange when time is about to run out. This affects anyone using the free tier of the service; previously the timer was hidden during idle periods, and now you'll notice the remaining time appears directly in the status bar at the bottom of the screen. The change is live today.

4d6e4c343641ea3c6e8789ac8dee87eb5c35233e.text: The automated system that double-checks the software still works end-to-end now gives itself more time to finish its checks before it gives up and reports a failure. You might notice that tests which used to time out and fail prematurely are now completing successfully, since the time limit was doubled from ten minutes to twenty, and longer-running checks get an even bigger allowance. This is a behind-the-scenes adjustment to the testing machinery, not a change to the software you use.

d79dc99d54cde0766206015a188840cb46678613.text: If you run a script today, it will talk to a test database by default. You can now tell it to talk to the real production database instead by wrapping the command with a special prefix that switches the environment, and you should still prefer read-only queries. Without this prefix, scripts always stay on the test data, so nothing you run will reach production unless you explicitly opt in.

5c0c0ac2515c4c1ca066fa70a22ddb4d3a4c0edf.text: The assistant no longer checks whether you have a paid account or have been signed up for at least three days before handling a chat request that uses the non-free mode. Paid subscribers and bring-your-own-key users can now run those requests right away, even on a brand-new account, whereas previously a new or unpaid account would get a 403 error asking you to wait or upgrade. This is in effect today across the completions endpoint.

060eb553eefe78c2d477e7363dfda2e3750aceb8.text: If you use the service on the Free Lite plan for Fireworks chat sessions, you may now see the system flag your session as 'degraded' a bit sooner when the wait time before your response starts getting generated gets longer. Instead of waiting nearly a full second in line before the system considers performance slipping, it now reacts after about six tenths of a second. This is internal monitoring logic, so it doesn't change how fast your chat actually responds, but it might affect when you see status warnings or when the team gets alerted to slowing servers.

1401668addb1c937cbb5763314294f47f4c8abd1.text: The automated checks that confirm the assistant works correctly now wait roughly eleven days instead of three minutes before giving up, so they stop falsely reporting failures during long-running tasks. This affects only the internal testing process; you will not see faster or slower responses, and nothing about your experience changes.

553387c77c78e9f73dad13f01aa76605030008f4.text: When you use a free agent, it now keeps its conversation notes cached for twice as long (10 minutes instead of 5), so you don't lose context as quickly between steps if you pause. Free users will also notice less leftover clutter, since the system quietly removes extra prompt tags that used to stick around during pruning. If you're on a paid plan, your agent still uses the default 5-minute cleanup window, so nothing changes for you today.

9e0bca43b9da195068a60d936e04e5484f05be61.text: If you're using Codebuff for free, the assistant will no longer automatically bring in a separate AI helper that uses Google's Gemini model to tackle tricky coding problems with files. Instead, free users will rely on the other built-in assistants already available to them. This change simply turns off that one optional helper for the free plan, while paid users and the rest of the system continue to work as before.

c341c025a0db4f1cf4c9586cee95aac61c126d2d.text: The internal assistant that counts how many lines are in a file was slightly wrong. For most files the count was fine, but for empty files it showed zero lines instead of one, so anything relying on that count for empty files got the wrong number. The fix makes the empty-file case report one line, matching the rest of the software. It is live today in the internal version of the assistant.

117cc3de13ecae4863068f4d4870ab01f60d8c25.text: Free accounts can no longer request expensive models like Opus while pretending to use free mode, which previously let them bypass billing checks and get costly responses at no charge. Going forward, an unpaid account that tries to set the request to 'free' must also pick an agent and model that are on the short allowlist; anything else is rejected with a 403 error before the request reaches the rate limiter or the model provider, and the failed attempt is recorded for review. This restriction is live today and applies to any free-tier account attempting to exploit the loophole.

07d2d7853bef1571195a1a9b051db169561ba40a.text: Behind the scenes, the team gave the subscription-limit tests extra time to finish on busy machines. Tests that verify subscriber access checks were failing just past the five-second mark, so the allowed window was doubled to fifteen seconds. This is internal test maintenance only; if you looked, you would see longer timeouts on the subscription enforcement checks, and you would not notice anything different in the product today.

506c5ab18679267f9ef76a9051f1f4943cf7f0cd.text: If you are a developer using this system to build apps, your code checks (a kind of testing tool) now run without errors related to a missing field on the fake user data used during testing. The testing utilities that simulate a user now include the account creation date field, which was previously missing and causing type errors. This only affects your local development and testing work, not anything your end users see.

c7e2926787e8a817c260246ce75dfdb89a6c7c0d.text: If an AI response you're getting cut off early—say, the connection drops or the AI hiccups mid-response—the system used to potentially skip charging you for the tokens already generated. Now, it captures the generation ID from the first response chunk and, after stream ends, waits 500ms before looking up the final cost from OpenRouter's records to ensure billing is still recorded. Developers reviewing the code would notice the StreamState type now tracks generationId, model, and billed status, with fallbackBillFromGeneration handling the delayed cost lookup.

9f3f274bf654c394f76472e10eec2f5b683bbf6e.text: The chat completions endpoint now accepts requests from free mode users, bypassing paid relationship and account age validation. Free mode users can now make requests to the chat completions API without needing a paid account or meeting the minimum account age requirement. If you looked at the code, you'd see a new conditional check that skips the paid relationship and account age validation when the request comes from free mode.

b992bec00d24351d7915f3ffb7ca9cf0c449f546.text: The automated checks that make sure the chat completion endpoint behaves correctly were crashing because two fields in the test data didn't match the expected shape. The developers corrected the test fixture so the fake billing object now declares its 'breakdown' and 'principals' maps as explicitly empty dictionaries, letting the suite compile and run. This is internal reliability work: nothing changes for you, but the team can trust their tests again.

61914917527ec0b8842fe3a015e34c957b4e3578.text: If you send a chat-api request using the email team@codebuff.com, the system lets your request through even before you have paid or waited three days for your account to mature, so the company's own integration tests can hit a real server without buying a subscription for every fresh test account. Today, any request not coming from that address still has to clear the pay-and-wait gate; the bypass only applies to that single email address.

bd3cface754bc88769a451f1b6f9ee4d2c74fe04.text: The test versions of the system's example user accounts now include a fake signup date of January 1, 2024. You wouldn't notice this yourself since it only affects internal testing files, not the live application. The testing tool flagged that these sample users were missing a date field that the system expects, so adding it stops the tests from producing confusing errors about missing information.

24c7a015a526af5c874f809a96ea1740a7c9c337.text: When someone signs up for a new account, they will no longer automatically receive free credits added to their balance. The signup process now skips the step that used to grant a set number of credits to new users, so brand-new accounts start at zero. People who already have accounts keep whatever credits they had before.

8f5254f7269d7dabb514d76c63f7eca69169a77d.text: The agent now gently suggests loading skills instead of making it a strict requirement. When you work with the assistant, it will look at what skills it needs, load them, and remember not to load the same ones again during your chat. You won't notice the change unless you're paying close attention to how the assistant handles its tools.

23efc014d99ccc747103b54a721bc28a356ce881.text: The assistant now uses a newer model version across all its default settings, so tasks run through the agent system will use the updated model instead of the previous one. If you interact with an integrated agent (such as the editor or thinker agents), you are affected. You would not notice anything visual, but the underlying model name changed in the configuration.

63db864d994664afaa6b0b01b5a4a4a08fd14e88.text: When someone signs up using a friend's referral link on Freebuff, neither person will anymore receive 500 free credits as a thank-you for bringing in new users. Referrals made through shared links will still be recorded so the platform can see who referred whom, but the actual credit rewards that used to be granted automatically have been turned off. This appears to be a response to cases where people created multiple accounts just to earn and then burn large amounts of free credits, and the company is now shifting away from relying on credits altogether in favor of Freebuff's credit-free model.

c1a63d8422c1b138b8a61e0dc27083b1f6145c4e.text: If you sign up for a new account today and immediately try to use advanced AI features that cost money, the service will now stop you unless you have a paid subscription or purchase history. Accounts must be at least three days old and linked to a real payment method to use anything beyond the free tier. People who provide their own AI service key (BYOK) skip this check entirely, since they're paying their own bill directly.

6aa4eb23f3ad33ab5334eb8305474fec2d34772d.text: When you ask a specific AI model through the internal system, it can now think through problems more carefully before replying, rather than always working at a medium level of effort. You don't need to do anything different: if you've already told the system to use more thorough reasoning, it will apply that; otherwise it keeps working the way it did before. Nothing changes for you today, but the system is now ready to support deeper think-throughs if that setting is turned on later.

0ff352d7420c8d8f9ffacdaea9e6b4568875c06a.text: When you chat with the assistant, it now knows which underlying engine is powering its responses, and that fact is stated right up front in its opening instructions. The assistant picks one of two engines depending on your selected mode and injects that engine's name into its system prompt. If you look at the conversation, you'd see a new line near the top that reads, "You are running on the [engine name] model," telling you exactly which version is active for that session.

fbb215c3b394bb8f70c501c7bbd24017a8bf0ae4.text: The internal test harness now includes the new kimi-k2.5 model in its long-context compatibility tests, and the assistant's backend now knows how to route requests for that model to a dedicated, pre-warmed deployment instead of the shared default. Only internal staff running these compatibility checks will notice the difference. The change limits its effect to internal testing and backend routing configuration.

c9a72f15599f448ed43719b0e9b4029bc1776138.text: The assistant's Fireworks integration will now always try the custom deployment path for all 24 hours in a day, rather than only attempting it during business hours (10am–8pm ET). Users of the web package's Fireworks API requests may notice more consistent behavior from the custom deployment fallback throughout the day. The system now logs 'Trying Fireworks custom deployment' instead of including the '(business hours)' qualifier.

c61e5d17a254cc80aac896edc1a7cb3472e41f83.text: The system's record of which database update to run at a particular step was pointing at the wrong file, so the update mechanism could not match it to the correct instructions. It now points at the file that actually exists, so when the system synchronizes its data structure it will apply the intended changes instead of failing or skipping them. This is behind-the-scenes maintenance that does not change any feature you see, but it prevents the update process from tripping over itself. The fix is live today.

d3bc905a3237c8ce84de761f6696803e8a40f840.text: The free version of the tool now uses a different AI model — GLM 5.1 instead of MiniMax M2.5 — so if you open the app or read its help pages, you'll see that name where MiniMax used to appear. The change is already live in the website and documentation, and the speed claim on the home page was also adjusted from up to 10× faster to up to 5× faster, but the actual coding experience for free users is otherwise unchanged.

c85611b367fb131b85f917fc943799d54363f43d.text: The system that finds and loads your custom instruction files now has a set of automated checks to make sure it keeps working correctly. These checks verify that it still looks in all the right spots (like your home folder and the project you're working on), follows the right override rules when duplicate instructions exist in multiple places, and gracefully skips broken or invalid files instead of crashing. This is a behind-the-scenes quality improvement for the development tools — you won't see a new feature, but it reduces the chance of surprises when the system reads your instruction files.

6a1ef293a535c2af8503668e8839ca95ccd36009.text: The system now runs more of its nightly evaluation tests at the same time, so the backlog of checks finishes sooner behind the scenes. If you monitor internal dashboards, the automated testing runs will show a higher number of tasks completing in parallel, which is why those scheduled checks wrap up faster each day.

a334a46deccf5e1caa990d649db6a232f453e1d8.text: The automated system that scores our internal test results was upgraded to use newer versions of its two main judging models, swapping in GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet-4.6 in place of the previous GPT-5.1 and Sonnet-4.5. Only people running these internal evaluation jobs will see any difference: the latest scoring results will now be produced by the new models instead of the old ones. Along with the model swap, the two nightly scoring jobs now cap how many tests they run at the same time to a slightly lower number, so they will pace themselves a little more conservatively. These changes are live today for anyone running the internal test harnesses.

b702ab96f9e87defdfd18594f0f494e9d284e1f5.text: When you chat with the Librarian agent that clones and explains a GitHub repo, or with the Tmux CLI agent, and with the free-tier editor/reviewer assistants, the system is now swapping in a newer model called Minimax M2.7 instead of M2.5. You won't notice a flashy difference, but the agents you interact with in free mode (the base orchestrator, the lite editor, and the lite code reviewer) are now pulling answers from this updated model, so responses may read a bit more smoothly or accurately. The change is live today for anyone using those free-mode agents.

bec1d40804df694a6030c2f9900084e5ef5cfdb6.text: The web app can now use the MoonshotAI Kimi K2.5 assistant as an option, alongside the other assistants you can switch between. It is live today, so you might see it show up in the list of available assistants when picking one. The cost for each usage unit has also been set up behind the scenes, so this new assistant counts as a real, priced option rather than a placeholder.

4965185c1a82c6cd29e55d5556c6308ceb2defb6.text: Agents can now use a new model called Minimax M2.7, which is the latest version replacing the older M2.5 model. If you looked at the system settings, you'd see pricing details showing that using this model costs money: 30 cents per million input tokens, 6 cents for cached inputs, and 1.20 for every million output tokens. The assistant now recognizes M2.7 as a valid choice and can route calls to the correct backend automatically.
