aaebab6ba804107ea5fc2277c287fb14d348b7b6.text: The project now sets a single, fixed version of React's typing helpers at the top level, instead of letting each sub-project point back to that same version. If you looked at the project files, you would no longer see duplicate version rules scattered in the web and freebuff/web folders. This is in place starting today and only affects people building or maintaining this codebase, not anyone using the published app. It just keeps dependency resolution simpler and more reliable behind the scenes.

f29ccc3e1876a5708f2589aaaa6ba667af47ce31.text: If you use the free version of the assistant through a base2 agent today, your requests are now being processed by a new underlying service called inceptron/fp8 instead of the previous fireworks service. You won't notice anything different in how the assistant behaves or responds, since both services handle the same free-tier model, minimax-m2.5. The change only affects the back-end routing for free-tier users and doesn't add new features or alter your access.

17612d804f3826973857304988d4c6cd08a0b322.text: When you ask the assistant to explore a codebase, the step-by-step guidance it follows no longer tells it to launch separate helper agents for searching files or browsing folders. Instead, the assistant can now use the search, folder-listing, and pattern-matching tools directly itself, which makes those searches faster and avoids relying on helper agents that were removed. If you looked at the instructions, you would simply see fewer agent names mentioned and more direct use of the built-in search tools.

ee5e984f9b354d71352cbca1ef9453fcb1e94ea4.text: When you use the command-line assistant, the space between each line of output — whether it's text, an image, or a tool result — is now always the same. Before, different kinds of lines were spaced using separate, hard-coded margins, which sometimes made the display look uneven. The software now uses a single, built-in spacing rule on every container, and the old custom spacing logic was deleted. You'd notice that lines no longer jump or crowd each other, and the layout stays consistent as new content scrolls in.

db37b85cf3e0e64e0beab185886ea30fc43b2dde.text: When you look at a side-by-side comparison of two files in the terminal, any extra blank lines at the very top or bottom of the panel are now gone. The tool that draws the comparison quietly discards that stray spacing before printing the lines, so the diff you see starts and ends on actual file content. This only affects that on-screen comparison viewer in the CLI; it doesn't change the files themselves or when the comparison runs.

d0b522ba55ee7857e935292f29ecffe9fccb4355.text: Your coding assistant now always sends its most advanced reasoning model (Opus) to a specific, trusted provider instead of letting the system pick any available one. This provider has its own copy of the assistant's instructions, so the assistant no longer waits while those instructions are sent over again with every message, which previously caused delays and wasted time. If you use a project that relies on this advanced model, your tasks will run faster and more reliably. Other assistants you might use (like the GPT-5 or Sonnet-based ones) are not affected by this change.

ac11f0809762c0c450be227d08607f5a698b5fa9.text: When you're using the CLI and messages are streaming in from the assistant, any blank lines that show up at the very beginning or very end of a message are now automatically removed before you see them, so the text doesn't appear to jump around as it loads. Previously, only blank lines at the very end of a message were being cleaned up. This makes the display look a bit tidier while messages are still coming in.

9fa5e732e6003051c79304b62761a3b2e3253f10.text: The tool the team uses to debug why prompt caching sometimes fails now sorts the snapshots by run by default, so it can isolate instability in the conversion layer from intentional cache-marker shifts. You can still compare across all runs with --cross-run or filter to a single run with --run <id>. When you run it, you'll see the run IDs compared and a new line showing the first message index where structural differences appear after stripping cache_control fields, instead of just saying messages differ.

7dc3fb96a92c35a2ac7703f2fb11359a12f6e7a9.text: When you ask the assistant to track a list of tasks, each item now lines up with a touch more space after its checkbox or checkmark. You'd notice the checked and unchecked items sit a bit more cleanly apart from their text. The change lands purely in how those todo lines are padded, so everything you type still behaves the same; only the alignment looks a little smoother.

580d90521384fa40268af32eead85438fd65abf3.text: Starting today, free-tier users can now use the assistant's built-in tools for searching code, browsing files and folders, and matching file patterns, which were previously locked behind a paid plan. If you are on the free tier, you will simply see these tools available when you open the assistant instead of them being hidden or grayed out. The assistant will also stop filtering out its own advanced helper tools in the free experience, and it cleans up old configuration that used to track who was allowed to use what.

a6026d1f5fb63b6f0ee4d122e95c05ba6a329e62.text: Starting today, people using the free version of the service can no longer use the two tools that let them draft and suggest changes to files. If you are on the free tier and try to use those tools, they won't be available to you. Only people on paid plans still have access to them.

a5aa4a5044ac3d47e494cebb025253ff215d43a3.text: When the assistant is configured for cache debugging, the system now records how many input, output, and cached tokens each step uses, so the snapshot file includes actual usage numbers instead of just request details. If you're collecting these debug snapshots to investigate caching, you'll now see cache hit rates and token breakdowns directly in the comparison report. This only applies to runs that pass a cache debug correlation ID, which is an opt-in behavior, so it doesn't affect standard assistant sessions.

ed1100f857836154e655880272ece2b2e033d3fb.text: The Freebuff assistant used to offer a /init command that created a knowledge file for you. It's now gone, so if you looked for that shortcut while chatting you wouldn't find it. The program still supports its other slash commands like /help and /new, and you can still work with a knowledge file manually if you need one.

a73857232d3ab61ed1d12790ecac5399f92ac92e.text: When you use the free version of the assistant, it now does simple tasks one at a time (like searching files, listing folders, and finding matching files) instead of splitting them off to specialized helper tools that could run at the same time. This avoids confusion when multiple tools try to work in parallel. If you are on the free tier today, the assistant simply handles these basic chores directly rather than delegating them.

ee320c3b975f1f75f073ec2c4d3752c18e3ca04b.text: When the system checked that its settings were valid, it tried to read an error report the wrong way and failed. The fix corrected how that error report is read so the system can now properly log a warning and stop safely instead of crashing. This affects anyone whose settings are missing or misconfigured when the app starts. If you looked right after this change, you'd see a clean, readable warning message in the log instead of a cryptic crash error.

b2c27168a27cc9da6a838be38d1b8c7a5b304718.text: If you run the free version of the assistant, you can no longer pass a starting prompt or pick a specific agent from the command line - the program now waits for you to type your request in the chat instead of taking it as an argument. The paid version keeps all those options, so only Freebuff users lose the ability to launch it with a preset prompt or clear old logs with a flag. --continue and --cwd still work for both versions. This change is live now, not something coming later.

43afde76e2a2f2d85fb5a1d72361df54fab988ae.text: When an assistant replies piece by piece instead of all at once, the system used to announce that a message was being prepared too early, before the reply was fully ready, which meant debugging tools sometimes logged incomplete information. The announcement now waits until the reply is finished, so debugging logs capture the complete, final message. This affects developers who use the SDK's streaming feature to build apps where the assistant responds in real time.

560f0ace43a7e2bcf5eebbfa7bb838503e411aef.text: You run a smart assistant that remembers what it was just thinking by caching parts of its conversations. In the live version of the software that runs that cache, a setting that would normally cause the system to write out a detailed journal of every cache lookup is now turned off, so the cache stops leaving those trace logs behind. That switch is flipped only in the production version of the software—the one actually running right now—so you wouldn't see those verbose cache logs in your current session.

f90fbb70c5b64cfcee458e25288cefd6c935f149.text: When you use the Freebuff version of the command-line tool and open the list of slash commands, you will no longer see entries for switching between modes (like mode:chat or mode:code). Those mode options are only generated and shown in versions that are not Freebuff, so Freebuff users get a shorter command list without the mode-switching shortcuts.

a45e5363c132b97909f6a97060e9b53ec65800ba.text: A new shortcut command was added to the project's build instructions that lets internal developers start up the Freebuff command-line tool for local testing with a single command. It only affects the internal development workflow and does not change any user-facing feature or behavior.

417b5ba3a4297703716d4e72791ed38dbadff99d.text: When you expand a block of the assistant's reasoning in the CLI, the text now shows with its original line breaks intact instead of being run together on one line. You only see this when you open a collapsed thinking section to read the full content; the short preview that stays collapsed still removes line breaks. The fix rewrites extra blank lines into a single blank line so the formatting looks correct without dumping huge gaps.

3c5f2b81ef5375c90a218b0d6e3e65cf58a14229.text: The team updated the tool that creates official release posts on GitHub to use its newest version. This affects every release you make through the automated system, across the CLI and npm applications. If you looked, you'd see the release-publishing steps now rely on the updated tool, which aligns with GitHub's current runtime requirements. It's live today and is a behind-the-scenes maintenance change that keeps the release process stable.

cfb6cbe07b75cbef94ddc92ea79b9c7b5a9d3adc.text: The guide for new developers joining the project now spells out exactly which secret keys and settings they must fill in before the software will even start locally. Previously the setup notes told contributors to copy a template file, but left them to guess which fields actually mattered; now they're listed one by one, along with reminders that the development server must be restarted to pick up the changes and that an OpenRouter key needs real account credits or it will flatly refuse to pay for model calls.

f658c35076ea52904412b671e168fdc382cba0ed.text: The behind-the-scenes automation that builds and tests the software has been updated to work with the latest version of its underlying platform. If you looked at the project's build configuration files, you'd notice references to newer versions of the tools it uses. This is routine maintenance that keeps things running smoothly and securely, similar to updating the engine in your car so it stays compatible with modern fuel and parts. You won't see any visible difference in the software itself, but it ensures the team's automated processes continue to function correctly.

2237ce99e973141912d251e90ea69144dd78e772.text: When an AI agent tries to save a file and it runs into a problem, it shows an error message to let you know what went wrong. This fix makes sure that error message actually displays the correct details instead of showing an empty or unclear message. It affects the behind-the-scenes process that handles file-saving actions in the agent runtime. If you use a tool or feature that writes files on your behalf, you'll now get a clearer explanation when something goes wrong.

af94dfb0e1b78acf86e55af4df5e8717ebdf8a7a.text: When you run the command that publishes your work, the system now checks exactly where the word 'publish' appears in your command instead of searching anywhere in the whole list of words. This stops accidental triggers if 'publish' shows up as a value inside another option rather than as the main action you intended. You'd notice this if you previously saw publishing start unexpectedly when 'publish' appeared as part of a flag value. It's live today.

9a6cc9d95123a1587958dc38f95415b5b3ca2854.text: When the software starts up, it now gives you a clearer, more helpful message if something is misconfigured in your environment settings instead of throwing a raw error that's hard to understand. The message also prints the specific details of what went wrong to the screen. Additionally, the guide now explains how to create your own custom AI workflows using a setup command. This applies to anyone running the software who encounters environment setup issues, and you'd notice the difference if the program fails to start due to a configuration problem.

a15b697b15ce465ef6b795a5579b534b9ae4a5ac.text: When the assistant asks a connected tool to describe what information it needs from you, that description used to come back blank whenever the tool's request form was built with certain advanced layout rules (specifically the allOf, anyOf or oneOf keywords) rather than a simple list of named fields. The assistant now inspects the whole request form and will correctly surface the parameters even when those advanced rules are used, so you're no longer shown an empty 'None' in place of the tool's actual expected inputs. This fix is live in the agent runtime package today.

a54e61b66c6f64af8e61791d106c8548222a6b3d.text: When the system is collecting detailed logs for debugging, it used to risk stopping everything if that logging step hit an unexpected error. Now, if that logging step fails, the system simply skips it and keeps running normally. You wouldn't notice anything different unless something went wrong with the debugging logs, and even then, the system would just quietly continue instead of breaking.

54c1386d5622b034b8a26ec4280e9cddf87bd27c.text: The web app's core interface library was rolled back a version to fix type errors that were causing problems during development. The affiliate dashboard's form now shows loading states correctly by passing the pending flag down to the submit button instead of checking it indirectly. Type resolution for the database ORM tools was fixed across three configuration files to point to the correct shared location. If you look at the affiliate page, the 'Set Handle' button will now properly show 'Setting Handle...' while the action is running, and developers will see fewer confusing type errors when working with the database layer.

19d1cd67d2075b8e47c0f4889bd4898715ce399e.text: When you run the assistant, it can now check a new toggle that switches it into a 'free-only' mode. This toggle is read the same way as the other configuration settings the assistant already uses, so it will work consistently in both real use and in the test environment. The change is already in place today.

de29db72df8d9fd2823f92a936f99b6bac42a972.text: When you download Freebuff software through the system, it now correctly fetches files from the Freebuff release folder instead of the Codebuff one, preventing mix-ups between the two products. This affects anyone downloading Freebuff releases through the platform. If you looked at the download links being generated, you would see they now use "freebuff-v" instead of just "v" in the URL for Freebuff files.

c4d97b201a80accb2dde5134ef53f656386fe287.text: The web app team cleaned up how the site's design system is stitched together, removing an unnecessary piece of the puzzle that was causing TypeScript to throw confusing errors about shared internal code. The site's appearance settings now get their configuration shapes from the component library itself instead of a separate type definition, and the TypeScript setup was taught new shortcuts to find shared internal modules without relying on a direct dependency that wasn't supposed to be there. If you looked at the site today, everything still works the same, but this behind-the-scenes cleanup means future changes to the design system are less likely to break the build or trigger type-related errors.

27d4960d7467b1464a50fcd89fe28c759356e3de.text: Folders that store individual coding tasks now get created without a colon (:) in their name. If an assistant follows the standard checklist of steps, you would see folder names like "03-03-0909-add-console-log" instead of "03-03-09:09-add-console-log". The colon was removed because it can cause problems on some computer file systems, so the naming rule was changed to avoid it.

5d98e790131598e3f38f2b43031e10e4d3a8bf5e.text: When you use the free tier of the Base2 agent, your requests are now always sent to the Fireworks provider instead of potentially bouncing among different providers. This locks the free path to one specific model routing, which also blocks that provider from collecting data about your usage. If you pay for access, nothing changes for you: you still get the default provider selection and the Claude Opus model, exactly as before. The change is live today for anyone using the Base2 agent under the free tier.

8a449e81a4a8062056d71cc8c03ee08d19e4520d.text: If you open the tips page that compares your personal coding preferences to project-specific settings, the side-by-side chart now displays correctly instead of showing raw formatting symbols. The fix wraps that one table in new markup so your browser renders the rows and columns neatly. Only readers of that single documentation page notice the change.

f09f86cba11df88d5c46a3f10971c631dc5b5893.text: The assistant has been switched to a newer model for thinking through hard problems and reviewing code. The previous model name was dropped from the instructions; the assistant now tells itself to use the new model when it needs to reason carefully. If you watched the assistant's internal plan, you'd see it call on a different specialist agent for complex steps. This is live today for the assistant's own decision-making, not something you toggle yourself.

a051d6395f9ebd84f1dcfc5c5c1e4fa534ec5b33.text: The table that compares when to use your personal settings file versus your project settings file now has evenly spaced columns, so the text lines up neatly from row to row. This only affects how the documentation looks in the source file; the published page already displayed correctly and continues to do so. Nothing about how the files work or what they control has changed.

b1957203eeb51dba493a545f238baa672aadde9c.text: The built-in helper that searches your project for relevant files now uses a newer, faster Google AI model instead of the previous Grok model. You may notice slightly quicker results when that file-search helper scans directories, especially in its thorough mode; the standard mode stays the same. This rolls out today for anyone using that file finder inside the agent tools.

de5a6d9cdd7d30b6066ea2b967cd176051dab988.text: All requests to count how many tokens a message uses are now always routed through Anthropic's method, even if the model belongs to another provider. You would notice this only if you were measuring token counts programmatically against the API, where previously some provider-specific models may have used a different counting path. This is live today as a behind-the-scenes switch with no visible impact to end users.

b493ab53110787a9c1cc7a02faf624ed4368a8f9.text: The system that manages your AI assistant settings now recognizes the newest versions of popular AI models (GPT-5.3, Claude-4.6, Gemini-3, Grok-4.1, GLM-5) plus a couple of other updated options. Older, outdated model names were removed. You probably won't notice this directly, but agents that get updated soon can now choose these newer models when you pick which AI you'd like to run a task. This is in place today and ready to enable those model options moving forward.

f845d424d49d74b5c3664eeedd402cea4b09bac0.text: The assistant now has an option to skip its final 'lessons learned' step, where it normally writes a takeaways file and updates its knowledge base after finishing a task. This only affects the version used to run coding competitions and evaluations, which turns that option on, so those runs stop one step earlier without writing the lessons file. If you looked at one of those runs, you'd notice it ends after validating results and never produces the lessons document.

69b64047d85d7aa17986b3d7ec47aa1af35ad0f6.text: The AI assistant now leaves any of your other ongoing work in the repository untouched instead of accidentally undoing it when it gets a new task. A new reminder in its instructions explicitly tells it to preserve unrelated changes sitting in your git status. The helper also tightens the rules for the shared tips it saves for future use: only broadly useful insights make the cut, and it now strictly avoids writing anything tied to the specific feature or run just completed, so the saved knowledge stays relevant across many different situations. The guidance is part of the assistant's base instructions today.

59d88d23d299030c7f9dc5af8cb47c79c3e98c26.text: The AI agent now follows a strict eight-step process when building something new: first it researches the code, then asks you questions, writes a spec document, makes a plan, writes the code, reviews it, tests it, and records lessons learned. Each step is defined and enforced, replacing the previous loose approach. If you ask it to implement a feature, you'll notice it takes a more structured, methodical approach with documentation saved along the way.

c29bbc207e8ceede2f0b877aab6a76c01f273323.text: If you use the service in free mode, the system now correctly recognizes when OpenRouter returns a model name that includes a date suffix. Previously, a model like minimax/minimax-m2.5-20260211 would be rejected even though it's allowed, because the check only looked for an exact name match. Now, the system also accepts any model whose name starts with an approved base name followed by a hyphen, so versioned variants like this one are no longer blocked. This fix prevents legitimate free-mode usage from being incorrectly denied.

6d01d07189ca915f61757a74da8eed6e431c8dc4.text: If you pay for the $100 or $500 monthly plan, you now get more credits each week to use the assistant - the $100 plan went up by about 20% and the $500 plan by about 5%. You'd see these larger numbers when you check your usage on the pricing page. The change is live today.

b5cf55edd5737f8dc858fbf424f8ee885aeb06cc.text: The benchmark test that measures how well certain assistants perform has been switched to use a different assistant variant called 'base-deep' instead of 'base2-free'. This only affects internal developers running these evaluation tests; regular users won't notice any difference. If you run the benchmark today, it will test the 'base-deep' configuration rather than the previous 'base2-free' one.

f9bfec097638416ef3d1757b7fea3c83ed61b8d2.text: If you work with Claude inside the terminal, the /connect:claude shortcut you may have seen is now switched off. Instead of opening a sign-in window for Claude, you will get a message telling you to use /subscribe, which is the new way to pay for usage across all models. This is now live today for the command line tool, so anyone typing /connect:claude will hit that message instead of the login flow.

df5a04df20ca02720f3f986a88c04de9b2043965.text: If you have an active subscription, the program now hides promotional messages and the /ads commands that let you turn ads on or off. The subscription check happens automatically, so subscribers see a cleaner experience with fewer prompts. For people without a subscription, nothing changes and ads still appear as before.

9552ba579472f17797bf9350982444258e7618b4.text: If you write code that uses the assistant, you now have a new way to make small edits to existing files, similar to how Codex-based assistants edit code. The old method of replacing whole files still works the same, but it no longer guesses at keeping parts of the previous file when you leave placeholder comments like "//... rest of the function..." instead requiring you to overwrite the entire file. This is live today for users of the SDK package, and if you relied on those placeholder comments, you will need to switch to the new editing tool or the replacement method to make partial updates.

7612d494f6ba94f0641abf30410adbc21a3ffb86.text: When the system looks through folders to find available helpers, it now skips any folder named 'skills' so those files aren't treated as helper definitions. This only affects how the system organizes helper files internally, and you won't notice anything different unless you're specifically managing those files. The change is live today.

be3c2a3d639710f50d2f6daa7573320d02e85ebd.text: When you look at the pricing page and hover your mouse over the small question-mark icon next to a plan, a small box pops up showing how many credits you get for each dollar spent on that plan. This helps you quickly compare which subscription gives you better value. The tool that analyzes code changes rated this as a very minor update, meaning it's a small addition rather than a major overhaul.

b7dfc25889af3fcaf6ff17147ea8d5987d252cc4.text: Paying subscribers who run out of pay-per-use credits can now make requests again even when their account balance shows zero. After verifying your subscription block grant, the system will let your request go through if you have subscription credits available; if the subscription check fails for any reason, it errs on the side of letting the request proceed. What you'd notice: if you're a subscriber and your a-la-carte credits are exhausted, your chat requests no longer get rejected with a 'out of credits' message when your subscription block grant is active. This only affects subscribers; non-subscribers with zero balance still see the out-of-credits message.

44db78128e3e40441b4b7945e3b1349455870f37.text: When you ask the system to use a specific version of a Claude model through a particular provider, it now connects to the right model instead of failing or picking the wrong one. If you were trying to use that version before, your request would not have resolved correctly, and now it does.

f67ecd430e3766470583662754da873a9c14dedd.text: The system now checks your subscription credits (like a prepaid block of usage) at the same time it checks your regular balance when you make an API call, so those credits are counted toward what you can do right away instead of only showing up separately. Previously, freshly created subscription grants could be invisible to the credit-check step, meaning a newly created block grant wouldn't be recognized until later. If you use the chat completions or web search/docs search endpoints, any eligible subscription block grant is now created and applied during the same request instead of being delayed.

14fbb52ffa1149b49cf9293371cc5531ee08dae9.text: When you turn on the automatic top-up feature while your balance is already below the trigger level, you will now see a confirmation dialog asking you to explicitly accept the immediate top-up charge before it goes through. This prevents accidental charges if you did not realize your balance was low. The feature is live today for users managing their auto top-up settings through the web app.

51bf4282d902f44d797956ef786b85d02e9ec640.text: When you ask the Discord bot about your account, it now explains that you must use the primary email tied to the GitHub account connected to your Codebuff profile, and it points you to the account settings page where that email is listed. If you forget to include an email or provide one that cannot be matched, the bot's error message spells out exactly where to find the right address instead of leaving you to guess. This applies to anyone using the Discord bot to manage their Codebuff account starting today.

3f6de551d04a9dc45132e68878ef980ba0956514.text: The help page that explains the different working modes now displays its comparison table correctly instead of showing jumbled columns. If you opened that page in a browser, you would see a clean table with four rows—Default, Max, Plan, and Free—each showing the mode, the assistant used, and whether code review is available, rather than text running together. This is a documentation-only fix that is live today.

427e35f32dd64d15a118db9ac88cf4c93b973d84.text: The tables in our advanced documentation page were showing up jumbled and unreadable because the formatting was broken. We fixed the table layouts so the information about which AI models handle different tasks now displays clearly when you read the docs. You would notice that the mode and task tables on the 'what-models' page now render as properly structured tables instead of running rows of text together.

f6607057b83163683840f5ef1f061a905fa77537.text: The quick-start guide has been shortened so it's easier to read and navigate. If you opened it, you'd notice it no longer explains each setup detail inline—instead it points you to other pages for things like project modes and troubleshooting. Some optional setup steps are still there but with less background text. The guide is live today and applies to anyone reading the help documentation.

1226e08dc65010d303b274d2578e471923d4fead.text: The troubleshooting guide for Codebuff has been reorganized to focus on the issues you're most likely to actually hit. The old instructions that walked you through clearing out a hidden npm cache folder and decoding a specific connection error message have been removed, so you won't be sent chasing fixes for problems that rarely matter anymore. In their place are two new, simpler sections: one that points you to download the underlying tool (Node) if it's missing, and one that tells you where Codebuff keeps its local files so you can delete and restart if something looks stuck. If you open the help pages today, you'll see the slimmed-down version that skips the technical error copy-paste and leans on these straightforward cleanup steps.

e96fc5bc74a277a2c963ca27c994de467656eca8.text: Behind the scenes, the testing setup used by the development team got a small tidy-up so its internal checks line up correctly. The automated test helpers that simulate certain responses were adjusted to match the expected data format, keeping the test suite stable. You won't see this change anywhere in the product itself—it only affects how the team verifies everything works during development.

e9cbb031f37a29a3ff75673f8aed0545c75a2d3d.text: The instructions for new contributors were corrected so they no longer claim a single command starts both the web interface and the command-line tool. You would notice this if you followed the guide: the old steps that promised one command would launch everything are gone, replaced by clear steps showing the web server must be started first, then the command-line tool in a second step. This affects anyone trying to set up a local development copy using the project's own guide.

aed5699db1345178ed99d031a97a57570430aef9.text: When you run the command-line tool, the promotional banner now shows the call-to-action text in bold, making it stand out more clearly. The web address shown next to it is now also clickable, so you can jump straight to the advertised site instead of just seeing it as plain text. Both elements respond visually when you hover over them, so it feels more interactive.

419ea9ea24a0d76f129ce34c00b3aed76f41a31d.text: Your assistant can now use a new model that produces more accurate and relevant code suggestions for you. Behind the scenes, a setting that controls how the assistant generates code was fine-tuned so its output matches your intent better. This change is live today for all users.

aa83b05ff418e46a4c508ce209da88b43707f964.text: The test that checks whether reusing a previous conversation makes the assistant cheaper to run has been rewritten so it now talks to the real online service instead of a pretend stand-in, and it also confirms that simply having files change on your computer between requests does not wipe out that savings. You, as someone running these tests, will now need an API key set up as a secret environment variable for the test to actually run; if you do not have one, the test quietly skips itself instead of failing. When you do run it, you should see two real cost figures printed in the logs instead of the fake ones used before.

da1d2ed9b21ba5bec138c63a84309afdb4788751.text: The assistant's helper tools can now be stored in a custom folder instead of only the default one. If you looked, you would see an extra setting where you type the address of your own folder, and the assistant would go look there for its skills. This change is live today for anyone using the helper toolkit in their own project.

538f982782ec25624e12fdefff87c429cb96878f.text: The side-by-side feature chart that compares Codebuff and Claude Code has been made easier to read. If you looked at the comparison page, you would see the columns now use clearer color-coded labels and friendlier icons for each feature, instead of a plain grid of checkmarks. This only affects how the table looks; nothing about the tools themselves changed. It is live today.

310f353fe60e9f05e5292fb22dfd1de8c46f6a0d.text: The text on the subscription page now reads 'Subscribe to use all modes with higher usage limits', and a small question-mark icon next to it opens a brief note saying the plan comes with 5-hour sessions and weekly limits. The only other difference is that the spacing above the rest of the page content changed slightly so things look a bit more balanced. These tweaks are live today for anyone looking at the pricing page.

6fc9d8c2bd75caf2584a33cc37e65e5eac947afc.text: If you use the service without a paid account, you can now get help reviewing source code through a lighter-weight version of the code review feature. It draws on the same underlying model as the editor tool, so the quality should feel familiar, and it appears alongside the other free tools you already have access to. The change is already in place, so you can try it out the next time you open the free mode.

841150ec209cce82f55caeade2a4544338a9d2e8.text: The assistant can now pass its current pricing setting to helper agents it spins off, so those helpers stay on the same billing mode as the main session. You wouldn't notice this directly, but it keeps subagents from accidentally using a different cost mode than the one you're working under.

f538e7ffabb6b0c2bbcc1649706f8cd9f40de76f.text: If you use the command-line assistant and press Ctrl+U to erase to the start of the line, you won't see any new hidden debug entries in the tool's internal logs. The developers removed the special logging they used to track cursor math during that keystroke, which were only visible to people actively debugging. You probably never noticed these messages, so the deletion cleans up the background output without changing how the shortcut works.

47f88beeaab13c5bfff7e652691a9abbe32dea5b.text: If you run the assistant from your own software using the toolkit, you can now tell it to load custom skills from a folder you choose instead of the default locations. The toolkit passes that folder path through to where skills are gathered, so any skill placed in your chosen directory will appear in the assistant's skill list and be ready to use. This is already live in today's toolkit version.

34d768eb96e9cdc03772e4e2dfed5c9d7c4525d0.text: The automated checks that verify the tool works correctly have been updated to match how the tool actually behaves now. If you ever inspect these checks, you'll see that tests which previously expected the tool to report "null" or a placeholder message for empty results now expect an empty string or bundled agents even without a local directory. These are behind-the-scenes maintenance updates to keep the verification process accurate; no live user behavior changes today.

ba531540bdad0bb161148debb50a9b23aa6e1bce.text: When a tool returns a result, the system now handles cases where that tool doesn't actually produce any content, instead of crashing or showing an error. This makes the experience more stable, especially when tools finish a task but don't have a specific message to pass back.

13a411578d705e06f6f7487537f54e60bfa13d8f.text: If you use Codebuff for free, the helper that checks your code for mistakes now runs on a different system called MiniMax M2.5 instead of the old one. The free helper also joins the main editing helper, so your free code reviews should look more consistent with the rest of what the tool does. The public docs and FAQ now tell you which system handles free work, replacing the old name everywhere it was mentioned.

1ad32d436b2433106ba0549bb663d2de61920e5e.text: When the system runs certain AI coding tools on your behalf, it used to tell the tool it was already doing the work before actually handing off the task, which confused one of Amazon's AI services into rejecting the request. Now it frames those same instructions as something the tool should do next, so the handoff completes without error. If you watch the system start one of these coding tools, you'll see it set up a workspace session and then immediately begin working, just without the brief miscommunication that was causing retries.

74e25483f7660125e88f066816429ecb881fe44b.text: You might have noticed the assistant occasionally tried to use skills that didn't exist, as if pretending they were there. Now, when no skills are available, it explicitly says there are none and won't try to use any, stopping these fake attempts. This affects anyone relying on the system's tool usage behavior. The change went live today.

0e8d8adcfb2f995375dc80ebd5c80821864e4c67.text: When you type a command and a list of suggestions pops up, each suggestion now decides for itself whether its hint text sits on the same line as the command name or wraps to the next line. Previously, the menu looked at every suggestion at once: if even one hint was too long, every suggestion got pushed onto two lines. Now each suggestion fits as tightly as possible, so short commands with short hints no longer waste vertical space just because another, longer command is in the list.

e2d1e227bce8efc8b39a011a6d32040293be0f62.text: When the assistant is deep in thought and its reply comes back containing nothing but its internal reasoning, it now keeps thinking and continues its turn instead of stopping. This affects the assistant's runtime behavior so that moments of silent, reasoning-only processing no longer cut a turn short, letting the assistant reach a more complete response before handing control back. The behavior is live today.

3a503134b62fc72842fc81e9118775ecfc141c6c.text: When you type a command and the assistant shows you a list of suggested next steps, each suggestion used to decide on its own whether its hint text could sit on the same line as its label. That quick decision depended on how much total width the whole menu had, without thinking about how long each particular label was. Now, the whole menu looks at every label and hint together and decides in one go whether all hints can sit aligned on the same line, so the layout switches smoothly from stacked to side-by-side instead of some hints jumping to a new line while others stay put. You would see the suggestion menu line up its descriptions more reliably, without the crooked wrapping that happened before.

37f5ddf350b79edc494586cbeca21757d11d91c3.text: When an assistant is interrupted mid-task (aborted), it used to send incomplete tool usage records to its response system, which the system didn't understand and rejected with an error. Now, it checks that every tool action it references actually has a matching result before including it, avoiding the confusion. You would notice fewer errors appearing when the assistant is stopped or interrupted during a task. This fix is live today.

ff9f6e8944d5a061af8a951291b9c34a5d1c5ab9.text: When a table with long text in its cells is printed to your terminal, the text no longer gets cut off with dots at the end. Instead, the text now wraps onto multiple lines so you can read the entire content without anything being hidden. This makes tables easier to read when they contain lengthy descriptions or data.

ee3e0e3cc6e745ab5ceac079827315797956eb65.text: If you read Codebuff's documentation today, you'll see updated references to a newer version of its main AI model, replacing the previous version name everywhere the docs mentioned a specific model. The FAQ, model list, and feature comparison pages now describe how the assistant picks different AI systems for different jobs (like code editing vs. research). You'd notice the text mentions a newer model name where it used to say an older one, but the list of which AI handles which task stays the same. The change is live in the published documentation right now.

f4dbe3107e8cdb6cabb4ccfbf949ec634a6dae67.text: Starting today, anyone who has connected their paid Claude account (Pro or Max) to Codebuff will see a new warning in the app’s main screen and beside the /connect:claude command: the link to use that subscription will be cut off on March 1st. The help page repeats the same cutoff date and adds that some users have reported being blocked by Anthropic after heavy use through Codebuff, advising people to run the /subscribe command to move to a Codebuff Strong plan instead.

c961ffad7a8d6ce06e8900082b1529c9861bd7b5.text: The pricing label that used to appear next to paid subscriptions created through the Codebuff sign-up flow has been removed, so new subscriptions no longer carry a fixed description like "Codebuff Strong — $X/mo" in Stripe. The change is live now and only affects subscriptions created from the main subscription-creation endpoint; Stripe metadata and billing tiers themselves are untouched, so existing subscribers notice no change and new ones simply won't see that extra text. If you checked a freshly created subscription in Stripe's dashboard, the description field would just be blank now. This is a small maintenance tweak the team rated as minor.

737e8a0c1fe7b13e9cad264c2e4b88be9667d343.text: You can now ask your assistant to run on three newer AI models (Claude Opus 4.6, Kimi K2.5, and GLM 4.7) that weren't selectable before. The software's configuration files now list these models as valid options, so the tools that build and set up agents recognize and accept them when you pick a model. This adds support without changing anything else about how the assistant behaves.

46de4ded3f387148406e516df730a7f97de410b1.text: The assistant no longer drops instructions it was supposed to follow (the ones that tell it to call tools or use external services). You would notice by checking: things that used to sometimes not happen now happen reliably. Developers who depend on the assistant working with other software will see fewer errors where the assistant just stopped mid-task. It's like fixing a dropped phone call where one side stopped hearing the other.

1fa1ede5b2915c94a438455edbcc05f4af9cf392.text: The release tooling that packages and publishes the SDK will now run on a newer version of the underlying runtime engine (Node 24 instead of Node 20). This change only affects the automated publishing process for SDK releases, not the SDK features themselves. If you looked at the release configuration, you'd see the version number of the runtime engine had been bumped from 20 to 24.

bb00fb7bc8e3c6cb156e14f0e4b7fd552583cd38.text: When you click the small 'Ad' label on a promoted message in the assistant, a small information panel now slides open next to it with a 'Hide ads' button you can click to make all ads go away. Free-plan users see this hide option right away; paid subscribers do not. The ad banner stays visible otherwise, so you just get the extra choice to tidy up your screen if you want.

62fd54667bd81aadcaace15ff17372b51b3869ff.text: The credits buying screen has been simplified to only show fixed dollar amounts ($10, $25, $50, $100) instead of letting you type any custom amount. Auto top-up now defaults to $20 instead of the previous minimum of $5. The subscription page also has slightly clearer wording, and paying for credits now uses a new command line command called "subscribe" instead of "buy-credits".

240a6d83a7bdb4d644e0e1a3396c85290725d325.text: The behind-the-scenes test that checks your CLI commands was updated to reflect a recent rename of a command. A few weeks ago, the '/referral' command—which gives you a link to invite friends—was renamed to '/refer-friends' to better describe what it does. The test that makes sure everything still works was finally updated to match the new command name, so the test suite accurately reflects the current program you use. This is internal housekeeping only; you noticed nothing today, and the rename itself already happened before this commit.

ef6c525a2328e66eee9363b5e1a89d06df76942f.text: When you type the old command to get a referral code, it now answers to a new name and shows you a ready-made link you can copy with one click. The referral feature itself — earning credits for inviting friends — is unchanged, but the command was renamed from the old name to the clearer new name, and your unique referral link is now displayed in a banner with a copy button instead of requiring you to build the link yourself. If you still type the old name, it works as a shortcut to the new command, so nothing breaks. This is live today for anyone using the CLI referral command.

d16dd743087445adaf57103bdd5788486683d9e7.text: The text people see while signing up for the service was made shorter and simpler. If you're someone walking through the signup steps now, the headings and explanations read more quickly—titles like "Get the CLI" and "Run Codebuff in your project" replaced longer phrases, and the referral code step dropped a celebratory emoji and extra wording. This only affects the web-based onboarding screens you view in a browser; nothing about how the software works behind the scenes changed.

e2175c4348d342580d5da89e75d4dfce79568b8e.text: The automated process that publishes new versions of the software development kit (SDK) has stopped using a stored password-like secret to log into the package registry. Instead, it now relies on a newer, more secure method called Trusted Publishing, which is set up directly through the npm website. This change only affects the internal release pipeline itself; nobody using the SDK needs to take any action, and the published packages remain exactly the same.

8de679e7a997feac9bb6a84b921cb2a28af4ac34.text: The marketing page that compares how fast two assistants are now shows a concrete number instead of a loose "three times faster" claim: it says Codebuff finishes a real feature roughly 100 seconds quicker than Claude Code on average. If you read the page, you'll see the headline now reads '100+ Seconds Faster Than Claude Code' and the explanation points to specific tricks like running multiple helpers in parallel and grabbing related files all at once instead of one by one. Nothing about how the assistants actually work changed today—the wording update just makes the public claim match the measured test results, so the comparison reads like stopwatch data rather than a rough boast.

b19028b5468eafc23442f2293c16b224b5c362da.text: You can now use the assistant through the API even when you have no credits left, as long as you explicitly ask for a free request. When someone sends a request marked as 'free' in the system, the billing check gets skipped, so it won't be blocked for lack of credit balance. This only applies to specific agent and model combinations designated as free; regular requests still require available credits.

b3a26524d27f2ad674ba50bfdba5237632ad7dae.text: Today the command-line tool that some power users run from a terminal can update your a la carte preference in production, just like the website could. The preferences page no longer rejects that command-line tool; it now accepts its bearer token the same way the site handles it, so you can flip the fallback setting from either place without the call failing.

c5e6ef867a7fa08f4fbed10b840a35d41ce45172.text: The routing system that decides which artificial intelligence model to call has been updated so that a newly released version of the assistant, referred to as Opus 4.6, is now recognized and handled correctly when traffic is sent through an external service that distributes model requests. This corrects the situation where the new version was previously unknown to the routing table and could fail or fall back to an older model. If you were to send a request specifying the new model today, it now resolves to the right destination instead of being ignored. This fix applies to any setup that routes through the external service.

96a8378aa63af776c02b36b1be57b10b592b8f47.text: When the assistant begins writing code, it now always reminds itself to first load any relevant pre-built skills before doing the actual implementation work. This affects everyone who uses the coding agent, and if you watched closely you'd see an extra instruction step appear right at the start of every implementation attempt, making sure nothing useful gets overlooked. The change is live today.

e1d8726dbfaf592e2d5ca2bdc5e02b1886782630.text: When you visit the pricing page, the headline and short description that show up in your browser tab and in search results have been rewritten. The title is now simply 'Pricing | Codebuff' (no more 'Simple, Usage-Based Plans'), and the description now reflects the current pay-as-you-go model: 500 free credits each month, then 1 cent per credit, with enterprise plans for organizations. Who this affects: anyone who lands on the pricing page, either directly or via a search engine result. What you would notice if you looked: the browser tab for the pricing page displays a shorter title, and the snippet shown in search engines or when the page is shared has changed from emphasizing "no subscriptions" to highlighting the option to "subscribe for higher usage limits" versus paying per credit.

51f8943c9e8c68f14a91d0b0563872d581de292c.text: The assistant can now prove its identity to one part of the service using a bearer token instead of only the standard web login session, which lets automated tools talk to it without a browser. You would notice that the same shortcut for looking up who the assistant is has been reused for two related commands, so they both accept the token and both now check whether the login has expired before responding. It is live today for those two commands in the web interface, with no changes for CLI or documentation.

63d3a7692d4a3c1f9bc668b4317f37c1c4ac9ef7.text: If you use the command-line assistant and hit your monthly usage limit, you'll now see a clear switch labeled "Credit spending: enabled" or "Credit spending: disabled" instead of the old checkbox and multi-button setup. Toggling that switch directly controls whether your paid credits get used after your subscription runs out, matching how the system actually tracks that setting behind the scenes. The status line and available actions update instantly to show either that your credits will keep working or that you've paused that automatic spending. This is live today for anyone who sees those usage banners in their terminal.

746093347cf3ab3a01ada4aeac298382cf134b3f.text: When you run a command in the assistant's terminal preview, the output now stretches across the full width of your screen instead of being squeezed into a narrow column with extra blank space on the sides. You'll notice wider, less cramped text in the preview window when a tool runs a command. This affects only the visual layout of terminal command output in the assistant interface.

6ab7d2d0c9ffbe0c67444a76f95286042633179a.text: When the system talks to certain advanced AI models (like GPT-5) through OpenRouter, those models can take several minutes before they start sending a response. To keep those conversations from failing, the software now waits up to 10 minutes for the model to begin streaming its answer instead of giving up after a shorter period. If you use a deep-thinking model through OpenRouter, you’ll notice the system no longer times out while the model is still thinking and preparing its reply. No action is needed on your part; the extended wait now applies automatically whenever an OpenRouter request is made.

e4c2bbb3dcaf0c767ed14fd0d41e900709612082.text: When you hit your monthly or weekly usage cap, the assistant used to let you press Escape or Backspace to close the notice and keep typing. Now that notice stays on screen until you click to buy more credits or tap to open the pricing page. The exit shortcuts were simply turned off for that specific screen, so you can't dismiss it by keyboard anymore.

ce23b852c37d3341bb1962973efddb129588ce52.text: When you run the assistant at work in your terminal, the small credit-usage message that appears now shows the real website address we point you to instead of always showing codebuff.com. That means the link you see at the bottom of the usage banner will stay correct even if we change our domain in the future, so you won't be sent to a wrong or broken page.

5fa8a029096d594c513b8ba482e41c67e5d0b26d.text: The example setup file that tells new developers which settings their local copy needs now lists which port the web interface should run on. If you copy this template to start your own local environment, port 3000 is pre-filled for the web server so you don't have to guess. Nothing about the live site changes; this only helps people running the software on their own computer.

75109377ca3c2600aa30493939eef98794842b21.text: The internal database update process has been switched back to a faster method that pushes changes directly, instead of the step-by-step migration approach that was added earlier. This only affects the internal tools team and how they manage the database during development and setup. If you looked at the system logs or setup process, you would see the database preparation using the direct push method instead of running through the migration steps. This change is live today.

c564dac5d3681443df760b0752501d8c3de769b5.text: When the internal team sets up or updates the database for this package, the command now builds a careful step-by-step record of the changes instead of immediately rewriting the database structure to match the code. This makes the database updates safer to run in production, where directly changing the live structure can cause problems. If you ran the setup steps, you would not notice anything different on screen, but the underlying process that modifies the database is now more cautious and reliable.

efb9f5d4576330b8d6f3d7a68149e323987df9fa.text: When you create a new database, the system reads a list that records every change made to its structure. That list had a stray comma at the end of one entry, which strict reading rules treat as a syntax error, similar to a misspelled word tripping up a spell-checker. Fixing that comma ensures the list is read correctly when setting up the database, but otherwise you will not notice any difference in how things work.

34c7aaadc5259a9b329e41bcd1910351956cd4a4.text: The CLI stopped printing a debug message that previously appeared in the console when the assistant's message queue was temporarily blocked from sending responses. You may have seen technical diagnostic text about the queue being blocked in your terminal before; that line of text will no longer appear. This is purely a cosmetic change that reduces console noise during normal CLI operation, with no impact on functionality.

7a83297f47d8e25387f7e5bcc56e6d4e6e7e8e56.text: If you visit a page that asks for a sponsored post and the ad service behind it returns an error instead of an ad, the page now stays calm instead of crashing. It checks whether the service said ‘all good’ before trying to read the response, so broken or non-ad replies (like a plain text or HTML error) are logged quietly and you simply see no ad rather than an error screen. This only affects the server-side tool that picks which promoted post to show, so nothing on your end changes except fewer surprise breakages.

4e10365fd9f9fc1dba7c0ee557306cc1d31d7f12.text: You will no longer see two specific assistant options — one labeled as the Opus agent and another labeled as publish — when you open the slash command menu in the CLI. These entries were commented out in the command list file, removing them from the picker without deleting anything permanently. The change affects anyone using the CLI slash commands today and live.

a175054234a1be11eaa0f31276842e32aa2c85ee.text: You can now press \\/theme:toggle at the command line to instantly flip your screen between the light and dark color scheme, and a brief message will confirm which one is now active. Behind the scenes, the program reads your current theme choice from its shared settings, switches it to the opposite option, updates those settings so the new look sticks, and then clears the command line so you can keep working. The command is also now visible when you start typing a slash, so it shows up in the autocompletion list alongside the other built-in commands. This is live today for anyone running the CLI.

7f7c6d6b2d01e8af50d71600da3e478db859d3e2.text: When you open the command or mention menu in the CLI on a large terminal, the list now shows up to 15 options at once instead of 10. This applies to both the slash commands menu and the mention menu, making it easier to browse more suggestions without scrolling. The menu automatically switches between 10 and 15 items based on whether your terminal has more than 35 lines of height.

fc2d2f13ba01421a10b7c1f3222460759f746ea5.text: When you ask the assistant to do something, the system now tells callers in a clear, structured way whether the request succeeded or was cancelled, instead of returning blank or error-like values. This affects the underlying software kit used by apps that connect to the assistant. If you looked closely, you would not notice a visible difference in the assistant's behavior, because the wording and responses stay the same.

f9cdd1d365a762fde877ed7b8f186ba85c829dcb.text: When the assistant tries to double-check your agents before sending a message and that check hits a temporary server hiccup, you will now simply see your message go through without a noisy "network error" popup. The system used to show a generic error notice whenever the validation step returned no specific problems; now it quietly treats that blank result as a pass and only surfaces real, specific validation issues if any appear. Behind the scenes, the error list display also guards against missing identifiers so it won't break if an agent ID comes back empty, and the underlying validation tool now labels a missing file path as 'unknown' instead of leaving it blank.

b76866a5955f1c058321a4eaf2fd955a096acb09.text: The automated editor agent is now calling its file-editing helpers by the correct, namespaced names instead of generic ones, so it consistently uses the proposal variants of the tools rather than plain replacements. This corrects a mismatch between the instructions the agent was given and the actual tools available to it, preventing it from attempting to invoke tools that aren't properly scoped to proposing changes. If you watched the agent working today, you wouldn't notice this directly, but it ensures the agent's edit operations are properly routed through the correct proposing workflow rather than generic ones.

7970c2dee83b155434da93abdaad98ea2f0a0461.text: When you sign in from the command line, the tool will no longer try to launch your web browser automatically. Instead it prints the login address and tells you to open it yourself in a browser tab. You'll see the same login URL as before, but the line that used to say "Browser opened" now says "Please open the URL above manually to complete login." This is live today for anyone using the plain login flow on a server or machine where no browser is guaranteed to be available.

0ec9fa0acfde1fd0235ec3c1adf7e8b1091eaaf5.text: Behind the scenes, the code that simulates how the agent talks to AI models was updated so those simulations now return results in the same structured format the real system expects. This only affects internal testing tools, not the actual assistant you interact with, so there is no change to what you experience when chatting or running agents. Nothing user-facing changed.

37e11effc629201edc6776246bd6318ff94c3232.text: When you press cancel while the assistant is working, it now stops right away instead of quietly trying a backup model first. You may have noticed that cancelling a request sometimes still seemed to keep going or took longer than expected before giving up. That happened because the system treated your cancel as a routine failure and moved on to the next model. It now recognises a cancel for what it is and gives up immediately. This only affects requests that support fallback models, so the behavior you see will depend on which task you were running when you hit cancel.

7f9613cdda455a9edda444f35fb5079de51c03c9.text: The system that builds and ships the developer command-line tool now uses a newer version of its underlying JavaScript runtime and no longer relies on a manually stored password-like secret to publish releases. If you looked at the release process, you'd see it runs a newer Node.js version and the publish step no longer reads a special token from the project's secure settings, because publishing is now handled through GitHub's trusted publishing mechanism. This is live today for the CLI release production workflow.

befef2c6bbf198faa2e798f55b4ffe2cfb1c8a68.text: When the system asks an AI to evaluate commits or generate a changelog and the request is stopped early, it now gracefully handles that situation instead of crashing. Previously, trying to read the result after an abort would cause an error; now, it checks for the abort condition first and returns a safe fallback. This affects internal tools used by developers for automated commit screening and changelog generation, as well as the admin panel used for relabeling user data — if an AI request gets canceled mid-way through, the tool will log that it was aborted and continue without breaking the workflow. You wouldn't see this change directly, but it means these background tools won't fail unexpectedly when network timeouts or manual cancellations occur.

1bb1c6853036244ac1d440ccbe3cd1c6d96d6afa.text: When something goes wrong while the assistant talks to an API, the system now records more details about the failure: the exact web address it tried to reach, the error message the server sent back, whether it might work if retried, and the data it tried to send. It also handles tricky cases like self-referencing data and very large responses without crashing. You'll see this when looking at diagnostic logs for errors that happen during API calls. The change is live today.

a24ae19af0e80221114f35ffed9b7cbc9e646176.text: The system's built-in self-checks for the command-line tool were updated so they expect information to be grouped inside a 'data' container, matching how the tool actually organizes its responses. This affects only the internal testing process used by developers and does not change anything you would see or do when using the tool. It is live today as part of routine quality-control housekeeping.

4695192b8fd9050c351590b83511098b5ecbd078.text: When you paste text into the command-line tool, it will stay in your message as long text only if it's shorter than 2,000 characters. Text longer than that will still get attached as a separate file. The difference is nothing if you paste something shorter than 2,000 characters, but if you paste something longer, it will be attached as a file instead of staying inline. This change is live now for the command-line tool only. If you paste something shorter than 2,000 characters, nothing changed. If you paste something longer, it will now be attached as a file instead of staying inline.

61d4975f84aa6c9da41331ec5c4784451a64cc19.text: When you type an @ symbol and start searching for a file or folder in the command-line tool, matches are now found with looser, smarter logic: it no longer demands a perfect path match, and it can also surface folders (not just files) in the suggestions, scoring each result by how well its name lines up with what you typed (fewer gaps, longer consecutive runs, and word-start hits rank higher). You would notice this right away if you've ever tried to grab a file by a partial or misspelled name, since results now appear and improve even when the characters aren't typed in exact order. The improvement is live as of today.

4f45568ffa49272ba10dcc2c4e50f1b1fd531ff6.text: When you open the slash menu to pick an assistant skill, any skill description longer than 50 characters now gets cut off and ends with an ellipsis, so long descriptions no longer stretch or overlap the menu. This affects anyone using the command-line interface and choosing skills from the slash menu. You would notice that some skill descriptions appear shorter with "…" at the end where they used to run on. The change is live today.

5937834199b395521cd14e84a850d0e204c949af.text: When you're using the tool in development mode and it tries to log information about complex data, it used to crash if that data contained circular references (like an object that refers back to itself). Now it handles those gracefully by replacing the circular part with a placeholder text instead of crashing. If you looked, you'd see the word [Circular] appear in logs where the problematic data was, rather than the program stopping unexpectedly.

b45a8cca698a67999d6c8b35d9ad42cca6e76f99.text: When you run a multi-step coding task in the command line, the tool can now correctly show which approach it picked and why. Previously, it looked for the answer in the wrong spot, so the strategy and reason were missing from your screen. Behind the scenes, the tool was wrapping its response data in a 'data' container, but the code was reading from the wrong place. This fix makes it open the right container so the information displays properly.

0e2633a858d947a582ba57248c1d5272229992b0.text: The code examples in the documentation now appear in a compact dark theme layout instead of the previous bordered, lighter design. When you look at a code example, you'll see the language label is gone for regular (non-diagram) snippets, and the copy button sits inline on the right with simplified styling instead of appearing as a separate header row. This affects only the documentation pages that render code demos, and the change is already live today.

02f131b89966bff249f1e1c157234591b028d5cb.text: When you start your computer's command-line tools, a small setup step loads special environment variables that Direnv manages. A background check that verifies which parts of the system are allowed to read those variables was previously blocking that load, causing the tool to fail during automated testing. That check now permits the Direnv setup file to read the variables, so the startup sequence runs without being stopped. The change is live now in the tool's source code, though you wouldn't see any visible difference if you weren't watching the testing process.

585742806f8f389a76da2aff99d032e961f710dd.text: The reliability checklist that confirms the assistant connects to the appointment scheduling system correctly now includes one extra step, so the team can be sure the connection parameters the assistant actually uses are exactly the ones the checklist is verifying today.

66d02a7ddb897fec57232e58e92d65efb1ddb8a4.text: Your Discord bot will now start reliably instead of getting stuck or crashing during startup. The bot uses a coordination system where only one instance is allowed to run at a time by claiming an exclusive lock on the database; several bugs were preventing that lock from being acquired or monitored correctly. Those bugs are now fixed, so the bot should boot up and stay running without manual intervention. The fix is live and applies to all internal services that depend on this startup coordination.

2a3bf3c9cc9e7041dd804e4bc44a4378d235db42.text: When the CLI polls for activity and hits repeated errors, it now waits longer before retrying instead of hammering the server over and over. If there hasn't been a successful response yet, the tool considers an entry fresh as long as an error happened within the configured wait window, so persistent failures don't trigger a tight retry loop. You'd notice this as fewer frantic retry attempts in the logs when something keeps erroring out during polling.

84f283a51e6ac354b0a8f54ba40aa51229ad8422.text: The help documentation for the program's operating modes has been updated to use the new name 'Free' instead of the old name 'Lite'. If you look at the modes guide, you will see that the cheaper and faster option is now called 'Free' and the instructions for switching to it use the new slash command '/mode:free' instead of the old flag. This only changes the written help text, so existing shortcuts you use to run the program still work the same way.

0d9a8a2107a299ad81f12dde7a2e9f2b09143f5d.text: The system that loads your AI assistant's external tool connections can now read your secret passwords and settings correctly again, fixing a problem where it would crash before it could use them. When you had a configuration entry that referenced something like $API_KEY, the program would fail to look up that value and stop working. Behind the scenes, the code now retrieves environment settings through a different pathway that avoids a build-time restriction, so your tool configurations load properly. This fix is live now and applies to anyone using MCP-based tool integrations through the SDK.

5c129d57b23ad86db8cb9b7aacde501be26a9b4e.text: When an AI is thinking through its response, you'll now see the last 5 lines of that thinking displayed as a preview, instead of the thinking being completely hidden after it finishes. This affects anyone using the command-line version of the AI assistant to have a conversation. If you looked at a thinking block, you'd notice it shows a few lines of the AI's internal reasoning rather than appearing completely collapsed, giving you a glimpse into what the AI was working through.

aac0817bae2921bcaf1fa91be5e98b906b79260e.text: If you use the code search feature and pass in search terms wrapped in quotes, those quotes are now automatically removed before the search runs. Previously, typing something like "'filename.md'" would treat the quotes as part of the name and fail to find matches. Now the quotes are stripped, so your search works as intended. Live today.

f1accc200beda280aa54011c8adfa8cc685d9355.text: When you ask the assistant to show you the different strategies it's considering and which one it ultimately picked, the screen will now reliably display which option was selected and why. Previously, the program looked for the selection information in the wrong place, so the chosen strategy and its reason were sometimes left blank. The fix makes it search for that information in the correct spot before displaying the result. This applies to anyone using the command-line version of the assistant and is working today.

cc23c66e706d9816db3d96b53b50cf79385fa8f7.text: The program now starts up by simply beginning and walking away instead of attaching an extra safety net to catch startup failures. For you, the CLI behaves exactly the same: normal successes and failures still play out just as before. The difference is only in how the code is organized behind the scenes.

d2ab2877a07a46bf2e58f1342b2c1925dde3bf16.text: When you ask the system to start multiple helpers at once, you must now name a real helper (like 'commander' or 'code-searcher'), not a direct action (like 'read_files' or 'str_replace'). The instructions now warn whoever uses this feature that picking a tool-name instead of a helper-name won't work, and that you should just call the tool directly if that's what you wanted. This only affects the part of the system that launches several helpers in one go, and you'd notice it right away because the wrong names are now explicitly blocked with a message.

040c7041cf3f5140635b2492e337dacf384de2ee.text: When you ask an AI to spawn (start) additional specialized agents, the system now checks beforehand whether each agent name you requested actually exists and is allowed. If any requested agent is invalid—for example, it doesn't exist or is actually a tool rather than an agent—the call is either stopped entirely or proceeds with only the valid agents while returning an error message listing what failed. This prevents the AI from streaming an invalid tool call that would later fail, giving you clearer feedback about which agents could not be spawned. The update is live today in the agent runtime.

698b29200760a302869c6687ec3291d4f297bdb7.text: When the assistant runs a tool, it can briefly summarize what happened instead of showing the full output. That summary line now spreads across the entire width of your Terminal window, and long sentences wrap onto the next line instead of being cut off at the edge.

eb46bbff184fdb9b42ba8a4ed9d640eed47797b7.text: When you copy text while connected to a remote server through SSH, your copy now reliably reaches your local computer's clipboard instead of getting stuck on that remote server. When you copy text on your own computer directly, it still uses your computer's native clipboard tools as before. The change adds a smarter check that detects whether you're working on a remote server or locally, then picks the best method for your situation.

3a07ea51161e323d25c544e19dc49e6fb00bc2eb.text: If you've turned off internal reasoning for OpenRouter or Codebuff in your settings, that internal thinking text will no longer appear in streamed responses. The system now respects your choice to hide it, so you won't see the hidden scratchpad notes that the assistant uses behind the scenes.

9054900a3f68da7de0acb4ae7d2047a95a3d9063.text: The internal system that helps the assistant navigate files and summarize long conversations had some duplicate helper logic that was temporarily removed in a previous cleanup. That cleanup was rolled back because the shared helpers broke how the system saves and resumes work sessions (known as serialization). The original duplicated implementations are back in place, so the assistant's file-picking and step-tracking behavior works the same as before. If you looked, you'd see the extra helper functions were restored inside two specific workflow handlers, with "DUPLICATE" markers removed from shared comments.

d7b2ad8730aca61f27f58f37995ca05c83e5d68b.text: The test file that runs the browser-based end-to-end checks was renamed from one name to another, and the configuration that tells the testing tool which files to skip during quick unit runs was updated to match. If you peek at the test runner while it’s doing its fast pass over the codebase, you won’t see this renamed file being picked up and accidentally run as a regular unit test anymore. This keeps the quick checks fast and prevents them from stumbling into heavier browser tests by mistake. It’s live today, behind the scenes, with no direct impact on what you see in the app.

d2d075805ca94adcb02e71fe10ad0ead8f35a163.text: Links that start with /b/ on the company's main website now automatically forward to the short link service at go.trybeluga.ai. If you clicked such a link today, you'd briefly land on the main site and then be sent to the matching short link; this replaces the previous behavior where those paths probably didn't go anywhere.

9389ab66cd4c47e106b2b4df3bf0d3bace3b0c69.text: The team deleted an old file that had been sitting unused, which was a leftover test script for running browser-based checks the old way. It does not affect anything you see, and you would not notice it working or not working. This was just cleaning out a digital junk drawer, and it is already done.

017850d16cb9a501b22498e41f95630281cd8a4e.text: When someone uses an affiliate link that sends them to a referral page, the site now keeps all the extra bits already attached to the link instead of throwing them away. Previously, it only passed along one piece of information and dropped anything else; now it carries everything forward before adding its own tracking code. You wouldn't see this directly, but links you click that pass through those referral pages will behave more consistently, keeping the full set of parameters that were already there.

c933800c629cf3333831dc106304ec05f130035f.text: The command-line tool now shows clearer error messages instead of failing silently when something goes wrong. If you paste an image or send a follow-up message and it fails, you'll see a brief note telling you it didn't work instead of nothing happening at all. When typing mentions like @someone, the tool is less likely to crash if there aren't enough matching names or files to choose from. These improvements are live today and make the tool more reliable to use.

3ed910a5818f86c79252356d2f1503902d859b00.text: The website's underlying publishing system was updated with a small patch that closes known security holes. You won't see anything different when browsing the site, but if you're responsible for the website's code you'll find a newer version number recorded in the site's configuration.
